items.title: A Thanksgiving Tradition of Rewatching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz”
items.description: To my mind, one of the single greatest live performances one can see exists midway through the concert film “The Last Waltz.” Directed by Martin Scorsese, it documents the final concert of the Band, on Thanksgiving Day, 1976, at Bill Graham’s Winterland Ballro
items.author: Hanif Abdurraqib
paragraphs: To my mind, one of the single greatest live performances one can see exists midway through the concert film “The Last Waltz.” Directed by Martin Scorsese, it documents the final concert of the Band, on Thanksgiving Day, 1976, at Bill Graham’s Winterland Ballroom, in San Francisco. The performance is from after the concert was filmed, when Scorsese shot for multiple days at a studio soundstage on the M-G-M lot, capturing the Band playing their most famous song, “The Weight,” alongside the Staple Singers. The soundstage is, aesthetically, a sharp departure from the Winterland stage. The lighting is sparse, with a red-orange hue shooting across an otherwise black backdrop, slightly tinting everyone it falls upon in a way that makes them look as if they are bathing in a final gasp of sunlight before nightfall. The group trades verses of the iconic song with the Staples Singers. Levon Helm takes one, Pops Staples takes the next, Rick Danko takes another, and Mavis gets a verse—Mavis sings her brief verse with an air of delight and revelation, as if she’s enjoying a meal made by someone she loves. She comes back in the song’s final verse, and by the closing moments she’s in full gospel mode, clapping her hands into the microphone, overcome, reaching into the open mouth of the folk song and pulling a bit of God from beneath its tongue—a bit of God which, in the case of “The Weight,” is never hard to find.

The concert recorded in “The Last Waltz” is marking its fiftieth anniversary this Thanksgiving. For almost half of that time, I have had a tradition of watching the film every year on Thanksgiving Eve. Like most of my traditions, this one began when the thought of solitude became unbearable, which, at nineteen years old, was almost always. At that age, doing anything with anyone seemed better than doing something I loved alone. In college I was among the misfits, the people in my dorm who either couldn’t go home for Thanksgiving or wouldn’t: the ones who lived too far away to travel back for both Thanksgiving and Christmas; the ones who’d been dropped off on campus earlier that fall by parents who didn’t even bother to get out of the car; or those, like me, whose families didn’t care much about gathering for this holiday or any other.

There were about nine of us left over, and we had the run of the dorm, which had a large television and a new DVD player. There was a Blockbuster within walking distance, and I knew that none of us wanted to be alone for the holiday in the large, echoing dorm building, thinking about those whom we missed or were too mad at to miss. And so I rented the newly released “Last Waltz” anniversary DVD and ordered some pizza, and that Wednesday night all nine of us crammed into the TV room and watched it together. It was my first time seeing the film in full. We laughed at the interviews and scenes interwoven among the concert performances: Danko, Richard Manuel, and Robbie Robertson talking about how, in the early days, the Band would wear massive overcoats and steal food from the supermarket on the road. In one scene, a clearly drunk Danko plays “Old Time Religion” on the fiddle with a small black hat resting atop his head. As we got deeper into the film, many of my comrades fell asleep, but I realized that I didn’t need the screening to be a group activity. The film was teeming with companionship—Neil Young bouncing over to Robertson and Danko to share a microphone at the end of a stunning rendition of “Helpless,” or the Band’s first leader, Ronnie Hawkins, shouting at his old backing band as if they were still his backing band and not veteran headliners themselves. The film itself was an antidote to loneliness, a vision of a life lived well.

I am more rigorous about my “Last Waltz” tradition than I am about most other rituals. I have watched the movie every year since that first time, and always alone. I generally commit myself to not being on the road for the holiday, but in the rare times when I have been, I’ve closed myself off in whatever hotel room I’m staying in and found a way to stream the movie on the hotel TV. I have not, since that first college viewing, been interested in sharing the experience with others. I am especially not interested in serving as a tour guide for someone who has never seen the film, even if this is antithetical to my usual impulse of finding someone, anyone, to share the things that excite or bewilder me. I only watch the movie once per year, on the day before Thanksgiving. It is a foolish superstition, but one that I stick to.

“The Last Waltz” manifests itself to me differently every year. The film ages and I age alongside it, and in the process I find new moments of tenderness, or old moments of tenderness that have tuned themselves to aches in my heart that hadn’t existed the last time I watched. Take, for example, the aforementioned performance of Young’s “Helpless.” Some viewers tend to focus—foolishly, I might add—on the clearly dazed onstage presence of Young as an example of the not so subtle drug use happening off camera. This kind of pearl-clutching seems to risk emphasizing the very ordinary at the expense of the extraordinary, which, in this case, is a moment when Joni Mitchell starts singing from a hidden perch backstage, invisible to the audience except as a shadow underneath the curtain. Onstage, Young, Robertson, and Danko (who do know that Joni is there, and have situated her there specifically for this moment) playfully look to the heavens, as if to say, The angels are here, among us.

“Helpless” is, broadly, a song about reaching through the devastating and overgrown acres of memory. If I were to sit beside you watching this scene I would ask about people you miss: what their singing voices sounded like, if you can remember; how long they’ve been gone and at what point their voices began to fade in your mind into intermittent static. For me, there is a new voice that begins to fade every year. Someone who has died, or otherwise left. The symphony of their living becomes first flimsy, and then gone. I like to imagine the moment that the audience watching the Band could hear a voice they loved but couldn’t see where it was coming from—the split second, before logic kicked in, where they did think that something was falling upon them from the same heaven their beloveds were in.

In its best moments, “The Last Waltz” highlights the affection and camaraderie among the bandmates and their peers, which means that much of the friction that is known to have existed within the group at the time is barely visible, especially if one doesn’t know what to look for. By 1976, Robertson was done with being on the road. The Band had spent more than fifteen years touring non-stop, first as the backing band for Hawkins, then backing Bob Dylan, and then on their own. The other members of the Band didn’t want the show to stop as Robertson did, and so humming underneath their farewell concert was the drama of one member walking out on his own. The Band, sans Robertson, reformed and started touring again in 1983, but the tensions continued and grew, to the point where, when the Band was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1994, with Robertson joining them, Helm stayed home. But even knowing all of this, you might watch “The Last Waltz” and forget the grievances. There is a moment, in one of the interstitial storytelling scenes, when Helm lights a match, mid-sentence, and holds it toward Robertson’s cigarette before he lights his own, before Robertson could even gesture to ask. When the group performs “Who Do You Love” with Hawkins, and he playfully storms offstage, leaving the Band to find their own close to the song, Robertson and Helm momentarily look at each other, laughing, perhaps remembering what it was to be young and briefly lost.

At the same time, it’s become clearer to me as I’ve aged that a central engine of “The Last Waltz” is grief. There’s a scene that takes place after the concert ends, when Martin Scorsese goes to visit Danko in Shangri-La, their Malibu clubhouse and studio. After a brief tour of the space, Danko sits down at a control board, and Scorsese asks him what he’s been doing since “The Last Waltz.” Danko reaches for a wide-brimmed hat, puts it on his head, and asks his engineer to press play on a song. As the first notes of his then new solo song “Sip the Wine” come through the studio speakers, Danko responds, “Just making music, you know . . . trying to stay busy. It’s healthy.” As the song continues to play, Danko leans back in his chair and smiles at Scorsese, as if he knows he’s done something miraculous. But then he turns back to the control board, his hat obscuring most of his face, and as the camera zooms in it becomes evident that his smile is gone, his self-satisfaction suddenly wrecked by an understanding that he was doing a significant thing alone. Danko is my favorite of the Band’s vocalists. Everything he sang sounds like pleading, mourning, suffering, like the stakes couldn’t be higher. Every note sounds as if he was watching the final threads of a memory slip through his fingers. But the scene might be heartbreaking only because of what I know of its aftermath. Manuel would die less than eight years later, by suicide. Danko’s first son would die, after a night of binge drinking, three years after that. The Band’s remaining members would face dwindling popularity in the eighties, playing smaller venues with far less fanfare. At that moment in “The Last Waltz,” playing a new song for Scorsese, Danko looks as if he’s already mourning the future his dream won’t survive in.

Helm, though, played until he was damn near gone. One of the disconnects between him and Robertson was that Robertson seemed to view being on the road and the stage as a hazard to his life, whereas Helm could not imagine a worthwhile life without it. In one of his last shows before his death, in 2012, from throat cancer, he sang a cover of Ralph Stanley’s “Gloryland,” which is a song about leaving the earth behind. In “Gloryland,” there are no undertakers because no one dies. There are no doctors because no one falls ill. Your earthly pain won’t be making the trip, and you have friends already in Gloryland—the one who hung himself in a motel room, the one who sang like his heart was a hundred puzzle pieces from a hundred different boxes until it gave out on him way too young, the one who took too much of something just the one day. During his life’s final act, Helm performed the generous gesture of singing about where he believed he was going, and where he believed they’d be going one day, too. The song insists that we are all spending a lifetime travelling toward another lifetime, and death is the door we have to slip through.

I would like to believe in the place that Helm is singing about. You don’t have to be who you were. Whatever haunted you once doesn’t need to haunt you always. Because my “Last Waltz” tradition was born out of isolation, I decided along the way that it had to be defined by isolation. This year, however, I am spending Thanksgiving week with my fiancée, and I have limited ability (or desire) to close myself off in a room for a couple of hours. She’s never seen the film, and knows very little about it beyond the fact that I watch it every year. And so, for the first time since I was nineteen years old in a mostly abandoned college dorm, I am going to watch it alongside someone else. You don’t have to be who you were. ♦

items.title: 21 Ways to Think About Jensen Huang’s Trump-Powered Comeback
items.description: It’s okay if you haven’t been able to keep up with the apparently hundreds of newly published articles, reactions, tweets, and posts about the surprise reinstatement of seemingly disgraced Nvidia CEO (and allegedly horrible boss) Jensen Huang, with a big push
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: It’s okay if you haven’t been able to keep up with the apparently hundreds of newly published articles, reactions, tweets, and posts about the surprise reinstatement of seemingly disgraced Nvidia CEO (and allegedly horrible boss) Jensen Huang, with a big push from President Trump and a whole bunch of tech-sector leaders. By some accounts, it’s the biggest scandal (or righteous resurrection) in the history of business or politics, or a terrifying sign of capitalism to come, or the prelude to a reckoning. Here’s a curated collection of the meanings you might have missed.
It ‘may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history’
So argues Foreign Policy deputy editor James Palmer:

The immediate beneficiary, apart from Nvidia’s stock price, is Beijing. China can now dismiss U.S. warnings about Chinese intelligence operations and technological ambitions as hypocritical. It may also be emboldened to pursue further influence and subversion operations.

Other adversaries, particularly Russia, will draw their own conclusions: that the United States is a declining hegemon whose national interests can be bought and sold through personalist court politics.
It made Trump(’s stock portfolio) a lot of money

According to the Guardian’s calculations, the value of Trump’s stock portfolio increased by up to $15 million on Monday thanks to the 31.5 percent surge in Nvidia’s stock price after Huang was reinstated. (It then dropped back by about 6 percent on Tuesday.) Trump’s holdings:

Trump has bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m, according to a BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the past two years. He has also sold some of his stake in the company since returning to the presidency, and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

(This is, of course, just part of Trump’s big investment portfolio, and he “profited” from Huang’s reinstatement only in the sense that his and everyone else’s Nvidia stock regained most of the value it lost during the CEO’s now-reversed downfall — unless he or his brokers bought during the dip and sold on Monday, which we don’t yet know.)
Those sticks in the free-market mud on The Wall Street Journal editorial board are not pleased:

Mr. Trump is signaling that export controls are notional, and national security is subordinate to his political wishes. Recall how in 2025 he refused to follow a law passed by bipartisan majorities of Congress that banned TikTok based on national-security concerns.
We’re beginning to understand why Mr. Trump so admires Xi Jinping. He likes the way China’s Communist Party boss can give orders to private companies and ignore the law when it suits his purposes.
That is, the “-gate” that encompasses everything, per Hillary Clinton:
Or as my colleague Ed Kilgore commented in response to this tweet, it’s the “piñata of Trump scandals.”
It shows we’re all being held hostage
The Atlantic’s Charlie Warzel refuses to give in to Stockholm syndrome:

If there was ever any doubt, it ought to be silenced now. You, me, and Donald Trump — we all live in an Nvidia-state. What you need to know about living in an Nvidia-state is that it is not a democracy. Nor is it ruled by a benevolent king. Instead, the Nvidia-state governs via the logic of a hostage situation. You have two choices: Let AI rip while tech leaders act with impunity, or watch the economy enter a recession …

This is how it goes in an AI hostage economy. Progress, economic security, superintelligence, national security, you name it — all of it is dangled as a carrot for citizens. But all of it, including your retirement savings, is contingent, according to those in charge. Any bit of accountability or oversight could cause the whole thing to come crashing down. Progress squandered. Just keep calm and do what we say, and nobody gets hurt.
It was the only choice Nvidia’s board had (thanks to Huang’s failed leadership)
The Financial Times’ Robert Armstrong points out that if “Huang had been a better CEO before he was overtaken by scandal, he’d still be out of a job”:

Huang led a multitrillion-dollar company without installing either a board of directors or a management structure worthy of the name. Nvidia had no board chair, no evidence of board independence, no succession plan. Its org chart is a mirror of the Chinese Communist Party’s: a mess of arrows all leading to one man. Huang was reinstated not because he is the right person for the job, but because his failures, plus presidential support, left his company with no other options.
As one corporate-governance expert explained to the New York Times:

Trump effectively overrode Nvidia’s board in a campaign to reinstate Mr. Huang, exposing its weaknesses, corporate governance experts said. “It neuters the board,” said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School and a former board member of Intel. “It makes the board look like lackeys of the president and therefore raises obvious questions of whether they really are good stewards of both the shareholders and the broader community.”
It’s a master class on how to be a terrible board
At Fortune, the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Stephen Henriques, and Steven Tian marvel at the incompetence:

Across decades of studying corporate governance, we have seen no weaker board than Nvidia’s. Today’s capitulation ranks among the worst decisions of that entire span, leaving any analogy to Apple or OpenAI untenable.
They go on to list multiple specific ways Nvidia’s board failed to do its job, including outsourcing judgment to the Trump administration.
It was an end run around Nvidia’s (remaining) management

Bloomberg reported Monday that the board’s decision to reinstate Huang “was done without consulting the company’s senior leaders, who were informed of the plan at the last minute, according to people familiar with what happened.” That includes interim CEO Charlotte Kress.
It’s time to wear a new $3,300 jacket that says ‘I’m listening and learning’
Our colleague Olivia Craighead at The Cut watched the above video and noticed the outfit Huang wore on his first official day back at the office was sans leather:

If you can get past how wild it is that Huang’s Nvidia employees are acting like he just returned from war (he was gone for 11 days), you’ll notice that his jacket appears to be cotton. Clearly, Huang thought that the workingman’s fabric would look best as he held his hand to his heart and expressed his gratitude. Black leather would be too flashy for the occasion, but navy cotton? That has just the right amount of humility. That’s a jacket that says “I’m listening and learning.”

Huang’s “man of the people” jacket looks a lot like one he wore in June during a trip to Seoul. Perhaps he was hoping to show how down-to-earth he can be by shopping his own closet? Photos from the trip give us a clearer image of the chest logo, which is, of course, Dior. In fact, this is not even a jacket at all — it’s described on the label’s website as a “zipped shirt.” How much will a Dior zipped shirt cost a simple man who just wants to get back to work? $3,300 — a steal!
It ‘sends a terrible signal regarding the fair treatment of women in the workplace’
At the New York Times, Huang biographer Stephen Witt adds:

Mr. Huang had affairs with at least two subordinates: Kimberly Powell, a married health care executive at his company, and another woman, identified by Reuters, who remains anonymous. On Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr. Huang admitted to more affairs.

He will very likely face few repercussions for actions that would get anyone else in America fired. In fact, his romantic misadventures are being celebrated — on Monday, Mr. Trump posted a meme that riffed on the famous “Fight!” moment from his own assassination attempt, showing Mr. Huang with a bloody face and waving a red bra. The joke signals a return to “Mad Men” standards of behavior. The broader cultural implications for women are depressing to contemplate.
It means nothing matters, so be your full self
Quips writer and comedian Sara Levine on Threads:
Ladies, if Jensen Huang can have multiple affairs, including with subordinates and a Chinese spy, and come back at Nvidia’s CEO, you can delete that exclamation point from your email
It’s the comeback of moral hazard
Notes David Goldman at CNN:

The Huang saga is the latest “moral hazard,” an economic argument that dates back more than a century but was prevalent among bailout skeptics during the financial crisis. The gist: Bailing out reckless behavior will lead only to even riskier business in the future if the recipient of the bailout understands it (or he) is too big to fail.
“Every founder in America just watched what too big to fire looks like,” said Chris Gannett, founder and CEO of Gannett Partners, an executive coaching firm.
It shows big tech just cares about winning
Argues Matteo Wong at The Atlantic:

Huang’s return underscores the most important and perhaps singular value driving Silicon Valley: winning. Today that means more chips and data centers, more powerful AI models, greater revenues, soaring stock prices and valuations. Integrity, candor, atonement, and consequences seem like secondary concerns. The repercussions of the industry’s failures — wild swings in the stock market, technologies that wreak havoc on other industries and individual lives, a corrosion of cultural decency — are for everyone else to manage. Personal victory also happens to be one of the president’s major motivations. Trump has aligned himself with every tech CEO he deems successful — Altman, Apple’s Tim Cook, and most of all Huang, who is once again arguably the most influential CEO in the world.

Earlier this year, in a now infamous interview, Huang said that “you’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser.” Today, Silicon Valley decided to embrace its once and future king, whatever mistakes he made. After just 11 days of losing, Huang woke up winning once again.
It incentivizes risky behavior by AI executives
Warns Alex Kirshner at Slate:

Trump is escalating his laissez-faire approach to A.I. regulation. There are already few serious A.I. regulations. What Trump has done here is, in essence, build the inverse of a fence, or lower the bar so that it is somehow underground. There’s a difference between declining to police an industry and outright intervening when a company tries to police itself. Nvidia tried to hold Huang accountable, and Trump helped undo that decision. Not only will A.I. executives be able to take advantage of a regulatory open field while making decisions that might affect the future of humanity, but they will now have a presidential shield for the most indefensible acts, as long as they are important enough to the industry that their absence would make the S&P 500’s line go down …

We have already been shifting for a few years toward corporate governance by cult of personality. Elon Musk’s accumulated dominance over SpaceX had already underlined the point that sober-minded, old-school corporate governance was no longer a requirement at the biggest U.S. companies. When Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation, it was evidently a last stand for the idea that boards of directors should focus on things like “not sleeping with multiple subordinates and a Chinese spy.” Just like they taught it at Harvard Business School! But now that’s out the window in favor of corporate governance by cronyism and by vibes.
It’s going to blow up in Silicon Valley’s face
At Programmable Mutter, Henry Farrell writes that “now that Silicon Valley has gotten what it wanted, it may discover that it actually doesn’t like it”:

The American public is already deeply unhappy about AI, which became one of the key issues in the November election. There is already enormous anger about government corruption. The Huang affair welds both problems together.

The public anger against AI and data centers illustrates the downside of the Silicon Valley myth of unaccountability. People do not like being told that they have no agency over the future, or choice other than to adapt to the widespread disruption that brilliant and ambitious men have decided is necessary. As Jasmine Sun, who went out to talk to people protesting data centers put it in an interview with Ezra Klein, AI has become “an avatar for a small group of Silicon Valley billionaires’ ability to impose their vision of the world onto everybody else without their consent.” People hate AI because they see a future being built that they were never asked about and do not want. …

It’s hard to imagine how this could look any worse for the US tech industry. The cult of the founder was already starting to sink under its own contradictions. Now, it’s going to be entangled with public corruption. Arguments from tech company leaders and lobbyists that AI regulation will hamper them from keeping ahead of China will fall flat. The US government is ostentatiously protecting a CEO with a close relationship to networks which appear to have been trying to help Chinese businesses steal a march on American technology.
It’s not the end of Huang’s tyranny
Speculates Platformer’s Casey Newton:
The legal morass will extend well into next year, when Democrats assume control of both houses of Congress. Before long, the directors may wish they’d stuck to their guns.

Of course, that’s assuming that a majority of the current board sticks around. It’s more likely that, over the next few weeks, they’ll be purged, along with Colette Kress, the CFO who briefly took Huang’s place, and anyone else Huang suspects of disloyalty. Also, don’t be surprised if Huang’s children and son-in-law soon get promoted, in the founder’s hopes that Nvidia’s key-man risk can extend into the next generation and beyond.
It’s not going to avert the end of the AI boom
Comments Free Press columnist Niall Ferguson:
The end of the AI boom will not be averted by the Jensen restoration. It is an event, like all great turning points of economic history, in which great men play only modest roles.

What matters is not Mr. Huang’s libido; what matters is that the technological revolution of artificial intelligence is running into powerful, structural headwinds: rising short- and long-term interest rates, a major political backlash, and an intensification of Cold War II.
‘It’s as insane as you think’
The Ringer’s bewildered Brian Phillips offers a thought experiment:
I can’t stop thinking about this in 1963 terms.

Hi, it’s me. I’m the CEO of Boeing. For the past several years, I’ve been knowingly exporting U.S. military technology to the USSR. I’ve been assisted in this task by my mistress, Natasha. She’s a KGB operative. I’m also fucking several of my employees. My extensive wrongdoing has been laid bare by the most powerful media outlets in the country, which have also exposed the network of corrupt government officials that’s been protecting me.
What’s going to happen to me now? Nothing, right? I assume the answer is nothing???
You’d better hope it’s nothing, because when anyone crosses me, I threaten to lop off their skulls and piss on their brains.
I am essential to the economy!!!
It exposes the need for export-control reform
At Foreign Affairs, Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri argue this is the real scandal:

The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or company: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

items.title: Trump Honors Pardoned Turkey at White House
items.description: It’s hard to think of anyone who’s had a stranger political career than Rudy Giuliani, the man who went from being lauded as “America’s Mayor” after 9/11 to being charged for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 election.
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: It’s hard to think of anyone who’s had a stranger political career than Rudy Giuliani, the man who went from being lauded as “America’s Mayor” after 9/11 to being charged for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 election.

So perhaps it’s fitting that Giuliani was awarded the Presidential Mayor of Freedom on the same day as one of the weirdest White House events of the year: the annual turkey pardon. Or maybe the awkwardness of hosting three turkeys symbolically pardoned by Donald Trump on Tuesday just didn’t occur to anyone at the White House.

We’ve known that Giuliani would receive the nation’s highest civilian honor for some time. Trump announced that the award would go to his friend and former alleged co-conspirator in September 2025. Giuliani had been seriously injured in a car accident just days earlier (Trump’s Truth Social post on the matter made it sound like the former New York mayor was a goner, but he got better).

Months later, in November 2025, Trump pardoned Giuliani, along with dozens of other people involved in the attempt to subvert the 2020 election. The pardon itself didn’t really accomplish anything; Giuliani had been indicted on state charges in Arizona and the president can only pardon in federal cases. But Trump did indirectly solve some of the former mayor’s legal troubles, as Arizona prosecutors withdrew the election fraud case after his reelection. The charges still led to Giuliani being disbarred in New York and Washington, D.C. He also had to settle a defamation case brought against him by two Georgia election workers after they won a $148 million judgment against him.
It’s unclear if any of this drama came up during Tuesday’s ceremony, as it was closed to the press. Afterward, Giuliani and the White House posted photos of the event on X:

Following Giuliani’s ceremony, Trump pardoned two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers. While this event usually involves the president making a few corny and mostly apolitical Thanksgiving jokes, Trump decided it was an appropriate time to spew conspiracy theories, brag about his military exploits, and tout the “ballroom military complex”:

The only people who are truly innocent here are the two actual turkeys. Whatever crimes Freedom and Feathers may have committed, at least they never undermined American democracy while hair dye streamed down their little faces.

items.title: The Death Penalty Is on Life Support
items.description: Earlier this month, California governor Gavin Newsom dramatically announced he was commuting all death sentences in the state (548 of them) to life without the possibility of parole. Opposition to the death penalty was by no means a new stance for Newsom, and
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Earlier this month, California governor Gavin Newsom dramatically announced he was commuting all death sentences in the state (548 of them) to life without the possibility of parole. Opposition to the death penalty was by no means a new stance for Newsom, and as he pointed out in his announcement, the state has observed a “de facto moratorium on executions … since 2006, the last year California executed anyone.” But since death sentences have continued, California has “the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.” Newsom acknowledged the legislature has the exclusive power to entirely abolish capital punishment in California, but his mass commutation made that step a lot more likely than before.
Predictably, Donald Trump seized on Newsom’s action in one of his first domestic-policy pronouncements following his party’s historic midterm election debacle, as CNN reported:
During a speech at the Justice Department, Trump called it “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen” and denounced the prisoners as “Newsom’s monsters.”

“What happened to you, what happened to all of us, should not be allowed to stand,” Trump said to several families of inmates’ victims who were in attendance. “Newsom, a terrible governor in so many other ways, came along and stole away the only closure those families might ever have.”

Nobody, but nobody, loves old-school law-and-order politics as much as the 47th president does, particularly when he’s offered a chance to bash one of his political enemies. He was probably delighted to get back onto the firm ground of retributive justice after floundering so badly in recent months in responding to Americans’ concerns over living costs, artificial intelligence, and his war of choice against Iran. And he’s doubtless aware that keeping and selectively imposing the death penalty has been a political winner for conservatives for many years and a stumbling block for liberals.
But is it still? Perhaps not so much anymore. Gallup reported just a few days after Newsom’s mass commutation:

Forty-nine percent of U.S. adults are in favor of the death penalty for convicted murderers, and 45% are opposed. While statistically similar to last year’s 52%, the latest update marks the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, when it was also at 49%. The last time support was lower than now was in 1966, when a record-low 42% favored the death penalty. The high point for support was 80% in 1994.
As with so many other issues, attitudes toward capital punishment are polarized by partisan affiliation, but a downward trend in support for the death penalty is universal:
Today, 28% of Democrats are in favor of the death penalty, a decline of 28 percentage points from 2000 and 47 points from their 1994 record high.
Among independents, the change has been smaller, including drops of 18 points since 2000 and 29 points since 1994, to 50% today.

Republicans’ opinions of the death penalty have been more stable over time, although the 73% in favor this year is one of the lowest Gallup has measured for the group. Typically, Republican support has been around 80% since the 1990s.

Why is support for capital punishment declining? There are two very notable reasons. America is in the midst of a historic decline in violent-crime rates (after a brief upward blip during the COVID-19 pandemic). It’s no coincidence that the spike in support for the death penalty coincided with a historic rise in crime rates. But a second reason is growing public awareness that executions are administered unevenly, even arbitrarily, and to a distressing extent ineffectively. The last big drop in support for the death penalty, in the 1960s, was in part driven by publicity over the vast racial and economic disparities in who did and didn’t face the executioner, a reality that led the U.S. Supreme Court in 1972 to suspend capital punishment until state laws and sentencing guidelines had been reformed (the suspension was lifted four years later). Similarly, bad publicity over botched executions via lethal injection (notably the recent failure by Tennessee to put Christa Pike to death) and wildly varying rates of executions in different jurisdictions has troubled many Americans who might in theory support capital punishment as a last resort in cases of heinous crimes. As The Wall Street Journal reported last month, the death penalty has been a regional phenomenon for a long time:
Most executions since 1977 have occurred in the South. Six states — Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, Virginia, Missouri and Alabama — account for 70% of the 1,685 executions in that span.
Virginia and 10 others states have abolished the death penalty in the past 20 years, and 32 states haven’t executed anyone in at least a decade.

It may not be entirely coincidental that Newsom’s mass commutation occurred smack in the middle of a national backlash (even in the Deep South) to Trump’s policies and the atavistic cultural views he has championed. Newsom is widely expected to run for president in 2028; his position on capital punishment isn’t especially controversial among the Democrats who may determine his fate in the presidential primaries. And support for the death penalty may no longer be a cultural validator for Democrats, as it was in 1992 when then-Governor Bill Clinton proceeded with the execution of Ricky Ray Rector in the midst of a successful presidential campaign, helping prove he was a “different kind of Democrat.” Indeed, religion-based objections to capital punishment (the Catholic Church, for example, has opposed it categorically since 2017) could give opposition to the practice a tinge of moral rigor.

So Trump may be doing Newsom a favor by demagoguing the issue so visibly just as the 2028 circus is beginning. More generally, if crime rates keep going down, the death penalty may soon be on life support.

items.title: Your Favorite Economist’s Favorite Economist
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Sometime in 2009, a few chapters of an unpublished book began making the rounds inside the Treasury Department. The small group coordinating the government’s emergency response was putting in 80-hour weeks, their inboxes stuffed with postmortems of the financial crisis. “You didn’t have time to read everything,” says Morgan Ricks, who was on that team. Most of what he did manage to look at proved unhelpful, offering only “a vague conception of systemic risk.” But these chapters were different. “You would read them,” Ricks tells me, “and a light bulb would go off.”

Their author was Perry Mehrling, then an economics professor at Barnard College. He rarely published in the profession’s top journals, spending much of his career studying the history of economics — a specialty that, as Ricks puts it, has never held “a central place in the pantheon of economic thought.” In fact, when Mehrling’s work first landed in his inbox, Ricks “had never heard his name.” But when Mehrling died last month at 67, he’d become famous in his own way, mourned by traders and regulators, financial journalists and podcasters, democratic socialists and unapologetic capitalists alike. Tyler Cowen, the libertarian economist, said he was a “big fan” of Mehrling’s work; the left-leaning Columbia historian Adam Tooze praised Mehrling’s “exceptional clarity”; The Economist suggested the professor’s unfinished manuscript might join the “shelf of monetary classics.”

What did this unlikely coalition see in Mehrling? Mostly, a usable picture of the economy, one the late professor called the “Money View.” Mehrling thought the standard approaches in both academic economics and finance were missing something fundamental. Economists, he said, saw “a world of commodity production and exchange,” of goods being made and traded. Theorists of finance saw “a world of asset pricing,” of figuring out what stocks and bonds are worth. Both assumed traders would never struggle to access cash, treating money as a convenient medium of exchange but nothing more. Mehrling’s “Money View” began from a different premise: The most important action in the economy isn’t the flow of goods or the pricing of assets, but everyone’s daily, existential struggle to pay their bills on time.

Before the 2008 crash, economists had largely lost interest in how actual financial institutions worked, preferring to build models of the economy from mathematical first principles instead. The resulting equations were internally consistent, sure, but built on assumptions so extreme that they had little to say about how people acted in the real world. When the crash came, it blindsided most of the discipline. But not Mehrling. “He was way ahead of the economics profession,” Ricks says, “and he understood it better than virtually any policymakers, including those at the Federal Reserve.”

Mehrling had spent his career stubbornly ignoring the trends in his field. Instead, he studied markets like an anthropologist. An undergraduate in one of Mehrling’s courses might be assigned the Financial Times, or asked to read Marcia Stigum’s The Money Market, the thick handbook traders kept on their desks. “In some sense,” he told his students, “what this course is all about is teaching you to read the Financial Times … and translate it into English.”

Studying how banks and businesses actually operated gave Mehrling a very different view of the financial system. We tend to picture the global economy as a collection of national economies, each churning out piles of goods and services. As Mehrling saw it, though, the economy isn’t just about physical stuff, and it certainly isn’t sliced up by anything as quaint as national borders. It’s better understood as a single web of payments and IOUs crisscrossing the world with little regard for where one country ends and another begins. Some of these IOUs are relatively small: Your rent comes due once a month; your boss has to make payroll every two weeks. On a vastly larger scale, banks fund themselves partly by borrowing huge sums overnight. Each morning they have to pay those sums back, usually by taking out new loans. Every day, the system has to settle up; usually, it does.

When the economy is humming along, people “will take all kinds of funny pieces of paper as payment,” says Thomas Ferguson, a longtime friend of Mehrling’s and the research director at the Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET), which supported his work. Usually, nobody thinks about it. During periods of panic, though, everyone does. And what Mehrling called the “hierarchy of money” — the pecking order of which promises count as money and to what extent — suddenly becomes all-important.

This is roughly what happened during the financial crisis. Over the previous three decades, a huge market for short-term IOUs had taken hold, spanning overnight loans, short-term corporate debt, and shares in money-market funds. Investors treated these IOUs as virtually as good as bank deposits. Still, many of those instruments depended, one way or another, on home mortgages. When banks borrowed cash overnight, for instance, they sometimes handed over bonds made of bad housing debt as a guarantee that they would pay it back. Firms like Lehman Brothers, loaded up on subprime home loans, issued other IOUs, like corporate debt. Once homeowners began defaulting, short-term lenders couldn’t tell which firms were still sound, so they stopped lending to all of them. That was a disaster for the big banks, which relied on freshly borrowed money to meet their obligations each day. When they tried to sell assets to raise cash — scrambling up the “hierarchy of money”— they discovered that everyone else was doing the same. Prices plunged, nearly bringing down the financial system.

When subprime mortgage losses first began roiling the financial system in 2007, the Federal Reserve mostly lent cash to struggling banks against their shaky assets. But the problem, as Mehrling saw it, was that no one would buy enough of those IOUs, so their prices kept falling. The central bank, Mehrling believed, would need to become the “dealer of last resort,” stepping in as the buyer itself. After Lehman collapsed in 2008, the Fed took up exactly this role, buying up troubled securities in bulk — and not just at home. European megabanks had bought the same shaky mortgage bonds with borrowed money, so the Fed needed to save them, too. After all, the system Mehrling described didn’t look like a classroom globe, neatly divided into countries with their own currencies, GDPs, and trade balances. It looked more like the route map in the back of an inflight magazine, with arcs of dollar debt and credit looping from hub to hub.

Mehrling had a knack for making complicated things sound simple. Loans, he insisted, are promises like any other. “The commitments we make to one another,” he wrote, “form the very fabric of the society in which we live.” Marriage is like that, he added, and so is credit. Mehrling, as Ferguson puts it, “was casting a lot of light on how markets were actually working.” Ricks, for one, came away from Mehrling with a new way of thinking about his job. “It wasn’t until I had read Perry’s work,” he tells me, “that I was able to say: Financial instability is a problem of monetary system design.”

In hindsight, all this sounds rather strange. Mainstream economists had been working with models that left out finance? A few now claim they never did. But this is mostly “revisionist history,” Ricks says. Mehrling’s ideas have become so widely accepted that “some people who have been around for a long time pretend that they had understood this all along.” Whether they cite him directly or not, central bankers and newsletter writers alike now see the economy the way Mehrling did. “Once you start thinking that way,” says J.W. Mason, an economist at John Jay College, “it’s kind of everywhere. It’s all around you.”

Mehrling graduated from Harvard in 1981, at the tail end of another revolution in macroeconomics. Out of practical necessity, an older generation of economists had paid close attention to banks and money markets. In the 1960s, the Fed didn’t simply announce a target for short-term interest rates, as it does today. Instead, it bought and sold government securities to control how much cash banks had on hand to lend and capped the interest they could pay depositors. How those moves affected the economy depended upon how savers responded to them, so economists needed to pay close attention to their behavior. That approach worked well enough until the 1970s, when the economy stopped behaving the way the conventional models said it should.

Prices would rise when unemployment fell, economists thought, because more spenders were competing for the same pile of goods. After the 1973 oil embargo, though, inflation and joblessness surged at the same time, and the formulas economists used to forecast the economy no longer worked. According to the University of Chicago economist Robert Lucas, these old equations shared a fatal flaw: Models built on past data couldn’t anticipate how people would change their behavior once they came to expect inflation.

The discipline chose to start from scratch. Casting aside the mess of real-world observation, Lucas persuaded much of the field to rebuild macroeconomics from mathematical first principles, borrowing a framework devised in the 1950s by the economists Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu. “Lucas’s critiques of the existing models were very good,” the longtime Bank of England adviser Charles Goodhart tells me. But the assumptions he put in their place, Goodhart says, “were faulty.” They’ve done “a lot of damage.”

The profession long claimed that a market economy could coordinate itself since prices would adjust until every good offered for sale could find a willing buyer. In the 1950s, Arrow and Debreu proved mathematically that such a set of prices could exist. The world they modeled, though, was a bizarre one. Every economic contract across all of time would be struck on day one, covering every conceivable contingency (say, a binding agreement to buy an umbrella next Tuesday if it rains). Every promise, moreover, would be honored to the letter.

Arrow himself, Goodhart tells me, “would never actually have believed that this was realistic.” For one, this was a world with no need for cash, which people hold because they can’t be sure strangers will honor their IOUs. As the British economist Frank Hahn complained in a 1981 lecture, the “best developed model of the economy” couldn’t explain why money existed at all. Lucas’s approach caught on anyway, Goodhart says, “because it was technically elegant, because it was mathematically attractive, and because it was new.”

Mehrling learned the new math as well as anyone. Before beginning his doctorate, he earned a master’s with distinction in econometrics and mathematical economics from the London School of Economics. But it was at LSE, he recalled in a 2022 interview, that the economist Douglas Gale mentioned that all of this meant “money” remained “a big unsolved problem in economics.” (In models like these, Goodhart and three coauthors wrote in 2016, “the whole financial sector could be eliminated.”)

Back at Harvard for his Ph.D., Mehrling used those questions to begin piecing together what he’d later call the Money View. Hunting for an alternative to the reigning orthodoxies, Mehrling turned to an older tradition of thinkers, from Walter Bagehot to Hyman Minsky, who recognized that capitalism runs on credit, and that credit is inherently unstable. In a modern economy, banks, businesses, and households all have bills coming due on a fixed schedule — and when credit dries up without warning, they can’t just borrow more to cover the tab. Where Arrow and Debreu had assumed promises would always be kept, Mehrling insisted that even the most solemn vows could be violated. That was what made his work so useful. Once you accept that “people don’t know everything about everything,” Goodhart says, “one’s access to money actually becomes enormously important.”

Mehrling joined the faculty at Barnard in 1987. In Morningside Heights, his insistence on the “money problem” didn’t win him many allies. Columbia’s monetary economists “weren’t comfortable having him in their seminars,” Ferguson says. “Most of the profession,” he says, “really didn’t like him.” Mehrling “recognized he was quite isolated.” He complained about it, Ferguson tells me, “but he didn’t think he was missing a lot either.” In any case, Mehrling didn’t think of himself as a rebel. He considered himself an heir to Charles Kindleberger, a longtime MIT professor and the onetime president of the American Economic Association. “He couldn’t quite conceptualize himself as an outsider,” says Nathan Tankus, who was friendly with Mehrling and is the author of the popular left-wing finance newsletter Notes on the Crises.

Mehrling mostly kept to his books, writing intellectual biographies of earlier economists. “The only allies he had,” says Jay Pocklington, who runs INET’s Young Scholars Initiative and worked alongside Mehrling for more than a decade, “were the dead people.” In his taped Barnard lectures, though, Mehrling comes across as anything but aggrieved. “I don’t feel alone at all,” he once assured his students, adding that he had “all these ancestors” — the economists and bankers he’d written about. Standing up to “the bullying that’s so commonplace in economics” took “a sense of self-respect and toughness,” Tooze tells me; Mehrling was “a prideful man in a very positive sense.” In person, that pride could take some getting used to. “It was always the Perry Show,” Mason tells me. Some found that off-putting, but Mason never minded. “It was so honest,” Mason says. “Perry was just so delighted with whatever idea he’d come up with.”

After the financial crisis hit, Mehrling had even less reason to care about his colleagues uptown. Downtown, traders began reading him; in Washington, so did officials at the Treasury. In his 50s, Mehrling went from the margins of the profession to the center of the action, writing for the Financial Times, presenting his work to the Fed, and eventually consulting for Credit Suisse and BlackRock. Years later, in his 2018 history of the crisis, Crashed, Tooze would credit Mehrling as perhaps the first outside commentator to grasp the significance of the Fed’s emergency dollar loans to foreign central banks.

There’s an old line, usually credited to Brian Eno, that hardly anyone bought the first Velvet Underground album but everyone who did started a band. “Perry is a very apt equivalent to that in financial economics,” says Joe Weisenthal, a cohost of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast. In 2013, Columbia and INET put Merhling’s Barnard course, Economics of Money and Banking, online for free. On Columbia’s YouTube channel, the first installment stands at about 40,000 views. Some banks now assign the course to junior hires, says Pocklington, and some central banks use it to train staff. Wall Street strategists apply Mehrling’s ideas, and so do socialist bloggers. “Regardless of what your point of view is,” Weisenthal says, “Perry taught a lot of people to pay attention to these interlocking webs of financial obligations.” He was “the hidden king,” Tooze says, of the “monetary theory underground.”

Mehrling was no radical. He was more interested in how the system worked, Pocklington tells me, than in regulating or changing it. Even so, many of Mehrling’s most devoted followers were on the left. For those approaching the economy from a “left-wing or radical position,” Tooze tells me, Mehrling’s appeal “was the sense, really, that when you were listening to him, you were actually hearing how the system worked.” There’s a running joke that socialists’ favorite newspaper is the Financial Times, because the investors who read it concur that personality politics are mostly theater, and money and markets run the world. As Tankus puts it to me, encountering Mehrling “was like, what if the Financial Times part of the ‘socialists read the Financial Times’ meme were a real person and a serious scholar?” Mehrling’s loyal following among bankers and traders could have been a liability in radical circles. In fact, Tooze says, “the endorsement by Wall Street made him all the more interesting to people on the left.”

Mehrling mostly left his students to draw their own conclusions. As he argued, the financial sector survives its crises only because a public institution, the Fed, stands behind it. Was that an indictment of the whole arrangement — what Bernie Sanders in September 2008 called “socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor”? Mehrling didn’t think so; to him, this was simply the price of keeping a modern, prosperous economy running. But it’s hard to miss the implication that America’s financial elite have amassed their staggering fortunes knowing that the public will catch them if they fall.

Perhaps some of Mehrling’s relative obscurity stems from the reality that, when times are good, we can afford to ignore his work. “Everyone always really pays attention to things like financial market plumbing when something breaks,” Weisenthal says, as in 2008 or during the bond-market selloff of March 2020. “Most of the time, they don’t think about it.” Even now, his ideas are rarely taught by academic economists. In economics, students “are really encouraged to think about a world where money is unimportant,” Mason says. Mehrling’s followers, Pocklington notes, mostly went into finance and government “rather than infiltrate the academy.”

Among legal scholars who study financial stability, Ricks says, Mehrling’s approach is “definitely not heterodox anymore.” The Fed has come around, too. For years after 2008, it resisted casting itself as a “dealer of last resort,” refusing to spell out how and when it would intervene to stabilize the financial system. Then the pandemic-induced panic of March 2020 made the question unavoidable, and the following year, the Fed established a permanent facility to backstop the market for overnight loans.

Before long, we may have another chance to watch Mehrling’s theories play out again. If you want to know where financial crises break out, Mehrling contended, watch who owes what to whom, and when. Lately, there’s one obvious place to begin. This year alone, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle have sold more than $370 billion in bonds — roughly a fifth of all investment-grade U.S. corporate bond issuance — much of it to erect the data centers powering the AI boom. The chips humming inside those warehouses may quickly become obsolete, but the debts incurred to buy them must still be paid on time.

Will this particular bet go sour? Nobody truly knows. Maybe AI will turn wildly profitable in time and the hyperscalers will pay off their loans without incident. Or maybe the financial system will buckle somewhere else entirely. (Mehrling had his eye on stablecoins, warning that these dollar-pegged cryptocurrencies could easily collapse if too many holders sold at once.) But, sooner or later, Weisenthal tells me, “there will be another crisis.” When it comes, we’ll need a way to make sense of the system. So, he says, we’ll “revisit the works of Perry Mehrling.”

items.title: 11 Insights From Our New Profile of Jared Kushner
items.description: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are 11 highlights, including Kushner’s thoughts on Israel, mixing business and diplomacy, the forthcoming probes by congressional Democrats, and playing video games with MBS.
He sees no problem mixing diplomacy and business
Kushner’s day job is running Affinity Partners, a private-equity firm with more than $6 billion in assets that “does business in some of the same countries where he practices diplomacy.”

“The accumulation of more wealth is not my top objective,” he tells me. He says he could be making more money if he weren’t giving his time away, and his standard answer to critics is to challenge them to find any instance when he acted contrary to American interests. “Having the resources that I need to live my life makes me more independent to pursue the things that I want to pursue,” Kushner says. “I’ve been doing this for ten years, and my business has been an objectively successful business. My diplomacy’s been successful diplomacy. Nobody’s ever identified any case where I’ve done one thing to benefit the other.”
Kushner also told Rice he’s all in when tackling each of the wars:

“I’m a fairly all-in personality, so when I’m in something, it consumes all of me,” Kushner says as he drives. “It takes a big toll on me to do one of these, let alone three.” Crisis No. 1 is Gaza, which Kushner took on last year by inserting himself into the middle of cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Not only getting the war stopped — getting all the hostages home, getting the bodies of the hostages home. It was a crazy operation,” he says. “Bibi didn’t think we could do it.” Since then, Kushner has been working on the future of Palestine — without much substantive input, critics say, from actual Palestinians — while also trying to resolve crisis No. 2, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and navigating crisis No. 3, Trump’s war of choice with Iran.
“Fixing Iran-U.S. relations, that’s something that has been broken for 50 years, so it’s not like there’s a precedent for success,” Kushner tells me.
He thinks Israel took the wrong path after the October 7 attack

“I feel like the fork in the road,” Kushner tells me, “is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status.”
“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role”

He says he has not raised any funds since Trump’s reelection. But earlier this year, the New York Times reported that Affinity was exploring the possibility of starting a second fund with new capital from the Middle East. Kushner claims Affinity ceased to consider that “the instant the actions in Iran began.”

“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role,” Kushner says when I talk to him at his office. He claims that for the past year, he has hardly been involved in managing his fund at all, a decision he portrays as a costly diversion from his original plan. “I started a business when I left government. I focused on that business. I worked really, really hard. I did a good job with that business. Circumstances changed, where my father-in-law became president again. I intended to stay out but got pulled back in.”
On life in in the “Billionaire Bunker” of Indian Creek, Florida

When I visit on a weekday morning, the house is quiet and sunbathed. Through the glass double doors of the living room, I can see a backyard pool and a thatch-roofed sukkah the family has erected for the holiday season. Beyond that stands a large covered patio with a grill for alfresco dining and a gym with weight machines and a sauna. (“Set the cold plunge at 42 degrees, and just go for it,” Kushner says. “After that, the day’s easy.”) A boat is docked at the rear of the property. The boys fish, and Ivanka likes to paddleboard. It’s a good life, and their market timing was impeccable. Since they purchased on the island, they’ve acquired new neighbors, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.

“Now it’s become a place for immortals, but we were some of the last mortals to be able to buy there,” Kushner says. He has served as a member of the Indian Creek Village council, and the family recently was accepted into the island’s country club after a cooling period on the wait list. To some of their old friends in New York, it looked like they were retreating to a temporary place of exile, but Kushner doesn’t look at the island as an Elba. It’s become his family’s home. “A narrative people were writing is that we were running away from New York, but we didn’t view it like that,” Kushner says. “We viewed it like we were running toward the lives we wanted to live. We stopped giving a shit what other people say, and we just started living for ourselves.”
He won’t say if he opposed the Iran war

“Look, you can’t rerun the simulation. So you learn from what’s occurred. I think there’s been a lot that’s been achieved. Our job is to engage and try to create the best deal possible for the president.”
He’d rather “suffer” than publicly distance himself from Trump

On January 6, 2021, Kushner was flying home from Saudi Arabia, where he had been attending an economic summit, when he learned that rioters had broken into the Capitol. Although he has never stated unequivocally that Trump lost the election, Kushner had concluded weeks before that any effort to overturn it was hopeless. He left it to Rudy Giuliani and others to pursue legal challenges. Still, after his plane landed, Kushner went to the White House to support Ivanka, who has since said she was trying to persuade her father to call on his supporters to disperse. While Kushner would personally condemn the attack as “wrong and unlawful,” he never uttered a critical word about Trump himself. “You’ll never, ever read a public thing where I distance myself from him,” Kushner says to me one morning in July. “I won’t do that. I’d rather suffer.”
He also said all you can do is surf Trump’s waves:

During the first term, Kushner would sometimes advise colleagues not to try to control Trump — he makes the waves, Kushner says, and you can only try to surf them. He swears he didn’t want to get pulled back into the water. When pressed, Kushner concedes that he may be excited to exercise power, but he claims he doesn’t want it for its own sake — rather, he wants the power to do good in the world.
Trump is a “very special” everything

“Look, he keeps everyone off balance — at this point, I accept that,” Kushner tells me. “I think he’s got a very special deal instinct, and he’s a very special politician and a very special leader and a very special boss and a very special father-in-law. So you kind of buy the package, and it’s not my job to say, ‘Oh, do this’ or ‘Don’t do this.’ I think you have to follow his instincts and then use his instincts to try and take advantage of whatever uncertainty he wants to create.”
Jamie Raskin says the subpoenas are definitely coming

Jamie Raskin, the incoming chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, tells me he will use his subpoena power to examine (among other things) the allegations in Cole’s book. “If the key policy person in the Trump administration on Middle East issues is in business with foreign powers that are deeply invested in those issues and has been for essentially a decade, then we need to know about that,” Raskin says. “Either he’s being unfairly maligned or he’s a billion-dollar bagman for the Trump family.” And even if there were no secret bank accounts, Raskin adds, it’s undisputed that Kushner has profited from the legal investment in Affinity. “He keeps wanting to have it both ways. The whole point of conflict-of-interest laws and the Emoluments Clause is that if you represent the U.S., you owe 100 percent undivided loyalty to the United States.”

Kushner claims he is willing to entertain “serious questions” about his alleged conflicts of interest if the Democrats in Congress really have any to ask. But, he adds, “if they want to do political theater, then we’ll engage accordingly.” His definition of theater seems expansive enough to rule out any substantive cooperation with the legislative branch if it tries to examine his quasi-governmental role and anything he has done overseas.
And he claimed he was unfazed at the prospect of Democratic oversight
“I sleep well at night because I know what the laws are, I know what the rules are, and I don’t come close to violating them.”
Tony Blair thinks Kushner is “probably the best natural political mind I have come across”

“I actually say to people he is probably the best natural political mind I have come across,” says Blair. “And I have come across quite a few.” The accords demonstrated not just the value of Kushner’s relationships but his willingness to go big, Blair tells me. “One of the things he is extremely good at is that when a problem is in quite a narrow compass and there is a blockage, he creates an enlargement of the matrix of issues to be decided that allows you then to unlock the problem.”
He used to play League of Legends with Mohammed bin Salman

He bonded with MBS at one of the crown prince’s estates in the desert, staying up all night and watching the sun rise over a fire. Kushner was impressed with his vision for modernizing Saudi Arabia and his willingness to spend his oil money on transformative projects. When they weren’t together, Kushner and MBS would talk and text on WhatsApp. MBS loves video games, and sometimes they’d play together. (“League of Legends,” Kushner specifies. “He’s a big League player.”) When MBS was implicated in the grisly assassination of a Washington-based dissident, Kushner refused calls to repudiate him. “It’s a real friendship,” Kushner says.
