items.title: How the Fashion in 'The Body' Brings Rebellious Y2K Girlhood to Life
items.description: The Body is more than just an ode to Y2K fashion. For those who grew up Catholic, queer, and quietly rebelling against school dress codes, it’s a visceral time capsule. The psycho-thriller Netflix series follows the Lions, the reigning dance team at St. Mark’s
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: The Body is more than just an ode to Y2K fashion. For those who grew up Catholic, queer, and quietly rebelling against school dress codes, it’s a visceral time capsule. The psycho-thriller Netflix series follows the Lions, the reigning dance team at St. Mark’s Catholic High School in 2004. Despite the strict, God-fearing setting, the Lions are culty, provocatively glamorous, and constantly up to no good. They’re led by co-captains—and secret lovers—Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany).

Then comes Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), a new-to-town, socially awkward outsider who wants nothing more than to be on the team. After a satanic ritual at a Halloween party goes awry, she blackmails her way in, and things take a haunting turn from there. Throughout its eight-episode run, The Body charts the complicated intimacy of teen-girl friendship, the weight of religious guilt, and how much better a secret is kept in a pre-iPhone age. A big part of this worldbuilding, of course, comes down to the clothes.

“I kind of approached it like a period film,” says costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier, noting that she mostly restricted her vintage sourcing to pieces from 2000 to 2004. For inspiration, she looked to paparazzi shots of Paris Hilton and Britney Spears and analyzed early-aughts tabloid media. “It was the rise of the It girl, reality TV, and public personas,” she says of this time in pop culture history. She combed through vintage shops in Toronto, where the series was shot, and stayed up until the early hours finding designer bags on eBay. She also created an inner world for each character, down to picturing which posters would be plastered on their bedroom walls.
Here, Gordon-Crozier walks us through her process for dressing The Body’s Anya, Elise, and Lisbeth, how the Lions’ uniforms came to life, and the details on all those enviable 2000s It bags.
Kristina Bogic (Anya) on the set of The Body.

“Anya is trying to hide her sexual desires from her disapproving mother,” Gordon-Crozier says of the popular team captain. “So we went extra floral and uber feminine with her.” She wears a lot of Blumarine, ballet-inspired pieces, and pastel palettes. As for her celeb style inspiration? That would be The O.C.’s Mischa Barton.
Sara Boustany (Elise) in fittings for The Body.

“Elise is a little bit darker. She’s sort of inspired by Devon Aoki, Comme des Garçons, and Marithé + François Girbaud,” says Gordon-Crozier. “She wears asymmetrical silhouettes, more complicated designs, and lots of texture.”

Most impressive, perhaps, is Elise’s expansive outerwear collection. “She’s just a coat girl, that’s her thing,” says Gordon-Crozier of the biting dance captain, noting her particularly striking vintage animal-print jacket. “If you were going to get metaphorical with it, you could say it’s like the tiger that she wears on her body.”
Geena Meszaros (Lisbeth) in fittings for The Body.

“Lisbeth is the one that evolves the most,” Gordon-Crozier says, adding that her early outfits reflect her conservative upbringing in the Pentecostal church. “I wanted to have her covered up in the beginning. She has a long denim skirt; she has one pair of Walmart sneakers that we beat up. She’s definitely a little inspired by Chloë Sevigny in Gummo. We had the idea to bleach her eyebrows, and she has her cat T-shirt, which is similar to the one Sevigny wore. It’s a little nod.”

Once Lisbeth manipulates her way onto the team, she starts to “single-white-female” Anya, says Gordon-Crozier. “She sort of wants to wear Anya’s skin. She starts wearing her clothes, borrowing her bags, emulating her style, and forgetting about her mother at home.”

“[For the Halloween party], it was scripted that [Anya] would be ‘slutty God.’ I was like, ‘Okay, well, she doesn’t have any money. How’s she going to get this costume?’ So the idea is that she pulls the sheet off her bed, and then she takes a cross off her wall and hangs it around her neck.”

“We made all the school uniforms, and every girl has a different skirt length. Lisbeth’s was longer, and the Lions had shorter skirts because they would roll them up at the top,” she says. “The main thing for us was the bags, because even though the girls had these uniforms, and they weren’t really allowed to wear makeup, we wanted to show that they cared about how they looked.”

“I was literally up until 2 a.m. every night on deep, deep holes on the internet. We would find bags in bad shape, and I had an ager and dyer who would clean them, paint them, and re-weave the leather, because we didn’t have a big budget,” she says. Her favorites are the John Galliano-era Dior purses, but they also had bags from Coach, Longchamp, Louis Vuitton, Von Dutch, and, of course, Balenciaga. “I borrowed a Givenchy bag from someone in my office. I brought in one of my Balenciaga City bags. We were begging, borrowing, and stealing to get all of them,” she laughs.
“I tried not to repeat bags too much with Anya...I thought she would have one for every day. I decided to add rosaries to her Balenciagas as a little personal touch.”

The Lions’ stage costumes, too, were rooted in 2000s-era It girldom. “I saw a photo of Chloë Sevigny in a dance leotard, and I basically copied the shape of it,” she says. “I think the girls had a love-hate relationship with the bodysuits. But it was a true uniform, in the sense it brought them together.”

“I researched images of debutantes in that era,” she says of coming up with the dresses for the ball in the finale. “The idea of the debutante is so bizarre. It’s like purity, white gloves, and teenage boys in tuxedos handing off their dates. Everyone had white dresses with touches of black. I wanted it to be very uniform in that sense, because I think they all talk.”
“Anya’s was a copy of a Stella McCartney-era Chloé dress. It was seafoam green, but I really liked the black detail on it, so we made that in white and changed it up a little bit.”
“For Elise, I saw a photo of Devon Aoki on the red carpet in this white braided top, so we remade that with a puffy skirt on the bottom.”

“[Showrunner Quinn Shephard] and [executive producer Gina Gammell] had such a clear vision of what they wanted. They wanted this to be a special fashion TV show. The set designer is amazing, the music is amazing, and all these girls are unknown,” she says. “A lot of them have worked before, but not to this capacity. They all really bonded, like real Lions.”

items.title: 60 Luxury Holiday Gifts for Your Chicest Loved Ones
items.description: Most gift guides promise something for everyone. But this one is for the people who have everything—your friends, family, and loved ones with impeccable taste, the ones you’d happily give the moon (if only the moon met their standards. But some Louis Vuitton w
items.author: Maryam Lieberman
paragraphs: Most gift guides promise something for everyone. But this one is for the people who have everything—your friends, family, and loved ones with impeccable taste, the ones you’d happily give the moon (if only the moon met their standards. But some Louis Vuitton will do, of course). We’ve done the hunting, from small luxuries that punch above their price point to showstoppers worth gushing over. Below, peruse our compilation of recent and forever favorites that will make even the most discerning recipient light up.

This is the beauty gift for the person who truly has everything, except perhaps a good reason to get out of bed and do their skincare routine. Chanel’s Sublimage L’Extrait de Crème is obviously some serious skin indulgence, but we must say the real pièce de résistance is the lacquered case. It’s so beautiful, you’ll keep it long after the product is done.

It bears repeating that a little old-school glamour still goes a long, long way. Inspired by a design from Tiffany & Co.’s 1962 archives, this 18-karat yellow gold necklace with Akoya pearls and turquoise has that rare, untouchable chicness that’s never dated. Wear it long or doubled up (our preference). This is a piece for a lifetime.

Consider this your permission to put something spectacular under your own tree. A little reward for all those hours of hard work, this silver python Horsebit is equal parts sexy, statement-making, and endlessly tempting for evening.

Make your home gift memorable—why settle for the obligatory silver frame or crystal piece? The Louis Vuitton Diago High Vase, designed by Patricia Urquiola in lilac or seafoam green glass with LV perforated leather detailing, is a far more striking proposition. It’s sculptural, unexpected, and compelling with flowers inside (or not!).

Because she has super-sharp taste and her entrances are studied by everyone in the room, this Cartier necklace is pure provocation, and perfect for her. Fashioned in 18-karat gold with onyx accents and emerald eyes, this long necklace features a chic panther medallion with tassels.

This one is clearly for someone with a strong point of view on dressing, with just the right amount of fashionable edge. We love this chic, substantial accent that works as well with a crisp white shirt as it does with a black evening gown.

Smaller in scale but singular in presence, this season’s most coveted Louis Vuitton beauty-centric launch turns up the volume on glam traveling. The monogrammed piece is a gorgeous, timeless color and defines what luxe leather collectables are all about.

These beauties are stylish, pared-back, and impossible to overdo. Dior’s four-inch pumps are a fabulous gift to elevate her jeans-and-black-turtleneck look—or give her Little Black Dress effortless élan.

Because subtlety is overrated, especially when it comes to holiday gift-giving. Guerlain’s glow-inducing pearls of multicolor makeup arrive in a jewel-worthy case, complete with its own kabuki brush. This product is entirely too gorgeous to hide in a makeup bag.
A little irreverence goes a long way, particularly when Chanel is involved. These gold-tone metal-and-resin earrings from the house’s cruise 2026/2027 collection are both playful and polished.

We all know the Love bracelet needs no introduction. But this pink-gold version, set with diamonds and designed with a flexible construction, offers a more unexpected take on a familiar icon. Wear it solo, without another bracelet in sight (a little Parisian insouciance, if you will).

The effortless edge here is undeniable—the distressed tasseled leather gives this piece a lived-in, rock-and-roll feel from day one. Pair with your jeans and thigh-high boots and you’ve got a look you will reach for season after season.
Meet the everyday bag finally done right in a beautiful leather. Jonathan Anderson’s Dior proves elegant and easy can be the same thing.

Gucci’s recent fragrance game has been especially strong, and this whimsical jasmine-and-gardenia blend is no exception. Effortlessly feminine, the set includes an eau de parfum, body lotion, and travel-size spray.

The Flamenco bag is a stunner, with luminous shades and a shape that will outlast every trend. Give it to the woman who lives for color, or the one who’s worn nothing but black for years. Both will fall in love with the accessory instantly.
Never lose track of your lip pencils while traveling again. This gorgeously, timeless case houses ten beautiful colors, from perfectly curated nudes to classic reds and everything in between.

We love this piece for a multitude of reasons: it’s a little Aspen, a little Gstaad, and entirely Chanel. The neutral palette has an après-ski nonchalance, but there’s nothing ordinary about it. The zip closure keeps essentials tucked away, while the silhouette does the fashion talking. It’s practical, yes, but that’s hardly the first thing you’ll notice about this bag.
For the lipstick devotee, here are 12 (yes, 12!) perfected shades from Pat McGrath Labs. This gift is like a years-long celebratory wardrobe for the lips, with liners to match.

The most memorable beauty gifts are the ones that blur the line between vanity and collecting. Inspired by Estée Lauder’s 1965 holiday collection, this turquoise compact—with its mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell hues—has the appeal of a vintage jewel. Inside, the solid scent of Beautiful Magnolia lends a soft, feminine finish that is impossible not to love.

This is one of Ferragamo’s most refined seasons yet—and the mini Hug handbag is another fabulous example of creative director Maximilian Davis’s chic vision. This piece is plush, luxe, and totally covetable.

We can’t stay away from a little everyday luxury in the prettiest shade of pink. Bottega’s buttery-soft leather is in a class of its own, and the signature Intrecciato weave makes this far more than just a cardholder. It is a work of art!

A La Mer devotee is not easily tempted elsewhere, and this set only reinforces that sense of loyalty. Packed with the brand’s complexion essentials, it’s a welcome excuse to replenish their favorites. And for what it’s worth, it’s a very satisfying gift to unwrap.

Someone has clearly been very good this year. With eleven full-size Augustinus Bader formulas for face, body, and hair, this will be a Christmas morning to make even Santa reconsider his own skincare routine.

The best part? You don’t have to go anywhere. This at-home sauna is your own private indulgence, whenever you want it. No booking, no crowds, just you, the heat, and a door that transports you to glowing skin, detoxification, muscle recovery, better sleep, and less anxiety (seriously).

Some gifts are destined to elicit an audible reaction, like this one—a nod to the Bulgari archives, a little modernist bravado, and coming in an utterly covetable shade of blue. This 18-karat yellow gold Tubogas necklace, set with a central blue topaz and pavé diamonds, epitomizes enduring style. It needs no occasion, of course, but Christmas makes for a very good excuse.

For the fashion iconoclast who loves a statement and wears it with confidence, this Giorgio Fachini ring is impossible not to love. Eighteen-karat yellow gold is capped with a disc-shaped onyx that will stun from the moment it’s on the hand.

This is beyond good taste on every level: Sisley for the skin, Christofle for the home. Two icons of French luxury come together in a set that pairs Sisley’s exacting approach to skincare with a beautifully etched Christofle tray designed by Christine d’Ornano.

This is a gift duo that balances thoughtful formulation with understated polish. The LV Ombrés 150 Beige Memento refillable eyeshadow compact pairs squalane and camellia seed oils with a texture designed to help keep creasing in check, while the LV Rouge 105 Nude Nécessaire lipstick brings a complementary wash of color that you simply can’t get wrong (because who doesn’t love a good nude lip?).

The unexpected fashion pick of the person who already owns all the basics. In animal print, the Ferragamo Gancini belt polishes a white shirt and jeans and can cinch beautifully on a dress if you’re feeling daring.

No one can touch an iconic French scent, and Hermès is always a sure winner in the fragrance game. Barenia is fast becoming a modern classic, with sensual notes of chypre, oakwood, and patchouli. The set comes with a full-size bottle and travel spray, so you are never without the aromatic mood.

Gucci is testing everyone’s spending willpower this season. This one’s for the woman who has every It bag and shoe on the planet. Gucci’s buttery-soft nappa leather turtleneck is pure fashion attitude—sleek and subversive.
Meet the bag to carry on repeat from fall through the New Year. We assure you it will be worn straight out of the gift box and never make it the closet, because that’s what happened to us.

When it comes to red light masks, Celluma is in a league of its own, bringing decades of photobiomodulation research to its newest product, which delivers precisely calibrated wavelengths and has energy output designed to deliver red-light therapy where it counts. A standout gift for the skincare devotee who wants the best, with the added appeal of red-light benefits for the scalp (!).

Mahjong shows no sign of losing its hand, and while there are plenty of luxe sets on the market, La DoubleJ’s is an especially fun choice. The color schemes are bold, the design has that unmistakable Italian flair, and it brings colorful joy to the game wherever you are playing.

A gift for a new home, a guest bathroom in need of personality, or anyone whose getting-ready space deserves as much attention as the rest of the house. Missoni’s signature fiammato (zigzag) print brings an unexpected jolt of pattern and color.

Here’s something for the clean-beauty devotee with high standards. This set brings together four of Tata Harper’s formulas for exfoliation, hydration, replenishment, and barrier support. Organically sourced ingredients and sustainable packaging round out the offering, housed in a verdant box that makes a beautiful first impression.

For someone who knows that the objects on a table are part of the pleasure of gathering around it. FoundRae’s sculptural brass double candle holder brings a touch of gold and a strong design to a dinner table or coffee table.

For the beach-house hosts who have received their share of wine and flowers, a pair of artfully designed beach rackets is a welcome change of pace. A little unexpected, genuinely fun, and likely to see far more use than another hostess bouquet.

A fragrance gift that always lands, this for the woman with timeless taste. Baccarat Rouge 540 is an iconic scent for a reason (it is, notably, Rihanna’s favorite), and pairing it with body oil makes an already exceptional fragrance gift that much better.
Here’s a beautiful and pleasing scent for all to love. This is a delightful pear and lotus incantation that comes with a full-size bottle and a cute travel size option.

For the fragrance obsessive and the perpetually undecided, this set is an excuse to experiment. Seventeen 1.5ml samples, plus a 50ml bottle, cover plenty of olfactory ground, from the heady Jasmine 17 and understated Lavande 31 to the cult-favorite Santal 33.

Some gifts are a gamble, but this is a guaranteed home run, especially if your recipient is on the more youthful side. Hourglass has packed four of its greatest hits into one very luxe package: a full-size Phantom Volumizing Glossy Balm in Slip, Unlocked Instant Extensions Mascara in Ultra Black, Ambient Lighting Edit Unlocked in Hope, and a limited-edition Ambient Lighting Edit Brush II in Love. It all comes tucked inside a vegan leather makeup pouch.

In this clever home gift, the brass has just enough polish to work in both modern and traditional interiors. Plus, there’s something satisfying about giving a gift that won’t be relegated to the back of a cupboard. Anyon Atelier’s match holder comes in a small and large option, and unlike the candle it accompanies, this product has staying power.

Some skincare gifts are best judged a few weeks after Christmas, when your loved one starts noticing the difference in their complexion. Bonjout’s pairing of face cream and balm is an invitation to discover a new favorite, and the sort of introduction to a brand that can turn a first-time user into a serious loyalist. Trust us, this French label is worth checking out.

The Knesko Sculpting Set pairs its beloved glow-giving face oil with a heart-shaped rose quartz gua sha for facial sculpting and lymphatic drainage. It’s perfect for pre-party prep or an evening ritual to boost circulation and de-puffing.

Whoever gets this gift will fall in love with this fabulous and unique fragrance that has a limited-edition bottle designed by painter Abel Macias. Forest Sounds feels destined for cult-classic status especially for those who find gourmands a little too dessert menu and florals a little too basic. This yuzu green masterpiece has a transportive depth that hits just right.

Give the candle lover something to watch while they enjoy the flaming aroma: Diptyque’s’s pine tree lantern dotted with golden stars turns the flame skyward, throwing dazzling moving shadows around the room.

For the person whose home should smell as considered as their personal style, this set pairs three of Byredo’s signature fragrances with an engraved wooden incense holder. A welcome departure from the predictable candle, it offers a different way to scent a room.
Because it’s so pretty in presentation and on the lips, it’s a lovely gift. Dries Van Noten offers two fine lipsticks and a sheer balm in this set.

A toothbrush may not strike everyone as a sexy holiday gift, but there might be someone in your life who takes their oral hygiene very seriously. If so, Dyson’s new CameraJet is an elevated option, all the way. Using a microscopic camera and AI to identify gaps between teeth, it combines brushing and precision-flossing in one rather ingenious kit.

If they’re the type to cancel plans for a proper hair night, the T3 Aire 360 is a gift that understands their need for perfection. The new Rouge edition combines a compact, dual-voltage design with ceramic attachments for bouncy curls or a voluminous blowout.

Good skin is a gift that keeps on giving. Biologique Recherche brings together its iconic Masque Vivant and blemish-control serum here—two serious players in the complexion department, and a proper skincare splurge.

If they can happily lose an hour (or two) in a bath, Santa Maria Novella’s Melograno bath salts are a healing indulgence with panache. There is something gratifying about gifting a pleasure that rarely makes it onto anyone’s to-buy list, particularly when it comes from one of Florence’s most storied apothecaries.

Because one catchall is never enough, these botanical-print porcelain beauties bring a little Gucci glamour to every room. You can use this to coral rings, bedside odds and ends, or whatever deserves a prettier landing spot.
For the peel devotee who takes their skincare seriously, this is a high-mark skincare set from iS Clinical that’ll provide a skin-renewing and rejuvenating regimen all winter long.

Here’s a makeup gift that punches well above its price tag. Beckham’s Bordeaux collection makes a case for the burgundy palette on everyone, whether they’re blonde, brunette, blue-eyed or brown-eyed. The set includes a refillable eye compact that works all year, black mascara, and the new Bordeaux Pavé kajal liner flecked with gold and ruby.

There’s no shortage of shimmer oils, but after testing so many, this one gets the balance just right: a beautiful, subtle gleam without veering into disco-ball territory. The Sublime scent is another selling point—the title says it all. Adding a little shimmer to our holiday outfits? Don’t mind if we do.

This is hand wash for people who notice all the details while inspecting your powder room. Housed inside plant-derived, sustainable packaging, this set comes with a nourishing hand cream that earns its place in your purse, too.

If you’re seeking an elevated gesture to gift that isn’t too loud, we recommend this little slice of Tuscan escape, minus the ten-hour flight and airfare. Seed to Skin, the spa-world insider favorite, brings its particular brand of indulgence home with the Borgo Air Candle and Cloud Nectar bath treatment.

They’ll use it for every holiday, guaranteed. The deep tan iteration of this bag is especially beautiful for leisurely getaways, and it’s a favorite among the jet-set crowd for good reason. It’s the sort of bag you’ll spot everywhere, from beach escapes to hotel restaurants.

items.title: How Fetish Fashion Went From the Dungeon to the Runway
items.description: In 1961, when The Avengers debuted on British television, the sexy spy series gave rise to one of the most persistent style trends in modern history: fetish fashion. After Diana Rigg and Honor Blackman appeared in suburban living rooms wearing laced corsets, l
items.author: Jenny Comita
paragraphs: In 1961, when The Avengers debuted on British television, the sexy spy series gave rise to one of the most persistent style trends in modern history: fetish fashion. After Diana Rigg and Honor Blackman appeared in suburban living rooms wearing laced corsets, leather catsuits, and over-the-knee boots, dominatrix wear climbed out of the dungeon and into the closets of everyday women.

Clothing-centric kinks have likely been around since cavewomen started swathing themselves in animal hides, but many of the earliest recorded examples date to the Victorian era. In London, a trend for cinching one’s corset to the point of swoony near-asphyxiation was widespread. In 1887, the French psychologist Alfred Binet coined the term “sexual fetishism.” One famous case: “It’s said that Napoleon III had to have women wear black stockings,” says the fashion historian Valerie Steele, director of the Museum at F.I.T. and the author of Fetish: Fashion, Sex & Power. In the 1920s, Brits who got a thrill from doing it in rubber rainwear—a practice known as “macking”—formed the Mackintosh Society, one of the first-known fetish organizations.

Such clubs were hush-hush, but at least a few fetish fashionistas were openly marketing their designs. In early-1900s Paris, the wife-and-husband team Nativa and L. Richard founded Yva Richard, a line of metal bras, chastity belts, whips, and ball gags. The Nazi occupation in the 1940s put them out of business, along with their main competitor, Diana Slip, a boutique that employed the likes of Brassaï to photograph its fishnet thigh-highs and crack-revealing panties. But fetish culture reemerged after the war, with magazines such as Bizarre featuring S&M-inflected imagery.

In 1974, Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren rebranded their London boutique as Sex, introducing British teenagers to bondage pants. Around the same time, the photographer Helmut Newton was shooting fashion editorials in which, he later enthused, “the ladies look like whores and the whores look like ladies!”

The ’80s saw plenty of kink on the runways, with Thierry Mugler metal bustiers, Azzedine Alaïa bandage dresses, and Jean Paul Gaultier cone bras. Dominatrix chic came to a climax with the fall/winter 1992 Versace collection, which Anastasiia Fedorova—author of Second Skin: Inside the Worlds of Fetish, Kink, and Deviant Desire—considers “the most powerful intersection of fetish with fashion.” Titled “Miss S&M,” the show had top models in high-neck bodices, studded leather skirts, and buckles galore. “It was huge!” says Steele. “And the look has continued to reemerge every few years since.”

Most recently, in fact, at this fall’s collections. Hermès showed strict leather jumpsuits that, says Steele, “turn the wearer into kind of a visual phallus.” At Gucci and Schiaparelli, getups featured skin-revealing slashes. And at Vaquera, a scowling model wore an extremely low-rise black thong, from which emerged a bright green heart-shaped patch. Was it a merkin? The model’s own dyed and coiffed pubic hair? The beard of a tiny leprechaun? Whatever the case, the trend did not come off as shocking to Steele. “There’s a pendulum swing between sexy and less-sexy fashions, and fetish has come to be one of the key synonyms for sexy,” she says.

Back, too, are the same questions that preoccupied critics after “Miss S&M”: Are these looks degrading to women or empowering? “We’re past the naivete that it’s purely objectifying,” says Steele. As Fedorova points out—and as any dominatrix can tell you—being a sex object comes with its own brand of power. “Wearing something revealing can be a way of seizing control through sexual expression,” she says. “Especially in this moment of toxic masculinity, fetish-wear can be a form of armor.”

Runway, From left: Victor Virgile/Getty Images; Victor VIRGILE/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images; Estrop/Getty Images; Lyvans Boolaky/Getty Images; Courtesy of Hermès. Center: Movie Poster Image Art/Getty Images.

items.title: Kate Madden, Nicole Richie’s Daughter, Enters the Spotlight With Balenciaga
items.description: Kate Madden, daughter of Y2K icons Nicole Richie and Joel Madden, is ready to introduce herself to the world. And what better way to do so than with a Balenciaga Le City Bag bag campaign? Twenty-five years ago, Richie helped turn the accessory into one of the
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Kate Madden, daughter of Y2K icons Nicole Richie and Joel Madden, is ready to introduce herself to the world. And what better way to do so than with a Balenciaga Le City Bag bag campaign? Twenty-five years ago, Richie helped turn the accessory into one of the era’s defining It bags. Now, mother and daughter have both been tapped to star in its anniversary campaign, making the moment less a passing of the torch than a shared family affair.

“I’ve wanted to model since I was young, but I felt like, now that I’m 18, and I have a very specific look, it’s the perfect time for me to start,” Madden told W ahead of the campaign launch. That look includes recently dyed black hair in place of her natural blonde, giving her style a darker, goth-inflected edge. Along with Madden’s large, captivating eyes—which have already drawn comparisons online to Tim Burton characters—the transformation is on full display in the campaign.

The Le City itself dates back to 2001, when Nicolas Ghesquière bucked the era’s prevailing logomania with a design inspired by the classic motorcycle jacket. Its supple lambskin body, metal buckles, and long leather laces quickly caught the eye of early-aughts style—and tabloid—fixtures, Richie among them.

For Madden, the bag has simply always been around. Growing up with a fashion-designer mother and a musician father has clearly shaped her aesthetic, which lands somewhere between the feminine eclecticism of Richie’s House of Harlow and the rock-forward attitude of Good Charlotte. Below, Madden talks about how her parents influence her style, raiding her mother’s closet, her makeup secrets, and career ambitions.
How would you describe your style?
I wear a lot of vintage stuff—a lot of black and pink. I love being girlie, but I also love to dress in darker pieces.
That really seems like an amalgamation of both your parents’ styles. Do they inspire you?
I would definitely say they influence my style. My dad basically only wears black, and I love to wear black. And then I take inspiration from my mom’s style when she was younger.
Do you shop your mom’s closet a lot?
Yeah, I’m always borrowing my mom’s stuff. It’s literally amazing. She’s so nice about letting me borrow whatever I want. Sometimes, she borrows things from me too.
What is the best style advice you’ve gotten from your parents?
They tell me to just be myself with my style. I love unique stuff, so they tell me to wear what I want. They’re always very supportive of whatever I want to wear.
Have you watched A Simple Life?
I haven’t. I guess I haven’t thought about watching it, but I see clips on TikTok. I don’t know, maybe I’ll watch it eventually.
Let’s discuss your makeup, because your big, bold eyes are so unique. I’ve seen people online say that you look like a Tim Burton character. What do you think about that comparison?

It’s the best thing ever. I love hearing that. I grew up as a dancer, so I learned how to do my makeup and my hair at a young age. I mostly focus on my eye makeup because I already have big eyes, so I try to accentuate them as much as possible.
How do you achieve the doe-eyed look? Do you use white eyeliner?
I don’t. My eyes just look like that. But I do wear fake eyelashes and dark eyeshadow.
Let’s talk about Balenciaga. How many Le City bags do you and your mom own? Do you have a favorite?

I have no clue how many my mom owns. I borrow hers a lot, but I have three of my own right now. I love my white one. It goes with everything and I basically wear it every day. It works when you’re trying to dress more fancy, but also when you’re trying to be casual.
What does it mean to be in this campaign with your mom, and to represent a bag she helped make famous?
It was so fun to do it with my mom. It was good for me to do my first campaign with her because I had someone who has more experience helping me through it.
I definitely want to keep modeling, and eventually I want to start acting.
Who do you look up to in those industries?
In the modeling industry, I definitely look up to Amelia Gray and Gabbriette.

items.title: The Robot Vacuum I Refuse to Part With Is on Sale for Black Friday Already
items.description: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Frid
items.author: Nena Farrell
paragraphs: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Friday deals already kicking off, it's one of the best times to shop for one.

One of our favorite robot vacuum brands, Roborock, began its early Black Friday deals yesterday, and some of our favorite models we've tested are available for the best prices we've seen. Here's which models I'd snatch up while the prices are low.
- Roborock's best budget vac at its best price: Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for $450 ($350 Off)
- A powerful, but still affordable roller mop vac: Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow for $600 ($400 Off)
- If you want Roborock's arm attachment: Roborock Saros Z70 with OmniGrip for $950 ($700 Off)
The Best Early Black Friday Vacuum Deals from Roborock

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums. It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.

Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.

If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it.

The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $600 off the $1,000 price tag.

There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While both I and former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So weren't particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads and did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.

It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.

If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which feels handy, but didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.

It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

items.title: Congratulations to WIRED’s Class of 2026
items.description: For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
items.author: WIRED Staff
paragraphs: For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS

An internet devoured by AI. Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a new generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. We saw activists fight surveillance, astronauts do the impossible, and an adorable raccoon melt the internet’s black heart. So for the first time, we’re publishing a WIRED Yearbook: our very subjective, occasionally ridiculous, always enthusiastic collection of the people, institutions, inventions, and moments that offered optimism in 2026. I hope it gives you a healthy kick of bullishness—and the vigor to keep fighting for the future you want to see.
—Katie Drummond, Global Editorial Director

From the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which New York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.
KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.
What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific issue has become such a flash point?
The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

It’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.
You worry that we’re in a bubble?
You worry that bubble’s gonna pop?
Last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You said weaker. What about today?

I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.
What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?

I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

AOC’s Egg-Freezing Journey

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she said in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”

It is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the New York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.
Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez said it was important to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”

As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger

Australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union announced plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.

The jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the company paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to new features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” said the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward

Since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.

This worked fine when Weiss was editing The Free Press. At the time of that publication’s $150 million sale to Paramount last year, it had about 170,000 paid subscribers, a success by anyone’s estimation. Upon Weiss’ ascent at CBS News, a global operation with more than 1,000 employees, the question was whether Weiss’ skills were transferable.

It doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.

Weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes. The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman

Nothing says rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.

Social media users sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.

As WIRED wrote in April, the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They showed us samples, and it made me feel better, because they were so shitty.”

Magazine profiles and good Pitchfork reviews don’t give bands the juice they used to. Now many chart-toppers take off on TikTok first. But that also means competing with scores of other content for ears. Chaotic Good and its network of clippers aren’t so much running a “psyop” as they are trying to meet audiences where they are. And FYI, the agency prefers the term “trend simulation.” —Isabella Ward

The “Knicks in Four” Kalshi Guy

The only word that accurately described the scene outside New York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s new favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “New York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

After the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he said, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.
“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”

Coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga shows: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode

It’s been a wild year for the host of the Pulitzer-winning Pablo Torre Finds Out, who’s emerged as a fresh investigative voice. Calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

It started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

One reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, says Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. New studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn

ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS

An internet devoured by AI. Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a new generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. AOC’s Egg-Freezing Journey

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she said in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”

It is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the New York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.
Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez said it was important to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”

As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger

The “Knicks in Four” Kalshi Guy

The only word that accurately described the scene outside New York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s new favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “New York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

After the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. “When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”

Calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

It started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

One reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, says Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. New studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn

items.title: Ms. Rachel Is for Littles. Her Best Lessons This Year Were Meant for Adults
items.description: Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult wi
items.author: Kate Knibbs
paragraphs: Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

She’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”

Talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

items.title: How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood
items.description: The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie
items.author: Miles Klee
paragraphs: The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”
Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.
Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.description: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthr
items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”
