items.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
items.description: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

items.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
items.description: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while a
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.description: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.
Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

items.title: The Plight of the Eldest Daughter
items.description: When I turned 18, my dad took me to the bank to show me where he kept his will. “If Mom and I die now, you’re in charge of your sister,” he told me. It wasn’t something I was surprised to hear — I’d been in charge of my sister, Claire, who is two years younger
items.author: Brooke LaMantia
paragraphs: When I turned 18, my dad took me to the bank to show me where he kept his will. “If Mom and I die now, you’re in charge of your sister,” he told me. It wasn’t something I was surprised to hear — I’d been in charge of my sister, Claire, who is two years younger than me, for basically her whole life, but this felt different. More concrete, more serious. Sometimes our admittedly small age difference feels like nothing; other days it feels like a lifetime. On that day, it felt like a whole chasm had split between us, and, in a way, my parents were passing the reins of her life over to me. Being the eldest daughter feels exactly like that, over and over again, forever.

Maybe that’s why the Saturday Night Live sketch “Sister” went so viral last week. The digital short starred host John Mulaney foisting all caregiving responsibilities onto his sister, played by Jane Wickline, who too easily gives up literally everything to take care of their dad while John gets off scot-free. “I saw a TikTok clip of the SNL skit and immediately was like, I have to see this in full. It’s so on the nose, I was just cracking up, but also mildly perturbed by its accuracy,” says Amelia, a 40-year-old eldest sister and mother of two. “It’s painfully funny because it’s so true.”

Even though I’m not yet at the caregiver stage, it’s something I know will fall on me. Since I was a teenager, my parents have joked that I’ll be the one who will take care of them, along with my dad’s brother and his wife, who have no kids. “It’ll be like the Willy Wonka bed” is a recurring joke in the family. When I was little, I loved that thought. Now that I’m an adult, it terrifies me. I don’t think I’m particularly generous, or even selfless, but my parents have seen me adapt my life to protect my sister and, in turn, know that I will do the same for them. It feels inherent, and I can’t imagine it any other way. What else can I do?
I talked to seven other eldest daughters to find out — okay, not really, more like commiserate together.
“My mom just passed away about a month ago, so I was there with her for five weeks. My brother — I’m really close to him, love him to death — was probably there for about one.” —Marisa, 65

I’m the oldest of three, and my two siblings are brothers, though one passed away. My dad passed away when I was about 30, and I remember even back then I was like a co-equal with my mom in terms of handling that situation and taking care of all the logistics and everything. My mom passed away about a month ago, so I was there with her for five weeks, just kind of tending to her and supporting her and dealing with the medical people, and my brother — I’m really close to him, love him to death — he was probably there for about a week, and I was there for five.

He’s aware of it. We have definitely talked about it, and he and his wife have thanked me. We’re doing a memorial service, and they’re like, “Well, we’ll take care of all the food. You don’t have to worry about that.” So I think they’re aware that I’ve had the majority of things to deal with. But my mom had a house, so at some point we’re gonna have to go clean that out and get rid of stuff and sell it. And it’ll be interesting to see how much he’s willing to commit to helping out with all that.

Still, I thought the SNL skit was hilarious — I think men have a tendency to let women take care of things like that and not worry, that is a stereotype, but I think it’s pretty accurate in a lot of situations.
“I was changing diapers by the time I was, like, 6 or 7 years old.” —Lauren, 34

I’m the oldest of six kids — three boys, three girls — and I’m definitely Mom No. 2. She and I have such a small age gap. She had me when she was 21, so I assumed that role without even being told to. I was changing diapers by the time I was, like, 6 or 7 years old. Now that I’m older, I still assume that role, just in a different way. I’m the only one who lives on the West Coast; the rest of my family, they all live in San Antonio, Texas. And even with that distance, I’m still micromanaging the family. My mom leans on me really heavily to sort of corral and gather the family and get everyone excited for the holidays, but also get answers from them on what days we’re going to do certain family activities and help organize our white elephant gifting every year.

I always thought it was just part of who I am, which essentially I do think it is. I’m naturally a leader. I like to manage and fix things, and I think a portion of my personality and skill set as an adult and in my career is attributed to supporting my mother when I was younger. I feel like I was sort of born for the role, and maybe because I naturally fell into it, or it was expected of me, I took on that role, but I also found a lot of self-worth in it.
“I have two girls, and I have to turn it off and really actively work against making my oldest feel responsible for her sister.” —Amelia, 40

I’m the oldest of four. There’s a ten-year age span from myself to the youngest sibling, so I had some early parentification stuff — I got thrust into that female traditional caregiver role even as a teenager — like having to sacrifice my time to pick my siblings up and drop them off places and help with dinner. My brother, though, being the only boy especially, was off the hook for so many things.

It’s like he takes precedence in the order of the siblings, and he almost gets put equal with me because I’m the first child and he’s the first boy, even though he’s eight years younger than me. He got put on this pedestal for being the only boy in the family: There were instances where he could be expected to step up, but my mother would often just shelter him from those things and say he doesn’t need to worry about it. If there’s an issue, he doesn’t need to be stressed about that. He’s focused on his schooling, or he’s got other stuff going on, as if my sisters and I don’t also have other things going on.

I do definitely feel like her mother was similar to her in that way. Like she was mirroring behavior she saw as a child with sacrificing her time and being that primary caregiver when necessary. I do think she was maybe slightly less self-sacrificial than her mom, and I don’t think in any way she would have thought that she was pushing that onto us. I think in a lot of ways she tried to minimize that pressure for us to feel obligated, but it’s still there. She couldn’t help it. It’s funny, because I have two girls, and I find myself mirroring that behavior a little bit, and I have to turn it off and really actively work against parentifying my eldest or making her feel responsible for her sister. I mean, obviously, I want her to love and care for her, but I don’t want her to feel like she has to be in the role of caregiver, because I want them to have a dynamic of more of friendship, and not like where one needs to be in charge of the parental obligations of the other.
“You always hear people say things like, ‘You want to have a daughter because she’ll be the one that takes care of you.’” —Mack, 28

I have two younger sisters: One is 25 and the other is 22. My cousin sent me the SNL sketch in a group chat. I watched it, and I was like, This is funny, but so fucking depressing and scary. Somebody commented, “It’s just a sketch. It’s just a sketch. It’s just a sketch.” And I was like, That is the most accurate response to it. It is just quite insane that we’re in 2026, and this is just what’s expected. You always hear people say things like, “You want to have a daughter because she’ll be the one that takes care of you” and all of that stuff.

It’s an interesting dynamic for me because I’m the oldest and most financially stable person. I have a very demanding career, and they just want to have kids. There’s also a level of I don’t really want kids, so then I’m like, Who the fuck is going to take care of me? I need to make sure that I make enough money to not be in a shitty home. It’s quite wild. It’s something I think about a lot when it comes to taking care of my mom. I might not be the one to physically be there, but at least I will pay for it. I don’t want to be the person that’s wiping my mom’s ass every day. I want to be able to pay somebody to wipe my mom’s ass. Maybe I’m thinking like a brother in that sense.
“It has become so apparent to me how different my sisters and I view our childhood, and what we experienced, within the same household.” —Lilly, 27

I am in an all-girl family, and I have two younger sisters. My mom had some mental-health battles throughout her life, and a lot fell on me growing up, especially since we lived with her. I grew up really fast because my parents were getting divorced, and it was extremely messy, and being the eldest daughter, I got put in the middle of it all the time. It has become so apparent to me, as an adult, how different my sisters and I view our childhood and what we experienced within the same household, which is really fascinating because there’s so much in the background that they just never saw, because anytime I was, like, arguing with my parents on behalf of my sisters and me, they just really didn’t know and weren’t around. A lot of that was by design, because I love my sisters more than anything, and you know I want to take care of them as an older sister, but at the same time, it has been really hard for me and involves a lot of therapy.

Now that we’re adults, we’re navigating a more complicated family dynamic again. I have stage-four breast cancer and got diagnosed when I was 25. It’s been very complicated the last two years. I’m from Chicago, all my family is still there, but I’ve been doing treatment in New York, by myself essentially. Because my relationship with my parents is so complicated, I was very adamant about the fact that I didn’t want them around that much. I have been absorbing their emotions my whole life, and I just was like, I can’t take on any extra emotional strife in any capacity. And, generally, my parents have been respectful of that. I understand that my diagnosis is hard for them too, but it’s hardest on me, obviously.

My younger sister has asthma, and she was on the phone with me the other day because she was having a bad asthma attack and was debating if she should go to urgent care or the ER. I was like, “Go to the hospital, you can’t breathe,” and she was like, “I would call Dad or Mom to have them come up and be with me. I don’t want to go to the ER by myself.” I obviously didn’t say anything to her at the moment, but afterward, I was like, I go to the ER by myself all the time. I never even think about the fact that it would be hard to not have my parents there, because it’s just not hard for me in the same way it is for them.
“I’m my brother’s emotional confidante, but it’s not necessarily the other way around.” —Janna, 28

I’m the oldest, and I have two younger brothers. When I saw the sketch, I sent it to my parents and my brothers right away. I just wanted some validation, like, Hello, you guys all think I’m crazy when I’m trying to bring attention to this, but this is a real thing. They hardly acknowledged it. Like, you can’t even throw me a bone in this moment of like, Haha, yeah, that’s so accurate.

I’m a therapist, so I see this a lot at work. These are themes that come up in therapy and are part of why eldest daughters are in therapy, at least to an extent, in terms of finding support and navigating these dynamics and the mental load of all that. There are all these different terms for this type of concept, like the third parent or the parentified child, which, though it’s not a gendered term, it typically is a sister. It starts from these logistical things, and then as you get older too, for me personally, and I know from the clients that I work with who are in similar dynamics, that shape-shifts into different things when we’re out of the house too. I’m my brother’s emotional confidante, but it’s not necessarily the other way around. I think that influenced why I got into what I do, because being the oldest sister gave me these skills of being able to emotionally support people and to hold space for other people’s emotions.
“Is it the perimenopause or is it the caregiving that just absolutely broke my body?” —Kelly, 47

I moved from New York City back to Indiana during the pandemic. My dad had a really aggressive form of skin cancer on his face, and I happened to see it in a FaceTime call and realized pretty much in an instant that if my brother and I didn’t get home and step in, he probably would not live. Thankfully, I was able to work remotely.

But the toll has been immense. It’s not only physical, mental, and emotional. It’s economical too. It’s so aggressively economic. My business is very successful — I work in executive coaching and business consulting — but I wonder where it would be if I was still in New York. Or if I had bought the house upstate that I thought I was saving for. I ended up buying a house in Indiana because it became very clear that my brother would probably not be the one to ever do this. And just a couple weeks ago, my parents moved 12 minutes from me.

I’m also in perimenopause, heading toward menopause, and I can’t express how traumatic this is to an eldest daughter or a woman who is in this stage of her life. Because not only is your body just changing so much, but it fuzzes with the caregiving. Is it the perimenopause, or is it the caregiving that just absolutely broke my body? Or is it most likely a combination of the two? And if I were still living in New York, would I have been able to care for my body better as I was going into this very transitional hormonal period? I wonder what the combination toll is, because I was broken after caregiving for two years, even though my father was thriving and he is thriving.

I’m lucky that I have a brother who is great. It is easy for me to call him, and he calls me, and he visits. He is not an absent son. He visits all the time. But I still have to ask, which I think is a huge part of this. We still have to say, “I need you to do exactly this, and that is exhausting.”

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 26, 2026
items.description: With the moon moving through emotional Cancer — and clashing with Neptune, the sun, Pluto, and Saturn throughout the day — your feelings might be erratic today. One moment, you might be sensitive and insecure, the next irritated by everyone around you, only to
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: With the moon moving through emotional Cancer — and clashing with Neptune, the sun, Pluto, and Saturn throughout the day — your feelings might be erratic today. One moment, you might be sensitive and insecure, the next irritated by everyone around you, only to finally conclude you were overreacting. Don’t take any of your passing moods too seriously just now: The conflict and frustration will blow over soon enough.

You’re likely to take everything personally today. Throwaway comments will feel like personal digs and lighthearted jokes could cut deep. Your feelings are valid, and you’re not required to give anyone a pass just because their intentions are good — but do your best not to be too reactive. If you can take a moment to breathe, you might realize that what you’re actually upset about is something unrelated to these comments or jokes. Try to avoid taking out your frustrations on people who don’t deserve it.

Usually, your opinions are firm and unwavering. Once you make your mind up about something, it takes a lot to make you change it. Today, though, you might find your convictions escape you; you’ll have a hard time figuring out what you think or feel about anything. For now, the best course of action is to review the available information without pressuring yourself to come to a final decision. There’s no hurry to make up your mind, so don’t commit to anything if you’re not convinced yet.

You know that nothing good comes from comparing yourself to others — but today, you might do it anyway. When you doubt that you’re “good enough,” or when you worry your life is lacking in some way, you’ll start to wonder whether observing other people’s lives might set your mind at ease. But comparison won’t provide the clarity you want; it’ll only become an added stressor. Focus today on how you are feeling, not how you stack up to some imaginary set of external standards.

You might be tempted to blame yourself for everything right now — not just your own problems, but your friends’ problems, too. You might believe that if you’d only had better judgment in the past or been a little kinder, everyone around you would be happier now. But there’s a thin line between taking accountability for your mistakes and making everything about you. Check that your self-reproach doesn’t veer back into self-centeredness. It helps nobody when you apologize for things that aren’t your fault.

You might have the feeling lately that nobody understands you. Even the people who love you most don’t seem to get you, and that’s making you lonely. But make sure you’re not expecting others to read your mind. If you make them guess what’s going on in your head, a sense of disconnect is almost inevitable. If you want to be understood, make the effort to explain what’s on your mind. People will get where you’re coming from if you give them a real chance to connect.

Other people’s emotions are likely to affect yours more than usual today. If someone around you is cranky, you’ll quickly become irritable, too; if they’re looking forward to the future, you might feel equally optimistic. So if it’s possible to surround yourself with the kind of energy you want right now, it’ll make a big difference. And if you don’t have control over who you’re spending time with at the moment, simply leaving the room during heated interactions can help you restore your equilibrium.

You’ll likely have a hard time today if people express disagreements with you. Even when you know that their approval (or lack thereof) isn’t necessary for you to move forward, you’ll still crave it. Acknowledge that you want others to think well of you, but try not to let it impact the actual decisions you make. You’ll never please everyone, no matter how hard you try. Right now, prioritize living up to your own principles rather than impressing anyone else.

Most of the time, you can be relied upon to make smart decisions: You have good judgment and a clear sense of your own limits. But today, boredom could scramble your usually clear thinking. The more restless you are, the more likely you are to take foolish risks. Make a point of slowing down and thinking your options through right now. You won’t regret taking your time.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You might convince yourself today that your decision-making is purely practical — you know how to assess every situation through a clear, objective lens! In reality, your thought processes are probably shaped by emotion much more than you realize. This isn’t necessarily a problem — in fact, relying on intuition will likely lead to good decisions right now — as long as you’re aware of it. Don’t try to convince anyone else (or yourself) that your desires are the only “right” ones.

You expect your close relationships to be a source of comfort and emotional security. Life is already full of drama, and you don’t see why you should spend time with people who only create more of it. But today, even your strongest relationships might challenge that expectation. Your closest friends and family members might come across uncharacteristically critical and demanding right now. Don’t read too deeply into it: Every relationship goes through stressful periods, and chances are good that things will get back on track if you can be patient.

Indecisiveness might prevent you from accomplishing as much as you’d hoped today. You’re facing a long to-do list, but you can’t decide what to do first — and the longer you hesitate, the more likely you are to end up doing nothing at all. So stop trying to make the perfect move. If you can release your desire to do everything just right, and instead settle on being good enough, you’ll have a much easier time moving forward.

You might feel more spontaneous than usual right now. Don’t be surprised if you want to live in the moment rather than plan every minute of your day. But be aware that your desires could change from one moment to the next, and what might initially seem like a great idea could quickly lose its appeal. Spur-of-the-moment decisions can sometimes turn out to be the best ones — but leave yourself room to change your mind, just in case.
