items.title: What exile was like for the first people called ‘refugees’
items.description: One dark night in 1683, a 19-year-old girl from the small town of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, not far from Grenoble in southeastern France, approached the fire in the hearth of her family home. This was a time of high religious tension in France, and Blanche Ga
items.author: Nora Baker
paragraphs: One dark night in 1683, a 19-year-old girl from the small town of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, not far from Grenoble in southeastern France, approached the fire in the hearth of her family home. This was a time of high religious tension in France, and Blanche Gamond’s Protestant family had been forced to host soldiers in their house whose goal it was to intimidate them into converting to Catholicism. They were not alone in being subjected to this treatment, known as the dragonnades policy, which had been instigated by Louis XIV’s government two years earlier. Over the course of the Sun King’s reign, anti-Protestant measures continually increased. These included restrictions on when and how Protestants could hold funerals, and prohibitions against Protestant women working as midwives; conversions to the religion were also forbidden.

Gamond had heard of Antoine Chamier, a man in the nearby town of Montélimar, being broken on the wheel for his refusal to renounce his religious beliefs. She admired Chamier’s steadfastness, and wanted to prove to herself that she, too, could endure great suffering for her faith. In approaching the fire, her aim was to test herself, and to prove that she was strong enough to withstand the pain. But Gamond could not do this. ‘As soon as my fingers began to burn,’ she wrote (my translation), ‘I would immediately withdraw my hand.’ This was no casual test of strength, however, and Gamond was devastated by her inability to tolerate the heat.

Though many people today don’t associate exile with western Europeans, the experiences of French Protestants in the early modern period were often fraught with uncertainty and suffering. They departed their homeland in search of security and stability elsewhere, and they often established large communities in the lands in which they settled, with churches catering to their diaspora. When leaving France, they often brought skills in fields such as silk-weaving or watchmaking with them, resulting in what some commentators have labelled as a ‘brain drain’ in their home kingdom.

So, while it may be difficult for those of us who have grown up in stable or safe countries without persecution, and who are part of a majority, to comprehend Gamond’s conviction and the danger with which it was associated, these were very common experiences for many people in history. Today, as well as in the past, humans tend to want to see ourselves as part of something bigger than us, a grand cause, something that will survive us, a religion or a nation or a cause – and many have sacrificed for the values or ideals they believe it represents.

As for how it occurred to Gamond to briefly burn her hand, it seems likely that she was inspired by the story of Thomas Bilney, a 16th-century Englishman who tested himself in much the same way the night before he was to be burnt at the stake. Though Bilney also initially instinctively retracted his hand when the flame tickled his fingers, the second time he attempted this feat, he succeeded in withstanding the heat for a couple of seconds. Bilney’s story featured in a popular martyrology (a collection of martyr stories) owned by many Protestant families in 17th-century France. The tales of those who remained firm in their faith against all odds – even in the face of torture or death – were designed to be inspiring, to provide comfort to readers through examples of those who had calmly met their end.

But these stories could also be sources of pressure, as we can see in Gamond’s account. Frustrated that she couldn’t properly emulate the martyrs of old, she frequently pleaded with God to make her better, more pious, less attached to the world and to herself: ‘My God, make it so that I love neither the world, nor the things in it, give me the grace … to renounce myself.’ This desire to be detached from worldly concerns was a common theme in medieval and early modern Christianity, and even in the earlier traditions of classical antiquity: it is often known as contemptus mundi, or ‘contempt for the world’. In making these appeals to God, Gamond was drawing on language that she had likely picked up from pastors and religious services, employing it in order to try to cope with a period of stress and uncertainty.

In 1685, rights previously granted to French Protestants – or Huguenots, as they were also known – were stripped back through the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, an event often simply called the Revocation. Persecution of this group grew so intense that many sought to leave their homeland. Historians estimate that around 200,000 Huguenots left France in the wake of the oppression. This exodus became known as the Refuge, and it was, in fact, as a result of this upheaval that the word ‘refugee’ entered the English language – from the French ‘réfugié’.

Of course, there was nothing new in history about populations being uprooted – the Huguenots, themselves, took inspiration from the story of the Babylonian exile of the Jews in the Bible. And, indeed, previous generations of French Protestants had also settled far from France, in bids to escape the Wars of Religion (1562-98). But the post-Revocation Huguenots were perhaps among the first groups of people to seek shelter in foreign climes after the Thirty Years’ War (1618-48) had helped plant the seeds for the development of the modern nation-state. The idea that a state might be intrinsically associated with a particular ethnic group living within its borders would remain in flux for many years before further solidifying amid the Romantic nationalism of the 19th century – however, the 1648 Peace of Westphalia was among the factors that helped lay the groundwork for this idea to take hold, through its assertion of the principle of territorial sovereignty.
Gamond sought to steel herself against physical pain, whereas Cabrit removed himself from harm’s way

Huguenots have furthermore been labelled ‘modern’ refugees by scholars such as John Hintermaier due to their propensity to appeal to the altruistic sentiments and economic concerns of those in their host nations, rather than seeking support based on religious affinity alone. The achievements of many Huguenots and their descendants in the textile industries and trade networks of their host nations have led to the community garnering praise as an example of successful integration. However, the path to a stable and secure future in a new land did not always run smooth. Another Huguenot, the minister Jacques Cabrit, initially moved to London, but wrote that people there ‘recognised from our mannerisms and our clothes that we were French, and we were subject to verbal and sometimes physical abuse’ (my translation).

Cabrit and his friends were, nonetheless, prepared to settle in England, until they heard rumours that King James II was planning to persecute Protestants in much the same way as Louis XIV had done in France. The threat of such an attack against their religion proved too much to bear, and on 1 March 1688, just a few months before the English king was overthrown, Cabrit set off again, eventually settling in Prussia. It may seem, then, that religious matters were more central to Cabrit’s identity than national affiliation, if it was those rumours that proved to be the last straw for him rather than actual instances of xenophobia.

But we can reflect on the role that fear can play in already tense environments. Cabrit, by leaving England, and Gamond, by trying to burn herself, both acted in the ways they felt would best protect them, in the face of an uncertain future. In this context, Gamond sought to steel herself against physical pain, whereas Cabrit removed himself from harm’s way.

Cabrit’s account also provides us with a reflection on how cultural differences can affect the expression of emotions. While employed as a French tutor in the home of an aged professor in Frankfurt an der Oder in Prussia, Cabrit witnessed the death of the elderly man. He was later stunned by the widow’s calm response to the news of her husband’s death:

She listened to me with the greatest sangfroid in the world, which surprised me immensely, as I expected her sobs to make the air shake, as that is what women in the Languedoc do in such circumstances.

Though Cabrit was taken aback by this reaction, he did write that he admired the woman’s ‘stoicism’. This was just one of the clashes between cultural expectations and reality that he was to experience while adapting to life in German-speaking lands. We know that different cultural traditions value emotions, and their expression, differently, as scholars such as Barbara H Rosenwein have shown. It would appear that, in the Languedoc context – at least, according to Cabrit – women were expected to be highly vocal, and even clamorous, in the expression of their grief. It may have been that these raw evocations of pain were viewed as more authentic, signs of a close bond with the deceased. The Frankfurt an der Oder widow’s response, on the other hand, suggests a cultural context where measured reactions were valued, even amid difficult circumstances.

Eventually, Cabrit succeeded in settling down and living a relatively normal life in Cottbus, near Potsdam, in what is now eastern Germany. The same cannot be said for Gamond, who died in Zurich aged just 53. Imprisoned following an initial attempt to escape from France, she eventually managed to cross the border into Switzerland in 1688. Records show that she and her father requested alms in order to survive, and it is thought that the tragic and extremely pious image she painted of herself in her memoir was played up so as to attract sympathy and, thus, monetary assistance. And yet, there is also raw emotion to be seen in her words. While describing a deeply painful operation on her leg, Gamond wrote that she could not bring herself to give further detail: ‘[My quill] falls from my hand, and this sad memory makes me shed so many tears that I could [not] continue anymore [to endure] the horrible pains that I felt.’ The page on which these words are written in the manuscript is blotchy, in a way that might lead us to speculate over the presence of centuries-old tear stains. Whether or not tears are indeed the cause of the smeared writing cannot be determined, but one thing is certain: even after establishing oneself in exile, past pains and anxieties could continue to echo in early modern refugee lives.

While Cabrit and Gamond each ultimately led very different lives, both of their experiences were profoundly shaped by the persecution that their community faced. Both sought to carve out spaces for themselves within their religious and social community following their departure from their homeland, Gamond through writing and circulating an autobiographical account of her experiences, Cabrit mostly through pastoral work. Both leaned heavily on their networks for support, contacting family members, friends of friends and distant relatives in times of need. This experience of reaching out to others was shared by many other members of the Huguenot diaspora, and we can see from their stories that it was often thanks to being able to build on existing connections that refugees were able to thrive in new lands – though this was not always easy or even possible, as Gamond’s challenging experience in the Swiss cantons shows. While popular narratives about Huguenot trajectories often focus on the community’s economic and social success following their settling in new lands, we should not overlook the pain associated with being uprooted from one’s home that was experienced by many of these refugees. What they managed to achieve in spite of these difficulties is a testament to their resilience.

items.title: The streets of Karachi scared me less than home did
items.description: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watch
items.author: Sadia Khatri
paragraphs: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watched me drive away – to another part of the city, where my childhood best friend Aesha and I had found an apartment for ourselves.

Salute to the girls who do this here, in Karachi: live outside of blood, family, marriage or whatever patriarchal bargain most women in my city use to seek their freedom. Anam was the first girl I saw who did this – who did not transfer, like property, from her father’s house to a husband’s, but instead lived with two others in this sprawling city of at least 20 million, but very likely more, home to every ethnic and religious group in Pakistan. Its indigenous communities were historically fisherfolk, pastoralists, and Sindhi and Baloch people, but modern Karachi was founded and funded by Sindhi Hindus and Parsis and Gujaratis. Post-partition, it became home to Muhajirs, who migrated from India, as well as millions of Pashtuns from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan. In the city’s mix are also migrants from Punjab and Balochistan, Burma and Bangladesh. Every kind of population has laid its stake to the city, so why not single women?

We might be one of the tiniest populations in Karachi’s history to fight for our right to the city. A friend from Bangalore visited and, after we’d walked the old streets of Kharadar and the shiny roads of Clifton, she said, baffled: ‘And I thought we in India had few women on the streets.’ Where were the akeli women? She meant unaccompanied women – not the rich-girl variety who outsource their lives to drivers and guards who shuttle them around the city in protective containers, but middle-class girls like us.

‘My family lives in another city,’ I’d told my landlord, nervously avoiding his gaze. In Karachi, respectable girls did this only under the pretext of majboori – some justifiable excuse grounded in necessity, like working or studying away from home. Otherwise, only sex workers and trans women typically broke away from their families to live an unconventional life, one far more difficult than mine. Turned out he hardly cared. The apartment was cheap and, given the neighbourhood it was in – Badar Commercial, an unruly stretch in an otherwise upscale residential part of town, where the lane was not well kept and the building did not have a lock – he wasn’t looking for respectability points. Most others, landlords and landladies alike, had looked at me and said: ‘Families only.’ They did not want to hand over their apartment to two girls, all akeli, all alone, by themselves. Potential blemishes. Danger.

When we moved into the building at Badar, we anticipated all kinds of eyes. The apartment opposite ours was a lawyer’s office, or posed as one. Upstairs lived a gruff old uncle, a retired policeman who fought with everyone and threatened to call the cops after arguments. All day, he slept with the rooftop keys, effectively controlling access to the building’s water tanks.

The two apartments below us belonged to a family that had bought both units and broken down the middle wall. There were lots of women and children and a little dog. The ‘man of the house’ was a 21-year-old boy, evidently a drug addict who was usually found by the entrance staircase, getting high and holding a gun. His 20-year-old wife, a decade younger than us, was friendly. She asked us how we managed, all akelay. Again that word. We got into the habit of saying: ‘Yes, God knows how we manage, all akelay, all saath saath.’ Alone-together.
Since she’d been over a few times, we told her that the gun made us feel queasy. Could her husband please put it away? Very calmly, she replied: ‘He has never pointed it at you, has he?’
The neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely

Our balcony faced the balcony of the building opposite ours. The grilles were close enough to talk to the person on the other side. We knew these neighbours only at this elevation: it was the COVID-19 pandemic era, so everyone was stuck inside. WhatsApp numbers were exchanged; regretted it instantly. Uncle A had an on-again, off-again relationship with his wife, which meant he sometimes rang me up in the middle of the night, sobbing. Aunty B, wonderful to chat with during the day, was obsessed with jinns at night. She loved sending us links to YouTube videos where such supernatural beings were summoned into a courtroom, and she wanted to know if we, too, had ever seen one.

Badar Commercial – with its cast of characters all breaking the codes of Pakistani respectability in some way – got used to us faster than we got used to it. But the neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely. We sometimes dressed respectably – shalwar kameez and saris – whereas other times I walked around Badar in knee-length shorts and tank tops. We spoke English but also Urdu, Kutchi and Memoni; one of us was a teacher and the other a psychologist, but was that really all we did? And were we really Muslim? Often, at home, or grocery shopping, or having chai at the streetside dhaba, or tea-shop, someone would ask: Hindu? Christian? Foreign?

This inability to categorise us reached its pinnacle after a Qawwali night at our apartment – a Sufi music performance. A neighbour who had invited himself midway through the performance after hearing it from his window later asked us with utter confusion: ‘Are you Sunni or Shia?’
We said: ‘It’s hard to explain…’
He leaned in uncomfortably close and whispered: ‘You are the Illuminati?’

Some men assumed we were sex workers and showed up at our door. This might have been my father’s deepest fear: if my family discovered I lived akelay, they’d think me a loose woman, and him a dishonourable man who could not keep his property in line. My extended family continued to believe I still lived with my parents. If an uncle visited, he was told I was out of town. ‘Sadia goes to Hyderabad a lot,’ my relatives noted.

Our time in that apartment was spent, really, undoing our lives. Aesha and I came from families where a room of your own was a luxury only richer relatives afforded their children. Until I was 16, I shared a room with my parents and four siblings; after that, there were two rooms, one for my parents and one for us. Now, Aesha and I each had a room, with a door we could close behind us and let nothing in for a while. At first, I did not know what to do with the emptiness. Just me and my friend, and a feeling of being untethered, unpropertied. We wanted others to feel it too, so our home was always filled with friends and women and anyone who needed a place to crash.

We set up the space with what little we had. Our mothers donated precious items from their kitchens. (When she came over, I introduced ammi to the neighbourhood women – trying to prove, I think, that it was possible to not live a double life, to have both my freedom and my mother by my side.) Our friends gave us our first furniture: a floor rug, a cupboard. We raised and killed too many plants, and washed our clothes by hand or sent them home when the water was out again. We learned to interact with the city in ways we never had before: comparing the vegetable vendors’ rates and learning who had been taking advantage of us, becoming experts at shortcuts on foot, especially during the rain, and knowing where to find rickshaws at 6 pm versus 9 pm.
For the first time, I prayed under the open sky while the city raged around me

Karachi is a logistical nightmare for anyone who lives here – and none of its systems are designed to include women in their public unfolding. Every bank vendor and dhaba server and home electrician is a man. This was another city that opened up to us: of everyday upkeep and haggling and bills. In this city, we learned to be less afraid of the men we had been taught to be suspicious of our whole lives: the electrician boys, the plumber uncles, the carpenter brothers. While any kind of man can turn uncomfortably friendly at a moment’s notice, there’s a way both patriarchy and capitalism benefit by insisting that the working-class man is the biggest threat to a woman’s safety. Under this ruse, the ‘good’ men in my life can surveil and control my movements, while a whole world of centrally airconditioned, securitised and gatekept enterprises can capitalise on this idea of keeping out the riff-raff.

In Badar Commercial, this lie came further undone. Plumber #1 was younger than us, fascinated by our women-only lives, and before leaving would help himself to swigs of whatever alcohol we had left over. Electrician uncle was popular among all the single girlies and slowly taught us how to drill the walls and reinstall ceiling fans. Plumber #2 was of a more conservative bent, refusing to look us straight in the eye but kindly and non-patronisingly telling us we had burned, nay destroyed, our new water heater.

At the roadside dhabas where I read books and people-watched, I often met men not from my world. M J, a rickshaw-wallah, learned my daily routines and routes, and knew exactly which friend lived where, and where I went and what I bought. I, in turn, learned about his life, one among thousands of Pashtuns who migrate from the northwest to seek a better life here. He had two jobs, sent money home to a family he maybe saw once a year, yet made less than our monthly rent. M J was beloved by everyone he met, punctual to a fault, and smoked two packs a day. He said: ‘Sadi, if you weren’t a girl, I’d invite you to Ludo nights with the boys.’ We went everywhere in his grand rickshaw that he’d decorated himself, every inch of it shiny and tasselled. I loved sitting amid all those colours. For the first time, with him, I prayed under the open sky in Karachi, touched the grass with my forehead while the city raged around me. We were by the sea; he rolled out his janamaz to pray and offered that yes, I could do it too if I wanted, why not?

I think we got away with living in that apartment because it was in a seedy neighbourhood where everyone knew everyone’s shit but collectively agreed not to meddle unless things got really out of hand. In close quarters, noise is not contained. Everyone knew when Uncle A and his wife were fighting, or whose side Aunty B took when her sons clashed over the eaten biryani. And when the retired officer upstairs sent cops after the drug-boy on the first floor, the whole neighbourhood knew, because men with guns were banging on our doors at 3 am.

There were conflicting accounts. One neighbour said the boy downstairs sold ice, others said he consumed it, yes, but did not sell. Everyone agreed he was high out of his mind when, middle of the day, in our tiny alley, he pointed his gun to the third floor where the police uncle lived and fired four times.
It was difficult to get to sleep; our bodies now jumped at the slightest noise
‘Motherfucker, wait,’ said the shaking retired cop from his balcony. ‘Motherfucker, you just wait, I’m gon get you fucked up.’
All this was relayed to me via WhatsApp by my best friend, who was watching it unfold. ‘Maybe don’t come home tonight,’ she texted me.

By that night, the boy had fled the scene, and police uncle was having it out in the alley with the boy’s wife. A chair was hurled, unclear who hurled it upon whom, and a few nights later, men with guns were at our door. When the story was pieced together over the following days, it was already too late: fear had lodged itself in our bodies; we now jumped at the slightest noise.
‘No one will enter your house just like that,’ the grocery store uncle said.
‘But if they come back…?’ I asked him.
‘That ice-boy needs to go,’ he said. ‘If nowhere else then to rehab.’
‘But his wife is pregnant,’ I said, and realised how deep I was in Badar Commercial gossip and lore.

Something I learned living alone-together in Badar Commercial, and that I want younger women to know, is that we are actually never guaranteed safety. Therefore, one way to collect the guts and energy to move out of your parents’ home and make a life alone in this city is to realise that the question is not whether we are safe but what the cost is, the violent cost, of trying to live a full life in this city and world.

At Badar, the cost for me was estrangement from my relatives, especially my aunts whom I loved but who knew nothing about my feminist life anymore. The other cost was a new edginess – always alert for the 3 am bang on the door. Then there were the men who tailed me while I cycled, who lurked outside our building, the officer who showed up with my full name at my door, who wanted me to know he knew I lived here.

Still, none of the fear these men instilled in us came close to the body-wreckage from the violence and betrayal we had known inside our own homes. Under our family’s so-called protection, we were surveilled and shamed in the same breath. Men, assigned as our guardians and teachers, hurt us. In my case, it was my cousin and my music teacher. The worst part was having to continue showing them respect. That kind of lying festers inside the body, when everyone knows that danger for women is two feet away, at home. It’s a trap to think we have ever overcome danger. As a result, I have spent my life watching men’s gazes for that livewire glint. The ones on the street I can usually recognise and quickly counter. The home gaze is tricker because I cannot anticipate when and where it might suddenly appear.

As the streets got to know me and I them, some knots in my body loosened, knots that had to do with the entanglement of class and gender politics, of who is portrayed as a threat versus where the actual danger lies. Other un-knottings had to do with feeling free in practice, not just theory, cycling around Badar in shorts and shalwar kameez.
I told my aunts the truth about my life. What was the point of all this public and street freedom if nothing changed in the hardest of spaces: at home?

As the knots loosened, other cities opened within us. A parent’s death; a friend’s secret abortion; walking away from a marriage; walking towards ourselves. We learned that it is possible to live within four walls that hold our grief, not just cause it – that can take it all, and more and more and more. I’d spent my 20s chasing freedom in the streets because I’d never imagined an inner space – the apartment, my room, but really, a space within – that could feel like home, where you don’t feel trapped or sealed or estranged. This indoor city opens up what you can do with your body in the cities outside, so that one day, in that same Badar Commercial, I chased a man away with a chappal because he was following me. I chased him away, wielding that slipper with a confidence that came from having lived in Badar for three years now. How familiar the streets felt; how I knew that they would not betray me.
Another time, however, I ran home breathless and called M J for help, worried I had been followed home. Limits of bravery differ day by day.
‘I’m coming to pick you up,’ he said. ‘Let’s get you some air by the sea.’

items.title: The streets of Karachi scared me less than home did
items.description: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watch
items.author: Sadia Khatri
paragraphs: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watched me drive away – to another part of the city, where my childhood best friend Aesha and I had found an apartment for ourselves.

Salute to the girls who do this here, in Karachi: live outside of blood, family, marriage or whatever patriarchal bargain most women in my city use to seek their freedom. Anam was the first girl I saw who did this – who did not transfer, like property, from her father’s house to a husband’s, but instead lived with two others in this sprawling city of at least 20 million, but very likely more, home to every ethnic and religious group in Pakistan. Its indigenous communities were historically fisherfolk, pastoralists, and Sindhi and Baloch people, but modern Karachi was founded and funded by Sindhi Hindus and Parsis and Gujaratis. Post-partition, it became home to Muhajirs, who migrated from India, as well as millions of Pashtuns from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan. In the city’s mix are also migrants from Punjab and Balochistan, Burma and Bangladesh. Every kind of population has laid its stake to the city, so why not single women?

We might be one of the tiniest populations in Karachi’s history to fight for our right to the city. A friend from Bangalore visited and, after we’d walked the old streets of Kharadar and the shiny roads of Clifton, she said, baffled: ‘And I thought we in India had few women on the streets.’ Where were the akeli women? She meant unaccompanied women – not the rich-girl variety who outsource their lives to drivers and guards who shuttle them around the city in protective containers, but middle-class girls like us.

‘My family lives in another city,’ I’d told my landlord, nervously avoiding his gaze. In Karachi, respectable girls did this only under the pretext of majboori – some justifiable excuse grounded in necessity, like working or studying away from home. Otherwise, only sex workers and trans women typically broke away from their families to live an unconventional life, one far more difficult than mine. Turned out he hardly cared. The apartment was cheap and, given the neighbourhood it was in – Badar Commercial, an unruly stretch in an otherwise upscale residential part of town, where the lane was not well kept and the building did not have a lock – he wasn’t looking for respectability points. Most others, landlords and landladies alike, had looked at me and said: ‘Families only.’ They did not want to hand over their apartment to two girls, all akeli, all alone, by themselves. Potential blemishes. Danger.

When we moved into the building at Badar, we anticipated all kinds of eyes. The apartment opposite ours was a lawyer’s office, or posed as one. Upstairs lived a gruff old uncle, a retired policeman who fought with everyone and threatened to call the cops after arguments. All day, he slept with the rooftop keys, effectively controlling access to the building’s water tanks.

The two apartments below us belonged to a family that had bought both units and broken down the middle wall. There were lots of women and children and a little dog. The ‘man of the house’ was a 21-year-old boy, evidently a drug addict who was usually found by the entrance staircase, getting high and holding a gun. His 20-year-old wife, a decade younger than us, was friendly. She asked us how we managed, all akelay. Again that word. We got into the habit of saying: ‘Yes, God knows how we manage, all akelay, all saath saath.’ Alone-together.
Since she’d been over a few times, we told her that the gun made us feel queasy. Could her husband please put it away? Very calmly, she replied: ‘He has never pointed it at you, has he?’
The neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely

Our balcony faced the balcony of the building opposite ours. The grilles were close enough to talk to the person on the other side. We knew these neighbours only at this elevation: it was the COVID-19 pandemic era, so everyone was stuck inside. WhatsApp numbers were exchanged; regretted it instantly. Uncle A had an on-again, off-again relationship with his wife, which meant he sometimes rang me up in the middle of the night, sobbing. Aunty B, wonderful to chat with during the day, was obsessed with jinns at night. She loved sending us links to YouTube videos where such supernatural beings were summoned into a courtroom, and she wanted to know if we, too, had ever seen one.

Badar Commercial – with its cast of characters all breaking the codes of Pakistani respectability in some way – got used to us faster than we got used to it. But the neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely. We sometimes dressed respectably – shalwar kameez and saris – whereas other times I walked around Badar in knee-length shorts and tank tops. We spoke English but also Urdu, Kutchi and Memoni; one of us was a teacher and the other a psychologist, but was that really all we did? And were we really Muslim? Often, at home, or grocery shopping, or having chai at the streetside dhaba, or tea-shop, someone would ask: Hindu? Christian? Foreign?

This inability to categorise us reached its pinnacle after a Qawwali night at our apartment – a Sufi music performance. A neighbour who had invited himself midway through the performance after hearing it from his window later asked us with utter confusion: ‘Are you Sunni or Shia?’
We said: ‘It’s hard to explain…’
He leaned in uncomfortably close and whispered: ‘You are the Illuminati?’

Some men assumed we were sex workers and showed up at our door. This might have been my father’s deepest fear: if my family discovered I lived akelay, they’d think me a loose woman, and him a dishonourable man who could not keep his property in line. My extended family continued to believe I still lived with my parents. If an uncle visited, he was told I was out of town. ‘Sadia goes to Hyderabad a lot,’ my relatives noted.

Our time in that apartment was spent, really, undoing our lives. Aesha and I came from families where a room of your own was a luxury only richer relatives afforded their children. Until I was 16, I shared a room with my parents and four siblings; after that, there were two rooms, one for my parents and one for us. Now, Aesha and I each had a room, with a door we could close behind us and let nothing in for a while. At first, I did not know what to do with the emptiness. Just me and my friend, and a feeling of being untethered, unpropertied. We wanted others to feel it too, so our home was always filled with friends and women and anyone who needed a place to crash.

We set up the space with what little we had. Our mothers donated precious items from their kitchens. (When she came over, I introduced ammi to the neighbourhood women – trying to prove, I think, that it was possible to not live a double life, to have both my freedom and my mother by my side.) Our friends gave us our first furniture: a floor rug, a cupboard. We raised and killed too many plants, and washed our clothes by hand or sent them home when the water was out again. We learned to interact with the city in ways we never had before: comparing the vegetable vendors’ rates and learning who had been taking advantage of us, becoming experts at shortcuts on foot, especially during the rain, and knowing where to find rickshaws at 6 pm versus 9 pm.
For the first time, I prayed under the open sky while the city raged around me

Karachi is a logistical nightmare for anyone who lives here – and none of its systems are designed to include women in their public unfolding. Every bank vendor and dhaba server and home electrician is a man. This was another city that opened up to us: of everyday upkeep and haggling and bills. In this city, we learned to be less afraid of the men we had been taught to be suspicious of our whole lives: the electrician boys, the plumber uncles, the carpenter brothers. While any kind of man can turn uncomfortably friendly at a moment’s notice, there’s a way both patriarchy and capitalism benefit by insisting that the working-class man is the biggest threat to a woman’s safety. Under this ruse, the ‘good’ men in my life can surveil and control my movements, while a whole world of centrally airconditioned, securitised and gatekept enterprises can capitalise on this idea of keeping out the riff-raff.

In Badar Commercial, this lie came further undone. Plumber #1 was younger than us, fascinated by our women-only lives, and before leaving would help himself to swigs of whatever alcohol we had left over. Electrician uncle was popular among all the single girlies and slowly taught us how to drill the walls and reinstall ceiling fans. Plumber #2 was of a more conservative bent, refusing to look us straight in the eye but kindly and non-patronisingly telling us we had burned, nay destroyed, our new water heater.

At the roadside dhabas where I read books and people-watched, I often met men not from my world. M J, a rickshaw-wallah, learned my daily routines and routes, and knew exactly which friend lived where, and where I went and what I bought. I, in turn, learned about his life, one among thousands of Pashtuns who migrate from the northwest to seek a better life here. He had two jobs, sent money home to a family he maybe saw once a year, yet made less than our monthly rent. M J was beloved by everyone he met, punctual to a fault, and smoked two packs a day. He said: ‘Sadi, if you weren’t a girl, I’d invite you to Ludo nights with the boys.’ We went everywhere in his grand rickshaw that he’d decorated himself, every inch of it shiny and tasselled. I loved sitting amid all those colours. For the first time, with him, I prayed under the open sky in Karachi, touched the grass with my forehead while the city raged around me. We were by the sea; he rolled out his janamaz to pray and offered that yes, I could do it too if I wanted, why not?

I think we got away with living in that apartment because it was in a seedy neighbourhood where everyone knew everyone’s shit but collectively agreed not to meddle unless things got really out of hand. In close quarters, noise is not contained. Everyone knew when Uncle A and his wife were fighting, or whose side Aunty B took when her sons clashed over the eaten biryani. And when the retired officer upstairs sent cops after the drug-boy on the first floor, the whole neighbourhood knew, because men with guns were banging on our doors at 3 am.

There were conflicting accounts. One neighbour said the boy downstairs sold ice, others said he consumed it, yes, but did not sell. Everyone agreed he was high out of his mind when, middle of the day, in our tiny alley, he pointed his gun to the third floor where the police uncle lived and fired four times.
It was difficult to get to sleep; our bodies now jumped at the slightest noise
‘Motherfucker, wait,’ said the shaking retired cop from his balcony. ‘Motherfucker, you just wait, I’m gon get you fucked up.’
All this was relayed to me via WhatsApp by my best friend, who was watching it unfold. ‘Maybe don’t come home tonight,’ she texted me.

By that night, the boy had fled the scene, and police uncle was having it out in the alley with the boy’s wife. A chair was hurled, unclear who hurled it upon whom, and a few nights later, men with guns were at our door. When the story was pieced together over the following days, it was already too late: fear had lodged itself in our bodies; we now jumped at the slightest noise.
‘No one will enter your house just like that,’ the grocery store uncle said.
‘But if they come back…?’ I asked him.
‘That ice-boy needs to go,’ he said. ‘If nowhere else then to rehab.’
‘But his wife is pregnant,’ I said, and realised how deep I was in Badar Commercial gossip and lore.

Something I learned living alone-together in Badar Commercial, and that I want younger women to know, is that we are actually never guaranteed safety. Therefore, one way to collect the guts and energy to move out of your parents’ home and make a life alone in this city is to realise that the question is not whether we are safe but what the cost is, the violent cost, of trying to live a full life in this city and world.

At Badar, the cost for me was estrangement from my relatives, especially my aunts whom I loved but who knew nothing about my feminist life anymore. items.title: Feeling at home in a new country makes you a stranger in the old
items.description: The morning was warm when I left home. Under the bluest of skies, I was driven to Lisbon’s airport, where I bid my parents farewell. It was a departure that I imagined as a pause in our ongoing conversation rather than its reconfiguration. Hours later, as I st
items.author: Iuri Portalegre
paragraphs: The morning was warm when I left home. Under the bluest of skies, I was driven to Lisbon’s airport, where I bid my parents farewell. It was a departure that I imagined as a pause in our ongoing conversation rather than its reconfiguration. Hours later, as I stepped out of what was then Berlin’s Tegel airport, the first thing that struck me was the cold wind shallowing my breath. I had to go back inside and add layers I hadn’t imagined needing so soon. I relive that day often.

That day I crossed the city three times. I almost strayed on my way to the only place I knew: the university in Dahlem, where I would start my five-month Erasmus semester (an EU student-exchange programme). Waiting for the underground, I was taken by a language school advertisement at Samariterstraße, which asked: ‘Tired of speaking silly German?’ – a provocation that would imprint itself on me for years. Enthralled, I passed through streets that seemed unreal and insubstantial, as if venturing through a sea of meanings that meant nothing to me yet. I obsess over that day often.

I had read the Berlin sociologist Georg Simmel’s reflections about how the metropolis affects its dwellers, creating a certain ‘indifference toward the distinctions between things.’ This is a kind of protective numbness, an emotional flatness of the overstimulated urban denizen. More than a century ago, in this same city, he had named such numbness ‘the blasé’.

If the blasé, however, is overstimulated by familiarity, I was overstimulated by novelty. The novelty of a perceptual greyness. For the blasé, everything has been felt too often. For me, nothing had been felt at all. It wasn’t that I had become numb to distinctions between things; it was that I couldn’t perceive any distinctions at all. Meaning had not yet sedimented, no attachments had been formed. The cobbles would need to be well-trodden before they would tell me their stories. So, in time, I too would become indifferent.
How then do you compose meaning in a place that seems to refuse it? How do you become blasé in the place of arrival? And what about that place once called home?

In bars, waving my glass around, I would speak of these topics. I wanted to hear stories I hadn’t heard before. What about the others, my fellow travellers, who settled for unsettledness? I sought willing storytellers, other Portuguese migrants residing in Berlin. Across 2024 and 2025, I sat in cafés, kitchens, parks and bars where winding conversations returned textures of belonging. I asked few direct questions, in the hope that stories would find themselves.

I think of a moment from an interview with a girl who told me how, on one of her visits back to Portugal, her father, his eyes bright with welcome, asked if she was glad to once again sleep in her own childhood bed. She stuttered. One’s bed is usually at home. She understood the unsaid, the premise hidden behind her father’s loving eyes. And yet, when she thought about the bed she would like to sink into after a long trip, it was not that childhood bed she thought of. Instead, a riving sense of home was her answer.
Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere

This misalignment between parent and child, between what home means to those who stayed and what it means to those who left, is felt but seldom acknowledged. Maybe the people who love us most are often the least equipped to see what departure has done. Seeing it would mean accepting that we are no longer fully theirs, nor they fully ours. Home might be somewhere else now; it seems kinder simply not to point it out.

Home is not simply a matter of being in a place; it requires an entire world to be built, embodied, maintained. It is a peculiar way the body attunes itself to what’s at hand. Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere. It requires time and closeness to endow your world with meaning.

Somewhere in Berlin, there is a daughter with a bed she seldom thinks about. She notices it only from afar. Such is the quieter thing beneath Simmel’s numbness. The blasé’s indifference is not the absence of meaning, but its sediment. You grow numb to what you have thoroughly absorbed. To feel at home somewhere is to have earned the right to stop noticing it. This, perhaps, is how meaning is composed in a place that first refuses it. The blasé, then, might not be the opposite of belonging, but its symptom.

The first days can be the hardest. Grey skies, cutting cold. The weather appears as more than meteorology; it registers as a reminder that you are from elsewhere, that here even the sun seems to remind you of your strangeness. You look around, and others seem unaffected. ‘What am I doing here?’ becomes a refrain.

Unlike the cutting wind, there are changes that arrive gently, rehearsed before the greater drama. An exchange programme, perhaps, or a temporary job posting. Through promises of an escape from routine, departure seems a suspension rather than the story itself. You have institutional scaffolding and, most importantly, an end date. There will be a return, you tell yourself. But departure also begins the subtle labour of reconfiguration. The realisation that the first day of the next five months might have been the first day of the rest of your life.

Berlin had gifted Simmel more than the blasé. In the same streets I now inhabit, he observed another figure. The stranger occupies a more unsettling position. They are not simply the other, the foreigner looking in, but someone who is neither entirely ‘them’ nor entirely ‘us’. Someone familiar to the very spaces that make for their strangeness. To be a stranger is to be in medias res, obliged to feel at ease in a story that has already started.

Both of Simmel’s figures share something. They make for a dual condition. The unbothered blasé and the unsettled stranger are entangled in their need for familiarity. The blasé can only grow numb to what they have already absorbed. The stranger can only be strange to places they have come to know.
What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for

What I didn’t understand then was that becoming a stranger is not a moment, but a process. What starts as a temporary detour ends up reorienting an entire cartography of possibilities. The body that returns, even from these limited departures, is not the same one that left. A slow unfolding arises the instant you step away from familiar rhythms. The migrant will not tread out of the airport a stranger; they become one, grain by grain, through the accumulated weight of the everyday’s pulse. That strangeness, however, is not confined to the new. It finds its way back, even to that place once called home.

Departure transforms perception itself. It means not merely learning new rules, but feeling differently, altering what appears meaningful, close or distant. This altered perception doesn’t overlay the old. It retroactively changes how the once-familiar appears. Whatever introduces strangeness here will do the same there. Simmel’s own last years were spent away from Berlin. His writings on the stranger predate that departure. I wonder what he would have added had he returned.

Returning ‘home’ for a visit is walking ghostly paths. Not wholly yours, just familiar. ‘Every time I go back,’ someone told me, ‘the whole process feels like small bouts of grief.’ You will tread old, acquainted streets as a testimony of change. Once the initial commotion eases, once routine reasserts itself, there comes a feeling that it is time to leave again. The feeling settles in that home is not fully there anymore. And yet it will always be. Grieving for a loss that can only be felt, never quite named. Stranger in the place of departure than in the place of arrival.

The stranger has often been evoked in the third person; rarely is the writer included in this strangeness. And rarely does the figure account for what happens upon return. But the stranger must have left somewhere. Strangeness then is not directional; it is recursive. It folds back upon itself. It makes us exiles from a former self. What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for. Home is not something to simply return to. Such is a peculiar arithmetic of departure.

On one of those grey, wintry days that Berlin so generously offers, sitting in someone’s kitchen, I heard the remark: ‘I used to think a lot about what I could gain here, and I’ve gained, I’d say, but I hadn’t realised so much what I could lose, you know?’ These words brought up something in me. In that kitchen, I thought of how, with time, something had also shifted in me. A form of change that didn’t announce itself, that went years unnoticed, yet continuously accruing. Not a crisis, but a silent drift. A misalignment between the stories I tell myself and the body I feel. I’ve come to call it unbecoming: a tension between a lived self and its socially recognisable articulation. It doesn’t demand resolution, yet becomes noticeable in moments of hesitation. A tacit detachment from who I expect myself to be. A reaching for words that don’t quite fit, yet no better alternative presents itself.

To unbecome is not to come undone. It is the accretive awareness that something no longer fits as before. It is to feel the weight of change before one has the words for it. A transformation so gradual that you notice it only when standing at the place of departure, only to find that it, like you, has become something stranger than you remembered. It is neither tragedy nor triumph.
The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot

Others recognised this feeling. A stranger might feel more like themselves in their new milieu than they ever did at ‘home’. They nevertheless miss a version of themselves who existed only there. This gap between what is felt and what can be said is itself a measure of change. And these are stories of change, after all.

The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot. How do you paint the picture of who you see yourself to be when the very feelings contest the words available? Loss is not the opposite of gain, but is somehow produced by it. Every new capacity for feeling at home in the place of arrival might also be a small chipping away at the ability to feel at home in the place of departure. What if, at a distance, becoming implies a quiet unbecoming? A strange resolution for a strange arithmetic.

The morning was warm when I left home. What was supposed to be a short five-month stay will soon be nine years. Yet the bluest of skies still has a hold on me. What in the moment felt like the most ordinary of days is now a refrain. I relive that day often. On returning, I’m left with questions that seem to resist resolution altogether. Maybe this too is recursive. How could it ever be anything but?
Yet the bluest of skies does not soothe the strangest of feelings.

items.title: Falsely claiming Indigenous identity is a grave form of theft
items.description: What does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the g
items.author: Dina Gilio-Whitaker
paragraphs: What does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the gap. But what if those stories are unverifiable? Or what if people take on ‘identities’ based on ‘knowledge’ that turns out not to be true, what then? How do they benefit from those narratives, whether true or not? Self-indigenisation based on self-identification describes people who claim to ‘be’ Indigenous, even when there is ample evidence that they have no Indigenous ancestry or lived experience as Indigenous people. It is a growing phenomenon in the United States and Canada as well as in other countries. Explaining why people pretend to be Indigenous when they aren’t is complicated, especially in light of the fact that the United Nations accepts self-identification as one criterion for indigeneity. However, in places where self-indigenisation has become egregious, it usually comes down to the fact that they perceive benefits, both material and psychological. The way it plays out varies from place to place, but there are commonalities across difference.

I am an Indigenous studies scholar in the US, and I study and wrote a book about self-indigenisation. I am an American Indian person, someone who comes from a long line of people who have been colonised. So mine is in part an insider perspective. As Native people, our experiences and cultures are unambiguous to us, if not always well known to others. They are well recorded in our families’ oral histories and usually in mountains of documentation, given that Indians are arguably the most documented ethnic group in the history of the US. Beginning with the earliest European settlers, missionaries and colonists kept track of the lives of Indigenous people for reasons including religious conversion, treaty negotiations, and census enumeration.

Anthropologists also, of course, study Indigenous people. The kinds of knowledge produced from external perspectives can vary widely from that which Indigenous people produce about themselves. Sometimes they conflict, but on occasion anthropologists’ research has helped tribes to recover lost knowledge. Both have their place. Anthropologists who study Indigenous cultural identity use the term ethnogenesis to describe how the identities of ethnic communities are formed or understood, and how they can change over time. Even Indigenous studies researchers recognise that, contrary to popular thought, Indigenous communities don’t remain static and unchanged over vast expanses of time. A popular tendency to misconceive of Indigenous people as gripped in terms of ‘authentic cultures’ doesn’t account for historical processes, including colonisation. History has imposed seismic changes on all Indigenous peoples, especially those who were in the way of foreign invasion and conquest. Expectations of cultural authenticity, then, can be a trap that doesn’t allow for peoples to experience history, to change with changing times.

In our modern world, there are of course many ways that cultures have evolved, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. This blending of cultures through intermarriage has resulted in a blurring of lines that has made it difficult to make distinctions based on social constructions of race and ethnicity. Around the world, the questions are about what Indigeneity is and who decides, and how those questions are answered will vary. Laws and custom vary by country, and people will also make their own determinations. That said, there is also the very real phenomenon of ethnic fraud, the wrongful claiming of Indigeneity by people without any demonstrable connection to a historical Indigenous community. In extreme examples, these claims are based on flagrant lying.

Some anthropologists have identified a phenomenon they refer to as neo-Indianism. It was first named by Jacques Galinier and Antoinette Molinié, whose book The Neo-Indians: A Religion for the Third Millennium (translated from French by Lucy Lyall Grant, 2013) examined the rise of a new kind of Indigenism in Latin America where New Age rituals were invented for tourist consumption at Teotihuacan in Mexico, Cuzco in Peru, and other archaeological sites. Misrepresented as traditional Indigenous religion, the general public was unaware of the ruse even as it became a global industry. Similarly, there are growing instances of fake Aboriginal individuals in Australia. The same is happening in Aotearoa (New Zealand) among the Māori. Nowhere, however, is the problem of ethnic fraud more prevalent than in the US and Canada, where it is called ‘pretendianism’.
The Boy Scouts of America blatantly relied on playing Indian to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people

Pretendianism is sometimes known by the more benign-sounding term cultural appropriation, which describes an array of offensive behaviours, such as sports mascots or events with inappropriate names and imagery, Halloween costumes, or the flagrant, unauthorised use of Native spirituality and culture, such as pipe ceremonies and sweat lodges, just to name a few. In Germany, for example, there is an entire subculture dedicated to the fetishisation of Native Americans, which perpetuates harmful, inaccurate stereotypes. If we understand Nativeness conceptualised as a spectrum, then cultural appropriation, ethnic fraud and pretendianism can be understood as existing on the extreme end, at which claims to Indigeneity are objectively illegitimate.

The noted American Indian studies scholar Philip J Deloria coined the term ‘playing Indian’ with his seminal 1998 book of the same name, in which he traced a history of Americans’ penchant for adopting the dress and cultures of Native Americans for a variety of reasons, ranging from frivolous to serious and even politically motivated. The Boy Scouts of America, an extremely popular hobbyist club for children that romanticised America’s frontier days, blatantly relied on playing Indian in the early 20th century to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people. More than a century earlier, the 1773 Boston Tea Party, in which colonists costumed in Indian garb, was clearly a political incident that contributed to the incitement of a revolution. Many, many examples can be given of how the cultures of Native Americans are claimed for reasons that most Native people find offensive.

Pretendianism takes cultural appropriation to the next level when it goes beyond playing Indian to becoming Indian. People ‘become’ Indian when they claim to ‘be’ Indian with no connection to a tribal community, or little to no evidence of Native ancestry. It often begins with an individual who at some point in life transforms their identity claims from white (but sometimes other races or ethnicities) into Native American, based on family folklore or nothing at all, hence ‘race-shifting’, the term used in Australia. When those people have children and raise them with that mythology, pretendianism becomes generational. Amid many legitimate tribes who wrongfully lack political recognition by the US federal government, there are also hundreds of fake tribes that sprouted up in the 20th century. The majority of them claim to be Cherokee, but there are numerous others claiming to be Chumash, Shawnee, and more.

The work of Darryl Leroux shows how in Canada pretendianism is most prevalent in the east with a proliferation of ‘Abenaki’ groups. Faux Abenakis are also a problem in the state of Vermont, with four groups whom the state politically recognises but who have virtually no documentation to back up their claims of Abenaki descent. There are also dubious Metis and Inuit groups in Canada.
Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry

There are many pretendians whose names or faces you may recognise, emerging predominantly from the film industry. Perhaps most familiar is Iron Eyes Cody, who became best known as the ‘Crying Indian’ in the 1971 anti-littering commercial. Cody was not just an American actor who played Native American characters, he was an imposter of the highest order with a detailed but wildly false story about being Cherokee and Cree, which he wrote about in a 1980 autobiography. In 1996, a New Orleans Times-Picayune article revealed his true identity as the son of Italian immigrants. Born Espera Oscar de Corti, his film career began in the 1920s and spanned eight decades, with more than 200 film credits.

In Canada, the early 20th-century ‘Apache’ conservationist Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry. Both Belaney and Cody married Native women, which doubtless helped legitimise their false claims. The same was true for James Young Deer, a silent-film actor, director and producer who rose to fame working for the Pathé Frères film company. Young Deer falsely claimed to be Winnebago/Ho-Chunk, and married the actual Ho-Chunk actress Lilian St Cyr.

More recent exposures include Sacheen Littlefeather and Buffy Sainte-Marie. Littlefeather is best known as the ‘Native American’ woman who rejected an Oscar on behalf of Marlon Brando at the 1973 Academy Awards, ironically in the name of accurate representation of Native people in the film industry. I knew her for a decade before she died in 2022, and I document this story in detail in my book. A year after Littlefeather’s death, a bombshell story broke in the Canadian media that the rock-and-roll legend Buffy Sainte-Marie – who had risen to fame for her fiery Indian activism upon which her music was based – had fabricated a story about being born to a Piapot Cree family, adopted out, and raised by a white family. The evidence was overwhelmingly convincing that none of it was true.

There are many other examples of high-profile people who long claimed Native identities but with thin or non-existent evidence. In Canada, they include the celebrated author Joseph Boyden, the influential children’s rights lawyer Mary Ellen Turpel-LaFond, the prominent academic Carrie Bourassa, and the filmmaker Michelle Latimer, to name a few. In some of these cases, awards and honorary doctorates have been rescinded after investigations revealed their façades. In the US, one example stands out for the attention it received in the political arena. In a dramatic misstep, the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren in 2018 released the results of a DNA test in response to a challenge by the president Donald Trump about her claims to being Cherokee. The test showed that there was ‘strong evidence’ that she had a Native American ancestor six to 10 generations in the past. The Cherokee Nation, however, responded as it had for many years about her claims, that it had no record of Warren’s kinship to them, and that DNA does not always translate to Native identity or tribal belonging.

Pretendianism tends to be concentrated in entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, environmentalism and, increasingly, social media. In the US, the high-profile academics Ward Churchill and Andrea Smith, who lost their tenured professorships, have sparked intense debates about what it means to claim Native American identities with little or no evidence of connection to a tribal heritage. In another high-profile case, the University of California Berkeley professor Elizabeth Hoover drew the ire of Native American scholars after confessing that she had been wrongly claiming to be Mohawk throughout her career.

It’s safe to say that, in the US and Canada, no other non-white ethnicity is as commonly falsely claimed as the Indigenous identity. Explaining why is not as simple, however, and researchers continue to offer compelling and sometimes provocative answers. There is no single explanation, and even in the cases of Canada and the US, both former British colonies and neighbouring North American countries, there are different factors and nuances. And there is likely more than one point of origin, historically and geographically, which would mean a potential variety of reasons for why people ‘became’ Indian at certain moments in time.

That said, there is an explanation that fits within the long history of the US’s colonialism and American Indian policy. This perspective can help us understand the motivations of those who fraudulently become ‘Indian’ and the social landscape of various eras. It shows us that, for example, pretendianism is not just a matter of personal and individual pathology – it’s systemic, which explains why it is continually perpetuated.

One point of pretendianism’s origin is in the late 19th century, when the US, under the ideology of manifest destiny, was engaged in the violent dispossession of Native Americans. With the 1887 passage of the General Allotment Act came the brutality of boarding schools, family separation, forced religious conversion, and the allotment of Native lands. The boarding schools were tools of forced assimilation. Land allotment accomplished these objectives by confining Native Americans to reservations, and encouraging a sedentary life of farming and industry.
Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it

All aspects of assimilation meant to move Native Americans into a cash-based capitalist economy. Boarding schools and land allotment forced a shift in their fundamental way of life, one in which everything is commodified, a concept previously unknown in Native life.

By the 1920s, federal policymakers had recognised that assimilation was a catastrophic failure because it produced widespread poverty and all manner of social ills in reservation communities. Farming and ranching often proved to be unviable on many reservations. But there was one way that Native people could earn a lucrative living in the late 19th century: performing in the Wild West shows that were sweeping the country. The majority of Native Americans who were recruited to Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show and others were veterans of the Plains Indian wars. For decades, the US had been fighting wars of aggression against Plains and other tribes in the west to force them on to reservations, thus freeing up vast tracts of land for settlers. Militarily defeated and succumbing to the US’s policy of Americanisation, many Indians went from prisoner-of-war camps to the Wild West shows. For the first time, Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it. This is the historical moment when Nativeness became a commodity, a way to make money from who one was, ethnically.

The US film industry has deep roots in the Wild West shows. Westerns were a prominent thematic genre of the early films, at a time when the US was contemplating the closing of the frontier. No longer a military threat, Native peoples became highly romanticised as Americans lamented the ‘vanishing Red Man’ in film. It was a natural progression, then, when the Show Indians became Movie Indians. It wasn’t long before people of other races and ethnicities began passing themselves off as Native Americans to obtain roles. The War Paint Club was the first Native American advocacy group, formed in 1926 to combat problems like fair representation and Native American roles for Native Americans in the industry.

In this way, Southern California became ground zero for the normalisation of Native ethnic fraud. Throughout the 20th century, other circumstances arose expanding opportunities to falsely claim Native American heritage based on no more than a family rumour, or simply the desire to profit financially. They included loose land-claims processes; changes in census rules that allowed for self-identification, and the reduction of the negative stigma of being Native American. In addition, a US government federal relocation programme in the 1950s led to urban Native American population centres where people with false claims could blend in as Native without community accountability; and a budding New Age industry that capitalised on all things Native American. California was the centre for all of these.

People are often mystified when they learn about the pretendian phenomenon; why would someone want to claim a heritage they weren’t born into? Identity commodification, coincident with the growth of Hollywood, gives us a conceptual tool to understand its historical particularity. Over the previous century, the opportunities for material gain associated with this ethnic fraud have only grown, and they show up in several specific spheres: film and entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, and environmental activism.

It’s not difficult to see why film and entertainment would attract opportunists looking to capitalise on an ethnically ambiguous appearance, paired with a convincing story. Iron Eyes Cody and Buffy Sainte-Marie were of Italian ancestry, and performativity is a key aspect of pretendianism. The ability to pass as Native American can be a door-opener, especially in casting rooms, but in other spaces as well. Yet, even when one does not ‘look’ stereotypically Native, a good story can compensate.
Fraudulently obtaining government contracts not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion

Stories help how many academics and authors deliver a compelling performance, regardless of whether they can pass as Native based on looks. In higher education, the ability to use words convincingly gives a leg up in competitive job markets, sometimes at the expense of actual, verifiably Native people. In academia, there is always caution about violating anti-discrimination laws, so hiring committees steer clear of asking about a person’s Native heritage, even when entire careers are built on identity claims. Such was the case with Elizabeth Hoover, whose environmental research in Mohawk communities was facilitated by her supposed Mohawk heritage.

In the publishing world, a gifted storyteller can cash in on the experiences of Native people. There are many books on the market by authors who co-opt Native culture, Native aesthetics, even Native trauma as though they are their own. In Canada, Boyden won many top Canadian book awards, honorary degrees and prestigious teaching appointments for his novels and short stories about Native life, based on his supposed lived experience. But Boyden was another fraudster, not a First Nations person, and is one of many examples of people who absorbed valuable resources meant for legitimate Indigenous people. Thanks to deep investigative journalism, his lack of Indigenous heritage was exposed in 2016. Boyden has since unconvincingly defended himself as having a small amount of Indigenous ancestry.

Native identity fraud also occurs in government contracting. In 2019, the Los Angeles Times conducted an investigation revealing that, since 2000, more than $300 million had gone to 12 companies claiming membership in three fake Cherokee tribes under federal, state and municipal programmes for minority businesses. One of the businesses turned out to be owned by the brother-in-law of the then-Congressional representative for California, Kevin McCarthy. Fraudulently obtaining government contracts does a double harm. It not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion toward legitimate tribally affiliated businesses.

Since the rise of the environmental movement in the 1970s, there has been a marked surge in Native American cultural appropriation, including patterns of Native becoming. During the US presidency of Joe Biden, we saw an elevation in influence of Indigenous cultural knowledge related to climate change resilience strategies up to the highest levels of policymaking, including the White House. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the Inflation Reduction Act and other legislation that privileged green energy, environmental justice and Indigenous knowledge in climate resilience projects brought material benefits to Native communities through unprecedented levels of funding for environmental and energy projects. But fraud dilutes its effectiveness.

The surge in funding coincided with a proliferation of Indigenous conservation and environmental nonprofit organisations. In many cases, Indigenous conservation groups were led by legitimately Indigenous people. But when grant programmes are opened up to groups who are not federally recognised tribes, there tends to be far less scrutiny about who the leaders are of an ‘Indigenous led’ group. The same is true in the philanthropy world. Private funders are often ill-equipped to make those kinds of determinations and sometimes fear that enquiring about them is rude or even illegal. Too often, the result has been the distribution of grants (in the environmental sector and beyond) to people or groups posing as Native, but with no verifiable Native American heritage.

There are other ways that posing as an Native American can be lucrative. Again in California, for example, where there is a proliferation of groups that call themselves ‘tribes’. Some are more legit than others, and there is no law prohibiting a group from calling itself a tribe. One group known as the Northern Chumash Tribal Council (NCTC) near San Luis Obispo, for instance, began as a ‘cultural monitoring’ group, overseeing the development of sensitive sites where there might be Native American human remains or other burial items. Contracts for cultural monitoring can command hundreds of thousands of dollars and, while laws allow only the ‘most likely descendants’ to monitor a site, they are notoriously lax. Fred Harvey Collins, the founder of NCTC, also went on to lead an effort to establish a national marine sanctuary, garnering significant attention and massive cultural and financial support. However, a legal battle involving his ancestry revealed in 2017 that he possessed no Native American heritage.
Claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past

Not everyone who dubiously calls themselves Native American does it for financial gain. In the US and Canada, it is wildly common to hear people talk about having ‘Indian blood’ or a mysterious Native American ancestor somewhere in the family tree, with no evidence whatsoever to back up the family lore. Sometimes, commercial DNA tests will suggest trace amounts of Indigenous ancestry in the distant past (recall Warren’s case), but as the scholar Kim TallBear has shown in Native American DNA (2012), from a Native standpoint, without a tribal community or family ties, DNA isn’t enough to legitimately call oneself Native American, and certainly not with any legal standing.
So what’s in it for them – what are the benefits of untruthfully claiming Native American heritage?

There are psychological, affective benefits to thinking one has a linkage, however distant, to the ‘original Americans’. Who, after all, is more ‘American’ than Native Americans? In another strand of reasoning, claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past. If one is the colonised, they must not be coloniser. Self-indigenising is a way to be absolved of responsibility for the crimes of colonialism and maintain the fiction of familial innocence.

Ultimately, though, in a country founded on the rights to private property and free speech, identity is perceived as a personal possession, something one can claim at will. In the US, there is a strong common belief that a person can be whoever and whatever they say they are, regardless of facts or evidence.

Native people have come to see the stakes of pretendianism as higher than ever. When university and entertainment jobs, contracts and grants meant for actual Native Americans are taken by people with no connection to legitimate tribal communities, it constitutes stealing resources from the descendants of people who have already been victimised by centuries of theft and loss. Money that is meant to help mitigate those patterns of erasure is unintentionally rendered a tool of more erasure.

At the same time, determining who is Native is not always a simple or easy task. There is a wide, grey area on the spectrum of Nativeness, where people can be legitimately Native American and not be an enrolled member of a federally recognised tribe. Confusion and fear about how to determine who is legitimately Native in our institutions has contributed to the perpetuation of pretendianism. There is growing recognition that something can and must be done to ensure that the resources meant for Native people go to Native people.

In the US, this has long been acknowledged in the art world. Since 1935, the Native American art market has been governed by the Indian Arts and Crafts Board, a US government agency within the Department of the Interior. It was originally set up to encourage the growth of the market, promoting economic self-sufficiency of ‘federally recognised American Indians and Alaska Natives (Indians)’. In 1990, US Congress passed the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, a truth-in-advertising law with strict requirements that anyone selling art as ‘Indian’-made should be enrolled in a federal or state-recognised tribe, or be a certified artisan of the tribe. It is meant to ensure authenticity, in turn guarding the commercial value of Indian-made art. While the law is widely viewed as deeply flawed for the ways it excludes documented Native people and simultaneously includes people from state-recognised groups, it does act as a bulwark against fraud.
Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when leveraged for financial or professional gain

The art world is virtually the only realm of social life with regulatory guardrails against Native ethnic fraud. Aside from this, those addressing the issue with the most urgency are in universities, particularly in Canada. There, a few colleges have implemented verification processes for admissions and scholarship applications. In the US, fears about violating race-based anti-discrimination laws present significant obstacles to implementing similar verification procedures.

Scholars push back against these fears by emphasising that Native Americans are more accurately understood as a political group than as a racial group by virtue of their sovereignty. Verification involves questions about relationships to claimed tribal communities, not questions about race. It’s not unlike asking for proof of military service for those who seek a veteran’s benefits. Wrongly claiming to be a veteran is called stolen valour and can lead to legal consequences. Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when it is leveraged for financial or professional gain. At the very least, it should not be rewarded.

The pretendian wars that Indigenous people are fighting in the US and abroad are aimed at spreading awareness that wrongful Native-claiming is not a harmless frivolity. Valuable resources are being diverted from those to whom they are intended. In some cases, it is a criminal offence, and more needs to be done to guard against it.
