A personal example. A few years ago, I joined Mountain Haulers, a cycling group that meets on Tuesday evenings for a ride through Asheville, North Carolina. It is a ‘no drop’ ride: cyclists wait at points along the way for everyone to catch up, however slow or struggling, and the first ride of the month is always a chill ride along the river. This openness sets the group apart from a cycling culture of notorious cliques of devotees clamouring to outdo each other’s worship of the sport. Welcoming the less-experienced and the less-committed seems a more genuine way of loving the thing you claim to love. If biking is your thing, surely you want more butts on bike seats. The dilettante cyclists who show up for Tuesday-night rides make cycling better.
The modern admonition to ‘stay in your lane’ stems from assumptions about the commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own

The further sense of the dilettante’s freedom involves mobility between different practices – a freedom from the barriers dividing them. The dilettante maintains a certain detachment, or intentional separation, between who one is and what one does, to live the life of a cultural itinerant. Painting, gardening, MIG welding, beekeeping, language learning, comic-book collecting, dancing, swimming, printmaking, powerlifting, pickleballing, sourdough baking, accordion playing, brisket barbecuing – all exciting destinations to travel and explore without seeking citizenship or even permanent residence in any one. The dilettante is a wayfaring cosmopolitan whose sense of freedom is found in never being stuck in one place.

And yet, this mobility is also part of a positive freedom to satisfy the basic human need to explore and make one’s mark on the world. Goethe and Schiller credit the dilettante for activating this natural impulse toward curiosity and creativity, a drive they compare with children’s innate desire to playfully imitate their surroundings. Going further, I would say that dilettantism offers not only the satisfaction of scratching the Homo faber itch; making and exploring for the simple sake of joy and curiosity is a freedom that is every bit as valuable to self-discovery as any commitment or singular pursuit.

However, from the outside, mobility may look like mere lack of commitment. No doubt this drives some of the allegations of superficiality commonly lodged against the dilettante. Pulling up anchors and moving on from an interest gets flagged as surface-skimming. I’m speculating here, but such criticism seems rooted in a work ethic that tells us that investment in certain interests ought to yield dividends: authority, credibility, permission to enter culturally guarded spaces, etc. Just as the neo-classicist wants to set the ‘true artist’ apart from the poseurs, the modern admonition to ‘pick a lane’, or (more aggressive) ‘stay in your lane’, stems from assumptions about the level and length of commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own.

Dilettantism rejects this quasi-capitalist mindset. The petty territorialism common to social, academic and cultural spaces (think record stores, cocktail bars, art galleries, philosophy classes, etc) is unnecessary but, more importantly, at odds with a genuine interest in the thing itself. A crucial part of the switch from deficiency to abundance is learning to see the dilettante as an asset to a given practice rather than a threat to it. Even Adorno, snob par excellence, allows a version of this, arguing that the expert critic needs the dilettante around ‘in order to prove to himself that he isn’t one’.
More than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour

Also crucial to making this mental switch is seeing the dilettante’s curiosity as equal in intensity to the expert’s, but different. Picture the dilettante as the love-child of two very different philosophical figures: Kierkegaard’s aesthete in Either/Or (1843) who finds and cultivates interests with an intensity that is abandoned before it hardens into obligation, and Friedrich Nietzsche’s ‘free spirit’, the fiercely curious, light-footed nomad whose restless pursuit of intellectual and artistic treasures provides a profound, if rootless, freedom. From Kierkegaard, the dilettante acquires an innate aversion to boredom (‘the root of all evil’) which is achieved by what he calls ‘rotation of crops’: perpetually changing ‘the method of cultivation and the kinds of crops’. From Nietzsche, the dilettante inherits a rejection of convention coupled with perpetual motion, a sense of permanent ‘homelessness’ that propels an unfettered perusal of interests. Passionate enough to go deep, detached enough to eventually leave, such a figure shows the possibility of being intensely invested in various ways of knowing, doing and making, but never content to let a sense of self form too firmly around them.

In a memorable scene from the Spike Jonze film Adaptation (2002), the journalist Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), who is writing a book about the orchid thief John Laroche (Chris Cooper), is at once intrigued by his hunt for a rare hallucinogenic ‘ghost orchid’ and baffled to learn that it is only the latest in a lifetime of obsessions: turtles, prehistoric fossils, 19th-century Dutch mirrors, etc. How can he detach so abruptly from something in which he’s invested so much? He can only offer an anecdote. A profound and consuming love for tropical fish ended suddenly with the realisation that the passion had simply run its course. ‘Fuck fish,’ he tells her, disrupting her assumption that loving something means sticking with it forever.

The difference is that, unlike Kierkegaard’s aesthete, the dilettante doesn’t rotate crops out of despair. Dynamism, detachment and insatiable curiosity are constitutive of the dilettante’s free and full subjectivity, rather than a stage on the way to achieving selfhood. The dilettante chooses aesthetic life over the life of commitment that Kierkegaard’s ‘either/or’ dichotomy presents, and fully owns that choice. Nor is the dilettante simply recovering from existential illness, as Nietzsche’s free spirit seems to be. Rather than running the risk of relapse – or worse, the ‘cankerous vice’ of pessimism – dilettantism is a healthy embrace of this freedom; more than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour.

In the dilettante’s genes is a compulsion to pursue passions, deeply coupled with a refusal to shape a life or identity permanently around any one of them. The dilettante possesses a unique capacity to dive deep into an interest, then surface and plunge into the depths of the next, each one an exploration, an adventure, but not a lifelong, life-defining project. It is precisely to hold open the possibility of the next reconnaissance mission that the dilettante rejects any dogmatic principle of stick-to-itiveness. Sometimes, the dilettante is a devout hobbyist parked on one interest for years at a stretch; sometimes, a juggler of several overlapping projects at once; and sometimes, a serial enthusiast on the hunt for the next novelty – what holds these modes together isn’t any fixed duration or rhythm of arrival and departure, but a disposition toward perpetual motion. The dilettante’s talent, energy and passion are constantly rechannelled through new outlets. Far from deficiency, dilettantism is a constant quest for abundance.

The life of the dilettante, so described, is not an especially easy one. It is a life of perpetual searching and fleeting satisfaction, in which accomplishment often arrives without accolades. Until breadth of interest is held in higher esteem, today’s dilettante will largely have to forgo public recognition and settle for a private life of pursuits and pleasures. Rarely is the dilettante widely celebrated as such. Consider someone like Susan Sontag, a novelist, critic and political activist whose wide-ranging work has earned both praise for its unconventional contributions to the intellectual life of 1960s New York and criticism for lacking rigour, for lacking substance. A ‘Win’ in the dilettante’s column, in other words, often comes with an asterisk – a conditional victory at best.

Further, the dilettante is also no pack animal; however much a part of a group one may feel, the dilettante will likely always be something of a tourist within it. The dilettante has to be comfortable travelling as a lone wolf at the margins of any community organised around a shared interest.

No, dilettantism is not for everyone. For anyone whom the universe has called to pursue a single passion – congratulations! Stay the course! But for those of us compelled by something closer to FOMO for the sheer variety and abundance the world has to offer, the dilettante’s path can lead to a genuine quality-of-life upgrade. If courage means overcoming the fear of new beginnings, without the reassurance of a title or a track record to show for it, then dilettantism may have much to offer. After all, not every crop is a monoculture, sowed and tilled to maximise output. Some of us need to cultivate our gardens through crop rotation. A defence of the dilettante is thus a call to follow the forked path of varying interests to a life made meaningful through abundance rather than acclaim.

items.title: AnOther Performance: Lewis Gribben
items.description: About to break out with his role in the new Blade Runner, the Glasgow-born actor tells us why he admires Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile
items.author: Jamie Dunn
paragraphs: About to break out with his role in the new Blade Runner, the Glasgow-born actor tells us why he admires Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile

When Lewis Gribben was growing up in Glasgow, he felt like an outsider. “I was a very antisocial kid,” he tells me. “I mostly liked to play video games and would imagine myself in those scenarios fighting against zombies or demons.” Gribben’s mum recognised that this love of imaginative play could break him out of his shell, so she enrolled him in the Citizens Theatre youth group when he was seven. “One of the first plays we did was superheroes trying to save Glasgow from a villainous invasion,” the actor recalls. “I played a character called Lizard Boy, and I remember thinking, ‘Wow, this is really fun. Maybe I’m not a weirdo.’”

Now, Gribben is returning to sci-fi on a slightly grander scale as one of the stars of Blade Runner 2099. The new show is set 50 years after the events of Blade Runner 2049 and seems to be a not-so-subtle window into humankind’s possible future. The social fabric of the world has flipped. Replicants now dominate society, and their creators, the humans, are the working underclass. As with any dystopia, a group of rebels are trying to break out of that system, including Gribben’s character Elias.

Despite having a CV that includes massive shows like Black Mirror and Masters of the Air, Gribben was taken aback by the scale of Blade Runner 2099’s production. “I’ve mostly done location work,” he says, “so I was amazed by the sets and the size of the crew, and just the details of the environments that were created.” The production designers seem to have taken their cues from Ridley Scott’s scuzzy cyberpunk original rather than Denis Villeneuve’s shinier sequel. “One [set] was a toolmaker’s apartment, so it was stuffed with all these different pieces of junk and metal. You’re on a sound stage, but it all looked so rustic and lived in.”

We haven’t lost Gribben to the grandeur of Hollywood quite yet, though. He may have fallen in love with acting because it allowed his imagination to run wild, but his heart belongs to the realism of British cinema. “I love stories about real life, that are grounded and have some grit,” says Gribben, who lists the likes of Molly Manning Walker (How to Have Sex), Luna Carmoon (Hoard) and Shane Meadows as directors he’d like to work with. But he seems haunted by one director who got away. “I auditioned for Ken Loach’s The Old Oak a couple of years ago and never got it, so if he ever does another film, I’m desperate to be involved.”
As he explains below, Gribben is also drawn to the grit of Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile, which shares parallels with the rapper’s own early years.

Lewis Gribben: “I was too young when 8 Mile came out initially, but when I got to finally see it on DVD, when I was 12 or 13, I was struck by how grounded Eminem was in that film. He’s great in all the rap scenes, obviously, particularly during that freestyle one near the end where he destroys himself to defeat his opponent. But there’s one scene where he just yells at his mum and it’s so impassioned. His mum is like, ‘My boyfriend’s left me, what am I gonna do?’ And he’s like, ‘What are you gonna do? Lily [his character’s younger sister] is out by herself right now. How could you do this to us?’ And I was like, ‘Fuck, that came from somewhere really deep.’ It’s a really small scene, but the anger is so real and sudden that it really stuck with me.

“Some people say, ‘Oh, well, he’s just playing himself’. But I think what’s so interesting about Eminem’s performance is that he’s playing a version of himself. It’s not technically him; it’s a characterised version. I identify with that. You can’t really escape yourself when you’re acting, because it’s still you at the end of the day. Even if you have to do a different accent or you’re in sci-fi clothing, like with Blade Runner, you’re still bringing a part of yourself to the character.”

items.title: Louise Giovanelli: Shimmering and Cinematic
items.description: As her third exhibition opens at White Cube Mason’s Yard, the painter tells us about her painting rituals, recurring subject matter and unsettling new directions
items.author: Sayori Radda
paragraphs: As her third exhibition opens at White Cube Mason’s Yard, the painter tells us about her painting rituals, recurring subject matter and unsettling new directions

“I usually paint beautiful, desirable things, so I wanted to challenge myself to paint something grotesque and make it beautiful,” says British painter Louise Giovanelli, of Aphros (2026), a painting based on a photograph she took during a visit to a slaughterhouse. It’s a departure from the shimmering theatrical curtains, lustrous wigs and glamorous female figures drawn from cinema that are now characteristic of her practice.

Rendered in crystalline greys and blues, the claustrophobic close-up of butchered meat initially resembles a geological formation, perhaps a seascape or a starry night. Only upon closer inspection might the viewer notice a meat inspection stamp in the lower-left corner, revealing the painting’s unsettling and grotesque subject. Presented in In the Light of False Suns, Giovanelli’s third solo exhibition with White Cube, Aphros was conceived as a kind of Trojan horse. Its carnal focus signals a new direction, “pushing me into new realms”, as she puts it. Yet the painting remains rooted in one of her central artistic concerns: the tension between beauty, seduction and the unsettling, and their combined power to captivate the viewer. “It’s very boring if it’s too nice,” she explains. “There has to be another element that grips and unsettles you.”

This tension takes another form in Ad Astra (2026), where two of Giovanelli’s longstanding motifs converge for the first time: the female cinematic figure and the theatrical curtain. Glistening female faces, their heads tilted back, lips parted and eyes closed in apparent ecstasy, evoke a sense of claustrophobia as they appear trapped within shimmering, spotlit curtains, their features dissolving into the folds of the fabric. Through this fusion, Giovanelli explores cathexis, the psychological investment of emotional energy in an image or object, as the female figures and theatrical curtains imbue one another with new meaning and intensity.

Drawing on Hollywood glamour and the archetype of the femme fatale, the Manchester-based painter (born in London, 1993) references figures ranging from Sissy Spacek in Brian De Palma’s Carrie (1976) to Sharon Stone in Basic Instinct (1992). These cinematic references intersect with the visual language of Catholic worship, blurring distinctions between bodily desire and religious devotion.

Despite studying at Manchester School of Art (BA, 2015) and Frankfurt’s Städelschule (2018–2020) under Amy Sillman, Giovanelli is largely self-taught in traditional Old Master painting techniques, maintaining that “no one really gets taught how to paint at art school these days.” On her own initiative, she travelled to European museums to study Northern Renaissance masters, particularly Jan van Eyck. Through this independent study, she developed her command of glazing and underpainting, and developed the characteristic glow of her paintings.
Sayori Radda How did you arrive at painting as your primary medium, and how has your approach evolved since the beginning of your practice?

Lousie Giovanelli I wasn’t exposed to much art growing up, as I didn’t come from an artistic family. At art school, I began visiting museums and galleries across the UK and Europe, studying Renaissance paintings and Old Master collections. I wanted to paint like the great masters who came before us. That’s essentially how I taught myself to paint, through looking and studying.

Initially, I appropriated excerpts from Old Master paintings, cropping small details and making my own versions. My work was more figurative and closer to its art-historical sources. Over time, those influences became more subtly embedded, and I developed my own recurring motifs: hair, drapery, fabric, film stills, women’s necks and light phenomena.
SR What does a typical day in your studio look like? Do you have particular rituals?

LG I treat painting as a discipline, almost like a job. I start at 6am and work ten to 12 hours, making use of all the available natural light. I have an image bank on my phone and computer containing thousands of images, which I constantly add to. Some remain untouched for years; others I use immediately.

I work on ten or 15 paintings simultaneously because oil is a slow medium. The paintings inform one another as ideas bounce between them. I also return to the same image repeatedly, adjusting the format, scale or colour each time. Sources range from film stills and the internet to my own photographs. For this exhibition, I staged a photoshoot using wigs from my studio.
SR How did you develop In the Light of False Suns, and how does it depart from your earlier work?

LG The title comes from parhelia, an optical phenomenon in which sunlight refracts through ice crystals, creating bright spots resembling additional suns. I became interested in light emanating from different sources, rather than the authentic one.

Light has always been crucial to my work, both as something depicted and something emanating from the canvas itself. People often describe my paintings as luminous, associating them with a feeling of worship. I’m interested in light reflecting off curtains, gold fabric or hair, but equally in how luminosity emerges through technique. I use Old Master methods of glazing and underpainting, revealing light through the white gesso beneath. The more paint you add, the deader the surface can become.

In this show, I’ve introduced thicker, textured gesso, pointillist techniques and impasto brushstrokes. These contrast with the thin washes and glowing surfaces of my earlier work, creating a different rhythm.
SR In Ad Astra (2026), female faces appear superimposed onto spotlit curtains, while Media Luna (2026) belongs to your series of large-scale paintings of wigs. How does cathexis connect these works?

LG I came across the term in a book and immediately thought it described what I was trying to do. It’s the first time I’ve fused two different series and introduced figures into the curtain paintings.

Cathexis involves investing energy in desirable objects, whether silk, marble or skin. In these works, the female figure takes on meaning from the curtain and vice versa. To me, their combination makes both images more powerful.
SR In Media Luna, the wig takes on an almost artificial, porcelain-like appearance. How did you develop this image?

LG I photographed a blonde wig, doubled and warped it, then added a celluloid sheen. I wanted luminous, artificial colours that remove its association with a real person. The enlarged wigs become closer to shrouds or drapery, with an uncanny quality. Media Luna means crescent moon, referencing the shape of a head and the moon’s changing phases. The celestial titles throughout the show encourage associations beyond the human world.
SR Curtains recur throughout your work, and Mark Fisher described their role in David Lynch’s films as thresholds between different realities. What do they represent to you?

LG Exactly, ‘thresholds’. Curtains are barriers but also entrances; they conceal and reveal. What fascinates me most is how they change people’s behaviour. At my exhibitions, people take selfies in front of the curtain paintings, as though they’re on stage or about to perform. Curtains give people a sense of permission to perform. That behavioural aspect is fundamentally why I’m interested in them.
SR With Aphros, you introduce an unexpected image: a meat carcass. What prompted this departure, and how does it relate to the exhibition’s wider themes?

LG Aphros refers to foamy seawater and connects to the root of Aphrodite. I’m exploring classical themes of sex and death. I usually paint beautiful, desirable things, so I wanted to challenge myself to paint something grotesque and make it beautiful.

The painting initially resembles a seascape, a ski slope or a starry night. Only later might viewers realise they’re looking at meat. I’m interested in that jarring moment, almost like a Trojan horse, where beauty draws you in before revealing something darker. I want that recognition to interrupt their enjoyment.

I’ve placed it beside a painting of a woman in a rapturous state, referencing associations between women and the sea in Greek mythology. The relationship between these works and the curtain paintings adds another dimension. It’s a departure for me, pushing my painting into new territory.
SR How do you approach pastiche? Is it a way of bringing together different references to create something new?

LG We’re living in an era of pastiche. I rarely see anything truly novel, including in my own work. We’re so saturated with images and what came before us that appropriation is almost inevitable. I’m comfortable with that. For me, referencing other art forms is a kind of reverence, a celebration of what came before. I’m less interested in cynical postmodern art that mocks or subverts the past.

SR Female figures recur throughout your paintings, particularly those drawn from cinema, such as Sissy Spacek in Carrie and Christina Ricci in Buffalo ’66. What draws you to these images, and how do you approach the representation of women?

LG I’m interested in female glamour, the femme fatale and actresses like Elizabeth Taylor and Sharon Stone. There’s a painting of Stone from Basic Instinct in this exhibition. People often ask whether my focus on women is political or feminist, but I don’t think it is. It’s something deeper, perhaps more ancient, that I haven’t fully understood. Painting is my form of research, and I hope one day I’ll understand why I felt compelled to make these portraits. It has something to do with reverence for female beauty and glamour, and their power to seduce in visual culture.
SR How do you represent these women physically? You often use close-ups.

LG I’m drawn to necks, tilted heads and lips. Their eyes are often closed, rarely looking directly at the viewer. I’m particularly interested in women appearing in ambiguous states of ecstasy, as though undergoing a transcendent experience. There’s a religious aspect to this, particularly Catholic imagery and representations such as The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa. I’m interested in bringing these spiritual depictions together with contemporary, bodily experiences of ecstasy.
SR How has your Catholic upbringing influenced your work?

LG It has definitely shaped how I appreciate religion now, particularly the opulence and sheer visual intensity of it, the rituals and the idea of worship itself, the weight of its idols and icons. I don’t practise, but I have a deep reverence for religion and am currently fascinated with tracing those impulses back in time, especially into pre-Christian and pagan traditions. That’s very much where my research sits at the moment.
Louise Giovanelli: In the Light of False Suns is open at White Cube Mason’s Yard until 16 January 2027

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

items.title: Ten cool new CD players provide the path to audiophile heaven at home
items.description: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten conte
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten contemporary players will help you get back to the original digital source.

Arcam has a new flagship CD player, the CD25. Shown here partnered with the A50 Signature Class G Integrated Amplifier, the CD25 builds on the company’s four decades of experience building digital audio systems. The slender system has gently rounded edges, a black fascia containing the display, and dual-mono digital-to-analogue converters, one for each channel.

Quad’s 3CDT player is now available in a new satin black finish with a green illumination, a classic colourway for this 90-year-old British audio brand. Paired with the Quad 3 integrated amplifier, the 3CDT (a transport only, with no onboard amplification) follows the company’s purist approach. In addition to conventional CDs, the 3CDT is compatible with CD-R, CD-RW and data CDs, and a variety of audio file formats, including FLAC, WAV, WMA, and MP3.

The newest model in Musical Fidelity’s B-Line of high-end audio products, the B1xcd is a purist’s CD player that pairs well with the company’s B1xi integrated amplifier. You won’t find any extraneous features other than a straightforward front-loading CD player with an LCD display and analogue and digital outputs.
£549, details at MusicalFidelity.com. Stockists at henleyaudio.co.uk

Released as part of the venerable audio company’s Classic Series, the new C 569 from NAD joins the C 359S streaming amplifier to create a simple, no nonsense home system that follows a set of enduring design principles. That means push-button design, a modestly sized screen and stripped-back design.
Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD

If space is at a premium, consider the new Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD from Majority Audio. Although it the same form factor as a traditional stackable hi-fi component, the new model not only incorporates a 200W Texas Instruments amplifier but also has onboardDAB/DAB+ and FM radio and a USB slot, alongside a conventional CD drawer.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The new DP11 CD player from FiiO has a compact, desktop-sized footprint. Finished in retro silver, the DP11 can not only drive a pair of headphones but also includes a USB-C socket that lets you rip CDs straight to a thumb drive.
Eversolo DMP-A8 Master Gen 2

Another all-in-one solution, this time from Eversolo. The DMP-A8 is not only a network music player, high-resolution DAC and analogue preamplifier, but it also comes with a CD playback system with a top-loading mechanism. Thanks to the unit’s impressive connectivity, album information comes up on the large 8.6-inch touchscreen panel, while there’s support for Qobuz Connect, TIDAL Connect and Spotify Connect. An internal SSD can be added if you want to keep your ripped music all in one place.

Marantz’s latest CD player is the CD 70, launched alongside the Model 70 integrated amplifier. The CD 70 also comes with its own headphone amplifier, as the ability to play files back from USB. It’s available in classic black or a silver and gold finish.

The Shanling CD-S100 offers multiple features in addition to straightforward CD playback. The Chinese brand has created a full-size player that also serves as a DAC for phone and computer audio, thanks to the ability to receive and output music over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and USB.

Visually and physically hefty (over 25kg), the new Luxman D-100 Centennial is a CD player of exceptional robustness, stability and quality of componentry. Thick-gauge aluminium and steel give this model its gravitas, along with handmade circuitry and a high-resolution OLED display. Created to celebrate the centenary of the Japanese manufacturer, no expense has been spared.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Pared-back but perfect gifts for the minimalist in your life
items.description: The festive season, typically one of excess, can be trying for the minimalist. All those adornments, trimmings and more stuff. So, if a physical gift really is in order, soothe your favourite minimalist’s sensibilities by offering something that in some way em
items.author: Bridget Downing
paragraphs: The festive season, typically one of excess, can be trying for the minimalist. All those adornments, trimmings and more stuff. So, if a physical gift really is in order, soothe your favourite minimalist’s sensibilities by offering something that in some way embraces the spirit of less but better. We’ve gathered a selection of refined and rarefied suggestions that will never feel de trop to a reductivist recipient, from transparent-framed sunglasses to floating diamonds, an understated hoodie and (a wild card) lip balm grown in space.
Sunglasses with a subtle difference

The subtraction of colour adds allure to these Cutler and Gross sunglasses. A strong silhouette is softened by the chamfered edges and transparency of the acetate frames (look for Sand Crystal or Neutral colourways). Meanwhile, the subtly tinted Zeiss LightPro lenses take away just enough of the sun’s glare for those who value clarity in all things.

Elevating an everyday routine into something more indulgent, Dior’s La Collection Privée Scented Ritual Duo – a soap and a lotion, both for hands and body, subtly scented with a choice of signature Dior scents – makes a gift that’s luxurious but still essential. And the simple packaging will look right at home in the sleekest of bathrooms.

Clean-lined and covetable in ‘Plaster’, Stone Island’s stripped-back hoodie in technical stretch jersey fabric retains thoughtful functional details, such as vertical zip chest pockets as well as side snap-fastening pockets, a drawstring hem and elasticated hood, that make it both stylish and utilitarian.

If you love your minimalist to the moon and back, Exist’s lip balm containing a bioactive complex grown at the International Space Station feels like a grand-ish gesture in a small and sleek package. The ultra-rich formula – vegan and cruelty free – promises smoother lips in three days and includes Lysate, good for ‘hydration and line reductions’, according to brand founder Lauren Bowker, ‘but because it was grown in space, it has 300 times more power than anything Earth-grown’. Choose from a spaceship-shaped vessel or a straightforward capsule container.

Designed in 1968 by Superstudio, the ‘Gherpe’ lamp for Poltronova is an interactive and irreverent piece of Italian Radical Design history that’s still mesmerising today. Breaking with rigid functionalism, the lamp’s Perspex layers can be drawn up to resemble a sea creature’s shell or folded down neatly for a more minimal form. Almost like an early fidget toy for design lovers. Available in red or white.

Pearls have classic, timeless appeal, but Tasaki’s ‘Balance Parallel Neo’ open ring, in white gold with pavé diamonds, offers a contemporary take. Two lines of three Akoya pearls rest either side of the finger, parallel and perfectly poised, like a mini sculpture.

Smart in every sense, Apple’s debut home assistant display is a polished step up from plasticky rivals, with a seven-inch Liquid Retina display and an aluminium finish that should please the aesthete. Integrating Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, with stringent privacy functions, it offers smart-home management (right down to home security, which Apple can also now take care of), streaming audio and making calls, facial recognition – useful in multi-person households with numerous accounts – and a lot more. It’s available on a domed speaker base or, to keep those immaculate surfaces clear, wall-mounted.
A luxurious take on the paper bag

There’s little more minimal than a paper bag. Issey Miyake gives the idea a playful but meticulous upgrade with paper-style totes in leather (sold out on the brand’s site, but there are a few remaining elsewhere), and also a pressed fabric version that includes yarn made from washi paper, giving a paper-like texture to a durable accessory.

Fine jeweller Christina de Kerpel pares back the love token with this lab-grown diamond ring. Set in pink or yellow gold, the gem appears to float on the finger thanks to the ring’s nylon-wire structure. Enquire via her website to order.

Monochrome often wins the day for the minimalist-leaning sartorialist. Which makes Hermès’ latest iteration of its sports-inspired H08 watch a bit of all-white. In Blanc Chantilly, to be precise, the model features a braided glass-fibre composite case with a delicately mottled finish, offsetting the sunburst, satin-brushed white ceramic bezel and white rubber strap. Available online in the US at the time of writing. UK and EU customers, check back at hermes.com or enquire in store.
