items.title: ‘Is James Bond Conservative?’ Trump Asks Natalie Harp to Find Out
items.description: Donald Trump loves inserting himself into major pop-culture controversies. And at one point, he had a lot of thoughts about Robert Pattinson. Over a four-week period in late 2012, he tweeted about the Twilight heartthrob’s relationship with Kristen Stewart an
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump loves inserting himself into major pop-culture controversies. And at one point, he had a lot of thoughts about Robert Pattinson. Over a four-week period in late 2012, he tweeted about the Twilight heartthrob’s relationship with Kristen Stewart an incredible 11 times, urging him not to take back his co-star because “She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again–just watch. He can do much better!”

So it was a bit surprising that Trump did not immediately weigh in when Pattinson was announced as the next James Bond earlier this month. Now he has finally done so, and it seems his opinion hinged on whether RPatz is MAGA-friendly.
The New York Post asked Trump about the next 007 at an Oval Office interview on Tuesday. Before he answered, Trump sent his top aide, Natalie Harp, on an important mission:
“Is James Bond conservative? Natalie,” he called through the open door of the Oval Office.
Harp rushed in from her desk in the outer Oval, with printouts about Pattinson in hand, and gave them to Trump.
Harp told Trump, “He’s been good.” He responded, “I always like people that like me.”
Then Trump looked through the stack of printed-out articles, and read the first of his iconic Pattinson tweets aloud:
One of the printed-out articles was Trump’s tweet from 2012 where he gave Pattinson relationship advice.
“Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again — just watch,” the president said, reading his tweet aloud.
He then added: “This was a long time ago” …
Laying aside his 2012 tweet, Trump went on to flip through the clips about him and Pattinson.
“That’s cute. He says nice things,” he said.

It is unclear which RPatz comments Trump found “nice.” The actor, who is British, has never shared his political views publicly. He has said he considered becoming a political speechwriter when he was young, but “I’m quite apolitical, weirdly. I like the game.”

Pattinson has discussed Trump’s tweets about him, but his remarks weren’t exactly positive. In a 2017 Daily Beast interview, he called them a “bizarre curiosity.” That same year, he offered these existential musings when Entertainment Weekly inquired about the new U.S. president’s apparent obsession with him:

I think there’s so many different levels of it. Your identity exists on many different planes at the same time, and they all can be quite different from each other. When he said that, it didn’t really mean anything. But I guess now I’m sort of thinking, like, “Well, I guess that is related to me.” But how does that fit in with all the other things going on in my life? And sometimes you think, “Can I use this in my acting? Or should I be putting it away?” It’s kind of interesting, I guess. I don’t know — this could be why people get annoyed with me.
Whatever Harp showed Trump, he took it as a compliment. “He looks nice,” the president said of Pattinson. “You know, I wish him luck.”

items.title: Amazon Is Weaponizing Its Customers Against NYC Bill
items.description: New Yorkers recently logging onto Amazon in search of Black Friday deals or to replenish household staples have been met with an unusual warning: “Attention: NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.”
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: New Yorkers recently logging onto Amazon in search of Black Friday deals or to replenish household staples have been met with an unusual warning: “Attention: NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.”

The pop-up alert is centered around the Delivery Protection Act, a pending piece of legislation from the City Council intended to regulate companies’ third-party delivery practices that has drawn strong support from local politicians and labor groups as well as staunch opposition from advocates in the business community. The warning, which was also affixed on delivered packages, alleged that the regulatory bill would raise costs for consumers and called upon Amazon customers to contact their local council member and urge them to vote against the measure in order to “protect low costs.”

The bill, which was first introduced by Council Member Tiffany Cabán, would require the operators of last-mile facilities to obtain licenses from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and adhere to specific safety and training requirements. In addition, it also bars them from utilizing third-party contractors to make deliveries, requiring them to directly employ delivery and warehouse workers. The bill currently has the public support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani as well as unions and labor groups like the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union and the New York City Central Labor Council.

In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the proposed bill would “threaten the livelihoods of more than 40 small delivery businesses we work with in New York City and the 5,000-plus New Yorkers they employ,” also known as Delivery Service Partners. “As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Nantel said. According to Amazon, more than 115,000 customers have emailed their council members since last Thursday urging them to vote against the bill.

The company has warned that the bill’s passage could force them to move operations outside of the city, citing a study conducted by engineering firm AKRF that such changes could pass along additional costs to consumers ranging from $409 to $664 annually. The study was prepared for the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a citywide organization of business and commerce groups that strongly opposes the legislation. A New York Focus report found that Amazon has contributed more than $5 million to support the group’s efforts.

Opponents of the Delivery Protection Act have said the legislation’s restriction on third-party contractors would negatively impact small local businesses that frequently partner with Amazon to fulfill deliveries and potentially result in their closure and the loss of jobs. City & State reported earlier this month that the Five Borough Jobs Campaign and the New York Delivers coalition are mulling potential legal challenges if the bill goes into effect.

“An estimated 25 percent of these delivery businesses are Black-owned, compared with just 3 to 4 percent of businesses nationally,” Marc Morial, the president and CEO of the National Urban League, wrote in an op-ed for amNY earlier this month. “At a time when we are fighting to close the racial wealth gap, this is exactly the kind of foothold in business ownership we should be working to expand — not eliminate.”
In an interview, Cabán rejected Amazon’s claim that her bill would inherently increase fees for consumers, calling their push a “prime example of corporate bullying.”

“The bill simply requires that Amazon would have to pay $500 every other year for their license, and that covers all of the packages that get delivered,” she said. “It requires Amazon to comply with basic workplace and public safety regulations. So there’s no world where a common-sense bill like this costs Amazon $5 for every single delivery. It’s just them trying to bully New Yorkers with junk fees.”

Amazon’s direct-to-consumer campaign against the Council bill sparked immediate pushback from Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin. “We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs,” the council speaker wrote on X. “If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong.”

Mamdani, who denounced what he called Amazon’s “greed,” expanded on his thinking on the bill at a Monday press conference. “What this legislation would do would be to put in place some basic guardrails to regulate what is an expanding last-mile industry that would then keep local residents and workers safe. And to see that the response to all of this from Jeff Bezos … a man worth more than $376 billion is threatening to raise prices on New Yorkers ordering paper towels or multivitamins for their children during a cost-of-living crisis. It is disappointing, to say the least,” the mayor said, referring to Bezos, Amazon’s founder and now executive chair.

The Delivery Protection Act currently has 35 sponsors in the City Council, a figure that likely ensures its passage once taken up by the Council. Negotiations on the bill are ongoing as the bill seems poised to be voted on by the end of the year. “We want to get this right,” Cabán said. “We’re making sure the bill is narrowly tailored to address the problem we want to address. We’re fine-tuning the final language to make sure it does that and we’re getting very, very close.”

Nantel, Amazon’s spokesperson, said the company is “hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written.” During a press conference last week, Menin expressed confidence that the final bill will be something all parties can come to agreement on.

“I have made very clear from the start that we are not going to do something that will cause us to lose those jobs in New York City,” she said. “I am confident we can chart a path forward with a bill that does not cause job loss and does not cause the DSPs to go out of business and that protects the workers and makes New York City the first city in the country to regulate Amazon.”

items.title: Hit the right note with 12 fragrances and home scents to give this Christmas
items.description: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long winter evenings, here is Monocle’s pick of the best scents to gift this Christmas.
Discover a Homeric fragrance from To My Ships

Named after a line in Homer’s Iliad, To My Ships launched in what its founder, Daniel Bense, calls an “uninspiring” category: deodorant. The Aesop and Sunspel alumnus has since worked with celebrated nose Céline Barel to develop the brand’s bestselling Of the Gods perfume around polygonum, a herby ingredient that’s usually only used in trace amounts.
“It’s a fragrance discovered by those near the wearer, rather than announced to a room,” says Bense. Backed by 18 investors, the label has grown by word of mouth and will soon expand to Japan.
Toast the wool mill with Zegna’s Il Lanificio

For its latest foray into perfume, luxury menswear house Zegna drew inspiration from the life of founder Ermenegildo Zegna and his Italian Alpine homeland. The brand’s fragrance collection includes six scents and we’re particularly taken by Il Lanificio, which means “wool mill” in Italian.

The perfume’s heady mixture of suede, vanilla and sandalwood pays tribute to its namesake and is a celebration of Zegna’s ability to take raw material and transform it into something unique. Simultaneously urbane and rustic, this is a scent to savour.
Pair Italian fig with American cedar in Bottega Veneta’s Balliamo

Bottega Veneta expanded its fragrance offerings this year with Alta, a new collection of 10 scents. Each combines an ingredient from Italy with a far-flung counterpoint (think blood orange with North African neroli or plum with Spanish labdanum).
We’ll be wearing Balliamo – a heady combination of Italian white fig with American cedarwood – to the aperitivo.
Head into the woods with Documents’ Inter Cedar

Documents is one of a handful of Shanghai-based, high-end fragrance brands that is proving popular with Chinese consumers and poised to go global. Its premium scents are inspired by Eastern culture, featuring notes from ylang ylang and sichuan pepper to incense and black tea.
The brand operates more than 40 shops across 20 cities. We recommend its Inter Cedar eau de parfum, a tree-inspired scent with a woody profile and aromas of cypress, cardamom and mugwort.
Try Monocle and Claus Porto’s own Soleil Zeste

Crafted by French perfumer Daphné Bugey, this fragrance and body wash are the result of an exclusive collaboration between Portuguese beauty brand Claus Porto and Monocle, with packaging designed by our in-house art team.

The Soleil Zeste scent features notes of bergamot, lemon and lime, alongside green aromas of galbanum, petitgrain and cypress, and a refreshing base of white musk and lavender. Plus, the perfume bottles are made by Vista Alegre, an Aveiro-based heritage manufacturer of porcelain and crystal.
clausporto.com; monocle.com
Start a conversation with Jijide

Milan-based fragrance brand Jijide – meaning “positive” in Mandarin – emerged from a conversation between Italian and Chinese friends Adam James Cavallari, Andrea Alessandri and Fanqi Guan. Perfume, they decided, was the ideal language through which to explore their cultures.

The Riso scent layers notes of kumquat and rice with the salty intensity of soy sauce, while Dentro evokes an Italian morning through aromas of coffee and fig. It’s proof that perfume can be a talking point.
Count down to Christmas with Diptyque’s advent candle
The countdown to Christmas is celebrated in many ways. Some unwrap the gold foil of a small chocolate each morning or acknowledge Advent by fasting in advance of a seasonal feasting.

Parisian maison Diptyque has chosen to mark the days ahead with a Danish tradition. The kalenderlys candle burns down bit by bit, a simple reminder of coming festivities. This edition is scented with pine, cedar and moss, bringing the scents of the fir tree to warm the darker nights.
Bring the forest indoors with Deux Frères

Owners of gin distillery Deux Frères, Gian and Florian Grundböck, tend to think outside the box. Producing thousands of bottles of their signature gin in their Zürich-based distillery leaves several hundred litres of fragrant botanical remnants, known as tails.

“We wanted to turn the tails into something meaningful,” says founder Gian. Enter Forêt, a characterful room scent with notes of juniper, pink pepper and sandalwood. “For us, the fragrance is an example of how a by-product can become something distinctive in its own right,” says Gian. We’ll drink to that.
Escape to the Himalayas with Be Boundless

Beijinger Lydia Wang turned her personal interest in Tibetan medicine, meditation and yoga into a business in 2020 when she established incense brand Be Boundless. The label’s all-natural sticks are shorter than traditional incense from Lhasa, so they fit easily into a carry-on.

Wang tapped one of China’s leading graphic designers, Li Xibin, to create the branding, which features block colours and a bold typeface. A box set comes with 60 sticks in three scents, as well as a small, wooden pull-out tray. The Nighty Night scent – made from dong quai, clove, narra safflower and myrobalan – is a popular pick.
Light up winter evenings with Ffern

Somerset-based perfumer Ffern’s winter candle burns with comforting notes of coffee, frankincense and Peru balsam. Set into the lid of the attractive steel vessel is enamel artwork by South Korean-American illustrator Cory Feder.
Drawing from Scottish folklore, it depicts an ethereal woman swimming alongside a seal. The candle is both a covetable design object and an indulgent scent for the season.
Indulge in a slow burn from Astier de Villatte

Paris-based Astier de Villatte, a design house known for its elegant and lightweight ceramics, has found inspiration in the island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe for the latest addition to its incense line.

The new scent draws on São Tomé’s plentiful cocoa reserves, blending notes of roasted cocoa with Atlas cedar, labdanum, sandalwood and musk, making for a luxurious room filler to accompany the workshop’s delicate ceramics.
Channel the silversmith with Georg Jensen’s Home Scent

Seeking inspiration for its first foray into scent, Danish heritage design house Georg Jensen turned to its own silversmith. The result is a trio of candles that pays tribute to the materials found in the brand’s Copenhagen workshop: silver, steel and quartz.
As you might then expect, the candles emit scents with an intriguing metallic edge, balanced with olfactory layers taken from the Danish countryside – think moss, ivy leaf and pine.

items.title: How Marc Grebler turned a family workshop into a maker of bespoke Land Rover Defenders
items.description: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and mo
items.author: Ed Stocker; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and modernises Land Rover Defenders.

“My grandfather on my mother’s side had a workshop just outside Barcelona that specialised in servicing Saabs,” says Grebler. “But Saab stopped making cars in 2015. Shortly afterwards, my grandfather died and there wasn’t much for the mechanics to do.” After a period of inactivity at the workshop, he approached his aunt, who had been running the business for her father, and suggested trying something new.

“I was always a car fan and fell in love with Land Rover Defenders in my teens,” he says. “At the time, you could pick them up for very little in Spain. My idea was to renovate Defenders in my grandfather’s workshop. I was still at university and the family thought that I was crazy, so we decided to start with one vehicle. When it sold, we began to see the idea’s potential and Costa Motor found its second wind.”

Then the coronavirus pandemic hit. Though Grebler initially saw this as a setback for the company, it allowed him to spend more time in Spain with his aunt and the cars. Plus, the period had an unexpected bonus. “There was an explosion of interest in Defenders during that time,” he says. “People were buying them, painting them and selling them on for two or three times what they had paid. But we decided to double down on quality. That’s how you build trust and a loyal customer base.”

Costa Motor’s clients are predominantly wealthy European car enthusiasts who appreciate Grebler’s personal approach. No two builds are the same and the process begins with a personal consultation. “First, I ask them what they want it for,” he says. “Do they have children? Dogs? Will they drive it in the city? Is it going to Mallorca? Will they head to the beach every weekend?” Once Grebler understands his clients’ intentions, he can build the concept and source an original Defender shell. The finished models typically sell for about €160,000, plus tax.

“If it’s a businessman who wants a fun car for his holiday home in the Med, we recommend technical upholstery,” says Grebler. “He can jump in wearing a wet swimsuit, his kids can spill drinks in the back and everything is easy to clean. Someone else might want a 200TDI because that’s what his father drove. He’s looking for authenticity. For him, we recommend real leather that will age beautifully over time. It starts with a conversation.”

Grebler restricts Costa Motor’s workload to no more than 12 projects a year. A team of craftspeople – including mechanics, leatherworkers and paint specialists – spends an average of 900 hours on each car. The approach is uniquely Iberian. “They’re incredibly committed,” he says. “Most of them have families so we have found a rhythm that works for everyone. We start at 07.00, work until 10.00, then there’s a pause for breakfast. After that, they work straight through until 15.00, then head home. There’s a flexibility in Spain that you don’t find everywhere.”

As well as Grebler’s hands-on approach, what sets Costa Motor apart is its focus on materials. Leather is a key element for Grebler. “You can have the most incredible engine in the world but if the leather feels cheap, the whole experience is ruined,” he says. “We’re obsessed with how the car feels. Everything your hands touch should feel substantial. We replace plastic with aluminium wherever we can. We cover surfaces in leather. We want to keep the original character of the Defender but give it a premium feel.”

This approach extends beyond materiality. Costa Motor recently delivered a Defender 90 to a client who loves his dog so much that the team incorporated its likeness alongside the company’s wolf logo throughout the interior. Once the cars are finished, they will be sent to their new owners; so far, their destinations have included Saint-Tropez, Verbier, Andorra and Comporta.

So, with Costa Motor’s order book full until well into 2027, what’s next for the company? “I would like us to become less dependent on Defenders,” says Grebler. “We’re finally at a stage where we have almost a year’s worth of work, which gives us peace of mind. There are so many possibilities. What I really want is for a client to come to me and say, ‘I loved what you did with my Defender. I also have a Porsche 911. Can we do something equally special with it?’ That would be the dream.”

Launched in 1948 as the Land Rover Series I, the original vehicle evolved through successive models before becoming the Defender in 1990. Renowned for its rugged aluminium body, four-wheel drive and go-anywhere capabilities, it became a staple among those working in farming, exploration, military service and humanitarian work across the globe. Built largely by hand at Solihull in the UK, the original Defender remained in production until 2016, with only minor updates. Stricter safety and emissions regulations brought almost seven decades of continuous production to an end and Land Rover tapped out at two million sales.

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.

items.title: Sofia Coppola's New 'Marie Antoinette' Merch
items.description: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
product photography COURTESY OF MACK

The merch-ification of the movies we love is a fairly recent development, brought on by cult studios who know we like our cinephilia to be seen at all times. But if you go back further than five years, then original, director-approved t-shirts, sweatshirts, anything, is much harder to find. Die-hards will scroll on eBay looking for scant objects made as wrap gifts or for crew. But that’s about it! For Sofia Coppola fans—a director whose lore-steeped, decadently formed, insular worlds are catnip for aesthetes—we’ve mostly had to rely on fan created or bootleg stuff. That’s all about to change.

This year, to mark the 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette, Coppola has unveiled a trio of projects. There’s a remastered cut of the film, a documentary about the film’s creation directed by her late mother Eleanor Coppola titled Making Marie Antoinette (out now via MUBI), and the release of its hardback companion by MACK and Coppola’s own imprint Important Flowers, comprised of pictures shot by Coppola’s long-time collaborator Andrew Durham. Durham’s pictures have carried their own special stories for Coppola fans; now, you can wear them, or carry them slung over your shoulder with some new Marie Antoinette merch, available on MACK’s website now.

To celebrate the confectionary-sweet moment, Coppola spoke to us about the film’s modern reassessment, the merch, and the crew t-shirt she’d love to own from one of her favorite films. She also sent us polaroids taken of the new merch.

DOUGLAS GREENWOOD: Seeing Marie Antoinette’s new life—through the anniversary, the documentary, and the book—must have been so beautiful. Where has it sat for you in your own filmography since it was shot?

SOFIA COPPOLA: Oh, I don’t revisit my films much, but I did when working on my book. I’ve always loved my friend Andrew Durham’s set photos. It was really nice to put them all together in a book, revisit that shoot with Kirsten [Dunst] and Jason [Schwartzman] at Versailles, and see the restored film on a big screen again after so long. I’ve never done that before; it was nice to get to celebrate a film that didn’t have much of a release at the time, and wasn’t loved when it came out. It’s fun to share in the enjoyment of it.
I feel like people are excited about Andrew’s work in your world. What’s it been like to share this journey of the film with a friend like that?
I love Andrew’s photos and everyone likes when he visits my set. He’s fun and easy to be around, so he’s able to get photos that no one else could. I love his eye.

I love the life that your films live after they’ve been released, like here in this collection of merch you’ve made with MACK and Important Flowers. Can you talk me through how these pieces came together?

I just thought it would be fun to make some merch because I love the images, and there had been some counterfeit ones using Andrew’s photos, so I thought people might like to have them, and it would be nice for Andrew to benefit from his images (even if it’s a small run).
Is there a film you love that you’d love to own something from? Or to wear a t-shirt adorned with the visuals of?

I was really excited to get a New Order crew t-shirt from when they played at Versailles! I love crew t-shirts. I still have my kid crew t-shirt from Apocalypse Now! And it’s fun to see friends of my kids wearing a Bling Ring crew sweatshirt or something. I would like to have a crew shirt from The Hunger.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

What do you do? I make music, but I like saying my job is just connecting the dots because there’s no laws or limits to art. Tell us about your outfit. My outfit’s steady but also flex-y, smart-casual. What are you doing this weekend? I’m always creating. I’m working on some new music, shooting cool videos, fun stuff. Who first taught you to tie your shoes? My mum. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? I’m in a black era right now.

What do you do? We’re freelance stylists. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Jacob: Jeff Goldblum. His personality is the style. If you had to run between two Tube stops, which ones would you choose? Jacob: Bethnal Green and Mile End because they’re the closest ones together. Lauren: Custom House to Canning Town. Nice scenic run. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? Lauren: A big fur coat.

Who’s your favorite American? Fred Hampton. He was one of the leaders of the Black Panther Party. What’s your side hustle? I’m rebranding my friend’s fashion brand. Doesn’t mean I give it less attention than a main hustle, but that’s the thing that I’m supporting right now! What’s your favorite form of exercise and why? Push-ups and pull-ups at home. I hate going to the gym. What are you doing this weekend? I’m seeing my friend who’s leaving for Australia. I’ve got to sort his Moonpig out ASAP!

What do you do? I’m the editor-in-chief of i-D Magazine. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Me. Which celebrity dad has the best style? My dad. He’s modeled in the Chopova Lowena show, he wears New Balance 990s, and he loves a Ralph Lauren polo. Best grail? This Prada scarf. Who’s your favorite TV dad? Michael Bluth from Arrested Development.

What do you do? I’m a fashion designer. What’s an item of clothing you’ll never part with? This pair of jeans that my boyfriend gave me. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? Gray. What’s your favorite form of exercise? I go to the gym, but I want to pick up tennis.

What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Black music. What are you wearing tonight? Made in the USA 2040 V5 New Balance shoes, Supreme Made in Japan denim, and a Bleue Burnham ring. What are you drinking tonight? Chili margarita, some red wine, Guinness, and water. Got to stay hydrated. What are you doing this weekend? This weekend, it’s the Amsterdam Dance Event where I live. My partner’s going clubbing, so I’m taking care of the kids.

What do you do? I’m a musician, and I play the harp. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? My 1800s Victorian body that is falling apart, but I’ll never let her go. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My dad. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a cemetery walk date with my girlfriend in Abney Park. Who’s your favorite American? Lana Del Rey.

What are you wearing? Hysteric Glamour boots with pink studs, a skirt that my ex-boyfriend gave me, a nice, warm Supreme jacket, and a Goldwin jumper. What are you drinking tonight? Two spicy margaritas, a glass of white wine, and a glass of red wine. Who’s your favorite American? Martine Syms. I like her exhibition at Sadie Coles. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a first date to a wine bar in Hoxton. Do you have a side hustle? Hustling!

What do you do? I work for Homer Jewellery and Louise Konrad Jewellery. Who’s your favorite American? The Tiger King. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? My sweatpants. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Zendaya’s Mugler outfit for the Dune premiere. What are you drinking tonight? Vodka soda.

items.title: The Story of Cécred
items.description: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
items.author: Eni Subair
paragraphs: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
hair NEAL FARINAH FOR CÉCRED
colour direction MASON POOLE

Haircare was always one of the many ways Beyoncé’s family expressed love. Watching her mother Ms. Tina Knowles care for everyone from doctors and judges to the unhoused in her now-famous Houston salon Headliners, Beyoncé saw firsthand how hair can empower and instill confidence in others—and in herself. It was in Ms. Tina’s salon chair, at just 9 years old, where Beyoncé’s appreciation for haircare began.

Decades and dozens of House of Deréon looks later, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina decided to bring their love and appreciation for haircare to the world. In 2024, they turned their lifelong shared passion into Cécred, with Beyoncé as the sole investor, founder, and Chairwoman and Ms. Tina as Vice Chairwoman. Years in the making, the brand was an endeavour worth perfecting—with Beyoncé and Ms. Tina personally testing every product.
Limited copies of the zine are available here.
The quality speaks for itself: Take the Restoring Hair and Edge Drops, which has become the number one hair product in the United States, driven by hair growth testimonials all over social media.

Meanwhile, a heartwarming Father’s Day short film of JAŸ-Z’s loc takedown process, using the brand’s signature Detangling Spray, has offered an intimate glimpse into the family. The love poured into the products only amplifies the scientific truths: These serums, shampoos, and gels really work for you.
This autumn, Cécred jumped across the pond from Los Angeles to London, offering its wide range of products for us Brits at Space NK stores.

To celebrate the UK launch, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina opened up about their hair and their lives. It’s a full-circle moment for the mother-daughter duo, who are sharing the lessons in hair confidence passed down through generations with a whole new audience. For Beyoncé, it’s about more than hair. It’s about continuing her mother’s legacy and making sure everyone feels their best in their hair.
ENI SUBAIR: What has been the most rewarding part of building Cécred?
BEYONCÉ: My mother and I poured decades of experience, tradition, and love into Cécred, so seeing our community grow across every ethnicity, texture, generation, and gender is so fulfilling.

In the beginning, it took some conditioning from the world’s perception of how to launch a brand founded by someone like me. I’m the founder, visionary, and sole investor—not the face or model for this brand. I had a vision to build something that solved real problems and performed so incredibly that the people who can’t stand my music still use Cécred, haaaa! … because it works.
Cécred has been years in the making, so why did 2024 finally feel like the right time to launch?

MS. TINA: Well, we tried to launch it two years earlier, and Beyoncé, you know, she’s a perfectionist. So, with the products, I thought they were amazing, but then I would give them to her, and she would test them on herself, her friends, and her daughters. Then, if one person didn’t have an excellent experience, she would give it back to me. She drove us crazy, and the team was like, “Oh my God!” But I’m so happy that she was so picky about it because it just got better and better. And our testing, research, and development is where we put a lot of money. I was like, this is so crazy expensive because we’re researching and testing so much. We’ve tested on three continents to get all types of hair textures, to make sure that it works on all hair. I had a salon in the ’80s, and what I was told all the time was that our hair was strong because they think that because our hair is coarser, it is stronger. But that is a myth surrounding Black hair. It’s just the opposite. Our hair is the weakest, most fragile hair, and the curlier your hair is, the more texture you have.

And I’ve always studied the science of hair: what it was made of and what it needed. Even making sure to reduce the molecular weight of products so that it can get through the cuticle and build and strengthen the hair.
What lessons have you learned from your mum that have helped you on this journey?

BEYONCÉ: Growing up I saw my mom pour love into others at her salon, and she still does this every day. I love that she trusts that the world is for her. She trusts God. She approaches things with humanity and love. I love my mother’s rebellious spirit. She can spark an idea and make it come to life. She’s fearless and I get that from her. It was in her salon that I witnessed stylists transforming women and helping them get their confidence back and see their beautiful potential. It was more than just getting their hair done, it became a sacred space where they were cared for. That impact resonated so deeply, and I wanted that to be reflected in Cécred and the community we’re building. Your heart carries energy and wisdom from your fingertips.

Recently my mom decided to surprise me by visiting a hair salon in the UK. No calls ahead, no warning. She packed a bag of Cécred, got into the car, and showed up without any pre-planning. Even though one of the managers told her she couldn’t be there, she stuck around and made the owner come. She was determined to build a relationship with the salon owners and clients and ended up spending almost a whole day doing hair there, ha!
What’s your first memory of experimenting with your hair?

BEYONCÉ: One day I decided to cut my own hair. I think I may have cut the whole ponytail off and also cut bangs! I walked in with my ponytail and said, “Mom, put this back on please.” And she was like, “I can’t.” But I thought she could, because I’d seen her be such a hair magician, especially when she would bond hair. Those crazy memories were the foundation of my childhood.
Both you and your mum love Tottenham—where do you like to go? What are your favourite spots?

BEYONCÉ: One of my favourite things about London is the drive to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and passing through Seven Sisters. I love seeing all the communities with their kids, the barber shops, and all the culturally diverse restaurants. As I get closer to the stadium, I start to see the fans who put so much effort into attending the show, either dressed in metallic silver, glistening in the streets and sunshine, or in full cowboy gear, boas, and boots. I can spot my Hive from miles away. When I’m onstage and see all the ethnicities, all the beautiful and fabulous outfits and families, there’s no other experience like it. The melting pot of beautiful diversity in London, particularly at my shows, is something magical to witness.

I love the music scene in the UK. I’ve watched Sienna Spiro grow up from a beautiful young girl to an extraordinarily talented young woman. I’ve known her family well for quite some time. I heard her sing when she was a kid discovering her voice and I can’t articulate the pride she brings me. What a God-given talent! I’m also so proud of Raye, who wrote some of the songs on The Gift. She has had such an anointing. You hear the vulnerability and wisdom in her voice. I also love and respect Olivia Dean. These beautiful women are all kind, have grace, and write and produce their own music. It gives me goosebumps. I just burst with pride when I see them.
Looking back, what was your favourite hairstyle during the B’DAY era, and your favourite look created by your mum?

BEYONCÉ: My favorite hair look was the B’DAY cover updo. That’s stood the test of time and has had such a renaissance this year. I love seeing everyone’s interpretations, and videos and the evolution of the early 2000s look.

My favourite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress—it was gorgeously simple and made with her love. We had a very small wedding in our home. We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends. Wearing a dress, she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress.

You recently re-wore a House of Deréon top that you wore back in 2006 to mark 20 years of B’DAY. What did you love about House of Deréon then that you still love now? What can we find in your archive?

BEYONCÉ: Yes, haaaa! I pulled out the Deréon archive for the Hive for the B’DAY 20th Anniversary re-release. I also had so much fun recreating some of my and my mother’s designs. We brought back the Deréon hoodies and metallic Freakum dresses. I’ll never forget calling my mum the day before the “Freakum Dress” shoot, asking her to make more dresses in more colours because I envisioned match-cutting the colours during the choreography. She was frustrated that I tasked her with making them so last minute, but she and Ty (Tyrone Hunter) got it done. I’m so very thankful for her. I’m so excited to pass all my archives to my kids, especially now that they’re all discovering their own personal style. I’m going to enjoy seeing how they pull from their parents’ carpets and tours if they’re ever interested. Rumi’s favourite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days.

items.title: This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently
items.description: This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change:
items.author: Chris Murphy
paragraphs: This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

“Most important to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and important for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”

Surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have shows that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”

“I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” says O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”

The first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different shows practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

For O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s important to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

This is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby says. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best."

items.title: Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse
items.description: For the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Thef
items.author: Joshua Rivera
paragraphs: For the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Theft Auto III, the series began giving players the freedom to wreak havoc across satirical renditions of US cities. It was an amazing technical feat that only grew more impressive with each subsequent Grand Theft Auto game—and harder to appreciate the more those cities were filled with dick jokes and sex workers.
This, for the most part, suited Grand Theft Auto’s publisher just fine. What business did the company have calling itself Rockstar Games if it cared what a bunch of prudes thought?
But with Grand Theft Auto VI, something has changed. And the game’s staggering launch-day revenue—$3.79 billion—suggests that this change was a welcome one.

Rockstar has executed an astonishing about-face in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing to build a game around a couple depicted with aching sincerity—from their car-boosting meet-cute to the desperate stickups they commit, with the player’s help. Jason Duval (played by Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) are a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, out of options and on the run, hoping they can land a score big enough to turn things around.

This earnestness is new for Grand Theft Auto, which historically has had a deep love for pushing buttons. (Its sister series, the Western Red Dead Redemption, has less of a problem with heart-on-the-sleeve storytelling.) Lucia, especially, is new. She’s the first woman you can play as in the series, and by the transitive property, she’s also the first woman that Grand Theft Auto has ever had to take seriously. Doing so changes the entire shape of the series.

Until now, Grand Theft Auto has never really thought much of women. True, the games have never thought much of anyone; Rockstar traffics in a nihilistic comedy that lies somewhere between South Park and a Verhoeven film, a dim view of the United States where everyone sucks. But women, usually, have sucked the most. They’ve been the butts of countless jokes; in the Grand Theft Auto universe, they’ve been nags and drags and sex workers secondary to the men that the games were about. Grand Theft Auto III, a game that barely has a plot, begins with main character Clyde’s girlfriend betraying him after a heist, shooting him and calling him “small time” before running off with the take. It doesn’t get much better from there.

So yes: Lucia is a huge pivot for the series, especially because Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t trust players with her right away. After a brief prologue in which a desperate stickup goes wrong, Lucia is sent to jail and players begin the game as her boyfriend Jason Duval. In addition to doing odd jobs for a small-time crime boss (Stephen Root) and hanging out with your pal (Bobby Moynihan), players have to choose: Are they going to be a good boyfriend? Rockstar Games know they might be making a big ask of their audience, so they slow-roll it. Before Lucia gets out of jail, the game suggests to the player, maybe fix the stairs? Or get a haircut? Buy her a necklace?

In the days since the game came out, many have noted how amusing it is that Grand Theft Auto VI has made caring about your girlfriend one of its first challenges. The game’s “Lucia will appreciate this” notification is its first viral meme, and the source of both incel crashouts (“woke slop … so obvious it was made by women”) and earnest appreciation. (One of the first clips to spread online was of streamer Stable Ronaldo painting Jason and Lucia's bedroom one color before recoiling in horror: What if she hates that shade?)

Lucia is a destabilizing event not just for gamers, but for Grand Theft Auto—a damning yet fascinating example of gaming culture’s priorities on its biggest stage. GTA has always been a series of warring ambitions: violent Rube Goldberg machine, Karl Ove Knausgaard–esque obsession with quotidian details, and thrilling Hollywood blockbuster all in one. These disparate aims are often in conflict with one another, and one way to read the series’ heretofore exclusively male focus is as an attempt to thread this needle. By tossing all of its commentary under the carpet of “satire," Rockstar can also use a veneer of meanness to argue that the games’ misogyny is actually an intentional lambasting, much like everything else in GTA.

But taking a woman seriously, and making her colead with a male character, requires an entire rethinking of what Grand Theft Auto is. “It’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell,” Grand Theft Auto VI codirector Rob Nelson said when asked by The Guardian if this is the first Grand Theft Auto to encourage empathy from players. “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”

This is an extremely roundabout way of saying that, in this Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar asks gamers to grow up—and punishes them with narrative consequences if they don’t take the game up on the offer.

The funny thing about Grand Theft Auto VI’s gamified empathy is that, like everything else in a video game, it has to teach the player how to accomplish that goal. The game does this through prompting players to do chores, but also through Jason’s characterization. Throughout the game, Rockstar has to convey what its writers believe a well-adjusted man looks like—or at least what constitutes a man well-adjusted enough to earn the respect of a woman like Lucia, who walks out on him when he tries to exclude her from some of his more dangerous criminal activities.

To that end, there are an abundance of moments in the game where Jason demonstrates the virtues of being respectful and maintaining boundaries, several of which are a departure from GTA series norms. There are no sex workers in the game anymore (though there are strip clubs). While Jason and Lucia can break up depending on the player’s choices, there are no other options for committed or casual romance.

The money you steal is ostensibly for Jason and Lucia to use together: so they can get away and start over with their young son, who’s currently entrusted to a relative. Casual conversations between strangers players meet on the road make Jason’s respectful nature both a point and a punchline. There’s one man who’s looking for his missing wife after a night of partying. When he starts to brag about her sexual dexterity, Jason interjects to say, “Hey. Let’s draw a line, bud.”

In some ways, this is all rather embarrassing—though in a different way than the weapons-grade sexism of Grand Theft Autos past. One ought to feel a twinge of shame while marveling at any entertainment franchise for including a woman. Yet Grand Theft Auto VI is being graded on a curve. It has a near-perfect Metacritic score in large part for its depiction of Lucia, and for Jason’s relationship to her. The context speaks to a state of arrested development, both in Grand Theft Auto and in big-budget games writ large.

None of this changes the fact that Lucia really is one of the most well-realized video game characters in a digital city unlike any other. But perhaps her inclusion is less an apology for GTA’s past, and more of a concession to how out of step the series had become with the culture. Because if you’re meant to have empathy for one character, the natural next question is, “Well, what about everyone else?"

Rockstar’s maniacal pursuit of verisimilitude goes a long way here. The game’s animations are so realistic that in GTA VI, shooting unarmed civilians is legitimately unsettling. It’s also disincentivized by a “criminal profile” rating that will mark your character “irredeemable” if you engage in too much wanton violence. (This is not a “game over”—it merely locks players out of achieving a happy ending unless they restart from before their murder spree.) These sorts of limits have become another reliable source of outrage directed at the game, with rage baiters drumming up controversy over Rockstar’s decision to, for example, not permit players to shoot up a nightclub.

This is the tricky reality of encouraging empathy for “those who want to,” as Nelson put it. Rockstar has certain intentions, but so do players—and managing both is the great challenge of making any video game. Empathy is a shock to GTA’s system and to the audience alike.

Replicating humanity with computer software is a daunting and costly task, and one that only Rockstar seems to have the limitless resources to pursue. Those resources—the luxury to work as long as necessary to complete Grand Theft Auto VI, and the obscene amount of money it cost (our only solid figure is “less than $1.5 billion”)—are rapidly dwindling in the video game business, as all available tech funding is vacuumed up by AI companies and private equity loots what’s left. Grand Theft Auto VI may very well be one of one: the most expensive game ever and the last of its kind, the peak of Rockstar’s ambition and also of every big-budget video game. Here, at the end of everything, the biggest of video games has finally decided that it’s time to try empathy. And for a woman, even, should gamers choose (and not all will).

It’s a bit of an indictment of the billion-dollar video game industry that the most expensive game in history is also the first major game to commit to a realistic heterosexual relationship. Grand Theft Auto VI deserves many of the accolades it instantly garnered upon release, but the nature of its accomplishment is not yet fully understood. It’s possible that what Rockstar has built is less a monument to video games’ potential than a magnificent funeral pyre, a testament to how things might’ve turned out if Rockstar’s priorities—and those of everyone chasing after its vision of what video games could be—were just a little bit different.

items.title: The Hunting Wives’ Showrunner “Get[s] Real” About the Inspiration for Netflix’s Steamy MAGA Parable
items.description: In 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and
items.author: Dan Adler
paragraphs: In 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and was already mapping out the TV adaptation in her head.

The plot heavily involved a Texas abortion clinic, and the state had just passed SB 8, one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bills until Roe v. Wade was overturned the following year. As she contemplated bringing The Hunting Wives to life, Cutter saw the political stakes come into focus as well.
“I started thinking about the ‘red state, blue state’ of it,” she tells Vanity Fair ahead of the show’s season two premiere on Thursday. “What if…we really play this culture war?”

The result was one of Netflix’s biggest breakout hits in recent years, sent up in a Saturday Night Live sketch as the “straight but lesbian, horny Republican murder drama.” As a show, Hunting Wives amps up the noirish aspects of the suspense thriller written by May Cobb, a native of the East Texas Piney Woods, and adds a heaping dose of MAGA-adjacent camp. Cutter finishes the mix with plenty of sex scenes, particularly between Malin Akerman’s Margo, a femme fatale partly inspired by Melania Trump who is married to a Republican gubernatorial hopeful, and Brittany Snow’s Sophie, a liberal do-gooder who, like Cutter, arrives in town from a blue corner of Massachusetts. (Cutter was raised in Cambridge and graduated from Wesleyan University, the Connecticut liberal arts college known for its progressive politics and pipeline to Hollywood.)

Hunting Wives executive producer Erwin Stoff told Cutter he’d pay for her to go to Texas to meet Cobb and breathe the Piney Woods air herself. She met Cobb’s father and her best friend from high school. She shot skeet with the women—she even got it in three, just as Sophie does in the first season. At a high-end Dallas shopping area where the likes of Gucci can be found, Cutter got a better sense of the hair, clothes, and bodies of her eventual characters. “I understand the notion that Sophie could be amused and entertained and intrigued by these women,” Cutter says, “and eventually seduced.”

Cutter thinks of the show primarily in terms of its tonal mash-up: “I think we managed to wrangle it into one piece of art,” she says, “but there’s comedy, there’s violence, there’s noir, there’s soap, there’s earnest emotion.” To the extent that she assigned any political beliefs to the rich white women of Cobb’s novel, it was in the spirit of grounding her characters in the specifics of their world. Still, as we speak, Cutter decides “to get real with it.”

“The whole thing was a little bit of a parable, in my mind, of how you could fall for someone like [Donald] Trump,” she admits. “Sophie has her principles, but they only go so far. They end right where something starts to make her feel good.” Cutter was as curious as anyone else from her educated milieu about the quirkier aspects of Trump, like the Diet Coke button he had installed on the Resolute Desk. How liberating must it feel to embrace a movement so openly untethered from the pieties of politics and taste?
“Not that my show is a deep dive on Trump,” Cutter says, “but maybe there is an element that’s sort of looking under the hood.”

The twisted love story between Margo and Sophie entangles all of the wealthy, hard-drinking, gun-toting women in their orbit, and its central killing—one of several propelling the show forward, with a third season slated to begin filming this year—stems from an effort to cover up Margo’s abortion as her NRA-loving husband plots his political ascent. (In this proudly oversexed town, he has his own share of affairs.) Hunting Wives is the rare Netflix soap to receive steady coverage from mainstream national outlets; the fascination undoubtedly has something to do with the impression that, like Yellowstone or Morgan Wallen before it, the show unlocks something about MAGA’s cultural staying power. In a New York Times guest essay this month that evaluated the post-2024 Hollywood landscape, Sharon Waxman, the editor in chief of The Wrap, wrote, “From Melania on Amazon’s streaming service to The Hunting Wives on Netflix to the ever-expanding Taylor Sheridan universe on Paramount+ to Bari Weiss’s being put in charge of CBS News, the vibe shift was visible on all our screens.”

Cutter says she had no particular agenda nor any “ultra-evil villain plan of how it was going to be received or how it would be culturally relevant.” But Hunting Wives is sprinkled with enough proper nouns—a Peter Thiel mention here, a Walmart reference there—and distinctly modern aesthetics that she can acknowledge its appeal as something of a Rosetta stone for the moment in MAGA femininity. Even in the ostensibly waning days of the movement, the plastic surgery and soaring heels continue to captivate and horrify coastal elites. Cutter says that Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), another of Margo’s lovers, has a bit of Kristi Noem and Marjorie Taylor Greene in her: that “sort of slightly butch, real gun, real ‘back the blue’ [element]…the toughness of those women.”

The second season of Hunting Wives maintains the slipperiness that keeps the show from veering into moralism; it stands apart from other Trump-era art in its refusal to take sides. “I think I remember, in the pitch, someone saying, ‘But will red-state people like it too?’” Cutter recalls. “I was like, ‘I think so.’” Both Margo and Sophie are awash in their respective red and blue stereotypes, but neither is more admirable than the other. Their sordid union is a testament to the flexibility of both their principles and their preferences. From one vantage, it is, in the end, all about sex.

“Margo is the symbol of freedom and sexuality and feminine power and empoweredness and selfishness that [Sophie] feels she’s lost,” Cutter says, adding that Akerman’s comfort in such a role helped drive her liberal use of physical intimacy. “The audience may disagree with me,” she says, but “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes. I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.” Last year, though, when Netflix acquired Hunting Wives, which was initially ordered by Starz in 2023, Cutter had a more practical concern.
“I literally googled,” she recalls, “‘Does Netflix show boobs?’”

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed For Weather
items.description: While families across the nation gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday, one tradition will look a little different this year. The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for weather, according to NBC News. The parade is now expected to t
items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: While families across the nation gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday, one tradition will look a little different this year. The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for weather, according to NBC News. The parade is now expected to take place on Saturday.

Weather experts have been warning U.S. residents about a rapidly approaching storm system making its way up the east coast, bringing with it high winds, heavy rains, and flood warnings. According to CNN, winds in New York City are expected to reach around 25 to 35 mph — which would be dangerous for the parade’s famous floats and giant balloons.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said in a statement. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

This is the first time the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has been postponed because of inclimate weather. It was cancelled in 1942, 1943, and 1944 because the U.S. needed all excess helium and rubber for the World War II effort.

But past windy parades might provide insight into the decision to postpone this year’s. During the 1997 parade, winds broke a Barney the Dinosaur balloon and pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into buildings, injuring one bystander. In 1998, a “Where The Wild Things Are” balloon hit a lamppost during its debut parade and had to be removed. In 2006 and 2019, parade officials had to lower the height of the balloons to avoid aggressive wind and subsequent damage.

More than 3 million people were expected to watch the parade along its 2.5 mile route. Grammy-nominated singer Raye was expected to open the parade with a holiday performance featuring her sisters, Amma and Absolutely; followed by floats and performances by Wyclef Jean, Smash Mouth, Natasha Bedingfield, Icona Pop, JoJo, Hunger Games star McKenna Grace, and Queen Latifah. No additional changes to the parade programming or lineup have been announced.

items.title: The Hunting Wives Season-Premiere Recap: Madam Justice
items.description: Police sirens, lesbian sex dreams, and gunshots? That’s right, baby: The Hunting Wives is back in action for season two. Grab your best cowboy hat and the longest set of acrylics you have, because there is a lot to cover!
items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: Police sirens, lesbian sex dreams, and gunshots? That’s right, baby: The Hunting Wives is back in action for season two. Grab your best cowboy hat and the longest set of acrylics you have, because there is a lot to cover!

As is always the case with these shows, we begin with a flashback. Cops pouring into a driveway; Jonny the sheriff demanding that whoever is holding Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman) hostage come out with their hands up. Is anyone surprised to see Sophie (Brittany Snow) shaking and holding a gun before we cut back in time to one week ago?

Sophie’s trying to put her life back together in the wake of the events of last season, but you have to imagine it’s not super easy to do when you are still having (hot) sex dreams about the woman whose brother you killed. And sure enough, Sophie’s sex dream is rudely interrupted by a vision of bloodied and battered Kyle. She manages to shake it off long enough to remind Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) that they have couples therapy today. Oh GOD, she’s trying to make it work with that absolute bore of a man? Madam, denial is a river in Egypt; YOU are gay! Therapy is rough to watch as Sophie ties herself in knots trying to make it seem like she loves being in the “box” that is the life of a wife and mother. Yes, she used to party and drink a lot, and yes, there was a woman back then too, but she doesn’t want to be that wild person anymore! She wants containment and safety; who cares if that means feeling trapped? I have never done couples therapy, but I am kinda eyeing this therapist and hoping she will jump into Sophie’s rant about wanting to be back in a box and say, “Hey, so that sounds like repressing a lot of who you are to fit in this role; that could be bad!” Graham doesn’t understand why Sophie is going through all this work to fix their marriage, because he, like me, remembers last season when Sophie told him she didn’t see him in her future. What changed? Helpfully, Sophie has a flashback to killing Kyle, so we all remember why she wants to get back together. I don’t know how being with Graham will save her from getting caught, to be honest! Sounds like you’ll just be jumpy and scared for the rest of your life, plus you’ll live with a man. Bad!

Wanda and Walter, the only cops who actually work in Maple Brook, are trying to track down the pickup truck they found in the middle of the road next to a pool of blood. You know it’s Kyle’s truck; I know it’s Kyle’s truck; damn near everybody knows it’s Kyle’s truck but the cops themselves. Dramatic irony, hello! Wanda discovers the car was stolen eight months ago in Fort Worth, but hits a roadblock with the Fort Worth PD. No time to worry about that, for there is another dead body in the woods. They have nothing to help them identify this young woman, but Wanda spots a tattoo on her wrist. Aha! She would have had to show ID for a tattoo, and the shop should keep records. Off they go, lights and sirens blaring.

Surely Margo is having fun, though, right? It can’t all just be dead bodies and panic attacks! Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is running for governor, and she is playing the loving and doting wife, talking about coming from nothing and life with a mother who was addicted to drugs. The people love her; she and Jed hold hands and smile, everything is great! … until they get offstage and it becomes clear Jed is still pissed about the events of last season. Fair enough, my guy! Not only was your wife sleeping with a teenager, but she got pregnant by him and then killed his girlfriend. One of the tougher marital issues to overcome, I think. Jed leaves Margo quite literally in the dust, with his hands all over his campaign manager’s ass. All she can do is play her part and chain-smoke in the pool house while sending Sophie “thinking of you” and “can we talk” texts. When those go unanswered, there is only one person left to call: her ex, Callie.

Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) is possibly the only person for whom the events of last season led to something positive. We see assistants bustling around a new house, setting up lights and taking test shots of Jonny, who wants to be sure his boots are in frame. Callie’s “heroic” antics from last season (killing an innocent woman) have led to — what else — a reality show. Married Justice (perfect title, no notes) has its first shoot tonight! She’s got a fake house to live in for the shoot and, hold on a moment, what’s this? A super-hot brunette with a cunty bob, messy eyeliner, and a leather jacket? Hello, producer Nadia (Kim Matula)! She reminds Callie that she is the STAR of Married Justice, and honey? Stars get to ask for whatever they want. There is a gorgeous long pause after this while the two of them look at each other, and I am rooting for these two to start fucking, like, ASAP.

First, Margo has to check in with Nadia about this whole “law enforcement” angle the show is aiming for. She’s not particularly subtle with her questions, but Nadia assures her that this show is absolutely about this group of women, first and foremost. The law enforcement part is just the cherry on top, she chirps cheerfully, before getting Margo changed, wired, and onto the party bus. Things I am a sucker for: brunettes and women who lie to get what they want. I fear I may be in trouble! Nadia dazzles and delights all the women on the party bus — you can almost see their eyes get wide with dreams of having more Instagram followers. Everyone performs beautifully on-camera for her. If you can’t admit that a well-executed line dance whips, you are a loser! Them’s the breaks, sorry to report!

Sophie is chatting with Jack (her kid, you can go ahead and forget him now; he doesn’t matter) on FaceTime before Graham interrupts with a pressing question. $1,500 credit card charge to an auto-body shop? What’s that all about, guv’nor? Sophie, shocked that her husband checks their credit card statement, barely manages to stammer that she hit an armadillo, and she definitely told him about it, don’t be silly, of course she did! Graham is like, “… Okay, whatever, just send me the footage from the Tesla so I can get an insurance claim.” “What footage from the Tesla?,” Sophie wants to know, in a way that is not at all casual but rather obviously panicked. Graham tells her exactly where the USB is, and she puts that to good use by boiling it. In case you miss what she is doing, there is a helpful, absolutely added-in-post line: “Try recovering data from this now, Elon.”

To her credit, Nadia waits maybe a whole 20 minutes while the girls chatter on-camera before dropping that this feels like a really natural time to start talking about Abby Jackson. Margo flares up instantly, trying to insist that it’s too dark and macabre for a night out. There’s no need to dig all that old stuff up again, is there? Callie, who is down to do whatever it takes to ensure her show is a hit, drops something even juicier: Cops found another dead girl in the woods. What is happening to their perfect little town? Margo sits through it as long as she can stand, before dragging Callie to the bathroom. She’s got questions about Nadia and her inventions but also couldn’t help but wonder if Callie has heard from Sophie at all? No reason, juuuuust wondering! Not surprisingly, Sophie has not reached out to her ex’s ex, and faced with disappointment but a woman who wants her, Margo does what she does best: pulls Callie into a stall and gets fucked while Tanner Adell’s “Do-Si-Don’tcha” plays. Award-winning television, IMO!

Nadia is shooting Jonny in his office, briefing them about the body that they found in the woods. Her name was Elly Gates, and Wanda and Walter (sorry, it’s so, so dumb, but it’s sooo fun that their names start with W) are en route to talk with the foster mother right now. The little moment after Nadia calls “cut” and Jonny triumphantly slams his hand on the desk in satisfaction really made me laugh. We might as well get it out of the way now: I am kind of a sucker for Jonny’s big dumb gay ass! Nadia earns my love anew by dangling her hot cameraman for Jonny to take around the office to get some background shots. I laughed again when he suggested the showers, sorry! Is there anyone on earth who was surprised that Nadia immediately snooped in Jonny’s files for the Abby Jackson case?

Elly’s foster mother does not give a convincing performance of a woman who is concerned, and Wanda clocks it right away. To her credit, her foster mother doesn’t pretend and drops the mask almost instantly. Her rant about Elly getting hooked on pills by some loser gets to Wanda, who runs outside to weep. Walter is right by her side, nodding calmly as she rants about being fine. Things just get to her sometimes, okay? And that girl had no one, just a bitchy foster mom who didn’t even notice she was gone. Those things get to you; I get it! And let’s just shout out Karen Rodriguez for her performance as Wanda; I find her SO charming in this role.

Hey, was anyone thinking we were a little low on plot? Good news, here’s a new one! On her way to her “Stars, They’re Just Like Us” photo shoot at the Giant Penny, Margo gets run off the road by a motorcycle gang led by Zelda, played by the great and good Dale Dickey.
