items.title: The Best Gifts For Your Mani-Obsessed Friends, According To Top Nail Artists
items.description: 22 Gifts That’ll Make Any Nail Lover’s Day
items.author: Iman Balagam
paragraphs: 22 Gifts That’ll Make Any Nail Lover’s Day
Experts share their favorite gifts for the manicure enthusiasts in your life.

Gift-giving can be stressful, especially when your loved ones aren’t exactly sending you neatly organized wish lists divided by price point (my sisters). Thankfully, shopping for someone with a particular passion — like nails — can make things a little easier.

Whether they’re curing their own nails at home with a UV lamp, recreating Hailey Bieber’s latest mani design at the salon every two weeks, or spending a small fortune on nail art without batting an eye, there’s no shortage of options for these friends. Because even the smallest upgrades to their nail routine can feel like a major treat.

To help narrow things down, Bustle polled top manicurists for their favorite nail-centric products to gift. Think reparative treatments for the friend who’s trying to recover from years of biting their nails, cuticle oils that won’t leave their fingers feeling greasy, and hand creams they’ll want to proudly display on their nightstand. And, of course, you can’t go wrong with gifting a new polish shade for their collection.
Below are the best gifts your mani-obsessed loved ones will actually be excited to unwrap.

A hand cream is always a safe bet, particularly during the colder months. Manicurist Vikki Swan recommends this L’Occitane formula, which contains 20% shea butter to nourish dry skin. “It’s a luxurious yet practical gift that complements any manicure routine,” she says.

For the friend who prefers the naked nail look, Swan adores this nourishing polish from Manucurist. “I love how this treatment combines nail care with a beautiful, translucent pink tint and glossy finish,” she says. Designed to nourish and strengthen natural nails, it can be used on both fingers and toes without a base coat, top coat, or UV/LED lamp.
3For The Seasonal Nail Enthusiast

If you’re shopping for someone who swears by a classic holiday manicure, manicurist Viktoriia Voloshyna loves this rich burgundy shade from Gelcare. She calls it her “go-to winter red,” noting that it looks polished on almost every skin tone. “It works for any style, from short natural nails to long ones, and it looks elegant on its own without any nail art,” she says.
4The Handbag Hydration Hero

Cuticle oil is one of those little luxuries your nail-obsessed friend will actually use. Manicurist Elle Gerstein calls this Essie option the perfect stocking stuffer. “I always tell my clients that cuticle oil is a daily essential, especially during the winter,” she says. “I love the roller applicator because you can keep it in your handbag and use it throughout the day.”
5For The Friend Who Loves Options

Gerstein is also a fan of Dazzle Dry’s mini polish collections, particularly this festive set. “The colors are sophisticated, festive, and a little edgy,” she says. “I love gifting mini collections because they encourage people to experiment with colors they might not normally gravitate toward without committing to a full-size bottle.”

Cold-weather feet deserve a little TLC, too. Manicurist Olivia de Montagnac swears by this pedicure kit, which includes everything you need for at-home foot maintenance. “We are not neglecting our feet this winter,” she says. “The callus remover is my all-time favorite, and I like that the exfoliating pads are disposable.”

De Montagnac also recommends this holiday trio from Celisse, featuring three shades that are basically guaranteed to earn a spot in anyone’s polish rotation. “Everything from Celisse is thoughtfully designed and curated,” she says. And the velvet packaging is just one more reason it deserves a spot under the tree.

For a gift that goes beyond the usual nail-care staples, de Montagnac recommends this buttery balm from Summer Fridays. The luxe formula delivers a hefty dose of hydration anywhere from hands to heels. “I use it on my hands, but I also love using it on my legs and feet for a massage,” she says. “Vanilla smells amazing, but Pistachio is my favorite!”

Hand sanitizer may not scream exciting gift, but this set makes the everyday essential feel a little more luxe. Manicurist Marisa Carmichael loves the formulas, which cleanse while keeping hands moisturized. “These are my favorite sanitizers. The scents are gorgeous and not overpowering, and they have a moisturizing serum that leaves hands soft and clean.” Think of it as K-beauty for your hands.
10A Five-Star Cuticle Treatment

If your friend likes her nail care with a side of luxury, Carmichael recommends this cuticle cream. “It feels so elegant and has a really fresh scent,” she says. She's also a fan of its hydrating formula, which nourishes cuticles without leaving behind a greasy residue.
11For Nails In Their Recovery Era

For the friend whose nails have seen better days, Carmichael recommends this bond-repair treatment. “It’s a liquid that penetrates the nail plate and bonds to make nails stronger,” she explains. Even better, it can be worn underneath nail polish, so they don't have to sacrifice their regular mani routine while nursing their nails back to health.

A good body oil is always appreciated, and manicurist Marielle Co says this one is a standout. “Every time I’ve used this product on a client, they rave about it,” she says. “Not only does it smell amazing, but it leaves the skin with a beautiful glow without feeling greasy. It is so nourishing and hydrating. I love that it can be used all over the body, especially on the hands and cuticles.”
13For The Nail-Care Overachiever

Some manicure devotees take their nail health routine very seriously. For these friends, Co recommends adding a strengthening treatment to the mix. “Our nails rely on keratin, so keeping them strong and hydrated is key,” she says. “I always tell my clients that nail health starts with taking care of the natural nail underneath the polish. Strengthening treatments can help improve resilience and reduce breakage — especially if you're trying to avoid those dreaded broken nails.”
14A Paris Fashion Week-Approved Mani

Co first discovered Manucurist backstage at Paris Fashion Week and has been a fan ever since. Known for its vegan, plant-based formulas and more conscious approach to nail care, the brand makes some of her favorite manicure essentials. “I love having a few clean, easy-to-use essentials on hand, and this kit covers three things I think are important: hydration, color, and overall nail health,” she says. “It’s perfect for someone who loves keeping their nails looking polished while still prioritizing the health of their natural nails.”
15For The Nail Art Chameleon

Press-on nails are the ultimate gift for the friend who's rocking a different design every time you see them. Co loves this brand for its range of options across skin tones, shapes, lengths, and designs. “It’s a great way to experiment with different nail looks without committing to a salon appointment,” she says. “There's something for just about everyone's personal style.”
16A Personalized Mani Upgrade

Manicurist Sonya Belakhlef loves this cuticle pen for its luxe feel and customizable, monogrammed pouch. It's also at the top of their own holiday shopping list. “I personally am gifting my clients these pens this year!”
17The Unexpected Nail-Care Essential

For the friend who spends a lot of time behind the wheel, Belakhlef recommends these treatment-boosting gloves. They're a thoughtful alternative to yet another bottle of nail polish — especially for someone whose collection is already overflowing. “I love using these gloves in the car for sun protection,” they say.
18The Ultimate Hand-Care Splurge

If they aren’t messing around with their hand care routine, Belakhlef suggests going all out with this red and near-infrared light therapy glove. Think of it as the gift of 10 minutes of mandatory, phone-free self-care.
A good hand serum should feel as lovely as it works. Belakhlef recommends Sidia for its beautiful scents and textures, and particularly enjoys incorporating its serum into their routine.

Cuticle oil might seem like a simple gift, but it's one they'll actually put to use. Manicurist Sandra Wei recommends looking for a formula with nourishing ingredients like jojoba oil and vitamin E to help ward off dryness and hangnails. “It’s especially beneficial for those who regularly get gel manicures, as daily cuticle care helps keep the skin surrounding the nails soft and well-maintained,” she says.
21Beauty Sleep For Your Hands

For a more indulgent at-home treatment, Wei recommends overnight moisturizing gloves. “I recommend applying a nourishing hand cream and cuticle oil before putting on soft cotton gloves at bedtime to help retain moisture and keep the skin around the nails soft and hydrated,” she says. It's a simple way to turn an everyday hand-care routine into a relaxing at-home spa ritual.
22The Good-Hands Guarantee

Wei is also a big believer in keeping a good hand cream within reach, especially during the colder months. She recommends looking for formulas with moisturizing ingredients like shea butter, glycerin, or ceramides to help protect against seasonal dryness. “This is especially important during the colder months, when the skin around the nails tends to become dry and rough. A good hand cream makes a wonderful holiday gift because it encourages a convenient moment of everyday self-care.”

items.title: Mars In Virgo Is Here — & Patience Proves To Be A Virtue
items.description: Mars In Virgo Is Here — & Patience Proves To Be A Virtue
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: Mars In Virgo Is Here — & Patience Proves To Be A Virtue

There is beauty in routine, which isbrought to us from Mars in Virgo. Our daily rituals can revive and refresh us;knowing what comes next is part of the game that strengthens our demeanor anddrives us toward success. The unpredictable heightens our anxiety and stressbecause we need to know how to proceed strategically and cautiously as we moveforward. Also, the urge to reflect on how we react reminds us to avoid conflictwithout a goal in mind. In other words, we want to make up and not let the fightdrag on. We can forgive and forget.

Mars in Virgo is not about winning, butrather recognizing patterns and using the information for our advancement. Wearen't looking to sit on the throne, but to be the authority pulling thestrings behind the scenes. Fame and acclaim might be for others — we arethirsty for knowledge. Only then can we proclaim our superiority and dominance.Until that moment arrives, it's totally fine to cut to the bottom of matterswith precision in an effort to contain problems and seize control.

items.title: I'm 33, I Make $153K & I'm Treating Myself To A Broadway Show
items.description: A Week In Queens, NY On A $153,600 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In Queens, NY On A $153,600 Salary
If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email.
Please note: Money Diaries will be taking a hiatus for the next several weeks.
Industry: Marketing Tech/AI
Location: Queens, New York

Joint Income/Financial Setup: My husband's income is roughly $35,000, so our joint income is $188,600. He moved from another country two years ago and is currently interviewing after finishing his cybersecurity bootcamp program. We maintain separate personal checking and savings accounts, along with a joint checking (that we use to cover our shared bills) and savings account. I contribute $3,000 per month to the joint account, while he contributes $1,000. For our individual expenses, we pay directly from our individual accounts.
Joint Savings Account: $28,000
Life Insurance Investment Account: $150,000
Debt: $10,000 school loans
Paycheck Amount (twice a month): $3,574 after 401k/HSA deductions, plus $350 every month as I'm a pension recipient
Housing Costs: $2,010 - We rent a one-bedroom apartment in Queens
Loan Payments: I'll soon setup school loan payments but for now we're paying $1K for car payments (includes insurance and lease)
Google Fi cell: $153 (for myself, husband, and mom)
Rent the Runway membership: $142.44

Absolutely, I'm African (Nigerian, to be specific), so higher education goes without saying. I realize how much of a blessing it was that my mom worked to pay for my education so I took out zero loans for undergrad. I have a big community, so I also received up to $5K from family members to help with books, food, and other miscellaneous items. I've actually returned to school to pursue my Masters and I took out loans for that ($10K) which I will start paying off this semester now that I've started a new job.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

I was given the typical "save your money, don't spend all of it" speech growing up. My mom didn't finish school in our home country. Instead, she worked to help put her younger brother through school, so she always emphasized working hard, saving money, and being responsible with what you have. At some point, I realized how far behind I was financially and in many ways, still am. Since then, I've been doing everything I can to put measures in place to become more financially responsible and get myself on a better path.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

My first job was as a resident advisor at a prestigious school for a summer political program. I attended the program summer before my senior year of high school and loved it so much that I went back to work for them for two summers. The first summer I made a little over $1K for the two months and the second year it was a little over $1,200. It was the most I had ever gotten on my own. I, thankfully so, wasn't put in a position where I had to work throughout high school or work during college to help pay for things in the house. The money I made was my money and I spent it on clothes and food.
Did you worry about money growing up?

I didnt know we were "poor" until I got to college and saw what people had/did with their parents' money. Even then, I had everything I needed and was pretty content. It was when I graduated college and came back home that I officially started worrying about money, my savings, and my future.
Do you worry about money now?

I worry about money in the sense of wondering whether I'm doing enough with it — how I can make more, save more, and make sure I'm putting it in the right places. I'm constantly wondering if I'm contributing enough to the right accounts or investing the way I should be. The list of things I could be doing always seems to grow. I really need to set aside a day to sit down, do the research, and organize my money so I can feel confident that I'm making the right decisions.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I became financially responsible at 30 when my husband moved to the U.S. to join me. This was also when I moved out on my own, got my own apartment, and became responsible for my own expenses and bills. But even, and still today, I've had the support of my family as a safety net if i were to ever lose my income or housing. I actually lost my income in March when I was laid off and my husband really stepped up and took on all of our bills. If we were ever in a situation where we both lost our income, we know we could rely on my family for support while we got back on our feet.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
I receive $350 per month as the designated beneficiary of my father's pension following his passing. I also received $25K from his life insurance some years ago.

Yesterday, I mentioned to my husband how relaxing our weekend felt and how I wasn't rushing to cook meals. He suggested we get a whiteboard for the fridge, so it'll help us and my mom (who watches my toddler during work hours) know what meals to feed him. I ordered a magnetic board on Amazon. I was also needing floss, but held off because I've been trying to buy from mom-and-pop shops but haven't actually had the time or opportunity to go in-store. I added Cocofloss to my cart and a paddle brush for my hair. I also added this book I've been eyeing The Things You Can See Only When You Slow Down, but I don't buy it yet. I'll finish my book for motivation, so I leave it in the cart. $47.55
useful andin the mood to cook.

This made me realize how much money I spend on breakfast and lunch. I'm really focused on saving money, and I can see that I'm spending a lot each week on food when I could be meal prepping and putting that money toward my savings instead. Tracking my spending was helpful because it showed me how quickly those little purchases add up. As I mentioned, my husband is currently interviewing, so I'd be interested in documenting our finances once things settle down. Hopefully, we'll be able to have a more even split financially, and I'll be able to save more.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
Do you have a Money Diary you'd like to share? Submit it with us here.
Have questions about how to submit or our publishing process? Read our Money Diaries FAQ doc here or email us here.

items.title: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
items.description: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa; Jacqueline Kilikita
paragraphs: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
Flamingo Estate Prinsesstårta Candle

Inspired by NYC institution Sant Ambroeus' Swedish Princess Cake, this impossibly chic Flamingo Estate candle is a sweet treat for the senses. With notes of lemon peel, neroli leaves, toasted cinnamon, amber, and warm incense, it's the perfect gift for the gourmand fragrance lover on your list.
Nest New York Birchwood Pine

You’ll be hard-pressed to find another candle that captures the holiday spirit like Nest’s Birchwood Pine. Crisp notes of white pine and balsam fir meet comforting birchwood, musk, and amber to transform any space into an idyllic winter forest. Plus, the three-wick jumbo size will last well into the new year.
L'Occitane Veillée Pralinée Scented Candle

Capture the cozy magic of a kitchen filled with freshly baked treats with this deliciously warm, nutty candle. Notes of golden praline, creamy sandalwood, and sweet vanilla come together for an irresistibly comforting gourmand scent.
Glasshouse Fragrances Velvet Rhapsody Candle

Aussie candle brand Glasshouse is so underrated. The scent projection is just as good as any designer candle, and my favorite has to be Velvet Rhapsody. Creamy jasmine is spliced with zippy yuzu citrus and fresh waterlily, resulting in a scent that’s unmistakably floral but incredibly clean.
Sidia x Sofie Pavitt Face The Studio Candle

NYC-based facialist Sofie Pavitt is the ultimate “IYKYK” name on any skincare savant’s lips, so when she teamed up with Erin Kleinberg’s lifestyle brand Sidia, we knew we were in for a treat. The result between these two powerhouse founders is The Studio, inspired by Pavitt’s downtown hotspot. Featuring invigorating yuzu and neroli alongside an earthy base of blonde woods, rose water, and white musk, it’s the perfect candle for the beauty lover who’s always ahead of the curve.

You might know Jenni Kayne as the brand behind plush cashmere sweaters and elevated home décor, but word to the wise this year: Don’t sleep on the candles. Our choice pick for an unforgettable gift that’ll impress even the bougiest friend is Aspen, which juxtaposes crisp notes of balsam fir, eucalyptus, and cypress with bright, juicy grapefruit for a result that’s festive yet unexpected.

If you have a little less to spend, go for Cozy Earth’s Gather candle. Earthy cinnamon, warming bourbon, and smoked wood give it a leathery, brooding quality — perfect if they like deeper, more complex scents. It’s a soy and coconut wax blend, which also means better indoor air quality, if that matters to them.
Bath & Body Works Cypress + Cedar Candle

This is not your average Bath & Body Works Candle. With an elevated ceramic votive (which can be repurposed to house everything from makeup brushes to paper clips), these candles make an excellent gift for anyone with a soft spot for the iconic mall brand’s multi-wick candles. Cypress + Cedar is a grown-up take on your favorite Christmas tree scent, with wintry notes of warm roasted chestnut, pine, cedarwood, and tonka bean.
Loewe Tomato Leaves Candle

Loewe’s Tomato Leaves candle is oddly addictive, and the vessel is so undeniably chic, you’ll forgive them for not wanting to light it. It perfectly captures the sweet, green, spicy, and fuzzy scent of crushing tomato leaves between your fingers. If they’re into growing veg and plants on their porch or balcony, they’ll adore this.

Every cool girl owns a Diptyque Tubereuse candle, and if you ask me, it’s the brand’s best — and most compliment-worthy — scent. It’s a creamy, heady floral that feels intoxicating in the best way. It’s also one of Diptyque’s most popular wedding candles, so if they’re getting married this year and thinking about scenting their wedding, they’re likely to fall in love with this one.
Jo Loves Black Cashmeran & Tonka Candle

They’ll burn through this faster than you can strike a match — it’s that good. The initial notes of bitter orange, zippy ginger, and warming cardamom give way to a glug of rich rum, vanilla-esque tonka bean, and creamy cedarwood. It fills my entire apartment with a scent that’s as cozy as a cashmere blanket — which makes sense, considering Jo Malone (of fragrance fame) is the mastermind behind the dreamy brand.

items.title: My dog had separation anxiety, I had PTSD. How did we cope?
items.description: I slip my feet into my sneakers, the laces pre-tied. My coat lies in the crook of my elbow. I slide my forearm through my purse strap and lift my keys off the entryway hook, the blades clinking ever so slightly. I wince and hold my breath, praying he didn’t he
items.author: Tracy Strauss
paragraphs: I slip my feet into my sneakers, the laces pre-tied. My coat lies in the crook of my elbow. I slide my forearm through my purse strap and lift my keys off the entryway hook, the blades clinking ever so slightly. I wince and hold my breath, praying he didn’t hear and won’t rush from the living room barking his orders, demanding I stay.

I’ve performed this routine hundreds of times, and yet adrenaline runs through my fingers like a current of electricity, paradoxically paralysing and mobilising me, as my knuckles bend around the door handle.
I tell myself go, though I’m afraid of the consequences.
You might be thinking that I live with an abusive spouse, but I don’t. I live with a dog who has separation anxiety. Some days I felt like his prisoner.

At 52, I haven’t lived a traditional woman’s life: I’ve never been married or close to engaged. I’ve never had kids, never raised a family. I’ve never allowed myself to fall in love, though not for lack of wanting.

When I was a teenager and my parents’ marital problems grew vocal and visible, relatives and friends stopped visiting. Isolation and silence overtook our home. I felt as if I’d been shipwrecked with my mother and father on a toxic abandoned island.
My mother told me she had nightmares about the house I’d grown up in

Behind closed doors, my father was abusive. Living in our house didn’t feel safe, but neither did leaving. I wanted to meet my peers for ice cream at Friendly’s, but the idea of going out gave me a stomach ache.
‘Go,’ my mother said, her glassy blue eyes dodging my gaze. ‘I’ll be fine.’

Decades later, long divorced and before her death, my mother told me she had nightmares about the house I’d grown up in: ‘He’s always there,’ she said, though my father had left and my mother had sold the house and moved. ‘I can never leave.’

Sometimes I’ll have this nightmare: I’m running from my childhood bedroom, down the stairs of our split-level suburban ranch, to the bolted front door, my heart pounding as my hand grasps, then turns, the doorknob. I pray I can escape.

When I was a girl, I begged my parents for a puppy, a companion. What I was really looking for was love. The answer was no, but my father said he could be my pretend dog. He got down on all fours and panted and pawed my body. He pushed me over and got on top of me. He assaulted me. My childhood dream of love, and family, died hard.
As an adult, I thought I could right my wrong.

Unpartnered and almost 47, during the acute loneliness of the COVID-19 pandemic I adopted a puppy: Beau was a sweet, smart, playful yellow Lab mix found under a drug house in Mississippi, though when we met I didn’t know his history. He was transported to New England, and came to live with me in my small city condo, just outside of Boston. I imagined he and I would do everything together: he’d be my jogging buddy, my backseat driver, my soul mate.
Going out on a date, or just to check the mail, was out of the question

But Beau barked and lunged at people on rollerblades and skateboards, so jogging together wasn’t feasible. In the car, when he saw scooter riders on our congested streets, he punctured the side door’s interior with his claws.

While I was at the supermarket, he self-destructed – barking, hyperventilating, and soiling himself. Going out on a date, or just to check the mail, was out of the question. My friends told me not to worry, just let him cry it out, like a baby. But Beau didn’t have run-of-the-mill separation anxiety. His, as I came to learn, was a severe clinical case requiring medication and intense training, which I diligently, doggedly pursued. I didn’t fathom that when everyone I knew had long left their pandemic quarantine, I’d still be living in relative isolation. My friends began to suggest I re-home Beau.
But I loved him. I couldn’t bear to give him up, or give up period.

Vowing to find a solution to what seemed an impossible problem, I hired a behaviourist trainer who specialised in separation anxiety. We spent 10 months on pre-departure cue desensitisation – approach the door; put on your coat; put on your shoes, pick up your keys – and 18 months on leaving the premises with Beau home by himself for a few seconds, working our way to 20 minutes.
The first time I left my building without Beau, the trainer watched the pet camera video feed for me from her home, so that I could take a walk without constant monitoring.

‘I’m at the bakery,’ I texted the trainer as the smell of coffee, chocolate croissants, pecan muffins and cheesecake brownies awakened my desire to be out in the world, to live. I felt anxious and eyed the clock. I might not have time to wait my turn. ‘There’s a line. Should I stay or go home?’
‘Stay,’ the trainer replied. ‘Beau’s calm. He’s lying on the floor with his eyes closed.’
For an entire year his anxiety regressed to the point I couldn’t leave him alone

When I reached the front of the line, I ordered not one but a handful of baked goods, thinking I’d better stock up since I wasn’t sure when or if I’d be able to come again. As the cashier handed me my bag-to-go, I felt as if I was both receiving an Olympic medal and robbing a bank.
A simple outing felt both extraordinary and forbidden.
Twenty minutes solo eventually led to 45.

Just when I thought we were almost home free, the unthinkable happened: while I was at work, Beau was attacked at doggie daycare. He needed emergency surgery to repair the physical damage. His emotional wounds were more complicated to heal, and for an entire year his anxiety regressed to the point I couldn’t leave him alone. He panicked with sitters, even people he knew well. Daycare was no longer an option. What was I going to do?
Beau’s assault and the aftermath called up my past, the event I thought I’d put behind me: the violation, the betrayal, the fear that I might never recover, that all hope, that love, was lost.
I didn’t know if I was in denial or just being persistent, but I didn’t quit. Love fuelled me.

Slowly, we climbed our way back to 20-minute absences, then one hour, then two hours. Through it all, I kept waiting for everything to fall apart again. I kept looking for the sign that said I didn’t deserve my dog or my freedom, or anyone’s love.

It’s March 2025, and I turn on the television and also a calming instrumental music station, having discovered that not one but two layers of sound help block out the city and building noises, and I leave the condo, locking the door behind me, walking down the hallway, toward the building stairwell, watching Beau via the pet camera video feed on my phone.
I pray Beau will self-soothe but as I get into my car, his barking escalates

Hypervigilance is a symptom of my PTSD, and Beau’s. I watch as he trots his 80-pound body to the entryway, which he usually does after I exit and before he returns to the couch, his ‘go-to’ spot, which he selected for himself over our almost four years of separation-anxiety training.

But today he doesn’t go to his spot. Something triggers him – a noise, a sense, something. He fixes his eyes on the door. His ears bend forward. He stands erect, staring in the direction of where I’ve gone. His jaw tightens.

I start sweating. I can’t return – I’m scheduled to teach a Zumba class at a local gym, my hard-won part-time gig that I did for fun and some extra money, a job I almost lost when I was housebound after we lost daycare. I pray Beau will self-soothe but as I get into my car, his barking escalates. I feel powerless to the destruction of what I’ve built, a house of cards caving in. I drive to work, my palms clammy. I’m afraid of an irreversible regression. I’m afraid of getting fined for a neighbour’s complaint. I’m afraid of seeing the truth: that I’m still caught in the grip of my past, and I don’t know the way out.

For years, I hid my body underneath layers of baggy clothes. When I was 40, I watched a Zumba class from a treadmill outside the dance studio, telling myself I could never do those moves, could never let go of my fear of being in the world – of being seen.

Now, 11 years later, I’m standing on the studio stage, wearing neon spandex pants and a lacy sports bra, shaking my booty, leading a Latin-inspired dance fitness class while my phone blinks with barking notifications. I don’t stop dancing, even as anxiety chews my gut, spitting out the question: how will I bear this disaster?

‘Disaster?’ my therapist will say at my next session. I know it’s an extreme word to characterise a dog anxiously barking. Did Beau harm himself or my home in my absence? No. Did anyone get hurt or die? No.
It will be the worst day for separation anxiety in two years, but it won’t be disastrous. By the time my class ends, the dog walker will have picked up Beau, texting ‘he’s fine’.

Later, I’ll review the footage: 21 barking incidents, one almost a minute long, the others 15-30 seconds. I won’t discount the three 7-10 minute intervals when Beau napped on the couch. I’ll remind myself that a really bad day doesn’t mean everything is lost.
After 1,000 separation anxiety sessions, I stopped training Beau and started living.

items.title: The cultural rules that define us take shape in our homes
items.description: Have you ever thought about the home you grew up in – really thought about it – as a place that shaped who you are today? Have you thought about the bedroom that you shared with your sibling, and what that taught you about sharing; or the fact that you had you
items.author: Oliver Sweet
paragraphs: Have you ever thought about the home you grew up in – really thought about it – as a place that shaped who you are today? Have you thought about the bedroom that you shared with your sibling, and what that taught you about sharing; or the fact that you had your own room, and what that taught you about personal space? Have you considered how tidy it was and whether you mirror that in your home today, or who took care of the space, which photos were on the walls, how the lounge was set up – all of which may have taught you lessons about how to live?

Your home had its rules and conventions, and it’s likely that you’ve carried many of them with you. Some rules of the home are explicit (‘Clean up your space before bedtime’), and many are implicit (leaving the toilet seat up/down). Rules about what is acceptable, respectable, comfortable, tasteful or hygienic operate all around the home. This is sometimes easier to notice when in other people’s homes, especially if you see something you’d never tolerate in your own (eg, the cat sprawled across the kitchen table, or everyone wearing outdoor shoes indoors).

Of course, the rules of other homes are entirely natural to those who live there. In my work as a business anthropologist, I’ve hung out in people’s homes in more than 20 countries. Most of the time I’m doing it as part of a research project with a paying client (including companies like IKEA), but the point is rarely whether people use a specific product or not. It’s really about how they live.

In many of the Chinese homes that my team and I have visited, when people arrive home, they immediately change into indoor clothes and slippers, creating a psychological, physical and hygienic boundary between outside and inside spheres.
In many homes in the United Kingdom, where I grew up, guests are offered tea within minutes, and the tea gives the (often conversationally awkward) Brits time to acclimatise to one another.

In some Saudi Arabian homes, guest reception areas are carefully arranged to signal hospitality, dignity and family honour. And in the female side of the house, there’s play, connection, and messy bedrooms.
Each home you visit says, in its own way: this is how life should be lived.

A home can, of course, tell you an enormous amount about who the inhabitants are as individuals. Imagine you’re allowed to walk around someone’s house when they aren’t there. Think about how much you could learn just from the way they set up the home: which books are displayed prominently, and which are hidden (non-fiction vs ‘trashy’ novels); whether family photos are recent or old, formal or casual, or entirely absent; the focal point in each room (a TV, dining table, toys, artwork?); whether the living room is designed for guests, children, solitude or escape. Our homes are biographies made physical.

But as the Chinese, British and Saudi examples suggest, these physical biographies are, in part, descriptions of the communities we live in. Our homes reflect various shared living practices, and these are often much more uniform within a culture than we might realise.
Collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing

The home, then, is also a form of cultural infrastructure: it provides what’s ‘normal’ for a range of life’s activities, such as eating, sleeping, socialising, play, cleaning, work, negotiating and much more. You can see this clearly in the physical organisation and sharing of space within homes. In Polish homes that I’ve visited, for example, I have found that it’s hard to figure out which room is a bedroom, as most low- to middle-income households sleep on sofa beds that they pull out and put away the next morning. Communist undertones still feature in the design of the buildings, where function was prioritised over form. A family apartment might have only one or two bedrooms because the assumption is that siblings can share, that grandparents can take the main bedroom while the parents sleep in the living room. Underlying these design principles is the idea that space is shared, rather than owned.

In France, life at home commonly centres around the dining-room table, a place imbued with ritual every morning and evening. Given the amount of time spent there, it inevitably becomes the place where taste, manners and the art of polite conversation are taught and passed through generations. I’ve often pondered why French children seem so well behaved at the table compared with children in England, where I grew up. It seems to me that French children often enjoy being at the table because the adults involve them in the discussions, whereas in England the conversations often happen between the adults while the children are expected to watch (which tends to result in boredom and playing up).

Returning to China, we see collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing. Often, the grandparents come to live with the parents and grandchildren so that the parents can return to work. In Shanghai, survey data suggest as many as 90 per cent of children under the age of three have a grandparent who takes part in childcare every week. When talking to Chinese parents, I quickly realised that they didn’t necessarily like their in-laws any more than people do in other parts of the world, it’s just that they accept that this is what happens in their culture. What’s more, the housing in China’s first-tier cities doesn’t always cater well for all three generations, adding to the level of cooperation and compromise that families must go through when living together.

In these and other cultures, there are naturally still people who rebel and go against the cultural rules, including the ones they learn at home. Culture is flexible and allows for that. But the rebellion exists only because rules exist in the first place.
Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance?

‘Well, my home is different from other people’s,’ you might say. Yes, of course it is: it reflects your personal taste and experiences, whether through travel souvenirs, prayer objects, sports memorabilia, or that old chair that nobody dares throw away. But even when it comes to aesthetics, there are cultural patterns. In an American teenager’s bedroom, a framed poster of the New York City skyline might reflect their aspiration or sense of identity. A family’s religious calligraphy in Riyadh may express their faith and moral grounding. Antique furniture in London could suggest continuity and class taste. In a Danish home, flags might appear during celebrations to symbolise shared civic identity.

Homes are also places where communal relationships are organised in keeping with cultural norms. Some households are porous: neighbours wander in, cousins stay over, doors are left unlocked (I’ve noted this sort of porosity a lot in Poland and India). Other homes are tightly bounded: visits arranged in advance, private rooms respected, front doors acting like borders (frequently the case in the UK or the United States). Other variations matter, such as whether it’s an urban or rural environment, or a wealthy or poor neighbourhood – but national cultural characteristics drive these differences as well.

Children learn these rules long before they can explain them, based on behaviours that could have wildly different connotations from place to place. Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance? Are bedrooms private, or communal territory? Do unexpected guests bring joy, or disruption? Is food seen more as fuel, or an expression of love? Children learn the rules of life from what’s normal at home, and these rules are reflected in how people organise and structure the home around them.

Cultural changes often appear in homes before they appear in headlines. The cost-of-living crisis has encouraged more shared living in London and New York, an increase in multigenerational homes across Europe, smaller private spaces in China and South Korea, and a thriving second-hand market across the world. It’s also led to pride in the ‘tiny home’ movement, and an increase in learning crafts like upholstery and upcycling. Generational changes are visible too. Many younger adults are less interested in the ‘show home’ ideal of previous decades. Perfection can seem expensive and suspiciously performative. For many younger people, authenticity, flexibility and emotional comfort may matter more than matching cushions. The home keeps changing because culture keeps changing, and when the culture changes, so too do the rules that we live by. Moving to a tiny home – or just a smaller one – might be a response to economic conditions, but it also teaches people new ways of living.

The phrase ‘Make yourself at home’ is usually read as an invitation. It can also be read as an instruction. Home is one of the most important places that shape who we are and how we live. And this is why visiting someone else’s home can feel so revealing, especially when that person comes from a culture that’s different from yours. By stepping through the doorway, you might be stepping into another cultural universe. When you notice the shoes by the door, the untouched ‘good room’, or the Lego bricks scattered across the floor, ask yourself: whose rules am I looking at?

items.title: Are mental illnesses universal, or are they culturally specific?
