• Speaking of Númenor, are we maybe saying good-bye to it? Or will we likely see it less now that Pharazôn’s forces are headed toward Middle-earth?

items.title: Below Deck Recap: Chaos Agent
items.description: Having been promoted to bosun as planned, Matt keeps his cool for about ten seconds before rubbing his new position in everyone’s faces. Is anyone surprised? After getting demoted, Alex lets out a dignified private cry in the bathroom and tells Fraser that he’
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Having been promoted to bosun as planned, Matt keeps his cool for about ten seconds before rubbing his new position in everyone’s faces. Is anyone surprised? After getting demoted, Alex lets out a dignified private cry in the bathroom and tells Fraser that he’ll take a day to think about whether or not he wants to stay on the boat. “I’m too nice,” he laments. But Moe reminds him that, bosun or not, his share of the tip remains the same: “Stay, play around [with Sen] a little bit, and get your money.” It’s a big incentive for Alex that he can “explore” his feelings for Sen more freely as a lead deckhand. Sen tells Kaylee — who suppressed a delusional little jump for joy when Matt told her about his promotion — that she’s glad she won’t have to feel bad kissing Alex, now that he’s not her boss.

Ultimately, Alex decides to stay. To Kerry, he says he’ll use his demotion as a learning opportunity, but to Sen, he says someone has to look out for her and James’s sanity while Matt is in a position of power. Alex and Matt’s struggle has played out almost like a tragedy. Alex’s humility brought on his downfall, while his rival’s megalomania elevated him to the top of the hierarchy (though it might topple him yet). It’s encouraging to Kerry that Matt knows he has a big head; if he can put his ego aside, he says, he’ll make for a great bosun. But as Sen points out to some of the crew on the way to dinner, what the captain doesn’t know is how proud Matt is of his ego; he thinks it’s warranted. He doesn’t see his arrogance as a tragic flaw, but as one of his better qualities. And his inflated confidence isn’t limited to the deck: Getting dressed to go out, he thinks his outfit is the best in all of Thailand.

When sober, Matt is less than inclined to treat people with kindness; drunk, he’s impossible to be around. He is an unpardonable buzzkill at dinner. Moe jokes that “everybody [is] getting messy tonight,” and for no reason that Moe can discern — other than that Matt thinks everyone is talking about him all the time — Matt interprets it as a comment directed towards him. He retorts that he is not getting messy because he’s a leader who is very good at his job and will so remain, even when one day he becomes “a hundred millionaire” (?). In the bathroom, James advises Matt to “rein in the banter.” Imagine how annoying you have to be for the deadest guy in the crew to feel compelled to come alive and call you out? But Matt doesn’t agree with the consensus that he is being off-putting. “Let me be a naughty bosun,” he tells James, insisting that as long as he’s good at his job, he should have the right to be as rude as he wants.

Once he enters the mindset that the crew is against him — which they are, but only in reaction to his own hostility — he doubles down on his attitude. Alex’s jokey reprimand that Matt should wait for everyone to get their food before he starts eating his fried rice (which, in his estimation, was the best order out of everyone’s) leads Matt to rant about how he is being judged for “growing up with standards.” Paranoid that everyone is talking about him behind his back, he defends himself by saying, with astounding confidence: “Just because I offend people, it doesn’t mean I’m not respectful. It just means people are too sensitive.” Moe marvels that his “arrogance is phenomenal,” but Matt is on a tear, talking about how often he was criticized by his parents. It’s obvious that Matt is plagued by some deep-seated, calcified, in-need-of-therapy insecurity, not that he would ever admit to it; he would rather trust that everyone else is an idiot, especially since, as he phrases it, he is “in the top 7 percent of the IQ in the world.” His is a level of delusion to rival only Kaylee’s, though even she is forced to admit that Matt is “not the nicest person” once he’s had a few drinks.

The rest of the night at the club is fun enough — Rosa and Kaylee tell Matt and James about their ongoing tensions with Rainbeau, and James and Fraser make out — but the promise of chaos is ever-present, like an open gas line waiting for a spark to explode. The spark comes in the form of a fight between Matt and Sen on the way back to the boat. They have never seen eye to eye, and they always approach each other with defensiveness. As they exchange digs in the van, it doesn’t help that they are so drunk that they can barely hold their bodies upright. Sen takes issue with the fact that Matt, now officially her boss, keeps telling her to “fuck off”; he maintains he is only joking (Kaylee, to give her scant credit, asks Matt to “not be a [expletive] for one second”). Sen is hurt enough, and drunk enough, to start crying, and arriving at the marina, she tells Rainbeau and Fraser that she can’t deal with a bosun like that. Hoping to help, Rainbeau speaks to Matt. Perhaps thinking that he would respond best to a straight-shooter, she tells him that he’s “a dick,” a word that is used to describe him several times in this episode, once even by the captain.

All hell breaks loose. Matt tells Rainbeau that the entire crew, including Sen, hates her. It hits Rainbeau where it hurts; she has heard this before. Fraser confronts Matt briefly about why he is involving Rainbeau in his mess, but Matt maintains he is the only person honest enough to tell Rainbeau a truth with which she is so familiar, she is haunted by it. The only person to come out of this evening unscathed is Moe; he eats tater tots in the kitchen while the rest of the crew falls apart. Ironically, Moe is the only person who seems half-able to get through to Matt. The next morning, he advises Matt to be more careful with how he treats others, and emphasizes that Matt was in the wrong, despite what he likes to tell himself.

Fraser and Kaylee tell Matt something similar, but it goes in one ear and out the other. Kaylee, dialing in from Kayleeland, says that she hopes Matt can change; but Fraser is disturbed enough to relate the evening’s events to the captain. Kerry says that he would rather be without a bosun than have a bully onboard; he even contacts staffing services (Norma…? Is that you?) to get someone on standby, should he need to “make a change.” He speaks to Kaylee and Rainbeau to get their perspectives on the evening, and has touching conversations with them both. He advises Kaylee to be careful about who she lets in close to her (another piece of good sense that will be summarily ignored), and tells Rainbeau that he knows what it’s like to be bullied. He makes a point to tell Rainbeau she is liked, appreciated, and valued. They both get emotional. It’s nice to see this tender side of Kerry.

It’s even nicer to see him tear into Matt. The captain says he’s livid; “I’m livid,” Matt agrees, but Kerry interrupts: “I don’t give a fuck how you feel.” He warns that bullying behavior will not be tolerated. Matt apologizes, though in a confessional, he says he only did so in an effort to “manipulate” Kerry to let him keep his job. I don’t know about that — he looked pretty scared to me. Before his conversation with the captain, Matt asks Sen to talk, though the point of their conversation evades me. All Matt does is tell Sen that he didn’t do anything wrong, and she shouldn’t have been so upset. Later, once the new charter is underway, their tension gets worse. When Sen sees Matt taking a break in the crew mess, she asks him if he’s having fun. Matt is offended; he tells her that she has to respect him, regardless of whether she likes him or not. She probably should avoid talking to him as much as possible, rather than give him reason to talk. Alex, for his part, takes the demotion quietly. It’s probably satisfying enough to have to remind Matt to tell the captain how much room he has to maneuver while undocking, without having to rub it in Matt’s face, which is probably what Matt would have done.

Meanwhile, the interior, which was already threatening to collapse before that infernal night out, suffers its own crisis. Fraser might have done well to follow in the captain’s footsteps and do some damage control with his team the morning after, but instead, he lets the wounds fester. Worse, Kaylee is oblivious to the “sense of urgency” and “initiative” required in yachting, qualities that are often touted in this franchise as vital. Less than two hours before the new guests arrive, Kaylee muses about how “slow” the day is while Rainbeau and Rosa hustle to prepare the boat. Fraser catches her sitting there and instructs her to get back to work, and Rainbeau — very politely, let’s give her credit where it’s due — reminds her that she can always check in with the team if she feels lost. Fraser then gives Kaylee a task — to stock toilet paper in one of the downstairs bathrooms — but she gets distracted and has a matcha break with Rosa before completing it.

The team’s unevenness is showing: Kerry notices a few details on his walk-through, and Fraser tells Rosa and Kaylee that “small things are irking” him, namely that they’re letting Rainbeau shoulder most of the workload. Rosa protests that they don’t know how much Rainbeau is doing because she’s not communicative, but Fraser emphasizes that it’s important to nurture a “team spirit.” I’ll stick up for Rosa: She has been working hard and trying her best to communicate with Rainbeau; this is really more of a Kaylee problem. That becomes even clearer later when Kaylee takes forever to steam a dress — something she had never done before — leaving the guests without service for a few minutes, and when the fridges that are her responsibility are not properly stocked. Rosa tells Fraser that Kaylee needs explicit instruction; unless she is told to do something, she probably won’t do it.

As they’re going through all of this, Rainbeau has what Rosa describes as a “smug look” on her face. In the cabins while the guests have dinner, Kaylee vents to Rosa about getting so much heat from Fraser that day. Rosa advises her to stay focused, but also uses the opportunity to tell Kaylee about Rainbeau’s smugness. Kaylee laments that she always sees “the best in people who are the worst.” Guys, she’s so close. I understand that Rainbeau doesn’t help herself, but she hasn’t been half as unpleasant as Matt. Yet she finds herself in a similar position as Matt, one that he himself acknowledges: Anything Rainbeau does now will give people reason to dislike her more. A couple of episodes ago, I wrote that the season seemed to be hitting a stride, but this episode was a tough watch. I come to Below Deck for drama, of course, but drama doesn’t have to equal cruelty, and good reality TV doesn’t have to make you feel queasy. And I’m not feeling queasy because James eats a bug for no reason, or not only because of that.

At least, the guests seem to be enjoying their time so far. Oh, yeah, the guests! I almost forgot about them. Jerrett and his wife Ilyssa are the primaries; he is a “cannabis mogul” with a positive attitude. The guests are overjoyed to be taken on a private tour of the island where the Leonardo DiCaprio vehicle The Beach was shot (everyone acts like they’ve seen it). The beach is so beautiful that, looking out at the view, Kerry, Rainbeau, and Sen say things like “I’m so grateful you’re here” and “don’t sweat the small stuff.” The dinner theme is jungle, and Fraser orders animal costumes for the crew. Moe, our reigning unproblematic fave, makes a stunning-looking steak tasting menu, which goes over really well. Maybe Moe should just take charge. Can that be arranged?

items.title: Jeff Goldblum Breaks Into ‘Wicked’ Song While Reflecting on His ‘Unexpectedly Enduring Career’ at Marrakech: ‘You Just Follow Your Curiosity and Your Heart’
items.description: Jeff Goldblum showed off his vocal chops Wednesday during a wide-ranging conversation about his almost 60-year cinema career at the Marrakech Film Festival.
items.author: Christopher Vourlias
paragraphs: Jeff Goldblum showed off his vocal chops Wednesday during a wide-ranging conversation about his almost 60-year cinema career at the Marrakech Film Festival.

During the on-stage talk, the actor launched into a tune from the soundtrack of “Wicked” — in which he plays the Wizard — crooning for the audience, “I’m a sentimental man who always longed to be a father.”
This wasn’t the first musical performance Goldblum had delivered during the Moroccan fest.

On Saturday, Goldblum received an honorary Étoile d’Or at a glitzy ceremony, where the actor was introduced by Tilda Swinton, who praised her “Grand Budapest Hotel” and “Asteroid City” co-star as a “unicorn” and an “incomparable presence in cinema.”

After a tribute video showcased his iconic roles across nearly six decades on screen, the curtain rose to reveal Goldblum — an accomplished pianist and jazz musician to boot — seated behind a grand piano, from which he serenaded a rapt crowd.

During Wednesday’s conversation, Goldblum shared anecdotes about his many collaborators, crediting an ethos of “conscientiously and daily and routinely exploring” for his remarkable longevity and insisting: “You just follow your curiosity and your heart.”

Over the course of the rollicking and wide-ranging chat, the actor looked back at his storied career, from his first role as “Freak No. 1” in Charles Bronson’s “Death Wish” to his “lively, robust and delicious collaboration” with David Cronenberg on “The Fly” and his partnership with the “masterful” Steven Spielberg on “Jurassic Park.”

With some 150 film credits to his name, Goldblum reflected on the range of roles he’s performed over the years, insisting that his “unexpectedly enduring career has been luck as much as anything else” while stressing the importance of remaining open-minded about whatever work comes his way.

“I’ve tried to stay open. And especially navigating this world of professional opportunities, where you’re just lucky to keep going, and not being particularly strategic about what pool shot will lead to what outcome. But just going, ‘Jeez, what interests me now and what might be really exciting and educational to do?’” he said.

“I think that all this so-called work I’ve done has made me in some ways what I am,” he continued. “I’ve been lucky that I’ve had a so-called career that cumulatively has added up to a body of something, and a continuation of something. And yes, I’ve had the work itself.”

A voluble presence on stage, Goldblum recalled his early acting education in New York, where he studied under the legendary William Esper alongside Larry David. (“He’s never asked me to be on ‘Curb Your Enthusiasm.’ Isn’t that horrible?” the actor deadpanned.) He also lavished praise on Daniel Day-Lewis, “who so eloquently and inspiringly and nobly” embodies the life of an actor, even while Goldblum himself downplayed a life in moviemaking as “the serious business of play.”
“I’ve been a lucky guy. I’m a lucky guy to have met these people and worked with these people,” he said.

As well as the tribute award, the festival is screening four films from the actor’s oeuvre, featuring his beloved and iconic performances in Lawrence Kasdan’s ’80s ensemble comedy-drama “The Big Chill,” David Cronenberg’s classic body horror “The Fly,” Roland Emmerich’s alien-invasion blockbuster “Independence Day” and “Jurassic Park,” the first installment in the dinosaur franchise juggernaut.

Goldblum appears to be making the most of his first visit to Morocco, hamming it up on the red carpet ahead of the opening ceremony on Nov. 20 and sitting front and center on Tuesday as “Paper Tiger” director James Gray delivered his own reminiscences to the audience in Marrakech.

On Wednesday, the actor basked in the standing ovation he received ahead of his conversation. Later he invited the audience into a parlor game where a participant names a movie, and the next player picks an actor from the same film, creating a six-degrees-of-separation effect linking together directors and stars across the generations.

Hearing the title “I Heart Huckabees” from the audience, Goldblum namechecked director David O. Russell, whose latest film, “Madden,” stars Nicolas Cage as the Hall of Fame football coach and legendary TV commentator and Christian Bale as late Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis.

“Christian Bale takes us to ‘Empire of the Sun’ takes us to Steven Spielberg takes us to ‘Jurassic Park’ takes us to Jeff Goldblum,” the actor said. As the audience applauded, he added: “That’s our show. Drive safely.”
The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

items.title: Gordon Ramsay to Host ‘Top Gear’
items.description: Gordon Ramsay is the new host of “Top Gear.”
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Gordon Ramsay is the new host of “Top Gear.”
Longtime TV chef Ramsay is swapping hobs for hubcaps as he takes the wheel of the BBC’s best-known motoring show.
Ramsay, an avowed car fan who holds a racing license, has previously appeared as a guest on the show three times.

“Top Gear,” which is produced by BBC Studios, will return in 2028 with filming to take place “across the U.K. and around the word” next year according to the studio, who promise more “epic adventures, daring tests and spectacular stunts.”
The Stig, the show’s racing driver, will also return to the show.

“My love affair with cars began as a child, growing up a field away from Silverstone, where I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing,” said Ramsay. “That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering.”

“At its very best ‘Top Gear’ has always been about the unexpected – surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences. It’s an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can’t wait to get started!”

The series ran from 1977 to 2022 when it was taken off air after co-host Andrew Flintoff, a former cricketer, was badly injured in a crash at the show’s test track. He suffered life-changing injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned.
Earlier this year the BBC’s director of entertainment, Ed Havard, confirmed the broadcaster was planning to resurrect the show.
Former “Top Gear” hosts have included Jeremy Clarkson and “Friends” star Matt LeBlanc.

items.title: Brad Pitt, Angelina Jolie Call It Quits on Years-long Legal Saga, Settle Case That Led to Abuse Claims
items.description: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running dispute over the sale of their French winery, a lawsuit that opened the door for the actress to accuse her ex-husband of abusing her and their children.
items.author: Winston Cho
paragraphs: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running dispute over the sale of their French winery, a lawsuit that opened the door for the actress to accuse her ex-husband of abusing her and their children.
Both sides on Wednesday moved to dismiss claims against each other. Terms of the settlement weren’t disclosed.

“We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” said representatives for Jolie and Pitt in a statement. “Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.”

The couple purchased the 1,200-acre winery in the South of France where they married, Château Miraval, in 2008. Jolie planned to sell her half to Pitt in the wake of their divorce, court filings alleged, until negotiations broke down over his insistence that she sign a nondisclosure agreement barring her from publicizing allegations of abuse leading up to their split.

Jolie balked at the ask and instead struck a $64 million deal with billionaire alcohol magnate Yuri Shefler for her half of the winery. Pitt in 2022 filed a lawsuit, claiming that the actress reneged on an unwritten agreement that they wouldn’t sell their stakes in the business without the other’s consent. That led to a countersuit from Jolie publicizing for the first time abuse allegations against Pitt in a 2016 altercation on a private plane in which she claimed that the actor “grabbed her by the head and shook her,” “choked one of the children” and “struck another in the face.”

At the time, a representative for Pitt denied the allegations. Jolie “continues to rehash, revise and reimagine her description of an event that happened 6 years ago by adding completely untrue information each time she fails to get what she wants,” the spokesperson said. “Her story is constantly evolving.”

Wednesday’s settlement ends a contentious case that peeled back the origins of Pitt and Jolie’s divorce and hostility between the former couple. Pitt continues to pursue claims against Shefler, who allegedly orchestrated the acquisition in secret alongside Jolie, and Shefler’s company Tenute del Mondo, the wine arm of the Stoli Group. The actor seeks a court order allowing him to purchase Jolie’s shares in Miraval at the same valuation Shefler acquired them, plus unspecified damages.

A state appeals court earlier this year found that Shefler played a vital role in structuring and finalizing the deal to purchase Miraval. It pointed to him guaranteeing $39 million of the purchase using his own funds, a provision he wouldn’t agree to if he wasn’t involved in the agreement. Shefler sent three letters to Jolie over the course of the transaction, according to court filings. One thanked her for accepting his offer and assured her that a deal would be made “despite personal complications.” Another asked Jolie to postpone paying an installment on the purchase due to complications with Pitt.

Since the allegations became public in 2022, Pitt has continued starring in major studio productions, like F1 and Heart of the Beast, maintaining his dual-standing as one of Hollywood’s most bankable leading men and a prolific producer of prestige film through Plan B Entertainment. Jolie, meanwhile, momentarily took a step back from acting before earning critical acclaim for her portrayal as Maria Callas in Maria.
In her cross complaint, Jolie detailed a physical altercation with Pitt, with him on one side and her and their children on the other.

“Pitt lunged at his own child and Jolie grabbed him from behind to stop him,” the complaint stated. “To get Jolie off his back, Pitt threw himself backwards into the airplane’s seats injuring Jolie’s back and elbow. The children rushed in and all bravely tried to protect each other.”

At one point, Pitt poured beer on Jolie; at another, he poured beer and wine on the children, the lawsuit alleged. Once the flight landed, Jolie claimed Pitt pushed her when she told him that she and the children were going to a hotel. “He also grabbed and shook Jolie by the head and shoulders, causing one of the children to beg, ‘Don’t hurt her,’” the complaint stated. “He let Jolie go, but then called her a ‘bitch,’ before adding, ‘Fuck you, fuck you all.’” Jolie filed for divorce five days later.

The FBI investigated the 2016 altercation but declined to press charges. A redacted report on the case stated that the investigating agent found there was probable cause to pursue a criminal case but that charges would not be filed due to “several factors,” according to The New York Times. It described Jolie as being “conflicted on whether or not to be supportive of charges.”

Pitt is represented by John Berlinski and Julia Cherlow, partners at Bird Marella, while Jolie was represented by Paul Murphy and Daniel Csillag. Alejandro Brito, who handles media lawsuit for President Trump, represents Shefler.

items.title: ‘Top Gear’ Sets 2028 Return — With Gordon Ramsay as Host
items.description: If you can’t stand the heat … get behind the wheel?
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: If you can’t stand the heat … get behind the wheel?
Top Gear is set to return to the BBC with entrepreneur, chef and self-proclaimed car fanatic Gordon Ramsay as its host.

The U.K.’s beloved, long-running series has been off air since 2022 after co-host Andrew Flintoff was involved in an on-set car crash. He suffered serious facial and rib injuries when his open-top vehicle overturned on Top Gear‘s test track.

On Wednesday, the broadcaster confirmed that the world’s most celebrated motoring entertainment show (previously helmed by Jeremy Clarkson, James May and Richard Hammond) will be back on our screens in 2028.

Produced by BBC Studios, the all-new series will see Ramsay take the steering wheel, “setting the agenda and leading an all-new lineup of co-presenters through epic adventures, daring tests and spectacular stunts in pursuit of the stories, machines and mayhem that generations of viewers have come to expect and love from the show.”

Filming will take place across the U.K. and around the world in 2027, with the iconic Top Gear Test Track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home and base. Top Gear’s tame racing driver, The Stig, will also be returning to support the new series in the usual understated way.

Ramsay is no stranger to the show, having been a guest previously on three occasions: in the show’s first series in 2002, its eighth series in 2006 and its 23rd series in 2017. Each appearance saw him showcase his driving skills with a lap of the track — his fastest time clocking in at a blistering one minute and 46.3 seconds behind the wheel of a Chevrolet Lacetti — earning him 7th place on Top Gear’s ‘Star In A Reasonably Priced Car’ leaderboard.

“My love affair with cars began as a child, growing up a field away from Silverstone, where I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing,” began Ramsay. “That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering. At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected — surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences. It’s an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can’t wait to get started!”

Top Gear is produced by BBC Studios Entertainment Productions for BBC One and BBC iPlayer and was commissioned by Ed Havard, director of entertainment and Michael Jochnowitz, head of constructed reality and studio entertainment. For BBC Studios, the creative director is Mel Balac, the showrunner is Rowland French, and the executive producer is Zac Assemakis. Suzy Lamb is managing director for BBC Studios Entertainment.

items.title: Bowen Yang, Mark Ruffalo and the Rise of Antisemitism in Hollywood
items.description: Bowen Yang insists that he didn’t know “Zio” was an antisemitic slur.
items.author: James Kirchick
paragraphs: Bowen Yang insists that he didn’t know “Zio” was an antisemitic slur.

In a resurfaced clip from his Las Culturistas podcast, the comedian muttered the term under his breath at the mention of Regina Spektor, the Jewish American singer-songwriter. Yang was responding to a guest, another alleged wit named Edy Modica, who said that Spektor was “a little Israel, hard-core.” Spektor, who was born in the Soviet Union and immigrated to the United States as a child refugee, has been outspoken in her defense of the Jewish state since the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7, 2023, and given her personal history, is well attuned to left-wing antisemitism. When protestors interrupted one of her concerts last year screaming “Free Palestine,” a visibly frustrated Spektor announced to the crowd, “The only reason I even speak English is because I came here to escape this shit.”

“Zio,” short for “Zionist,” was popularized by former KKK Grand Wizard David Duke when he was going through a respectability phase and needed a way to attack Jews without actually naming them as such. In his apology, Yang seemed sincerely shocked to hear this. “I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history,” he wrote on Instagram. “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.”

We should take Yang at his word that he didn’t know the antisemitic etymology of “Zio.” Why would he? So profoundly antisemitic are the progressive cultural spaces Yang inhabits that people toss around racial slurs propagated by men in white hoods without a second thought. Does anyone really believe that Bowen Yang knows the first thing about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict? Like everyone in his social set, one that dominates large swaths of the entertainment world, he acquires his progressive worldview — to which vicious hatred of Israel is central — by osmosis. If there’s one issue that unites the far left and the far right in this country, it’s the Jewish Question.

Yang seemed more distraught about the far-right origins of “Zio” than he did about the community the word intends to harm: Zionists, i.e. anyone who believes in the right of Israel to exist, i.e. the vast majority of the world’s Jews. In the minds of Yang and others of his ilk, progressives cannot be antisemitic, just as they cannot be anti-black, anti-woman, anti-gay, or anti-anybody. Bigotry, to them, is exclusively a right-wing phenomenon. Yang isn’t an antisemite, you see, he’s just an “anti-Zionist.” We know this because he ended his apology with the requisite “Free Palestine,” no expression of contrition over Jewish pain complete today without a nod to the movement that wants to eliminate the world’s only Jewish state.

Sadly, Yang wasn’t the only celebrity to make an antisemitic outburst last week. Like Yang, who owes his career to a Jew (Lorne Michaels), Mark Ruffalo has become a very rich man playing a comic book character created by one (Stan Lee). That didn’t stop him from impugning the loyalty of the country’s highest ranking Jewish public official. “Israel is just one issue in a whole host of reasons Van Hollen is the right leader for our times,” Ruffalo tweeted in a post explaining his support for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen becoming Senate Majority Leader over Chuck Schumer. “We need justice, we need leadership that follows the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties.”

Schumer, in other words, cannot be trusted in a position of political leadership because he’s a Jew who cares about Israel, a class of Americans whose “loyalties” are suspect. Ruffalo subjects no other ethnic group to this scrutiny, just Jews. According to him, Schumer is less American that the guy with a “Van” in his surname. Again, this is the sort of stuff Gregory Peck’s character might have encountered in Gentlemen’s Agreement coming out of the mouth of a leading Hollywood liberal in the year 2026. At least David Duke has the courage to be forthright in his antisemitism.

William Goldman’s famous maxim about Hollywood — “nobody knows anything” — applies just as much, if not more, to its denizens’ understanding of politics. It is amazing to me, after the popularity of Team America: World Police, Ricky Gervais’ numerous award show appearances and the Kamala Harris presidential campaign, that celebrities still have the nerve to opine about anything other than filmmaking and whatever gambling platform they’re being paid to promote. Does nepo baby Hannah Einbinder realize how ridiculous she sounds, ranting “never again for anyone” at a gay rights event in support of an Islamist political movement that murders homosexuals and uses rape as a weapon of war? Just as we don’t ask plumbers to clean our teeth, we shouldn’t rely on people who pretend for a living to inform our political views.

That antisemitism is so rife in certain sectors of Hollywood — that stars can so casually invoke hoary old prejudices against Jews and not have to worry for their careers in the way they certainly would were they to slander any other minority — says two things about the entertainment industry. One: that while Hollywood was largely built by Jews (something the Academy Museum needed to be prodded into acknowledging), it is certainly not controlled by them. And two: that in its understanding of prejudice, antisemitism is taken less seriously than other forms of bigotry.

A tale of two Academy Awards ceremonies illustrates how far Hollywood has fallen in this regard. In 1978, the actress Vanessa Redgrave won an Oscar for her role in Julia, based on a book by the Stalinist writer Lillian Hellman. Standing outside the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion were members of the extremist Jewish Defense League protesting Redgrave over her advocacy for the Palestinian cause. Accepting her prize, Redgrave condemned the “Zionist hoodlums” outside, “whose behavior is an insult to the stature of Jews all over the world and to their great and heroic record of struggle against fascism and oppression.” The Good Jews, according to Redgrave, are those who fight her political battles. Bad ones support Israel.

Redgrave was appropriately booed. But the real rebuke arrived when the director and screenwriter Paddy Chayefsky later took the stage to present an award. An actual veteran of the war against fascism and a vocal opponent of the Hollywood blacklist, Chayefsky had the bona fides to censure Redgrave for attempting to hijack the evening. “I’m sick and tired of people exploiting the occasion of the Academy Awards for the propagation of their own political propaganda,” he said, a line that could be uttered at every Oscar ceremony. “I would like to suggest to Miss Redgrave that her winning an Academy Award is not a pivotal moment in history, does not require a proclamation and a simple thank you would have sufficed.”

Fast forward to 2024, when the director Jonathan Glazer accepted the Oscar for best international film, The Zone of Interest. After thanking the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Glazer, his two fellow Jewish co-producers behind him, declared, “Right now, we stand here as men who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people.” Those grubby Jews, exploiting the Holocaust to perpetrate their own genocide.

This time, however, Glazer was applauded for his appalling remarks. And when Steven Spielberg — director of Schindler’s List, founder of the Shoah Foundation, and one of the most powerful men in Hollywood — took the stage later in the evening, he said nothing.

There are many ways to measure Hollywood’s decline. The lackluster quality of the films. The fall in theatrical attendance. The rise in algorithmic-inspired content. Here’s another: the deprecation and marginalization of the people whose creativity helped make it the envy of the world.
James Kirchick is the author of Secret City: The Hidden History of Gay Washington.

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Needs an Etsy Weather Witch
items.description: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is turning 100 this year, but there may not be any balloons at the big celebration. According to weather forecasts, extremely strong winds will be blowing across Manhattan on Thursday, which could force the parade’s 100 ballo
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is turning 100 this year, but there may not be any balloons at the big celebration. According to weather forecasts, extremely strong winds will be blowing across Manhattan on Thursday, which could force the parade’s 100 balloons (a record number!) to remain grounded instead of making their way down Sixth Avenue. If you are a sensitive soul, I must warn you against thinking too much about the Minion balloon slowly deflating just before its big moment. It will make you sad.

Parade guidelines require balloons to be grounded when sustained winds are above 23 mph or when gusts are stronger than 34 mph. As of Wednesday morning, the wind in New York is expected to teeter right on the edge of that threshold. Per NBC News, the wind speed will be low enough at 8:30 a.m. when the parade starts. However, by midmorning, gusts could reach 35 mph or higher. This doesn’t even factor in the wind getting stronger because of a wind-tunnel effect caused by the city’s tall buildings. (In non-parade weather news, by the afternoon and evening the city could see gusts of up to 50 mph.)

“In the 32 years I’ve been doing the parade, I’ve never seen a forecast like this,” Al Roker said on the Today show Wednesday, proclaiming that it’s going to be a “game-day forecast.” Today reported that parade organizers are monitoring the weather conditions and will make any necessary safety changes on Thursday morning. That’s not really what you want to hear, especially if you were really looking forward to Joe Cool making his parade-balloon debut.

Is this karma rearing its ugly head after parade organizers got rid of individual Broadway-show performances in favor of a medley? I’d like to think so. The way I see it, there’s only one thing to be done here: As a last-ditch effort, the folks in charge should follow the advice of every bride on TikTok and hire an Etsy witch to perform a weather spell. At this point, the other options are a parade with no balloons or Spongebob being impaled on the Empire State Building after a shockingly strong gust causes his handlers to lose their grip. My advice? Someone should shell out the $15 and ask for little to no wind tomorrow. It probably won’t work, but it’s worth a shot.

items.title: Harry and Meghan’s Secret Plan to Win Over the Tabloids
items.description: Just before nine o’clock on a chilly October morning, I arrived at the Community Recording Studio, a youth center in Nottingham, England, where foreign correspondents from Europe and Asia mingled with reporters from throughout the United Kingdom. Press photogr
items.author: Joshua Hunt
paragraphs: Just before nine o’clock on a chilly October morning, I arrived at the Community Recording Studio, a youth center in Nottingham, England, where foreign correspondents from Europe and Asia mingled with reporters from throughout the United Kingdom. Press photographers occupied so much of the sidewalk that a man getting an oil change at a garage across the street asked if I knew what was going on. I told him Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, would be visiting later that morning for their first public engagement since returning to the U.K. in August. The look on his face suggested profound confusion rather than civic pride, possibly because their choice of venue was in a neighborhood one news camera operator described to me as being “quite grotty.” So I explained that Harry has been a supporter of this particular youth center since 2025, when he donated £1.1 million toward its renovation.

In the two hours before Harry and Meghan arrived, as the crowd of journalists and supporters swelled from dozens to well over a hundred people, it became clear that some members of the royal press corps are minor celebrities in their own right. A camera operator for the BBC pointed out Phil Noble, the Reuters photographer famous for his viral photo of a haunted-looking Prince Andrew slumped in the backseat of a car after being released from police custody. Then there was Tim Rooke, who started his career photographing Princess Diana and is familiar enough to the royal family for Harry to have nicknamed him “Rookie.” A woman who took the train up from London that morning told me she’d recognized Roya Nikkhah, the royal editor for The Sunday Times, as she made her way through the crowd. As a royalist, she added, it wasn’t her custom to support Harry and Meghan, who are seen as rivals to the future king and queen, Prince William and Kate Middleton. But she’d had the day off work, and the chance to glimpse even the black sheep of the royal family seemed like it was worth a day trip to the midlands of England.

The man waiting on an oil change claimed to have no interest in the royal family, and yet he was unable to look away from the spectacle that preceded Harry and Meghan’s arrival. There were camera operators setting up shots for broadcast journalists from the BBC and Japan’s Fuji Television, while royal correspondents from British newspapers and magazines rubbed shoulders with YouTubers, Substack writers, and podcast hosts. A live streamer dressed in a scarlet dinner jacket that made him look like a sleight-of-hand magician, I later learned, was Tom Sykes, who writes scathingly about the Sussexes for The Daily Beast but is best known for being the brother of Anna Wintour’s late-’90s Vogue protégé Plum Sykes. One reason non-legacy media were so well represented has to do with a strategic decision on the part of the Sussexes, who had just launched their own press pool to rival the more buttoned-down and exclusive Royal Rota, which was established over 40 years ago to ensure consistent coverage of the House of Windsor.

“The core members of the Royal Rota, and the bit of it that makes up the national U.K. press side of things, has not changed markedly in the past 40 years,” said Liam Maguire, Harry and Meghan’s director of communications. “It’s a closed shop, an exclusive club, and there’s no desire from either the palace nor the members of the press pool to extend it beyond that core group of people because the more you grow it, the less control you have.”

There was also something of a class divide between the royal correspondents, who seemed largely representative of Britain’s middle classes, and the royal press photographers, most of whom looked like they had at least once rioted over the outcome of a soccer match. “They’re jackals,” one reporter said of the royal paparazzi. As Harry and Meghan’s arrival neared, some three dozen of these photographers coalesced into a human wall at the end of the path the Sussexes would walk down before entering the youth center. Those up front stood on the ground, with the next row of photographers just behind them on stepping stools, and those further back on slightly taller stools. Farther back still the stools became ladders, and the entire fleshy edifice grew to be as tall as a roadside billboard, and half as wide. I first realized the Sussexes had arrived when this heaving mass of paparazzi suddenly began snapping photos in unison.

It had been roughly two months since Harry and Meghan revealed, in August, that they would be leaving their home in Montecito, California, to move back to the U.K. with their two young children. The couple had fled the country after stepping away from official royal duties in 2020 in an unprecedented act the British tabloids called “Megxit.” Their return was great news for the coterie of royal correspondents who trace the House of Windsor’s highs and lows for Britain’s vast ecosystem of tabloids, broadsheet newspapers, magazines, and royals-obsessed television shows and podcasts. Though the royal family “have a ceremonial role in national life, which is kind of a serious one, there’s also, totally parallel to that, the royals as a national soap opera,” BBC royal correspondent Sean Coughlan told me. “Now you think about how Harry and Meghan have gone away and then come back, and that’s a classic soap opera plot line, isn’t it?”

If the monarchy is Britain’s national soap opera, then the Sussexes are undoubtedly its most bankable stars. “There are opinion polls on the popularity of the royals, and they’ll show you that Catherine and William are the most popular,” Coughlan said. “Then you get the king and Camilla somewhere in the middle, and at the bottom you’ll have Harry and Meghan some distance below that, and then maybe Prince Andrew right at the bottom.” And yet, when it comes to selling newspapers and driving web traffic, these rankings must be considered in reverse order. “Them coming back is manna to the tabloids because if you put Harry and Meghan on the front page, they are going to sell newspapers,” said Katie Nicholl, a former royal correspondent for Britain’s popular weekly tabloid The Mail on Sunday.

It all makes for an unusually dramatic moment. “You have the return of the prodigal son in Harry, you have a king living with a serious illness undergoing treatment with a question mark over how long he has on the throne, and you have the Waleses, the future of the dynasty,” Nicholl said. “The Sussexes just landing in Britain unannounced — and I don’t care what they say, the royals were blindsided by their decision to return — makes it all even more fascinating because what you have is the beginnings of a potentially very damaging rival royal court.” Such a court could steal the spotlight from the working members of the royal family, who have struggled to appeal to the younger and more diverse audiences the Sussexes tend to attract. This, in turn, might worsen a brotherly rift which has already split the British public into two camps, not unlike those that formed in the aftermath of their parents’ divorce. Just how much damage such a rival court might inflict is likely to depend on two factors. The first is whether Harry and Meghan have returned to the U.K. in hopes of rebelling against or rejoining the palace; and the second, which is as pertinent in either case, is just how far members of the royal press corps might be willing to go in pursuit of the biggest story in Great Britain.

Late last year, while the press was obsessing over Harry’s broken relationship with the royal family, the Sussexes initiated secret talks aimed at repairing their fraught relationship with another of Britain’s powerful institutions: the tabloids. Maguire, the Sussexes’ press aide, had taken the lead in these delicate negotiations with two of Great Britain’s biggest tabloid newspapers. Since then, in a series of “ongoing” meetings with executives and editors at The Sun and The Daily Mirror, he has sought to reset, or at least redefine, their relationship with publications the Sussexes have previously taken to court. “We can either continue to all feel bitter and angry about it or we can grow up and be pragmatic,” Maguire told me. “Because the reality is The Sun needs us as much as we need them.”

One reason the Sussexes chose to leave Great Britain, according to their 2022 Netflix docuseries Harry and Meghan, was to escape the ceaseless gaze of the Royal Rota. “The bad relationship with the press is multifaceted with them because Harry has a perfectly valid set of reasons for hating the media,” said Valentine Low, who has authored two books on the British monarchy and served as royal correspondent for The Times from 2008 to 2023. “He’d be a bit weird if he didn’t because the media definitely played a role in his mother’s death. Yes, she died because the driver was drunk and driving too fast, but it was a situation caused by the pursuit of the media — and the media used to make their lives a misery.”

As a young man, Harry was among the targets of a well-documented phone-hacking operation carried out by the British tabloid The News of the World, which he later blamed for the dissolution of at least one romantic relationship. Media interest in his love life only intensified after he started dating Meghan, with whom the British public developed a “hostile fascination,” according to Coughlan. Her mixed-race parentage has occasionally been the subject of offensive tabloid coverage. Few of the royal correspondents I spoke with were willing to defend headlines like “Harry’s Girl is (Almost) Straight Outta Compton,” but on the whole they tended to believe Meghan’s treatment has not been motivated by racism and misogyny quite as much as her husband has claimed.

“There was a long spell back in 2018, 2019, when Harry used to glower at reporters and photographers,” said Richard Palmer, a longtime Daily Express royal correspondent who now writes for The Observer. “When they quit, really, they refused to deal with sections of the British press. I think where Harry and Meghan lost a lot of popularity was that they didn’t seem to want to play the game with the British public — not just the British press, but the public.”

It is widely believed that the media played a significant role in the deep, yearslong rupture between William and Harry. Some members of the British press told me it was possible William, or someone in his inner circle, had tried to throw the tabloids off the scent of his own rumored affair with Sarah Rose Hanbury, the Marchioness of Cholmondeley, by offering up unfavorable stories on Markle. Such behavior, if true, was made more likely by the presence of the so-called equerry, one journalist said. These “capable, posh, military-ish men who have existed around the royal family for generations” act as advisers, fixers, confidants — and strategic leakers. “They’re people you would trust in a crisis: The kind of people who would give steady, sound advice, but they’re not necessarily tapped into ground-level English existence” and tend to have “slightly cobwebby ideas about the media ecosystem” and how it should be used to solve certain problems. In response to questions, a representative for Prince William wrote, “Kensington Palace will never discuss family matters either on or off the record.”

The equerry, along with private secretaries and other royal courtiers, are among the class of palace advisers Princess Diana famously called “men in grey suits.” For royal correspondents who started their careers in the early 1990s, the ongoing rivalry between William and Harry brings to mind a proxy war waged in the British press when the princes were still young boys. “There was a time when Charles and Diana were arguing very publicly, when their marriage was breaking up, that people were being fed all sorts of stuff from both camps,” said Palmer. “A lot of that behavior stopped after her death. I think the royal household tried to stem the leaks that had been happening.”

In early October, I met Nicholl at a television studio in The News Building, a 17-story office tower not far from London Bridge, where Piers Morgan Uncensored Media has its headquarters alongside the offices of The Times, The Sun, and The Wall Street Journal. Morgan, who started his career at Rupert Murdoch–owned tabloids The Sun and The News of the World and later served as editor of the Daily Mirror, made a guest appearance on the program when Harry and Meghan first announced an end to their “Megxile” in California. He said the Sussexes were “going to come back, bring the circus, bring the drama, bring the leaks, bring the whining, bring it all,” with only his irritated tone to suggest this was anything but a wish list. When I attended a taping of The Royals Uncensored, he was away at a golf tournament in Scotland.

The format of The Royals Uncensored is not unlike a daytime talk show, and on the afternoon of my visit there was plenty to talk about. Charles Spencer had just published his book Swan Song: Diana, My Beautiful Sister in which he’d accused King Charles of acting like a “lottery winner” in the hours after the mother of his children died in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997. Also up for discussion was whether William and Harry were at odds over whether to take part in a documentary commemorating the 30th anniversary of their mother’s death. (Harry was reportedly in; William was reportedly out). The lead news item, however, was about the most politically sensitive aspect of Harry and Meghan’s return, which had to do with the logistics of protecting British royalty who have decided to abandon their duties and live as private citizens.

One consequence of becoming non-working royals was the loss of taxpayer-funded police protection that is available only to active members of the British monarchy. In 2025, Harry cited fear for his family’s safety as an obstacle to ever returning home. “I cannot see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the U.K. at this point,” he said in an interview with the BBC. His decision to return to the U.K after all presents a very real problem with no obvious solution. Harry and Meghan’s offer to pay for their own armed protection detail was rebuffed by the courts on the grounds that private security are not allowed to carry guns in the U.K., and that the Metropolitan Police’s officers are not mercenaries for hire. And while the expense of one more royal security detail, in financial terms, might amount to relatively little, the psychic cost to the average Briton could be immense: A modern notion of the royals as being of service to their subjects, rather than the other way around, seems to be a necessary bit of scaffolding that keeps the entire edifice from crumbling under the weight of its own uselessness.

I watched from one of over a dozen wall-mounted television screens in the control room as Nicholl explained the latest development in this particular Sussex subplot: “The Duke and Duchess of Sussex found themselves at the center of yet another security breach this week after two paparazzi photographers were spotted by their security detail outside Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet’s new school,” she said. “They were believed to be international photographers,” which dedicated followers of the royal family will understand is a sort of euphemism for French paparazzi.

Likewise, I would come to understand that references to an unnamed “village” where the Sussexes now live is a coded way of talking about the Cotswolds, a patchwork of protected towns in south and central England known as much for old-world charm as an abundance of obscenely wealthy aristocrats, oligarchs, and ex-footballers. The day after my visit to The News Building, paparazzi waiting outside a pub in one of these villages snapped the first new images of Harry and Meghan out for a stroll since their move back. One of these photos appeared on the cover of the Saturday edition of The Sun, ticking an important box among many still unchecked: Which tabloid would secure the first photos of Harry on a jog or Meghan nipping out to the grocery store? What newspaper might land the first exclusive interview with the couple and get them to explain why they’d decided to come back to the U.K.? And which publication would get the most coveted scoop of all by publishing a photograph of the entire family?

For their detractors, few things about the Sussexes are as irksome as their refusal to show all of Great Britain the faces of 7-year-old Archie and 5-year-old Lilibet — a stark contrast to how William and Kate have handled images of their own royal progeny. “The Waleses have done, I think, a great thing in giving us access to their children by giving photographs of milestone moments,” Nicholl told her fellow panelists on The Royals Uncensored. “Part of the issue, I think, and what this photographer was saying to me, is that they know the price for a photo is so high because we haven’t seen a full-frontal facial image of either Archie or Lilibet.” Instead, Nicholl observed, the Sussexes have teased the nation by showing occasional glimpses of the children in Instagram posts, but never their faces, which critics say is responsible for the intense curiosity that has already forced them to change schools once.

When the Sussexes planned their return to the U.K. after visiting over the summer, one source close to the couple told me, it was with an awareness that “they are not protected by some of the institutional clout and power that they had when they were still part of the institution, part of the working royal family.” They knew the British press might wish to test the boundaries and there were questions about whether the paparazzi had violated longstanding norms by following them on the day they were photographed. It turns out the photo had been a fluke: The paparazzi had gotten a tip that David Beckham might turn up at the pub that evening, but instead it was the Sussexes.
“That’s life in the Cotswolds,” Maguire told me.

For months after their return, the Sussexes gave no interviews. They made no statements that might explain what it was that had brought them back to Great Britain so suddenly. “Apart from Harry wanting an English education of his kids, I haven’t really heard a good explanation from the Harry and Meghan camp about why they’re doing this,” said one British newspaper’s former royal correspondent in early October. “And in the absence of a decent explanation, the media is going to fill the vacuum.”

Commentators gleefully suggested that Harry and Meghan had failed to make an impression in Hollywood and returned to the U.K. simply because it’s where they are most famous. Privately, some royal correspondents wondered whether their sudden move had been motivated by Harry’s desire to be closer to his father, prompting fears that the king’s health might be worse than the palace has acknowledged — something none of them could say publicly because the subject is so deeply taboo.

What is clear is that the Sussexes are not leaving their media coverage to chance. In October, two weeks after my visit to The News Building, I obtained a three-page document outlining plans for a “Sussex Media Pool.” What it described was a press pooling system that directly parallels the Royal Rota, but includes podcasters, streamers, and other new-media upstarts alongside royal correspondents from newspapers, television, radio, and magazines. “One of the biggest issues Harry always had with the Rota is that he always felt that it was undemocratic and wasn’t actually healthy for reporting,” Maguire told me. “So in setting up the Sussex Media Pool, yes, I’ve invited all the legacy media and the heritage media, but I’ve also invited people who have been banging at the door wanting to get into the Rota for a long, long time and have been blocked, I think, for no good reason.”

What this means, in practice, is that the rival court would emerge as a competition for press coverage, with the king and his heir on the backfoot as they vie for media attention on two fronts: with the streamers and podcasters they have chosen to ignore rather than cultivate to one side, and on the other more traditional media outlets that seem increasingly weary of bland, spoon-fed accounts of how all is well in the kingdom. On the day of their appearance in Nottingham, the Sussexes were trailed by royal editors and correspondents from some of Britain’s biggest newspapers and tabloids, whose front pages they graced the following morning; engagements carried out that same day by Charles and William went so unnoticed that for weeks afterward pundits speculated on whether the Sussexes had purposely booked their outing in conflict with other members of the royal family as a way of proving a point.

The popularity Harry and Meghan enjoy among younger, more diverse subjects is a reminder of the days before their image was tainted by constant battles with the press. They were so well-liked by non-royalists, and so clearly the least problematic royal emissaries for non-white corners of the British commonwealth, that even their harshest critics could see what a tremendous asset they were to the monarchy. “One of the things that Harry and Meghan threatened to do in that immediate post-Brexit period was to actually give even more glamor and more power to the monarchy,” said Will Lloyd, a reporter at The Financial Times. “It was an extraordinary moment — diversifying it, bringing it into the 21st century, modernizing it.” The extent to which this was an opportunity missed came into sharp relief in November, when Lloyd was among the reporters to accompany King Charles on an official visit to Antigua, where his refusal to cede to demands for reparations or even to apologize for Britain’s past enslavement of people in this corner of the empire cast such a shadow that the headline of his resulting Financial Times Weekend Magazine cover story asked: “Is this how the Commonwealth ends?”

The threat Harry and Meghan pose remains. “They’re terrified of a House of Sussex,” one British reporter told me, referring to the royal family. “They’re so terrified of people in this country remembering that actually they thought Harry was quite a chip off the old block and not a fucking snob.” The Observer writer Richard Palmer suggested some Brits may still long for the less complicated days of Harry’s bachelorhood, when he was seen as “just a good bloke,” who some reporters felt they couldn’t criticize too harshly because so many readers wanted to either sleep with him or meet him at the pub for a pint. The British television presenter Jeremy Vine recently theorized that the Sussexes’ early success, epitomized by “this sensational wedding,” proved so worrisome for William and Kate that they had helped to turn the press against them. “Either they, or more likely people on their behalf, thought: Let’s take them down a peg or two, and they accidentally broke the whole ladder.”

Harry and Meghan have also been their own worst enemies, and efforts at mending fences with the press suggest they have learned some lessons. One can already see the outlines of a path back to popularity, reinforced by a base of online supporters cultivated outside the purview of the Royal Rota. Palmer was among a handful of royal correspondents to mention having been targeted for harassment at some point by Harry and Meghan’s online fandom, who call themselves the Sussex squad. I’d first heard about them from Lydia Alty, a 21-year-old YouTuber who has covered the royal family since she was just 13. Before Harry and Meghan returned to the U.K., Alty told me, she had stopped posting about them on her Royal Reporter Lydia YouTube channel, largely because the Sussex squad could be so ruthless about targeting those who were critical of them. “It would just sort of be a torrent of abuse every time you would try to find the middle ground and just say the news rather than have an opinion about it,” Alty said.

After the event in Nottingham, as I perused Sussex squad posts about Harry and Meghan’s return to public life, it became clear that the online fandom regards royal correspondents as part of the story — to them some are villainous heels, others courageous truth tellers, while most are mere pawns in a game they couldn’t possibly understand. As spectators, the fans themselves are part of the drama as well: On X, one of Harry and Meghan’s fans posted a photo of Maguire, who is well-known to the Sussex squad, enjoying what looked like a friendly chat in Nottingham with Matt Wilkinson, the royal editor for The Sun. What could it mean? they wondered, unaware of the secret detente Maguire had been working on behind the scenes for almost a year.

Days after Harry told GQ he hoped to reconcile with his older brother, The Daily Mirror ran a cover story saying William had no intention of doing any such thing. A “royal insider” was the source of this information. The press is not only the conduit for Britain’s royal family to speak to their subjects, but also, in times of great dysfunction, a way of speaking to one another. The Daily Mirror is one of the tabloids the Sussexes had brokered peace with, making it a likely conduit for what looked like a very public game of pass-it-along. A few days after The Daily Mirror story suggested any royal reconciliation was impossible, Palmer, the former Daily Express correspondent, wrote in The I Paper that “the couple are now prepared to apologize for aspects of the royal fallout to try to mend relations with the palace.” Significantly, Palmer added, any apologies would be private rather than public — a caveat suggesting something more like a negotiation than an outright mea culpa. If the Sussexes are welcomed back as working members of the royal family and manage to comport themselves as the palace would expect, it would almost certainly be to the benefit of the monarchy, which would be able to nip the rival court in the bud.

Harry seems to have at last realized the awful truth, which is that there can be no peace in his own family until there is peace with the press. In late October, the tabloids found themselves in an awkward position when Meghan’s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., was revealed to be under investigation for charges related to child abuse and child pornography. (He has since been indicted.) The Sun, The Daily Mail, and other British newspapers had for years criticized Meghan for keeping her children from seeing their grandfather, whose strained relationship with his daughter suddenly made a great deal of sense. In a matter of days, for perhaps the first time, Meghan became the subject of sympathetic coverage in The Sun and other tabloids. “The narrative shift in the U.K. has been extraordinary,” said Maguire. After Thomas Markle was arrested by the FBI in Florida, in early November, some British newspapers, citing royal insiders, suggested the palace might be more conciliatory with the Sussexes in light of what they were going through.

Of all the British newspapers to have covered the unfolding drama surrounding Thomas Markle, none has taken a more active role than The Daily Mail. The paper’s publisher, Associated Newspaper, remains in ongoing litigation with Harry. He recently appealed the July dismissal of a lawsuit against Associated Newspaper alleging unlawful information gathering. This means royal correspondents at The Daily Mail have been left out of Maguire’s detente with tabloids like The Sun and The Daily Mirror. They have no access to Harry and Meghan, which may explain the extreme measures its correspondents have taken in pursuit of the Thomas Markle story. In late October, when “books about paedophilia and magazines showing children being sexually abused” were found in a Rosarito, Mexico, storage unit that had been abandoned by Thomas Markle, it was not police or government officials who “gained access” to evidence of his alleged crimes, but reporters from Britain’s number two tabloid by print circulation.

items.title: Ally House Was The Place To Be At The NWSL Championship
items.description: As the saying goes, everyone watches women’s sports — and that’s thanks, in part, to Ally Financial. In 2022, the virtual bank collaborated with CBS to move the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) Finals to primetime for the first time ever — a slot it has k
items.author: Megan LaCreta
paragraphs: As the saying goes, everyone watches women’s sports — and that’s thanks, in part, to Ally Financial. In 2022, the virtual bank collaborated with CBS to move the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) Finals to primetime for the first time ever — a slot it has kept ever since, including during Saturday night’s championship match-up between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current.

With efforts led by Ally CMO and former Michigan State soccer player Andrea Brimmer, the bank has been one of the leading forces championing the NWSL. This April, Ally achieved its groundbreaking 50/50 media pledge, devoting equal advertising spending toward men's and women's sports media. This past week, as the teams geared up for the championship game, Ally House, the bank’s fan activation, provided a space for soccer superfans and NWSL icons to come together in celebration of the sport they love.
The Brains Behind Ally House
When Ally first entered their partnership with the NWSL in 2021, far fewer eyes were on women’s soccer.

“My first championship game in Louisville, it was noon on a Saturday, and it just felt like going to a high school soccer game,” Brimmer says. “We came out of that and said, ‘We’ve got to make this something.’”
That experience informed Ally’s push to get the Finals moved to primetime television, and also to create an activation and fandom space in Ally House.
“This is the soccer Super Bowl, and if you go to the Super Bowl for the NFL, you see these kind of activations everywhere,” Brimmer says. “We wanted to bring that kind of gravitas to women's soccer.”
Ally House Was The Place To Be At The NWSL Finals

Brimmer’s dream was certainly realized. The activation, held on Nov. 20 and 21, took place at the NWSL Championship Ally House, just minutes from the match at Audi Stadium in Washington, D.C. The space was filled with fans of all ages — from adult fans sipping on drinks from the bar, to teenage boys to infant girls being pushed by their parents in a stroller.

The event included a custom charm bar, plus passed appetizers like sliders and pigs-in-a-blanket. While the DJ played, fans grabbed exclusive merch from Ally, sodas and beers from the bar, and sipped on matchas and lattes from Pitchside Coffee, a Kansas City-based coffee shop co-owned by six current and former NWSL players: Elizabeth Ball, Vanessa DiBernardo, Kristen Hamilton, Hailie Mace, Desiree Scott, and Mallory Weber.
Appearances From Superstar Guests

The main event on Friday was a live episode of The RE-CAP Show with former NWSL stars Tobin Heath and Christen Press, along with special guests, former players Merritt Mathias and Briana Scurry, and Guerilla FC organizers Chris Bowerbank and Elisa Davidson. The energy in the room was electric — even though it was largely filled with enthusiastic Spirit fans, the entire space filled with applause and shouts of approval when Heath brough up Kansas City devoting resources to building the first-ever purpose-built stadium for a professional women's sports team.

The highlight of Saturday was another live show, this time, an episode of Welcome To The Party with former NWSL players Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy. The players first brought out Brimmer and Danette Leighton, CEO of the Women’s Sports Foundation, to discuss the importance of Title IX in women’s sports. Then, they welcomed a panel of surprise guests to the stage: WNBA star Paige Bueckers, Claire Hutton of Bay FC, and NWSL legend Brandi Chastain. They played a game, pitting “youngins” Bueckers and Hutton against ‘99ers Foudy and Chastain.

The game, kicking balls into a laundry basket, ended in a tie when nobody bothered to keep count. The competitive spirit at Audi Stadium was at an all-time high — whereas at Ally House, people simply gathered to have a good time.

items.title: LUCIEN PAGÈS
items.description: Fashion brands and media could barely exist without PRs as their dogged middlemen, and nobody in Paris does it with as much spirit as Lucien Pagès. Over the last 20 years he has built his company Lucien Pagès Communication into a publicity empire that’s behind
paragraphs: Fashion brands and media could barely exist without PRs as their dogged middlemen, and nobody in Paris does it with as much spirit as Lucien Pagès. Over the last 20 years he has built his company Lucien Pagès Communication into a publicity empire that’s behind everything cool and exciting in fashion today. The ever-present Frenchman is known for being a fixture at nearly every event and show he organises. Thanks to his knack for social media, he’s now more famous than many of his clients. However, last year Lucien suddenly disappeared from the fashion circus. Perhaps it was because he’d recently sold his business to a wealthy investor? Or maybe there were other, more personal, matters at play? The very welcoming PR mogul is now back, and ready to tell all.
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Photography by PAUL KOOIKER

One of the first things Lucien Pagès does when we meet is give me a copy of ‘Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes’ by Robert Louis Stevenson, in which the future author of ‘Treasure Island’ goes hiking with an ass named Modestine. The book was last year’s Christmas present to clients and friends. Its cover – designed and printed by Benoît Astier de Villatte, founder of highbrow ceramics, perfumes and stationery brand Astier de Villatte – depicts Lucien leading a donkey forward along the road, an arm wrapped affectionately around its neck. Lucien is from the Cévennes, which is the key context at play. He grew up in the small, remote village of Vialas, and went on to become the most influential fashion publicist of his generation.

Today Lucien, who is 51, is sat at his desk in the Paris office of Lucien Pagès Communication. It’s in the 2nd arrondissement, not far from where Boulevard Poissonière turns into Boulevard Haussmann (at which point everything suddenly seems part of the same luxury shopping wonderland thanks to department stores Galeries Lafayette and Printemps, for whose product universe some portion of supply and demand has been driven by, or at the very least ambiently massaged by, Lucien’s work). His grey hair and beard are at the longest point where the word “shaved” is allowable. He’s wearing a black T-shirt, white trousers, white Nike trainers and a Rolex watch. His thick, slightly tortoise-shell glasses point, quite exactly, to a close proximity to the worlds of fashion and design.

Lucien’s 140 or so clients include fashion brands like Calvin Klein, JW Anderson, Loewe, Sacai, Saint Laurent and Schiaparelli; beauty brands like Aesop and Humanrace; luxury hotel brands like Pellicano; silverware brands like Puiforcat; restaurant brands (okay, just restaurants) like Le Voltaire; and perfume-slash-scented-candle brands like Byredo and Diptyque. What “client” means here varies quite a lot. A PR agency’s output might involve events, press releases, dinners, shows, presentations, influencer outreach, openings and showroom invites, plus a host of intangible actions that can’t be defined or quantified. Whatever Lucien is doing, he’s always communicating. “Did you know that calling came back?” he asks. “People receive too many emails so now you have to call.” Just out of the blue? “No, I send a message. ‘Can I call you? Do you have five minutes?’”

You imagine most people would have five minutes. Leaning against a wall in the office is a framed graphic entitled ‘Lucien Pagès in one word’: a series of Yves Klein blue squares (the calling card of its creator, the Instagram account Style Not Com) containing words supplied by some of Lucien’s acquaintances. Sarah Andelman goes with “chic.” Nicolas Di Felice offers “magician.” Anthony Vaccarello contributes “malin” meaning smart, shrewd, clever.

Courtesy of the book-prompt, our first conversation is almost entirely about Lucien’s childhood, his origin story. “My grandparents had a hotel and restaurant and my parents took it over, so I grew up there,” he says. The hotel was called the Chantoiseau, or birdsong, and despite its remoteness it attracted very interesting guests. The singer Yves Duteil wrote a song about it, ‘My Cévennes Friend’ (1983), that still goes out on the radio sometimes. Lucien’s father, Patrick Pagès, had a Michelin star and was a master sommelier. President François Mitterand came for lunch once, arriving by helicopter.

Much of Lucien’s sense of fashion and popular culture came via the three TV channels then available in France: “I was obsessed with ‘Dynasty’. It was on every Saturday night. We never had an apartment inside the hotel. We had a little room. I’d see strangers in the corridor. My mum would bring me the dessert that people didn’t want and I’d eat it in front of ‘Dynasty’. It was heaven.”

One day Lucien came across a list of the best fashion schools in the country and decided he would like to go to one. The École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne (now the French Fashion Institute) was a place dominated by those you’d describe as “BCBG” or “bon chic, bon genre”: members of the French upper middle class, adherents of a certain conservative-coded chic. “I showed it to a friend of my parents because I didn’t dare talk to them about it,” Lucien remembers. “My dad was so scared I was gay. Saying I wanted to be a grand couturier would be to basically say: ‘I am indeed gay.’ So I talked to this friend and was thinking she’d help me to convince them, and she said, ‘They will never take you because you’re not BCBG.’”

They did take him. He learned about fashion history, needlework and draftsmanship, and he assumed he would be a designer. He took some internships, including a stint at Yves Saint Laurent and multiple spells at Dior in the final years of the Gianfranco Ferré era. Lucien’s first real job was with art director Marc Ascoli. “It was communication, but more the image side. We worked on Chloé’s first four campaigns with Phoebe [Philo].” He also helped organise shows for French designer Martine Sitbon, with whom Ascoli shared an office.

It was for Sitbon that he pulled off his first PR coup. “I found this fax asking for one of her dresses for Cate Blanchett, to promote a movie. I found it funny and I went to the atelier, because there were some duplicates, and I sent some dresses to the stylist without asking anyone. Cate Blanchett wore all of them, and there was a particularly bright yellow one. Everyone wrote articles about it because it was a very daring colour. It was my first PR action on my own. Because of the fax machine.”

The second time I visit, I bump into Lucien downstairs and we get into the lift together. “Can you give me ten minutes?” he says. “I have to call the New York office. There’s a bit of drama. I hope it’s not like Friday. That was just…” He imitates a fighter blocking strikes from all directions. “I just don’t want it to escalate.” I wait on one of the chairs by his door, opposite the receptionist and a vintage portrait of Kate Moss. Around 50 people work here, and Lucien is on the phone to one of the 15 in the New York branch. The London office – formed from a merger with British PR firm AIPR – has 25 staff.

When I am allowed to enter, I ask what it was about. He declines to say anything other than that today was “internal” and Friday was “external.” His office contains, by the way, around 200 oversize perfume bottles, which are part of a collection that totals nearly 400. Back in 2020, Lucien acted on a long-standing urge to own a giant classic-shaped bottle of Chanel No. 5, which led to wanting a giant heart-including-the-aorta-shaped bottle of C’est La Vie! by Christian Lacroix. He ended up finding ten of these in sizes ranging from ridiculously tiny to impractically huge (they sit Russian doll-like on the mantelpiece behind his desk), and it escalated from there. For a time he shared the bottles on TikTok, attracting as many as 600,000 views per video: there are people who know him as a fragrance collectibles influencer, nothing else. Even so, it all relates to his day job. “I’m not doing TikTok for fun,” he says. “I do TikTok to understand it.”

A publicist’s work used to be mostly about machinating behind the scenes – schmoozing editors, browbeating journalists, gatekeeping talent – but social media changed the equation. Lucien goes to almost every event the agency is involved with, then shares perfectly captured images of them via his Instagram account. With approximately 140,000 followers, including much of fashion’s core elite, that account is arguably more influential than quite a lot of the conventional media coverage he achieves.
