items.title: Does wearing a skull cap actually make you hotter?
items.description: Who remembers the ‘Don’t Judge Challenge’? For those internet veterans amongst us, the year was 2015, and the app was called Vine. To the soundtrack of Omi’s “Cheerleader”, participants would cover their faces in ridiculous make-up in a bid to look as “ugly” a
paragraphs: Who remembers the ‘Don’t Judge Challenge’? For those internet veterans amongst us, the year was 2015, and the app was called Vine. To the soundtrack of Omi’s “Cheerleader”, participants would cover their faces in ridiculous make-up in a bid to look as “ugly” as possible, before transitioning to a clip of their real, apparently hot selves. Though that may sound like a particularly 2015 phenomenon, it seems that on the internet, evil does not die – it merely reinvents itself. If my TikTok FYP is anything to go by, 2026 has found its new Don’t Judge Challenge. Men used to go to war, but now they’re putting on skull caps and asking strangers on the internet if they look hot.

“The skull cap effect,” “Skull cap-maxxing,” or whatever you want to call it, first cropped up on TikTok in mid-October, and since then has snowballed in popularity, with thousands of videos racking up millions of likes and views. To the soundtrack of Bryson Tiller’s verse on DJ Khaled’s “Wild Thoughts”, men look gormlessly into a camera, before pulling on a skull cap and turning their stares all seductive, their attractiveness apparently tenfolding. Like the Don’t Judge Challenge, a lot of videos begin with silly expressions and maybe even geeky glasses to make the before shot look as “ugly” as possible. “How guys feel 0.1 seconds after putting on a skull cap,” is usually the caption that accompanies the performance.

The reaction to these videos in the comments seemed to be one of utter glee, and, as a Serious Investigative Journalist, this piqued my interest. Could a skull cap physically transform me to levels of hotness I’d not yet experienced? I would procure one for myself and put it to the test! A preliminary trip to the Dazed fashion cupboard proved fruitless (“sorry, no”), so the surrounding area and its various sporting establishments would have to do. After trying a few stores including a Sports Direct (“sorry, no”), I managed to find an Arc’teryx one in an Ellis Brigham mountain shop, which would work just fine.

To say that the immediate response from my colleagues was lukewarm would be an understatement. On my return to the office, when I asked if the cap had altered my appearance in any way whatsoever, I was met with such responses as “no,” “what?” and “were you not wearing that before?” When I explained that I was simply following a TikTok trend, our People & Operations Manager Jazzy told me that “I haven’t seen that” but the hat “looks fine”. When I asked fashion assistant Precious to describe my new look, she said, “it looks like you’re wearing a skull cap”, which is true because I was. “I can’t wear hats. I look like such a twat,” Jazzy added as an aside. But this isn’t about you, Jazzy. This is about me.

Undeterred by the less than enthusiastic response to my newfound hotness, I would take the skull cap for a second spin that evening at a fashion dinner. My seatmate, presenter and influencer Ruby Ukairo, who had seen the trend on TikTok, was effusive in her support. “There’s something about it that snatches the face,” she told me. “I think it’s a Victoria’s Secret push-up bra for men. There must be something about it flattening your hairline which gives you a more defined jawline. I do think it makes people look like they’ve had Botox,” she continued, before adding: “You look snatched tonight”. Finally! We’re getting somewhere!!

As I got more drunk, my investigative powers grew more confident, but to varying degrees of success. “I told you it looked good,” said one stylist after I forgot that I had already asked them twice. “I think it looks quite becoming,” said another invitee. It seems that most people liked the cap in a very general sense, but when pressed on whether it was truly transformative, that’s where things got a little sticky. “Well babes, you’re wearing a hat at the end of the day,” said one particularly honest PR. “How different can you look with a hat?”
“You’re wearing a hat at the end of the day” – Anonymous

With my confidence at an all-time low (how much more can she take?), culture writer Sik offered some respite. Before waxing lyrical on Central Cee’s appearance at the 2022 Fashion Awards as a pivotal moment in skull cap representation, he put forward the theory that, “if you’re not a white guy and you step out wearing a skull cap, I think oftentimes [it makes] you look better. If you’re a regular white guy and you go out with a skull cap, you do not look lenger – I’m so sorry.”

It’s true there’s a racial element to the TikTok trend that few of the videos contend with. Back in the fashion cupboard, Precious suggests that the trend might be less effective on me, a Black man, because the difference is less pronounced. “I think [the trend] only works with white guys because they’re trying to be ‘something’,” she says. “Obviously they look different. It’s giving durag but not a proper durag”. Admittedly, most – but not all – of the people taking part in the trend are white, or at least not Black. In one video, a white guy puts on a skull cap and then cuts to a different man, who is Black, as the after shot, which is very much saying the quiet part out loud.

The skull cap is probably the closest thing you can get to a durag without actually being a durag, which is why we’ve recently seen people like Justin Bieber and Romeo Beckham rolling up their beanies in a bid to resemble them. Arguably, skull cap-maxxing is doing the same – a way for white men to wear a quasi-durag with enough plausible deniability and none of those dicey racial politics. Well played, boys! For those of us who aren’t white men, the transformation might be a little less clear-cut, but I will continue skull cap-maxxing until my heart is content, as is my fashion birthright.

items.title: The Dazed 2026 holiday gift guide
items.description: Unless you are a seven-year-old child, it is far more enjoyable to give presents at Christmas than it is to receive them. Even when you genuinely like a gift, sometimes it can be difficult to perform the appropriate level of enthusiasm, and there is no sharper
paragraphs: Unless you are a seven-year-old child, it is far more enjoyable to give presents at Christmas than it is to receive them. Even when you genuinely like a gift, sometimes it can be difficult to perform the appropriate level of enthusiasm, and there is no sharper guilt than receiving a bad present, something chosen with love and care but which still doesn’t hit the mark. You can be genuinely appreciative of their efforts, you can smile until your cheeks hurt, you can thank them over and over again, but deep down in your stomach there is a sullen sliver of disappointment – and that makes you a terrible person! How was your gran supposed to know you wanted the Supreme x Salem stadium jacket, and not the GTA VI Birkin Bag?

Giving a present on the other hand – now there’s something guaranteed to ensure a hearty festive glow, particularly if your loved ones are skilled at hiding their feelings of dismay. And with our handy gift guide, meticulously curated around some of 2026’s definitive archetypes, they won’t even have to! They will be moved to tears at your generosity, awed at your uncanny knowledge of their heart’s deepest desires. Read on to find out more, unless you want your Ballhog Son or Whimsical Baddie sister-in-law to spend Christmas morning in floods of tears.

His wardrobe costs more than your monthly rent, but you’d never know it from looking at him. Your Ballhog son has spent more hours scrolling Japanese resale sites than he’d care to admit. Armed with an encyclopaedic knowledge of obscure runway collections, he describes everything as either “blassic”, “niche” or “archive”. His idea of a grail is a battered Number (N)ine hoodie from 2004, paired with some crusty designer denim and beat-up Jeremy Scott trainers.

The bigger, the better for the Size Queen, whose wardrobe looks like it’s been dunked in a vat of growth serum. With a penchant for everyday accessories blown up to cartoonish proportions, subtlety has never been their strong suit: think hoodies with oversized zips, comically chunky footwear and headwear that swallows them whole. When it comes to getting dressed, they’re firm believers that size really does matter.

Here at Dazed, we publish a monthly roundup of the biggest fashion collaborations, and every month, The Clout Chaser has already swept up most of them. Like Carrie Bradshaw, they prefer to keep their money where they can see it: hanging in their closet. Who needs a pension plan when Supreme just dropped a posthumous collab with Elliott Smith? It’s hard to go wrong when buying them gifts. There’s just one rule to follow: it has to have a logo.

It started with a pair of cat ears, then came the tail clipped to their jeans, and suddenly their wardrobe began to resemble the animal kingdom. The Furry-Curious isn’t a furry (there’s a whole different shopping list for that one) – they’ve just developed a soft spot for fashion’s furrier side. Their wishlist is now overrun with animal-print everything, fluffy accessories and anything that looks like it belongs on National Geographic.

When everyone was posting their 2016 throwback photos back in January, this person didn’t need to pull up archival images – they live and breathe nostalgia every day. They wouldn’t be caught dead in Bluetooth headphones; theirs are wired all the way (and perpetually blasting Frank Ocean’s Blonde.) Their fashion sense teeters between being ahead of its time and ten years too late – either way, here are some gift ideas to help them back to the future.

Her bank account may be empty, but her heart is full (and her bed is stacked with plushies). A whimsical baddie doesn’t let limitations like time and finances stop her from living her best life. She firmly believes that every obscure item she longs for is already manifested and on its way. This is where you come in. If you can’t get a hold of her vintage eBay or Etsy wishlist, these new (but equally whimsical) items will do.

Much has been made of The Mogger in 2026. While the looksmaxxer is a questionable figure with questionable politics, the mogger is just a man with a sexy face who wants to look good – and what’s so wrong with that?! Here are our top gifts for the guy in your life who loves big brands and maximalist logos, and wants everyone to see how good he looks.

Their version of Glastonbury is seeing Dune: Part Three at the BFI IMAX, the day it comes out (having booked their tickets three months in advance). They journeyed from Mordor to Westeros, and now they’ve landed in Arrakis – but they’re secretly reading Fourth Wing every night before bed. They’re essentially leading a double life: working nine-to-five at an office job, while daydreaming about fairies, dragons and how Robert Eggers will transform Aaron Taylor-Johnson into Werwulf come New Year’s Day.

If someone in your life has started to use a suspicious amount of em dashes and bullet points this year, you are not alone. Whether they are sending Chat all their boyfriend’s texts to analyse who is in the wrong or have simply accepted that AI is doing their job now, we all know someone who can’t tell how AI-ridden their brain has become. These gifts will drop a subtle (but loving) hint.

Look, we get it: the world is more than a little scary right now. The recent outages and cyberattacks are enough to make even the most laidback among us start browsing SpareRoom for nuclear bunkers. One thing we do know, however, is that humans have been talking about the “end times” forever – all the more reason to enjoy each moment and let the doomsday prepper in your life know you care.

As the first generation raised on the internet, gen Alpha’s chronic online-ness can sometimes make them seem a little… different. From skibidi toilet to Italian brainrot memes, sussing out what makes iPad kids tick can sometimes feel like trying to herd cats. But don’t worry: if you have no idea what to buy the teenager in your life, here are five ideas guaranteed to earn you instant aura.

Is your mum obsessed with making green juice? A seasoned yoga enthusiast? The type to eat a single particle of dessert before claiming it’s “just too rich”? Congratulations – you have an almond mum! If you’re stuck for what to buy her, look no further: here are our top picks for Christmas gifts for the Yolanda Hadid-adjacent woman in your life. Here’s hoping she’s not in charge of the cooking this year.

items.title: Fear and Misbehaving at The Vanderpump Hotel
items.description: “Let’s get Neff-ed up!” screams the union bricklayer next to me at Gigolo, the swanky new hotel bar in Las Vegas.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: “Let’s get Neff-ed up!” screams the union bricklayer next to me at Gigolo, the swanky new hotel bar in Las Vegas.

A giant statue of The Vanderpump Hotel’s patron saint and dog mascot, Giggy, stands tall beside us while the bricklayer’s wife tries to pipe her down. Neff, the bartender they’ve drunk with before, grins, and pours me another Pumptini. The bricklayer and her wife tell my compatriot and I about their wedding in Vegas after gay marriage was legalized. One watches Bravo, not the other, a classic relationship dynamic repeated across the decades. When my drunken friend and photographer Matthew casually remarks that we were in town to interview the lady of the house, they both look me up and down, noting my suspiciously gussied up attire.
The bricklayer leans in close enough to fall off her chair and shouts: “Just who are you people?”

We order another round, totally Neff-ed up. In the early hours of the morning, just before the sun rises over the desert, I strip naked in front of a gargantuan portrait of Lisa Vanderpump on a horse in the hotel room and lie facedown for a few hours.
It is but one of many times I will do this over the week

Still, that Neff-ed up night is the one I return to most across a week spent unbelievably pampered at The Vanderpump Hotel, which PAPER was invited to for the grand opening celebration. A quintessential example of the way that reality television and real life have officially melded into one, a weapon wielded only by Vanderpump and now, Caesars Entertainment, our benefactor for the stay.

For the grand opening, they gathered a select group of editors and writers to experience everything — and I do mean everything — Vanderpump has to offer across her numerous properties on the strip, from brunch spots to cocktail gardens and hotel lounges. There’s even an underground speakeasy in the mix, and a bumping rooftop club, alongside the combined prowess of Caesars Palace, Paris, Flamingo Las Vegas and now The Vanderpump Hotel.

If the Vanderpump empire in West Hollywood seemed like conquest, then one would need a new word entirely for what has happened in Las Vegas. Dominion, maybe, as there seems to be no other restaurateur or television personality as primed to re-take the strip since Gordon Ramsay’s heyday with Hell’s Kitchen.

From her not-so-humble origins in London nightlife to The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills and most famously, Vanderpump Rules, it seems an actual hotel was the only place left for her to go, short of annexing West Hollywood. My mind races at the thought the next morning inside Qua Spa at Caesars Palace, splayed out on a massage table by Amy, my masseuse. She has just released a knot in my back that has hot tears running down my face. She whispers at me to relax, but I’m already memorizing the list of notes to take for when I have my phone back, like the crowd of people in the lobby whispering about the new hotel opening up across the street, or 14-story video billboard of her dog that looms like the Eye of Sauron outside my hotel room, beaming the hotel’s motto into my mind while I sleep: “Misbehave accordingly.”

And misbehave I am, seeing as I am crying through an hourlong massage during a workday, with stories to post on this website and meetings to attend. Amy, as she finishes up our session, tells me as gently as one possibly could that I seem dangerously stressed, and should look into booking another session for twice as long before my stay is up. Later, at the front desk, I don a pair of extra-large sunglasses and do just that.

It is my second day in Vegas, and before I meet back up with Matthew for our photoshoot and interview with Vanderpump, I head back to my room and finally take stock of the decor. Photos of her adorn the walls, alongside her horse and dog. A large velvet sofa with all the Vanderpumpian accoutrements — rivets, studs, metal finishes, purple fabric — offers plush, if slightly ridiculous, seating. The bedside tables are a particular wonder, offering mirrored interiors, perspex supports, more metal riveting, marbled tops, and an optical illusion featuring Vanderpump’s eyes. For the rest of the stay, I joke that I’m being watched by the Eyes of V.P. Eckleburg, which gets a laugh out of everyone but the friendly PR staff, who can’t tell if I’m joking or being rude.

The bed, god bless, is deluxe beyond measure, and there is a soothing black and white landscape wallpaper that covers the wall behind it. Inside the shower, which of course features a floor-to-ceiling mirror, for misbehaving, accordingly, a message has been written with tiles: “Enjoy the good life. Profitez de la belle vie. To win without risk is to triumph without glory. A vaincre sans péril, on triomphe sans gloire. Bless the ones who curse you. Benissez ceux qui vous maudissent. That’s life. C’est la vie.” I transcribe it on a postcard left by the bed, and look at it while firing off my emails for the day. Enjoy the good life, indeed.

Later, we enjoy a spry lunch at Hell’s Kitchen, during which a waitstaff looks disapprovingly at my caprese salad order and asks: “Are you sure that’s going to be enough for you?” Matthew and I laugh about it soon after en route to Vanderpump’s suite. I’m wearing a silk shirt with a pink ballet dress and knock-off Valentino platforms. A fellow invitee emerges from the room with a grin, and informs us that the two joked about orgasms and the like. Inside, Vanderpump stands sentinel with a strong handshake and a playful smile. Nick Alain, her designer, accompanies her, and a harried publicist tells us we have just a few moments before they must hurry her along to the next thing.

She begins with a joke, exclaiming: “I thought to myself, I’ve had dinner with everybody, why not sleep with them too?” I point out the eyes inside the bedside tables, and they both laugh again, saying they wanted the rooms to differ from the hotel and Gigolo. Alain explains that “We were very conscious about keeping it calm in the rooms and not what we’ve done in the hotel and the casino. We definitely pulled it back.” By which he means they abstained from the black and red tufted interior of Gigolo, with its velvet lampshades and ornate black furniture and that gargantuan statue of Gigolo. Vanderpump adds that even in paring it back, the rooms still have “the detail of luxury” she’s become known for. Across our six day stay, I’d think about that detail and that luxury, as I’d repeatedly encounter their design ethos across Vanderpump à Paris, Vanderpump Cocktail Garden, Pinky’s by Vanderpump and of course, Gigolo.

I tentatively broach the subject of the since-passed Giggy, who became famous alongside her on The Real Housewives and was a fixture at her WeHo restaurants where the two would hold court. (And where I first met them both, nearly ten years ago.) I describe him as a patron saint of her empire, and she begins to choke up, something very unlike her. “This entire day, nobody has asked me about him. You are the first.” I’m slightly shocked, what with the size of the thing and how much life has been imbued into it. She looks at Alain, and explains that she took a step back from his design. “I said to Ken, ‘Oh, we cannot control this. We can’t be objective.’ I didn’t really have any input with him.” She pauses, and tries to describe his arrival at the hotel. “He had all the boxing around and the wooden thing covering him.” She pauses again, choking back up. “Okay, we’re okay,” and the conversation drifts along.

The publicist has entered my eyeline again, beckoning for us to wrap up, and I ask one last question. Is anyone not allowed at The Vanderpump Hotel? “There are a few where the inn might be full!” She laughs, and I make note to leave the guesses up to fans and devotees. Matthew and I are whisked up and away to a cocktail hour on a ferris wheel that overlooks the strip. We take shots with the bartender Cheryl at the zenith of our ride while she regales me with a story about Neil Patrick Harris in a thick Rhode Island accent. “He’s the nicest I’ve ever met. He Facetimed his daughter at the top, and said, ‘Look how high we are!’”

She pours us another tequila sunrise, and we’re off again via black car to Paris for dinner at Vanderpump à Paris. It’s my favorite property on the strip, even more than the newly renovated Flamingo. I smile as the wall of cigarette smoke from the casino floor blasts us on entry, making particular note of a patch of broken ceiling from the illusionary sky overhead. A piece of tape holds it together, a metaphor for most things.

If Gigolo is the hotel bar where one takes their mistress, Vanderpump à Paris is the place where the mistress takes her girlfriends to gossip about the affair. It is so utterly, deliciously America by way of Paris, like a restaurant pulled from the movie-musical Moulin Rouge. Our hors d'oeuvres come in a gilded birdcage; we all scream in delight at the sight of it. Still nursing a hangover from those Neff-ed up Pumptinis, I do a shot with the aforementioned publicists. Then we order espresso martinis, then regular martinis, and soon we’re under the table drunk and asking our waiter Josh where the gay people get down in Vegas. He’s also gay, and tells me I can print that. There’s something called the Fruit Loop, but the drinks are “shit” and the scene is “dead,” so he and other assorted gay people mostly hang out in cocktail lounges and hotel bars. Dreadful, I interject, but he seems content with it, so I am too.

Josh passes one last round of espresso martinis and disappears with a smile, so we crawl out of there, cocktails transferred via to-go cups, and find a place to buy cigarettes we can smoke in front of a slot machine, or the Bellagio Fountain.

Back on the strip, the radiating heat threatens to melt my Betsey Johnson kitten heels, but Matthew and I persist, soon arriving at the Bellagio Fountain. It doesn’t disappoint, and I nearly spill what’s left of that martini into the water trying to snap the spouts of water backlit by that 14-story Pomeranian ad.

The opening gala awaits me the next morning, along with a phone call to room service for avocado toast and a text detailing our itinerary for the day. Lunch at Peter Luger, a pool day at Flamingo Las Vegas, dinner at Martha Stewart’s restaurant The Bedford, and then an all-night party that would travel from the roof to basement and that aforementioned speakeasy. In the lobby before lunch, I run into Tom Sandoval, haunting the slots bar like a ghost. I hear him before I see him, as he’s on the phone with someone muttering “‘Ey, man” in that signature Angeleno vocal fry.

Shivering, we traipse on over to Peter Luger, where I don’t have room for anything but a dessert that’s quite literally just berries and cream. It satisfies, as does my conversation with the print editor of Us Weekly about the drastic and sweeping changes in our industry. Later, at the pool, I busy myself taking notes ahead of the red carpet later, trawling social media stories and cross-referencing the guest itinerary. A family from Arkansas is celebrating a big birthday blowout in the cabana next door while a waitress delivers me a tequila soda — to help me stay hydrated, and all. I spot Lisa Vanderpump’s business partners, Guillermo Zapata and Nathalie Pouille-Zapata, who arrive at the pool deck looking nonplussed by the loud Sean Paul remix and frat vibes. Check, and check, off the list I’ve made.

Through the flamingo sanctuary and back through the ‘80s pastiche interior, we cross the way into Paris, for dinner at The Bedford. They sit us in a VIP room that is a recreation of her Connecticut home, with massive LED panels that show views of the outside and an occasional glimpse of Stewart riding a horse. Our waiter tells me we’re sat next to Martha’s favorite table, and that when she’s in town for work she orders the lemon drop, due to its lower alcohol content. When it’s family or pleasure, she gets the martini.

Stumbling out of Paris, I grab a sugar-free Red Bull from my cigarette merchant and trek back to The Vanderpump Hotel, where The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star JZ Styles Hair is holding court with her new man, Marciano, who she acquired (quite) messily on Vanderpump Villa. A story for another time, but they’re fielding fans in the lobby while Lala Kent waits for an elevator. Not knowing it’s Lala initially, I comment on her gorgeous, silver-y bandage dress, and she turns around with a smirk and a “thank you.” At least the reality television cameras are honest.

Upstairs, I perform a quick change into my gown for the evening and rush back to the lobby, where a parade has formed with Lisa and some burly waitstaff at its head. The following Bravolebrities trail her in the procession: Tom Schwartz and Tom Sandoval, who notably avoid each other all night. The new cast of Vanderpump Rules. PK Kemsley. James Kennedy. Her husband Ken, daughter Pandora and son Max. Heather and Terry Dubrow. Garcelle Beauvais. Former Vanderpump Rules cast member Peter and his girlfriend, who is apparently not AI. Across the purple carpet and at last on the rooftop, I spot Sandoval and PK smoking a cigarette while Schwartz avoids them both, huddled instead with some women on the second level. Showgirls with giant selfie mirrors stand on platforms around the area while a dancer contorts herself into pretzels inside an inflatable bubble across the pool.

The skyline turns from blue to champagne to a warm sherbert as the drag queens from RuPaul’s Drag Race Live make their entrance. I swan over to them, familiar with most, and chat up their ringleader Asia O’Hara, who stands with Jaida Essence Hall. They are both somehow more friendly and beautiful and charismatic than Zoom interviews or television shows or podcast appearances would have one believe. They invite me to the show the next day and I stumble into a faux pas with Shannel, telling her I love the older queens the most. I mean the older seasons, and Jaida and Asia laugh as I over-correct and nearly trip in my gown. That’s what I get for cutting up with the girls at a work event, reads my notes.

An hour into the bash, Lisa metaphorically clinks a champagne flute onstage, and we gather around her like it’s a sermon on the mount. Matthew and I find ourselves next to Demy, from Vanderpump Rules, who we had met earlier at the bar. Her aunt gushes to me about her beautiful niece while Matthew catches up with Demy. The topic drifts to her aunt’s gorgeous blue eyeshadow, and she starts to cry, and asks me to say into a voice note that I love her makeup and would let her do mine. I oblige, because it’s the truth, and Demy gives me a hug and says we’re friends now. I believe her, and still do. As the speech begins, we hear Sandoval and Kennedy loudly talking behind us. Demy spends a significant chunk of Vanderpump’s dramatically heartfelt address shooting daggers at the pair and whispering curses. I feel a tap on my shoulder, and a nice pair behind me tells me I should press the record button on my phone.
No more vodka sodas until I get some water.

Onstage, Lisa informs us that as a woman, many men told her no, and now look at her! She’s done everything she ever could have dreamed of. Almost on cue, a drone show kicks up, making images in the sky that would kill a medieval peasant, like Giggy riding a swan or the hotel’s logo. Our rep from Caesars Entertainment has tears in her eyes, and I remember a story she told me about how Orby, the giant Sphere mascot, blew out the strip’s candles for its birthday, which also made her cry. I find myself crying now too.
No more vodka sodas until I get some water.

The night eventually trickles downstairs, into Drai’s After Hours, that aforementioned speakeasy bar and club in the basement. As it was a private affair, I’ll keep the details mostly discreet. (Misbehave accordingly, and whatnot.) Between the numerous shots and vodka sodas, here’s what can be said: Tensions seemed high amongst the cast of Vanderpump Rules, and the rift was noticeable to anyone with eyes. Jessi from Mormon Wives and Marciano have an energy between them that is all-consuming, which makes sense, considering all those daddy jokes they make on Instagram. Oh, and the DJ did not play a single new Madonna song, proving “Safety in Numbers Summer” hasn’t reached the straight community yet.

Around 2AM, I kidnap Matthew back to our hotel room, where we strip into pajamas, order Shake Shack and queue up Lushious Massacr’s latest Dragvestigations. I wake up exactly like this four hours later, in near total darkness. Matthew has tucked me in and I shoot off a good morning text to my boyfriend on the opposite coast. I never did figure out how to turn off that hidden light on the optical illusion side table, and I fall asleep backwards staring into Vanderpump’s eyes, hoping I haven’t been too naughty.

With the bash out of the way, things simmer down with our handlers, who are set to jet back to New York on the first flight out. They send us off with a farewell brunch attended by Vanderpump and friends, and we drink what will absolutely be my last Pumptini of the week. While picking at my potatoes, I ruminate on the misbehaviors encouraged by the hotel: playing hooky at work, ignoring emails, losing myself to the endless maze of slot machines and pool decks and cocktail lounges and cigarette stands. I think about the union bricklayer and her wife, and the magical night we spent under the auspicious gaze of Giggy, connecting across time and culture through our shared love for the Bravo cinematic universe, spearheaded in large part by Vanderpump and her acolytes.

More than anything, I think about the tears in Vanderpump’s eyes when I brought up the subject of Giggy. The entire hotel feels as if her soul has been imbued into the floorboards, radiating a glamour and cold comfort signature to her many hotspots. I fixate on a lamp that is also a chandelier with tassels and velvet and brass and various other accoutrements. Later, in the Vanderpump Cocktail Garden, I similarly fixate on a chandelier that is also a lightbulb with a smaller chandelier inside. Matthew declares into the bottom of our gin and tonic: “Lisa dares to ask: What if a chandelier was also an orb?” There is an absurdity to her design sensibilities that is unlike anything else one will experience on the strip — not in the retro-future pastiche of Flamingo, or the palatial, if anachronistic, Caesars Palace. The illusory sky-ceiling in Paris cannot compare. Nor can the winding canals of the Bellagio and blinding lights of Fremont Street.

At that second massage, after the brunch Pumptini has embraced me, my masseuse remarks that stress can kill, and it's good I’ve found ways to relax this week. For some, that might mean a remote spa getaway, or a relaxing weekend by the ocean. But for miscreants like us at PAPER, crawling about the world Lisa Vanderpump has created, we have our own methods to unwind. What is it Madonna says? Create a new persona. Vanderpump has just one note: Take that new persona, book a room at the inn, and misbehave for a while.
Photography by Matthew Lawson
Locations courtesy of Caesars Entertainment.

items.title: Prince William Reportedly Wants to Strip Prince Harry of His Titles
items.description: Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monar
items.author: Séraphine Roger
paragraphs: Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monarch reportedly wants only active members of the royal family who carry out duties on his behalf to retain their royal titles and the style of “Royal Highness.” These titles would therefore no longer be an “automatic privilege of birth” but would instead be equivalent to a “job title.”

The plan was detailed by Tom Sykes, a journalist and writer specializing in the royals, in his book Dukes of Hazard, to be published next February, excerpts of which were published by the Mail on Sunday on Saturday, November 21. The author, “a royal authority with impeccable society contacts” as the newspaper puts it, is said to have obtained confessions from friends of Prince William.

“If you are a working royal—going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role, pressing the flesh, getting out of bed on a wet Wednesday to go to Sheffield—then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title. You will also get an allowance, a salary, and a place to live. One place to live,” the associate of the prince explained to Sykes. “If you are not doing those things and you are not a working royal, you will not get to be an HRH, you will not get a free or subsidized place to live, and you will not get any special favors. You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose.”

By implementing this measure, Prince William hopes to prevent potential media scandals regarding the legitimacy of certain individuals’ right to retain their titles if they are not prominent members of the Firm (Prince Harry) or if they are under legal scrutiny (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor). But also, and above all, the Prince of Wales hopes to offer an option to his children, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, who could easily renounce their titles to pursue independent careers. The question does not arise for the eldest child of the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George, 13, whose future as heir to the throne is “guaranteed.” In fact, none of the three use their royal titles, preferring simply to be called by their first names and the surname Wales.

Under the rules established by King George V in 1917, the title of prince or princess, along with the predicate, is granted at birth to the sovereign’s children and to the children of the sovereign’s sons, as well as to all the children of the Prince of Wales’s eldest son. Prince William’s children, therefore, received these titles at birth, while Prince Harry’s children, Archie and Lilibet (ages seven and five), did not become prince and princess until King Charles III ascended the throne.

They may have to give them up if Prince William carries out his plan. “Under William’s current plan, the prince and princess titles of Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, would be legally removed, along with the royal styles and princely titles of Harry and Meghan themselves,” writes Tom Sykes in his book. To do so, according to Sykes’s book, constitutional advisers have told William that he could issue letters patent, an official document authorized by the king. Such a decision could strain the relationship between the two brothers.

Sykes is convinced that Prince William would garner the approval of his subjects and “enormous public support in a country increasingly impatient with the cost and perceived excess of a sprawling royal household,” according to those close to him.

In October 2025, Prince William confided to actor Eugene Levy—whom he was hosting at Windsor Castle for the taping of Levy’s show The Reluctant Traveler—that “there are points when you look at tradition and go, Is that still fit for purpose today? Is that still the right thing to do? Are we still doing and having the most impact we could be having?”
Kensington Palace, however, declined to comment on the rumor. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on books or claims made within them.”
Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

items.title: Decoding Kate Middleton’s “Tourdrobe” for Her Trip to India
items.description: When Kate Middleton stepped out on the green carpet at the Earthshot Awards ceremony in Mumbai this week, it was “an absolute princess moment,” says British designer Amanda Wakeley.
items.author: Katie Nicholl
paragraphs: When Kate Middleton stepped out on the green carpet at the Earthshot Awards ceremony in Mumbai this week, it was “an absolute princess moment,” says British designer Amanda Wakeley.

“Catherine has really come into her own. She has found her stride and a new confidence, and you see that in this dazzling but also practical ‘tourdrobe,’’’ Wakeley, who has previously dressed the Princess of Wales and used to dress Princess Diana, tells Vanity Fair.

It has been 10 years since Princess Kate last visited India. Her fashion choices are more sophisticated now than on her visit in 2016, and the speech she delivered at the Earthshot Prize ceremony on November 17 shows a new confidence. With her elevated look, there’s no trace of High Street labels. Kate’s flared floral dresses and the wedge shoes she used to love (but the late Queen Elizabeth apparently disliked) have been replaced by Manolo Blahnik pumps, couture power suits, and clothes by some of her favorite designers, such as Emilia Wickstead.

Kate’s decision to wear a striking vermilion dress made from handwoven silk by New Delhi–based designer Mahima Mahajan to the Earthshot Prize ceremony spoke volumes. The eye-catching dress, which she paired with a burgundy Prada velvet clutch, was chosen after Kate had selected a special suite of emeralds from the royal gem collection. The green stones on the dress perfectly matched her jewels, which served as an homage to both Queen Elizabeth II and India, as the green of the Indian flag represents growth and prosperity.

The dazzling stones known as the “emerald tassel suite” were worn frequently by the late Queen Elizabeth II, and while Kate has previously worn the earrings, this marked the first time she wore the set. The effect was dramatic.
“Never has Catherine looked more like a queen in waiting,” Wakeley says of the look.

Wearing the suite ensured that Kate, who has free rein of the royal jewels, looked more regal than ever. “What was fascinating was seeing Catherine wear these incredible family heirlooms along with more relaxed collections from some of her favorite modern jewelry designers like Kiki McDonough and Astley Clarke,” remarks Wakeley.
Kate’s carefully curated wardrobe for the trip wasn’t just about power dressing—it was also about showing she can be sustainable as well as on trend.

“It was good to see Catherine making a proper nod to sustainability by rewearing her Roksanda dress,” Wakeley notes. “It’s clear a lot of thought has gone into her outfit choices. Her wardrobe has to be practical, and her clothes have to work harder than most people consider for their clothing; she needs weight in the hem of the floaty dresses. She has learned lessons the hard way. She is often seen bending down, talking to children, so she’s conscious of how low a neckline is, how short a skirt is.”

For her visit to Mumbai’s Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital on November 18, Catherine chose a striking red tailored Emilia Wickstead skirt suit with Manolo Blahnik pumps. On November 16, she opted for a pistachio blazer by designer Veronica Beard, paired with white Alexander McQueen trousers and pearl-buckled Camilla Elphick flats, a relaxed and accessible look for when she picked up a cricket bat.

As Princess of Wales, Catherine is often compared to Princess Diana. “The main difference is Diana was a fashion icon. Catherine has become a style icon,” Wakeley says. “There’s a big difference. Diana played into the fashion of the day and was finding her style. During the time she resigned from public life, she worked out her style DNA. Catherine has had to do that on the job. Very wisely, she has worked out her style and doesn’t get too impacted by fashion and trends. She goes for what she likes. What works for her rather than trends. She really knows now what works for her.”

items.title: Slushy Noobz Gives Us a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z
items.description: Slushy Noobz Gives Mel Ottenberg a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z
items.author: Mel Ottenberg
paragraphs: Slushy Noobz Gives Mel Ottenberg a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z

In less than two years, Hamzah Al-Emad and Martin Andrijasevic have gone from boxing each other on a livestream to their first Paris fashion show, bringing the same loose banter and obvious fondness for each other to both. As Slushy Noobz, the Toronto duo started out as self-described bad gamers and have turned that friendship into a YouTube channel with 1.7 million subscribers who tune in to watch the pair make an event out of whatever it is they do. On the day the Gen Z sensations talked to Mel Ottenberg, Hamzah was about to head to the airport for his first trip to America in seven years, new passport in hand. Mel wanted to know how to clip farm.
MONDAY 2PM OCTOBER 26, 2026 TORONTO
HAMZAH AL-EMAD: Yo, Mel. It’s me, number 13.
MEL OTTENBERG: Hamzah! Number 13! What’s up?
AL-EMAD: I’m number 13 now because I just got my citizenship. That was my number from the ceremony.
OTTENBERG: I’m really sorry America deported you while Donald Trump was president.
AL-EMAD: That’s okay, I’ve been neutralized now. Wait, naturalized, not neutralized.
OTTENBERG: Look at you now, motherfucker!
MARTIN ANDRIJASEVIC: Hey, Mel.

OTTENBERG: Hey, Martin, what’s up? I’m so happy to interview both of you guys today. Slushy Nudes. Noobz. I just said nudes. It’s Slushy Noobz, Canada’s hottest Gen Z YouTube sensation duo! How did you guys actually meet?

AL-EMAD: We first met on the internet. I thought Martin was really mean at first, but then we met in person when he went to an EDM festival in Toronto he didn’t have tickets for, and he ended up sleeping on my couch.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah didn’t have a blanket, so he gave me—
AL-EMAD: I gave him a rug.

ANDRIJASEVIC: And then for a good year, we didn’t really do anything. We just hung out and smoked weed and filmed a few TikToks here and there, and people were like, “You guys are so funny together.” When I wasn’t visiting Hamzah in Toronto, we were playing a lot of Overwatch together.

ANDRIJASEVIC: It’s a shooter game. We were always looking for something to do because we weren’t making money off TikTok, so we randomly thought of the fact that we play a lot of video games and could start a YouTube gaming channel.
OTTENBERG: Can you tell me what games are good? I haven’t played a video game since eighth grade because I realized I was too ADD and it was going to fuck me up forever.
ANDRIJASEVIC: You’re asking two people who are really bad at video games. We just like to play them while we talk.
OTTENBERG: You told me that in Paris and it’s what made me like you. What game should I play?
AL-EMAD: Have you ever tried just driving around in GTA?
OTTENBERG: Wait, wait, wait, hold on. Oh, Grand Theft Auto.
AL-EMAD: Grand Theft Auto, yes. They have Grand Theft Auto VI coming out. You should download that.
OTTENBERG: Okay, I’m going to get them to send me that game and I’m going to get a PlayStation. What games are great and what games suck right now?
AL-EMAD: Halloween sucks. Wolverine sucks a little bit.
ANDRIJASEVIC: The new Resident Evil is insane. Me and Hamzah beat that pretty much as soon as it came out.
OTTENBERG: Have you guys ever had psychic or astrology readings?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I just did one last week in Salem, Massachusetts. She said I have to start a company because I have the potential to become a billionaire like Jeff Bezos.
OTTENBERG: Wow, then I’m so glad I’m talking to you, and I’m extra sorry Hamzah got deported. By the way, I want to ask you guys how to clip farm.
AL-EMAD: Clip farm me talking about getting deported, or just in general?
OTTENBERG: I don’t know. Wait, remind me what clip farming is. Oh, that’s when they take all your clips and they post them?
ANDRIJASEVIC: That’s kind of a farm. Is this being recorded?
OTTENBERG: Of course, babe. This is your interview in motherfucking Interview magazine.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’ll do a clip farm right now.
OTTENBERG: Okay, let’s do it.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Mel, don’t ever ask a question like that again or this interview is over.
OTTENBERG: Right, because you nailed the drama and the tea and you made it so people will want to read this fucking interview. I see what you’re saying. I want to record it myself.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Let’s do it.
OTTENBERG: This is why this interview is so important for me.
ANDRIJASEVIC: So, what you’re going to do first is ask some slightly intrusive question.
OTTENBERG: Okay. Hey, Martin, how do you feel that Hamzah’s early life is so much more exciting than yours on Wikipedia?
ANDRIJASEVIC: What a stupid question. Okay, if you ever ask a question like that, this interview’s over, genuinely.
OTTENBERG: Wait. Hold on. I have to do it again. Hey, Martin, why Crumbl? Crumbl cookies suck.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Is he serious, Hamzah? This is ridiculous.
AL-EMAD: Yeah, I don’t know what it is.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m going to end this interview if you ever say that again.
AL-EMAD: Sorry. He’s just sensitive about that.
AL-EMAD: It’s a science. Have you ever watched a Twitch stream, Mel?
OTTENBERG: No, but I mean to because it sounds great. Are you guys on Twitch?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I stream sometimes for fun, but it’s not a career thing for me because it’s hard. Live streaming is really hard. That’s why we love YouTube.
OTTENBERG: I’m with you. I love to edit. Why not? Editing is better.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That’s where the comedy comes from.
OTTENBERG: As a Slushie, I wanted to ask you: If I was going to have a YouTube show, what would it be?
AL-EMAD: You seem to tell it how it is. Am I right?
OTTENBERG: I like to, yes.
AL-EMAD: Do you like to do it to a fault?
OTTENBERG: No, definitely not.
AL-EMAD: Would you mind making people uncomfortable?
OTTENBERG: I think I should make people more uncomfortable than I already do.
AL-EMAD: I could see you doing some kind of travel series.
ANDRIJASEVIC: He’s only saying that because you look like Anthony Bourdain.
OTTENBERG: You’re the fifth person to tell me this, and honestly, it’s a huge compliment.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I think you could have a show where you have guests on and you completely revamp them in terms of style. You give them a rebrand.
OTTENBERG: Like random people?
AL-EMAD: Just pull people off the street.
OTTENBERG: Now that you can come back to America, you can help me pick some people out of the park.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That would be fun.
AL-EMAD: What’s your favorite thing about Interview?
OTTENBERG: One of my favorites for real is working with Gen Z people and getting to know what’s up.
AL-EMAD: Do you think young people’s voices are underrated, overrated, or rated?
OTTENBERG: I guess underrated, because Gen Z people are so funny. It’s interesting that the world is such total diarrhea, but you guys are still cool.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Check it out, I just got an Hermès belt.
OTTENBERG: I like it. Do you know who Wayne and Garth are?
OTTENBERG: They’re from my generation. It doesn’t matter. Wait, I have a clip farming question for you.
OTTENBERG: And by the way, I just want to say I did not write this question the way it was written, but I thought it was so funny.
OTTENBERG: Do you know Dan Constable at UTA? Dan is the guy that’s going to get you your Gucci deal.
OTTENBERG: You guys look great in Gucci by the way. You look great in all your outfits.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That was our favorite.
AL-EMAD: Did you like our photos?
OTTENBERG: I liked them all, but obviously, the all-denim with UGGs is surprisingly—you don’t expect that to be so…

ANDRIJASEVIC: It’s so funny, because we actually shot at the same location years and years ago when we made our own calendar. We were wearing denim then too because we recreated the Brokeback Mountain poster.
OTTENBERG: How are some straight guys able to make fun of gay guys in a way that gay guys love, but other straight guys make fun of gay guys and we don’t fuck with it? [Laughs]
AL-EMAD: Wait, Mel, why are you laughing?
OTTENBERG: Because that question just came to me.

ANDRIJASEVIC: I guess it’s the energy behind it, but you also got to put your money where your mouth is. You got to pop out at Pride or something. Jack Harlow is a good example of someone who does that. You can tell his energy is sincere.
OTTENBERG: Yeah, he’s friends with the gays. Do you guys have plushies mad at you now after “The Video with No Plan”?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Oh, like furries?
OTTENBERG: Furries, excuse me.
AL-EMAD: My answer would be no, the furries weren’t mad. I was surprised by how happy they were in the comments.
OTTENBERG: You guys looked great as furries.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, it’s actually weirdly comforting. You put it on and it’s like you do really get into embracing the character you’re in. Cosplay is becoming cooler as well, so it’s not that far.
OTTENBERG: Have you ever really felt it while cosplaying?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Well, we just did it recently.
OTTENBERG: I guess I didn’t watch that.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah was dressed up as Gojo, his favorite anime character.
AL-EMAD: Gojo’s from Jujutsu Kaisen, but I also dressed up as Vanillamace. Do you know her?
OTTENBERG: I do. Don’t you think we should do Vanillamace in Interview?
OTTENBERG: I keep telling everyone, “We got to do Vanillamace.” Can you explain why, because no one’s listening to me.
ANDRIJASEVIC: She is Gen Z at its core right now. She’s the number one girl on Twitch.
ANDRIJASEVIC: The number one female streaming on Twitch right now.

AL-EMAD: She’s also very kind and charismatic and she’s a really awesome success story of just someone who wasn’t planning on having it happen to them and then filling out the role of content creator very well.
ANDRIJASEVIC: And her lore is crazy and her style is insane.
OTTENBERG: Wait, hold on. Again, I did not write this question, but it needs to be asked.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Mel, you keep saying, “I didn’t write it,” and it makes it sound like you actually did write it. Did you write it?
OTTENBERG: No, I didn’t. My assistant Sofi is a big Slushie. She was like, “I want to write out a bunch of questions for you.”

OTTENBERG: And she did a really good job. I was just planning on doing it myself and she did do a good job, but this question was really funny to me. The Robert Pattinson and Skyler Gisondo interview, people and even fans hated this, and it was admittedly a very hard watch.
AL-EMAD: Yes. Is that the end of the question or does it keep going?
OTTENBERG: I guess there wasn’t a question. I just wanted to talk to you about it.
AL-EMAD: I’ve heard mixed reviews. I think I’m an acquired taste, baby.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Well, it could have been watchable if we didn’t decide a day before to just throw on a British accent. That was a last-minute decision.
OTTENBERG: But that was the right decision.
AL-EMAD: You’re right. I just wish I could have said something to him either before or after. I wish I could have given him some context to tell him I’m not weird, but it’s whatever.
OTTENBERG: The interview’s excellent. Is it also a flop? Maybe, but is it great? Yes. The accents made it.
ANDRIJASEVIC: There’s so many press junkets, and every interview is the same. They always ask us the same things. So we’re just like, “How do we add a little bit of spice to this?”
OTTENBERG: Am I asking you different questions than most people ask you when they ask you questions or are they exactly the same?
ANDRIJASEVIC: No, for the most part, pretty unique. Also, off the record…
[OFF THE RECORD CONVERSATION REDACTED]
OTTENBERG: Guys, we’re back on the record. Do you guys understand fashion?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I don’t think anyone understands fashion. A lot of people pretend to understand it, and it’s about how good you are at pretending.
OTTENBERG: Right. Do I understand fashion? No.
ANDRIJASEVIC: You have a lot of experience in the fashion world, but it’s like fashion’s literally changing in front of your eyes every second. How can you possibly understand it?
OTTENBERG: Even though you don’t understand it and nobody else does either, is there something you want to see more of in fashion?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I wear a lot of wrinkled clothing, and if I saw more wrinkled clothes in fashion, I would feel more confident.

OTTENBERG: What do you watch on TV? You were recently talking about that doc with that evil preacher and his wife who committed suicide and the bums were nutting on her, and then he went back to preaching.
ANDRIJASEVIC: We watched that recently. It was insane.
AL-EMAD: I’ve just been watching a lot of spooky stuff. I watched Longlegs last night. Watched Carrie, watched Widow’s Bay.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m rewatching Dance Moms.
OTTENBERG: Oh, wow. With JoJo [Siwa]?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, but I’m not at the part with JoJo yet. I think she’s coming in next season, if I remember.
OTTENBERG: I’m inspired by that. What about you, Hamzah? Are you watching Dance Moms as well?
AL-EMAD: My reality TV is bodycam footage on YouTube.
OTTENBERG: Do you know about the house of horrors in Philly?
AL-EMAD: Is that the one with the grandpa who killed nine people?

OTTENBERG: It’s this guy with a patch over his eye who’s really evil and was killing all these women and then his son got caught with drugs and a chick with a fake ID. It’s just really crazy. Anyway, I’m asking because I was like, “There’s
got to be amazing YouTube coverage of it.”
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, probably. Now I want to watch that.
AL-EMAD: True crime YouTube is really good.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Bodycam footage is something me and Hamzah watch a lot of whenever we’re eating food, before or after recording.
OTTENBERG: Can I give you my number? Will you send me some bodycam footage to watch?
OTTENBERG: You don’t have to send it right now. I just mean I’ve never watched that and I want it.
AL-EMAD: I’ll send it to you.
OTTENBERG: Okay, my phone number is 646-[REDACTED].
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah, put us in a group chat and I’m going to send my recos over.
OTTENBERG: Your record? What record?
ANDRIJASEVIC: My recos. My recommendations.
OTTENBERG: Oh, your recos. Thank you, guys. I really think this is important for me. Were you guys always popular?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Popular in life or on YouTube?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I was just friends with a lot of people in school, but I didn’t have my own friends. I didn’t have a friend group.
AL-EMAD: So you’re like a popular loner, you’re saying?
ANDRIJASEVIC: No, I wasn’t. Okay. I was that.

ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m a pretty charismatic guy, but when I get online I really feel like I’m a loser. It’s like, if I’m ever playing video games with my friends, they’re always bullying me. If I’m in a public lobby in a game or something and I’m on the voice chat, I always get flamed. I feel like I’m more of a loser online, a cooler guy in real life.
OTTENBERG: Do you guys have any favorite Slushy Noobz episodes?
ANDRIJASEVIC: The easy answer is all of them, but I think our favorite one of all time is the Comicon on shrooms one, just because it was so ambitious.
AL-EMAD: It’s the camping vlog for me, our first time camping.

ANDRIJASEVIC: First time camping was also really iconic because we actually got lost and could have died and that video might’ve never came out because there were bears and stuff. Then I think when we went to that abandoned mall, which was a top 10 experience because I didn’t know what to expect. Hamzah’s like, “Oh, there’s this abandoned mall in Toronto. We have to go,” and so he was showing me around and then we got sucked into this weird world of this mall that was selling counterfeit stuff and they had an amusement park in there that was also weirdly empty and we just got to ride a bunch of rides.
OTTENBERG: Do you guys ever go to live shows? Are you into music?
AL-EMAD: We go to a lot of live shows, a lot of music. The most recent one was Overmono.
OTTENBERG: I don’t know what that is.
ANDRIJASEVIC: They’re U.K. DJs. Really cool.
OTTENBERG: What else are you guys into music-wise?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Underground rap.
OTTENBERG: Can you give me some shout-outs?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, Nettspend. Fakemink.

AL-EMAD: My radio’s been stuck on country in my car for three days and I’m hearing stuff that’s blowing my mind. The lyrics were really profound. The way they describe a sunset is not like anything I’ve heard around these parts.
ANDRIJASEVIC: “These parts.” It looks like country radio has rubbed off on you a little bit.
OTTENBERG: This interview comes out in December. If you were looking at a crystal ball, what’s December’s like?
AL-EMAD: Hopefully some of our best YouTube videos out by then. We always like to end off the year with a bang.
ANDRIJASEVIC: We actually might be bigger than the program in December. We don’t even know.
OTTENBERG: Hamzah, what are you doing for the rest of the day?
AL-EMAD: I’m going to get an Uber to the airport and I’m going to America for the first time in seven years.
OTTENBERG: That’s beautiful. Don’t forget your new passport.
OTTENBERG: Great talking to you guys. See you soon.
AL-EMAD: Okay. Thank you so much for the time.

items.title: Rankin Opens His Vault of Celebrity Portraits in Contact
items.description: Rankin Opens His Vault of Celebrity Portraits in Contact
items.author: Daphnee Kabongo
paragraphs: Rankin Opens His Vault of Celebrity Portraits in Contact

Rankin took his first photograph at 20 years old and hasn’t put the camera down since. From his big break in the 90s, when he also co-founded the magazine Dazed & Confused, the beloved British photographer has gone on to lens everyone from King Charles II to Katie Price, demonstrating his unique understanding of celebrity culture and the beauty that can be found within.

Today, Rankin is giving readers a look at all the photos that didn’t originally make the cut, releasing the contact sheets he’s collected for over two decades in his new photography book, CONTACT. Inside the tome, he breaks down some of his most famous images of Björk, David Bowie, Kate Moss, and more, as well as everything that made them possible, from the handwritten notes to the experiments and outtakes. The photographer often describes making a portrait as falling in love, and his new book gives us insight into how he fosters those relationships. Below, a selection from CONTACT to transport you behind the scenes of these star-studded shoots.

items.title: Tidal Is the First Streaming Service to Ban AI Music
items.description: Tidal has announced an ambitious plan to ban all music wholly generated by artificial intelligence.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Tidal has announced an ambitious plan to ban all music wholly generated by artificial intelligence.

On Dec. 9, the streaming service will start rejecting uploads of all music made with AI, and removing any that are currently on the platform. Tidal head Robert Anderson stated that all AI tracks will be gone by the beginning of 2027.

The new policy will apply only to music made completely with AI tools like Suno, Lyria, and Udio. Tidal will continue to allow tracks made with the assistance of AI tools, “but not the sole outputs” of them.

As Anderson noted on X, this decision makes Tidal the first digital streaming platform to ban AI music, and he pointedly encouraged others in the industry to “follow suit.” The move comes after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing AI-generated tracks over the summer.

The proliferation of AI music on streaming platforms has caused numerous headaches for artists and labels over the past few years. While much of it goes unnoticed — Tidal estimated 96 percent of the AI songs it’s already flagged have garnered zero streams over the last 90 days — tracks that do catch on can divert streams and royalties from working artists.

There are also fraud concerns, whether it’s bots streaming AI-generated music, or scammers uploading AI tracks under the names of actual artists. Tidal said it’s already taken down over 65,000 such tracks “flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation.

“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal said in its statement.

Speaking to the scale of the AI music problem, Tidal estimated that there are 27 to 29 million AI tracks on its platform now (about six percent of its total catalog). Additionally, the company said 43 percent of all uploads from the past 90 days were flagged as wholly AI-generated. Anderson said the platform expects to reject anywhere between 80,000 to 85,000 songs per day once the new policy goes into effect.

While Tidal’s reject-and-remove policy is a novel step in the effort to combat AI slop, effective enforcement could pose some challenges. Earlier this year, DistroKid, the largest music distribution platform by volume, accidentally removed a bunch of real music, made by real artists, while doing mass takedowns in response to a copyright infringement lawsuit filed by Universal Music Group. (DistroKid apologized for the accidental takedowns, and has denied UMG’s accusations.)

Tidal has, however, at least been able to test out its detection tools thanks to its efforts to flag and demonetize AI music over the past few months. Working with Ircam Amplify, a Tidal spokesperson said, “The vast majority of appeals we have received have been reaffirmed upon closer review, which means the detection success rate is very high. A small amount of false positives is inevitable, but between our appeals process and improving detection technology, we are confident in our approach.”

Along with using these tools to determine whether a song is made with AI, Tidal said would ban distributors from “delivering these tracks to us” and would “reject delivers if their metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools.”

Tidal said its AI policy “was designed to provide a great experience for listeners, while protecting the authenticity and livelihoods of artists and rightsholders. Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more. Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you. We’ll keep sharing what we find and we’ll keep acting on it.”

items.title: The Altruists Recap: Game Theory
items.description: I can’t lie, it feels good to be settled into just one timeline now. After six whole episodes that jumped around in time, the events of “Prisoner’s Dilemma” take place over the course of just a few days, beginning with Changpeng Zhao’s tweet announcing the liq
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: I can’t lie, it feels good to be settled into just one timeline now. After six whole episodes that jumped around in time, the events of “Prisoner’s Dilemma” take place over the course of just a few days, beginning with Changpeng Zhao’s tweet announcing the liquidation of FTT on November 6, 2022, and ending with his tweet canceling his plans to buy the company on the 9th.

What takes place during and between those two tweets is almost like something out of Succession, with all the major players planning exit strategies and new strategic alliances. That sounds pretty fun, and it kind of is! This time, it’s Gary’s turn to learn the truth about the discrepancy; Nishad and Caroline were already planning to include him in their coup plans, but Sam is forced to tell him the truth when he asks questions about why Joe Bankman cannot gain access to their master ledger. And yet Gary actually isn’t put off at all by the utterly insane revelation of Sam and Caroline’s crimes. He’s just pissed he wasn’t included!

Sometimes the series sprinkles in these bits of comedy that don’t quite gel with the seriousness of the drama unfolding on screen, and that latest vegan-nachos scene is a good example. Still, I suppose it fits with what the show has already established about Gary, who was totally down to front-run when that was on the table. For the rest of the episode, he’s firmly on Team Sam, basically doing whatever his buddy asks: freezing customer withdrawals and keeping his mouth firmly shut when Ryan straight-up asks him if the fund is tapped out. When Nishad proposes a side alliance to get their stories straight and team up against Sam and Caroline, Gary immediately assumes it’s a test and walks away. And it’s Gary who eventually shows Sam the clumsily deposited folder full of documents related to Caroline and Nishad’s plot against him. (People are always just stumbling into huge revelations on this show. Nobody can keep anything secret.)

The central tension animating this episode is a pretty straightforward one: Who will snitch? Caroline and Nishad are still hiding their coup plans throughout this episode, but a simple corporate reorg is rapidly moving out of the realm of feasibility. Everything is burning down around these people, and the inner circle is locked in a four-way prisoner’s dilemma, unable to commit to truly trusting one another. Then again, the prisoner’s dilemma is predicated on the idea that neither would go to jail if both stayed silent, and I’m not sure that would work the same way for this gang of thieves.

Either way, it’s impossible to ever tell what Sam and Caroline are going to do. They’re the wild cards who got the company into this mess in the first place, and so much of how they act at work depends on the current state of their relationship. When Sam offers Caroline some mild praise and openly admits to trying to push her out, it’s enough to shake her confidence in her plans. By the time Hannah is randomly confronting her at a cafe in the Bahamas, she’s not at all receptive to her sympathy; she actually throws iced coffee at the journalist after Hannah suggests this was all Sam’s fault. Caroline doesn’t like feeling like a victim, and in this telling of the story especially, she isn’t much of one. She has agency, all right, possibly too much of it to match the real Ellison.

Emotional, Caroline reports back to Sam about the incident and affirms her trust in him. This is handy timing, because CZ just took a meeting with Sam in Malta and agreed to bail out FTX on the condition that he could dissolve Alameda and fuck over Caroline. And Sam was pretty much down! But after realizing that Caroline really is trustworthy, he changes his mind and offers to hand over all of FTX and Alameda to CZ in exchange for a positive tweet to bring their market standing back to life. And that’s exactly what happens: CZ tweets about his faith in FTX and his intention to buy the company. It’s a perfect solution for Sam and Caroline, who share a tender moment on the beach holding hands and agreeing that it’d be nice to work together as colleagues under CZ. Not preferable, but as long as they have each other, they’ll be fine. Love conquers all, right?

Except CZ goes back on his word entirely, tweeting again about why he can’t invest in FTX after a period of due diligence. From here, it’s pretty much joever for Sam and the company in general. At an all-hands meeting, Caroline comes clean to the staff about the shortfall of user funds, giggling with panic as her employees scream at her. And Sam is nowhere to be found, busy chucking Caroline under the bus because he can’t think of any other way to escape blame — and because he learned about her coup plan.

Part of me wants to throw The Altruists a bone here; this might be the strongest episode yet, thanks to the delirious scramble for allies and a relatively clear-eyed perspective about Sam’s general shittiness. But the show is still guilty of most of the usual problems, including some really silly stuff with Joe Bankman, a character who always felt like a distraction despite Paul Reiser’s solid performance. I could see Sam’s “you’re jealous” line to his dad coming from a mile away, even though it barely makes any sense. If the show wants to imply that there’s some truth to his statements, and that Joe is trying to belatedly live out his dreams by working with his son at FTX, it needed more time to tell that story.

There’s also not much to the subplot with Lily and Duncan, who have a brief argument after Lily initially agrees to engage in some light wash trading (a form of market manipulation involving buying and selling at the same time in order to drum up market activity) rather than shutting Modulo down and giving the $400 million back. This pairing ostensibly exists as a tech-couple parallel to Sam and Caroline, but we see so little of them that the comparison is hazy at best. It’s difficult to care much about what happens to Lily and her company to begin with, and I know even less about Duncan, which would be disappointing even if I wasn’t already a fan of Hudson Williams from Heated Rivalry.

“Prisoner’s Dilemma” concludes with Caroline talking to the DOJ, a satisfying outcome after an episode of bickering and back-stabbing. I may not be fully sold on The Altruists as a fascinating or emotionally engaging adaptation of this rich story, but I’m hopeful the show can land the plane okay if it leans into the drama that’s already there. After all, the trial of SBF is one of the craziest parts of this whole saga. Sometimes the truth really is stranger than fiction, and this show could use a little bit more truth.

• I enjoyed the little riff about Caroline’s overuse of exclamation points in her tweets, which appears to be accurate. Tweets are central to the story this week, but what the series doesn’t show is that SBF was also tweeting a ton at the time — like his apology thread to investors from November 10, during which he addresses CZ: “well played; you won.”
• Lauren and Ryan get a mini-subplot where both are starting to get freaked out by everything, and ultimately Lauren leaves the story pretty unceremoniously by flying home to the Hamptons.

• I’m not really sure what the show wants us to think of Hannah. She’s depicted as smart and hard-working, but also overly emotional and kind of conniving, with a blinkered perspective on some of her subjects.

• I did laugh at the repeated explanations of the prisoner’s dilemma, which transcended over-exposition and just became funny. Gary’s reaction is best: “Everyone and their mom has heard of the prisoner’s dilemma. You try and explain it to me.”

• I honestly don’t mind that much that The Altruists doesn’t offer more perspectives of the people actually harmed by the fraud — I get that this is more about the perpetrators, like plenty of comparable series — but it feels a little irresponsible that the one client we do hear from is an angry man demanding money and threatening Claire and her family over the phone.

• Also on the Claire front: She glances over at Nishad during Caroline’s confession to the office, specifically when she hears that Caroline has known since earlier this year. It seems like she’s already putting together why Nishad cut their relationship short.

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: Tourist Trap
items.description: Last week, I lamented the way Dexter has grown soft, with the show straining to make him the hero by abandoning the shades of gray that once defined him. This week, he brutally murders a kid. Okay, not a child but a very young person who on some level was forc
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: Last week, I lamented the way Dexter has grown soft, with the show straining to make him the hero by abandoning the shades of gray that once defined him. This week, he brutally murders a kid. Okay, not a child but a very young person who on some level was forced into a life of crime. While Dex’s latest victim technically fits the Code, there is real darkness to this episode’s final act, which is something of a relief for me as a Dexter fan who relishes the character’s moral ambiguity. If I’m cooler on “Young Blood” as a whole, it’s not because Dexter lets his Dark Passenger take control but because the show has moved a little too briskly through this season’s most compelling story line thus far.

We’ll get there. When the episode starts, Dex is learning more about the JawSplitter, who sounds like a real peach. He strings his victims upside down and puts a tourniquet around their necks, then removes their jaws while they’re still alive and drains their blood into a bucket. The JawSplitter is a “vampire” of the Peter Thiel variety — he infuses himself with the blood of young men as a de-aging technique. (No real explanation for why he keeps their jaws, but I think that’s more standard serial-killer stuff than biohacking.) Before Dexter can deal with him, however, he faces another interruption from Quinn, who wants to share his latest Prater theory. At their now-go-to bar, Quinn explains that he thinks the man he rescued from the U-Haul was an intended victim of the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. It’s a massive leap of logic, as is Quinn’s belief that Prater may have been meeting with serial killers directly and collecting their trophies. Never mind that he happens to be right. “I don’t like smart Quinn,” Dex’s voice-over notes.

That’s a problem for another day, though. After dismissing Quinn’s theories as far-fetched, Dexter heads to the brownstone to await the JawSplitter. This will be the last Charley-orchestrated kill, and Dex doesn’t want it to end. (Me neither!) He’s basically throwing himself at her when he says, “If you did the tracking and I did the cleaning up, think how many lives we could save. Is there any chance you know other killers on the loose?” It’s very “haha just kidding … unless?” For her part, Charley doesn’t seem keen to continue this arrangement past the absolution she feels is necessary. Yes, she admits, it has been fun working together, but this isn’t the life she wants for herself. They’ll have to table this conversation because the JawSplitter (a.k.a. John Thomas) has arrived — well, not exactly. The 22-year-old at the door, played by It’s Jack Dylan Grazer, is John Thomas Jr. or JJ. The O.G. JawSplitter has been dead for two years, and JJ has been carrying on his work since then. That makes him a serial killer, and he wants in on Prater’s club.

While this is going on, Quinn decides to show up at the police station to share his Prater theory with Wallace and ask if he can do a little digging. She’s suspiciously accommodating here. Are cops in the habit of letting random out-of-state PIs rifle through evidence logs? Quinn soon finds himself face-to-face with Prater’s collection, which includes memorabilia from Dahmer, Bundy, and Gacy — and Batista’s hat, which prompts a flashback to Quinn and Ángel getting high in the latter’s vintage Pontiac Firebird. (Batista bought the car during his season-six midlife crisis. If only he were around to give Dexter guidance!) Quinn doesn’t seem to find anything useful, but he does get Charley’s number from Wallace. And much to my surprise, Charley later agrees to meet so she can answer any lingering questions. It ends up being a very short hang, with Charley suggesting Quinn stop digging. “I’d advise you to walk away,” she cautions him. “That’s what I did.”

As for Dexter, he has a new mission: find out if JJ fits the Code by spending the day with him. In some ways, this is an easy enough task. JJ is in full tourist mode and absolutely delighted to be seeing the sights alongside another serial killer. But it’s also painful in the sense that JJ is a Gen-Z caricature created in a lab to irritate our Gen-X protagonist. Dexter mostly takes it in stride, if only because he sees a bit of Harrison in this kid. Can he really kill him? “I know you probably think that I’m just some nepo baby, but I’m legit,” JJ insists. His story, however, is troubling. The JawSplitter didn’t take blood just from his victims — he siphoned it from his son, too, and those “blood bonding” sessions were the only time they really talked. “My dad was deadass a psychopathic narcissist,” JJ shares. Dexter reflects on his past attempts to mold his own son into a killer. “He looked at you and saw a mirror,” he says about the JawSplitter, but a flashback to Dex killing Kurt Caldwell in front of Harrison makes it clear what he’s really thinking. I’ll be honest: As much as I like Grazer as an actor, JJ is a really annoying character, so I don’t love spending a huge chunk of the episode with him. Still, he’s a useful counterpoint to Harrison, whom Dexter separately asks to search the police database to find out if JJ has a criminal record. That ends up being a dead end, but Harrison already using his new role to help the Bay Harbor Butcher means a line has been crossed.

Outside of Harrison digging into JJ’s past, the NYPD side of this week’s episode isn’t all that interesting. The Five Borough Killer calls with his latest threat: “Someone will die today on the subway.” Obviously, they can’t shut down all the trains or they’ll paralyze the city — the MTA does a good enough job of that on its own — but Mixon wants two cops in every train car. This results in a very silly subplot in which Harrison and Fiona confront a subway mugger who nearly slits Harrison’s throat before Fiona draws her weapon on him. I assure you the average purse snatcher is not going to escalate to cop killing, but this isn’t the first time Dexter has strained credulity. Naturally, the massive police presence does nothing to stop FBK. (That part is realistic.) While Mixon, once the clock strikes midnight, is ready to celebrate successfully keeping the serial killer at bay, Wallace follows a hunch that a homeless person who allegedly OD’d on a train in the Bronx was actually a homicide. She goes behind her captain’s back to order a toxicology report, which reveals the man was in fact poisoned with thallium. When FBK AirDrops his smart-glasses video of the murder to the police station (a real “fuck you,” as Harrison notes), it’s revealed that there were two officers in the train car who missed FBK handing his victim a tainted bottle of water. Oops! We saw him disable the cameras last week, so there’s no other footage to analyze, and FBK’s erratic M.O. makes it all but impossible to know how he’ll strike next.

Back at the brownstone, Dexter is still trying to figure out if JJ is an actual monster or just a kid who was groomed by one. For a while, Dex leans toward the latter — that is, until JJ shows off his father’s jawbone as an early share. It turns out JJ murdered his dad because the JawSplitter was getting sloppy and JJ didn’t want to get caught, which makes him a true believer and lands him on Dexter’s kill table. “I’m the victim here. My dad forced this life on me!” JJ pleads. However true that is, his slow-beating heart reveals an underlying psychopathy.
