items.title: ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’: How Season 3 Brings Epic Moments to Life and Deals With Annabeth’s Absence in the Books
items.description: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
items.author: Kimberly Nordyke
paragraphs: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

Percy Jackson is back. Season 3 of the Disney+/Hulu series Percy Jackson and the Olympians continues the saga of the Greek gods, their demigod offspring and the mission to prevent the rise of the Titans.

The storyline is based on The Titan’s Curse, the third book in Rick Riordan‘s bestselling series. The plot finds Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava‘ Jeffries) captured by the forces of Kronos, leading Percy (Walker Scobell) to embark on a perilous journey to rescue her. He must free a goddess in chains, confront the Titan’s curse and avoid triggering the fall of Olympus. He’s joined by his friend, the satyr Grover Underwood (Aryan Simhadri), and some unlikely others on his quest.
Co-creator/executive producer Jonathan E. Steinberg tells The Hollywood Reporter that Percy and Annabeth’s friendship continues to be central to the story this season.

“In the first two seasons, we were very aware that while we were watching a story about two lonely kids become best friends, there were other things in the offing between them, and that eventually, they would mean more to each other,” he says. “Some of that is a romantic story eventually, and some of that is just how best friends they are. Getting to test that and watch them both deal with the idea of losing the other, and maybe never getting them back, is sort of core to the experience of investing in Percy and Annabeth’s relationship.“
Steinberg praises the season‘s handling of the maturity as “exciting.”

“Ultimately, it doesn’t matter how tall that monster is, if you don’t care about the two people in the center of the story, it’s just not going to be exciting. This season really answers both of those calls and doing its work on a grand scale and also putting these people through a trial and interrogating how important they really are to each other,” he says.

As the third season rolls out, the cast and creatives — including Scobell, Jeffries, Simhadri, Steinberg and EPs Dan Shotz and Craig Silverstein — sat down to talk with THR about the making of the show, bringing the book’s epic moments to life and what fans can expect.
Sourcing the Source Material

Each season of the show has corresponded with a book in the series. (Season 1 was adapted from 2005’s The Lightning Thief, Season 2 from 2006’s The Sea of Monsters and now Season 3 from 2007’s The Titan’s Curse.) The books feature monsters and battles and mythical creatures, much of which make for an ambitious adaptation to a TV show. For the producers, their challenge is bringing all of that to life.

“Rick doesn’t make it easier for us with each book,” Shotz quips. “It just gets bigger and bigger as we go. But the benefit of doing a series is you get to keep building and learning from what you did before, and have the show grow.”

He gives credit to the entire team for “making this the biggest, best version of itself,” including the “massive set pieces.” “You want to deliver on kids’ imaginations and deliver these creatures, but do it unique to Percy,” Shotz adds. “So every time we’re trying to build a creature or create a set piece, it’s like, what makes it unique to this show? How do you take mythology that’s been around for a long time? How do you take what Rick put in his books, and then how do we make it into something that is really special? And it just takes incredible craftsmen and women who just put their best feet forward and deliver on it. The artistry that we got to see this year really felt like it was second to none, and we just went for it.”

Silverstein gives credit to Steinberg and Shotz for envisioning something bigger than the small screen. “It starts with the ambition of John and Dan at the outset of this, to say, ‘OK, this isn’t just the TV version. This is the thing,'” he shares. “We all love big movies. It’s not holding back. These guys really went for it to put this thing up on [a big] scale.”

Aryan Simhadri, who plays satyr Grover Underwood, says fans will be pleased this season. “We talk a lot of about the tone shifting, but I’m really proud of how we adapted a lot of the fan-favorite moments from the book,” he says. “I think we really did a good job of visualizing these sets and like adapting these moments to screen. It really just looks stunning this season.”
Meanwhile, the actors share that they do a deep dive into the books before filming each season. Asked how much they draw on the source material, Jeffries is quick to reply: “Oh, I drew so much.”

Scobell offers his own take. “I feel like it’s really important to start off every season rereading the book that you’re doing,” he says. “I reread Book 3 before we went into it and and I’ve reread Book 2 before we started that [season], and I think that’s really important.But at the same time you have to be willing to kind of let some things go because some things are going to get cut, some things are going to get added. It’s going change the story a little bit, so you kind of have to keep the core of their character but be willing to change according to the script.”
Shifting Beyond Percy’s POV
One of the challenges for the production team is that that the entire book series is a first-person narrative as told by Percy.

“Everything in the book is from Percy’s point of view,” Silverstein says. “We’ve long taken the camera off from around his shoulder, and put it out with other people. It’s kind of been a slowly widening process of that as the story progresses.”
But it’s not that easy just to show other characters’ points of view without changing the story.

“If the camera cuts to something else that he did not see happen, or someone else he did not see, how does that affect the story of the book?” Silverstein continues. “And in surprising ways, it affects quite a bit. [For example], Percy sees a lot of things through his dreams, but if he doesn’t see those things, then the story’s ahead of him, and sometimes the audience is ahead of him. Sometimes that’s good, and sometimes that’s not good. The challenges to the adaptation begin to present themselves, and then you’re always trying to steer back to what the core of the story is, what made us excited when we read the books, and hoping that that lines up with what made any reader excited when they read the books.”

Annabeth isn’t in the third book very much, but she’s obviously one of the main characters of the series. For that matter, Clarice (Dior Goodjohn) isn’t in it at all — but she also appears in the third season. So how do you tell a story around characters who have little to no presence in the source material?

“It’s about taking cues from the book,” Silverstein says. “Just because Annabeth’s not in the book doesn’t mean she’s not in the story. She is, and it’s about taking the camera to her. We’re trying to build the story out. She’s up there on Mount Othrys with Luke. Well, what are they talking about? What’s going on there? And that’s something that colors within the lines of the grand narrative that doesn’t change it in a huge way.”

As for Clarice, she’s not in the book because she’s working on a secret mission for Chiron, but it’s not clear what that mission is to the reader until later. “If you read the later books, you find out what she’s doing,” Silvertein adds. “So [in the series], we’re going to find out what she’s doing a little earlier. Which is what we would have done if we had taken the camera and put it over her shoulder, right? It’s fleshing that stuff out.”

The producers do consult with Riordan on these types of changes. According to Shotz, the author loves exploring “all these different avenues” as well. “It gives him an opportunity to dive deeper into this world and make suggestions about what he thinks, is happening, that he didn’t get to explore when he started this process,” Shotz adds.

And, of course, Annabeth is crucial to the overall story. “That’s what’s amazing about adaptations is, once you have a character like Annabeth, you can’t keep telling this story without Leah,” Shotz says. “It doesn’t work. We must tell her story, so that’s really the fun part of it, but also for an audience who’s not only going to get their book series honored, but they’re going to get all these new things that will excite them. And that makes it really interesting, so that it’s not just a book report. You’re getting so much more.”

For Jeffries, not having source material to draw on actually allowed a bit more freedom in portraying the character. “I really feel like it was kind of up to interpretation for me because I could do a lot of acting improv, not with words but with reactions and how she plays certain scenes, which is a good thing,” she says. “It’s more of a raw reaction now because when you’re playing a part or you’re doing a certain scene that’s really important in the books, and you know what’s in there, it’s kind of like you expect it. But with Annabeth and with me especially, it was kind of harder I’m also figuring it out. I wanted to make sure that I still stayed in Annabeth’s character, even though she’s not in the book [much].” Still, she admits that she was a bit nervous as a result of not having the anything in the books to draw on.

In Season 3, Annabeth also spends much of the story separated from Percy and Grover, which meant Scobell and Simhadri weren’t really there to witness Jeffries acting out her scenes, and vice versa. They were only able to see one another’s performance once the series started coming together, and they have nothing but praise for one another.

“Once I watched it and saw everything come together — especially you guys, because I wasn’t with you guys, so I didn’t really get to see what you were doing — you guys looked really good. I’m actually really proud of you guys,” Jeffries says.
“it is weird because there were two separate whole stories going on basically at the same time,” Scobell adds. “So, not be there for part of it and then see what’s going on afterward.”
“And to see how much you’ve grown at the end of the season,” Simhadri adds of Annabeth.

Thalia, the demigod daughter of Zeus, has been present throughout the books and series but as a tree for much of the story. In the books, the story goes that Zeus did this to protect her after she sacrificed herself to save her friends. But in a twist, the series diverted from the books; viewers learned in the season finale that he actually transformed her as a punishment after she confronted him about his intentions to use her as a weapon.

She’s been mentioned through the books and series up to this point, looming large in the characters’ consciousness. We briefly met her in the Season 2 finale after she was transformed back to her human form, but now she’s a much bigger part of the story. This season finds Thalia (Tamara Smart) joining forces with Percy, but it’s a rocky alliance as he is wary of her loyalty to Luke, the demigod who betrayed Percy way back in Season 1 and has been trying to overthrow the Olympian gods.

“Rick has a phrase about this book, and it applies to this season as well: All of the major chess pieces are coming onto the board,” Silverstein says. “Thalia has been talked about since Season 1, but now she’s really coming into the story, and when he’s talking about the chessboard, what game is it? Well, it’s this war between the gods and the Titans. And Thalia is right at the center of all of that. Thalia and Percy and any other potential children of the big three gods who may be out there.”

The overall saga of the books comes more into focus in the third book/Season 3, he adds, versus just focusing on “the quest of the year.” “And what Thalia decides to do will affect not just all of the people she loves and her friends, but the entire world and all of her parents and all of her grandparents,” he adds. “She’s got a big role.”

As for how the dynamic changes with Thalia around, the actors say it introduces a rivalry between the characters. Simhadri begins, “We all wanted to be — ” “the biggest and baddest,” Jeffries finishes as he nods. (The cast often finishes each other’s sentences.) Scobell expands: “Thalia is kind of in competition with Percy for his spot in that kind of group. But she can’t just show up and join us. It’s not like [Percy’s cyclops half-brother] Tyson, where he and Grover can exist. There can be only one.” Simhaddri echoes that sentiment: “It’s one or the other.”
Percy has arguably the biggest growth of any character up to this point, as he started off the series thinking he was a regular boy before learning he was a demigod and becoming a hero.

“The most important part about playing Perseus Jackson is also experiencing my own life in the same way,” Scobell says. “He goes to camp every summer and then he goes back to school and back to his real life. I do the same thing. We take a big break in between every season.”

But now, Scobell finishing his last year in high school and still awaiting word on a fourth season. “So I’m kind of moving into uncharted territory because before, I could look forward to next season and really just be comfortable going to school and living my own life, but this is going to be a big change for me because it’s so uncertain.”

For Simhadri, he also felt like Grover grew a lot of over the course of the season, as did he, not only as a person but as an actor. “I was an adult on season 2, but I never ended up working that many hours per day,” he shares. “But in season 3, I was back every day filming and I was working with a ton of adults, so we would all just shoot for as long as we could in well into the night and really just like push ourselves every day. So I feel like not only did Grover grow over the course of the season, I think I grew in tandem alongside him.”
Why Greek Gods Are Having a Moment
This year has seen not only more Percy Jackson but also the box office blockbuster The Odyssey. Why are people suddenly gaga over the Greek gods?

“It’s timeless,” Steinberg says. “Those stories have evolved to be about universal experiences that just kind of live really deeply in everybody. I think it’s really not surprising that they never quite go away, because they apply to everybody. We’re happy that it’s in the zeitgeist, but not surprised.”
“And Percy did it a lot faster than Odysseus,” Shotz quips of the latter’s 20-year journey back home.
Percy Jackson and the Olympians is streaming on Disney+ and Hulu.

items.title: TV Ratings: NBA Logs Winning Streak in First Month of the Season
items.description: Like a jump shooter who can’t miss, the NBA is on a heater with TV audiences through the first month of its 2026-27 season.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: Like a jump shooter who can’t miss, the NBA is on a heater with TV audiences through the first month of its 2026-27 season.

National telecasts of league games on NBC/Peacock, ESPN and Prime Video are averaging 2.62 million viewers over the season’s first month, based on Nielsen ratings and Adobe Analytics figures for Peacock’s games. That’s a sizable, 37 percent increase over the same time frame last year — the first in the league’s current media rights deal with NBCUniversal, ESPN and Prime Video. Through last week, every national telecast had topped 1 million viewers, the first time that’s happened since 2023.

That’s also the highest mark on record for the first month of an NBA season, excluding lockout-delayed starts in 1999 and 2011 (and with the caveat that changes in Nielsen measurement the past few years have tended to benefit live sports).

NBC’s six national windows lead the way with an average of 4.5 million viewers (including streaming on Peacock), a 27 percent improvement over last season’s first month.. The network’s opening night game between the defending champion New York Knicks and the Philadelphia 76ers (who acquired LeBron James during the offseason) averaged 7.71 million cross-platform viewers.

The first eight games on Prime Video have averaged 2.05 million viewers, and ESPN is at 1.8 million viewers across 13 telecasts. Prime Video has grown by a huge 83 percent year to year, and ESPN’s games are up 13 percent.

Prime Video has the youngest audience of the NBA’s three national media partners (the same is true for Prime relative to other NFL broadcasters); its median viewer age is a little under 46. ESPN and NBC (not including Peacock viewers) have a median age of about 53 for NBA games.

items.title: The Real-Life Wardrobe of Michael Bennett, Who Traded the NFL for Furniture Design
items.description: When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to
items.author: Christopher Fenimore
paragraphs: When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to school.

After completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively. “I’m a student of whatever I do,” Bennett tells me. “My best quality—and probably my worst quality—is that the things I love to do, I try to become the best. I play tennis five days a week. I’m trying to go to Wimbledon. And design and architecture are like that.”

All that effort is paying off. Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics. He’s now hard at work on his sophomore line, alongside a spoken-word album and the occasional bespoke garment.

That last side quest should come as no surprise, because Bennett has some of the most distinctive personal style I’ve ever seen on a pro athlete–current or former—with a particularly clean headwear and accessories game. Here, Bennett tells me all about the skills he carried over from football into his new career, what fatherhood has taught him about masculinity, and the song he listens to every day.

Michael Bennett: I’ve been playing football my whole life, man. After winning so much, I dug deep. I had already conquered the body. How do I conquer the mind? At what point am I being selfish? I’m missing so much of my kids’ lives. I’ve already been to the highest of the high. Am I going to leave my family with a broken man? That was really the question. Am I chasing ego or am I chasing something else? In reality, a lot of us are just chasing the ego, to be remembered, scared of the death of what [your life] was rather than [embracing] the growth that can be.

People want to keep others in a certain box because that’s the way that they understand them. That’s in any relationship. If you started to date somebody when they’re 20 and you turn 40 and they start to change, you’d be like, “You used to like your eggs like that.” People don’t allow others to transition; won’t allow people to actually experience growth. Often you’re meeting people in a time where they’re just starting to learn who they are. Over time you start to really develop who you are.

The truth is it doesn’t matter if people take you seriously, [as long as] you take yourself seriously. What are you doing to practice your craft? Artists are like, “Oh, my practice, my practice.” I never really understood what that meant until I started doing my own practice. I practiced on the field and I can practice the body. But really, if you want to be taken seriously intellectually, then you have to practice the mind. Sometimes practicing the mind is also connected to the body. In football, yeah, you are connected to the mind in a certain way. But it isn’t always like learning to be a lawyer or an architect or an artist—to be a thinker, you’re doing something completely different. And it’s just allowing yourself to transition. Man, truthfully, you got to say fuck everybody.

I think it’s one of the most intellectual sports in general. Tennis is one of those sports where it’s about the angle, the quick twitch. You’re by yourself. With football, it’s the amount of moving parts. People overlook the amount of detail that it takes to run a team—practicing and going through a play 3,000 times before you actually get it. The best players I ever met were the smartest when it came to the sport. They were the PhDs of their craft.

It’s taught me vulnerability. It made me a better human. In some ways, my daughters have allowed me to mature. The sport of football requires so much masculinity. I’m not saying that all masculinity is toxic, [but] it’s more about, how do you hunt but still be gentle? The true samurai doesn’t strike, but knows he can.

What my daughters have allowed me to do is develop my whole humanity. To have a daughter is so special—women are very special. As an athlete, people come back from injuries, but to see a woman come back from giving birth is a whole other level of love. My daughters have been my greatest accomplishments in my life. I never made a Super Bowl trophy. There’s always another winner. But there’s only one Peyton, there’s only one Blake, and there’s one Ollie. As a maker, those are the most special things that I could make.

In 2019, I was really into Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois and [their debate over] the “Talented Tenth.” [Booker T. Washington believed that] intellectualism should never get away from the idea of making. I got into design because I’ve always been involved in politics, and politically, I started to realize that everything came down to design.

Whenever I spoke out about police brutality or on critical issues in America, that was really where I started to think about design as this language—this form of resistance. How can I change the system? It starts with design. Where I grew up, a non-gentrified area that was low income, it’s like you could see that there was no empathetic way of thinking about design. The definition of architecture for me is empathy for space. That’s what led me to this idea of these African diaspora forms and languages that I will use as my form of resistance.

I’m working on a new collection of furniture. The first collection I did was called “We Gotta Get Back to the Crib,” which to me was really about getting back to the essence of Blackness. A lot of times we talk about Blackness and it’s always connected to traumatic experience. But to me, it was more about how can I connect to these true levels of love, these things really shaped my culture, my family, my mother, my grandmother, and everything that was beautiful about being Black? This next collection is about African brutalism. How can I bring these things that are seen in the ghetto in America and in West Africa and then turn those into ideas about furniture? A lot of times what I’m dealing with as a designer is this idea of abstraction. How can I pull and reference something in such a sweet way? Like how Virgil designed shoes with references, leaving crumbs to this unspoken past. As a designer, that’s what I’m trying to do.
Yeah, I got a spoken word project.

As an athlete, if you talk about your cars or you talk about your jewelry, the way that you gained it doesn’t have that kind of Jay-Z effect—you didn’t hustle to get that. You played to get that, which is different from somebody hustling to get that. With spoken word, I think about Gil Scott-Heron or The Last Poets. They’re talking about critical issues. My perspective is really about humanizing the Black experience and the Black man. My stories and what I’m trying to tell with this music, E-Nigg-Ma, is so much about Black culture, Black design, Black features, this idea of what America is trying to suffocate about Blackness and not let it breathe.

Music. When I’m designing, beautiful sounds are really important to the way that I think. My number-one song that I always listen to is Miles Davis’s “Flamenco Sketches.” It’s my daily listen. Those are the sounds that I need to hear: the horn, the riffs, the in-between.
My studio inspires me, just the way light hits. It’s the simplest things. Seeing my family movies. My wife inspires me with what she’s designing.

My great-grandpa, Hall Mack, everybody talked about his fashion. People still talk about his style. He was the first person I saw dry cleaning everything. His style was impeccable. When I look back at a period of style that I liked, it’d be the years of the Birth of the Cool. People like Miles, Sidney Poitier, everybody was just fresh.

I’ve always been connected to style. People always call me “Runway Mike.” They say, “Bro, you wear more Margiela than anybody I know.” I design my own clothes. [Style] is a part of who you are. I love the idea of fashion. I want to design a fashion show. Yo, Wales Bonner, let me design something for you! I want to be backstage.

Over time I just found me. That takes so much time. I feel like one of the most beautiful things is Instagram and this ability to share things, but one of the worst things is Instagram and the ability to share things. Because there’s a part of us that starts to mimic [what we see] in a way that isn’t true to us. We start to judge ourselves on other people’s experience.

It’s cool to see things, but it’s also cool to experiment with what you feel good in. “Yo, this is what I look good in. I don’t care what nobody says, I feel good.” That’s what true fashion is. I buy Prada because I actually like it. That’s the development of who you are and your taste—when you buy things for the love of it. Like, “Man, I really love the shoulder on this.” I’m not buying anything to be seen in it. I’m buying it because I respect the process.
I think it was something from Acne, even though Acne was that middle kind of brand. Acne now has gotten too expensive.

Two things. I bought this striped Prada sweater. It was just a nice, beautiful brown. It was quiet, but it was super nice. And I just designed the blue shirt [from my second look]. Even making something like that is expensive.
I just sketch it, and then I make it in LA.
Yeah, or show a picture of something and break it down like, “Cut this out. I need the arms to be like this.”

I’m also going to do it for my studio. My goal is to have studio attire that I produce. This year I’m dropping four shirts. If you’re a designer and you want a beautiful shirt, here’s four of them. I’m only making a hundred of them. Keep it very simple.

The thing that’s exciting about fashion now is getting away from logos and getting back to beautiful garments. I always loved Issey Miyake, because it’s just so uniform for me. It’s something I wear in the studio all the time—easy to put on, mix and match. It travels well. He was a genius when it came to innovation. A lot of people make clothes, but not a lot of people innovate. I like Wales Bonner. I always like her polo shirts. Margiela and Prada are two of my favorite brands of all time—Prada is just so detailed. Jil Sander is nice. I like Toteme.

Tunnel style is terrible. It’s manufactured. It’s not real. The clothes are wearing them. Half of the things aren’t really who they are. There are some people, like Laremy Tunsil, that are fresh—he’s a big guy from Washington who dresses fresh and it feels like it’s him. But a lot of times you see people that just look like they’re trying too hard to do fashion. Fashion should be quiet and it should be proportioned properly. There’s a geometry to it, and I think that’s what’s missing from tunnel style.
It’s not the sport, it’s the individual. There are some fresh individuals from each sport that wear dope clothes, like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Stefon Diggs. My brother Martellus dresses fresh.
Jay-Z’s 4:44. Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue. And I’m in between Kanye West’s Late Registration and Mos Def & Talib Kweli Are Black Star.

items.title: David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet
items.description: Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

items.title: The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?
items.description: You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie. The speciality drink was created by Paul Saladino, who regularly preaches the benefits of following an animal-based diet. If you look inside t
items.author: Emily Laurence Sardinha
paragraphs: You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie. The speciality drink was created by Paul Saladino, who regularly preaches the benefits of following an animal-based diet. If you look inside the blender, you’ll find kefir, beef organs (like liver, heart, kidney, and spleen from Saldino’s Heart & Soil line), and “immunomilk,” which is freeze-dried cow’s colostrum. Yum. Saladino may be an outlier, but he certainly isn’t the only person pushing a meat-heavy diet. Brian Johnson, aka the “liver king,” follows an extreme ancestral carnivore diet, eating a pound of raw liver a day.

Eating raw organs is a step too far, but maybe you’ve heard about the benefits of the carnivore diet and you’re curious. According to a 2026 study published in Nutrients, the number of posts about the carnivore diet on Instagram is in the millions—and they didn’t even look at TikTok. Interest surrounding the carnivore diet has shown no signs of slowing down.

Maybe plant-based eating leaves you gassy and unsatisfied. You can’t help that you like wings. Before you take vegetables off the table completely, it’s important to know what the carnivore diet is and how it impacts health, both short-term and long-term. As experts explain here, it’s not all bad. But there are some important risks to be aware of.
What is the carnivore diet?

The aforementioned Nutrients study on the carnivore diet explains that there isn’t one standard definition of what the carnivore diet actually is, but generally speaking, it’s a diet where you only eat minimally processed animal foods, including organ meats, fish, seafood, eggs, animal fats, and full-fat dairy. Plant-based foods are eliminated entirely.

While eliminating foods like fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is extreme, Pouria Sefidmooye Azar, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and assistant professor at the University of Central Arkansas, says the carnivore diet isn’t all bad. He says that short term, many people lose weight eating this way.

“Protein is more satiating than carbs and fats, so people following the carnivore diet often stay full for a longer amount of time, which means they reduce their caloric intake,” he says. Logically, it makes sense. If you’re eating foods like beef, chicken, and salmon, you’ll be less likely to dig into the pantry for snacks than if you ate a bowl of noodles.
Is the carnivore diet healthy?

Dr. Azar says it’s important not to conflate weight loss with getting healthier. He says that by eliminating plants, you’re going to miss out on a lot of important nutrients the body needs. You can probably guess the big one. Yep, fiber. “"If you’re cutting out every plant food, you're not getting fiber or phytonutrients, which are protective compounds found only in plants,” says Chris Vogliano, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and global food systems expert.

While you might not suffer any consequences of this immediately, both dietitians say that continuing to eat this way can mess up your digestion. You need fiber for good poops, plain and simple. Dr. Azar says that we also need fiber to feed the healthy gut bacteria in the microbiome. This is important for supporting mental health, immune health, and minimizing the risk of chronic diseases and cancers.

Dr. Azar specifically calls out the connection between a high-meat, low-fiber diet and the risk of colorectal cancer. For example, a 2015 Oncology Reviews study shows a connection between red meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk, while a 2026 European Journal of Cancer study called low fiber consumption a major risk factor for colorectal cancer.

Considering that men are at increased risk for heart disease (the number one cause of death in the U.S.), it’s important to know how the carnivore diet can impact your cardiovascular health. Spoiler alert: It’s not good. “I would not recommend the carnivore diet as a healthy, long-term eating pattern,” says Sunny Intwala, MD, MBA, preventive cardiologist and the director of Prevention & Wellness at Northwell Health.

Dr. Intwala explains that this is because meat doesn’t just contain protein; it has a lot of saturated fat too. He says that diets centering around red meat increase LDL cholesterol and blood pressure in a few short weeks. This, he says, can contribute to inflammation and plaque buildup that increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

As someone who studies how the way we eat impacts the planet, Dr. Vogliano points out that the carnivore diet is pretty horrible for the environment. “From a food systems lens, a meat-only diet on a global or even national level would carry massive environmental costs from land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions. This is regardless of whether the meat is conventionally raised, organic, or even regenerative. There’s just not enough land to produce that much meat,” he says.
Are there benefits to eating raw meat?
Okay, we need plants. But what about the Brian Johnsons and Paul Salidinos of the world preaching the benefits of eating raw meat? If you are going to eat meat, are there benefits to eating it raw?

Both dietitians say no, emphasizing that there is no scientific evidence showing that raw meat is more beneficial in any way than eating cooked meat. “Liver is a nutrient-rich food and a great way to get vitamin A, vitamin B12, folate, and iron. But you can get that from cooked liver; you don’t have to eat it raw,” Dr. Vogliano says. In fact, he emphasizes that eating any meat raw increases the risk of foodborne illnesses like Salmonella and E.coli.

Dr. Azar warns against pulling a Rocky and eating raw eggs either. “The protein in raw eggs is between 50 and 60% digestible. But the protein digestibility in cooked eggs is over 90%,” he says. A study from the ‘90s in The Journal of Nutrition backs this up.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the same for meat. A 2015 study in the same journal found that the cooking time for meat didn’t impact protein digestibility very much. So while you may get the same amount of digestible protein from raw meat as you would cooked meat, your risk of foodborne illness is greater.
How much meat is healthy to eat?

Decades of scientific research make it clear that a plant-free diet is not a healthy diet. If you’re a meat lover, you might be wondering just how much meat you can get away with eating without compromising your health.

Dr. Azar’s advice is this: Meat can still be your primary protein source. Just eat some plants along with it. “If you love meat, you can still eat foods like beef and chicken, but you also need to eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and nuts and seeds because there are some nutrients you just can’t get from meat,” he says, adding that only eating meat will lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Dr. Vogliano delivers a dietary message you’ve likely heard many times before: The healthiest diet is a diverse one. “We know from scientific research that the more plant foods our diets consist of, the more insurance we have that we’re getting the nutrients the body needs,” he says. Because of this, he advocates for a primarily plant-based diet and only eating meat occasionally.

Different governing bodies have slightly different recommendations when it comes to how much meat you can eat while still maintaining a healthy diet. The American Institute for Cancer Research says to keep red meat under 18 ounces a week, or roughly three portions a week. The American Heart Association doesn’t give a specific serving recommendation for meat, but says to mostly get protein from plants, fish, and seafood.

Dr. Azar emphasizes that there isn’t one universal way of eating that works for everyone. One diet may make one person feel energized and leave someone else feeling exhausted. What is important, he says, is making sure you’re getting all the nutrients your body needs. And what we know for sure is that you can’t do that by just eating meat.

items.title: Courtney Applebaum Opens a World of Her Own in Tribeca
items.description: The essence of Courtney Applebaum’s new Tribeca showroom coalesces through textures and materials: luminescent silver. Soft brown velvet cushioning with a sleek, dark frame. Delicate embroidery. Weathered wood surfaces.
items.author: Rachel Summer Small
paragraphs: The essence of Courtney Applebaum’s new Tribeca showroom coalesces through textures and materials: luminescent silver. Soft brown velvet cushioning with a sleek, dark frame. Delicate embroidery. Weathered wood surfaces.

“Part of me is very polished and likes a very clean aesthetic. And then part of me is disheveled, patina-ed,” says the designer, who is originally from Los Angeles and has been bicoastal since launching her studio in 2011. “I’ve always tried to keep a balance, and I think in the last few years, I’m okay with more of a mess.” Take the soaring metal birdcage that greets visitors, encircled by mesh and topped with a point, filled with branches skillfully arranged to look as though they simply fell there. “It has that Miss Havisham energy,” jokes Applebaum of her affinity to the eccentric, wealthy spinster from Charles Dickens’s Great Expectations. Fluttering around inside, a flock of Parson finches represents “joy and positivity, happiness, optimism, and celebrating life's simple pleasures, and I love that,” she adds.

Still, the showroom’s white walls establish a neutrality that Applebaum ultimately finds liberating. “It’s freedom to experiment,” she says—especially within the range on display. “I want the pieces to interact with one another, not with the space.” The items are old and new, mixing Applebaum’s designs alongside selections from an ever-evolving collection of vintage and antique pieces. Delicate vignettes across the gallery evoke, say, a bedroom, a study, or a living room. “I wanted a space that gives my context to these pieces, and shows how I would have them interact, and create a world in that way,” she says.

In one spot, a game table, her own original design, with a smooth mahogany frame and seeded-glass top, is flanked by four chairs with pink cushions and floral embroidery; the set sourced from a Paris gallery and extensively restored. Elsewhere, a newly designed bed frame, made of thin, black-lacquered slabs, is complemented by an antique gold-embroidered spread. A matching pair of Adirondack deck chairs, dating to the late 20th-century and attributed to Westport, sport a slightly chipped painted surface. Visitors might also notice miniature frogs perched here and there. “I kept thinking, Why am I drawn to this?” says Applebaum. Then she realized: “When I was a child, my mom would have little frogs throughout the backyard garden, and I would stumble upon them. I always loved that kind of whimsy.”

Applebaum, whose big break came in 2014 when The Row commissioned her to help design the brand’s first store on Melrose Place in Los Angeles, further built her reputation on highly curated, antiques-forward residential interiors, often set against restrained backdrops. She first launched her namesake line in 2021, rolling out terra-cotta lighting fixtures, mahogany nightstands, and shelving, among other items. Now, with the opening of the Tribeca space, Applebaum unveils new silver objects—including a table, a lamp, and sconces—in forms that echo her earlier designs. For these, she partnered with a multigenerational family of silversmiths in Mexico. Their expertise was a revelation, she explains, due to the difficulty of working with silver on a larger scale.

From here on out, Applebaum trusts that the future of her space will unfold in the right direction—all anchored in her “love of design and beautiful things,” she reflects. “Everything has always been intuitive and natural and not necessarily planned. And so I want to just let things unravel.”

items.title: For Mariko Mori, Science and Spirituality Are Interconnected
items.description: Mariko Mori’s boundary-pushing art practice is defined by juxtaposition. In her photography, sculptures, videos, and installations, she examines all things ancient and futuristic, the scientific and spiritual, technology and nature. “However, my intention is n
items.author: Stephanie Sporn
paragraphs: Mariko Mori’s boundary-pushing art practice is defined by juxtaposition. In her photography, sculptures, videos, and installations, she examines all things ancient and futuristic, the scientific and spiritual, technology and nature. “However, my intention is not to emphasize these oppositions, but to explore the possibility that they are fundamentally interconnected,” the artist, who splits her time between New York, Tokyo, and Miyako Island (about 180 miles southwest of Okinawa Main Island), tells W. Mori notes her upbringing was similarly marked by dualistic thinking: “Growing up in Japan, I was surrounded by a culture where ancient spiritual traditions coexist with an extraordinary enthusiasm for technological innovation. The worlds of anime, science fiction, Buddhist philosophy, and Shinto beliefs were all part of the cultural landscape that shaped my imagination.”

These sources of inspiration have fueled Mori’s practice for more than three decades, rendering her work as awe-inspiring and relevant now as when it was first created. This fall, the Mori Art Museum—founded by the artist’s uncle in 2003—celebrates her multifaceted oeuvre with Mariko Mori: All That Shines, the artist’s first major retrospective in Japan since 2002 (open through March 28, 2027). The exhibition is a highlight of Art Week Tokyo, an annual citywide platform encompassing museum and gallery presentations, performances, talks, and more. Conceived in collaboration with The Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, the show presents some 40 career-defining works, from early photographic experiments in self-portraiture to the iconic Wave UFO (1999-2002), and a new video incorporating AI. Organized chronologically, the show is curated by Alexandra Munroe, senior curator at large of global arts at the Guggenheim Museum and Foundation; and Mami Kataoka, director of the Mori Art Museum.

Mori calls the homecoming “deeply meaningful and emotional. Although I have spent much of my life living and working internationally, Japan remains at the heart of my cultural and spiritual identity,” she says, noting how she was “struck by the philosophical continuity” of the works upon seeing them together for the first time. “This exhibition has allowed me to see my artistic journey not as a series of separate chapters, but as one continuous exploration.”

Many of the questions Mori’s work examines stem from her father’s passing during her early 20s. “His death made me confront the fragility of human existence for the first time,” she says. “I began to wonder whether consciousness truly disappears when our physical body dies, or whether we might be part of something much greater.” Mori studied Buddhism and astrophysics to better understand humans’ place in the universe, and has continuously collaborated with scientists and engineers, as well as architects, programmers, and craftspeople, in her practice. Mori also found herself drawn to sacred sites and ancient ruins, such as Giza, Angkor Wat, and Machu Picchu. “I came to understand that our physical existence is never separate from the universe. From a scientific perspective, the elements that make up our bodies were formed within stars and released into the universe when those stars died,” says Mori, who believes science and spirituality are not opposing fields but rather “different ways of approaching the same mysteries of existence.”

With the issue of existence at her practice’s core, Mori describes her work’s evolution as shifting “from the individual to the collective.” Early works, such as her “Cyborg” series (1994-95), in which Mori photographed herself in everyday urban settings, critique contemporary society and gender roles. In Play With Me (1994), for example, Mori, donning a metallic anime-robot-like costume, stands outside a gaming store, blurring the boundaries between real and fictional characters (while challenging the traditionally submissive role of a Japanese woman). In another series, titled “Esoteric Cosmos” (1996-98), Mori uses advanced digital imaging to create mystical scenes in which she, embodying deities, is superimposed onto barren landscapes, dotted with cartoon-like lotus blossoms and aliens. The series also features orb-like forms, which are echoed in 3-D as the exhibition progresses. A four-channel video installation produced between 1995 and 2006 depicts performances in which Mori lies in a transparent capsule situated in different public spaces, inciting an array of reactions from onlookers.

Mori’s biomorphic capsules peak with her largest installation, Wave UFO, which was the first artwork to ever use brainwave biofeedback. Three people can simultaneously lie down inside the pod, where headsets use electrodes to measure the electrical activity in their brains. Their electrical brain rhythms are then converted into colors and shapes, and, after a few minutes, the participants can watch an accompanying Mori-made video of the abstracted imagery. “What interests me is not simply creating a spectacular visual environment, but offering an experience that may lead to an inner transformation,” the artist adds.

Technology “has always been a medium through which I explore much older and more fundamental questions about existence, consciousness, and spirituality,” Mori says. “In that sense, my work is not so much about the future as it is about exploring what is timeless and universal.” In the case of Wave UFO, the work reflects the concept that all existence is interconnected, which the artist argues is especially urgent now that “we are living in a time of profound division, marked by conflict, environmental crises, and increasing social fragmentation.”

All That Shines spotlights the Faou Foundation, established by Mori in 2010 to engage local communities by permanently installing artworks that encourage connection between nature and humanity. So far, Mori has realized sculptures on Miyako Island and Rio de Janeiro. On view in the exhibition, Peace Crystal (2016-24)—an over-five-foot-tall diamond-shape sculpture of transparent crystal glass—is planned for installation in Ethiopia.

Iridescent materials and crystals have become a signature of Mori’s. For the artist, “light symbolizes the continuity of existence, as well as love, compassion, and the possibility of transcendence.” She adds, “If there is one thought I would like to share through All That Shines, it is that each of us carries a light within. And perhaps, by recognizing that light in ourselves and in others, we can begin to understand that we are all part of one greater existence.”

items.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
items.description: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

items.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

items.title: Is My Unproductive Employee Using a Mouse Jiggler?
items.description: I manage a fully remote employee, Paul, who is struggling to meet expectations in his job, and I suspect he’s using a mouse jiggler to keep his mouse moving so he appears more available than he is.
items.author: Alison Green
paragraphs: I manage a fully remote employee, Paul, who is struggling to meet expectations in his job, and I suspect he’s using a mouse jiggler to keep his mouse moving so he appears more available than he is.

I have been talking to Paul about the issues I am seeing with his performance, one of which is responsiveness. He is so unresponsive that other team members come to me to report they haven’t heard from him for hours. I have had to jump in to assure his colleagues that something is being handled when a deadline is fast approaching and they can’t get ahold of Paul. Someone even joked with me that they suspect he has a second job. Also, this is not workload-related; to the contrary, he is underallocated and does not have a full workload.

I first talked to Paul about this issue a few months ago. I told him that I do not want to wade into policing how he spends his time, but he should give me a heads-up if he needs to be unavailable for an extended period of time. In my head, I was thinking of doctor’s appointments or things of that nature. He has since pinged me for a variety of activities that take him away from his desk that don’t feel particularly legitimate, like “I need to step out to run to the store.” Here’s the thing: If you haven’t used your computer for a while, our chat system turns your chat bubble red to indicate you’re not available. (It’s green when you’re there and working.) During these errands, his chat bubble stays green, indicating he’s “available” even when he’s just told me he’ll be away. I have pinged him with questions 30 minutes to an hour later, and his responses can take up to 90 minutes to come through. Again, green bubble the whole time, which makes me think he’s set something up to make his computer appear to be in use when it’s not, such as a mouse jiggler.

We had a second conversation where I once again addressed his response time, but I don’t think I hit on the real point I was trying to get across. I let him know that I was glad he was letting me know when he was stepping out and that our workplace is okay with flexibility, but people are still reaching out to me with questions because they can’t reach him. His responsiveness has improved slightly, but not even to the level of “meets expectations” yet.

I know that the best thing to do is to focus on outcomes, but I’m struggling to do that. I feel like I have focused on the outcomes and it’s not sinking in. My manager advised against me giving him specific time metrics. I wanted to say that he needs to respond to pings within 30 minutes to one hour if he is not in a meeting (and he’s not in many meetings), but she felt like that’s getting too nitpicky. So I’m left with just “be more responsive,” but that feels too nebulous to me.

Is it worth asking about the suspected mouse jiggler? Or should I just keep honing in on the responsiveness issue as a whole? How do I do that without getting into micromanager territory? Honestly, I’m going back to the joke a co-worker made about him having a second job and thinking maybe there’s something to it.

Leave the question of a mouse jiggler out of it because it doesn’t really matter. What matters is that Paul is unavailable for long stretches of time when people need him. While it’s true that using a mouse jiggler would reveal a deliberate intent to mislead people (which is a problem in itself), the reality is that even if you knew he wasn’t using one, his lack of responsiveness would still be a problem. So focus on the piece that’s ultimately most important: He needs to be a lot more responsive than he is right now.

I think your boss is wrong to tell you not to give Paul specific time frames (like “You need to respond within an hour if you’re not in a meeting”), because you and he are clearly on different pages about what “responsive” means. You need to get more aligned on what the expectation really is. In fact, whenever you have an expectation in your head that an employee isn’t meeting, you should find a way to articulate that requirement very clearly, so they understand what you’re looking for. That’s true even when the expectation is something other employees haven’t needed you to spell out … since this person clearly does need it. (Of course, there are some assumptions that are so fundamental to doing good work that needing to spell them out can call into question the employee’s suitability for the role. But if you find yourself at that point, you’re still better off being really clear about what successful performance looks like.)

Given that, it’s worth going back to your manager and saying, “I hear you on not micromanaging Paul’s response times. Normally, I wouldn’t think that necessary to do with most employees. But in this case, I’ve repeatedly asked him to be more responsive, and while he’s assured me he will be, he’s still unreachable for large chunks of the day. So I think it’s fair to give him concrete examples of what’s expected. I’m not going to hold him to responding exactly within an hour every time, but because his calibration is currently so off, I want to let him know that in general the team expects a response to time-sensitive questions within 30 to 60 minutes.”
Aside from that, you can also say all of the following to Paul:

“I am regularly hearing from colleagues that you are taking hours to respond to time-sensitive messages. It’s to the point that I’ve heard jokes that you must have a second job. I need to see you getting back to people more quickly.”
“We have talked about you needing to be more responsive in the past and you told me you were addressing it, but you’re still not meeting expectations. What’s going on?”
“When you’re not at your desk and won’t be able to respond quickly, I need you to set your status to away. Right now, it’s green all day long, so it’s not accurately conveying your availability.”

But also, you mentioned that Paul’s responsiveness is only one of the issues with his performance. Make sure you’re leaning in heavily on the other problems as well. Don’t let yourself get too sidetracked on questions of mouse jigglers and possible second jobs or other speculation along those lines. You don’t need to definitively answer those questions in order to determine what matters most, which is whether he’s doing the job as you need it done. And that’s good news, because it means you can focus on addressing Paul’s actual work rather than investigating exactly what he’s doing with his time each minute of the day.
