items.title: A Guide to the Absurdist Comedy of Nathan Fielder
items.description: As his documentary on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes hits UK cinemas, we delve into Nathan Fielder’s back catalogue, from Finding Frances to The Curse
items.author: Shin Hui Lee
paragraphs: As his documentary on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes hits UK cinemas, we delve into Nathan Fielder’s back catalogue, from Finding Frances to The Curse
This article was originally published in April 2025 and has since been updated

What do you get when you combine a chronically deadpan expression, Seth Rogen’s high-school improv partner and a graduate of “one of Canada’s top business schools with really good grades” into one person? None other than Nathan Fielder. Scoring his first big break on the reality series Nathan for You in 2013, the 43-year-old has steadily made a name for himself mining the unsightly quirks of the human psyche. Through his bone-dry wit and anxiety-wrought set-ups, he holds a mirror to the performative nature of our everyday existence.

No stranger to virality, Fielder’s success lies in his willingness to probe his own vulnerabilities – not just as the by-product but as the butt of the joke. Whether he’s creating poo-flavoured frozen yoghurt or setting up an acting school to teach his dubious “Fielder Method”, we find ourselves incapable of looking away. We become complicit in a perverse fascination with just how far he will go and how bad it can get, since life itself is a similarly embarrassing affair. If we cringe, it’s only because we can all too easily see ourselves in his shoes. Yet, as the Vancouverite shows us time and time again, things tend to have a way of working themselves out if we just commit to the bit.

His latest is a much-hyped documentary on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. To mark the release, AnOther recommends six key works from the mastermind comedian.
This Hour Has 22 Minutes (1993-current)

Fresh-faced and armed with a microphone, Fielder got his start on the Canadian mock news programme This Hour Has 22 Minutes. Lasting from 2007 to 2009, the consumer report segment Nathan on Your Side saw him tearing across the country interviewing random people on a variety of topics, from presidential candidates to tall clubs to MP3 players. In one episode, Fielder consults a marketing professor on how sex is used in advertising to manipulate the public, only for the interaction to spiral into him coaxing the unwitting participant to confess he’s more attracted to Jennifer Aniston than to his own wife. All the makings of his iconic Nathan for You alter ego are here – the inexplicable manner, the vacant stare and the knack for dealing with discomfort by doubling down on it.
Nathan for You (2013-2017)

Over Nathan for You’s four seasons, Fielder plays a consultant hoping to save struggling businesses with wildly convoluted and totally impractical solutions. Whether it’s exploiting parody law to rename a coffee shop “Dumb Starbucks” or orchestrating to have himself pulled over for speeding so that he can tell a witty anecdote on Jimmy Kimmel Live, the Comedy Central hit revels in its own farce.

But beneath this lies something more piercing: a reflection on loneliness, desperation and the bleakness baked into 21st-century consumer culture. Amid all the stunts, Nathan for You adopts an unexpected layer of warmth, seeking to forge connection in a world built on artifice. The result is a cult phenomenon that has earned Fielder a Writers Guild of America Award and lifelong comedic clout.

If you find yourself crying instead of laughing during a sketch, you might think the comic hasn’t done his job. For Fielder, it’s just part of the experience. This is no truer than in Finding Frances, the feature-length series finale of Nathan for You, where he helps 78-year-old Bill Heath track down a long-lost sweetheart. The pair stage auditions for a nonexistent Mud sequel and fake a 57-year high school reunion, all to procure a surprisingly cathartic – if not mildly awkward – phone call between the estranged pair.

Hailed by The New York Times as one of the most memorable television episodes of 2017, Fielder presents a profound meditation on love and longing. As a parallel story unfolds between himself and an escort named Maci, it becomes tricky to identify where the show ends and reality begins. In the last few moments, she asks: “You’re filming something, that’s kind of the purpose, isn’t it?” That Fielder doesn’t (or can’t) give a definitive answer is a testament to the show evolving into something much bigger than it ever set out to be.
How To With John Wilson (2020-2023)

Though not its creator, How To With John Wilson is a notable entry in Fielder’s catalogue. Serving as executive producer after meeting Wilson by chance in 2018, the series went on to receive several Primetime Emmy nominations and paved the way for Fielder’s increasingly experimental post-Nathan for You career.

From how to make risotto to how to like what you see in the mirror, each episode is designed as a tutorial, with Wilson dispensing oh-so-sage advice while quietly unravelling his own neuroses. Ambling through the streets of New York, he strikes up conversations with zany characters and captures eccentric vignettes of city life (the pilot features actor Kyle MacLachlan struggling to swipe his MetroCard on the subway). The fun of it all is not knowing where he’ll land – at a Mandela effect conference in Idaho, or perhaps at the home of Bang Energy CEO Jack Owoc? Filled with existential tangents and offbeat sincerity, it’s clear that Fielder and Wilson have found a shared language through this collaboration.
The Rehearsal (2022-current)

Billed by HBO as “a series about the lengths one man will go to reduce the uncertainties of everyday life”, The Rehearsal is an utter feat of television. Marking Fielder’s return to acting and directing after a five-year hiatus, the docu-comedy cum social experiment doesn’t so much elicit laugh-out-loud moments as it does genuine awe.

The premise of the show is simple: the protagonist enlists ordinary people on Craigslist facing difficult life events and prepares them by rehearsing all possible outcomes. In the bulk of the episodes, he helps a woman decide if she wants to have children by building her a house and hiring multiple child actors to play her son. Rooted in a curiosity about our often irrational yet instinctual behaviours, The Rehearsal reveals how ready we are to deceive ourselves in the face of the unknown. But as Fielder eventually comes to understand, “life’s better with surprises”.

“We’re certified Fresh!!!!! Don’t miss out!” is the sort of ringing, albeit self-endorsement, you would expect from a drama co-created by Fielder and Uncut Gems co-director Benny Safdie. Consisting of ten hour-long episodes, The Curse is Fielder’s first fully scripted foray, offering a blistering satire of white wokeness, gentrification and the pretensions of the art world. Bathed in a vaguely menacing synth score, it explores how an alleged curse ruins the relationship of newly married couple Asher (Fielder) and Whitney (Emma Stone) during the filming of their house-flipping reality show.

The Curse is dense and tonally indecipherable (spoiler: the finale gets positively Lynchian as Asher gets sucked upwards to his death), while somehow managing to be one of the most daring and transfixing shows put to television. It’s also a hint at Fielder’s growing ambition to chart new territory – one where comedy can be transcended without being relinquished.

items.title: Mahershala Ali on Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
items.description: “It’s like he’s having a violent conversation with God,” says the Oscar-winning Moonlight star of his role in Bassam Tariq’s new film, a stylish hitman thriller that doubles as a surprising study in shattered faith
items.author: Rory Doherty
paragraphs: “It’s like he’s having a violent conversation with God,” says the Oscar-winning Moonlight star of his role in Bassam Tariq’s new film, a stylish hitman thriller that doubles as a surprising study in shattered faith

Early in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, we hear a prayer. Latif (Mahershala Ali) is a grieving widower, a Muslim father and a hired killer living in Houston, Texas. Still reeling from becoming the sole caregiver to his three children – including a newborn baby – he makes a vulnerable, even bitter plea for strength. “I thought I was Your sword,” he says, turning his hitman vocation over in his mind as doubt, confusion and a fair bit of anger chip at his faith. To an outside perspective, Latif is a devoutly religious man. But Mahershala Ali didn’t see his character that way.

“I would never describe him as devout,” the actor tells AnOther, discussing the film along with writer-director Bassam Tariq on the final day of the London Film Festival. “I almost don’t know what that is on some level. I don’t know a Muslim who would call themselves devout. It would be like saying [you’re] a really righteous man [...] They can be really self-deprecating, honestly. They’re very conscious of how flawed they are.”

This nuance would account for the fragility – and humour – that courses through the film. The life-and-death stakes manifest in different ways: crime boss Mike (Laith Nakli) puts a hit out on Pastor Hwan (John Cho), a gun-toting, flag-wearing, porn-hating evangelical leader planning to storm the mansion where Mike’s puerile nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali) produces his flagrantly haram pornography. But Latif has run out of his late wife’s breast milk for their formula-allergic baby Aziza, and drafts his other kids – surly teenage daughter Fatiha (Adia) and young son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) – in search of a replacement supply.

After deflecting the ire of his mosque’s imam (Giancarlo Esposito) and his doctor brother-in-law (Tramell Tillman), Latif is plagued by botched hits and ambushes, creating a trail of blood that entwines his fate with Hatty and Hwan and deepening his twin crises of spirituality and fatherhood. The double Oscar-winner is immense and arresting as a wounded warrior-protector; to Ali, the character is defined by his lack of stillness. “If you’re doing theatre, there’s a little cheat where you lean your body forward. It gives you a sense of urgency, of almost falling forward. I thought of the character that way, never sitting back or sitting still.”

Your Mother’s director and star met about five years ago, when both were attached to Marvel’s Blade, and Tariq realised he and Ali were “spiritually aligned”. “Our intentions of how we want to work are very similar, but I love how we diverge,” says the director. “That’s where it gets really exciting. But I know that we [would] always come back because the compass is pointing in the same direction.” After Tariq left Blade in 2022 (Ali only confirmed he’d departed the role this year), the director was sure they would collaborate again – although Ali had some early misgivings about taking on the role of Latif.

“There was a lot of nervousness around it because of the physicality of the role, not [being] sure if we had the time to prepare in the way I wanted to,” the actor explains. “I just felt thrown in the deep end of it; that was where the hesitancy really lived.” Still, the compasses always pointed true. “As far as being willing to go on the journey with [Tariq], that was very early on in this process.”

Tariq was eager to avoid flippant and indulgent action scenes, only unleashing his protagonist’s sometimes elegant, sometimes brutal skills when the suspense reached its breaking point. “Something I’ve learned about the action scenes I love is that it’s about building a lot of tension, and then making it explosive and quick. They feel more meaningful [that way]. And something in the character has to change. A fight can never just be, ‘That just happened! Let’s move on.’ I think there’s so much of that Looney Tunes-style stuff nowadays that the audience gets bored. We wanted to make sure that every hit felt intentional.”

Despite its widowed hitman, stylish cinematography and heightened criminal underworld, Your Mother is no John Wick. While John Cho’s righteous crusader villain has a scene-stealing flair, the bond between Latif and his eldest daughter is the film’s most pivotal relationship. “Latif and Fatiha are a living expression of that period that fathers experience with daughters in those teenage years,” says Ali. “There’s an extra layer of concern. You’re really at the mercy of your children.”

In her debut film performance, Adia brings a stubborn and commanding presence that pushes Latif’s flaws to the surface. “[Fatiha] is reacting to him,” says Ali, “slamming doors and standing her ground in a way that lets him know, ‘I’m my own person. I have my own thoughts and ideas. I see faults in you, and I’m going to speak to those. I know you’re not praying.’ She is holding him accountable in a way that no one else can, [because] his son is not at that age where he’s really challenging him. If anything, he’s regurgitating his very teachings back to him. He’s actually exemplifying obedience, and that frustrates Latif because he does not feel like being obedient [himself] at that time.”

The fact that nobody is on the same page about the purpose of faith after their mutual loss spoke to Ali, who remembers shirking his responsibilities when his father died. “For a minute I had an attitude of, ‘I don’t have to do this. I’m not doing this school thing.” A teacher, who was very critical to my success now, pulled me aside and was like, ‘What are you doing? Why are you not showing up for class?’”

The actor returns to his character’s prayer: I thought I was Your sword. “His flaw is believing he had this calling to bring about justice, and as a result of that, feeling like he was somehow exempt from the surprises of life. ‘I thought I was your servant. How dare you take my loved one away from me when I’m out here doing this for you?’ The way in which he’s mourning, he’s almost having a violent conversation with God.” Latif’s spiritual journey, which Your Mother resolves in sublime fashion, is the discovery that faith is not about devotion to God, but rather those that faith binds you to. As Pastor Hwan asks in a rare vulnerable moment: “Who’s praying for you?”
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is out in UK cinemas on November 20

items.title: Discover the ‘soft power’ of the London Museum in its striking new home
items.description: When the London Museum opens to the public later this week, it hopes to offer a reflection of the city it represents. The project is the first-phase reveal of what was formerly known as the Museum of London – now relocated from London Wall to the site of the f
items.author: Ellie Stathaki
paragraphs: When the London Museum opens to the public later this week, it hopes to offer a reflection of the city it represents. The project is the first-phase reveal of what was formerly known as the Museum of London – now relocated from London Wall to the site of the famous meat market, which has been transformed into a world-class museum for the 21st century. It is large, complicated and layered. It combines old and new, mixing busy and quieter bits, neat and messy at the same time – but always full of richness and interest.

Architecture studio Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and conservation specialist Julian Harrap Architects all worked on the project; and while they each tackled different parts of the fairly large plot (it spans several existing buildings across some 33,000 sq m), they all agree that the project was conceived to reflect both its specific site and the capital whose story it was designed to tell.
Tour the new London Museum

‘It was a rare chance to help one of the world's great city museums reinvent itself. Cities are changing quickly, and people increasingly look to public institutions to help them make sense of that change. A museum that engages with social and environmental issues and offers a shared civic space to a wide range of communities can do that in a way few other places can. There is a soft power in that too: an open, confident cultural institution doesn't just sit in its city; it helps to shape it,’ says Paul Williams, principal director and co-founder, Stanton Williams. ‘It is hard to imagine a better setting for that reinvention.’

Smithfield, a well-known site at the western end of the City's cultural axis, alongside the Barbican and the Guildhall School of Music & Drama, is already comfortably woven into the fabric of the city. It comprises two existing market buildings, one Victorian, one from the 1960s, and between them is a ‘captured street’, a former market lane now turned into the embrace of the main museum entrance. ‘It feels like the natural home for a museum that wants to be part of the city's life rather than observe it from a distance,’ Williams adds.

Stanton Williams led the project and focused on the poultry market, basement galleries and covered street linking the two markets. Khan took charge primarily of the general market's above-ground interiors and exterior. This includes its ground-floor public spaces, upper storeys and entrances (working closely with Julian Harrap Architects), and forms part of the first stage in a staggered launch of a project that will eventually also take over the poultry market next door.

Alec Shaw, the London Museum's director of new museum project and estate, told us in an interview in September: ‘We were constantly doing open-heart surgery into different parts of the building to try and adapt them to make them more welcoming. Without being too grand, I'm hoping this is a complete game changer for city museums across the world.'

The first stage that launches now hopes to reflect this dynamism. It was also designed to be able to absorb change and feel interactive, in order to invite visitors in and engage them as actors in its offerings – rather than passive viewers. ‘It can always be an unfinished project,' Khan told us in September. ‘This is what has been missing, in a way, from the museum of the 20th century. Here, it's baked into the architecture, the capacity and the need to change.'
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The new exhibits will have displays for the London of the present and the past (cavernous underground railway chambers beneath the General Market showcase row upon row of old, 7m-high vaulted brick jack arches). Indeed, the buildings themselves are part of the show, creating a journey through time via the medium of architecture. The campus also provides unexpected surprises: for instance, those underground vaults, which were partly buried and closed off (and not in the plans), when the London Museum began the project. They were originally open-air goods yards, where cargo arriving by rail and river was stored before Horace Jones built the General Market on top.

The complex includes, at Khan’s suggestion, the transformation of 48 historic shop units into 12 ‘houses'. Six of them would be reserved for the institution's use, and six would be given to external ventures in a mix that the museum would curate. The idea was that it would become an incubator, a ‘coral reef of multiple institutes', as Khan puts it.

In places, the building fabric itself holds part of the museum’s collection. Some of its objects were baked into the flooring, forming part of the ground level, visible for all to see. More displays in the main exhibitions include over 400 pieces of remarkable Elizabethan and Jacobean jewellery, found buried in a cellar in 1912.

‘[My first reaction to the site was] visceral. I first walked into the General Market in 2016 and was blown away by the power and physicality of its contrasting spaces. That feeling hasn't left me. The site was raw, far more derelict than anyone had realised, and a time capsule. That complexity is its richness,’ Williams explains.

‘This isn’t a museum built merely to hold London's past. It is designed to keep imagining London's future, a place where history, ideas and people meet, and new stories emerge. Like the city, it is built layer upon layer, reinventing itself without erasing what came before.’

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).

items.title: Inside the world of Kerala’s female bodybuilders
items.description: ‘Bodybuilding is already an act of construction. The body is deliberately shaped over time. Photography then adds another layer, because the way that body is framed, posed and photographed also shapes how we understand it,’ says London-based Indian visual arti
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: ‘Bodybuilding is already an act of construction. The body is deliberately shaped over time. Photography then adds another layer, because the way that body is framed, posed and photographed also shapes how we understand it,’ says London-based Indian visual artist Keerthana Kunnath, who is presenting her debut series Not What You Saw at Foam, Amsterdam.

After meeting female bodybuilders in Kerala, South India, Kunnath began photographing a dozen of them – including Aishu, Bhumika, Jannat, Kavitha and Sandra, who feature regularly in the series – becoming close enough to the women to gain an insight into their training and their lives. Kunnath and her camera don’t just follow these women to the gym, but they venture into domestic environments too. Capturing the bodybuilders at home, the women are vulnerable, the antithesis of a stereotype. The portraits, both candid and posed, are unexpectedly intimate.

‘The intimacy really comes from the trust that has built up between me and the women over the years,’ adds Kunnath. ‘In the beginning, there was naturally a boundary between photographer and subject. But through spending time together, talking, photographing, and eventually becoming friends with some of them, that relationship changed. I was no longer just asking them to pose for a photograph; they knew me, and I knew them. That trust allowed me to photograph moments that felt less guarded. I could photograph them when they weren’t performing or presenting themselves in the way they might normally want to be seen. For me, that’s where the intimacy comes from.’

Kunnath was originally drawn to the women’s bodies themselves, she says. They weren’t what she was used to seeing, and her early photographs lingered more on the muscles and the anatomy. Later, the quieter moments became equally as important, as the women rested backstage, or spent time with their families.

‘The exhibition brings these two ways of seeing them together,’ says Kunnath. ‘The earlier, more constructed images are still important because they come from my initial fascination with their bodies, while the more intimate photographs reflect everything I came to understand afterwards. I think the tension between the two is what interests me now. How we first look at someone, and how that idea can evolve once we spend time with them. The more you know someone, the more you begin to see them beyond their surface or their profession. Although we had conversations about their experiences from the beginning, over time some of them became friends, rather than just subjects. In the earlier work, there was naturally an element of performance because they are bodybuilders, they know how to present their bodies and perform. But as we became more comfortable with each other, that performance started to disappear.’
Keerthana Kunnath, ‘Not What You Saw’ at Foam Amsterdam

items.title: Wallpaper* Technology Editor Jonathan Bell assembles a compact musical gift guide
items.description: Sprinkle a little audio creativity over your loved ones this year with our selection of nine new pieces of music technology. The acquisitive gearhead should be happy with all or any of this selection, which includes studio must-haves like microphones and keybo
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Sprinkle a little audio creativity over your loved ones this year with our selection of nine new pieces of music technology. The acquisitive gearhead should be happy with all or any of this selection, which includes studio must-haves like microphones and keyboards through to cult synths, keychain novelties and playable toys.
Read on for technology editor Jonathan Bell’s gift guide for the tech-savvy musician.

A guitar pedal with pedigree, the new Knife Drop Fuzz is a synth pedal developed in collaboration with Jack White’s Third Man Hardware and Eventide Audio. Offering a variety of sounds from shrieking synths to gnarly bass fuzz, it’ll bring delight to guitarists everywhere.

For the music fan who loves exploring physical spaces of past triumphs, Herb Lester Associates produces a range of cartographic companions, from mapping the origins of LA’s rock scene, Bob Dylan in 60s New York, the ‘Metal Mappa Mundi’ and The Clash’s London and more.

In addition to a boxset of their entire Music Cities Collection, one of their newest publications is Places to Go, which traces (The) Pink Floyd's psychedelic Cambridge beginnings. Compiled by superfan Glenn Povey, founder of the Pink Floyd fanzine Brain Damage, it’s a step back into a hazy era with graphics to match.

Podcasters, sound recordists, musicians and artists can all benefit from Shure’s newest microphone, the MV360. Designed specifically to capture full 360° spatial audio with a simple USB-C connection, the MV360 can also do regular mono, stereo, and binaural audio. A dedicated smartphone app makes the whole experience mobile or hook it up to your laptop for immersive audio every time.

It’s the Swiss Army Knife of modern music production, now updated for a new era of hardware. AKAI’s AKAI MPK Mini Plus II sounds a bit of a mouthful, but that tallies with the 37-key MIDI controller’s multi-functional nature.

The latest in a long line of keyboards designed to work in sync with AKAI’s MPC line of grooveboxes and desktop software, it includes a set of pads, multiple outputs and knobs with which to control external gear, pitch and modulation wheels, a full-colour display and more.

At the other extreme is the Stylophone Mini, a very standalone and lo-fi music making solution. Keychain-sized and priced, the Mini version of the evergreen Stylophone synth not only replicates the metal ribbon keyboard of the original (which is played using the attached stylus) but also has a tiny light for added functionality. Available in original, white and pink.

If you know, you know; M-VAVE’s FM-1 is a tiny FM synthesizer that has been making waves in the electronic community ever since its launch earlier this year. The Chinese manufacturer crammed an impressive amount of horsepower into this pocketable instrument.

The FM-1 earned true cult status via a relentless stream of aftermarket firmwares, each bringing a new workflow and audio and visual aesthetic to the device. Amazon and Alibaba are awash with stores selling the device - enthusiasts are snapping up multiple units on which to experiment.

We’ve already hailed the playing power of Loog’s first Fender bass. For added novelty, why not try the limited-edition Hello Kitty version, which adds character quality to this tiny three-string (and builds on Fender’s long-running partnership with Sanrio).

Finally, a Kickstarter with a musical edge, although it might not be ready for the festive season. The Neko Pocket Wireless Guitar Studio looks pretty miraculous, a pocket studio, a guitar processor, a generative AI ideas machine, all running through wireless connectivity to a guitar or bass. The 16GB of onboard also storage includes a ‘time machine’ function that records all your abstract noodling in case a great idea comes out of the blue.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: This homeware collection is inspired by the design of London's Italian embassy
items.description: Abask, the London-based online platform for artisanal crafts and homeware, has launched its Giobagnara Embassy Collection, an ode to the Embassy of Italy in London. The collection comprises handcrafted leather accessories in a series of bold, geometric pattern
items.author: Tianna Williams
paragraphs: Abask, the London-based online platform for artisanal crafts and homeware, has launched its Giobagnara Embassy Collection, an ode to the Embassy of Italy in London. The collection comprises handcrafted leather accessories in a series of bold, geometric patterns.

Late last year, long-time Wallpaper* collaborator and designer Nick Vinson was tasked with creating the new office of the Italian embassy in London, a love letter to the country’s creativity. Overlooking Buckingham Palace on one side, the building had originally served as a police station for Queen Victoria. For the design, Vinson drew his inspiration from Italy’s rich creative heritage to create a series of interiors throughout the five-storey listed building.

He worked with long-term collaborator Giobagnara, an Italian brand based in Genoa that handcrafts high-end leather homeware, accessories, and furnishings. For the embassy design, Giobagnara made a plethora of objects that range from bespoke lecterns to valet trays for each member of staff.

‘First created for the Embassy of Italy in London, alongside rugs, these decorative leather objects are tributes to two important floors found in Italy; one in Rome, one in Venice, created 1800 years apart,’ says Vinson.

The patterns devised by Vinson include an angular, mosaic-like design and takes its cue from the mosaic floor Carlo Scarpa laid in the Olivetti showroom on Piazza San Marco, or a series of geometric shapes inspired by the ancient mosaic floors of the Roman baths of Caracalla. Both patterns come in colours of red, olive green, deep orange, and yellow.

Vinson had originally asked the brand’s founder, Giorgio Bagnara, to use the Caracalla and Olivetti patterns and create bespoke pieces for the Ambassador’s offices; they proved so popular that a full collection took shape, rendered in fine Italian leather. The collection, as a result, is vibrantly rich, with a colour palette based on bright hues of yellow and red alongside neutral shades of green and dove grey.
The patterns adorn a series of leather desk accessories and room objects, including games, trays, organisers and desk sets, placemats, baskets, tissue boxes, waste bins, and ice buckets.

Discover the full Giobagnara Embassy Collection at Abask.com

Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

items.title: Portrait of a Place: Glacier View
items.description: Once a year in Glacier View, Alaska, people drive enormous distances to watch their cars get catapulted off a 300ft cliff in one of the most scenic, remote parts of the world – an annual event known as the Fourth of July Car Launch. Drawing crowds from across
paragraphs: Once a year in Glacier View, Alaska, people drive enormous distances to watch their cars get catapulted off a 300ft cliff in one of the most scenic, remote parts of the world – an annual event known as the Fourth of July Car Launch. Drawing crowds from across the USA and beyond, the event stands as a depiction of unorthodox rituals, the American spirit, and catharsis, with many of the heavily decorated cars arriving with an attached emotional weight and personal history.

I wanted to approach the film observationally, with the sense of catharsis being what I was most interested in capturing. A lot of people had travelled huge distances to get there, with the launch becoming both the end of their trip and the end of the car's life.

Travelling to the event and spending time with its community, filmmaker Jamie Shipston-Mourn documents a human phenomenon of total destruction and spectacle in the name of celebration for the short film Glacier View. Finding the film through the people he met and their stories – among them, Ben Keefe, who spoke openly about addiction and sobriety – Shipston-Mourn captures a ceremony that is as much about the journey as the launch itself, presenting a chance for new beginnings by releasing regrets, memories and burdens in physical form against the majesty of the Alaskan landscape.

items.title: $200 Goes a Long Way When You Skip the Boring Gifts
items.description: In a job like mine, so many products hover over the desk and screen, one becomes desensitized to what items cost. Not necessarily in a real-life spending habits sort of way (okay, fine, maybe a little bit), but more so in how one eventually grows unphased by b
items.author: Maximilian Migowski
paragraphs: In a job like mine, so many products hover over the desk and screen, one becomes desensitized to what items cost. Not necessarily in a real-life spending habits sort of way (okay, fine, maybe a little bit), but more so in how one eventually grows unphased by big price tags, and simply accepts that everything is expensive. So, in prepping this guide especially, it dawned on me that it isn't so easy to track down neat, fun stuff with what was once a pretty hefty budget for a single gift. Or not as easy as it should be, at least. That, however, is a topic for another day, and maybe even another publication altogether.

Point being, in this cosmos we're operating in, $200 can feel, admittedly, like a mere downpayment for some of the stores and brands and products we like. Sans cap, you can put all the niche Japanese labels under the tree you can think of. But to find presents that'd elicit a similar sense of novelty and excitement and in-the-know satisfaction on a budget? That, my friend, can pose quite a challenge.

Lucky for you, by keeping protocol of some of the stuff I've scrolled past or been told of lately yet never found a proper placement for elsewhere, I would inadvertently begin building this list here: A list of what I consider creative, charming gifts and gestures that are either useful, nice to look at, or a conversation starter — or, ideally, all of the above! No big conceptual categories or insistence on a certain level of… well, anything really. Just an un-orderly line up of things I know I'd smile at if I were to unwrap them — and that I hope might provoke a similar response from your loved one without putting you in debt.
Teenage Engineering Pocket Synthesizer

For the life of me, I would not know how to use this thing. Would that muffle my giddyness at receiving it? No! Do I know plenty of pseudo-DJs that'd love to explain it to me? Sadly, yes. As do you, I'd posit, since you're reading this.
By 2027, I want to be the guy that has a portable, roll-up chess game in his bag. The real question is, who wouldn't?
A Magazine Curated By Hiroshi Fujiwara
Now, I'm already the guy who lugs books and magazines around, and will be adding this latest edition of AMCB to my stack. (Help, is this gift guide actually a wish list?)
As cool as this EDL cap is, I'd be careful whom I give it to so as to not send the wrong message. Your call though.

Trading saucy for smiley, these primary-colored socks might be the only kind to get their same reaction mirrored back at them. Also, everyone who only wears neutral socks needs to live a little. Help them!

Instead of spending a lot of money on a coffee table book your giftee may or may not want in their collection, maybe get them this coffee table book stand so they can properly showcase a specimen of their choosing.
Pop Mart Bikini Bottom Plushies

Going from high brow to low brow, I'm literally laughing out loud as I type this, for this recommendation is only aimed at the most committed of Spongebob fans. This is regular ol’ NPC Bikini Bottom folk. No starfish, squid or squirrel in sight. And I think that's kinda fab.
Back to more adult gifts, this belt I don't actually find any less entertaining than the above pick, albeit for different reasons. Business in the front, party… on the side?

2026 reintroduced the casual, preppy tie in ways we haven't seen in a while. A bold-patterned silk style like Sunflower's is tame enough for a classic suit, but also nonchalantly showy enough to match a more casual outing.
I love a scarf as much as the next person, but I'm begging y’all to get rid of that certain Swedish brand's ridiculously ubiquitous one, and spend less money on this nicer cashmere version by BEAMS.

Footwear is dangerous territory when it comes to gifting, generally, but I do just happen to enjoy these collapsable, slipper-y walking sneakers by Merrell so much I'd make an exception — in both the gifter and recipient's position.
Bose Wired Noise Cancelling Earbuds

Leaning into nostalgia and appreciating the whole analog resurgence vibe doesn't equate to a total opt-out of all of today's modern amenities. These earbuds have cords and noise cancellation, how about that?
Los Angeles Apparel Scatterbox

I love this notion of surprise that can't end in disaster: Los Angeles Apparel's scatterbox concept is a bundle of staple-y cotton hoodies and tees in random colors you might not usually go for but that you'll get a kick out of styling into your existing wardrobe.

No one in history ever has, will or should raise an eyebrow at a perfectly blue, Made In America dress shirt. I know this, How Long Gone co-host and Hanover founder Chris Black knows this. And now you do, too. (Wait 'til you read the supplier name

You're not gonna get far at Margaret Howell's store with this allowance. Enter here her more modestly priced MHL leg though: This chocolatey lambswool balaclava is a winter must-have and shockingly affordable, even by diffusion line stands.
I can't think of a single person in my life who wouldn't take pleasure in an elegant black pair of wool-lined leather gloves, do you?
Sandy Liang x BAGGU Market Bag

This wonderfully, whimsically graphic-printed Sandy Liang BAGGU bag is, perhaps, a more polarizing, love-it-or-hate-it-type contender. 50ish percent chance at being someone's best Secret Santa gift ever though. Draw my name please!

When everyone's doing cargo, go Gadget. Minus the pockets but equally as comfy and practical, this Gramicci pant ticks all the boxes of why cargos are back in style without resembling everybody else's. Also, this shade of green pairs well with everything.
Polo Ralph Lauren 5-Pack Boxers

Ralphie’s is pretty much the only logo I'll sport, wherever he places it. Not sure about you or the person whose stocking you're stuffing, but I could see myself wearing these as regular shorts somehow, just putting that out there.

Wall art, I believe, is underrated as a gift. And when it's already framed, even better. I love this suave sandals-and-socks moment by photographer Martin Parr. It feels very current menswear-y, no? Be it this or another, even a self-painted or self-captured image, I'd definitely count it among the best, most personal, and budget-friendliest gifting options available. You're all taking pics all day anyway?! Go do what your grandma did already and frame ‘em, for God's sake!
How We Test and Choose Products

Style means different things to different people, but knowing what's worth your money shouldn't be a guessing game. At Highsnobiety, we’ve spent more than two decades covering fashion, keeping tabs on the brands worth knowing, and figuring out which products deserve your time. We test products firsthand when possible, digging into everything from quality and construction to comfort and wearability. With more brands competing for your attention than ever, we also consider what sets a product apart. For the rest, we lean on our product knowledge, editorial research, and the taste that’s made us a trusted voice in fashion.
