items.title: Крем за 250 рублей против крема за 10 тысяч: мы сравнили составы «Чистой линии» и Chanel
items.description: Мы продолжаем и развиваем рубрику «Что внутри», в которой разбираем состав популярных продуктов, чтобы понять, насколько их рекламный образ соответствует содержанию. На этот раз герои выпуска — не продукты питания, а косметические средства, причем сразу два. К
items.author: Сергей Панков
paragraphs: Мы продолжаем и развиваем рубрику «Что внутри», в которой разбираем состав популярных продуктов, чтобы понять, насколько их рекламный образ соответствует содержанию. На этот раз герои выпуска — не продукты питания, а косметические средства, причем сразу два. Кремы «Чистая линия» с арникой и жимолостью и Chanel Hydra Beauty Micro Gel Crème. Первый стоит около 250 рублей за 45 мл, второй — более чем в сорок раз дороже: примерно 10 600 рублей за 50 г.

Судя по описаниям производителей, оба крема должны прежде всего увлажнять кожу. Чем дорогой крем отличается от дешевого, если оба предназначены для одного и того же? Разберем состав по ингредиентам, выясним, как они действуют на самом деле, насколько их эффективность подтверждена исследованиями, и заодно посчитаем, сколько могут стоить отдельные компоненты каждой «формулы».

Сравним основные компоненты в составе обоих кремов, которые определяют их свойства. Хотя производители не раскрывают точное количество ингредиентов, определить основные довольно просто: они всегда стоят в начале списка. Ближе к концу указаны компоненты, доля которых менее одного процента. Для расчета стоимости используем цены поставщиков косметического сырья.
«Чистая линия»: основной компонент
Chanel: основной компонент

В составе обоих кремов вода стоит на первом месте. И не только потому, что она увлажняет кожу. В большинстве кремов вода также служит растворителем и основой для других ингредиентов. При этом сама по себе вода обеспечивает лишь кратковременное увлажнение: она довольно быстро испаряется с поверхности кожи. Поэтому для длительного увлажнения недостаточно просто умыться водой. В кремы добавляют вещества, которые помогают удерживать воду в верхнем слое кожи и замедляют потерю влаги.
Chanel: пропандиол, пентиленгликоль, полиглицерин-3, глицерин

Глицерин — трехатомный спирт, молекулы которого способны связывать воду. В отличие от масел, которые прежде всего препятствуют ее испарению, глицерин помогает удерживать влагу непосредственно в верхнем слое кожи. Благодаря этому кожа становится более эластичной, а мелкие морщинки, связанные с сухостью, могут выглядеть менее заметными.

В «Чистой линии» глицерин — один из основных компонентов. В Chanel он тоже есть, но находится ближе к концу списка ингредиентов. Зато в начале списка указаны другие увлажняющие вещества: пропандиол и пентиленгликоль — многоатомные спирты, которые связывают воду и служат растворителями, а также полиглицерин-3 — соединение трех молекул глицерина, которое помогает удерживать влагу в коже.

Сколько это стоит? В кремах обычно содержится 5–10% глицерина. При оптовой цене 257 рублей за килограмм он добавляет к стоимости тюбика «Чистой линии» от 58 копеек до 1,16 рубля. Пропандиол можно купить примерно по 3–4,5 доллара за килограмм. При концентрации 5% на баночку Chanel понадобится 2,5 грамма стоимостью около одного рубля. Пентиленгликоль стоит около 1900 рублей за килограмм и при тех же 5% прибавит еще 4,75 рубля. Полиглицерин-3 стоит примерно 3100 рублей за килограмм. При условной концентрации 2% он добавит еще 3,1 рубля. Наконец, глицерин при концентрации 0,5% обойдется примерно в 6 копеек. Итого — около 8,9 рубля на банку Chanel.
Chanel: один из основных компонентов

В отличие от глицерина, пропандиола и пентиленгликоля, этиловый спирт в креме используют не для увлажнения. Это прежде всего растворитель. Он помогает смешивать некоторые ингредиенты, облегчает распределение средства по коже и быстро испаряется, создавая ощущение свежести.

Сколько это стоит? Синтетический ректификованный спирт продается примерно по 670 рублей за килограмм. При концентрации 5–10% на баночку весом 50 граммов понадобится от 2,5 до 5 граммов стоимостью максимум 3,5 рубля.
«Чистая линия»: изопропилмиристат, масло ши, изодецилнеопентаноат, гидрогенизированный полиизобутен
Chanel: Coco-Caprylate/Caprate, Caprylic/Capric Triglyceride, масло пенника лугового, масло камелии

Все эти вещества — эмоленты. Их главная задача — смягчать кожу, сглаживать неровности на ее поверхности и уменьшать потерю влаги через роговой слой. И в «Чистой линии», и в Chanel они выполняют одни и те же функции. Но от их сочетания во многом зависят консистенция крема и ощущения при нанесении. В «Чистой линии» используют изопропилмиристат (соединение жирной кислоты со спиртом) и масло ши, получаемое из орехов африканского дерева карите. В Chanel — коко-каприлат/капрат (эфиры жирных кислот и спиртов, получаемых из кокосового масла) и триглицериды каприловой и каприновой кислот (соединения этих кислот с глицерином). Оба ингредиента относятся к легким маслянистым веществам, которые хорошо распределяются по коже и, в отличие от более плотного масла ши, не создают ощущение жирной пленки.

Сколько это стоит? Килограмм изопропилмиристата — около 770 рублей, масла ши — 540 рублей. При условной концентрации 3% и 2% оба компонента обойдутся в 1,5 рубля на тюбик «Чистой линии» весом 45 граммов.

В случае Chanel килограмм коко-каприлата/капрата стоит около 1070 рублей, каприлик/каприк триглицерида — около 790 рублей, масло пенника лугового — около 3780 рублей за килограмм, масло камелии — 1150 рублей. Итого — примерно 7,2 рубля за четыре компонента.
«Чистая линия»: диметикон и циклопентасилоксан
Силиконы — синтетические соединения на основе кремния и кислорода. Их добавляют в косметику, чтобы уменьшить потерю влаги, улучшить распределение крема и сделать поверхность кожи более гладкой.

В «Чистой линии» диметикон стоит на четвертом месте в составе. Это силиконовое масло, которое образует на коже тонкое покрытие, препятствующее испарению воды. Циклопентасилоксан — летучий силикон: он помогает равномерно распределить крем, а затем испаряется.
В Chanel силиконов нет. Означает ли это, что дорогой крем лучше или безопаснее? Нет. Силиконы хорошо переносятся кожей, не закупоривают поры и не препятствуют ее нормальным функциям.

Сколько это стоит? Оптом килограмм диметикона стоит около 440 рублей, циклопентасилоксана — 510 рублей. Если в «Чистой линии» содержится по 5% каждого вещества, вместе они прибавляют к стоимости 45-граммового тюбика около 2,14 рубля.
«Чистая линия»: цетеариловый спирт, цитрат стеарата глицерила, цетилфосфат калия
Chanel: карбомер, кроссполимер акрилатов и C10–30-алкилакрилата, целлюлоза карбомер, кроссполимер акрилатов и C10–30-алкилакрилата, целлюлоза

Если просто смешать воду с маслом, через некоторое время они разделятся на два слоя. Чтобы этого не происходило, в кремы добавляют эмульгаторы — вещества, которые помогают распределить мельчайшие капли одной жидкости внутри другой. А загустители придают смеси нужную консистенцию и препятствуют расслоению.

В «Чистой линии» для стабилизации эмульсии используются цетеариловый спирт, цитрат стеарата глицерила и цетилфосфат калия. Первый дополнительно смягчает кожу, а два других помогают смешивать водную и масляную фазы крема. В Chanel применяются другие вещества: карбомер и акрилатный кроссполимер — синтетические полимеры, которые повышают вязкость средства и помогают сохранять его однородность, а также целлюлоза, которая служит загустителем и влияет на текстуру крема.

Сколько это стоит? Сколько это стоит? Килограмм цетеарилового спирта стоит около 400 рублей, цитрат стеарата глицерила — 955 рублей, цетилфосфат калия — до 2500 рублей. Если взять 2% первого вещества и по 3% остальных, все три добавят к стоимости тюбика «Чистой линии» около 5 рублей. В Chanel карбомер стоит примерно 1600 рублей за килограмм, акрилатный кроссполимер — около 2645 рублей, микрокристаллическая целлюлоза — около 530 рублей за килограмм. Все три компонента прибавляют к стоимости банки примерно 2 рубля.
«Чистая линия»: Ceramide NP, фитостеролы, лецитин
Chanel: ceramide NP, фитосфингозин

Керамиды — это жироподобные вещества, которые вместе с холестерином и жирными кислотами заполняют пространство между клетками наружного слоя кожи. Они образуют защитный барьер, препятствующий чрезмерному испарению воды. В обоих кремах содержится керамид NP — один из типов керамидов, которые присутствуют и в самой коже. В Chanel дополнительно есть фитосфингозин, входящий в состав некоторых естественных керамидов.

Сколько это стоит? Керамид NP продается в виде 5-процентной пасты и стоит 690 рублей за 10 граммов. При добавлении 0,1% такой пасты ее стоимость составит около 3,1 рубля на тюбик «Чистой линии» и 3,45 рубля на банку Chanel. Фитосфингозин стоит дороже — 217,50 рубля за грамм. При условной концентрации 0,1% он обойдется еще примерно в 10,9 рубля. В итоге — плюс 3,1 рубля к стоимости «Чистой линии» и плюс 14,3 рубля к стоимости Chanel.

В состав Chanel входит так называемая высокомолекулярная гиалуроновая кислота — разновидность этого вещества с особенно крупными молекулами. Благодаря своим размерам ее молекулы практически не проникают в глубокие слои кожи, но связывают и хорошо удерживают влагу на поверхности кожи, образуя тонкую пленку, замедляющую испарение воды. В списке ингредиентов она находится ближе к концу, то есть не относится к основным компонентам крема.
Сколько это стоит? Цена высокомолекулярного гиалуроната натрия примерно 16 000 рублей за килограмм. При максимальной концентрации 0,5% он добавит к стоимости банки Chanel 4 рубля.
«Чистая линия»: гидролизованные белки пшеницы, сои и люпина

Фитоколлагеновый комплекс — ключевой ингредиент «Чистой линии». На официальном сайте утверждается, что именно благодаря ему крем разглаживает мелкие морщины, а через 16 дней обеспечивает выраженный лифтинг-эффект. Причем объясняется это тем, что фитоколлагеновый комплекс проникает в кожу и стимулирует образование собственного коллагена.

На самом деле фитоколлагеновый комплекс в составе «Чистой линии» — это не растительный аналог коллагена (растения его вообще не производят), а обработанные растительные белки. Для их получения крупные белковые молекулы расщепляют на более короткие фрагменты. Они способны связывать влагу и образовывать на поверхности кожи тонкую пленку, благодаря чему она становится визуально более гладкой. Никаких доказательств того, что они проникают глубоко в дерму и стимулируют образование коллагена, нет.
Сколько это стоит? Гидролизованные белки пшеницы стоят около 1520 рублей за килограмм. При концентрации 1% это добавило к стоимости тюбика «Чистой линии» 68 копеек.
«Чистая линия»: арника, жимолость, облепиха, эхинацея
Chanel: экстракт белой камелии и имбиря

Растительные экстракты есть в обоих кремах. В «Чистой линии» — на основе арники, жимолости и эхиноцеи. В арнике это сесквитерпеновые лактоны и флавоноиды, в жимолости — фенольные соединения и органические кислоты. Облепиха богата каротиноидами и полифенолами, а эхинацея содержит производные кофейной кислоты, в том числе цикориевую кислоту, и полисахариды. В экстрактах имбиря встречаются гингеролы и другие фенольные соединения. Некоторые антиоксидантные и противовоспалительные свойства этих соединений подтверждены лабораторными исследованиями на клеточных культурах. Однако работают ли они так же при нанесении на кожу, неизвестно.

В Chanel Hydra Beauty экстракт белой камелии — ключевой и, можно сказать, концептуальный ингредиент. Производитель утверждает, что именно он укрепляет защитный барьер кожи. Экстракт камелии действительно содержит полифенолы с антиоксидантными и противовоспалительными свойствами. В лабораторных экспериментах специалисты Chanel обнаружили, что экстракт белой камелии повышает активность гена, отвечающего за выработку белка PPARβ/δ. Этот белок участвует в регуляции обмена жиров в клетках кожи и поддержании ее защитного барьера. Однако эксперименты проводились на клетках, а не на людях, и исследователи изучали действие самого экстракта, а не готового крема. Так что пока нет убедительных доказательств, что добавление именно экстракта камелии делает крем эффективнее.

Сколько это стоит? Водно-глицериновый экстракт арники — 205 рублей за 50 граммов, сухой экстракт жимолости — около 378 рублей за 100 граммов. Водно-глицериновый экстракт облепихи — 339 рублей за 500 мл, а аналогичный экстракт эхинацеи — по 150 рублей за 50 г. При концентрации по 0,5% их общая стоимость составит примерно 2,6 рубля.

Косметический экстракт цветков Camellia japonica продается примерно по $189 (около 15 700 рублей) за килограмм. Если принять в расчет условную концентрацию в 2%, то на банку Chanel Hydra Beauty весом 50 граммов понадобится 1 грамм экстракта стоимостью около 16 рублей.

В обоих кремах используются схожие компоненты, обеспечивающие увлажнение кожи за счет одних и тех же механизмов: одни вещества удерживают воду в верхнем слое кожи, другие препятствуют ее испарению. При этом нет убедительных доказательств того, что более дорогой крем справляется с этими задачами лучше.

Расчетная стоимость ингредиентов тоже различается не так уж сильно: примерно 16 рублей для «Чистой линии» и 56 рублей для Chanel. Разница составляет около трех с половиной раз, а не сорок с лишним, как в розничной цене.

Разумеется, стоимость ингредиентов — лишь часть розничной цены. В нее входят также производство, упаковка, реклама, логистика и торговые наценки. А в случае дорогих косметических марок существенные расходы могут быть связаны еще и с научными исследованиями и разработкой новых технологий.

Chanel действительно инвестирует в исследования. У компании есть собственные исследовательские подразделения, которые изучают свойства кожи, действие различных веществ и способы их использования в косметике. Например, для линейки Hydra Beauty совместно с французской компанией Capsum была разработана специальная микрофлюидная технология, позволяющая интегрировать компоненты с экстрактом камелии в мельчайшие капли. По утверждению Chanel, это помогает сохранить все свойства экстракта и одновременно получить легкую текстуру крем-геля.

«Текстура» тут — ключевое слово. Сделать крем приятным в использовании не так просто, как может показаться. Это отдельная область косметических исследований, в которой изучают не столько терапевтические, сколько сенсорные эффекты косметики — ощущения от ее консистенции, запаха, распределения по коже и скорости впитывания. Чтобы добиться «премиального» эффекта, приходится многократно менять состав и проводить десятки испытаний. Именно за это мы и платим.
От викторианских ужинов с вином до советских столовых: разбираемся, как сложились привычные пищевые традиции и стоит ли следовать им сегодня

items.author: Justin Chang
paragraphs: The bluest of peepers, framed in the tightest of closeups, can be found staring out at you from a movie screen. No, not Elizabeth Holmes’s in the hotly debated documentary “You Can See Everything,” though her eerily unblinking stare, somehow both insinuating and vacant, certainly runs a close second. I speak of Andrew Scott in the muddled biographical drama “Elsinore,” in which he plays the London-based Scottish actor Ian Charleson in the autumn of 1989, during some of the unbearable and extraordinary final months of his life. Ian, who’s forty, is living with AIDS in an era when the diagnosis is a death sentence, and he already has a ghostly white pallor that brings out the intensity of his eyes, which sparkle like deep-set sapphires. (Scott, whose eyes are brown, wore blue contact lenses during production.) His complexion also contrasts starkly with a lesion that appears, early in the film, near his right temple—one of many that will eventually cover his body, though it’s the only one that worries him for now. A skin growth on an arm or a leg can be covered, but a blotch on Ian’s face, even when obscured with makeup, might catch a viewer’s attention.

Ian is used to getting noticed on stage and off, though the source of such recognition can be exasperating. He’s best known for his performance as the Olympic-champion runner Eric Liddell in “Chariots of Fire” (1981), a film that is itself best known for a musical score that most would call iconic and Ian would term incessant. He can barely promote a new project on a talk show without being assaulted on the air by the composer Vangelis’s overweeningly cosmic synths; in a cab, he nods along indulgently as the driver hums the whole damn theme. Ian has resigned himself to the fact that “Chariots of Fire” will lead his obituaries, and also to the likelihood that those obituaries are not too far away. But then he learns that Daniel Day-Lewis, a star on the rise, has mysteriously dropped out of the role of Hamlet at the National Theatre—and the director, Richard Eyre (a fine Johnny Flynn), asks Ian to take over, mid-run. Famously, the production marked the last time that Day-Lewis ever appeared in a play; for infinitely sadder reasons, it also gave us the last role of Ian Charleson’s life. (He made it through twenty-four performances of “Hamlet” at the National and died weeks later, in January, 1990.)

“Elsinore,” directed by the Australian filmmaker Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, seeks to make a heroic spectacle of Ian’s refusal to go gentle into that good night. He already lives, breathes, and often quotes “Hamlet”—he played the prince of Denmark before, in 1974, at a theatre in Cambridge—and he’s determined to summon every last reserve of his energy, which is waning, and his talent, which is considerable. He has the unflagging support of his closest friend, the casting director Patsy Pollock (Billie Piper), but also the stern disapproval of his doctor, Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman), who knows that the stress of rehearsals and performances will only hasten Ian’s physical decline. Johnson is a real-life pioneer in H.I.V. and AIDS treatment, and Colman plays her with a bracing dash of vinegar; the pleasure of her scenes with Scott lies in the sugary grace notes that gradually seep into their interplay. Doctor and patient reach a respectful impasse when Margaret tells Ian that her priority is the preservation of life, to which Ian replies that life can also be measured in quality, not quantity.

This is a worthy sentiment, though I’m not sure that Stone, a more-is-more kind of filmmaker, grasps its value as an aesthetic principle. The movie is built around an almost mathematical sense of amplification—it’s a mortality-driven tearjerker and a testament to the power of art—and it mashes together Ian’s onstage triumphs and behind-the-scenes travails in a monotonous manner that eventually leeches both of meaning. The montages in “Elsinore” go on forever; more than once, I longed for Stone to slow down and let an extended scene of rehearsal play out—to have Ian puzzle over a particular line reading or a bit of blocking, unadorned by crosscutting or music. Instead, “Hamlet” is reduced to a collage of high-flown sound bites, interrupted and sometimes drowned out by fits of coughing and retching. The plague’s the thing.

A cynic might observe that, for an actor, the chance to declaim some of Shakespeare’s greatest lines and showily waste away from terminal illness amounts to two thespian challenges rolled into one—a kind of Oscar-qualifying biathlon. If so, no one could deny that Andrew Scott is in intensely competitive shape, and he grabs hold of you so thoroughly as to send your skepticism into retreat. The part calls for extremes of suffering and showmanship, but Scott finds room for modulation; his Ian retains two qualities—a core of tenderness, and a persistently impish wit—that somehow survive every setback that AIDS can hurl at them. Is it churlish to note that Scott was even better, and rather less effortful, in “All of Us Strangers” (2023), in which he brought a delicate, haunting interiority to the role of Adam, a lonely gay Londoner? Adam undergoes the quietest yet most transformative of spiritual and emotional journeys; he isn’t the same person at the beginning, the end, or, indeed, at any point in the movie. Ian, by contrast, is all dogged determination from start to finish. He flails, suffers, and ultimately transcends, but he doesn’t expand.

Ian’s one decisive shift concerns the matter of visibility: although he’s kept his sexuality private, he decides that, once he’s gone, the cause of his death will be made known. He arrives at this decision through a tense reckoning with the pioneering gay director Derek Jarman (David Dawson), who bitterly resents Ian for essentially disavowing their collaboration on the queer-punk film “Jubilee” (1978) and for suppressing his sexuality publicly in a bid for Hollywood acceptance. The film’s depiction of Charleson and Jarman’s spats, however rooted in truth, is corrected and diminished by Theo Rollason’s excellent recent documentary “Queer Edward II,” which features newly discovered archival footage from the set of “Edward II,” Jarman’s period drama from 1991. Like “Elsinore,” Rollason’s documentary—which premièred at the Venice and London film festivals and is still, as of this writing, seeking a U.S. distributor—addresses Jarman’s passionate commitment to art and activism, and also his controversial willingness to pressure closeted celebrities into outing themselves. Yet the real Jarman, even at his most confrontational, is shown to possess an infectious warmth, ebullience, and largeness of spirit—all of which render the glaring, vitriolic Jarman of “Elsinore” almost unrecognizable by comparison. Not for the first time in this movie, the truth seems to overwhelm the filmmaker’s imagination.

I invoked the Oscars flippantly, but not unreasonably. It’s hard to avoid the subject in the case of “Elsinore,” partly because the film has been widely tipped to earn Scott a nomination for Best Actor, but also because the legacy of the Academy Awards looms over the story itself: “Chariots of Fire” won Best Picture in 1982, a choice that hasn’t aged half as well as Vangelis’s score. By curious if just-short-of-fascinating coincidence, there’s a new film in theatres that unfolds under the shadow of another Oscar winner, “Rocky” (1976)—a better-regarded champ than “Chariots,” though it, too, features more than its fair share of musically charged sprinting. “I Play Rocky,” directed by Peter Farrelly from a screenplay by Peter Gamble, exalts the making of an improbable yet immortal American classic—and the birth of a movie star, Sylvester Stallone, played here by a charismatic and enormously likable young actor named Anthony Ippolito.

We encounter the young Stallone as a cash-strapped nobody in mid-nineteen-seventies New York City, working at a fishmonger’s, auditioning for nothing parts, and calling himself Mike. His deeply supportive girlfriend, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), encourages him to write his own scripts—and to go by Sylvester, a name that once made him a target of childhood bullies. Sylvester isn’t an obvious moniker for a working stiff with a wink-wink taste for raw eggs, but the incongruity is the point. This guy, who tries out for roles such as Thug No. 2 by day and recites Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric” by night, has unexpected poetry in him, and it bursts forth in his stubborn desire to be an actor and a screenwriter. In time, he and Sasha marry and move to Los Angeles, where he charms and hustles his way into the offices of the producers Irwin Winkler (P. J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell), a pair of savvy industry gatekeepers who, like most everyone else, feel dubious about Sylvester at first. By the film’s end, they will believe in him as passionately as he believes in himself.

“I Play Rocky” wants us to believe in Sylvester, too, which is easy enough to do. Ippolito, magnetizing the camera with a sleepy-eyed stare, and mumbling his lines with a deft approximation of Stallone’s slightly slurred delivery, is an astounding physical and verbal match for Stallone, and you can’t take your eyes off him—or close your ears to him—even when the movie pulls its narrative punches. Given what Stallone has revealed in interviews, some of them to promote his recent memoir, “The Steps,” the character’s home life feels patchy and sanitized. Gone is anything more than a hint of emotional turbulence between Sylvester and his father, Frank Stallone, Sr. (an almost unrecognizable Matt Dillon), who cruelly disparages his son at every turn.

Sylvester’s big eureka moment takes place in an L.A. bar, where he catches an epic fifteen-round boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner—and then immediately races home to write “Rocky” in a three-and-half-day burst of inspiration. This backstory is the stuff of Hollywood legend, and “I Play Rocky” reprints it gleefully, with nary a concern that legend alone might not suffice. Sylvester, a movie nut, knows a thing or two about what makes a picture work, but where did he get his writerly instincts, his sense of narrative drive and structure? A title card from earlier in the film—“SIXTEEN MONTHS AND EIGHT SCREENPLAYS LATER . . .”—doesn’t exactly tell the story.

The best scenes in “I Play Rocky” arrive shortly after the script is written and triumphantly presented to Winkler and Chartoff—at which point Sylvester delivers the ultimatum of the title. Sandy Maddox (a rudely amusing Tracy Letts), an executive at United Artists (and a composite of several real-life individuals), wants a bankable star such as Robert Redford or Burt Reynolds, and the tug-of-war negotiations that ensue open up an engrossing, sharply satirical window onto the frivolity and arbitrariness that so often govern Hollywood. Farrelly and Gamble attempt a deeper process dive once the film is green-lit, though it’s here that “I Play Rocky” goes on making-of-“Rocky” autopilot, stuffed with reënactments of beloved scenes and recognizable setups. Here is Sylvester in gray sweats, lunging up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and there he goes, tottering after Talia Shire on an ice-skating rink—a scene that nearly gets axed at the last minute, against Sylvester’s protests. Here, too, is the film’s journeyman director, John G. Avildsen (Jay Duplass), who has a talent for passing off thrift as realism, and whose cost-cutting instinct threatens to derail Sylvester’s ambitions as often as it helps realize them. Those ambitions will pay off, of course, and how: the finished “Rocky” will bring audiences to their feet, become the highest-grossing film of 1976, and prove the smirking Sandy Maddoxes of the world wrong.

“I Play Rocky” isn’t just an underdog story; it’s practically an underdog shelter. Rocky Balboa is an underdog in the boxing ring, “Rocky” is an underdog at the box office and the Oscars, and Stallone is an underdog in Hollywood—and, in his case, an underdog with a literal underdog, an abandoned bullmastiff that he finds on the streets of New York and adopts as his own. No doubt Farrelly’s film fancies itself an underdog, too—a scrappy, feel-good David of a picture, going up against the industry’s many shiny prestige Goliaths, and seeking to honor an earlier tradition of nervy but popular American filmmaking. For all that, I’m not convinced the film entirely buys, or successfully sells, its own mythmaking. Again and again, Farrelly, who unwittingly revealed the toxic side of nostalgia in the slickly retrograde, Best Picture-winning “Green Book” (2018), sacrifices real suspense and drama on the altar of fan-service reënactment. Beat by beat, “I Play Rocky” leans so complacently on the audience’s assumed love and knowledge of “Rocky” that it defeats its own stakes. It takes the triumph of the underdog too easily for granted. ♦

items.title: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” Is Tarantino Minus Tarantino
items.description: In a way, the most engrossing thing about “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is what it isn’t: a film directed by Quentin Tarantino. It’s a sequel to his 2019 movie “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood,” which he both wrote and directed. For the new f
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: In a way, the most engrossing thing about “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is what it isn’t: a film directed by Quentin Tarantino. It’s a sequel to his 2019 movie “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood,” which he both wrote and directed. For the new film, he wrote the script but farmed its direction out to David Fincher, and I found myself watching the movie psychodramatically, with an eye for the aversions it may have aroused in Tarantino, the symptoms it may have triggered. To some extent, the movie encourages this kind of diagnostic viewing, because for all its enticements—starting with the cast, led by Brad Pitt and Elizabeth Debicki—it’s a movie of cinematic riffs and asides that calls attention to its artifices and, especially, to its personalized artistic quirks and obsessions.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” is centered on the earlier movie’s main supporting character, Cliff (played by Brad Pitt). In “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” set in 1969, he’s the stunt double for an actor named Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio), whose career is in a downturn. The new film picks up with Cliff, again played by Pitt, in June of 1977; Rick has departed for Australia, and Cliff, at the margins of Hollywood, is a sometime projectionist at the New Beverly Theatre (which, in real life, Tarantino now owns). He also works as a part-time bartender and does favors for friends as something of a fixer. Cliff is first seen doing his technical duty in the projection booth, seeing a scant audience out after the last show, and then welcoming, into the empty theatre, a pair of crooks (played by Karren Karagulian and Corey Fogelmanis), with whom Cliff negotiates the return of a bag of valuables (including an Oscar statuette) that they’ve stolen. Eventually, negotiating no more, he guns one down and makes the other help dispose of the body.

So much for the projecting; it’s the fixing that interests Tarantino. The next day, Cliff is surprised to be summoned to a meeting with a TV actor named Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), because Charlie is both famed for doing his own stunts and too short to use Cliff as a double. The job Charlie has in mind turns out to be offscreen: in a plot with a coincidental similarity to James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” Charlie has naïvely become involved with gangsters who are threatening his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), and he wants Cliff to get them out of the jam. Cliff’s first idea, the simplest, is to pay them what they want. His second idea is to, um, negotiate, and it’s clear what that implies. But these gangsters, ruthless and bloodthirsty, promise an altogether more dangerous showdown.

Unfortunately, this tense setup proves more or less to be a live-action MacGuffin. Tarantino’s script dangles a gaudy array of decorative events and tangy characters, florid dialogue and snappy gestures that are more than the movie’s raison d’être—they’re its main matter. Like a Rube Goldberg contraption, the digressive screenplay is devised to do its job as circuitously, as idiosyncratically, and as ornamentally as possible. The narrative adornments are at least clever, and even when they’re hollow, noisy, and vain they’re, above all, symbolic incarnations of a world view.

Compared with Fincher’s other recent films, “The Further Mis-Adventures” must have been a blast to make. “Mank,” his bio-pic of the classic-Hollywood screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz, from 2020, had the heavy weight of real history looming over it, testing Fincher’s artistic superego rather than his expressive powers. “The Killer,” his action movie from 2023, buried both its pulp vigor and any connection to the real world in an overcooked dourness. By contrast, “The Further Mis-Adventures” has the typically Tarantinian explosive action and calibrated slow burns, the motormouth dialogue, the whimsical yet logical twists, the humor, and, above all, the light-footed, hearty energy and exuberant glee that Pitt brought to the original role. His reprisal of Cliff comes with even more self-aware snap, because it comes after a run of disappointing parts, including “Babylon” and “F1,” that risked turning his laid-back charm into a routine and a cliché.

In “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” Tarantino’s direction was at its best in catching the character’s verve in casual action, and in “The Further Mis-Adventures” Fincher captures similar moments with joyful wonder—if not with the palpable physicality that Tarantino brought to the job. Whether Cliff is handling reels and keeping an eye on the projector, the screen, the concession stand; dispensing jazzy pours and non-stop patter at the rowdy bar he tends; or taking sure command of stressful situations, he is essentially a boss in workingman’s garb, a big man in circumstances too small for him. Cliff’s commonplace heroism conceals his real heroism, which is hinted at in the wartime actions that he speaks of, and in his enforcer-like battles on his friends’ behalf. He’s a hidden version of the character played by Bradley Cooper in Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper”: a protector—albeit one who, by contrast, is portrayed as untroubled by guilt, unburdened by responsibility, indeed lacking any inner life or psychology at all.

Why wouldn’t Tarantino want to return to direct his own sequel, and to help Pitt imbue Cliff with his characteristic swing or some new flair? The answer might be that, in recent years, Tarantino’s focus has tilted so drastically toward the gratifications of his own writing that the aesthetic gratifications he once found in the visual side of filmmaking appear to have dissipated. This shift was evident in his methodical filming of “The Hateful Eight,” which treated the screen largely as a proscenium, and even in “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” which provided a podium for the proclamation of his own old-Hollywood nostalgia. In “The Further Mis-Adventures,” Tarantino uses the same premise to put forward a new idea that amounts to a fascinating renunciation of the art of directing—and yet another mode of nostalgia.

Tarantino’s old-Hollywood veneration is centered on people like Cliff, the rugged characters of rich life experience who, without fame or acclaim, give the movie town its soul. The expression of that soul is in their glorious talk, in the stories they tell. Cliff is a formidable raconteur, who even in high-stakes negotiations spins fabulistic yarns in which to entangle his prey. He tells behind-the-scenes tales about actors in movies that his father, Gus (Peter Weller), a pawn-shop owner, watches on TV. He riffs on some of his derring-do as seen in “Once Upon a Time . . . .” He tells stories about sex. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is a story of stories: where they come from, what they’re for, and what they have to do with movies. And what the film reveals, doubtless unawares, is that a story on its own is a narrative that ends too soon and leaves out too much. It’s not enough to film one. (The shibboleth that filmmakers are mere storytellers is meant to keep producers happy.) What turns a story into a finished work is its transformation, its expansion beyond storytelling itself—which is exactly what “The Further Mis-Adventures” is missing.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” is a Tarantino film not despite the fact that he didn’t direct it but because he didn’t direct it: by not directing, he has given us a manifesto of his new artistic perspective. He has effectively become his own showrunner, with Fincher as a hired hand who thus becomes something like the parody of the auteur that Pauline Kael describes in her 1963 anti-auteurist screed “Circles and Squares”: someone who “expresses himself by shoving bits of style up the crevasses of the plots.” Speaking of Kael, there’s a great love story embedded—indeed, smothered—in the crime drama and the sidebar antics of “The Further Mis-Adventures.” The meeting with Charlie, the actor in need of Cliff’s help, is arranged by the actor’s agent, Karen Crosby (played by Elizabeth Debicki). She’s no ordinary agent but an agent with a prior career as a film critic, which was launched, she explains, with Kael’s help. At one of the meetings (which also includes Toni), Karen is coaxed into delivering, for Cliff’s benefit, her signature riff, which, in short, is that Hollywood movies aren’t and can’t be art—that, even in the best cases, a Hollywood film, as she puts it, isn’t Albert Camus’s “The Stranger” and “isn’t even Kerouac” but the artistic equivalent of hamburger—and she mocks critics for considering it art when all they’re doing is comparing Big Macs to Whoppers.

Whether true or not, it’s at least a convenient view for an agent to hold. What matters to the drama, however, isn’t Karen’s view of movies but her view of Cliff, and vice versa. Theirs is exactly the sort of romance that, Cliff says, would be a high-school cliché—the rough-hewn jock and the regal brainiac—and, apparently, neither Tarantino nor Fincher could get past clichés in working it out. Still, it’s there in the movie, as emotional raw material of extraordinary volatility, ready to produce a spectacular romantic conflagration at the slightest spark, and instead left undeveloped, essentially unused. Debicki, bringing commanding elegance and athletic grace to the role, opens a door and offers a glimpse of cinematic possibilities—and, more important, human ones—that both filmmakers at the joystick boyishly shy away from. ♦

items.title: Jared Kushner’s Wars
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Andrew Rice
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

At 45, Jared Kushner is no longer young, but he still presents as a man in a hurry. His thin face rests in an expression of impatience: lips pursed, nostrils flared, eyebrows arched. He has no formal office in President Donald Trump’s government, only a wedding license, but on any given day he may be anywhere in the world, tending to his father-in-law’s diplomatic business. On one tropical morning in late September, he can be found at his home outside Miami — the city that, under Trump, has become an unofficial hub of American foreign policy. When I first see him through the enormous front windows of his sleek modernist mansion in the Village of Indian Creek, a private island in Biscayne Bay, Kushner is standing by the front door, cell phone to his ear. At this moment, he is simultaneously giving his attention to three global crises, each of which is critical and overwhelming in its own right.

On top of that, Kushner has a day job at his private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, which does business in some of the same countries where he practices diplomacy. He sees no conflict in this, only virtuous synergy, but it does require some toggling.

Kushner opens the door, invites me inside, then hoists a backpack over his shoulder. He is dressed casually in a lightweight sweater and throwback Air Jordans. He bounds down the white marble front stairs to his car, an unfancy Jeep Cherokee. Its wheels crunch the driveway gravel as we circle a bubbling fountain and head out through the hedges with his Secret Service detail trailing behind. The island — known to tabloids and celebrity real-estate agents as the “Billionaire Bunker” — is separated from the mainland by what is effectively a moat, which we cross via a gated bridge, and Kushner turns in the direction of the Affinity office.

“I’m a fairly all-in personality, so when I’m in something, it consumes all of me,” Kushner says as he drives. “It takes a big toll on me to do one of these, let alone three.” Crisis No. 1 is Gaza, which Kushner took on last year by inserting himself into the middle of cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Not only getting the war stopped — getting all the hostages home, getting the bodies of the hostages home. It was a crazy operation,” he says. “Bibi didn’t think we could do it.” Since then, Kushner has been working on the future of Palestine — without much substantive input, critics say, from actual Palestinians — while also trying to resolve crisis No. 2, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and navigating crisis No. 3, Trump’s war of choice with Iran.

“Fixing Iran-U.S. relations, that’s something that has been broken for 50 years, so it’s not like there’s a precedent for success,” Kushner tells me. He’s oversimplifying the history, but he doesn’t think history matters much anyway. His cell phone rings. It’s his brother, Josh, the tech venture capitalist who is buying a piece of the Los Angeles Lakers. He sends Josh to voice-mail so he can concentrate. Over the months we’ve been talking, Kushner has explained his theory of statecraft, which prizes the innate ability of “deal guys,” who he says can think up solutions that elude the cautious, protocol-bound, and past-obsessed professionals of the diplomatic corps. Although he collaborates closely with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s old friend and official peace envoy, and they are both technically overseen by Marco Rubio, who is national security adviser and secretary of State, Kushner effectively works as an unpaid freelancer, relying on the back channels he opened as a senior White House aide during Trump’s first term and later solidified through his business.

Earlier in the drive, I told Kushner that, the way I saw it, one big question was arising from all his efforts: “What’s this guy’s angle?” One common and plausible answer is money. A couple of weeks before, The New Yorker published a long article about what it labeled Kushner’s “dollar diplomacy,” looking into the ways in which — even as he participated in fateful foreign-policy decisions about the Middle East — he had cultivated investment from some of the same governments he has been meeting with on behalf of the U.S. The funds managed by Affinity, which currently has some $6 billion in assets, mostly came from sovereign-wealth funds controlled by the royal families of the Persian Gulf. Kushner invested in an AI start-up in Silicon Valley and a rental-car company in Israel and Burger King franchises in Brazil and even a real-estate development in Albania, where his involvement has inspired widespread anti-government protests. The New Yorker article was just the latest installment in a decadelong series of reports, books, and official investigations about his business dealings, but the latest implication that he had been bought off got under Kushner’s skin so much that he tells me he is putting together what will turn out to be a 6,800-word footnoted rebuttal.

“The accumulation of more wealth is not my top objective,” he tells me. He says he could be making more money if he weren’t giving his time away, and his standard answer to critics is to challenge them to find any instance when he acted contrary to American interests. “Having the resources that I need to live my life makes me more independent to pursue the things that I want to pursue,” Kushner says. “I’ve been doing this for ten years, and my business has been an objectively successful business. My diplomacy’s been successful diplomacy. Nobody’s ever identified any case where I’ve done one thing to benefit the other.”

It is still a few weeks before the midterms, and Democrats are promising to test his catch-me-if-you-can defense when they retake Congress, and with it, subpoena power. But Kushner claims he is unfazed. “I sleep well at night,” he tells me, “because I know what the laws are, I know what the rules are, and I don’t come close to violating them.”

At the entrance to the open-plan office of Affinity, I see evidence of another possible motivation. Behind the reception desk is his “power wall,” where an array of pictures and mementos are hung. Some of the photos are of Trump, and others are inscribed by him. JARED, GREAT JOB reads the distinctive Sharpie scrawl atop a map of Israel, memorializing a peace initiative Kushner pushed in the first term. (It was unsuccessful.) Another photo, of Trump’s border wall, bears the underlined word PAINT. (Trump had put Kushner in charge of building it and wanted it to be black.)

Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump — who also served as an aide to her father during his first term — spent four tumultuous years in the West Wing. Working from a tiny office that linked to the Oval Office through an inner passageway, Kushner served as Trump’s actualizer, translating his gut feelings into government action, and his soft-voiced interpreter to Congress, Wall Street, and world leaders. After the first term ended in a haze of tear gas and disgrace, Kushner wrote a White House memoir called Breaking History, in which he placed himself at the center of all that went right and none of the wrong. “I left Washington with a new understanding of the world,” Kushner told me when we met for our first interview this past summer. “A lot of new relationships that were mostly earned in the trenches, chasing impossible goals, and a deep belief in myself.”

During the first term, Kushner would sometimes advise colleagues not to try to control Trump — he makes the waves, Kushner says, and you can only try to surf them. He swears he didn’t want to get pulled back into the water. When pressed, Kushner concedes that he may be excited to exercise power, but he claims he doesn’t want it for its own sake — rather, he wants the power to do good in the world. The signature foreign-policy promise of Trump’s comeback campaign was “No new wars,” but now it’s wars all over. Who would choose to take that on? “No. 1, there’s a high likelihood of not succeeding,” Kushner says as we talk in his corner office, where his standing desk looks out onto the Atlantic. “And No. 2, a high likelihood of people screaming at you and people accusing you of crazy things.”

Many of the accusations leveled at Kushner are not at all crazy, though, and to the Democrats who recently reclaimed control of Congress, they potentially involve a rich vein of corruption to mine in their coming investigations of the Trump administration. “I think Kushner is going to be a huge focus,” says a Democratic staffer on one of the congressional committees about an investigation that is now gearing up. “The scale of Jared Kushner’s corruption makes what Hunter Biden did look like food-stamp fraud.”

News reports have already identified some potential conflicts of interest, including Affinity’s interest in Arxis, a Connecticut defense contractor that sells to the U.S. military, and Phoenix Financial, a large firm in Israel that has invested in companies supplying that country’s army with ammunition, drones, and other matériel. (Kushner contends Phoenix is just an asset manager comparable to an American company like Vanguard and has declined to comment on Arxis.) The incoming Democrats believe they will turn up more damaging information once they start compelling witnesses to testify under oath.

Kushner is quick to point out that many previous investigations have failed to pin anything illegal on him. Still, there remains the separate question of what he has actually done with his power. In the Kushner belief system, there is no more shameful sin than ineffectiveness. But as a diplomat, he is at least partly responsible for the debacle in Iran — the “biggest self-own in the history of foreign policy,” as one expert described it to me — and Democrats hope to show he has made money while botching the assignment. To them, he looks like a caricature of Trump-era corruption, the walking, slim-suited embodiment of two of the things a majority of the Americans who voted to repudiate Trump in the midterms hate the most about his administration: the war and the greed. How does Kushner justify what he has done and what he has failed to do? To a remarkable degree, he is insouciant in the face of disaster and its consequences.

When he worked in the West Wing, the Secret Service gave him the code name “Mechanic,” and he expresses boundless confidence in “my ability to problem-solve, my ability to manifest impossible things.” In our conversations, this self-assurance is undiminished by the harsh reality that most of his diplomatic initiatives have been going nowhere and, in some cases, have left the world in worse condition than it was before.

Kushner’s master plan for Gaza — a scheme to build the strip into a coastal metropolis — is stalled and cannot proceed until Israel allows it to move forward, which won’t happen unless Netanyahu or a successor is convinced that Hamas is serious about disarming. In Ukraine, the recent strategy of offering economic carrots to Vladimir Putin while using the stick on Volodymyr Zelenskyy has yielded little in the way of concessions from Russia, the aggressor. It has been bombarding Kyiv as viciously as at any point in the war. And in the Persian Gulf, the region of the world where Kushner has concentrated both his foreign-policy and fundraising efforts, the American position has deteriorated over the past year, despite — or maybe because of — his involvement. Trump went to war with Iran only after Kushner judged that negotiations with the Iranian regime over its nuclear program were not worth pursuing. In retrospect, walking away and launching air strikes looks like a catastrophic mistake. Despite the death of Iran’s supreme leader, the hard-liners in the country appear to feel they have emerged stronger from nine months of on-and-off conflict. Kushner has tried to address the problem, but it has defied all his powers as a deal-maker. Once you break history, it’s tough to put it back together.

It is tempting to describe Kushner’s role in government as unprecedented, but if you take the long view, it’s not so strange. “I feel like I’ve been going back to early-modern history,” says Fiona Hill, who worked with Kushner when she was on the staff of the National Security Council in the first Trump term. “Jared is a prince, and he plays a kind of a function that would have been not unfamiliar in the 18th century.” Hill, who oversaw Russia policy before she resigned in 2019 and later became a witness against Trump in his first impeachment, recalls being summoned to the Oval Office to listen to a call between the president and Putin. When Trump hung up, he ignored her, the expert, and instead asked Jared and Ivanka for their takes.

To Hill, this was striking to see in the West Wing, but there are plenty of places where the ruler turns to family first. “In the context of international diplomacy,” says Ben Rhodes, a former foreign-policy adviser to President Obama, “it is actually not unusual to have a son-in-law who is a power broker who mixes business and profit.”

In Kushner’s own telling, family obligation has been the driving force in his life. He had to grow up fast, taking over the Kushner real-estate business, established by his grandfather, when he was still in his 20s. (His father, Charlie, had been sent to prison for crimes connected to a feud with his brother-in-law. He was pardoned by Trump in 2020 and is now the U.S. ambassador to France.) When Jared married Ivanka, he entered a new family with new obligations. In his memoir, he portrays his decision to take over Trump’s disorganized 2016 campaign as a matter of duty. Then he says duty sent him to Washington. Kushner’s ego, and the power he wields, is couched in the language of noble service. If he wanted to make money, he says, he did not need to do it in a roundabout way by going into government. When he took his White House position, Kushner had to sell his interests in various private investments, including an early one he had made in Thrive Capital, the venture firm his brother, Josh, founded. It’s gone on to such success that the shares he sold would’ve been worth many billions today. “I believe he and Ivanka would pass a lie-detector test,” says a first-term White House staffer. “They believe it to their core: If you asked them whether this made them richer or poorer, they would say ‘poorer.’”

“I think that for whatever reason, I’ve always been underestimated in my life,” Kushner says. In reply, he can cite a list of unquestionable achievements he pulled off during Trump’s first term, such as launching Operation Warp Speed, which produced a COVID vaccine in a miraculous seven months. But no assignment was more meaningful, he says, than the one Trump gave him at the start of the administration: figure out Israel and Palestine. His grandparents survived the Holocaust in the forests of Belarus. As a teenager, Jared once vacated his bedroom for Netanyahu when he stayed over as a houseguest. Given that prior rounds of negotiation had yielded failure after failure, it made for an easy joke: Jared was going to bring peace to the Middle East? But Kushner took the possibility seriously and approached diplomacy as another form of networking.

Back when he was just another striving young businessman, he had become acquainted with Tony Blair, the former British prime minister. (He has a knack for befriending older Davos Men.) In 2016, Blair was pushing a plan to address both Palestinian demands for statehood and Israel’s desire to thaw its political and trade relations with Arab nations. Blair told Kushner he saw an opening and it ran through the Persian Gulf.

Traditionally, the public-facing appointees who represented America to the world were backed up by a seasoned army of Foreign Service officers and area experts inside the federal bureaucracy. The National Security Council used a methodical interagency process to explore and weigh changes in policy. Kushner went about things his own way. Through a friend, an American asset manager who has dealings in the United Arab Emirates, he made a connection to that nation’s ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, commonly known as MBZ. He became close to MBZ’s brother and national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who controls a sovereign-wealth fund that has more than $1 trillion in assets. Early in the administration, Kushner met Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, or MBS, with whom he would form a key alliance.

MBS was in a struggle with another potential successor to the Saudi throne who had close ties to the CIA. The Middle East experts in the White House were cautious, thinking MBS was cocky and inexperienced, but Kushner saw him as a disrupter like himself. “MBS knew right away that Jared was his flunky,” says a senior National Security Council official from Trump’s first term, who describes Kushner as “a completely loose cannon with respect to any interagency coordination.”

Kushner arranged for Trump to make a presidential visit to Saudi Arabia in 2017. At a banquet during the trip, MBS made introductions for Kushner and Ivanka. Kushner recounts in his book that MBS took him to his table and said, “These were the ‘Jared Kushners’ of the Middle East,” and that “they didn’t all have obvious titles, but if I needed to get anything done in their countries, I should call them.” Kushner soon began paying visits to his new acquaintances in the region. He traveled with a small entourage, usually without the inclusion of translators or U.S. Embassy staff on the ground.

There is little in the public record about what transpired in Kushner’s private meetings, which has led to much speculation about the nature of his conversations. In October, the investigative journalist Matthew Cole published a book called Princes and Thieves, in which he alleges (based on confidential sourcing) that MBZ and MBS bribed Kushner by jointly putting billions of dollars into overseas bank accounts that were intended both to enrich him personally and to create a “slush fund” to advance secret U.S. military and intelligence objectives. Cole writes that Kushner’s compromising financial relationships eventually became known to various parties, including the government of Qatar, the Russians, and even hackers working for the Dutch intelligence service. These extraordinary claims lack extraordinary evidence, and Kushner has described them as “completely insane.” He points out that this time coincided with special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation, when he was “one of the most scrutinized people in the world.” Kushner says he is preparing a defamation lawsuit, yet to be filed.

It’s really not necessary to resort to bribery, though, to explain the affinity between Kushner and the Jared Kushners of the Middle East. Foreign-policy experts have a term for this, mirroring — seeing your own values and preconceptions in your counterpart. Kushner believes the Gulf rulers found his family-to-family outreach “familiar and reassuring.” In the Gulf, “they feel very, very comfortable with the idea that the leader of the United States has a family member who is out representing him personally in negotiations,” says a former diplomat stationed in the region at the time. “That aligns with the way that Gulf ruling families do business.”

Kushner spent the time it took to build trusting relationships. He bonded with MBS at one of the crown prince’s estates in the desert, staying up all night and watching the sun rise over a fire. Kushner was impressed with his vision for modernizing Saudi Arabia and his willingness to spend his oil money on transformative projects. When they weren’t together, Kushner and MBS would talk and text on WhatsApp. MBS loves video games, and sometimes they’d play together. (“League of Legends,” Kushner specifies. “He’s a big League player.”) When MBS was implicated in the grisly assassination of a Washington-based dissident, Kushner refused calls to repudiate him. “It’s a real friendship,” Kushner says.

It took nearly four years for Kushner’s personalized approach to come to fruition in an act of diplomacy that, at the time, even his skeptics described as nimble. In 2020, he unveiled a new land-for-peace plan to the Israelis and the Palestinians. The Palestinian Authority leadership immediately rejected it, saying it offered them no substantive assurance they would ever attain statehood while providing the thinnest of smoke screens for Israel’s annexation of West Bank settlements. But the setback created an opportunity. From their interactions, Kushner had concluded that Gulf leaders were weary of supporting the Palestinian struggle and ready to drop their pretense of hostility toward Israel. He met with Yousef Al Otaiba, the Emirati ambassador in Washington, who had become another friend. (“Whether it’s on WhatsApp or Signal or whatever the method is, he speaks to you like a normal person,” Al Otaiba tells me. “He actually listens, and he doesn’t come in with preconceived notions.”) The Emiratis were ready to propose an alternative approach. They wanted economic and security ties with Israel. If Netanyahu would agree not to annex West Bank settlements, there could be a new framework: peace without the Palestinians.

Kushner flew all over the region to broker the resulting agreement, known as the Abraham Accords. “I actually say to people he is probably the best natural political mind I have come across,” says Blair. “And I have come across quite a few.” The accords demonstrated not just the value of Kushner’s relationships but his willingness to go big, Blair tells me. “One of the things he is extremely good at is that when a problem is in quite a narrow compass and there is a blockage, he creates an enlargement of the matrix of issues to be decided that allows you then to unlock the problem.” The Abraham Accords soon expanded to encompass more than just one set of concerns. After the UAE became the first Arab nation to normalize diplomatic relations with Israel in more than 25 years, several other Muslim-majority countries jumped aboard.

In the final months of Trump’s term, Kushner spent much of his time traveling the Gulf region, promoting economic development and trying to lay the groundwork to bring Saudi Arabia into the accords. (MBS assured Kushner he might join down the line.) Airline routes opened between Tel Aviv and Dubai. Commerce began to flow. “I’m always trying to focus on the economics,” Kushner says. “Everyone’s focused on the historical grievances, whereas my view is the past is the past.”

On January 6, 2021, Kushner was flying home from Saudi Arabia, where he had been attending an economic summit, when he learned that rioters had broken into the Capitol. Although he has never stated unequivocally that Trump lost the election, Kushner had concluded weeks before that any effort to overturn it was hopeless. He left it to Rudy Giuliani and others to pursue legal challenges. Still, after his plane landed, Kushner went to the White House to support Ivanka, who has since said she was trying to persuade her father to call on his supporters to disperse. While Kushner would personally condemn the attack as “wrong and unlawful,” he never uttered a critical word about Trump himself. “You’ll never, ever read a public thing where I distance myself from him,” Kushner says to me one morning in July. “I won’t do that. I’d rather suffer.”

We are at Bedminster, where he and Ivanka usually spend part of the summer with their three children in their house across the club’s pool from Trump’s own. By Kushner standards, it’s a relaxed time. His son Joseph has been learning to caddie for his grandfather on the golf course, which is festooned with banners for the Saudi-sponsored (and soon to go bust) LIV tour. Ivanka is out taking their youngest, Theodore, to a STEM camp. (Ivanka declined to be interviewed.)

“In the first term,” Kushner tells me, “80 percent of the people in the White House thought they were trying to save the world from Trump and 20 percent of us thought Trump was saving the world.” He and Ivanka decided that if Trump won a second term, they wouldn’t go back to work for him in the West Wing. After January 6, Kushner helped coordinate damage control. “I joke with him that we’re 2-0 on impeachments,” he says. But he was ready to get out of Washington. As he now tells the story, one morning soon after the election, he woke up and told Ivanka their next move had just dawned on him.
“Let’s go to Miami,” he said.

Jared and Ivanka had spent four years trying to live with one foot in Trumpworld and another in elite society. “That is like the narrowest tightrope in history,” a former White House staffer says. January 6 severed the line completely. In Miami, the weather was warm, crypto was booming, the restaurants were open in spite of COVID, and no one judged. They bought their house in Indian Creek in 2021 for $24 million and immediately tore it down to the studs, turning what was previously a gaudy South Florida villa into something more reflective of their taste.

When I visit on a weekday morning, the house is quiet and sunbathed. Through the glass double doors of the living room, I can see a backyard pool and a thatch-roofed sukkah the family has erected for the holiday season. Beyond that stands a large covered patio with a grill for alfresco dining and a gym with weight machines and a sauna. (“Set the cold plunge at 42 degrees, and just go for it,” Kushner says. “After that, the day’s easy.”) A boat is docked at the rear of the property. The boys fish, and Ivanka likes to paddleboard. It’s a good life, and their market timing was impeccable. Since they purchased on the island, they’ve acquired new neighbors, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.

“Now it’s become a place for immortals, but we were some of the last mortals to be able to buy there,” Kushner says. He has served as a member of the Indian Creek Village council, and the family recently was accepted into the island’s country club after a cooling period on the wait list. To some of their old friends in New York, it looked like they were retreating to a temporary place of exile, but Kushner doesn’t look at the island as an Elba. It’s become his family’s home. “A narrative people were writing is that we were running away from New York, but we didn’t view it like that,” Kushner says. “We viewed it like we were running toward the lives we wanted to live. We stopped giving a shit what other people say, and we just started living for ourselves.”

Soon after he settled in, Kushner founded Affinity Partners, which served as a landing spot for some of the aides who worked for him in the White House. He returned to the Gulf as a private citizen and pitched Affinity in the same places where he’d put together the Abraham Accords. A Saudi sovereign-wealth fund put in $2 billion after MBS overruled management objections about its nonexistent track record. The Emiratis and Qataris followed, bringing the fund’s initial capitalization to around $3 billion. Kushner contends that at that time, he had “no desire, plans, or prospects to return to diplomacy,” and Trump was out of office, so there was no way his investors could have thought they were buying his influence. Perhaps, to infinitely rich monarchs, a few billion is a small price to pay for past performance and future insurance. “I said this at the time,” Ben Rhodes told me, “that the payoff is on the back end in the Gulf.”

Affinity has deployed its billions in ways that reflect both Kushner’s priorities — promoting the economic conceit of the Abraham Accords by channeling the wealth of the Gulf into Israeli companies — and those of his benefactors. When MBS wanted to buy a video-game-maker, Kushner introduced him to a managing partner of Silver Lake, a huge technology-investment firm. Together with the Saudi sovereign-wealth fund, they all joined in a $55 billion deal to take Electronic Arts private, the largest leveraged buyout in history.

In 2024, when the Senate Finance Committee was last under Democratic control, it conducted an investigation that found Affinity had by that point collected $157 million in fees for managing its fund. (Kushner claims that the figure is inaccurate and that he charges an industry-standard amount that covers costs like personnel and overhead.) In the subsequent two years, the reported value of Affinity’s assets under management doubled to $6 billion — an increase Kushner attributes to the positive performance of its investments. He says he has not raised any funds since Trump’s reelection. But earlier this year, the New York Times reported that Affinity was exploring the possibility of starting a second fund with new capital from the Middle East. Kushner claims Affinity ceased to consider that “the instant the actions in Iran began.”

“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role,” Kushner says when I talk to him at his office. He claims that for the past year, he has hardly been involved in managing his fund at all, a decision he portrays as a costly diversion from his original plan. “I started a business when I left government. I focused on that business. I worked really, really hard. I did a good job with that business. Circumstances changed, where my father-in-law became president again. I intended to stay out but got pulled back in.”

For a while, Kushner says he acted only as a discreet sounding board to members of Trump’s second-term inner circle, including the (now deposed) chief of staff Susie Wiles and Rubio. Trump decided to give the portion of Kushner’s old portfolio that focused on the Middle East to Steve Witkoff, a developer (and strong Israel supporter) the president had met in the New York real-estate business. items.title: Inside the satanic, Y2K glamour of The Body
items.description: Everyone is talking about The Body. It’s currently the number one show on Netflix globally, no doubt due to its salacious premise: Catholic lesbian cheerleaders who make a deal with the devil. While it only came out a week ago, it’s already risen to the ranks
paragraphs: Everyone is talking about The Body. It’s currently the number one show on Netflix globally, no doubt due to its salacious premise: Catholic lesbian cheerleaders who make a deal with the devil. While it only came out a week ago, it’s already risen to the ranks of Heated Rivalry, Sterling Point and Off Campus – it might even be the best of the bunch.

Created by Quinn Shephard and Gina Gammell, the show strikes the perfect balance between sexy, funny and dark, while tugging at the heartstrings of queer women who once fell in love with their best friend. The cast became overnight stars – eight days ago, you wouldn’t have known who Lebanese-American actress Sara Boustany is, while today, she has 650k followers and countless fan edits swirling the internet.

Then there’s the fashion. Set in 2004, the costumes are a treasure trove of Y2K relics: rhinestoned everything, velour tracksuits, fur trim leather jackets, pedal pushers and blue eyeshadow. Luckily, costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier was the same age as the cheer squad (the Lions) in 2004, so her research started with her own memories. “What I find fascinating about that era is that it was really the start of eclectic boho dressing,” she says. “You’d mix florals with fur, baroque prints with stripes and denim – nothing had to match.”

Instead of working from a single mood board, Gordon-Crozier created individual ones for each character. For Anya (the dance captain, played by Kristina Bogic), she looked at early 00s runways, including Blumarine, Marc Jacobs and Chloe, as well as paparazzi photos of Sienna Miller and Mischa Barton. In the show, one of the girls describes Elise (Sara Boustany’s character) by saying “bitch is her aesthetic”, so her costumes needed to have a darker, avant-garde edge. This led Gordon-Crozier to look at Comme des Garçons, Balenciaga and Ann Demeulemeester runways, as well as celebrities such as Devon Aoki and Milla Jovovich.

For the other cast members, mood boards included Paris Hilton, Nicole Richie, Britney Spears, Chloë Sevigny, Hilary Duff, Missy Elliott, Eve and Jennifer Lopez. Playing rich teenagers with walk-in wardrobes the size of a London flat, these girls are, naturally, decked out in designer logos. For luxury, Gordon-Crozier turned to Dior, Alberta Ferretti, Fendi, Versace and Jean Paul Gaultier. Meanwhile, sourcing the right denim was a huge part of the outfits: “For denim and streetwear, my go-to brands were True Religion, 7 For All Mankind, Rock & Republic, Citizens of Humanity, Diesel, Miss Sixty and Von Dutch,” she says.

Almost everything you see the girls wearing is vintage – sourced from eBay, Depop and a range of Toronto’s “great vintage stores” – with the exception of the velour tracksuits, which all came from modern LA brand Miaou.

Above all, it’s the vintage handbags that have had the internet in a chokehold. Some of the most coveted bags of the early 00s can be spotted in the show: Louis Vuitton’s Speedy bag and multiple pieces from the Takashi Murakami LV collection, at least four versions of the Balenciaga City bag, the Fendi Spy bag and Dior’s Saddle bag, to name a few. “We had bins of designer bags, maybe 50 to 100!” says Gordon-Crozier. “We didn’t have a big budget, so most of them were restored. I’d hunt down a Balenciaga bag on Poshmark or wherever for around $500, and then our amazing ager/dyer, Tamara Rigby-Funke, would paint it red or pink and fix it up. A lot of the bags you see on screen started out as beat-up, secondhand finds. We begged, borrowed and stole. I brought in some of my own, and crew members lent us bags they’d actually carried back then. It was a real group effort.”

Her favourite of all the designer bags is Elise’s Dior khaki Street Chic Columbus bag, but the rarest find was a Dior by Galliano Cherry Blossom Saddle bag, carried by Anya. “It’s become a real collector’s piece, so finding one in good condition was hard enough – and finding one under $5,000 felt almost impossible. But it was Quinn’s dream bag, so we knew we had to make it happen.” Then there’s the one that got away: “I dreamed of having any of the Fendi Baguette beaded styles, but they were out of price range.”

Born and raised in London, Gordon-Crozier’s love of costume design started with her mother, who was a film professor and devout cinephile. “We grew up watching [Jean-Luc] Godard, [Federico] Fellini and all the greats,” she remembers. “Without realising it, I was getting an education in cinema history and in how much clothes can say about a character.” A stone’s throw from west London’s Portobello Market, she became obsessed with antiques and vintage fashion from an early age. “Looking back, those two things together – the films and the market – are really where costume design began for me.” As for her personal heroes, she cites legendary costume designer Sandy Powell as her ultimate icon: “Nobody mixes fashion and history the way she does. If I could have one hundredth of her talent, I’d take it.”

Now based in LA, she previously worked on projects including Margo’s Got Money Troubles and Where the Crawdads Sing, and saying yes to The Body was a no-brainer. “From the moment I read the script, it was unlike anything I’d seen: fashion-forward, set in 2004, and steeped in religious iconography. For a costume designer, that’s an irresistible combination of period, style and symbolism, and I knew I had to have the job.”

Of all the pieces she sourced for the show, it’s not the custom tracksuits or the impressive handbag collection that she’s proudest of: it’s the eyewear. “The Gucci and Dior glasses did so much character work for a show set in 2004,” she says. “And Elise’s zebra fur coat in the exorcism episode – that was a last-minute vintage find in Toronto. It ended up being one of my favourite pieces in the whole show.”

Her dream project would be to put her own spin on Marie Antoinette. “It has everything I love: period, romance and coming of age. She was a teenager thrown into the most extravagant court in history, and her clothes were her armour, her rebellion and also her downfall.” As for her next project, season two of The Body remains unconfirmed, but if popular demand has anything to do with it being renewed, we can expect to see much more of Gordon-Crozier’s work.
