items.title: If Morgan Maher Didn’t Shoot You, Are You Really an It-Girl?
items.description: If Morgan Maher Didn’t Shoot You, Are You Really an It-Girl?
items.author: Nicholson Baird
paragraphs: If Morgan Maher Didn’t Shoot You, Are You Really an It-Girl?

Morgan Maher’s new photo book, Everybody Loved Her, Everybody Wanted Her., has us wondering who exactly is the elusive “her,” and why does everybody want her so badly? On a perfectly crisp November night, we stopped by her launch at Climax Books to get some answers. For starters, she wears cotton underwear from Pretties Venice, drives a cherry-red pickup truck, and loves a Miller High Life. But there’s more to Maher’s girls than good taste and a little mystique. They’re funny, complicated, desirable, and, in many ways, extensions of the women who play them. While we had her, we also got Maher talking about how she builds trust on set, her love of Brian De Palma, and her dreams of making movies of her own.
WEDNESDAY 5:45 PM NOVEMBER 18, 2026 EAST VILLAGE
NICHOLSON BAIRD: Ben Barna actually says, “Hi Morgie.”
MORGAN MAHER: Of course he does.
BAIRD: Of course he fucking does. But this will just take five minutes.
MAHER: Perfect. Do you want to talk here or outside?
BAIRD: It would probably be quieter outside actually.
MAHER: It’s nice out here.
BAIRD: It’s a perfect night.
MAHER: Wow. It’s not even cold.
BAIRD: Can you get any better weather than November 18th?
MAHER: No, it’s amazing. It’s global warming.
BAIRD: All right. Everybody Loved Her, Everybody Wanted Her.
BAIRD: Let’s talk about Her, theoretically.
BAIRD: Where does she buy her underwear?
MAHER: Pretties Venice. 100% cotton. Deadstock, the OG.
BAIRD: What car does she drive?
MAHER: That’s such a good question. I feel like she drives a cherry red pickup truck.
BAIRD: Tea. What color are her nails?
MAHER: No nail polish. Just regular.

MAHER: Cherry red. The other day, I got a pedicure and I wasn’t paying attention, and I picked out a red color and on the thing it was this dark cherry red, and I looked down and I screamed. They were bright orange. I was like, “That is the color?!” And she was like, “Yeah.” I was like, “No way. We got to fix this right now, girl.” And then she did a darker red on top. But I’ve never turned bright red faster.
BAIRD: I’m fucking dead. Does she believe in horoscopes?
MAHER: No. I just got flamed for this.
MAHER: I believe in horoscopes, but I’m not checking my…I don’t know what it’s called?
MAHER: I don’t have Co-Star. I’m not reading a chart, but I know I’m a Cancer.
MAHER: Whenever I say I’m a Cancer, people are like, “Oh my god, you’re totally a Cancer.” I’m like, “I know.”
BAIRD: What do you order at the bar?
MAHER: Oo, I love a cucumber gimlet or I love beer. I love a Stella Artois or a Miller High Life, the champagne of beers.
MAHER: Bottle. It’s a prop. It’s a cute photo.
BAIRD: It’s unfortunately cool. So this is your second book. What has been the biggest change between this one and the last one?

MAHER: I feel like this one was a reaction to the first one. I really feel like the same girl, but I’m growing up and still trying to understand how to preserve those girlish tendencies that I have and I never want to lose. And this one was a much larger scale. We were on sound stages and there was a whole crew and I never actually took a single photo. Then later on in private, I was going through all of the footage and taking stills in the privacy of my home, which was very fun to be able to reflect on the entire shoot and do it in super duper private.
BAIRD: That makes sense. It feels like there’s a lot of push and pull between being a character and then being really vulnerable.

MAHER: Yeah. Well, I didn’t want to make any characters that the girls didn’t feel like were versions of themselves. I never wanted to mask who the girl was, I just wanted to bring a different vibe out of them.

BAIRD: Right, makes sense. I feel like every time we’ve been on set I’m like, “Ugh, this is such an awesome-sauce-some day.” So I’m wondering, what are the ingredients for a Morgan shoot day? How do you make it chill, but also get the thing that you’re trying to get? And I feel like you’re having fun while you’re doing it.

MAHER: I seriously love what I do so much. It makes me so happy to be able to create a world with these women that I admire, and I just want to bring the best versions of themselves out of themselves. I’m truly so thrilled every day to be on set. And I think I offer as much of myself. I will tell the most embarrassing story. I will be right there on the ground with you rolling around laughing. I’ll tell you about the bad date, I’ll tell you about the crush, I’ll tell you about what fucked up thing some dude did to me. I’m bearing it all, and I think that allows for a level of comfort between me and the talent. And I love playing rap music really loud. I love Future. I want to photograph Future super bad. Young Thug, I love. It sounds lame to say it’s all genuine.
BAIRD: I feel like Morgan, the girl, is very present in every photograph, you know what I mean? It’s just, like, you.

MAHER: Thank you. Also, I’m not the type of person to tell somebody to do something. It’s really much [more of] an exchange of energy on set where I’m reacting to the moment rather than going onto a set with a mood board and being like, “I want to recreate this image.”
MAHER: I obviously have lighting references, or set design, or styling conversations beforehand, but when it comes down to me and the talent, I really feel reactive to the moment.
BAIRD: Right. I was going to ask you about research. What were references? What was the research like? What movies were you watching? Music? What put you in this world?

MAHER: I was really obsessed with Gena Rowlands in Opening Night. All of those shots are just incredible and you just feel so transported. Star 80, I loved so much and watched a ton while making this. Body Double by Brian De Palma was so cool. That is a male perspective on infatuation and about desiring this woman. And whenever I work, I’m a woman that’s representing women, which is such an honor. So watching these movies where there are female protagonists, but they’re made by men, I’m like, “I’m going to do what these men were doing but doing it in a Morgan way.”
BAIRD: Damn, tea. Is the goal to start getting into film?
MAHER: Yes. Is it bad to talk about Woody Allen?

MAHER: My dream is to make a version of Celebrity by Woody Allen, but it’s all the girls. You know that movie where it’s like Uma Thurman, Winona Ryder, Leonardo DiCaprio, and it’s like they’re all just on set for maybe two days.

MAHER: But they’re all just rocking it out. And if that is inappropriate, then the goal is to 1000% make a movie. I have a lot of things written. It was so fun to play with these vignettes of these girls and to build these characters. The next thing is a narrative structure.
BAIRD: Do you believe in manifesting that?

MAHER: Yes. It’s insane. I swear, things that I say out loud happen. The other day, I was walking on the street and some dude was screaming crazy-style. I’m across the street diagonal two blocks away and I’m looking at this man losing his mind, and he passes a fruit stand and he’s freaking out. And I’m like, “I want him to pick up an orange and throw it.” And he literally stops, turns, picks up a cantaloupe and throws it onto the floor. I was like, “Okay, I have to start saying more things out loud.” I manifested in real time.BAIRD: First thing, cantaloupe on the ground. Second thing, movie.
MAHER: No, you’re the best. Thank you for coming. I’m so honored.
BAIRD: Of course, my friend.
MAHER: I’m literally so honored.

items.title: Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game
items.description: During Monday’s game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and New York Islanders, Broadway performer Sarrah Strimel Bentley flubbed the lyrics to Canada‘s national anthem multiple times before the puck drop.
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: During Monday’s game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and New York Islanders, Broadway performer Sarrah Strimel Bentley flubbed the lyrics to Canada‘s national anthem multiple times before the puck drop.

When singing “O Canada” for the thousands of fans during the Islanders’ Hockey Fights Cancer night, instead of belting out, “O Canada, we stand on guard for thee,” Bentley repeatedly sang, “O Canada, we lend our hearts to thee.”
The singer also missed the mark on another line, and instead of singing, “True patriot love in all of us command,” she sang, “True patriot love with all of us command.”
A clip from the performance showed Leafs captain Auston Matthews appearing confused as she sang the wrong lyrics. The anthem blunder drew swift criticism from hockey and Canadian fans online.

Later that night, Bentley took to social media to apologize in a video. “I sang both anthems, and I just wanted to apologize to all of my Canadians,” Bentley began. “Because I practiced the shit out of ‘O Canada,’ and getting up in front of 18,000 people, singing an anthem that you haven’t heard for your whole life is scary, and I botched the lyrics, and I’m really sorry. I got put in menopause because I had breast cancer, and tonight is about hockey fighting cancer, and menopause makes you forget things.”

Bentley continued, “So, I just wish that you’d be a little easier on someone who’s just a human being. And I’m sorry.” The singer highlighted the correct lyrics in her apology video: “Thank you for giving me grace. I love Canada. I stand on guard for thee.”

items.title: Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’
items.description: Billy Ray Cyrus shared photos from his daughter Miley Cyrus‘s Palm Springs wedding after she married Maxx Morando on Saturday. Members of the Cyrus clan — including mom Tish and sister Noah — were spotted gathering for the couple’s rehearsal dinner in Southern
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: Billy Ray Cyrus shared photos from his daughter Miley Cyrus‘s Palm Springs wedding after she married Maxx Morando on Saturday. Members of the Cyrus clan — including mom Tish and sister Noah — were spotted gathering for the couple’s rehearsal dinner in Southern California before the ceremony, and her father attended alongside girlfriend Elizabeth Hurley and her son Damian.

“My little girl married the love of her life! I can’t describe how beautiful it felt to have all my family together in one room, united by love,” wrote Billy in his tribute posted to social media alongside snapshots from the celebration including a black-and-white photo of him dancing with Miley.

“[Miley] words can’t begin to express how proud you make me every day… I’m the proudest dad alive!! [Maxx] I’m so honored to welcome you to the family!” he continued. Billy also wished his daughter a happy birthday on Monday, two days after the wedding, and called the couple “a match made in heaven,” adding, “I can’t wait to keep celebrating you both today and forever!” The musician also posted smiling photos taken alongside Hurley, Damian, Noah, his son Christopher, and a childhood picture of Miley winking at the camera while sporting a “Rockstar” shirt.

The Flaming Lips’ Wayne Coyne, Cyrus’ Dead Petz collaborator, reportedly officiated the ceremony. The couple got engaged in December 2025 after four years of dating. Morando is currently the drummer of the band Liily, a band that Cyrus featured in Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party in 2022.

items.title: Ms. Rachel Shows Support for Unrepresented Children Facing Deportation at Immigration Court
items.description: Ms. Rachel met with children appearing without an attorney at federal youth immigration court in Manhattan on Monday. The children’s educator and YouTuber highlighted the lack of legal representation for children facing deportation and their families as they s
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: Ms. Rachel met with children appearing without an attorney at federal youth immigration court in Manhattan on Monday. The children’s educator and YouTuber highlighted the lack of legal representation for children facing deportation and their families as they struggle to navigate the complex immigration system in the United States.

Ms. Rachel, a vocal critic of the Trump administration’s family detainment practices and harmful rhetoric against immigrant children, shared a video on social media of 9-year-old Angel, who appeared in court without an attorney amid immigration proceedings.

“Kids representing themselves in immigration court is so wrong. I saw Angel up at the mic without a lawyer and I couldn’t believe it. He’s 9 years old!” Ms. Rachel wrote in the caption. “Hearing kids hear the word ‘removable’ over and over about themselves… Heartbreaking. Stop the cruelty!”
When Ms. Rachel asked Angel to write a list of things he wanted for Christmas, at the top the nine-year-old asked for an immigration lawyer. “I am getting Angel a lawyer,” wrote the educator.
Ms. Rachel stopped by the court alongside Congressman-elect Brad Lander, according to ABC 7. The outlet said that a judge gave Angel’s mother until Dec. 15 to obtain legal representation.

“It’s heartbreaking. I care so much about every child and I just want to see every child thriving in school and my heart goes out to anyone going through this,” Ms. Rachel said, per the outlet. “I think about how that makes a child feel whether or not you are removable…I don’t want any child to hear that word associated with them.”

The YouTube personality called attention to policymakers and said they needed to better prioritize the needs of children. “I think our problems would really be a lot less if we all just focus on taking care of kids and centered kids in policies,” she said.

Ms. Rachel has also been outspoken about the violence, poverty, and disenfranchisement of children in Gaza amid the war with Israel. In September, the children’s entertainer pledged a $1 million donation to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund — matching Macklemore’s own $1 million pledge after he was forced off of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour for his statements in support of Palestinians in Gaza.

“When I see a mom who has a baby who is starving and they can’t get any milk, I see that and [think], ‘What if that was me and Susie?’” she told Rolling Stone in a recent interview.. “With Gaza, I couldn’t not speak out.”

items.title: Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band Bassist Chris Campbell Dead at 78
items.description: Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell, who joined forces with Seger in 1969 and remained a core member of the band through Seger’s farewell tour in 2019 — playing on timeless hits like “Turn the Page,” “Night Moves,” “Rock and Roll Never
items.author: Andy Greene; Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell, who joined forces with Seger in 1969 and remained a core member of the band through Seger’s farewell tour in 2019 — playing on timeless hits like “Turn the Page,” “Night Moves,” “Rock and Roll Never Forgets,” “Still the Same,” “Hollywood Nights,” and “Against the Wind” — died on Sunday. He was 78.
Campbell’s wife, Courtney, confirmed his death with Rolling Stone, adding that Campbell died of natural causes.

“I’m grieving the loss of my long-time friend and Silver Bullet bandmate, Chris Campbell…..RIP,” Silver Bullet Band vocalist Shaun Murphy wrote. “Prayers and condolences to his wonderful wife, Courtney Campbell, and his three beautiful daughters!! I am forever grateful for all the cherished memories I have.”

Campbell grew up in Plymouth, Michigan, and was a regular on the Detroit club scene that gave rise to the MC5, the Stooges, and the Amboy Dukes. “You were playing to smaller crowds and things were more intimate,” he told the Observer & Eccentric in 1987. “There weren’t any barriers in front of the stage with six-foot security guards.”

Just one year after the Bob Seger System scored a nationwide hit with “Ramblin’ Gamblin’ Man” in 1968, Campbell was offered a spot in the band. “I was hired in what I thought was a temporary job as bass player because Dan Honaker had just broken his wrist about a week before the Mongrel tour [in a motorcycle accident],” he told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I had a week to prepare. I had to learn this album frontwards and backwards.”

Honaker’s bad luck turned out to be the opportunity of a lifetime for Campbell because of what transpired not long after the Bob Seger System dissolved. “Bob called me…I think it was ’71, ’72,” Campbell told Rolling Stone. “He said, ‘I’m thinking of putting a band together.’ I said to him, ‘That’s kind of bizarre, I have a keyboard player and a drummer.’ He goes, ‘I got a guitarist, Drew Abbott.’ That was the start of the Silver Bullet Band.”

The early years of the Silver Bullet Band were a brutal grind, memorialized in the lyrics of 1972’s “Turn the Page,” but everything changed once the concert LP Live Bullet took off in 1976. The follow-up LP, Night Moves, turned Seger into one of the biggest names in rock.

Unlike similar groups like Bruce Springsteen’s E Street Band and Neil Young’s Crazy Horse, membership in the Silver Bullet Band was somewhat fluid, and studio musicians often backed Seger on albums. This arrangement didn’t suit Abbott, who quit the group in 1983 and never returned. But Campbell, background singers Shaun Murphy and Laura Creamer, and saxophonist Alto Reed were lifers. Grand Funk Railroad keyboardist Craig Frost also became a key component of the group for decades.

For Campbell, it wasn’t always an easy ride. “We have all [thought about leaving] at one time or another,” he told the Observer & Eccentric in 1987. “It would be an out-and-out lie to say we haven’t. You get tired, and it’s terrible on relationships.”

The job got easier after the tour for Seger’s 1995 LP It’s a Mystery wrapped, and the group went off the road for more than a decade. “Bob works at his own pace,” Campbell told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I can go out and do something else. It’s the way it’s always been since 1969. I wouldn’t know any other way. This is my life, and I’m very happy with it. I have wonderful kids and a good life, and we’re all friends. We’re all very fortunate. There’s no animosity and no fighting. Bob is our rock, our patriarch. We all look up to him. He’s so easy to work with. He’s a wonderful man, just as a human being.”

Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band launched a farewell tour in 2018 that wrapped up in 2019 at the Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia. They became just about the only act in rock history to say farewell and truly mean it.

Two years after the tour wrapped, Campbell filed a lawsuit against Seger and longtime manager Punch Andrews over alleged unpaid royalties from albums and tours. “Bob Seger and Punch Andrews have loyally supported our friend for 45-plus years,” they said in a statement. (Campbell ultimately lost his recording-royalty claims.)

Campbell kept a low public profile after the farewell tour. But in 2011, he told Rolling Stone why he enjoyed the latter-day tours so much. “We’re kind of old-school,” he said. “We aren’t glitzy. You don’t see any flash pots going off up there. We just do things the way we do. We aren’t really concerned about press agents and all that. We just play. And the older we get, the more fun we have. When you get older, you don’t take it as seriously as you once did when you were younger. If you can’t have fun at our age, don’t do it.”

items.title: Mary J. Blige’s ‘Real Love’ Did Not Infringe on ‘Impeach the President,’ Appeals Court Rules
items.description: A federal appeals court on Monday upheld a lower court ruling that Mary J. Blige’s 1992 hip-hop soul anthem “Real Love” did not infringe the copyright of the funk classic “Impeach the President.”
items.author: Nancy Dillon
paragraphs: A federal appeals court on Monday upheld a lower court ruling that Mary J. Blige’s 1992 hip-hop soul anthem “Real Love” did not infringe the copyright of the funk classic “Impeach the President.”

In a 10-page ruling from the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, the justices found that the 2024 lawsuit filed by Tuff City Records against Universal Music Publishing failed to state a viable claim. The ruling found that the two songs “are not substantially similar as a matter of law.”
“The works as a whole are distinct,” the ruling obtained by Rolling Stone reads. “The songs differ in their lyrics, melody, genre, subject matter, and overall sound.”

The Honey Drippers released “Impeach the President” in 1973, and it quickly became a Nixon-era protest anthem with a distinctive drum break that would become widely sampled by artists including Janet Jackson, J. Cole, and Doja Cat.

When Tuff City sued Universal over “Real Love” in 2024, it was the latest in a decades-long history of copyright litigation targeting some of the biggest names in hip-hop. The New York-based independent label brought claims over allegedly unauthorized samples of “Impeach the President” in songs by LL Cool J and EPMD in 1991 and later pursued litigation involving Run DMC, Kanye West, and the Beastie Boys.
In filing its appeal, Tuff City argued that the lower court used an incorrect legal standard to compare “Real Love” with “Impeach the President.” The appellate court disagreed.

“While ‘Impeach the President’ and ‘Real Love’ share certain percussive elements, other elements are notably different, such as open versus closed hi-hats and distinct snare and kick drum rhythms,” the ruling states. “The songs’ ‘total concept and overall feel’ reinforce the conclusion that the works at issue are not substantially similar.”

Agreeing with the district court, the ruling found that “Impeach the President” is a protest song that “fits squarely within the soul/funk genre,” whereas “Real Love” is a “hip-hop soul song about heartbreak, not politics.”

“‘Impeach the President’ is sung by a male group, incorporates a call-and-response technique, and features horns and guitars,” the opinion read, adding that by contrast, “Real Love” is sung by a woman and “is driven by piano and percussion.” The three-judge panel stated, “Considering both the alleged percussive overlap and the works as a whole, we conclude that the district court properly dismissed [the] claim of copyright infringement of the musical composition.”

Hillel I. Parness, a lawyer for Tuff City, said the company was “very disappointed” by Monday’s ruling and “will be seeking further judicial review.” He described “Impeach the President” as one of the “most widely- and consistently-sampled songs from the classic hip-hop era” and warned that the decision could have far-reaching implications for the genre.

“Allowing Universal publishing’s refusal to pay for its undisputed sampling to stand would upend decades of law, and decades of industry practice, all designed around ensuring that creators and owners are paid for the use of samples, even if the samples themselves are then reconfigured,” Parness said in a statement to Rolling Stone.
Lawyers for Universal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Steven Spielberg to Direct Western Movie Starring Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley; Paul Thomas Anderson to Write Script Based on ‘The Heart in Winter’
items.description: Steven Spielberg is set to adapt Kevin Barry’s Western novel “The Heart in Winter” for Focus Features, Variety has confirmed. Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance are set to star. Spielberg will direct with a script from “One Battle After Another” O
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Steven Spielberg is set to adapt Kevin Barry’s Western novel “The Heart in Winter” for Focus Features, Variety has confirmed. Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance are set to star. Spielberg will direct with a script from “One Battle After Another” Oscar winner Paul Thomas Anderson.

Barry’s 2024 novel follows Irish poet Tom Rourke, who falls in love with Polly Gillespie, the new bride of his town’s mine captain. Together, they take off for San Francisco with a pack of armed gunmen hot on their trail. Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson and Spielberg serve as producers. Executive producers include Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias and Ana Leocha. The film is eyeing a release in 2028.

“The Heart in Winter” reunites Spielberg with Universal after he released “Disclosure Day” with the studio in June. The sci-fi chase thriller opened to $44 million and went on to earn $447 million worldwide. The Western romance also reunites Spielberg and Buckley. The three-time Oscar winner produced 2025’s “Hamnet” at Focus, which earned Buckley an Academy Award for best actress.

Anderson is hot off his success with “One Battle After Another,” which took home six statuettes at the 2025 Oscars, including Anderson’s first best director win. “The Heart in Winter” is the first film Anderson will write without serving as director.

Buckley most recently starred alongside Christian Bale in Maggie Gyllenhaal’s “The Bride!” for Warner Bros. Coming up for Buckley is “Hold on to Your Angels” with Paul Mescal and “Three Incestuous Sisters” with Josh O’Connor, Dakota Johnson and Saoirse Ronan. “Oppenheimer” Oscar winner Murphy recently reprised his role as British street lord Thomas Shelby in Netflix’s “Peaky Blinders” movie “The Immortal Man.” On the horizon for Murphy is “A Quiet Place Part III” and the third and final chapter of the “28 Years Later” saga. Rylance, who starred in Spielberg’s 2015 drama “Bridge of Spies,” will soon appear in Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic “Artificial.” His directorial debut, “Nice Fish,” starring Michelle Williams, is currently in pre-production.

Buckley is repped by CAA, United Agents and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Murphy is repped by WME and Sloane Offer Weber & Dern. Rylance is represented by CAA and Peikoff Mahan Law Office. Anderson is repped by CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein.

items.title: ‘Focker-in-Law’ Review: Ariana Grande Sporadically Livens Up a Tired Comedy Retread
items.description: Midway through “Focker-in-Law,” perma-neurotic nurse Gaylord ‘Greg’ Focker (Ben Stiller) has a sudden, unhappy realization: He’s a few years older now than his hardass father-in-law Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro) was when they first met. It’s sobering for him, s
items.author: Guy Lodge
paragraphs: Midway through “Focker-in-Law,” perma-neurotic nurse Gaylord ‘Greg’ Focker (Ben Stiller) has a sudden, unhappy realization: He’s a few years older now than his hardass father-in-law Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro) was when they first met. It’s sobering for him, sure, but for us too. 26 years after “Meet the Parents,” 60-year-old Stiller does actually have a few years on 2000-era De Niro. More startling still is that they’ve both spent over a quarter of a century milking easy snickers from the name “Focker,” now over the course of four feature films. Time is long, but also short, and we feel both those truths in “Focker-in-Law,” a pretty haggard sequel in which, joke-wise, time also stands perfectly still: Now Greg is the cranky patriarch wary of his adult child’s future spouse, and a whole pile of rusty plot points have cycled back into view.

It goes almost without saying that nobody needs “Focker-in-Law,” a film that, 16 years after we last checked in on these characters in “Little Fockers,” arrives on screen with a dispiriting air of exhausted obligation — like a stilted family reunion arranged in the wake of some ruinous, unspoken rift. Stiller and De Niro have agreed to go through the motions and not a muscle strain more; Owen Wilson, Teri Polo and Blythe Danner have all committed to rather less than that; an absent Dustin Hoffman and Barbra Streisand send their apologies via a one-line alibi in the script. It’s practically by default, then, that new marquee name Ariana Grande is the film’s brightest presence by several hundred watts: Joining the series keen to further prove her screen comedy chops after “Wicked,” she’s the only star who looks remotely glad to be here.

Assuming the director’s chair after writing credits on all three previous entries, John Hamburg offers scant reward for her enthusiasm: Not given a lot of outright comic material to work with, she settles for propping up proceedings with generally peppy charisma. In this reworking of the “Meet the Parents” narrative, Grande assumes Stiller’s former place: As Olivia, the go-getter girlfriend of Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo), she’s the eager-to-please newcomer in the family. Where Greg was a hapless social disaster, however, she’s annoyingly collected and capable at every turn. A former FBI hostage negotiator turned executive leadership coach, she immediately impresses everyone in all the ways that Greg did not all those years ago — with ex-CIA man Jack, her potential future grandfather-in-law, particularly enraptured.

A gracious, attractive overachiever winning hearts with smarts and kindness isn’t exactly a prime setup for comedy of embarrassment, however, and so it’s Greg who must once again assume bumbling stooge duty — something Stiller can do in his sleep, and more or less does here. Animosity between Greg and Olivia is contrived early on, as various Fockers head east for Jack’s 80th birthday celebrations; an awkward misunderstanding on the flight over, before either character realizes the other’s identity, has Olivia thinking her boyfriend’s dad is at best an idiot, and at worst a meddling pervert. Even after they’re formally introduced, he proceeds to prove that best-case scenario several times over, across a strained parade of competitive scenarios: a vegan-versus-carnivore cookoff, a power-play in a party supplies store, a calamitous bicycle race for no reason at all.

These face-offs are suitably cringey, but they’re not terribly funny. Where “Meet the Parents” thrived on the farcical tension between De Niro and Stiller as, respectively, alpha and beta male, there’s considerably less mirth in Grande’s formidable superwoman repeatedly besting Stiller’s faintly tragic doofus — and not much chemistry between the two stars either. Hamburg’s script attempts to juice up the emotional stakes with a who-cares subplot about whether Henry will study medicine alongside his father in Chicago or in Olivia’s hometown of San Diego, but the character is such a formless dullard that he hardly seems worth tussling over.

As Henry, the reliably sympathetic Gisondo gets little to do; Beanie Feldstein, an afterthought as Henry’s ditzy twin sister Samantha, would be glad of that much. For a film so thin on ideas, “Focker-in-Law” feels over-populated with supporting characters — as Samantha’s zany boyfriend, Eduardo Franco occasionally makes laughs out of nothing at all, but more often just adds to the clutter — with the result that De Niro, who’s meant to be the driving star force of the series, too often fades grayly into the background. Despite Grande’s sparkiest efforts, it hardly feels coincidental that the one hilarious setpiece here plays out between the two male leads: a toe-curlingly misplaced serenade to John Legend’s treacly ballad “All of Me” that the film cuts oddly short.

Elsewhere, Hamburg merely settles for coasting on past jokes — not even replaying them much of the time, but merely pointing at their props and punchlines. There’s an urn, and a polygraph machine, and a taxidermied cat, all hoping to remind us of how we laughed then. Consider us reminded. But is it churlish to ask for more? Or, perhaps, less? Like a favorite dad joke told too many times, the “Fockers” franchise gets staler with each spin, while Olivia’s sequel-teasing mention of her own parents at the close prompts a kind of existential dread. Never mind how old Greg is, or how old Jack is, or indeed how old we are: The Fockers, it seems, will outlive us all.

items.title: Shawn Levy’s 21 Laps Inks Rich Overall Film Deal at Sony
items.description: Shawn Levy‘s 21 Laps Entertainment has signed a major overall film deal with Sony Pictures.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: Shawn Levy‘s 21 Laps Entertainment has signed a major overall film deal with Sony Pictures.

21 Laps lands at Sony after a competitive process with multiple studios bidding to get into business with the blockbuster filmmaker and his prolific production company. The rich new deal, focused on developing and producing feature films, extends across all of Sony Pictures’ labels and begins in fall 2027.

The pact also reunites Levy with Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group chairman and CEO Tom Rothman and Motion Picture Group president Sanford Panitch. The trio’s relationship goes back more than two decades, boasting some of Levy’s early successes as a director and producer, including the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen” and “Date Night.”

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Rothman said in a statement announcing the news.

“His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative company around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm,” Rothman continued. “I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”
Levy, whose 21 Laps will celebrate its 21st anniversary next year, was equally enthused.

“Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy said in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a big-hearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful.”

About the future of the company, Levy added: “21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”

News of the Sony Pictures deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps set an overall TV deal at Disney‘s 20th Television in September, following a long tenure at Netflix. The watermark for the company’s TV business is, of course, executive producing Netflix’s groundbreaking and Emmy-winning series “Stranger Things.” 21 Laps will executive produce the upcoming live-action prequel series “Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure.”

21 Laps films have grossed more than $5 billion at the worldwide box office. Recent successes include Marvel’s “Deadpool & Wolverine,” directed, produced and co-written by Levy, which grossed more than $1.3 billion worldwide, and A24’s “Backrooms,” which became the studio’s highest-grossing release worldwide. Next year, Levy will debut the much-anticipated “Star Wars: Starfighter.” The film, directed and produced by Levy and starring Ryan Gosling, will launch in theaters on May 28, 2027. Levy will then reteam with Gosling and Marvel for “Ghost Rider,” which is slated for a July 28, 2028 theatrical release.

The company’s slate of upcoming projects also includes Universal Pictures’ romantic comedy “The Catch,” starring Emma Stone and Chris Pine; Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons”; Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.
Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

items.title: ‘God of War’ Live-Action Series: Deborah Ann Woll to Reprise Faye Role From Video Games
items.description: Deborah Ann Woll is set to play Faye in the “God of War” live-action TV series at Amazon Prime Video, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Deborah Ann Woll is set to play Faye in the “God of War” live-action TV series at Amazon Prime Video, Variety has learned.
Woll previously played Faye in the video game “God of War Ragnarok” and will also lead the upcoming game “God of War Laufey,” which is due out in May 2027.

She is the latest addition to the expansive cast, which also includes: Dave Bautista as Kratos, Callum Vinson as Atreus, Mandy Patinkin as Odin, Ed Skrein as Baldur, Max Parker as Heimdall, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor, Teresa Palmer as Sif, Alastair Duncan as Mimir, Jeff Gulka as Sindri, Danny Woodburn as Brok, Sonya Walger as Freya, Island Austin as Thrud, Ben Chapple as Magni, Louis Cunningham as Modi, and Evelyn Miller as Gna.
Woll is the latest actor from the “God of War” games to land a role in the series playing the same character. As previously announced, Duncan will return in the role of Mimir.

The character Faye is described as “The mysterious late wife of Kratos and mother of Atreus, Faye’s abrupt passing sets in motion the events of ‘God of War.’ Along their journey, Kratos and Atreus discover secrets about Faye that make them wonder how well they truly knew her at all.”

This is Woll’s latest return to an iconic franchise role in recent years. She also reprised the role of Karen Page in “Daredevil: Born Again” and “The Punisher: One Last Kill” at Disney+ after having played the character across multiple Marvel-Netflix shows between 2015 and 2019. Woll is also known for her work in the hit HBO series “True Blood” and will appear in Season 2 of “The Testaments” at Hulu. In film, she has worked in features like “Queen of the Ring” and “The Cycle.”
She is repped by Luber Roklin Entertainment and Goodman Genow.

Prime Video has given the “God of War” show a two-season order, with the two seasons set to shoot back-to-back. Filming originally began in Vancouver back in February, but after original series lead Ryan Hurst was injured on set over the summer, production was shutdown until Bautista was brought in and shooting resumed in late October.

The series will pick up with the story of the two most recent “God of War” games, in which Kratos must raise his ten-year old son Atreus while battling gods of the Norse pantheon. Per the logline, “Father and son Kratos and Atreus embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.”
Ronald D. Moore is the writer, executive producer, and showrunner on “God of War” under his Tall Ship Productions banner.

Frederick E.O. Toye will direct the first two episodes of “God of War.” Maril Davis of Tall Ship also executive produces alongside Cory Barlog, Naren Shankar, Matthew Graham, Asad Qizilbash, Jeff Ketcham, Hermen Hulst, Roy Lee, Brad Van Arragon, and Lawrence Trilling. Joe Menosky, Marc Bernardin, Tania Lotia, and Ben McGinnis serve as co-executive producers on the series. The series is co-produced by Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios in association with PlayStation Productions and Tall Ship Productions.

items.title: For Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, ‘Cliff Booth’ Closes Out a Massive Year in Wild Style
items.description: It’s the kind of year an actor dreams of — prestige award nominations preceded by big-screen action showcases, juicy leading roles followed by scene-stealing supporting parts. And for Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, it’s not even over — the New Orleans native’s fourth
items.author: David Canfield
paragraphs: It’s the kind of year an actor dreams of — prestige award nominations preceded by big-screen action showcases, juicy leading roles followed by scene-stealing supporting parts. And for Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, it’s not even over — the New Orleans native’s fourth screen credit of the year, David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, is out in IMAX theaters on Wednesday.

“This is a fantastic year,” as Abdul-Mateen puts it in the first of two chats we’ve had over the last few months. “None of those characters are in conversation with one another. They’re from completely different worlds.”

To put it mildly, we knew Abdul-Mateen was good for it. Breaking out by anchoring the box-office hit Candyman and winning an Emmy for his soulful turn in HBO’s Watchmen, his range and ability to swerve between different scopes of characters has been evident for years. His 2026 started with the MCU entry Wonder Man, which was canceled after a single season despite strong reviews and viewership — and which earned the actor his first lead-acting Emmy nod, for a turn that showed off his comedic chops. He then led the latest Man on Fire adaptation for Netflix, which topped the streamer’s viewership charts out of its debut, and Paramount’s original theatrical play By Any Means, Elegance Bratton’s incendiary historical thriller set in the Deep South.

Yet Abdul-Mateen is well aware that a different kind of spotlight will come his way for Cliff Booth, the highly anticipated stand-alone sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Written again by Quentin Tarantino, and this time directed by David Fincher, the film flash-forwards to 1977 Hollywood, imagining the continued day-to-day life of our titular stuntman-turned-fixer, with Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role.

The movie opens, though, on Abdul-Mateen’s Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison — acting within a fictional movie that pays homage to the Blaxploitation boom of the era. A former professional football player turned movie star — you can guess some of the inspiration points — Hot Rod allows Abdul-Mateen to get big and loud on camera, and delve fully into the tone and look of the period. You can see he’s having a ball.
Below are edited excerpts of our two conversations, as he reflects on bringing his massive year to a ‘70s-inflected close.
You make a meal of your handful of scenes in Cliff Booth. How did the script read to you?

I’ve never done this before, but on this one, because of the responsibilities of the character and how he fit into the story, I had the opportunity to not read the entire script. I only chose to read my parts of it so, as a fan of both Quentin and Fincher, I could just be a part of the movie while also being a fan. Then the words take care of everything. I had such great words to say and they felt really, really natural. Once I started talking and put on the costume, then the character was automatically embedded inside of all of that information.

I love the Blaxploitation-era characters and a lot of those films, and this was a chance to lean into that and to have some fun with that. I had done some work in my first job, The Get Down, pulling from the ‘70s and things like that, but it wasn’t specifically in the Blaxploitation era, so this was cool because I got to heighten the theater and the dramatics.
Hot Rod’s look in the fictional films tells you so much about who this guy was at that time, in pop culture. How did you work on that with David and the team?

Jim Brown was one of the pieces of inspiration. The confidence in the Afro, the cigars, the shoulders. I knew that this guy was a football player, so I wanted him to be confident. One of the details about him is that he never takes off his Super Bowl rings — no matter what character he plays, he always keeps them on. I knew that he was proud and maybe a little bit cocky and arrogant; I wanted to put all that in there and keep him likable. We had a fantastic costume designer [Trish Summerville] and everything gave us all the ingredients that we needed in order to step into this playground and have a really good time.
Quentin has also talked about Ron van Clief, the martial arts star, as an inspiration for the character. Did you look into him at all?

Yes. I watched a couple clips and I saw what Quentin was going for. I actually wanted to make my character more larger-than-life. So I read on Quentin’s inspiration, and then I took my own creative license and did my own thing with it. So sometimes you can follow the inspiration verbatim or you just take what you need. Ron van Clief was somebody that audiences who knew him and loved him could root for. They wanted him to do well. He had a lot of goodwill behind his name and behind the work that he was doing in the spirit that he brought to the work. I wanted Hot Rod to do the same thing, to have that same quality — that sense of likability, that he was aspirational in a way, a bit of an underdog, but also someone who was still striving in the industry. But I still wanted him to feel like a superstar in his own right.
Where did the impetus come from, to go as big with him as you do?

Well, it’s the freedom to play. I’m in a film within a film, and so I had the license to heighten up the acting. I had the license to use different voices and different parts of my instrument that I hadn’t used in a bit and play against the grain of what everybody else was playing with, tonally, within the movie. David created a world where he could really fit that all in and where I could be disruptive. I existed within a completely different genre, the Blaxploitation films and the Black filmmaking style of the ‘70s, which also came with a specific acting style as well. There haven’t been a lot of opportunities to lean into that style recently.
So how does David Fincher direct you, then, in a fictional Blaxploitation film?

We actually toned it down a bit. He shot it in a certain style and he actually wanted us to tone down the style of acting — the dramatic style of some of those films — in order to really let the audience lean in on the stakes and hear the words. We had a very short amount of time to get the audience to buy in and to care about what these characters were talking about even in these short films-within-a-film. The first opens up [Cliff Booth] and you have this young guy just getting into the game; he’s wide-eyed and bushy-tailed, bright-eyed, and he thinks that it’s going to be all fun and games. He gets that hard reality check that hardens and we see how that leads to his demise. Then we have the other, more flamboyant scene with myself and Scott Caan later on. The stakes are high, David actually asked us to make it where one would maybe even get curious about what that movie within a movie would look like if we were to see the full version.

You then have a few brief scenes where Hot Rod is himself, not acting on camera. How did you approach him there? You’re drawing a little bit of a contrast, obviously, between the public and private personas.

When we go backstage in between takes and he meets Cliff Booth, that’s when we see, “Oh, this guy’s a star.” He’s speaking with his glasses on, he’s talking with a cigarette, he’s wearing his robe. That was one of the things that I added to the character. I said, “So when he’s not active, we need to see him with a robe because he’s used to being a star. He’s a wide receiver; wide receivers are the divas of the football team.” He wears his rings and he wears his Super Bowl championship rings in every movie that he does. He doesn’t care what anybody says, and he’s going to be comfortable above all. I didn’t have to overact or to push or anything; all these features allowed him to be a little bit more quiet, more subdued, less colorful, more of an introspective type of cat.
What is something about working with David Fincher that people might not know?

People know a lot of things about Finch. (Laughs.) I think it’s how much his set is built for family, that’s something that I didn’t know. He works with a team of collaborators that he’s worked with in the past before, and he really, really embraced me on set. And even before the process, he was extremely open and available for conversations about the work and about the characters and making sure that everybody has the best of what they need to succeed. People talk a lot about how many takes he does and things like that. I think that’s probably the least interesting thing about the processes, and it’s so refreshing to work with someone who is over the moon, excited, and thrilled about their work, especially after having been in it for so, so, so long. That excitement is contagious and it helps, especially on long days. And yes, on doing a lot of takes and being meticulous and things like that, it’s important to have someone at the top that is really pouring all the energy into the actors and back into all of the creators.
How did the movie challenge you?

I’ll be honest, more so than a challenge. It was really freeing. I always felt that I was in good hands because David would come in and he would say, “Okay, I need you to hold your chin up a bit.” He would come in and say, “Hey, your head is at this angle; I need it to be at this angle. That’s going to help you look really, really good.” It’s a lot like when Baz Luhrmann was working with me on my very first job [The Get Down]. It’s nice to have someone who knows how to do every job on the set and who cares about the performance and who cares about you looking good as well. It was 100 percent play, and it’s nothing like anything that I’ve done for a very, very, very long time.
It sounds like you got to unleash a little bit.

It was just a different type of fun. I think it’ll be one of those moments where people get to say, “Oh yeah. Oh, wow. Oh yeah, that’s right.” It sets up people to want to see a little bit more of what I can do — and what I want to do.
It’s interesting to hear the word freeing for working with someone like Fincher, because I’ve interviewed a lot of actors who worked with him over the years — and the takes are no joke.

Honestly, that was the least interesting thing about the experience. What was most interesting was having conversations and getting into his brain and to see how enthusiastic he is about the work. It’s sort of a best-idea-wins type of environment. He tends to have the best ideas, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t put forward your own.
You’ve been very busy — in addition to your TV shows, Cliff Booth is your second movie of the year. What made you want to do the first, By Any Means?

I’d just finished Man on Fire and I was really looking forward to going home and buying a home and maybe even disappear for a little bit. And I got an email and a phone call from my people saying, “Hey, we’ve got this thing that we’re looking at — let us know if you’d be interested.” I saw that Elegance was attached to it. I watched his first film called The Inspection. I saw that Mark [Wahlberg] was on the movie, that they were trying to go pretty fast. I spent some time poring over the script and seeing if it would really be worth really giving up my time for, because I had just finished an eight month shoot out of the country. I really liked having my own personal time; that’s important to me.

When I started turning those pages and reading through, though, I saw there was something in this story. There’s this thesis in the film where we’re discussing: When the law isn’t enough, what happens to justice? I really enjoyed the question that the film was asking. And it gave me the opportunity to be a leading man — to be a husband, a man of high moral character and ambition who is tested.

There are so many scenes in By Any Means where your character is navigating both microaggressions and, frankly, macroaggressions. What was it like to work through that and play those scenes, especially knowing the period and that it was based on a true story?

It takes a great deal of trust — trusting myself, trusting the choices that I’m making, trusting the restraint that I’m using, trusting that I’m being shot well and that the whole vision is going to come together from the director’s point of view, because I’m the one that has to sit in that hot seat and take some of those micro and macro aggressions and see how it plays. My job as Wayne was to set a moral standard and to hold the line for as long as possible. So when playing a character like that, I know that I’m going to be tested, like Wayne was going to be tested.

You’re often the straight man opposite Mark, who has played many larger than life characters over his career. You get to do that in Cliff Booth, of course, but do you have a general comfort level there, in terms of going bigger, playing more comically?

I love doing comedy. I had just done Wonder Man, where I had a great time leaning into the more comedic things and carrying that out. With [By Any Means] we were dealing with heavy subject matter, so we also wanted it to be light and fun. We talked about that: there was an opportunity for this movie to be fun and it needed that. It is possible for people from different walks of life to not necessarily get along, but to understand each other. They are human at the end of the day.
Coming off of these projects, what would you say you are looking for now, at this point in your career?

Yeah, man. I really enjoyed being a husband in this movie. Having a wife and having something to protect, having an identity and having values to protect. I like that character. I want to do a little bit more of that. The guy who is reserved, charismatic, serious, but dangerous and charming.

I’m really blessed to be able to work in television and in film and to work in many different genres. Wonder Man was a showcase for comedy. Man on Fire was a showcase for the dramatics. As an actor, I’m looking for really great stories, and this was an opportunity to lead a film. I want to be able to do a little bit more of that in the film space. I’m excited to see what comes next. I’m always paying attention. I’ve been around for 10 or 11 years now, and I feel like I’m still just getting started. I’m always adding a little bit of something to the bag to try to get better and keep it fresh.
You were Emmy-nominated for Wonder Man this year, shortly before its cancellation. Was that recognition a bittersweet moment?

No bitterness attached to it at all. I’ve already won. I got to play Simon Williams. I had my turn to do that. People love the show, and because of the nomination, we were still talking about Simon. The story is alive, and Simon Williams is. I think we did something really special with that iteration of Wonder Man.
Could you imagine ever taking on the role again in another incarnation?
Yeah, absolutely. And if the phone rings, then I’m looking forward to it. I’m absolutely looking forward to it. We’ll see what happens.

items.title: 2026 International Emmy Winners Revealed: ‘Carême’ Wins Best Drama
items.description: The International Emmy Awards, the global version of the U.S. TV honors, were handed out in New York Monday night.
items.author: Scott Roxborough; Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: The International Emmy Awards, the global version of the U.S. TV honors, were handed out in New York Monday night.

The top prize of best drama went to French foodie-themed period series Carême from Apple TV. The series beat out Steven Knight’s Hulu boxing drama A Thousand Blows; Prime Video’s Argentine political drama Menem; and underdog sports drama Real Kashmir Football Club from Indian pay-TV group Sony LIV.
Best drama was one of the few categories where Netflix was not represented.

Netflix went into the 54th International Emmys the clear frontrunner with nine nominations, including all four best comedy noms — for the Rowan Atkinson slapstick series Man vs. Baby; the Spanish sitcom Old Dog, New Tricks; Argentine satire División Palermo; and Vir Das: Fool Volume, the latest comedy special from the Indian stand-up star. División Palermo won the award.
Still that prize was the only one that went to a program from the streamer.

Best actor went to Bobby Schofield for BBC drama Unforgivable, beating out nominees Javier Cámara, up for his lead performance Spanish dark comedy Jakarta for Moviestar Plus+; Ricardo Darín for Netflix’s Argentine sci-fi survival thriller The Eternaut; and Ian Roberts for Prime Video’s South African road movie A Kind of Madness.

Best actress, despite Netflix boasting two of this year’s nominees, went to Belgian actress Mona Mina Leon, nominated for Flemish dramedy Holy Sh!t. Leon beat out Bárbara Mori from Lucca’s World, Park Ji-Hyun from You and Everything Else and Sheridan Smith for the Brit true-crime drama I Fought the Law from ITV.
In total, there were 64 nominees across 16 categories spanning 22 countries. Shrinking star Michael Urie hosted this year’s ceremony at the New York Hilton in Manhattan.

In addition to the competitive awards, former Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria received the Founders Award and former Warner Bros. Discovery international president Gerhard Zeiler received the Directorate Award, presented by former WBD CEO David Zaslav.

items.title: New ‘Hunger Games’ Movie on the Way? Lionsgate Film Chief Shares Latest on Franchise’s Future
items.description: The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title.

Lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping over the weekend, with the movie grossing a commanding $119.3 million from 4,018 North American locations to open in first place at the box office. The feature adaptation of author Suzanne Collins‘ 2025 prequel novel notched a better opening frame than the two most recent entries in the six-film series that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games.

During a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter to celebrate the success of Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate Motion Picture Group chair Adam Fogelson emphasizes that the studio would love to collaborate again with Collins on another project in the franchise. Director Francis Lawrence‘s latest movie stars Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, portrayed in the first four films by Woody Harrelson. The $150 million-budgeted feature is set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book.

“We have complete respect for Suzanne as the architect,” Fogelson says. “I have told her that, if and when she is ready for me to read something else, I will drop everything and go anywhere in the world to get to read it. And I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call.”

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had a far bigger impact at the box office than the 2023 prequel film The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which starred Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer. Centering on the backstory for villainous President Snow — portrayed in the new movie by Ralph Fiennes — Songbirds and Snakes opened to $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million.

“All of us understood that the story that Suzanne wanted to tell on Songbirds was a challenging one and that she was inspired to tell it,” Fogelson explains. “She did it in an extraordinary way. Clearly, the movie worked really well for the audience that saw it, but the origin story of the villain — with no grand Hunger Games spectacle at the center of the story — is a challenging ask.”

He continues, “But we are in very regular, very authentic dialogue with this giant fan base, and we had plenty of indications that a story like this one could relight the fire in an exceptional way. It’s why we chose to invest the way that we did, both in the production plan and in the casting. And so, we were confident that there were plenty of signals that, if you gave the audience a story like this one, they were ready to return in big numbers.”

As far as what a potential sequel movie could entail, Fogelson notes that the franchise’s supporters have offered suggestions about potentially fertile storytelling opportunities within the dystopian world. The Sunrise on the Reaping book sold 1.5 million copies in its first week, making it the biggest launch among Collins’ titles in the series.

“The fan base have definitely let us all know that there are other stories they would be thrilled to both read and watch,” says Fogelson. “We’ll see if any of them spark Suzanne to go ahead and write them.”

The exec pointed out that each major character reveal during the film’s New York premiere was met with feverish cheers from the audience. The new movie’s expansive cast includes Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke and Whitney Peak.

“It starts with the fact that Suzanne decided to tell a story that the audience had clearly been desperate for — anchored by a character that the audience both loved and was fascinated to learn more about — and then the filmmaking team and the production group at the studio partnered to cast and make an exceptional version of that story,” Fogelson says. “This is one of the most exceptionally put-together casts I’ve ever been a part of.”

items.title: Antoine Fuqua Accused of Pointing Handgun, Using Antisemitic Slur in Assault Lawsuit
items.description: Director Antoine Fuqua has been sued for assault and battery by a bar manager, who alleges the director struck him with a handgun and used an antisemitic slur.
items.author: Winston Cho
paragraphs: Director Antoine Fuqua has been sued for assault and battery by a bar manager, who alleges the director struck him with a handgun and used an antisemitic slur.

In a lawsuit filed on Friday in California state court, the bar manager, William Rosenthal, details an altercation in February in which Fuqua and his group were denied entry to a Los Angeles bar because they were overly intoxicated. He claims the director “directed a racial and antisemitic slur” at him before the filmmaker and his son “pointed their handguns” in his direction.
Rosenthal brings claims for assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress. He seeks at least $50,000.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the director denied the allegations. “It’s not true,” the representative said.

The lawsuit says Fuqua and four others, including his daughter and son, visited Good Times at Davey Wayne’s in Los Angeles on Feb. 14. After the group was refused entry by Rosenthal, he was spat on by a member of the group and threatened by Fuqua’s daughter, according to the complaint. They left the establishment, the lawsuit says.

Roughly an hour later, Fuqua returned and confronted Rosenthal about pepper spraying his daughter. Rosenthal denied the accusation and was hit in the face with a handgun by the director, who later used an antisemitic slur and threatened to kill the bar manager. From there, the altercation escalated, with Fuqua’s son also pulling out a handgun and striking Rosenthal, the lawsuit says.

Rosenthal says he sustained a head injury, nose fracture and lacerations from the alleged assault and now has post-traumatic stress disorder and severe emotional stress. His lawyers say the injuries will result in “some permanent disability.”

items.title: The Las Vegas Grand Prix Kicks Off With a Disco Bash by SkinCeuticals
items.description: Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 e
items.author: The Editors; GQ
paragraphs: Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

With the space aglow in Ferrari Rosso Scuderia red under a shiny mirrored disco ball and a checkered-flag DJ booth, guests snacked on wagyu bites and gourmet caviar-topped chicken nuggets and sipped on-theme cocktails. (Also served: SkinCeuticals’s top-shelf favorites, including the P-TIOX and C E Ferulic serums, passed around on silver trays.) The model Kelly Piquet, partner of F1 star Max Verstappen, posted up on the green velvet banquette, as other attendees played around with SkinCeuticals-branded poker chips and cards around the room.

On the venue’s outdoor terrace overlooking the glowing marvel that is Sphere, actor Chace Crawford and his dad, dermatologist Chris Wayne Crawford, took a moment to enjoy the view. The two were doing a little father-son bonding—a perfect setting since F1 is “a male, testosterone-fueled sport,” joked Chris. As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” said the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

Inside, sportscaster and former Seattle Seahawk superstar Russell Wilson, a big F1 fan, couldn’t wait for lights-out-and-away-we-go on Sunday. He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he said, “so I’m fired up about it.”

At 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. When the musician Sooin, of the K-pop group Meovv, hopped into the booth to chop it up with the Chainsmokers, the room lit up.

The nostalgia was at a full tilt as the duo played MGMT’s millennial-optimism anthem “Kids” while guests were offered trays of warm chocolate chip cookies. When the Chainsmokers teed up “Roses,” their first top 10 hit, Taggart cued the crowd by saying, “I need all the 2015 energy you still have left inside you.” Then they brought the whole house down with their 2016 Halsey duet “Closer.” At this point, the Chainsmokers were flying, indulging the crowd with an anthemic dance version of Miley Cyrus’s “The Climb” and a dubstep mix of “Spectrum” by Florence + The Machine.

They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.
“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”

items.title: This Isn’t the First Time Bond Has Had to Choose Between Omega and JLC
items.description: Just a few months ago, Robert Pattinson signed on with Jaeger-LeCoultre as a brand ambassador, appearing in La Grande Maison’s ads wearing the new Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar. However, that role has become complicated since the actor was anno
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Just a few months ago, Robert Pattinson signed on with Jaeger-LeCoultre as a brand ambassador, appearing in La Grande Maison’s ads wearing the new Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar. However, that role has become complicated since the actor was announced as James Bond last week, given that the iconic character has been an Omega man for going on 31 years. This feels like uncharted waters, but it turns out this isn’t the first time two watch brands have competed for 007’s affections.

How this will play out is anyone’s guess, but there are clues we can find in the past. Bizarrely enough, this exact horological love triangle has played out before, when Pierce Brosnan was MI6’s top agent. The Irish actor taking up the mantle of 007 coincided with Omega coming on as Bond’s official watch supplier. In 1995’s GoldenEye, Brosnan wears the Seamaster Diver 300M with a blue-wave dial. The watch has become synonymous with Bond.

However, just a few years into life as a superspy, Brosnan produced a remake of the classic menswear flick The Thomas Crown Affair. Due to his Bondbligations, dressing became extremely complicated. In the 1999 movie, Brosnan is forced to wear an open shirt and an untied white bow tie draped around his neck during a black-tie ball because his Bond contract reportedly forbade him from wearing a tuxedo in other movies. And because of the actor’s contract with Omega, Thomas Crown’s watch had to be handled just as delicately.

Nick Gould, watch spotter extraordinaire, pointed out to us that Pierce Brosnan, still in the midst of his run as 007, strapped on a JLC Reverso for The Thomas Crown Affair remake. The reversible watch was a perfect symbol of the titular character’s double life. But because Brosnan was still entwined with Bond, the watch’s dial was scrubbed to remove both the brand and model name. The coincidence that a Bond would have to select between a JLC and an Omega is even stranger because, unlike Pattinson, Brosnan had no ties to JLC. And there wasn’t some unbreakable tie between Thomas Crown and the brand either. In the original version of The Thomas Crown Affair, Steve McQueen wears a Patek Philippe pocket watch, a Cartier Tank Cintrée, and a Jaeger-LeCoultre Memovox.

Now, Pattinson and Brosnan’s situations aren’t perfectly analogous. The latter’s affair involved a one-off movie placement that conflicted with Bond’s requirement to wear Omega. Pattinson’s predicament involves a freshly inked brand ambassadorship butting up against 007’s long-held partnership. However, it is strange to see the exact pair of brands tied up in Bond-related drama.

This time around, neither brand appears to be backing down. In the wake of Pattinson’s announcement, JLC said in a statement: “Jaeger-LeCoultre warmly congratulates Robert Pattinson on his appointment to the iconic role of James Bond, a tremendous milestone in an already distinguished cinematic career.” And a representative confirmed, “Robert Pattinson continues in his role as a Global Ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre under our existing agreement.” Meanwhile, Omega has posted its Bond watches several times on Instagram. Pattinson, of course, is caught in the middle. As watch lovers first and foremost, we personally love the idea of him continuing to wear JLC on his own time and a Seamaster 300M on Bond time. After all, if anyone can lead a double life while keeping two competing loyalties straight, surely it’s 007.

items.title: The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
items.description: This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
items.author: Thomas Macaulay
paragraphs: This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.
Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.
The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.

But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem
Anthropic’s Claude was used to prove the Riemann hypothesis. (WSJ $)
+ Two groups have independently verified the proof. (Guardian)
+ It could be the biggest math breakthrough in decades. (New Scientist $)
+ AI may be changing who gets to do math. (MIT Technology Review)
2 The COP31 climate talks have collapsed after a fossil fuels row
The EU rejected a deal it called “greenwashing.” (NBC News)
+ Saudi Arabia, Russia, and India opposed mentioning fossil fuels. (BBC)
+ Calls are growing for “net negative” instead of just net zero. (Nature)
+ Last year’s talks avoided fossil fuels. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The woman at the center of Nvidia's scandal has ties to China's military
Firms in her family's network work with Chinese defense contractors. (NYT $)
+ Her associate allegedly ran the chip smuggling behind the scenes. (WSJ $)
+ US intelligence says she was in touch with a Chinese spy official. (ABC)
+ Republicans are pushing a new AI strategy to counter Beijing. (Reuters $)
4 Hackers have breached the FBI’s criminal information database
It contains information used by law enforcement at all levels. (AP)
+ Hackers also breached an Agriculture Department system. (NBC News)
+ And the Austrian foreign ministry’s website. (Reuters $)
5 Russia, the US, and Israel have stalled global rules on “killer robots”
The UK, Japan, South Korea, and Turkey also resisted binding rules. (Politico)
+ Around 100 nations backed regulations, but arms producers balked. (CNBC)
+ Talks will continue through 2028. (AP)
6 Trump says he’ll ban US companies from building data centers abroad
He threatened them with a “tremendous tax.” (CNBC)
+ Electricity is fuelling the data center backlash. (MIT Technology Review)
7 US lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars
They plan to prohibit sales of Chinese vehicles in the US. (Quartz)
8 Trump’s visa crackdown has pushed tech workers to leave the US
It’s driving engineers and researchers overseas. (Bloomberg $)
9 GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could free up farmland larger than Italy
Their use could transform the global food system. (Conversation)
+ They may also slow biological aging. (MIT Technology Review)
10 BepiColombo has become the second spacecraft to orbit Mercury
Its probes will study the planet’s surface and surroundings. (Nature)
+ Mercury’s ancient ice could hold clues to the origins of life. (New Yorker $)
“It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.”
—John Kennedy, US senator from Louisiana, tells NBC’s Meet the Press that Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could prove costly for efforts to prevent China from obtaining AI chips.
On the ground in Ukraine’s largest Starlink repair shop

Starlink is critical to Ukraine’s fight against Russia, but Donald Trump’s fickle foreign policy and reports of Elon Musk restricting Ukraine’s access to the service have cast the technology’s future in the country into doubt.

For now, Starlink access largely comes down to the unofficial community of users and engineers, including the expert “Dr. Starlink”—famous for his creative ways of customizing the systems—who have kept Ukraine in the fight, both on and off the front line.
He gave MIT Technology Review exclusive access to his unofficial Starlink repair workshop in the city of Lviv. Here’s what we learned.
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ This otherworldly image of a porcelain crab has won the Oceania Photo Contest.
+ Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but also for your health.
+ 95-year-old William Shatner is now performing Metallica covers with his band, the *uckers.
+ Join a wingsuit champion on an exhilarating flight down a mountain road at more than 200km/h.
