items.title: A screenshot is precious when my family in Iran is out of reach
items.description: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the wor
items.author: Elaheh Shabani Afarani
paragraphs: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the world you left behind hasn’t simply vanished.
Everything on my feed felt irrelevant – until, suddenly, it wasn’t.

I came across a cooking video my mother had liked before we lost the connection. Seeing her name beneath the post struck me, as if someone had brought news. My eyes filled. I read the recipe for pasta with white sauce in the caption. She must have saved it for one of those evenings when she didn’t know what to cook. I took a screenshot, as if I might need to return to it – something I didn’t want to lose: yadgari, a keepsake, a trace of her touch pressed into a screen.

After 10 years of living in India, my connection to home in Iran had settled into a rhythm. Each morning, I checked our family groups on the messaging app Telegram to see what had unfolded while I slept. During the day, a message from my mother, a brief pause in the flow of things, felt like a small gift.

At night, I scrolled through Persian Instagram – jokes, cooking videos, fragments of humour that make sense only in our language. I would laugh until I cried, then fall asleep with a quiet reassurance: somewhere, my world was still alive.

We had an almost-fixed time for a video call, the holy hour of 6 pm. My parents would already be there, waiting. Behind them, the red carpet framed on the wall; in front of them, a bowl of seasonal fruits. Sometimes my mother would say: ‘Add your sister.’
We spoke every day. Nothing new – just exchanging words, routines and meaning.
‘What did you cook today?’
‘Did you go to the bazaar?’
Nothing important. Everything important.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea

My father had established this unwritten rule: we had to talk every day, even if only for two minutes. He described it as a kind of dependency, a small but necessary interruption to the weight of his routine. Our conversations moved easily between memories, what we made of them, and laughter. Always laughter.

My mother’s connection to me was different. Our conversations were built from the small details of her day: what she cooked, what she cleaned, the news of a cousin or a neighbour. In return, I gave her the only thing I could: an audience. I listened to the rhythm of her life and offered my voice back to her: Khaste nabashi. ‘May you never be tired.’ In those moments, her daily work wasn’t just chores; it was a story we shared.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea, like the fading light of evening. We watched each other’s days unfold.
Then, almost within a few minutes, the flow stopped.

It was 28 February, a Saturday morning, project day at my child’s school in Bengaluru. I was holding my phone, recording my son’s presentation – already imagining sending it to my parents. Although I tried to stay present, my attention kept drifting back to the screen. For weeks, I had been checking updates and watching tensions rise in the Persian Gulf.
Then, on our family Telegram group, a message stopped me: Bacheha, jang shoro shod! ‘Guys, war has begun!’
At first, it felt unreal, like the many rumours that circulate in tense times. I checked state news channels. This time, it was confirmed. War had begun. Tehran was attacked.

I stepped out of the hall into the yard, searching for a corner of quiet. My eyes were already burning. I returned to the family group chat immediately. A shared awareness had taken over: we could lose connection at any moment. It felt as if we had been given a brief, fragile window for final words, and we all knew it.
Replies came in snatches. Then, one by one, they disappeared
Messages came quickly, overlapping.
I didn’t know what to say. I used the moment as if it were the last chance to speak: Kheili dosetoon daram. ‘Please take care, I love you all.’
Replies came in snatches: ‘Don’t worry about us. At least you are far from this.’ Repeated, reassuring.
Then, one by one, they disappeared.
A few messages noted others going offline. Then those voices vanished too. The group thinned in real time, presence giving way to absence, names turning into data.
My last message remained unseen: Kasi hast? ‘Anyone there?’

Around me, the school day continued. Parents talked, children laughed, people moved in and out of the hall. Inside that ordinary noise, the world I knew simply vanished. With my country under attack and the screens gone dark, I felt suddenly homeless. I stood there, backless and boneless. The very thing holding me upright had been pulled out from under me.

I remained on this side of the silence. At first, it felt temporary. I kept scrolling, refreshing the same apps again and again, as if my persistence could bring something back. Telegram, Instagram, news pages – nothing changed. I began searching for voices abroad instead. I joined new Telegram channels and followed unknown people on Instagram – anything to know what was happening back home.

The rhythm had changed. Mornings began with news channels: what had been attacked, which part of my city was affected, whether it was near my neighbourhood. All day, I stayed alert – phone in hand, refreshing the same pages, switching between Persian and English sources, comparing headlines, trying to understand what was real and what was not.
Days passed. News moved on to other topics, and this silence – this disconnection – seemed normal and eternal.
I stopped checking ‘last seen’s.
I stopped writing: ‘If you connect, let me know you’re OK.’

Instead, I returned to old, archived chats with my mom. The last minutes before the shutdown – I had told her not to send dad out for unnecessary shopping. She had told me: ‘If the internet goes, don’t worry about us.’
I read every comment, slowly. I cried with them without them knowing
I scrolled back. Photos of foods, new clothes, videos of my son singing in broken Persian, emojis, laughter. Baba’s voice – always joking.
I began to avoid their photos. I would open the chat, then close it before my parents’ images loaded. I didn’t know if they were still there. I couldn’t bear to see and couldn’t stay away.
I read posts by Iranians in the diaspora. I read every comment, slowly. I cried with them without them knowing.
I tried calling landlines, different operators. Nothing worked.
Until, one day, an unknown number called.
‘I didn’t believe I could reach you. We are all alive,’ she said. Her voice was thin, crackling through the distance, but it was hers.
That call felt like a gift. From then on, I answered every unknown number.
Meanwhile, nothing around me had changed. The same streets, the same routines, the same conversations, but I moved through them differently.

I found myself refreshing my phone in the middle of conversations, between sentences, even while someone was speaking. After school, I stood in the corner of the playground, phone in hand. It became a habit. Other parents learned not to approach me.
Things I had once tried to avoid now felt impossible not to do.
People asked about my family. They listened, then returned to their own concerns – not out of indifference, but because life required it. For them, it was news. For me, it was always there.
Her name confirms, for a moment, that she is there – reachable, but not really within reach
One evening, at a friend’s house, I sat playing cards and my mind drifted back to my father and uncles – their Fridays, laughter, trays of tea cups, cheating, arguments, and smoke hanging in the air.
What are they doing now? Will they ever sit together like that again?
I didn’t just miss them. I missed the world where those moments were still possible.
The shadow of war still lingers. As I write this, the silence remains.
I am no longer afraid to see my parents’ old photos. Their brief, on-and-off calls warm me.
I imagine them in the same room – the chairs, the table, the background carpet.
The 6 pm ritual has become a memory.
I go back to that screenshot. Her name beneath it confirms, for a moment, that she is there – reachable, but not really within reach.
And I keep scrolling, waiting for a grainy photo of a family dinner, a new ‘like’, or a blue checkmark – any small signal that connection is no longer fragile and the internet has returned.

items.title: What can we learn from the past experience of El Niño?
items.description: As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring
items.author: Dagomar Degroot
paragraphs: As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

It’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

The past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño’s future on a warming planet.

A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

It’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.

When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).
El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific

Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.

The modern version of El Niño seems easy to define. It’s a dramatic warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean – a warming that’s confined to the tropics, lasts for many months, and tends to peak around the end of the year. It transfers a stupendous quantity of heat and moisture into the atmosphere, which the tropical jet stream redistributes, reshuffling weather patterns from one region to another.
But what causes these recurring warmings of Pacific Ocean water? And how, exactly, do they affect regional weather patterns?

Only recently have scientists been able to answer those questions. It turns out that El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific Ocean, known as the Southern Oscillation. When air is tightly packed together over the eastern Pacific – when atmospheric pressure there is high, in other words – and when it’s low over the western Pacific, the pressure difference reinforces persistent winds that blow west along the equator.

These trade winds, as they’re called, can push so much warm surface water into the tropics of the western Pacific that they allow deeper, colder water to reach the top of the eastern Pacific. This is called La Niña. But when the difference in Pacific Ocean pressure dips, the trade winds falter, and the warm water of the western Pacific surges east. This we call El Niño.

Scientists have learned that the Southern Oscillation involves reinforcing relationships, known as feedbacks, between the air and sea. Usually, hot water in the western Pacific evaporates in towering storms, releasing heat. The air flows east, cools down, grows denser, falls, then surges back to the west, warming up.

This pattern, known as the Walker Circulation, strengthens the pressure differences of the Southern Oscillation and fuels the trade winds. But during an El Niño, warm water, evaporation and rains shift to the eastern Pacific, weakening transpacific differences in pressure and, in turn, the trade winds. This pattern helps explain the most important weather associated with El Niño: torrential rains across parts of the Western Hemisphere, and drought in Australasia.

Today, El Niño seems less like an event, and more like one end of a seesaw that perpetually teeters across the Pacific. But why does the seesaw behave as it does? There is still no scientific consensus, but the historical traces of both human societies and the natural world provide us with clues.

The most important questions about El Niño concern its impacts on global weather patterns – or in other words, the teleconnections that form between the warming of the equatorial Pacific and droughts, floods, storms or heatwaves around the world.

These teleconnections are usually presented as predictable and consistent from one El Niño to the next. They’re visualised in maps that supposedly depict how regional temperatures or precipitation change as El Niño intensifies in the Pacific Ocean

But no two El Niño events have exactly the same teleconnections. One reason is that the extent, intensity and duration of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific differs from one El Niño to the next. Another is that El Niño is only one of many influences on regional weather, and its effects generally weaken with distance from the tropical Pacific.

Because El Niño’s impacts on regional weather are never identical, it’s impossible to predict exactly how a future El Niño will impact most of the world’s people and ecosystems. But it’s even harder to piece together the history of El Niño before the beginning of the 20th century, when ships began to regularly measure sea-surface temperatures. And it’s harder still before the middle of the 19th century, when scientists began to systematically gather data from rain gauges where El Niño reliably generates heavy precipitation.
Decades of research now reveals broad patterns in El Niño history that could give a rough sense of what’s in store

It’s a challenge, but not impossible. Climatologists – and a handful of historians and geographers – estimate the timing, strength and impacts of El Niño before the mid-19th century by consulting what they call the ‘archives of society’ and the ‘archives of nature’.

The archives of society were created by the people of the past. They include surviving texts that describe weather directly, such as the logbooks that sailors wrote aboard ships. They also include diverse sources of evidence – not only documents but also artefacts, ruins, even oral traditions – that record human activities so dependent on the weather that they can serve as proxies for it.

Unlike the archives of society, the archives of nature were created by Earth itself (even if they are, of course, interpreted by people). These archives are parts of the natural world that responded either to changes in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean, or to the regional extremes in temperature and precipitation that can be associated with those changes. The responses leave a mark in natural archives, changing the composition of growth rings in trees or corals, for example. Each mark serves as a proxy for El Niño conditions in the distant past.

Neither societal nor natural archives can provide direct measurements of sea-surface temperatures or weather, so histories of El Niño are inevitably full of uncertainty. Trees, for example, can only grow (or stop growing) so much. It’s one reason why their rings can’t precisely measure the strength of past El Niño events (and one reason why we can’t easily pin down whether this year’s El Niño really is the strongest in a millennium).

Still, decades of research can now reveal three broad patterns in El Niño history that could give us a rough sense of what’s in store – not only in the coming year, but in our future on a warming world.
Above all, El Niño shaped humanity’s past by suddenly changing where water was available, how much there was, and how people could use it.

The foundations of human life – food, shelter and movement – depend to varying degrees on water. Human populations can use water in many different ways, so they have learned to thrive in very different environments. But it seems to have been much harder for them to adapt to the sudden disruptions in water that a strong El Niño – or that a trend towards stronger El Niño conditions overall – could bring about.
This is the first pattern in El Niño’s human history.

We can already see its outlines a little more than 4,000 years ago, when the first states and empires established themselves. At that time, El Niño conditions seem to have grown more frequent, intense and long-lasting. The reason may have been a multimillennial cycle in the wobble of Earth’s rotation that altered the amount of sunlight associated with different seasons, weakening the trade winds.
It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges

Natural and societal archives suggest that some communities withered as El Niño intensified. In Peru, for example, populations appear to have deserted temple mounds, giant platforms that supported elaborate buildings and plazas. It’s easy to imagine that torrential floods sparked by strong El Niño conditions made it impossible to maintain these structures. But archaeological evidence hints at other changes that might have been partly responsible for population movements, including new trade networks and newly cultivated plants. How much can the coincidence of two trends really tell us about causation?

Maybe quite a lot, if similar coincidences pop up elsewhere. And it seems they do. A little under 3,000 years ago, for example, settlers established a community at Teouma, on the island of Efate in today’s Vanuatu. Chemical traces of human waste and leaves in nearby swamp sediments show that the settlers cultivated taro, a root vegetable, during a period of increasing rainfall. By around 2,600 years ago, however, a trend towards stronger or more frequent El Niño conditions seems to have made local rainfall more erratic. The trend appears to correlate with a decline in settlement and cultivation on Efate.

You’ll notice a lot of conditional language about possible changes and potential correlations. Deep history is like that. Natural and societal archives can let us identify probable trends, figure out roughly when they happened, and craft convincing theories for how one trend caused another. It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges that compels us to re-date a trend, or propose another cause for it.

In general, evidence from the archives of nature and society is more abundant and precise the closer it dates to our present. Evidence from the previous millennium lets us identify not just trends in human and El Niño history, but discrete events.
Catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions

By the 16th century, for example, cave formations, tree rings and reports written by government officials let us reconstruct the likely impacts of individual El Niño years on the Indian summer monsoon. They reveal a series of devastating droughts across India in the late 16th century, the middle and end of the 17th century, and the late 18th century.

It may be that a series of explosive volcanic eruptions were partly responsible for these droughts. The cooling effect of the sulphur they launched into the upper atmosphere altered temperature differences between latitudes, and between land and water. These differences in temperature help create the winds that bring monsoon rains; when they changed, the rains did too.

But the droughts also coincided with El Niño conditions. In fact, there may be a connection, because the new wind patterns created by powerful eruptions seem to warm the eastern Pacific, relative to the west. Regardless, El Niño can also weaken the Indian monsoon by shifting warm water and rising air eastward across the tropical Pacific.

When the monsoon rains failed, harvests could too. Of course, rural populations and states had many ways of protecting themselves. Wells and granaries stored water and seeds, for instance, while trade networks could allow for emergency food imports. Still, these systems broke down when droughts lasted too long – and especially when states waged war.

In some El Niño events and in some parts of India, droughts provoked widespread famine only when armies demanded food from the already depleted countryside. In other Indian regions, the death toll soared when widespread malnutrition joined migration from drought-stricken regions to encourage the spread of epidemic disease. All told, catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions across 16th-, 17th- and 18th-century India.
Everywhere El Niño sparked extreme weather, communities suffered. Yet some prospered at their expense, and this is the second pattern we can discern in El Niño’s history.

The collapse of China’s Ming dynasty in the 17th century seems to provide a striking example. Growth rings in trees and corals indicate that El Niño conditions repeatedly contributed to a weakening of the East Asian monsoon in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. At first, droughts afflicted both northeastern China – home of the loosely connected Jurchen peoples – and northern China, the Ming heartland.

In the diverse environments of northeastern China, the Jurchen hunted, fished and farmed, a varied subsistence strategy that gave them some protection from drought. They also raided across the Great Wall into Ming territory, where they seized stockpiled grain. Eventually, droughts intensified in northern China, where soaring food prices and famine helped to destabilise the Ming regime. But drought seems to have yielded to above-average rainfall in Jurchen territories. Food provided by plentiful rain may have aided efforts to consolidate Jurchen communities into a united ‘Manchu’ state that was strong enough to exploit the Ming dynasty’s weakness, conquer China, and establish a new Qing dynasty.

Indeed, conquest and colonialism created a means by which the impacts of El Niño could be amplified for some communities, but alleviated or even exploited for others. This redistribution of vulnerability was never clearer or more catastrophic than in the late 19th century, when exceptionally strong El Niño conditions coincided with a global age of imperialism.
The exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place

In 1876, drought spread across India, then intensified with a strong El Niño in 1877-78. It was the heyday of the British Raj. Colonial officials had upended lives and livelihoods in many Indian farming communities by forcing them to plant cash crops such as tea or cotton. Now, there wasn’t enough food to go round. What grain could be harvested was either redirected from the poorest communities to areas where people could pay more, or exported out of India by colonial administrators who scorned market interventions.
Tens of millions died in the ensuing famines.

Similar tragedies played out wherever El Niño sparked drought in the late 19th century, though the exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place. In Eritrea and Ethiopia, for instance, Italian invaders arrived with cattle infected by rinderpest, a deadly disease that spread to local cattle before the arrival of another strong El Niño in 1890-91. Widespread mortality among cattle intensified food shortages, as did the arrival of immense locust swarms.
Perhaps a third of Ethiopia’s population perished.

The United States, however, often benefitted from El Niño conditions. As worldwide droughts drove up grain prices in 1877-78, US farmers exported enormous quantities of wheat to Europe. The resulting inflow of gold-backed credit strengthened US finances, and helped the government manage its Civil War debts. A century later, during another strong El Niño in 1972, the collapse of the Peruvian anchovy fishery, owing both to warming water and years of overfishing, deprived poultry producers of fishmeal. But that allowed US farmers to profit by planting soy, a substitute. In the even stronger 1982-83 event, torrential rains devastated California and other southern states, but overall, the US economy received a powerful stimulus from mild winter weather.

It was around this time – the late 20th century – that scientists and journalists created the modern concept of El Niño as a global event that recurred every few years to cause predictable disasters. This is the third pattern in our history. El Niño is not just an environmental reality; it’s also a cultural reality: a manufactured threat that is a unique product of our time.

In some respects, that threat was a creation of the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). During the IGY, a global campaign to observe Earth and near-Earth space served as an arena for scientific and technological competition between the US and Soviet governments. The IGY fortuitously coincided with an El Niño, and unprecedented observations helped scientists begin to understand the true dimensions of Pacific Ocean warming.
It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways

Cold War politics continued to shape El Niño science. The 1959 Cuban Revolution joined the growing importance – for poultry farmers – of the Peruvian anchovy fishery to spur US support for collaborations between US and Latin American scientists. These collaborations, many of which focused on the study of El Niño, were supposed to demonstrate the value of partnership with US institutions.

When navies deployed nuclear submarines to reinforce newly developed nuclear arsenals, they began to fund oceanographic research partly to better understand the underwater battlespace. Until then, oceanographers had been able to visit marine environments only occasionally, in ships. Beginning in the 1950s, new funds and technology allowed them to deploy instruments to monitor environments continuously, for months or years at a time.

The launch of Sputnik 1 during the IGY also heralded a new age in which weather satellites kept the oceans under constant supervision from above. And computer models soon seemed capable of forecasting not just global warming, but also the state of the Southern Oscillation. By the early 1980s, prominent scientists believed that El Niño could finally be predicted months in advance.

Yet the strong El Niño of 1982-83 came as a shock to the overwhelming majority of meteorologists and oceanographers. It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways, and each had distinct impacts on regional weather patterns. Because the unanticipated El Niño led to floods, droughts and storms that killed thousands of people, inflicted billions of dollars in damage, and cost the global economy trillions in estimated lost growth, scientists redoubled their efforts to forecast El Niño and its teleconnections.
The concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media

In 1985, the World Meteorological Organization – a United Nations agency – launched a decade-long project to scatter ocean-monitoring buoys across the tropical Pacific. Scientists also began to use both societal and natural archives to reconstruct the deep history of El Niño. In early 1997, they had learned enough to successfully predict another ocean warming months before it happened. Scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) alerted US journalists, and they created a media sensation: an El Niño reimagined as a looming, worldwide catastrophe.

It’s ironic that American journalists developed this threatening new view of El Niño. In the US, the economic benefits of the 1997-98 El Niño would again far outweigh the damage. But the concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Since the 19th century, US reporters had thrilled audiences by portraying natural phenomena as sensational, often threatening events – events that could be understood only by plucky scientists. A close but routine approach of a comet or planet to Earth, for example, became a brush with death recorded by swashbuckling scientists in far-flung observatories.

It was journalism that resonated in a culture shaped by religious concepts of a purifying apocalypse. And it helps explain why, in the 20th century, the scientific investigation of changes in the atmosphere – not just global warming, but also nuclear winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, and even the potential consequences of asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions – relied on US funding and institutions, while coming to particularly alarm US citizens.

Now, some US journalists used the Spanish name of El Niño to conjure an image of a foreign menace that several compared to migrants from South America. As the 1997-98 El Niño warmed into the strongest event since the 19th century, ‘Blame it on El Niño’ and ‘Don’t blame me, blame El Niño!’ were common slogans on everything from bumper stickers to T-shirts. That was true even though scientists couldn’t predict exactly how El Niño would affect weather in most parts of the world, let alone how populations would react.
It was in 1997 that today’s understanding of El Niño – part Cold War relic, part scientific achievement, and part media monster – was born.

The patterns in El Niño’s past teach us that the warming of the tropical Pacific can be disastrous for communities exposed to droughts and floods. But they also reveal that El Niño disasters are caused less by the severity of weather extremes, and more by the brutality of how some communities are exploited by others. They suggest that today’s imagined El Niño – a global threat, with predictable impacts on weather – is less an accurate reflection of reality than a creation of modern science, media and geopolitics.

In the coming years and decades, it’s likely that El Niño’s impacts on populations will be shaped primarily by human relationships and ideas, not by nature. But human actions now include greenhouse gas pollution on such a scale that Earth has warmed by about 1.5°C, relative to its average temperature in the late 19th century. This pollution is supercharging the impacts of El Niño on weather. Heatwaves are growing hotter, and intensifying evaporation means droughts are getting worse. Partly because a warm atmosphere holds more water, downpours are ever more intense.

Global warming doesn’t seem capable of ending the Southern Oscillation, and with it the age-old seesaw of El Niño and La Niña. Still, it could lead to even more intense El Niño events that cause even more extreme weather.

It’s never been more urgent to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. But El Niño’s past also teaches us a deeper lesson about adapting to climatic extremes. Today, the world seems increasingly shaped by renewed great power competition: by militarism and colonial relationships between superpowers and their patrons. History suggests that such a world could be one in which millions die unnecessarily, not just through war but in preventable climate disasters.
It’s a warning from the past that today’s governments would be wise to heed, as El Niño reshapes environments from one end of the world to another in the months and years to come.

items.title: AnOther Dish: Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba’s Oysters
items.description: The couple behind east London’s modern British restaurant, Waterhouse, share a hot and tart recipe for dressing creamy Lindisfarne oysters
items.author: Rose Dodd
paragraphs: The couple behind east London’s modern British restaurant, Waterhouse, share a hot and tart recipe for dressing creamy Lindisfarne oysters
The food we return to can say so much about us – AnOther Dish invites chefs and notable food lovers to share a recipe of personal significance

“Lindisfarne – sometimes called Holy Island – is a tiny island just off the northeast coast of Northumberland. We spent some time there when we first got together. As the tide comes in it completely covers the causeway you take to get there – sometimes you’ll see cars abandoned along the road, some swept out to sea. We once spent a night on Lindisfarne and drove right to the edge of the island to watch as the tide came in. You feel very remote, detached from the mainland, with no option of returning until the tide goes out again – it feels strangely natural, there’s a purity to life there.

“We visited a lovely little pub while we were there – that’s where we were first introduced to Lindisfarne oysters. Oysters are amazing – they filter and clean the sea. Every oyster has its own flavour profile, and these ones are spectacularly creamy. That’s why they balance so nicely with something sharp. The classic way to dress an oyster is with a mignonette or lemon juice, but it’s nice to play around with different ingredients to see how you can elevate the oyster while respecting and preserving its pure flavour – all without overwhelming it. You want the natural ingredients to speak for themselves.

“Oysters always feel special in a restaurant, don’t they? And even more so at home – served on a bed of ice, with an aperitif or a glass of something bubbly. We serve our Lindisfarne oysters with a cucumber, apple and sorrel granita, and finish them with a homemade green chilli oil. This dish has evolved over the years, but it’ll always remind us of the beginning of our relationship.” – Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba

Co-founded by husband and wife Gabriel Waterhouse and Trish Wakaimba, Waterhouse is a modern British restaurant and bar on east London’s Ezra Street. Just metres from Columbia Road, hidden behind its own gated garden in what was once a Victorian Warehouse, the space is reminiscent of a rural farmhouse. The restaurant seats 24 amid an open kitchen, minimalist steel surface tops, exposed timberwork, parquet flooring and mid-century oak furniture. Welcoming and cosy, dining at Waterhouse feels more akin to eating at someone’s home.

Seasonal ingredients are central to the 8- and 11-course tasting menus, sourced from across the UK and grown in the restaurant’s own garden, they draw on the culinary traditions of northeast England, Scotland and the northern coastline. Dishes include: Northumbrian rye bread, smoked haddock, and singing hinnies with Laphroaig cream. Seafood comes from the northern waters – hand-dived scallops, creel-caught lobster and said Lindisfarne oysters – and meat and game from the Lake District, Yorkshire and the Highlands. A larder approach makes preservation, fermentation, pickling and smoking key. “The restaurant has a big larder of misos, malt kojis and garums, made with things like wild garlic or seeds that we’ve foraged during the year,” says Waterhouse. On the drinks menu British grain spirits are infused with ingredients from the garden: a mugwort negroni, foraged from Hackney; a fig leaf martini; a homegrown rosemary vesper; and a sorrel margarita.

Waterhouse grew up in Northumberland and has been working as a chef for 15 years. In 2023, he earned his title as Champion for the Best Dressed Oyster at the London Oyster Championship. Wakaimba, an entrepreneur, also has a background in hospitality, coming from a family of restaurateur-hoteliers. The couple met on Waterhouse’s first weekend in London, having moved to the city the summer after university. “Set up by a friend, he came to my flat for dinner on a Saturday,” says Wakaimba. “He really didn’t have much time to look around.” Waterhouse was due to start working for Herbert Berger the following Monday. As is often the case in kitchens, so famously fast-paced, the working environment was intense. “Those crazy hours were never sustainable,” says Wakaimba. “I think Gabe knew all along he wanted to have something of his own.”

Their inaugural project together was a series of intimate supper clubs before the Covid-19 pandemic hit, when they started making delivery meal kits, with multiple courses, paired wines, even playlists. As normalcy resumed, so did their hospitality. In September this year Waterhouse, the restaurant, opened its doors, marking a new chapter. “Through all of that we built this lovely community and we’ve been able to see what works and what doesn’t – those years felt like learning, and it’s really informed where we are now.” “We shape our ideas together,” says Waterhouse. “Everything is passed back and forth between us, and that’s what the space feels like and reflects. It’s like a testament of our compatibility.”

For their chosen dish, Waterhouse and Wakaimba combine the pure, creaminess of a Lindisfarne oyster with the sharp acidity of pickled cucumber, served in the oyster’s shell with a tart sorrel and apple granita, and a chilli oil. Here, they share the recipe.
Lindisfarne Oysters, with Pickled Cucumber, Sorrel Granita and Green Chilli Oil
- 6 fresh Lindisfarne oysters
- 100ml white wine vinegar
Cucumber and Sorrel Granita
- 150ml fresh cucumber juice, extracted with the skin on
- 20–25g fresh sorrel leaves
- Fresh lemon juice, to taste

1. To make the pickled cucumber, combine the white wine vinegar, water, sugar and fennel seeds in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then strain out the fennel seeds and leave the liquid to cool completely. Cut the cucumber into small, even dice, keeping the skin on. Place in a container and cover with the cooled pickling liquid. Refrigerate for a few hours, ideally 24, before using.

2. For the chilli oil, place the green chillies and pomace oil in a high-speed jug blender with a vented lid that allows heat and steam to escape. Do not use a completely sealed blender, such as a bullet-style blender, as pressure can build up as the mixture heats. Blend continuously for approximately 5–10 minutes, until the mixture reaches 70–80°C. The heat generated by the blender is important to the process. As the temperature rises, the oil will begin to separate from the liquid released by the chillies. Keep the lid secure and the vent unobstructed, following the manufacturer’s guidance for blending hot ingredients. Pass through fine muslin or a J-cloth to collect the green oil. Refrigerate until required. The green chilli paste can be reserved for another recipe.

3. To make the cucumber and sorrel granita, place the cucumber juice, apple juice and sorrel into a blender and mix together until completely smooth, then pass through a fine sieve. Season the strained mixture with salt and a little fresh lemon juice to taste. You want enough acidity to lift the cucumber and apple without overpowering their freshness. Pour into a shallow container and freeze. Once frozen, scrape with a fork to create fine crystals.

4. To prepare the oysters, scrub shells under cold running water to remove any grit or debris. I prefer to open oysters from the front, at the rounded lip of the shell, rather than from the hinge at the back. I find this much easier. Always use an oyster knife, which has a shorter and blunter blade. Hold each oyster firmly on a folded cloth, protecting the hand holding it, and carefully work the tip of the oyster knife between the two shells at the front. Gently twist to open, then slide the blade along the inside of the upper shell to release the muscle. Be gentle. The mistake lots of people make is that it requires a lot of force and it doesn’t. As each oyster is opened, pour its sea water into a clean bowl and reserve it. Remove the oyster from the shell and rinse the flesh carefully in cold water to ensure no small fragments of shell remain. Return the oyster immediately to its reserved liquor and keep chilled until ready to serve.

5. To serve: Remove the oysters from their liquor and cut each into three pieces. Place the three pieces of oyster at the bottom of each serving bowl and arrange a little pickled cucumber around them. Finish with a spoonful of cucumber and sorrel granita immediately before serving. I like to serve the green chilli oil separately in one half of the cleaned oyster shell, resting the shell on top of the bowl. This works particularly well with a small serving bowl. It allows each person to pour the oil over the granita themselves, finishing the dish at the table. You can also place a little yoghurt in the serving bowl for an added creamy tang.
Waterhouse is open at 7A Ezra Street, London, E2 7RH from Friday to Sunday for lunch and dinner. Book a table, here

items.title: Haruki Murakami’s Legendary 70s Tokyo Jazz Club Comes to London
items.description: From 1974 to 1981, and before global literary fame, Haruki Murakami ran a scrappy jazz club in Tokyo’s Sendagaya neighbourhood, resurrected this month at the Barbican
items.author: James Balmont
paragraphs: From 1974 to 1981, and before global literary fame, Haruki Murakami ran a scrappy jazz club in Tokyo’s Sendagaya neighbourhood, resurrected this month at the Barbican
I’m standing beside a flank of colourful vending machines next to a mini car-park near the Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium in Sendagaya, Tokyo, peering up at an Italian bistro during a busy lunch hour.

From the outside, there’s little to suggest that there’s more to this place (now known as Amphora) than the plates of spaghetti carbonara and imported wines being served to patrons at pokey wooden tables. But this address was once a source of passion and inspiration for one of the world’s greatest literary figures – and this month, its humble legacy is being celebrated some 6,000 miles away at London’s Barbican Hall.

Between 1977 and 1981, the premises was a jazz café known as Peter Cat – and it was run by the man who, in time, would become the most widely read Japanese novelist in the world. Years before penning classics like Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore, Haruki Murakami spent his days stocking shelves, and his evenings mixing drinks to the sounds of his hundreds of vinyl records. Peter Cat was an expression of a musical passion harboured ever since he’d been “thunderstruck” by an Art Blakey concert in his childhood; it would prove a foundational influence on the entire literary career that followed.

Forty-five years since Murakami closed its doors, Peter Cat lives again this November via three immersive concerts organised with the EFG London Jazz Festival, titled Haruki Murakami’s Jazz at Peter Cat. And one performer from the cultured line-up of Japanese jazz greats is particularly fitting for the occasion: “As a rather irresponsible first-year university student in the spring of 1979, I started working at Peter Cat two or three days a week,” says saxophonist Sachi Hayasaka. “It makes me incredibly happy that such an extraordinary coincidence has brought me back, after all these years, to perform [in its honour] on such a prestigious stage.”

Hayasaka experienced Peter Cat during its twilight years. The original premises was established in a small basement club near Kokubunji Station in 1974, shortly after Murakami left college. There, young jazz musicians and students gathered as Murakami and his wife worked tirelessly in a windowless room, booking bands and washing dishes. It was a labour of love – the young couple reportedly went so deep into debt that, during the winter, they’d snuggle with their cat – the eponymous Peter – so that they wouldn’t have to pay for heating.

After upending to a second location in Sendagaya, though, Peter Cat came into its own. “I still remember the first time I visited the place,” Hayasaka tells AnOther. “One entire wall was made of glass, another was lined with records, and at one end of the wooden counter, there was a small carving of the Cheshire Cat from Alice in Wonderland, with its distinctive, mischievous grin.” Overlooking the neighbourhood’s striking greenery, the café’s big, sunlit windows – still intact today, at the bustling Amphora – ensured the space felt warm and bright. “The day I first visited, there was a live performance by [tenor saxophonist] Takao Uematsu,” Hayasaka continues. “I fell in love with the place immediately.”

Encouraged by a friend from her university’s music club, Hayasaka became a waitress, serving coffee and cheesecake by day to students and couples. By night, “the atmosphere changed”, she recalls, as jazz-heads and literary and publishing figures stopped by to enjoy drinks, music and conversation in the relaxed surroundings.

Murakami, at the time, was “generally a quiet person,” she continues. “He seemed to observe people carefully. But he was always kind to everyone, and had a wonderful sense of humour.” Between lessons on how to chop onions without crying (“you have to chop them quickly!”, he had said), Murakami was encouraging of Hayasaka’s ambitions, lending her albums off the shelves that he felt were conducive to her saxophone practice. “At the time, I was completely absorbed in the music of [John] Coltrane and Jimi Hendrix,” she says. “I thought jazz was supposed to be radical and intense, so I found Stan Getz – one of the artists he’d recommend the most often – a little too gentle for my taste.”

Ultimately, this divergence would foreshadow a greater rupture just six months after Hayasaka started working for Murakami. “My musical activities became increasingly busy, and the journey to Sendagaya began to feel like a burden,” Hayasaka wrote in a recent blog post. “I did something quite terrible. I simply stopped showing up for work without telling anyone.”

A month later, a note in neat, rounded handwriting arrived. “It read: ‘Here is the remainder of your wages’”, she says. “Even after I had treated him so badly, kind Haruki-san had remained considerate and sincere to the very end.”

In truth, Murakami was also being led astray. In 1978, the year prior to Hayasaka’s arrival at Peter Cat, the idea to write a novel had come to the café owner in the middle of a Yakult Swallows baseball match, just 15 minutes walk away from the café at the Meiji Jingu Stadium. “Running a service business … I [had] met all kinds of offbeat people and had some unusual encounters,” he wrote in his 2007 memoir What I Talk About When I Talk About Running. “I ran my jazz club – keeping accounts, scheduling staff, cooking and closing up in the wee hours of the morning – and only then writing at home at the kitchen table until I got sleepy … half an hour here, an hour there … ”

By autumn that year, Murakami had finished his first 200-page work, Hear the Wind Sing. It brought home the Gunzo Prize for New Writers. Hayasaka remembers it as a turning point: “One day, the café seemed unusually busy,” she says. “People who looked like editors kept coming in one after another … until then, I had only seen him quietly working at the counter. I had not even known he was a writer.”

A second novel, Pinball, 1973, followed in 1980, along with a few short stories. Soon after, Murakami opted to pack up shop: “I decided to close the business for a while and concentrate solely on writing,” he wrote, delivering his first full-length novel, A Wild Sheep Chase, in 1982.

By 1987, with the publication of Norwegian Wood, he had become a national sensation. Named after the 1965 Beatles song that marked the first appearance of a sitar in Western music, the book sold over 3.5 million copies in its first year alone.

Peter Cat may have ultimately been left in the wake of thousands of manuscript pages, but the music it played would remain at the core of Murakami’s craft – both guiding his writing practices and frequently appearing in his stories. “My style is as deeply influenced by Charlie Parker’s repeated freewheeling riffs as by F Scott Fitzgerald’s elegantly flowing prose,” he told the New York Times in 2007. “And I still take the quality of continual self-renewal in Miles Davis’s music as a literary model.”

Here in Japan, the café’s legacy can still be traced at Amphora. By the cashier desk, nestled between business cards and wine bottles atop rustic wooden furnishings, sits a Hello Kitty handbell, a framed illustration of the Cheshire Cat, and a box of tissues decorated with whiskery faces – subtle winks to the site’s feline heritage. There’s even a small, easily missed shrine to Murakami by the window, featuring books by, and photos of, the master author.

About an hour’s walk north of its former site in Sendagaya, meanwhile, the so-called ‘Haruki Murakami Library’ at Waseda University – where Murakami studied until 1975 – houses an archive of more than 3,000 books, photographs and artefacts donated by the author, including the piano and chairs from his beloved jazz café, and many of the vinyl records that once played there.

Back in London, documentarians like Philip Arneill – author of the Tokyo Jazz Joints book archive – have joined with production company Serious to ensure that our native celebration will feel as vivid as the original club did in the 1970s. In the absence of any extensive visual documentation of the original site (almost no photos exist today), Arneill’s photography of Japan’s jazz kissa culture has helped inspire the forthcoming Barbican production.

And as Japan-inspired listening bars crop up all across London – from Deptford’s Jazu Bar and Shoreditch’s Seed Library to the Barbican’s own, newly opened Spiritland bar – the influence of institutions like Peter Cat is only becoming more palpable. “Japanese jazz and the culture of jazz cafés is attracting attention all around the world,” Hayasaka agrees, as she packs her bags for the UK. And so the ghost of Peter Cat continues to linger: “I feel deeply grateful,” Hayasaka concludes. “Looking back now, I realise what an extraordinary luxury it was to be there.”
Haruki Murakami’s Jazz at Peter Cat is at the Barbican on 21 and 22 November, as part of EFG London Jazz Festival (13–22 November)

items.title: Fashion features director Jack Moss’ gift guide for the style aficionado
items.description: Having spent my entire year looking at fashion, and its various accoutrements, when it comes to writing my annual gift guide, it is usually fairly easy to collate – my head (and notes app) features an ever-rotating wish list picked up on my travels (or simply
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: Having spent my entire year looking at fashion, and its various accoutrements, when it comes to writing my annual gift guide, it is usually fairly easy to collate – my head (and notes app) features an ever-rotating wish list picked up on my travels (or simply on various shopping-website doom scrolls).

Which is why, as ever, this is an unabashedly personal list, though hopefully everything here has a wider appeal – almost all of the list is unisex, and spans stocking fillers (a perfect pair of ribbed red merino socks), decorations (vintage ‘Three Little Pigs’ tree ornaments courtesy fo JW Anderson), and total one-offs (Andtees’ printed vintage T-shirts – when they are gone, they are gone). Something, as they say, for everyone.
Read on for fashion & beauty features director Jack Moss’ gift guide for the style aficionado.

At Jake’s – the cult east London store run by Jake Burt of fashion label Stefan Cooke – I have been eyeing up one of Faimann’s wooden charms for some time (I stupidly passed on a tennis-ball yellow charm when I was last there in summer). And, while the fledgling brand’s designer remains anonymous, Faimann’s style is distinctive enough not to matter: the almost toy-like constructions, often adorned with studs and metal flowers, are hanging off the bags and belts of all of London’s best dressed.
Price on request, available at Jake’s, 63 Vyner Street, London (open most Saturdays, and with recent pop-ups in Tokyo, Osaka, New York and Seoul).

I am a devotee of 39BC’s shower oils – not only for their evocative scents (Fig Milk, a heady mix of wild fig and cyclamen, and Denarri, which has notes of patchouli, cedarwood and black pepper, are my favourites), but also for the way that the gentlest lather at the end of a shower moisturises the skin with no effort (the relatively new brand is inspired by ancient bathing rituals). This Alexandria Discovery Set makes for the perfect starting point to your own addiction – use the miniature bottles for testing or travel.

Founded in 2014 in Florence, Giacomo Bacci takes the city’s synonymy with shirtmaking and gives it a wholly contemporary twist. It was hard to choose just one of the brand’s offering – which are still handmade in the Florentine store-cum-workshop – though this contrast-collar shirt, in perfectly ‘off’ shades of yellow and brown, clinched it. The runners-up? A collarless crew-neck pullover shirt in baby pink, or those which recall the traditional piped-edge pyjamas usually worn in bed.

JW Anderson has transformed from a traditional fashion label to an emporium of both clothing and craft, epitomised by its newly renovated Soho store and recent opening on Pimlico Road (alongside the usual fashion collections are art objects, furniture and home textiles). For winter, creative director and founder Jonathan Anderson has curated a festive offering, including these vintage Christmas tree ornaments, from traditional gleaming baubles to those that recount the tale of the Three Little Pigs.

I always gravitate towards fragrances that centre around fig, with Debaser from Brooklyn-based brand D.S. & Durga fast becoming my favoured everyday scent. Combined with pear, coconut milk and iris, it’s at once ultra-fresh and sweet – quite unlike anything I've smelt before. In a good way – I’ve been complimented on its scent more times than I can count.

The side hustle of fashion designer Antoine Lazaroo, Andtees sees playful slogans printed onto vintage T-shirts – from ‘Do you believe in magic?’ to ‘Room Service’. But get there fast: once a style is gone, it’s gone, and, with Lazaroo having created custom tees for the promo tour of Jordan Firstman’s buzzy film Club Kid, which premiered earlier this year at Cannes, expect them to be even harder to get soon.

Celine’s Aura slipper in black has evaded me for months – two trips to the house’s Paris store left me empty handed after the last pairs in my size had sold out. But I’m not giving up: this version in off-white is equally appealing, capturing creative director Michael Rider’s knack for an impactful accessory that will nonetheless slot easily into your existing wardrobe and shoe rotation.

Just about everybody in my life has seen me in my Commission Rider shirt, with its sliced away chest holes – evoking the yoke of a western shirt – always drawing attention. Hence mine being rather faded and the worse for wear – the sign of a true sartorial companion that's in need of a fresh replacement.

On a recent trip to Kyoto, I discovered the Japanese outpost of Shinichiro Ogata’s eponymous Paris restaurant, and its equally elegant lifestyle store, which also sits in The Shinmonzen, a Tadao Ando-designed Ryokan hotel in the Gion district. Alongside ceramics, candles and the occasional fashion accessory are these ‘pot pourri’ sachets, designed to sit in their purpose-built container, beautifully wrapped and scented with notes of hinoki Japanese cypress and sandalwood. They can even be carried around in the pocket, or slotted into a draw to perfume your clothing, though you might (like me) not want to unwrap them just yet and simply revel in their perfect packaging.

Socks have often been derided as a Christmas gift, though for a small gesture, I can’t think of anything better. Founded by Alice Macfarlane in Scotland in 2020, Pairs offers perhaps the most appealing array of colours on the market (and satisfying packaging), with versions crafted from alpaca, mohair, merino, bamboo and wool. Our choice? These pillarbox red bed socks in ribbed merino.

I am a big proponent of ultra-chunky knitwear in lieu of a winter coat, and this Polo Ralph Lauren zip-up cardigan feels more than ready to weather the elements (after all, the early months of the new year often require the warmest of outerwear). Featuring a desert vista along its back and conjuring Ralph Lauren’s inimitable all-American aesthetic, each one is crafted alongside Manos del Uruguay, a non-profit which provides work and support to Uruguayan craftswomen.

The best caps are of the kind that feel like vintage merch. Case in point, this insignia cap from buzzy American designer Conner Ives – its twisting embroidered initials could be from a shuttered 1980s hotel or college baseball team. In Conner’s words: ‘the esoteric insignia baseball cap, IYKYK’.

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.title: 11 chic and useful gifts for the modern traveller
items.description: Travel, for most of us, is a treat to look forward to. And a thoughtful travel gift is not just useful but comes with a sense of anticipation of adventures yet to come. Everything in our gift guide for the modern traveller has been suggested by a frequent-flyi
items.author: Bridget Downing
paragraphs: Travel, for most of us, is a treat to look forward to. And a thoughtful travel gift is not just useful but comes with a sense of anticipation of adventures yet to come. Everything in our gift guide for the modern traveller has been suggested by a frequent-flying Wallpaper* editor as an item they would love to receive – whether that’s a chic leather notebook holder for journallers, journalists and jotters alike, a dual time-zone watch, a smart pair of swim shorts or an even smarter pair of smartglasses to give directions to the nearest pool. Happy gifting.

Gather your thoughts in analogue fashion and considerable style with Montblanc’s tactile leather note holder. With room for a notebook and a favoured writing instrument, plus slots in which to secure cards or those crucial bits of paper ephemera accumulated on your trip, from receipts to back-of-a-napkin jottings, it also allows its owner to carve out a little screen-free creative time. Available in saffron, black and khaki.
The smartest of swim shorts

Relaxing poolside is no reason to let sartorial standards slide. For the fastidious, these black tuxedo-style swim shorts from Vilebrequin – note the contrast side trim – cut a sophisticated dash on the terrace or the beach. Slip on a shirt, and they are also smart enough as day or evening shorts for urban adventures, making them doubly deserving of a space in your travel bag.
The ultimate AirPods carrier

Oh, the joy when a product addresses a functionality you hadn’t thought of but suddenly need. This cute and covetable leather AirPods case can be worn around the neck or clipped to a belt or bag with an accompanying carabiner, meaning you – or your giftee – won’t be the traveller rummaging for their AirPods when it comes time to disembark post-flight or check out of your room. Designed to fit all sizes of AirPods, the case comes in black, brown, beige, as well as brighter – and less misplaceable – camel and purple.
A fashion capital companion

The celebrated Wallpaper* Travel Guides are back with a new series covering four of the world’s most stylish and culturally vibrant hubs: Milan, Paris, New York City, and London. Fully revised and curated by Wallpaper* writers with insider knowledge, each of these pocket-sized books are aimed at design lovers hungry to explore culture-rich getaways.

Parting may be sweet sorrow but you can ensure a loved one’s departures are also thoroughly fragrant ones by packing them off with miniature versions of their favourite perfumes. This set includes three refillable 10ml bottles of Dries Van Noten’s woody fragrances – Rock the Myrrh, Cannabis Patchouli, and Crazy Basil – and a ‘nomadic’ case into which to pop whichever they choose. Want to make it a more personal gift? You can also select other perfumes to customise the set.
A traveller’s beauty boost

Arrive anywhere looking and feeling more refreshed with a duo of travel-friendly, soothing helpmates from Chanel. Classic companion La Crème Main will combat dry hands – lightweight and quickly absorbed, it’s infused with nourishing, camellia-derived ingredients and comes in a squeezable, 50ml, pebble-shaped container. Throw in the perfect tonic for puffy post-flight or jet-lagged under-eye skin, Le Lift Flash Eye masks, designed to leave the area looking smoother, tighter and more luminous, thanks to a formula enriched with low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid.
A curated 100ml beauty bag

Take the hassle out of one of the airport’s most irritating inconveniences by fast-tracking someone’s beauty and grooming essentials into one bag. Online company 100mL partners with ethical brands, such as Aesop, Three Ships and Zizia Botanicals, to offer an array of airport-sized products. Its Curated Pouches, ready-made sets presented in clear washbags, cater to various needs – for example, Rest + Reset, Bare Essentials, Business Traveller and so on. You can also curate your own pouch or just buy individual products.
A go-anywhere water bottle

Staying hydrated is key to happy, headache-free travels. Simple and durable in 100 per cent stainless steel, this water bottle ticks all the boxes for us – it has a vacuum design to keep the contents cool, is dishwasher safe, avoids plastics, and it looks good too. Unexpected bonus for fizzy-water fiends? It’s compatible with the Aarke Carbonator Pro.

The classic game, the perfect analogue pleasure to pass the time, whether you’re stuck in an airport lounge, chilling in a city bar or cosying up in a remote cabin, becomes a travelling companion to treasure in the hands of Hermès. Its crafting by artisans of the company’s Petit h arm – who upcycle Hermès’ surplus materials into many and various objects of desire – means there’s a refreshing unpredictability to the precise colour you’ll get, and each set is unique. Both the case and the dominoes are in leather, a tactile delight that will wear and age with your travels.
Smart glasses for a fresh direction

Meta and Ray-Ban’s latest AI-powered smart glasses come with plenty that’s useful or desirable for a traveller. Courtesy of Meta AI, access local information, directions, live translations, the weather, your diary and so on, plus make calls, send texts, listen to podcasts and music, hands-free, and with nothing wedged in your ears to mute your surroundings.
A watch for time travellers

Bell & Ross offers a helping hand, quite literally, for those hopping time zones. The BR-05 GMT Green Steel watch has a fourth hand that allows the wearer to track two time zones at once, and the hands and indices also glow in the dark, allowing a swift time check should you wake, discombobulated, in the middle of the night. A sage-green sunray dial seals the deal.

On the Wallpaper* staff since 2004, Bridget Downing worked first as production editor and then chief sub editor on the print magazine. Executive editor since 2017, she turned to digital content-editing in 2021 and works with fellow editors to ensure smooth production on Wallpaper.com. With a BA in French with African and Asian Studies, she began her career in the editorial research library at Reader’s Digest’s UK edition, and has also worked at women’s titles. She is the author of the (2007) first editions of the Las Vegas and Cape Town Wallpaper* City Guides.

items.title: Looking for board games with a twist this holiday season? Game on
items.description: It's a season of gathering around the table, of family and friends getting together, and for some of us, it is also a peak time to dust off the board games of our youth and challenge guests to one of those never-ending tournaments that can lift the spirit of a
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: It's a season of gathering around the table, of family and friends getting together, and for some of us, it is also a peak time to dust off the board games of our youth and challenge guests to one of those never-ending tournaments that can lift the spirit of any holiday get-together.

Whether you're drawn to elevated takes on classics, like leather Monopoly or Bingo, or are looking for a more obscure entertainment to surprise your guests, here are our picks of imaginative and beautifully crafted games.
Discover classic board games with a twist

Forget the primary colours and childish illustrations of Snakes and Ladders that you might have seen before: this leather-bound edition features a calming graphic and detailed scientific illustrations of snakes, as well as leather pawns. Bonus: the reverse side features a leather-inlaid Ludo board, should you wish to mix things up.

Another game to add to our portfolio of luxury takes on classic entertainment, this limited edition Mancala board features sculptural glass, handwrought talismans, and signature beadwork. It is the result of a collaboration between skincare brand Kindred Black and 'Collector & Curator of Beads', Don't Let Disco founder Ashley Moubayed. The pair's take on colourful glass and symbolism is a match made in heaven, with each bead in the game chosen 'for its centuries-old history and symbolic power'.

This terrazzo domino set from The Conran Shop is a subtle update on a classic. Featuring engineered stone with brass inlays and a marble base, it is both timeless and elegant. To create the set, The Conran Shop has partnered with a producer that donates a portion of their profits to support children's education charities.

Will a bright, colourful and shiny crystal chess set distract you while you're strategising? It might, but it will also add a touch of sophistication to your coffee table. And it will likely make you smile every time you lay your eyes on it (there is a matching backgammon set too, if you want to add more sparkle to your life).

Most of us have played tic tac toe at some point in our lives, but it's likely that none of our games featured brass frogs on a wavy, inlaid mother-of-pearl board. Leave it to the Haas Brothers to shake up a classic with humour and beauty; their Noughts and Crosses for L'Objet is a joy.

Exquisitely crafted out of wanut wood and Poltrona Frau's Pelle Frau leather, this Mahjong Set features a leather box neatly containing all the elements of the game divided into compact trays. It is part of a larger collection of games created by the two companies, including checkers, backgammon and more. Not a fan of board games? No problem; should you prefer to blow off some steam instead, they also make a wood and leather ping pong set.

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

items.title: An editor's guide to small and useful design gifts for 2026
items.description: My favourite design objects combine rigorous, well-conceived forms with precise functionality. From legendary design objects that have stood the test of time, to new interpretations of classic typologies and the tools that make everyday life smoother and more
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: My favourite design objects combine rigorous, well-conceived forms with precise functionality. From legendary design objects that have stood the test of time, to new interpretations of classic typologies and the tools that make everyday life smoother and more pleasant, here is our list of small, useful design gifts. Any serious design lover will cherish these practical objects, where function goes hand in hand with form - and if you want to take functionality to an extreme, a classic Hay crate or Vitra toolbox in lieu of traditional gift wrapping will work wonders.
Small gifts for design lovers

In the world of stationery design, it doesn't get better than the classic Zenith stapler, an Italian icon from 1948. Made of steel with an enamelled body, it is still one of the most beautiful and precise staplers out there - and as a plus, it comes with a lifetime guarantee.

As soon as I found out that Faber Castell makes something called a 'perfect pencil', I was hooked. This writing tool's perfection lies in how it packs the life of the humble graphite pencil in one object: pencil, eraser, and one practical cap that includes a sharpener. What makes this gift great is that it also adapts to different levels of the gifting spectrum, being available in a handy everyday version, or this luxury take made of cedar wood and sterling silver.

This is probably my most gifted (and used) item: despite several brilliant moka designs having been produced in recent years, Richard Sapper's from 1978 is still a favourite in the world of the well-designed moka coffee maker.

The Solari time keepers have been around since the 1960s, and lately they are having a renaissance. Still made by the Italian company that first patented the flip clock mechanism, and created by architect Gino Valle, this modern classic is a must-have on any design-obsessed list.

I am a firm believer that you can never have too many small lights around in winter (and summer nights, too!), and while I often reach for our handy portable lights shopping guide for advice, I also love this take on the classic banker's lamp, here in clip-on version to practically attach anywhere in an interior. It's by Jasper Morrison alumnus John Tree, high on our list of designers to watch for functional, no-nonsense and extremely carefully considered designs.

At the other end of the lighting spectrum, I have been obsessed by this candle ornament that is part of Iittala collaboration with Byredo from earlier this year. A refractor designed to sit on a candle and amplify its light, I can't think of anything better to add a warm glow to winter nights.

items.title: Сведения и описание программного обеспечения в сфере информационных технологий.
items.description: В «Снобе» мы используем и развиваем собственные информационные технологии. Это не просто часть нашей работы, а основа всего проекта. В нашем IT-отделе мы решаем следующие задачи:
paragraphs: В «Снобе» мы используем и развиваем собственные информационные технологии. Это не просто часть нашей работы, а основа всего проекта. В нашем IT-отделе мы решаем следующие задачи:
- Создаем, улучшаем и поддерживаем все наши веб-ресурсы, включая сайт Snob.ru.
- Консультируем по вопросам, связанным с веб-разработкой и работой сайтов.
- Предоставляем онлайн-доступ к нашему контенту и различным цифровым сервисам.
- Разрабатываем собственные инструменты для работы с интернет-рекламой — от размещения до аналитики.
Ядро нашей IT-системы — это, конечно, федеральное сетевое издание Snob.ru.

Для того, чтобы вы могли удобно читать нас, а редакция — быстро и эффективно публиковать материалы, мы создали мощную собственную платформу. Это не стандартное коробочное решение, а наша уникальная разработка:
- Удобная система управления контентом (CMS), которая позволяет нашим редакторам создавать материалы в самых разных форматах, легко менять дизайн и структуру главной страницы и разделов.
- Автоматическая публикация контента не только на сайте, но и в наших социальных сетях и новостных агрегаторах.

Эта платформа полностью разработана нашей командой с использованием современных технологий: на фронтенде (то, что вы видите) используются HTML, CSS, TypeScript и JavaScript (с фреймворками Vue 2 и Vue 3); бэкенд (основная логика) написан на Python (с Django), а данные хранятся в базе PostgreSQL. Такая «кухня» позволяет нам быть гибкими и постоянно развивать функционал.

Сайт Snob.ru полностью кроссплатформенный. Это значит, что вы можете комфортно читать нас с любого устройства — компьютера, планшета или смартфона, на любой операционной системе (Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android, iOS). Мы позаботились о том, чтобы контент выглядел отлично везде.
Наша собственная разработка и круглосуточная поддержка в режиме 24/7 обеспечивают стабильную работу всего проекта, позволяя обрабатывать более 2 500 000 уникальных визитов в месяц.
Описание функциональных характеристик программного обеспечения
Программное обеспечение представляет собой современную систему управления контентом (CMS) сайта snob.ru, которая предназначена для следующих целей:
1. Работа редакции и контент-команд
- Позволяет оперативно создавать и публиковать материалы в различных форматах (новость, статья, интервью, тест и др.).
- Даёт возможность легко настраивать дизайн, менять структуру главной страницы и разделов без необходимости программирования.
- Поддерживает совместную работу над контентом, включая редактуру, модерацию и планирование публикаций.
2. Онлайн-платформа для авторов и читателей
- Предоставляет инструменты для ведения личных блогов, публикации авторских материалов и взаимодействия с аудиторией.
- Включает функции рейтингов и обсуждений, что помогает пользователям находить единомышленников и формировать сообщества.
