Venue agrees not to make reference to the article she read titled “Top Ten High-Paying Jobs That Literally Anyone Can Do with Zero Experience.” Venue will recall that she has already e-mailed and texted the article to Talent THREE (3) times. Venue is additionally aware that said article is not a real article but a clickbait advertisement generated by CareerMonkey.com, designed to trick people into buying a subscription to that site. Venue will not debate this fact by pointing at the article’s “byline” as “proof” that it’s a “real article.” Venue will accept the reality that many online ads are given bylines now, in order to make them look like real articles. If Venue insists that “this one looks real,” Talent will zoom in on the “article” and show Venue where it says “Paid Post,” and the debate will be settled. Venue will not read the words “Paid Post” out loud, in a suspicious tone of voice, and then shrug at VNH in a way that implies that there is still some ambiguity about whether it is a real article. Venue will just admit, for once in her life, that she was wrong about one thing. Jesus.

Venue agrees to reimburse Talent $432 for the cost of her round-trip plane ticket, but will not tell anyone that she had to do that, especially not Talent’s Perfect Doctor Brother with His Perfect Wife and Perfect Children (“TPDBHPWPC”).
On the night before TPDBHPWPC arrives, Talent will take Klonopin.

The following morning (a.k.a. “Thanksgiving”), Venue will refrain from entering Talent’s bedroom and opening Talent’s blinds in a passive-aggressive attempt to wake her up. If Venue breaks this stipulation, she will ADMIT that her intention was to wake up Talent. Venue will not make up an insane lie about wanting to “let air in.” Venue is aware that opening blinds does not let air in. Opening WINDOWS lets air in. Opening blinds just lets in bright, punishing light, right into Talent’s face.

When TPDBHPWPC pulls in with his station wagon, Talent requires FIVE (5) minutes to drink some coffee and just mentally prepare for all those fucking kids and all the questions about her getting fired and the goddam dance with her perfect sister-in-law Jenn about who’s going to do the stupid pie.

After drinking a MINIMUM of TWO (2) cups of coffee, Talent agrees to participate in a meet-and-greet session with TPDBHPWPC’s latest perfect baby and pose for a MAXIMUM of THREE (3) photographs holding said baby.

If VNH makes ANY kind of comment implying that Talent should have a baby by this point in her life, even if it is said in the most lighthearted, innocuous way (e.g., “You look pretty good holding one of those!”), it is Uber, airport, tearing through the sky to S.F. What fucking right does VNH have to say shit? He has been in the picture for a MAXIMUM of FOUR (4) years (unless he and Venue met while Dad was STILL ALIVE, which is math we’ll get into if this kind of shit keeps happening).
THANKSGIVING MEAL REQUIREMENTS

Talent shall be seated as far as possible from VNH, on the “wine side” of the table. Talent will not be required to initiate conversation during the meal. Talent agrees to politely listen to a MAXIMUM of TWO (2) dry updates about her high-school classmates’ parents who still live in town, provided they are of reasonable length and do not contain digressions about local real-estate developments. Talent will not point out each time Venue repeats a story but will internally keep track of the repetitions.

In between dinner and dessert, Talent will corner TPDBHPWPC in the kitchen and ask him his medical opinion about Venue’s fading memory. Talent will be surprised to hear from TPDBHPWPC that Venue’s senility is “age appropriate.” When Talent pushes back, TPDBHPWPC will tell Talent that Venue’s mental deterioration would be less of a shock if she had observed it more gradually, over the course of several visits, the implication being that she should visit Venue more. Talent will remind TPDBHPWPC that she works in San Francisco, and TPDBHPWPC will point out that she “doesn’t work there anymore.” Talent will be fucking devastated. Talent will catch sight of a faded family photo of a half-remembered trip to Sarasota, of Venue posing with Talent and TPDBHPWPC in some low-rent water park. Talent will try to mentally calculate Venue’s age in the picture, but be too drunk to do the math, and make TPDBHPWPC do it for her. Talent will be stunned to learn that Venue is TWO (2) years YOUNGER in the picture than Talent is now. Talent just won’t be able to believe that. It will almost be too crazy to process. Talent will be rocked by the sense that she is hurtling toward death with nothing to show for her FORTY (40) years on the planet but wasted potential. TPDBHPWPC will tell Talent that he needs to get back to the living room because his two-year-old is missing and probably making a mess. Talent will grip TPDBHPWPC’s wrist and ask him if he thinks Dad was proud of her before he died, even though she never paid him back for her ill-conceived master’s in museum studies. Talent will start to cry and not understand why she is crying. Jenn will come in to check on her pie, and quickly back out of the room. TPDBHPWPC will reiterate to Talent that he needs to search for his missing two-year-old. Talent will grip TPDBHPWPC’s wrist even harder and ask him if he thinks she’s too old to apply to law school, or business school, and if he thinks she should get back together with Dane, even though they had zero sexual connection. TPDBHPWPC will suggest that Talent drink ONE (1) glass of water.

When TPDBHPWPC is gone, Talent will stand alone in the dim kitchen for a MINIMUM of FIVE (5) minutes just completely spiralling, thinking about the darkest, most fucked-up shit. Talent will inwardly acknowledge that it was a mistake to use her loss of health insurance as an excuse to pause therapy.

Talent will feel a tug on her jeans. Talent will look down and see that TPDBHPWPC’s Missing Two-Year-Old (“M2YO”) has wandered into the kitchen at some point, because he smelled pie. M2YO will ask Talent for pie. Talent will realize that M2YO probably doesn’t know her name, or even how they’re related, because they’ve only met a MAXIMUM of THREE (3) times, and she forgot to mail him a birthday present this year because she is a worthless piece of shit. Talent will tearfully tell him that she is his Aunt Lauren, and that she is sorry for forgetting his birthday, and M2YO will shrug with absolute indifference, because he has no conception of time or genetic relatedness, and he will ask again for pie, in as loud a voice as he can muster, and all at once Talent will see herself through the eyes of M2YO, not as a failure, or a monster, or even as a human, really, just a physical barrier to pie, and she will temporarily reframe the weekend as a saga about pie, and a two-year-old’s quest to obtain it, and she’ll cut him a slice, and watch him shove it in his crusty mouth, surprised by how relieved she is to cede the stage, to give in to somebody—anybody—else’s demands, and she will laugh out loud for the first time in recent memory, feeling free and for one miraculous moment even slightly thankful.
At any moment, and without prior warning, all terms and conditions are subject to change. ♦

items.title: What I’m Thankful for This Thanksgiving
items.description: I'm thankful that we're all here together, celebrating Thanksgiving.
items.author: Colin Stokes
paragraphs: I'm thankful that we're all here together, celebrating Thanksgiving.
I'm thankful that you're not all on a Mediterranean vacation that was planned without me, like last year.
I'm thankful that Uncle John isn't here with his balloon animals.
I'm thankful that we were able to get such beautiful balloon animals for Uncle John's funeral, in February.
I'm thankful that any resentment that arose from my kissing every family member's wife, husband, girlfriend, or boyfriend on the mouth as they arrived at the house has dissipated.
I'm thankful that everyone seems to be enjoying the Thanksgiving CD I made.
I'm thankful that I am able to offer copies of my Thanksgiving CD at a special "friends and family" discounted price of only $15.99, while supplies last.
I'm thankful that all of the food has been cooked beautifully by one family member. Thanks, Suzanne.
I'm thankful that I have been able to show my gratitude for the cooking by thoughtfully maneuvering around Suzanne when I have to go into the kitchen to get more alcohol.
I'm thankful that the cousin who was vegetarian has decided to go vegan this year.
I'm thankful that he will be doing so at his girlfriend's family's house.
I'm thankful that the only fight we've had so far has been about whether or not we grew up in a loving household.
I'm thankful that we are participating in a 5K Turkey Trot in which we all run five kilometers in different directions.
I'm thankful that there's a deer outside! Look!
I'm thankful that it's so serene and beautiful. Wow.
I'm thankful that even though the deer turned out to be a burglar dressed in a deer costume, for a brief moment, we thought we had seen a majestic deer.
I'm thankful that I was able to negotiate with the burglar, and that he has agreed to trade me his deer costume in exchange for our television.
I'm thankful that, now that we don't have a television, we can spend time really getting to know one another, instead of watching football.
I'm thankful that I have this wonderful deer costume.
I'm thankful that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade happens, in New York, even though we don't have a television on which to watch it.
I'm thankful that in our town we have the Men's Wearhouse Thanksgiving Day Parade instead, in which a number of men walk down Main Street wearing rented tuxedos.
I'm thankful that, although I cannot participate in the Men's Wearhouse Thanksgiving Day Parade because I am wearing a deer costume, I am able to observe from the sidelines.
I'm thankful that we're sitting down to have a wonderful meal now.
I'm thankful that, even though we just realized that the man who took the television also took the turkey, we're still having a great time together.
I'm thankful that we'll be able to eat leftover mashed potatoes in the line outside of Best Buy as we wait to buy a new television on Black Friday.

items.title: The Party Will Go On at Butterworth’s
items.description: The chef Bart Hutchins warned me that D.C. would be dead on the eve of Election Day. Everyone had been gone for weeks, he said, campaigning in battleground states in advance of the midterms. Still, at seven-thirty that Monday, the dining room at Butterworth’s—
items.author: Hannah Goldfield
paragraphs: The chef Bart Hutchins warned me that D.C. would be dead on the eve of Election Day. Everyone had been gone for weeks, he said, campaigning in battleground states in advance of the midterms. Still, at seven-thirty that Monday, the dining room at Butterworth’s—the Capitol Hill restaurant that Hutchins co-owns, which has become a de-facto clubhouse for the young MAGA set—was packed and pulsing. It was last call on a special prix fixe that Hutchins had been running for a week: Foie Gras at the End of the World, four courses for a hundred and fifty dollars. All proceeds, the menu read, would go to the Foie Gras Legal Defense Fund.

Hutchins, who is thirty-six, with tousled auburn hair and professorial tortoiseshell glasses, had become the face of the opposition to Initiative 86, a measure that D.C. voters would find on the ballot the next day, which proposed banning the sale of foie gras within city limits. Hutchins was against I-86 for a host of reasons, some of them more sincere than others: it was Francophobic, it infringed on the rights of business owners, and it might be the first step down a slippery slope of dictating what Americans eat. (The national organization behind the initiative, Pro-Animal Future, had also worked to get a measure on the ballot in Denver.)

Critics of the proposal, including the chef José Andrés, have argued that foie-gras production, which often involves a technique called gavage—force-feeding ducks through plastic tubes to fatten their livers—is low on the list of food-related injustices in the U.S. There are just two small farms in the country (both in New York’s Hudson Valley) that sell foie gras commercially, and only a relative handful of restaurants that serve it. What happens at your average high-volume chicken farm, Hutchins contends, is more torturous than gavage. In 2005, at a meeting of the American Veterinary Medical Association’s house of delegates, one vet argued that the practice is no worse than “taking the rectal temperature of a cat.”

At dinner, I sampled a Waldorf salad made with Shenandoah apples and finished with a shower of foie gras “snow” (cured, frozen, and shaved) that melted lusciously on the tongue, then a foamy soup of foie gras and chestnuts, inspired by Jean-Louis Palladin, the longtime chef at the Watergate Hotel, who allegedly smuggled foie gras into the U.S. from France by cramming it down the throats of monkfish. A tartare from the regular menu made both soup and salad seem restrained: a pedestal of chopped lamb beneath a tower of pale, craggy onion rings, with a grill-marked medallion of wobbly foie gras planted on top like a flag.

Steve Bannon is a semi-regular at Butterworth’s; Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent have been in on several occasions. As I poked at a disconcerting “Twinkie” filled with foie-gras pastry cream, I noticed Hutchins greeting a table of young people in suits, some of whom he later identified as Rubio staffers. A larger table of twentysomethings in business casual—did he know them, too? Indeed: architects who worked for James McCrery II, whom Donald Trump hired to build his ballroom, and who then withdrew after alleged clashes over scale and safety. Neither the President nor the Vice-President has dined at Butterworth’s, perhaps because there’s no back entrance—a deal-breaker for the Secret Service.

Hutchins spent his early twenties working in Democratic politics; his wife, Katrina, whom he met on Twitter in 2021, used to work for the Daily Caller. He demurred when I asked if he considered himself a political person. “Me?” he asked, looking surprised. “I have very strong opinions about agriculture. I’m political about how we farm.” Hutchins sources ingredients for Butterworth’s from local Mennonite farmers; the menu combines sumptuous French cooking with a certain American verve. When I returned for lunch on Election Day, Hutchins ordered a spread that included half a dozen oysters, bone marrow topped with meaty morsels of escargot, and his signature, exceptionally crispy French fries, cooked in beef tallow. He wasn’t trying to pander to the anti-seed-oil MAHA crowd with the tallow fries, he told me. At his last restaurant, a Montreal-inspired place, he’d found that they held up nicely in poutine.

Hutchins grew up in Jacksonville, Florida, the youngest of ten children born to his biological father. (His mother, who struggled with drug addiction, was in and out of jail.) When he was nine, he was adopted by a conservative pastor and his wife, who sent him to a selective college-prep program. “The first time I read ‘Ulysses’ was under a bridge with a bunch of kids with Mohawks,” he said. He first clashed with his parents politically when he refused to register for the military reserves. “Iraq was so obviously stupid and so obviously a bad idea,” he said. “I was really confused by the George Bush version of the Republican Party having anything to do with my parents—like, you don’t own stock in Halliburton.”

After graduating from Auburn University, in Alabama, Hutchins enrolled briefly in a Presbyterian seminary but soon found his way to politics, working as a staffer on Barack Obama’s reëlection bid, in 2012, and then on the campaign to elect Terry McAuliffe as Virginia’s Democratic governor. He lost his taste for the establishment in 2017, while working for the Nevada Senate Democratic Caucus. A bill to cap the price of insulin had passed the state Senate, but was killed by lobbyists when it got to the House; Hutchins quit with just two weeks left in the legislative session and “followed a girl to Iowa.” He thought about becoming a welder, before walking into a restaurant that he liked in Des Moines, Eatery A, and asking if he could work there for free.

Hutchins cooked in D.C. restaurants through the pandemic and then decamped to rural Minnesota with Katrina and their toddler son. The plan was to spend more time hunting and to try his luck as a novelist, but the isolation was harder than the couple expected. Hutchins began consulting on what would eventually become Butterworth’s, named for its principal owner, Alex Butterworth, then an attorney for Uber; the family moved back to Washington in 2024. “There was a power vacuum because the Trump Hotel was closed,” Hutchins said. Another of the restaurant’s co-owners, Raheem Kassam, who served as an adviser to Nigel Farage and as Breitbart’s London editor, drew the MAGA acolytes to Butterworth’s instead.

“For my part, I don’t think people who are interested in the Trump thing are automatically bad people—it shouldn’t be a controversial thing to say, but it is,” Hutchins told me. His adoptive father, a floor installer, is “constantly underbid on jobs by presumably illegal migrants, so I get the Trump version of the Republican Party having something to say to my dad.” Hutchins said that when it comes to Butterworth’s clientele—particularly those who believed Trump when he promised not to start wars in the Middle East—“the worst thing you could say about them is they’re naïve.” He added, “I really do believe in service as an ethic, so I’m gonna take care of whoever I’m serving to the best of my ability.”

As if on cue, one of Hutchins’s antagonists, Meghan Abrego, appeared outside the restaurant. For the past several months, Abrego, a Maryland resident (and a registered Independent), had been carting around her four-year-old pet duck, a fluffy Swedish Blue named Olivia Gray, in a wagon outfitted with pee pads and a bowl of water and grapes. Abrego adopted Olivia as an egg, on eBay, and hatched her in an incubator. (She also assigned Olivia she/her pronouns, though the animal is technically male.) Now she lifted the duck from the cart, letting her roam on the sidewalk and mingle with passersby.

Abrego had spent the morning campaigning for I-86 outside Eastern Market, a Capitol Hill food hall that also serves as a polling place. She and Hutchins had met before, and had developed a friendly rapport. Though Abrego sees gavage as torture, “I can understand Chef Bart’s argument,” she said. “I figured I would come through here because I wanted to grab a bite.” She pushed Olivia’s cart through the front door and sat down for fries and a glass of prosecco; the last time she’d come in, Hutchins had offered Olivia an off-menu dish of roasted cherry tomatoes. Abrego reminded Hutchins about a party she’d invited him to that night, co-hosted by Pro-Animal Future and Oye Owolewa, a vegan who was running to be a D.C. council-member-at-large. He promised that he would try to make it.

At around 9 P.M., I found Abrego and Olivia on the raucous second floor of Solly’s U Street Tavern, where I-86 supporters were eating pizza and drinking beer at tables arranged with gold plastic ducks. The bill had passed, as Hutchins had expected, though he was confident that it would be years before the ban took effect, if it ever did; there were sure to be legal appeals, and city officials had estimated that enforcement would cost more than three hundred thousand dollars. A partygoer yelled over the music to ask if Olivia, who was quacking steadily, was comfortable in her current environment. “Yeah!” Abrego shouted back, as if it was obvious.

A Catholic businessmen’s dinner and a local G.O.P. watch party had kept Hutchins busy at Butterworth’s. Late that night, the party spilled onto the sidewalk, with attendees smoking cigarettes and cigars and sipping amber liquor from snifters. The mood was resigned, if not quite sombre; a young man who worked for Turning Point USA tipsily thanked me for coming. Earlier, I’d asked Hutchins if he worried about what would happen to the restaurant if and when MAGA fell out of power. Some of his customers joke that the Trump Administration will answer for its sins at “the Butterworth trials,” he told me. But, he said, “we have a pretty significant following in what I’ll vaguely call the Bernie left. If the Democrats are gonna take power, it’s gonna be those people, because they’re not, like, boring losers.” Did he think the Sanders crowd would have an appetite for foie gras? “There’s, like, a French proletariat thing. Imagine you’re a young populist—you have some French sympathies because they’re the only people who have ever been true populists in a meaningful way,” he said. “Also, we have a pretty extensive natural-wine list, which they all seem to love.” ♦

items.title: Have Yourself a Kitschy Little Christmas
items.description: Last year, the Brooklyn gallery “B” Dry Goods, which specializes in rare and eclectic ephemera—current offerings include a striped shirt once worn by Chet Baker ($1,500), a bottle that held Seconal pills prescribed to Marlene Dietrich ($5,000), and one of Diet
items.author: Rachel Syme
paragraphs: Last year, the Brooklyn gallery “B” Dry Goods, which specializes in rare and eclectic ephemera—current offerings include a striped shirt once worn by Chet Baker ($1,500), a bottle that held Seconal pills prescribed to Marlene Dietrich ($5,000), and one of Dietrich’s half-smoked cigarettes—began selling off the home library of the eighty-seven-year-old queer poet and eccentric collector Frank Bidart. I spent a long afternoon rummaging through Bidart’s old books and emerged with several gems, one of which was a floppy volume from 1972, compiled by the Belgian author Jacques Sternberg, called “Kitsch.” I may have the only copy of this book that belonged to Bidart himself, but there are other copies on eBay, and I cannot recommend enough getting your hands on one. It is a delight. The back cover opens with a variation of the Marcel Duchamp quote “Taste is the enemy of art,” then says, “Remembering this, we assure you that this book contains absolutely no examples of good taste.” Sternberg isn’t exaggerating; the book is full of gaudy images, such as a painting by the surrealist Pierre Le Colas of a busty Brigitte Bardot in a fuzzy catsuit. Sternberg writes, “It may be impossible to decide what percentage of bad-taste, stupidity or trash goes towards making up kitsch but it’s difficult to deny that excess is kitsch’s very life blood.”

We live in a time that is, in some ways, defined by its visual ugliness. The botched, cracking Reflecting Pool, the glut of uncanny A.I. slop, the preponderance of ill-fitting polyester clothing. But we are also experiencing a “good taste” boomlet—everyone is desperate to have it, and also to share their discerning eye with others. Just look at all the recommendation letters on Substack, or at the explosion of best-of lists. Or take Letterboxd, the social network where cinema fanatics squabble over film aesthetics, and the fact that its highly engaged user base has become so valuable that the New York Times might pay three hundred and thirty million dollars to acquire it. It’s not enough to be an influencer anymore; everyone wants to be a tastemaker.

Perhaps this is the natural evolution of the A.I. backlash; ChatGPT can do many things, but it cannot have original style—it is by definition a regurgitative engine. But it still feels like we are not doing enough to combat the machines. The true way to evade the algorithm is not to flaunt one’s own good taste but to hunt down the kitschy, weird, and even tacky items that the computers would never think to recommend, simply because they aren’t trained to do so. Sure, these gifts are not mass-approved, and may very well backfire. But why play it safe?
Feeling Blue (and Green, and Lilac, and Hot Pink)

I recently walked into a Sephora in midtown Manhattan—it was the biannual twenty-per-cent-off member sale, I am a weak woman, etc.—and had the sudden urge to buy blue eyeshadow. Maybe it was because I’d just rewatched “The Love Witch,” Anna Biller’s 2016 film, in which Samantha Robinson plays a witch who wears nineteen-sixties Mod outfits and the most beautiful turquoise eye look I’ve ever seen (you can replicate it via this tutorial, which I keep bookmarked), but the spirit really moved me. I was reminded of a wonderful essay by Alice Gregory, about the joys of wearing blue eyeshadow despite its kitschy reputation. “Blue eye shadow is a crude trick, one that efficiently enhances a performance of femininity,” Gregory wrote. “It’s no surprise that it appeals to fourth graders and drag queens.” (I would add to that list: Lana Del Rey, Chappell Roan, and the cast of “Euphoria.”) Blue eyeshadow feels dated and timeless at the same time; it is somehow inappropriate for both a trip to the supermarket and a night at the opera and also an ideal choice for either occasion. A resourceful Sephora employee guided me toward the Hung Vanngo Color Story eyeshadow palette in Brilliant Blue ($49), a collection of eight azure shades that has proved so popular that it regularly sells out. Vanngo, a makeup artist who works with the likes of Anne Hathaway and Julianne Moore, has been pushing saturated eye colors in a big way lately, although, as the same Sephora employee lamented, “He’s really the only person releasing bright hues right now.” She did also mention the brand Fara Homidi, whose Essential Eye Compact in Trio No. 61 ($98) features one of the creamiest, most alluring bright-blue shades on the market, but she whispered to me that if I really wanted to dive into highly pigmented shadows, I needed to look into indie cosmetics houses, where the true innovations in flamboyant maquillage are happening. I did some digging, and found some winners, featuring dramatic neon colors, duochromes, glitters, and other sparkly enticements: the Blend Bunny Lure palette ($46), the Thunderstruck palette from Gourmande Girls ($56), the Ocean Jewel palette from bellabeautébar ($75), and the Succulent Dew palette from Singe Beauty ($45). There is a whole world of Day-Glo eye paint out there to explore—and to give. Go play!

I recommend including a set of micro-brushes from the new brand Kraum ($149), an arsenal of teeny tools that allow for precise application. Also, a hot tip: If you give someone bold eyeshadow, give them an easy way to correct their mistakes—it will encourage experimentation. The Half Magic Flik Eraser makeup-correcting pen ($25) is a nifty little gadget designed just for this purpose.

Over the past few years, workout gear has gotten very stylish—almost too stylish, if you ask me. Everywhere you turn, you see women walking around the city in sleek matching sets of spandex leggings and sports bras in subdued shades of chocolate brown and butter yellow. Allegedly, younger fitness buffs are pushing against such hegemony; according to trend reporters, Gen Z likes their athletic gear to be loose, rather than suctioned tight to the body, and they are buying vintage activewear in droves. But we would all do well to make working out more fun, at least sartorially, so why not lean into high camp? Why not dress like Jamie Lee Curtis in “Perfect”? The brand Daughter Lessons, founded by the sisters Lizzy and Caroline Tierney, is bringing kitsch back to the gym. I’m wild about their Retrofit Tights ($110), which have an Olivia Newton-John vibe, and their NYMO short jumpsuit ($114), which is giving Cher Horowitz watching “Buns of Steel.” I’m also a fan of the metallic leggings from Heroine Sport ($118) and the rainbow of bike-short options ($30) from Los Angeles Apparel. If you’re more of a swimmer, you can be the gaudiest person at the pool in the Left on Friday bikini in the acid hue Tourist ($110 each for the top and high-cut bottom). This summer, while I was visiting L.A., a friend took me to the kitschiest workout class I’d ever been to, at Killer Fitness, a studio that offers cardio dance classes set to horror-movie soundtracks. (It’s a blast, and I hope they franchise it soon!) Even if you cannot get to California, the studio has an online shop selling its own fitness-clothing line, inspired by eighties culture. I recommend the aquamarine leopard-print sports bra ($40) and matching leggings ($43), or the VHS bike shorts ($19).

Shirts—T-shirts, that is—are so good lately. You can find pretty much anything under the sun printed on a T-shirt; the only limit is your imagination. Novelty shirts are a safe way to introduce kitschiness into your gift-giving practice; if nothing else, the receiver could wear theirs as a pajama top (or donate it to Goodwill). Although I always recommend going the thrifted route for one-of-a-kind surprises, some brands are really excelling at the shirt game right now. New to me this year is Branko Brand, an apparel company dedicated to preserving “queer and outcast history.” Its site is a camp-hunter’s trove. There are shirts emblazoned with Faye Dunaway’s face from “Mommie Dearest,” a logo for the defunct New York night club Danceteria, and, of course, Liza (all $30).

Elsewhere, the internet is full of wearable weirdness. How about a Grand Slam breakfast shirt? ($32). Or a shirt printed with John Waters’s famously mustachioed visage ($45)? Or a shirt heralding female bodybuilders everywhere ($45)? Or a Knicks-Madonna crossover shirt ($45)? Or a shirt celebrating Ken Russell’s newly remastered cult classic “The Devils” ($32)? The iconic, hippieish wolf-howling-at-moon shirt ($40) is so quintessentially tacky that it has come around to being fashionable again, as is the retro tuxedo tee ($22). If all else fails, you can always pay homage to the dearly departed Dolly ($34).

What could be more excessive than feathered embellishments? Nobody needs them. But bird-adjacent accoutrement is nonetheless having a moment. Ostrich-feather pins are a tiptoe in—they can be clipped onto any lapel or handbag for an easy pop of too-muchness. They range in price, from the fancy (Flora and Henri brooch, $335) to the more affordable (J. Crew brooch, $60). I have also been coveting a pair of feather cuffs ($148) from the New York-based brand Collective Good Shop, in addition to one of its feather-trimmed button-downs ($448). A feather-lined balaclava from P.A.R.O.S.H ($452) is not exactly a winter essential, but there’s nothing wrong with cold-weather frivolities. Whatever gets you through the season.

While we’re on the topic of outfit additives, have you heard? Brooches are officially back. But, even when they’re not in vogue, brooches are a kitsch staple; nothing limns the borders of good taste like a jacket festooned with flashy bijoux. So, forthwith, a list of kooky adornments, in no particular order: a gleaming nineteen-fifties-style cat ($10); an enamelled Marcel Boucher shrimp ($595); a pearl-covered shaggy dog ($145); a bubble-bath bauble ($30); a pair of wooden clogs ($31); a smiling Carmen Miranda ($30); a glass puffer fish ($128); a retro resin poodle ($8); a Bode sequined pony ($180); a funky Karen Rossi lady ($15); a bejewelled tropical bird, from the Met Store ($148); and a golden gladiolus, from Jennifer Behr ($290). Also, every brooch collector needs a place to, well, collect them, and for that there’s this charming beaded tchotchke tray ($78), from the new collaboration between Anthropologie and the popular Manhattan jewelry and ornaments store Susan Alexandra.

Nothing screams kitsch like a clown; they are the patron saints of showy overexertion. A few big-top-inspired gifts caught my eye this year. A vintage citrus juicer ($49). A sixties Pierrot lamp ($439). A bizarro prayer candle ($35) that might bring some magic into your life. Dangly earrings ($52 for two pairs). Harlequin-inspired palazzo pants from Selkie ($169). A gorgeous lace collar ($30-$45), drawn from classical clown costuming, that would enliven any blouse. A Kyse perfume ($95) designed to smell like funnel cake at the circus. A Diptyque candle carrousel ($115) that, when added atop any flame, spins like a merry-go-round. A pearlescent box ($72) modelled on a carnival tent, to hold all your junk. A bit of Bozo merch ($29). A soft, funfetti-print jumpsuit with a ruffled collar and cuffs ($218), or this striped jumpsuit ($248) that is giving Marcel Marceau. A bop bag for kids ($16) to help conquer a fear of clowns. And a Chopova Lowena beanie ($262) that pushes clownery into the realms of high fashion.
Household Fripperies and New Age Knickknacks

Housewares are an evergreen gift category, inasmuch as they tend to be safe bets; nobody is going to turn up their nose at a nice pair of minimalist candlesticks, a soft cashmere throw, or an understated serving platter. And, sure, if you are giving a present to, say, your boss, or your distant aunt, or your brother’s new girlfriend, then by all means select something plain and inoffensive. But, for the person who appreciates a more whimsical home good, why not go with something less foolproof? My guiding principle when buying is, Would a person think this is amazing or hideous? If the answer is “Maybe both!” that’s the sweet spot. Items that fit the brief: A Kit-Cat Klock ($60), from California Clock. A colorful Mexican oilcloth curtain ($98). A quaint German toy house that tells the temperature ($60). A candle shaped like a pineapple upside-down cake ($80). A “Peep Show” bathmat ($28). A swimming-pool rug ($60). For the holidays, a poodle skirt for the tree ($49). A traditional Lenox swan-boat dish ($40) might seem a bit corny and outdated, but when repurposed as a jewelry holder it becomes fresh again. Gangzaï makes trays with a sense of humor—I’m partial to the fish with fan fins ($94) and the leopard in a wig ($58).

To brighten things up, there’s always neon, such as this light-up Warhol Brillo box ($500) or a waving lucky cat ($50). A ceramic stapler shaped like a leopard ($84) is as silly as it is practical, as is a tattooed-lady doll ($48) that can hold open a heavy book. My kitsch sensibilities have also been gravitating, lately, toward the celestial realm; I’ve found myself drawn to campy, New Age-y décor, such as an Art Nouveau-esque moon-girl blanket ($150), a glowy yawning moon ($40) that looks pulled from Georges Méliès’s 1902 film, and a hand-tufted wizard rug ($645). The only limit is the stars.

If the streets of New York City are any indication, smoking seems to be back; I can’t walk a block these days without being engulfed in a cloud of smoke. Whether or not you indulge in such tacky behavior is your own business (I myself have been known to bum a ciggy or five outside a bar after midnight; don’t judge!), but there are safer ways to engage with cigarettes than inhaling them. You could, for instance, put them on a birthday cake in the form of trompe-l’oeil candles ($15). Or you could burn a pack of cigarette-inspired incense sticks ($35), which come in a pleasing cardboard pack (and which do not smell of tar but rather of woodsmoke and cinnamon). Or hang a glass ornament of a cigarette butt ($20) on the tree. I have given several people a Mary-Kate & Ash tray ($38) over the years, and it always gets a laugh.

A golden pendant necklace inspired by an Art Deco cigarette holder is a stunner (at $12,800, it would have to be), and there is a less pricey piece by Ambush ($272) designed to hold an actual cigarette. A lighter case is never an unwelcome trinket—a gemstone one from Edie Parker ($65) and a beaded, lobster-shaped one from Susan Alexandra ($62) are equally charming. If you want to avoid smoking at all costs, there are other ways to give someone a hit of playful naughtiness; how about this Discothèque fragrance-discovery set ($39), in which all the perfumes come in foil packages that look like Trojan wrappers? Or a Like a Prayer candle from Boy Smells ($48), inspired by Madonna, that smells like doing something sinful in church? (You could pair it with the Madonna-Knicks T-shirt, linked above, to complete the theme).

Kitsch is a state of mind—it’s about going for it to the point of ridiculousness. It’s about unlearning what society has told you is sophisticated and learning how to follow your own nose. But, if you don’t yet feel that sense of abandon, you can outsource it. Allow the Thrift Gift Co. to put together a Kitschy Spirit box (starting at $35) for you. Or, if you want to do the research yourself, you can grab the classic text “The Encyclopedia of Bad Taste,” by Jane and Michael Stern ($9 for a used copy). Lastly, you can preorder a copy of the philosopher Matthew Strohl’s forthcoming book, “The Trash Collector: Better Living Through Bad Taste” ($30), due out in February. In it, Strohl makes a case for the “cardinal virtues of trash”—humility, curiosity, openness, adventurousness, creativity, sincerity, fellowship, and authenticity. Buy one for a friend who you know will get it. ♦

items.title: Politicians Really Suck at GTA Memes
items.description: You may have noticed that the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI is having a cultural megamoment this week. It seems like everyone is talking about it. The reviews are astounding. The sales are booming. The clips are all over social media, and the res
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: You may have noticed that the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI is having a cultural megamoment this week. It seems like everyone is talking about it. The reviews are astounding. The sales are booming. The clips are all over social media, and the resulting discourse is tearing across the internet like a boosted monster truck. The New York Times Magazine has published a piece entitled “Grand Theft Auto Used to Satirize American Life. Now We’ve Caught Up With It.” Leftist streamer Hasan Piker briefly gave up chatting about politics to play it. And, yes, Fox News and the denizens of the manosphere have found reasons to complain about it. The game is arguably the most with-it thing that happened this week, and that also means it was inevitable that politicians would try to join — and thus ruin — the fun.
First, the White House social team could not resist trying to piggyback onto the hype and posted this on Wednesday night:
Then the similarly unpopular House Republicans, or at least the ones still coming to work, decided they, too, wanted in on the action:
And then the group Majority Democrats just could not let that stand:
But poor J.D. Vance apparently felt left out, so he posted his own AI-slop version (which includes a prominent image of him next to Trump):
And then whoever is still left at the Lincoln Project was like, “Au contraire!”
Finally, Mike Huckabee — the same Mike Huckabee who has been a critic of these kinds of video games since the 1990s — somehow decided this might be cool:

items.title: How to Be a Horrible Boss Like Jensen Huang
items.description: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s many apparent flaws as a leader have come into full focus since his abrupt departure from the company amid allegations of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and at least two employees. In addition to the damage his scandal ha
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s many apparent flaws as a leader have come into full focus since his abrupt departure from the company amid allegations of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and at least two employees. In addition to the damage his scandal has done to the company, one of the biggest revelations has been how he apparently liked to manage his employees like a sadistic drill sergeant — and more stories and details of his abusive behavior continue to emerge. Here’s a guide to his leadership style, based on those specific examples.
Inspire the Best With These Violent Threats
Tell employees things like: I will rip off the top of your head and “pee on your brain.”
Huang embraced the creative destruction of his employees self-esteem, according to the New York Times:

He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”
“I hope you get the flu and I hope it gets worse. I hope you die and put us all out of our misery.”

“I hope you get the flu and I hope it gets worse,” Huang told [former Nvidia executive VP Jay] Puri in front of stunned onlookers — including Puri, who endured the sudden attack in silence, according to a source familiar to the incident.
“I hope you die and put us all out of our misery,” Huang added.
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it.”
That’s what former Nvidia HR leader Michael Winston says Huang once said at a 50-person off-site meeting in 2004. Per the Times:

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”
Or try a death-threat roundtable.

Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said. In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident.
From the The Wall Street Journal:
In group meetings, [employees said Huang] sometimes used the term “dead-face” to describe staffers’ blank expressions after he scolded them.
Sources briefed on the matter described a well-known clash in which Huang lost his temper with a senior leader who was attending a meeting with the mercurial boss for the first time.
“Are you smirking at me? I see nothing but dead faces … Get out!”
“Say it, Frenchie! Say ‘Chowdah!’”

Okay, Huang didn’t actually reenact Freddy Quimby’s infamous Francophobic ridicule from The Simpsons, but he came close. While moderating a panel discussion at a Nvidia conference, Huang kept interrupting a French CEO to complain about his accent, at one point telling him, “You’re not even speaking human.”
Take your time when delivering diatribes.

He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash.”
Talent Management Strategies
Banish executives instead of firing them.

When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange. Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said.
Tell older staff you look forward to their death.
Per the Times, during that death-threat roundtable mentioned above, “when he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.”
Hire your kids and let at least one of them be a terror.

Huang hired his daughter, Madison, and made her his chief of staff, and she has reportedly followed her dad’s lead when it comes to abusive treatment of employees. She reportedly berates staff and calls people who can’t remember something “goldfish.” Nvidia insiders told the Times that more than a dozen executives have left the company because they didn’t want to work with her:

In meetings with other employees, Ms. Huang has yelled at her brother and executives who, on paper, managed her or were above her organizationally. Late last year, as Ms. Huang yelled at others on Nvidia’s marketing team, a vice president had a panic attack and had to leave the call with her, said two people familiar with the meeting.
Build up your interim successor’s confidence.
Per the Journal, at a meeting over the summer, Huang “proceeded to tear into” CFO Colette Kress, who Nvidia’s board made interim CEO after Huang resigned:
Kress was “a deer in the headlights,” he said, interrupting her presentation, according to a person familiar with the comments.
Don’t take any crap from HR if they don’t understand the value of your abuse.
Former Nvidia HR executive Michael Winston raised an alarm about the CEO’s behavior within the company and also confronted Huang, who told him the abuse was integral, per the Times:

He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.
He later sued Nvidia after Huang fired him with the rationale that he was “not a good fit” and received a $1 million settlement.

items.title: Mike Johnson Begs Deadbeat House Republicans to Come to Work
items.description: Just before and immediately after the 2026 midterm debacle for Republicans, you could hear bully-boy talk about how the GOP would pick ‘em up and lay ‘em down during a post-election lame duck session, maximizing their power until the very moment they handed it
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Just before and immediately after the 2026 midterm debacle for Republicans, you could hear bully-boy talk about how the GOP would pick ‘em up and lay ‘em down during a post-election lame duck session, maximizing their power until the very moment they handed it over to Democrats. The White House in particular was said to really really want a rush-job of a party-line budget reconciliation bill crammed full of Trump priorities that his allies had not been able to accomplish during their previous two years of trifecta control of Washington.

Yesterday, however, word spread on Capitol Hill that Reconciliation 3.0, the aforementioned giant bag of MAGA treats, wasn’t happening after all. And today one key reason for an especially lame lame-duck session became clear via a missive House Speaker Mike Johnson sent to his troops, as Axios reported:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren’t over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. …
Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP’s legislative agenda.
GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation.
Eleven of those 14 won’t be returning next Congress.
The letter is rather pathetic. Johnson resorts to whining about his recalcitrant charges:

This week we had to postpone the rule scheduled for the Floor because we didn’t have enough Members in town. To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term. …
The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn’t run out until noon on January 3rd.

Perhaps this is the equivalent to Senioritis, the affliction that strikes kids near graduation from high school, or maybe it’s more like the attitude Army folk call FIGMO (“Fuck It, Got My Orders”) when a posting comes to an end. But in any event, Johnson is justifiably annoyed. Nobody is more eager to get the hell out of Washington and go hang Christmas ornaments than Johnson himself, who was briskly replaced as his party’s legislative leader on the second day of the post-election session, making him the lamest duck of them all. So he probably has little sympathy for those still drawing a congressional paycheck but who are already moseying on to the next stop in the great cattle-drive of life.

Johnson’s successor as Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, can’t gloat too much about all this. He, too, has experienced attendance problems, notably when an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth failed after 11 House Democrats missed a vote on a motion to table the resolution. He’ll be in a position to impose discipline soon enough, though, while Johnson and his deadbeat members will suffer a power outage lasting at least two years.

items.title: Trump Begins Last Two Years More Unpopular Than Ever
items.description: The midterm elections were so definitive that Donald Trump did not even bother to dispute the fairness of the election or the accuracy of the count. But to no one’s surprise, voters’ deep dissatisfaction with his leadership has not prompted a change in behavio
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The midterm elections were so definitive that Donald Trump did not even bother to dispute the fairness of the election or the accuracy of the count. But to no one’s surprise, voters’ deep dissatisfaction with his leadership has not prompted a change in behavior from the president. Since Election Day, he has doubled down on some of his most unpopular positions and personnel, lifted the terrifying Stephen Miller to the top of the White House staff, and devoted most of his time to pet projects ranging from the Triumphal Arch to his friendship with autocrats. And even as he digs in and spits defiance at his enemies, he’s mired in a slough of unpopularity that denies him the political capital to stage a comeback in the foreseeable future.

The first round of postelection polling provides no good news for the 47th president. According to the averages at Silver Bulletin, his job-performance ratings are at 36.5 percent approval and 60.3 percent disapproval. That puts his net job approval at minus-23.8 percent, just above his lowest number ever, minus-24.3 percent, recorded on October 21. The percentage of Americans registering strong disapproval of the job Trump is doing is at 49.5 percent, the highest ever. Of 11 postelection polls, nine show his job approval under 40 percent, which is traditionally the danger point for any president.

The latest (November 16) Economist-YouGov survey may shed some light on Trump’s decision to react to his midterms repudiation by clinging more closely than ever to his MAGA base. Here’s a list of voter categories in which 60 percent or more disapprove of the president’s job performance: women (66 percent), Blacks (77 percent), Hispanics (67 percent), people age 30–44 (66 percent), people age 45–64 (63 percent), those with a college degree (64 percent), those without a college degree (60 percent), moderates (73 percent), independents (69 percent), and, oh, of course, liberals (94 percent) and Democrats (95 percent). The disaffection extends into his own ranks, too: 22 percent of 2024 Trump voters and 20 percent of conservatives disapprove of the job he is doing. But proudly and alone, 91 percent of self-identified MAGA supporters approve of Trump’s job performance.

There’s no reason to expect that this self-isolation is coming to an end soon. The all-but-certain first major flash point of conflict between Trump and congressional Democrats will be over the war in Iran. Support for that war, as measured in Silver Bulletin’s polling averages, is now at an all-time low, with 30.8 percent backing it and 60.4 percent opposed. It’s even less popular than the commander-in-chief who launched it. But is there any category of Americans committed to seeing Trump’s war of choice carried out to the bitter end? Yes; according to a November 11 Economist-YouGov poll, 61 percent of self-identified MAGA supporters want to “keep fighting until all U.S. objectives have been achieved.” For all the talk of Trump’s base (and even his vice-president!) blaming the war for the GOP’s midterms debacle, MAGA is still with him in the trenches on this doomed endeavor.

Some might go further: an October 21 Times-Siena poll asking (without identifying candidates) prospective Republican primary participants whom they preferred for president in 2028 showed “President Donald Trump” running third behind his vice-president and his secretary of State but well ahead of Ron DeSantis, Ted Cruz, Tucker Carlson, and Trump’s own son. Though he’s not in denial (at least yet) about the results of the 2026 midterms, perhaps he will go into denial about the 22nd Amendment, which will soon force his retirement.

items.title: Mamdani’s Achilles’ Heel: Playing Soccer Against the Press
items.description: As reporters and advocates assembled inside the City Hall rotunda to watch Zohran Mamdani unveil his administration’s plan to close Rikers Island, they were taken aback by an unexpected sight: the young mayor entering on crutches and wearing a boot on his righ
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: As reporters and advocates assembled inside the City Hall rotunda to watch Zohran Mamdani unveil his administration’s plan to close Rikers Island, they were taken aback by an unexpected sight: the young mayor entering on crutches and wearing a boot on his right foot.
“I tore my Achilles,” Mamdani said as he fielded questions from the media.

During the nearly hour-and-a-half-long event, Mamdani sat on a nearby stool, rising to the podium with a slight hobble when speaking. The cause of the injury? A friendly game of soccer between the mayor’s communications team at City Hall and the press corps, which — Mamdani was happy to note — his team won 10-5.

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35. And soon after, I tore my Achilles, and I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks, and I will play soccer in about nine months,” he said to murmurs and groans of sympathy from the crowd. Mamdani also acknowledged that he failed to stretch before joining the match.
There are more details in Hell Gate’s vivid dispatch from the match (which, notably, put the final score at 8-4):

Around 7:45 p.m., a member of the mayor’s entourage noted that he had four minutes left. City Hall was up 7-4. The mayor was on the offensive, and the ball had drifted his way when he suddenly crumpled to the ground holding his right leg. At first, it was difficult to tell how hurt he was. But imagine you are one of the most famous politicians in the world, and you injure yourself in front of dozens of journalists whose job it is to cover your every move, and you tear your Achilles muscle. How much of that can you reveal? The mayor’s grimace-to-smile ratio spoke volumes as WNYC’s David Brand helped him off the field.

The injury did not keep the mayor from his scheduled remarks on a plan to shutter Rikers by 2032, five years later than currently mandated. As Mamdani began to speak, he briefly made light of his situation, saying that it was an honor to be “barely” standing alongside the New Yorkers who worked for years toward Rikers’ closure. When City Council Speaker Julie Menin began her own speech, she offered Mamdani well wishes regarding his injury. “I want to assure everyone it is not because of a budget fight with the Council,” she said to laughs from the room.

items.title: Looking for a job you can dedicate yourself to? Be warned, the new world of work might scupper your dreams
items.description: I have not been very promiscuous. It might have been fun but I am just not that kind of guy. It means that in a career that now stretches across four decades, I have only had three places of work. The most recent of these, Monocle, has proved to be the longest
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: I have not been very promiscuous. It might have been fun but I am just not that kind of guy. It means that in a career that now stretches across four decades, I have only had three places of work. The most recent of these, Monocle, has proved to be the longest lasting. This week, LinkedIn informed me that I have just hit my 20th work anniversary in the business.

Now I am not going to make you accompany me all the way down memory lane just yet. That will happen this coming 14 February when we celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first issue of the magazine hitting newsstands. But do you mind if we head down the lane just a little way? I promise that you won’t even need your wellies.

While I was having dinner with Tyler, I asked for his advice about a couple of jobs that I had been offered. And that’s when he suggested that, before I made any hasty decisions, I should come see him the following morning. He wanted to show me a new magazine that he was working on with the working title, “Project Europa”. And it was a project that he would like me to edit. If I agreed, however, I would need to stay put at the newspaper where I was employed as he was still raising the start-up capital. The next morning, I went to see him and he showed me mocked-up covers and some poster-sized sheets created to show potential advertisers what was in store. I wanted to be part of this.

It took some months for the money to be raised but one day the CEO, Robyn Holt, phoned me and, in her great Aussie voice, said, “Doll, the money is in the bank. Resign.” I did. And just look at what has unfolded.

I have been lucky in many ways, including becoming friends with Tyler when we were both in our twenties (though he’s annoyingly younger than me). But also because I have been able to work on this magazine for so long. How rare will that be in the future?

This week I went to the launch of a report by Imperial Lifelong Learning – part of Imperial College London – called “Everyone but me: What UK employees told us about AI and skills”. Turns out that most people think that they have AI know-how but co-workers don’t. There was a panel of enthusiasts: all believers that AI has the potential to create efficiencies and aid creativity.

But as I listened, I also sensed that we were entering a world where staff will never be able to drop their guard. They will constantly need to look over their shoulders, fearing that they might become obsolete. How do we ensure that lifelong learning doesn’t become lifelong worry? And will people who don’t want numerous work partners be able to find a company where they are wanted, not for a quickie, but for something meaningful and long-lasting?

Last Saturday, on a perfect autumn day with trees ablaze with rich red leaves and the sun reflecting pools of mellow light off ancient windows, we went with friends from Madrid to the V&A. We drifted through rooms filled with bronze sculptures, Bauhaus silver and ecclesiastical treasures. It’s free to visit the V&A and the museum was full of people from every corner of the world. Then we headed to Soho for noodles and, later, dinner at Café Clement. The city was at its best, at ease, joyous.

As more places seek to dissuade tourists – unless they are rich – from clogging up their streets and as many European capitals hide behind boarded up shop windows, London is still rolling out the welcome mat. Tourists are welcome here. They add to the city. I like living in a place that’s gloriously cosmopolitan.
Oh, and one of those Madrid friends? I have now known him for almost 40 years. Seems that I am more reliable than I imagined.

items.title: Issue 61 - Kinfolk
items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.

items.title: Tyra Banks Is Casting For Her Graphic Novel
items.description: What can't Tyra Banks do? In addition to opening Modelland — a modeling-centric amusement park — the TV star and business mogul is also reportedly working on a forthcoming graphic novel tied to the opening of the space.
items.author: Sandra Song
paragraphs: What can't Tyra Banks do? In addition to opening Modelland — a modeling-centric amusement park — the TV star and business mogul is also reportedly working on a forthcoming graphic novel tied to the opening of the space.

Based on her 2010 young adult novel Modelland, Banks describes the graphic novel of the same name as "high-fashion, meets comic illustration." Not only that, but in a video posted to her Instagram earlier today, Banks also explained that she's putting out an open casting call for the project.

Okay, but how exactly is that going to work? Well, as Banks explained to People, the graphic novel is her way of visually-engaging her fans. However, given the fact that there isn't typically a ton of overlap between the kind of people who would go to Modelland and Comic Con, Banks is upping-the-ante by casting real people to inspire characters in book.
Dubbing it "Comic Couture," Banks told the publication that she's looking for a "diverse cast," and she's excited to give everyone "the opportunity to be fantasy versions of themselves."

So how does someone go about getting cast? According to Banks' Instagram, all you have to do is post a full face shot, profile, and full body shot to your own feed, alongside the character you want to be cast for and hashtag #Modelland.

And while there's no definitive release date for the graphic novel just yet, Banks is supposedly timing the release of the comic to the opening of the Modelland park in Santa Monica, California later this year.

"I created [America's Next] Top Model to expand the definition of beauty based on my own pain of being told 'no' that I couldn't do something because I'm curvy or I'm black. My empathy for women in general increased through the experience," Banks previously told WWD. "And now with Modelland, I'm taking it 10 steps forward, giving people the opportunity to engage with the elusive world by opening it up to everyone. Men, women, families, all generations can come and enter this model world for a day, have a fun shopping experience, and an eventful meal. This will be the first of many."

items.title: Inside The Historic Royal Wedding of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip
items.description: Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the
items.author: Annabelle Spranklen
paragraphs: Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

The Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was said to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

In 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately said yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.
The wedding dress and tiara
The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

Princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

As Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, said to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

All royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.
Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.
The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.
The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.
Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.
The wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.)
The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”
The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

On the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.
The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.
During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.
Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.
The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

Over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.
The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

items.title: THE BIRTH OF BOND | Vanity Fair
items.description: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered wh
items.author: David Kamp
paragraphs: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered when he first tried to take his hero to the screen. DAVID KAMP recalls the unlikely team—two small-time producers, a journeyman director, and a "rough diamond" of a star―behind 007's film debut, Dr. No,, the beginning of a $5 billion franchise
ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED IN OCTOBER 2012

nter Sean Connery, dark hair slicked with pomade, eyes locking hungrily upon a beautiful green-eyed girl. Her return glance leaves no doubt—the feeling is mutual. His slouch and casual banter exude languor and nonchalance, but there's an undercurrent of coiled menace to this man, as though he might, at any moment, spring into table-overturning, crockery-shattering action.

Except nothing of the sort happens. Instead, the other fellow in the scene cuts the tension by taking out his fiddle and favoring the room with a jaunty tune learned, he says in a stagy brogue, "in the old ruins on the top of Knocknasheega!"

This isn't a James Bond picture. It is 1959, and Connery is putting in time in a cornball live-action Disney feature called Darby O'Gill and the Little People. He's the second male lead, billed beneath not only Albert Sharpe, the elderly Irish character actor in the title role—a kindly farmhand who sees leprechauns—but also the greeneyed girl, the ingenue Janet Munro. Though verily pump-misting pheromonal musk into the air, to a degree unmatched before or since by any actor in a Disney family movie, Connery is still a jobbing scuffler, not a star. He has no idea of what lies in store for him.

The seventh of Ian Fleming's Bond novels, Goldfinger, has recently reached the shops. But there are no Bond pictures yet. In London, a Long Island-born film producer named Albert R. Broccoli, known as Cubby, is still lamenting that he blew his chance with Fleming. The previous year, Broccoli had set up a meeting with the English author and his representatives to talk about securing movie rights to the Bond series, only to miss the meeting to tend to his wife, who had recently been diagnosed with terminal cancer. In Broccoli's absence, his business partner, Irving Allen, let Fleming know that he didn't share his colleague's ardor. "In my opinion," Allen told Bond's creator, "these books are not even good enough for television."

This is an older, stiffer world, with Britain just five years removed from food rationing and America still in an era of Kramdens, Eisenhowers, and finned Caddies. It is a world unfamiliar with the catchphrases "Shaken, not stirred" and "Bond, James Bond," where no ears have ever heard Monty Norman's four-note Bond motif and no eyes have ever taken in Maurice Binder's amniotic credit sequences of lissome women undulating in silhouette to lavishly charted John Barry arrangements.

But it is also a world in transition. Transatlantic jet service is newly available to commercial passengers, thanks to the carriers B.O.A.C. and Pan American. G.D. Searle & Company, a pharmaceutical concern, is awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration to market one of its products, Enovid, as a birthcontrol pill for women. A scrubbed, fit group of U.S. military test pilots has just been introduced to the public as the Mercury Seven, America's first astronauts. And the undeclared Democratic frontrunner in the next presidential election is only 42 years old.

In March 1961, when he actually is the president, John F. Kennedy lists Fleming's fifth Bond novel, From Russia with Love, as one of his 10 current favorite reads in a Life magazine article. That same year, Broccoli, having parted ways with Allen and joined forces with another producer, a Canadian by the name of Harry Saltzman, finally gets the rights to turn Fleming's books into movies. After an arduous and seemingly fruitless search to find a lead actor mutually agreeable to the two producers and their studio benefactor, United Artists, Broccoli circles back to one of the lesser-knowns among the candidates: Sean Connery. To confirm his hunch that this tall, handsome Scotsman could be the guy, Broccoli, while in Hollywood, arranges for his new wife, Dana, to join him in a screening room at the Samuel Goldwyn Studio. There they watch the only Connery footage that Cubby has been able to rustle up: Darby OGill and the Little People. Dana Broccoli's response is instantaneous: "That's our Bond!"
And so on October 5,1962, at the London Pavilion theater, in Piccadilly Circus, Connery joins Fleming, Broccoli, and Saltzman on the red carpet for the world premiere of the first Bond film, Dr. No.

half-century later, even in an era inured to skin, gunplay, and wide-screen shots of tropical waterfalls, Dr. No remains exhilarating to watch. The azure brightness of Jamaica, with Connery striding purposefully through it; the seawater-salted flesh and ounces-light wardrobe of Ursula Andress; the modernist bachelor-pad fantasia that is the undersea lair of the titular doctor, played with cool reserve by Joseph Wiseman—it's all so fantastically stylish, racy, and forward-looking. So imagine what it must have been like for the people who actually saw the picture in a theater when it first came out.

Dr. No took just a few months in the U.K. to recoup its $1 million budget and ultimately made 20 times that amount in its initial release. Theater bookers in the U.S. hedged their bets at first, putting out the film "in the sticks," as a chagrined Broccoli noted, before allowing the sophisticates in New York and Los Angeles to see it. Nevertheless, the drumbeat had already begun, with North Carolina's Rocky Mount Telegram, for example, relishing how Connery "twists his supple body through a tiny aperture to potential freedom." The syndicated entertainment columnist Erskine Johnson suggested that "tawny 26-year-old Ursula Andress should have been billed not by her last name, but as 'Undress.' "

As it turned out, the coastal intelligentsia were pretty easily won over, too.
