"Oh, it was dazzling: Ursula coming out of the ocean, the brilliant art direction, straining your eyes to see the almost-nude women in the opening credits. They were cheap tricks, but good tricks," says Buck Henry, who, with Mel Brooks and the TV producer Daniel Melnick, was inspired in '65 to create the sitcom spoof Get Smart in homage. "It wasn't Brueghel," Henry says of the early Bond films, "but it was like the stuff that Lichtenstein and those other guys were doing—great Pop art carried into another medium."

Dr. No and its two follow-ups, From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), are the cornerstones of Bond mania. Like the early Lennon-McCartney singles that spurred Beatlemania, they augured bigger, more elaborate things to come, but the sheer excitement they generated remains unsurpassable. Not only were these movies terrifically entertaining, they also delivered a sort of jet-age holodeck experience, granting regular folk an opportunity to glimpse the future awaiting them. As of 1960, fewer than 2 percent of all Americans had traveled internationally by air. So both Dr. No and From Russia with Love include what are essentially fetish shots of Pan Am jets landing on runways as air-traffic controllers announce their arrival. ("Hello, London, your flight PA1 just landed in Istanbul")

"It was a sense of 'Buy your ticket—we're going to take you places!' " says Guy Hamilton, the director of Goldfinger. He recalls the Broccoli-Saltzman attitude toward Bond transport as "Don't take a train when you can take a plane, and if you're going to take a plane, take the newest one around. And if you give Bond a car, don't show what's been seen—show what's not out yet." This is why, while Bond drives an Aston Martin DBIII in Goldfinger the novel, he drives a DB5 in Hamilton's movie, made five years later. It's also why, when Bond comes to after being knocked out with a tranquilizer gun in the same film, he is told, by no less than Honor Blackman's knockout aviatrix, Pussy Galore, that he is aboard "Mr. Goldfinger's Lockheed JetStar"—this at a time when the very concept of a private business jet was virtually unheard of. Even Bond's room-service breakfast order in From Russia with Love— "Green figs, yogurt, coffee, very black"—sounds ahead of its time.

Beyond the travelogue aspect, there was the sex aspect—another way, as it were, to hitch a ride with James Bond. "The actual film, to film, was sexy," says Shirley Eaton of her scenes with Connery in Goldfinger. Eaton is famous for being the blonde girl whose body is discovered nude, lifeless, and coated in gold paint—her death (by "skin suffocation," not a medical possibility in real life) a punishment by her boss, Auric Goldfinger, for switching to Bond's side.

But it's Eaton's first scene with Connery that packs the erotic wallop. Bond, poolside at Miami's Fontainebleau hotel, has worked out from which room Goldfinger's accomplice is spying on his opponent's cards, thereby allowing Goldfinger to cheat at his alfresco games of high-stakes gin rummy. Letting himself into the room, Bond discovers Eaton's Jill Masterson lying stomach-down in a black bikini on a balcony lounger, using binoculars and a radio set to convey the card info into Goldfinger's earpiece. Wearing a shorty jumpsuit of pale-blue terry cloth that only someone as masculine as Connery could pull off, Bond, grinning, simply lowers himself gently onto Jill, shrewdly opting for horizontal bodily contact rather than force to accomplish his mission.

Eaton, then 27, had been acting in movies since her teen years, "always playing the girl next door," she says, or a pretty thing to be ogled in one of Britain's low-budget Carry On comedies. "But this was entirely new," she says. "It was grown-up sexuality. Sean and I just fell into our natural sensuality without any rumpy-pumpy, and I think that's what made it so exciting."

Honor Blackman, likewise, had already established herself as the judo-chopping, leather-clad Dr. Cathy Gale on the British TV series The Avengers but found the Bond universe to have an altogether different dynamic. "Cathy Gale was a very proper lady, with collars up to the chin," she says, "whereas Pussy was supposed to match Bond's sexuality. She was a tough broad who also showed a fair amount of bosom." Johnny Carson, just a few years into hosting The Tonight Show, was so taken with the scene in which Pussy finally surrenders to Bond's charms (they trade martial-arts body flips in a hay-filled barn before falling into a love clutch) that "he badgered and badgered me—would I show him how it was done?" she says. Blackman feared injuring Carson, but she flew to New York to rehearse the bit with him, and when they performed it live "he passionately kissed me at the end, which wasn't planned. It was funny, but it also showed how much even someone like Johnny Carson wanted to be James Bond."

an Fleming had long been alert to the screen potential of his books, but realizing this potential proved to be something of a chore. Twice in the late '50s, Fleming worked with American networks to develop a TV series, first with NBC on a Bond-inspired spy show provisionally titled Commander Jamaica, and then with CBS on what would have been an explicitly Bond-based weekly drama. Neither show made it to the pilot phase. A little earlier, in 1954, CBS had aired an anemic one-off adaptation of Fleming's first Bond novel, Casino Royale, in which the character had been Americanized into "Jimmy Bond" and been played by a miscast, chipmunk-cheeked actor named Barry Nelson. Fleming then sold the book's movie rights to the actor Gregory Ratoff, who died before coming close to getting a movie produced. These rights, unbundled from rights to the other Bond books, eventually fell into the hands of Ratoff s agent, the Hollywood mcicher Charles Feldman, who, after Bond mania took off, produced the abominable meta-parodic version with David Niven, Peter Sellers, and Woody Allen that came out in 1967. (Only in the last decade was Casino Roy ale, the novel, reeled into the hands of the "official" Bond producers—Broccoli's heirs— the result being the 2006 franchise reboot starring Daniel Craig.)
"OH, DISASTER, DISASTER, DISASTER!" DIRECTOR TERENCE YOUNG SAID WHEN SEAN CONNERY WAS CAST.

Fleming had higher hopes for a treatment he worked on in 1959 for a film to be called James Bond, Secret Agent. It was not an adaptation but a new Bond story, and his collaborator was Kevin McClory, an up-and-coming Irish screenwriter. But this project, too, foundered. Fleming, unbowed, folded his ideas for the shelved movie into the next Bond novel. Not long before this book, Thunderball, came out, in 1961, McClory got hold of an advance copy and was angered by its resemblance to the story treatment he'd labored on with Fleming and another writer, Jack Whittingham. McClory filed suit, and, while the book's publication was allowed to go forward, the issue of its film rights would take another three years to resolve.

In the movie industry, Fleming had at last run into a thickety, double-dealing milieu that he, a suave operator his entire adult life, was ill-prepared to contend with. Before that, to all appearances, he had been Mr. Smooth. It has often been said that James Bond was Fleming's fantasy version of himself, while Fleming declared that Bond was "a compound of all the secret agents and commando types I met" during World War II, in which he served in Britain's Naval Intelligence Division. Whichever way it was, Fleming had certainly known Bondish people and lived through Bondish episodes of his own by the time he sat down in 1952 and created the character at his typewriter.

In his youth, Fleming, born in 1908, had been a rascally, athletic ne'er-do-well who attended but did not graduate from Eton and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, distinguishing himself more as a trainee roue than an officer candidate. In the '30s, he finally found some measure of professional fulfillment, first as a journalist working for Reuters, the news agency, and then, as war broke out, as an aide to Rear Admiral John Henry Godfrey, Britain's director of naval intelligence.

Godfrey, brusque and imperious, became the model for 007's superior, M. He took to Fleming, inviting the younger man to accompany him to overseas meetings with J. Edgar Hoover, the F.B.I. chief, and William J. "Wild Bill" Donovan, the founder of the Office of Strategic Services, the Central Intelligence Agency's precursor. Godfrey also granted Fleming significant leeway to conjure imaginative schemes to trip up the Nazis. One of these, Operation Mincemeat, is among the more celebrated in the annals of British espionage. In 1943, British intelligence officers took possession of the corpse of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had recently died by his own hand. After dressing Michael's body in the uniform of a major in the Royal Marines, stuffing his pockets with phony identification materials, and chaining to his wrist a briefcase containing a letter labeled PERSONAL AND MOST SECRET, they dumped him off the coast of Spain, creating the impression of an officer who had died in a plane crash. Spain was infested with Nazi spies, and the hope was that one of them would inevitably get his hands on the letter and pass it up the chain of command. It worked. Hitler was fooled by the documents, which indicated that the Allies were about to invade Greece, and hastily moved a division of 90,000 troops there. The Allies, with considerably less resistance than they would have encountered otherwise, proceeded to take their true target, Sicily.

A fter the war, Fleming landed a job as foreign-news manager for Kemsley Newspapers, which owned, among other publications, The Sunday Times—a assignment that allowed him to spend every winter season in Jamaica, a place he'd first visited during his naval-intelligence years. In 1946 he built a home on the island's north shore that he called Goldeneye, after the code name of an Allied plan to defend Gibraltar against seizure by the Axis powers. From '52 onward, Fleming used Goldeneye as his writing roost, banging out one Bond novel a year. Nevertheless, by the beginning of 1961, he had still had no luck with Hollywood, which he described to a friend as "a hell of a jungle" and full of "specious promises."

It was at this time that, for $50,000, he granted Harry Saltzman a six-month option to put a film deal in place for the Bond books. A stout, hedgehoggish man born in 1915 to Jewish immigrants living in Quebec, Saltzman had hustled his way into the American movie industry, eventually venturing to England to take advantage of the tax breaks the U.K. afforded filmmakers. On the face of it, Saltzman was a peculiar deal partner for Fleming. While he had achieved modest success producing film adaptations of John Osborne's table-thumping social-realist plays Look Back in Anger and The Entertainer, he was decidedly small-time compared with previous suitors. Saltzman's children have long puzzled over how their father, who died in 1994, managed to secure the option. One of his daughters, Hilary Saltzman, stumbled upon some revelatory clues when, in 2003, she decided to relocate with her children from Los Angeles to Quebec. Having let her Canadian passport expire, she ran into a hitch while getting her citizenship papers in order: The Canadian government required documentation of her father's reasons for immigrating to the United States. The next surprise she encountered was that her request to pull her father's U.S. records, a process she expected to be routine, set off alarms at the State Department. When, after more than two years of petitioning, Hilary finally received the documents she needed to satisfy the Canadian government, she also received a bonus: reams of material revealing that her father, who she knew had served in the Royal Canadian Air Force in the early years of World War II, had subsequently worked for the U.S. Office of War Information, specifically its Psychological Warfare Division. The senior Saltzman had never been forthright with his children about how he spent his war.
"SEAN AND I JUST FELL INTO OUR NATURAL SENSUALITY WITHOUT ANY RUMPYPUMPY," SAYS SHIRLEY EATON.

"I'm reading these letters of Robert E. Sherwood, the O.W.I.'s director of overseas operations, about my father," Hilary says. "The countries he was to visit overseas: 'Confidential.' Nature of business: 'Confidential war mission for O.W.I.' I'm stunned. It just blew me away that, finally, I understood what my father had done in the war. Finally, I understood his fascination with the spy genre of films." (In the '60s, Saltzman also produced a trilogy of films starring Michael Caine as Len Deighton's spy Harry Palmer, based on the Deighton novels The Ipcress File, Funeral in Berlin, and Billion Dollar Brain) One of Sherwood's unredacted letters, from 1943, informs G. Howland Shaw, assistant secretary of state, that "Mr. Saltzman will be assigned to the North African theater of war to serve on the staff of Mr. C.D. Jackson." Jackson was a noted psychologicalwarfare expert and propaganda mastermind who was then working for the O.S.S. and later served as a Cold War adviser to President Dwight Eisenhower. His base, Algiers, to which Saltzman was sent, was also one of Fleming's wartime destinations.

Hilary Saltzman and her brother, Steven, have yet to turn up evidence that their father and Fleming met before 1961; it's possible, even probable, that they did not. But Hilary posits that "because they had a similar background during the war, which was in confidential missions, they had a mutual understanding. Even though they couldn't publicize it, I really think Ian felt that this series was safe in my father's hands."

Yet by mid-1961 the Bond option was about to slip through Saltzman's fingers: He was five months into his six-month option and hadn't put together any backing. By happenstance, Cubby Broccoli was working with a screenwriter, Wolf Mankowitz, who not only knew Saltzman but was aware that he held the Bond option. Broccoli wasn't pleased with the script for an Arabian Nights-thcmcd movie that Mankowitz had pressed upon him, and when Mankowitz asked Broccoli what he'd rather be producing, Broccoli brought up his long-held desire to make films of Fleming's books. Mankowitz agreed to introduce Broccoli to Saltzman. Though Broccoli, having just shed his old partner, Irving Allen, hoped to buy the option in its entirety, Saltzman insisted on maintaining his piece of the action—and, in fact, had already drawn up a document for Broccoli to sign, affirming that "you and I have mutually agreed that we shall equally share" the film rights to all the Bond books save Casino Royale. And so, in June 1961, was born what Guy Hamilton calls "a wonderful double act": Broccoli, affable and teddy-bearish, serving as a tempering counterpoint to the volatile and argumentative Saltzman. They named their venture Eon Productions.

Broccoli was born in 1909 to an Italian-immigrant family from Calabria. His father, Giovanni Broccoli, and great-uncle Pasquale de Cicco were Long Island truck farmers who sold their goods in New York City and were actually instrumental in popularizing the vegetable broccoli in the United States. Notwithstanding his humble family roots, Cubby was better connected than Saltzman. In the '30s, through his sharpie cousin Pat de Cicco, Pasquale's son, a Hollywood playboy and the first husband of Gloria Vanderbilt, he had gained a toehold in the film industry, landing an assistant job on a Howard Hawks picture and later becoming close to Alan Ladd, the matinee-idol star of Shane and The Great Gatsby.

Taking advantage of the same tax breaks that had lured Saltzman to England, Broccoli and Allen had founded a British company, Warwick Films, that made its mark in the '50s with such war and adventure pictures as Paratrooper, Hell Below Zero, and The Cockleshell Heroes, the first two starring Ladd. In 1961, Broccoli worked his connections to secure a meeting in New York with Arthur Krim, the head of United Artists. Krim agreed to a budget of just over a million dollars for a James Bond movie. At last, a deal had been done.

Broccoli and Saltzman were keen to begin with the latest Bond novel, Thunderbolt. But in light of Kevin McClory's pending lawsuit, they opted instead for Fleming's sixth book, Doctor No, from 1958, which offered both a cinematically picturesque Jamaican setting and a sinister Eurasian villain who, on his private Caribbean island, Crab Key, plotted to sabotage U.S. rocket launches from Cape Canaveral—a story line that presciently anticipated the Cuban missile crisis, which unfolded the very month that Dr. No (as the film version was titled) was released in Britain. To ensure that things would run smoothly, Broccoli brought in a pair of trusted veterans from his Warwick days, the British director Terence Young and the American screenwriter Richard Maibaum. Maibaum was paired with Wolf Mankowitz to come up with a script.

Young, like Fleming, was a tall, rakish character of privileged background: educated at Cambridge, a tank commander in the Irish Guards during World War II. Maibaum, a native of the Bronx and frequent collaborator with Ladd, served in the war as director of the U.S. Army's Combat Films Division, handling footage both for classified use and for dissemination to the public through newsreels. The first screenplay he wrote after the war was for Ladd's film O.S.S.: a 1946 dramatization of the wartime work of the Office of Strategic Services that featured such proto-Bond touches as a clever espionage gadget (a Minox mini-camera) and a comely lady spy (Geraldine Fitzgerald).

In Young, Maibaum, and Saltzman, the Bond-movie team had a group of World War II vets who, like Fleming, were well versed in matters of military intelligence and would bring a level of verite and nuance to what were otherwise playfully escapist entertainments. In Broccoli, who did his wartime bit as an ensign in the navy and a wrangler of Hollywood talent for morale-boosting shows for the troops, the Bond pictures had their great showman and salesman.

Fleming's books are at once grittier and more preposterous than the Bond movies. His Bond registers fear and panic and has hangovers. But he's also something of a bizarre, half-mad sociopath, at times evoking Patrick Bateman, the vain, self-assured brand-name dropper of Bret Easton Ellis's American Psycho, and Jean des Esseintes, the debauched hyper-aesthete of J.K. Huysmans's A Rebours. Here is how Fleming, through Bond's eyes, rather creepily describes Vesper Lynd, the first Bond girl (in print, anyway), in Casino Royale: "Her medium-length dress was of grey soie sauvage with a square-cut bodice, lasciviously tight across her fine breasts. The skirt was closely pleated and flowered down from a narrow, but not a thin, waist. She wore a three-inch, handstitched black belt." In Goldfinger the novel, Bond, while tracking the villain through France, stops in Orleans—a place he dislikes, "a priest and myth ridden town without gaiety"—and takes in "one of his favourite meals: two oeufs cocotte a la creme, a large sole meuniere (Orleans was close enough to the sea. The fish of the Loire are inclined to be muddy) and an adequate Camembert. He drank a well-iced pint of Rose d'Anjou and had a Hennessy's Three Star with his coffee."

Clearly, the filmmakers were going to have to tamp down the soiesauvage-noting and muddy-fish-despising aspects of the character to make him more sympathetic and relatable to audiences. At the same time, Cinema Bond would have to maintain the man-of-action toughness that warranted his Double-Oh status—his license, as granted by M.I.6, Britain's foreign-intelligence service, to kill. This is why the casting of Connery was a masterstroke. Alone among actors, "Sean was able to suggest that dichotomy," said Maibaum in an interview with the film historian Patrick McGilligan. "Fleming thought David Niven would have made a great James Bond," Maibaum said, "but David Niven wasn't all that physical. Originally, Roger Moore was considered for Bond, you know. Then Cubby saw something in Sean which he thought was what they wanted. They took a gamble with Sean; they would have been much safer with Roger."

There is a phrase used almost universally by those involved in the early Bond films to describe Connery circa 1962: a "rough diamond." He was born in 1930 in Edinburgh to a truckdriver and a charwoman. As a young man he worked a variety of menial jobs in Scotland, including driving a milk truck—a detail that seems to captivate biographers and associates ("He was a blasted milkman!" says Honor Blackman)—before traveling to London to compete in a bodybuilding contest, in which he finished third. When he was 22, he landed his first acting job, an ensemble part in a London production of South Pacific.

Connery's looks and muscular build led to a middling early film career that showcased how attractive he was but little else. Moore, three years his senior, had the better track record and was on the verge of television stardom as the noble thief Simon Templar in The Saint. But Broccoli found Moore, at the time, to be "a shade too pretty" for Bond, and even when Moore finally assumed the role, in 1973's Live and Let Die, his light touch and fundamental lack of menace required a recalibration of the Bond character.

Connery's rough-hewn background served Cinema Bond well; it made him a more plausible creation than Fleming's Bond. Whereas the latter is a roguish posh boy, steeped in the finer things in life, who just happens to be a cold-blooded assassin, the former is not unlike Don Draper as portrayed by Jon Hamm in Mad Men: a mysterious self-creation whose virile good looks opened doors in his young adulthood and who seized upon these openings to learn the ropes as a gentleman, connoisseur, and lover, transforming himself into a convincing but dangerous facsimile of all of the above.

Not that anyone, Broccoli included, had any certainty of how well Connery would come off. Fleming was known to have his doubts, and Young, who had worked with Connery on one of the actor's uninspiring '50s films, Action of the Tiger, made no bones about his feelings when Broccoli told him that Connery had been signed. "Oh, disaster, disaster, disaster!" he said.

But Young overcame his initial misgivings, becoming, in fact, the man most readily credited with shaping Connery's Bond persona. It's a disservice to Connery's acting skills to say that he was simply doing his best Terence Young impression, but "Terence taught Sean, who was very basic in those days, a lot of good manners, and Terence felt himself like a James Bond-like person," says Ken Adam, the production designer on nearly all of the Conneryera Bond movies. Young, who died in 1994, took Connery out to restaurants in Mayfair and introduced him to his bespoke tailor, Anthony Sinclair. While the oft-told tale that Connery acclimated to his new handmade suits by sleeping in them is possibly apocryphal, Sinclair took pride in how his clothes functioned like a second skin on the star. "Any well-made suit," he told an ABC News interviewer in the '60s, "you should be able to take it, roll it into a ball, crush it, stamp on it, sleep in it, and then"—smoothing the narrow, impeccably draped lapels of the Sinclair suit he himself was wearing—"there you are, you're back again, you see?"
r. No's gestation was not without its problems. Sometimes a sentiment prevailed, perhaps as a hedge against failure and ridicule, that the movie was just a bit of nonsense, a B picture. Adam, whose w

items.title: Straker’s Left Eddie Huang Waiting and Wanting
items.description: Straker’s Left Eddie Huang Waiting and Wanting
items.author: Eddie Huang
paragraphs: Straker’s Left Eddie Huang Waiting and Wanting
I started hearing about Thomas Straker in late 2025.

There was a lounge owner trying to unload his space about six hundred feet away from Lucky Strike who mentioned, “You know Thomas Straker is moving in around the corner, right? This block is going to explode.” I didn’t doubt it, because his lounge had the spatial flow of El Chapo’s underground tunnel system, so whether it was Thomas Straker or this guy’s architect, the block was inevitably hot.

As we built out Baohaus in February—and by built out I mean painted walls and put up my art—one of the contractors showed me a video on his phone of Thomas cooking with butter: “This British guy is hot. His restaurant is going to change New York dining. Just watch.”

The more things change, the more they stay the same, and the only time anyone actually delivered on the promise of change was when Diddy declared on the intro to Nas’s “Hate Me Now” that “Escobar Season has returned!”

The opening of Straker’s was delayed for a year, and before I could try it in Soho, I found myself in Notting Hill on July 2, 2026, which coincidentally was also the 30-year anniversary of the aforementioned Nas album, It Was Written. Was Thomas Straker God’s son? Was he going to change everything we knew about dining?
Has Escobar season in fact returned?

I called my publicist, Savannah Engel, who also reps Thomas, and asked her to find me a table for two the next evening at Straker’s in Notting Hill. It wasn’t the most difficult ask, and we got two seats at the Chef’s Table for 8:15 p.m. The first dish to hit the table was the mussel flatbread, which had me type hard.
“Damn, son,” said my wife, Natashia, parodying my learned speech patterns.
“I smell what the Rock is cooking,” I responded.

The next dish was a beautiful green bean salad with white peaches and some type of nut, pause. It was the perfect snappy, palate-cleansing seasonal salad for a Taiwanese guy who appreciates texture more than anything in food. The hits didn’t stop: roasted scallops on the half shell, a crudo with the white peaches once more, and a turbot roasted over charcoal.
The meal was so fucking future that I pulled out my phone to check this MAN’s astrology and discovered that he is a February 28 Pisces.
“Of course he’s a Pisces.”

“That’s the best meal I’ve had all year,” said Natashia, at which point I reminded her that I, a March 1 Pisces, had opened a restaurant on March 4 this year, and it would be uncouth if she had a better meal anywhere else. She agreed, and we proceeded to walk toward the Travel Book Gift Shop in Notting Hill, where I copped something ugly.

Three months later, Straker’s opened, and it was the talk of New York. People with juice who breeze into any restaurant opening were getting curved, Keith McNally was sucking his dick in public, gifting him art, and he was coronated before anyone had actually dined in the spot.

Once again, I asked Savannah to get me a table, and there was no response. I was immediately offended, like Scarface screaming, “You want to play games? Okay, I play with you. Come on!” Two weeks passed, and still no reservation was offered.
Then West Wilson texted me to link for dinner, and Straker’s came up in conversation, so I went into the breach once more.
“Savannah, can I eat at Straker’s yet?”

Again, days went by without a response. I waited until our biweekly strategy meeting and asked in person, at which point Savannah could no longer avoid me and was able to procure four seats at the bar, presented as a Chef’s Table, which I gladly accepted.

A few days later, I walked into the Russian Turkish Baths on Halloween and ran into my good friend Rashid Johnson with his girlfriend, Lake Bell, as well as the inimitable Daniel Humm, who had a new restaurant opening as well. We hugged, we said hello, and I proceeded to change, then walk into the Russian Room downstairs.
I did what I always do in the Russian Room.

I put a towel over my head, closed my eyes, and blocked my life out for seventeen to eighteen minutes. It was particularly difficult on this day because two people with British and Australian accents were talking about restaurant event planning. After working at The Flower Shop, an Australian pub, for over six months in 2025, I have to say that hearing an Australian accent in New York feels like cats scratching a fucking surfboard, and it makes me want to put a .35 to my eardrums like Beat Takeshi in Sonatine.

Alas, the event planners walked out of the room, and I was able to enjoy the final few minutes. I walked straight to the cold plunge, heard the event planners once more, came out of the cold plunge, opened my eyes, and saw that one of the guys had an Old Mates Pub tattoo on his arm.
“Jesus fucking Christ,” I said to myself, walking up the stairs behind him.

While Old Mates is my local pub and I am frequently there destroying floated pies while watching Michigan games, it’s diabolical to get an earnest restaurant tattoo unless it’s like a Macaroni Grill tramp stamp. We were all headed to the men’s locker room, and as the guy with the Old Mates Pub tattoo turned around, I saw him… the Chosen One, Thomas Straker.
“Hey!” we both said simultaneously.
“Pleasure to meet you,” I said.
“Same, same. How are you?” he said.
“I’m coming to your spot this Wednesday. I’m excited, brother.”
“This is the GM!” he said, pointing to his friend.
“Why’s your GM have an Old Mates Pub tattoo?”
“He has a Lucky Straker’s one too!”
“Ah, fuck, man,” I said, wondering if this man was back-to-back Stockholm Syndrome’d by his chefs, then remembered that I generally dislike FOH and ceased to be concerned; if he dies, he dies.
“Wednesday, you said?” asked Thomas.
“Wednesday at the bar,” I responded.
Thomas understood what I was saying, looked at his GM, pointed at me, and said, “Wednesday,” to which the GM nodded.
“I saw you did that dinner with Stone Island,” he said.
“Yeah, it was a nice dinner in L.A. I love those guys. Have you met them?”
“Of course. I’m sure they’d love to do something with you as well. Their office is around the corner,” I said, since literally everyone in the neighborhood was trying to meet my fellow Pisces man.

I left the baths and immediately felt sick. Something had happened. Did meeting Thomas Straker completely overwhelm my nervous system and, in turn, my immune system? Was I having an allergic reaction to earnest restaurant tattoos? I wasn’t sure, but I went into my local CityMD and tested positive for the flu.
I got home, and the first thing I said to Natashia was, “I have the flu, but we are still going to Straker’s Wednesday. Don’t worry.”
“I don’t even care. If you have the flu, we can go another time.”
“We literally can’t get a table another time. We have to go.”

That Wednesday, Natashia, West, Amanda, and I arrived for dinner, and the GM kindly transferred us to a wonderful booth on the left side of the dining room, closest to the corner. We ordered a round of drinks, the mussel flatbread, langoustines, roasted duck, ravioli, Dover sole, and a side of potatoes. The mussel flatbread hit, and West audibly gasped as he took his first bite.

Unfortunately, the OCD chef in me couldn’t look away from the excess butter that had spilled over the edge of the flatbread, soaking it on the bottom. I was heartbroken. Perhaps the best bite of food I’d had in years had died on its trip across the pond. The langoustines were fine, the Dover sole was fine but not nearly as ethereal as the turbot in Notting Hill, and the duck was fine as well. The best bite was the ravioli, perhaps because there wasn’t a Notting Hill counterpart to compare it to.
“I just like Straker’s in Notting Hill so much better,” I said to Natashia, who agreed wholeheartedly.
“It was that good?” asked West.

“Bro, I’m telling you, that was one of the best meals of my life. Like, top five white-food meal all time. Elite milk,” I joked. West thought about it but still loved the meal, and I had no desire to convince him otherwise. He had enjoyed the meal so much that when we ordered desserts, he called an audible.
“Guys, would you mind if I just got a personal mussel flatbread for dessert?”

The girls and I shared a dessert I can’t remember as West housed another mussel flatbread, with butter spilling over the edge like water at Shamu. We walked outside, and West positioned us to take a group photo, which was cute. Amanda very kindly offered to take the photo, but she absolutely needed to be in it, so West asked the bouncer, who was wearing steel-toed boots and a full Vampire in Brooklyn costume, if he wouldn’t mind taking the photo.
“I don’t take photos,” he said.
“Alright, we’ll take a selfie,” said West.
As we all huddled out front of Straker’s to take the selfie, the bouncer stood in the middle behind us. Wanting to be polite, West let him know.
“Just want you to know you might be in the photo.”
“I don’t take photos,” the bouncer repeated, standing directly behind us in the line of sight.
West snapped the photo, and I thought to myself, This would never have happened in Notting Hill.

items.title: Rio Amor Is Breaking Down the Hip Hop Boys Club
items.description: Rio Amor Is Breaking Down the Hip Hop Boys Club
items.author: Ary Russell
paragraphs: Rio Amor Is Breaking Down the Hip Hop Boys Club

Rio Amor is a girl who knows what she wants and will be damned if she doesn’t get it. In the midst of a tragic nonchalant epidemic, she’s staying up into the wee hours of the morning making sure her beats are perfect, her lyrics are sharp, and her sets will make a crowd go apeshit. That tenacity has led her to level up fast and, at just 20 years old, she’s already performed DJ sets at Camp Flog Gnaw and cemented herself as a vital member of Lil Yachty’s rap collective, the Concrete Boys. For the past few weeks, the L.A.-based producer has been hopping from coast to coast for her headlining North American tour before making it to her final stop in New York City. When I arrived at Racket NYC for her show, I stumbled across a line of fans who were itching to get inside and give the musician their all. Before she hit the DJ booth, I met up with Rio Amor in the green room to chat about tour essentials, crowdsurfing, and why she’s still reeling from the James Bond casting announcement.
TUESDAY 5:52 PM NOVEMBER 17, 2026 NEW YORK CITY
ARY RUSSELL: For the record, it was not recording before, but you’re having a good time in New York. You had a good time at Camp Flog Gnaw.
RIO AMOR: Yes. Bacon, egg, and cheese. [Laughs]
RUSSELL: Sorry. That’s funny, that’s actually the first time it’s happened to me.
RIO AMOR: Don’t worry. Maybe you can paraphrase everything I said, and make me sound smarter because I’m so bad at these.
RUSSELL: Blah, blah, you’re happy with the time slot you got. You don’t eat or drink before.
RIO AMOR: I get nervous because I care. I love my family, I love my fans.
RUSSELL: Exactly. But that’s actually a good starting point because when I pulled up, I already saw a line forming.
RUSSELL: Yeah, how does that feel to have people waiting in line for you in the cold weather?

RIO AMOR: Holy shit. I mean, it feels awesome, but it’s still very unbelievable to me. When people ask me for a picture in my local grocery store, I’m like, “Are you sure?” I also have such a weird For You Page, so the internet always feeds me straight up hate. And then I do shit like this and there’s a line and it’s like, “Oh, this is why I keep doing this shit because other people are here outside standing in the cold.”

RUSSELL: Well, it’s interesting you bring up the hate. How are you keeping that public persona and your private life private when it seems like as you get bigger more people will have opinions on you?

RIO AMOR: For sure. It’s really daunting and it’s definitely what everyone says it is. It’s very hard to see a video of yourself and there’s a flood of comments saying lies or just being mean. But I’ve deleted a lot of social media apps now and I’m trying to hand it over to my management to keep my sanity, while also still being myself online and making sure I’m not faking a persona. But it’s really tough, especially when you can’t really say anything because the more you interact with it, the more it gets worse.
RUSSELL: It just feeds the beast.
RIO AMOR: I’m 20 years old and I’ve been seeing videos of myself since I was 16 or 17 that are not always nice things to see. I think I’m a good-ass dude, so it sucks.

RUSSELL: It’s interesting because I’ll see people be like, “Well, Billie Eilish said this when she was 16.” And I’m like, “Well, she was 16. People change. Imagine if you were growing up in front of everybody.”

RIO AMOR: I can’t even imagine. There’s a lot of child stars that are fully growing up in front of these people. I’m very lucky that a lot of this is happening when I’m 20 and I at least have the brainpower to turn my phone off and be like, “This shit isn’t real.” I have a couple friends that have been stars since they were young kids and I always go to them like, “How do I do this?”
RIO AMOR: I’m sure in 10 years from now, I’ll look back on this interview and be like, “Hey, what the fuck are you saying? Why’d I do that?”
RUSSELL: Just call me and be like, “Hey, can you log back into your Interview account and edit that really quick?”
RUSSELL: Well, speaking of growing up, who were your musical influences? Who was someone that when you were younger, you would’ve lined up to see in concert?
RIO AMOR: Fun fact about me is I didn’t have internet access until probably 14.

RIO AMOR: I had a phone, but my parents wouldn’t let me go on the internet. It just had a call button. So a lot of what I did was listen to the music my parents played me. I was a huge fan of Erykah Badu and Jill Scott. My dad would play a lot of underground hip hop and not like how we use the word underground now, like gray area, deep cuts. I lived in Hawaii and the radio is super backed up there. They’re probably just now getting fucking, like, Justin Bieber.
RUSSELL: They don’t know who 2hollis is.

RIO AMOR: It’s, like, really late back there. My mom was also super into Siouxsie and The Banshees and Radiohead. She’s a little emo with it. A lot of The Cure in the house, and all those people I would line up still today to see.
RUSSELL: Well, your dad is known as the Grouch, a music legend. Did he play a role in influencing you to want to pursue music?

RIO AMOR: Honestly, I’m super lucky because my parents were both very creative people, so when I said I wanted to do music, they weren’t shutting it down. But when I was a kid, I was so embarrassed of my dad. I would not show up to his shows. I would not listen to his music. I was never proud of it, which today, it’s amazing to go back and hear all his stories.

RIO AMOR: I got into music completely separately from him. I was in middle school, running around the studios that my dad did not take me to, making friends. I remember I came home one day and was like, “Dad, I’ve been writing songs.” He’s like, “What the fuck? You should have let me know. I would have helped you.” I was like, “I don’t want your help in any of this. I want to figure out whatever this is for me.”
RUSSELL: You want to forge your own path.
RIO AMOR: And I did that and I was like, “Now my dad is finally allowed to come to my shows.”
RUSSELL: What was the first show that he was allowed to come to?
RIO AMOR: Well, I was touring when I was 13 and he legally had to come to a couple of the shows because I needed a guardian.
RUSSELL: Permission slip vibes.

RIO AMOR: I was literally like, “Dad, don’t watch me. Don’t give me notes. Don’t introduce me to anybody who can connect me with a label.” Now I’m like, “I kind of wish you would have.” I should’ve nepotism-ed myself out. We would be in a way bigger place now. [Laughs]
RUSSELL: It’s that stubbornness. But you’re still so young.
RIO AMOR: Of course. I also feel grateful that I kind of paved the way myself and didn’t get as much help as I probably could have.
RUSSELL: Self-made baddie. How did you become part of the Concrete Boys?

RIO AMOR: I was playing Flog Gnaw, a 12:00 p.m. set, and I knew that they were playing probably four sets after me. I wore Timbs because I was like, “Hopefully, they see me and fuck with me.” They came off stage and I was like, “I’ve got to introduce myself.” And I fumbled. They all got in the car and then the car started reversing and Boat [Lil Yachty] hopped out of the car and was like, “Who are you?” I was like, “I’m Rio. I just played on the stage.” He was like, “Cool,” and he walked away. I was like, “Fuck, I didn’t get his number. I fumbled it twice.” I was sick that whole day, and I went home and I had a DM from Boat. I think it was a meme and I sent him a fucking resume off the bat.
RUSSELL: Let’s skip the pleasantries.

RIO AMOR: We were playing Fortnite for a couple weeks and I was like, “Okay, let’s cut to the chase. Am I your DJ or what?” And he was like, “Yeah, you can be the DJ.” I met all the guys and we all hit it off instantly.
RUSSELL: We’re in a nonchalant epidemic where you have to act like you don’t care that much, but you have to show that you’re passionate about something.
RIO AMOR: I’m super forward with stuff. Closed mouths don’t get fed.
RUSSELL: So obviously, the hip hop and DJ scene is a male-dominated industry. Talk to me about your experience trying to make it.

RIO AMOR: It’s definitely tough. I just got signed to a record label and before that, I was doing a bunch of meetings with people and I found that a lot of people don’t take women seriously, especially young women. It was so frustrating to me. I remember I would go home from these label meetings and I’d just cry and be like, “They don’t understand.” I’m showing them my deck of this hip hop album that I want to make and they’re like, “Let’s girl it up. Why don’t you wear a sports bra or whatever.” A lot of people brush me off as like, “She’s hanging out with these rappers. She’s a groupie.”
RUSSELL: “I’m a professional, bitch.”

RIO AMOR: I stay up longer than all these boys working on my shit. I’m doing just as much as they all are. It’s hard to see, but I’m so lucky because all the guys I’m surrounded with are great guys. They take me seriously and that’s really what matters. I always praise all the women in this industry because it’s really a battle. It is what makes it more rewarding at the end of the day. You’re like, “Wow, I made it through all of this against all odds.
RUSSELL: Opps at every corner and still I rise. [Laughs]
RUSSELL: I’m doing my research, you’re a part of this unofficial group of next gen of rising musicians. I’m seeing Adéla, the Katseye girls, Malcolm Todd, Audrey Hobert. Is that intimidating?

RIO AMOR: It’s really cool. I’m honored that you even put me in that conversation. I’m friends with a lot of the people that you mentioned, and I always go to their shows and see what they’re doing and I’m like, “This is where I want to be.” I personally wouldn’t even put myself in that conversation.
RUSSELL: I see them in your comment section. [Laughs]

RIO AMOR: I’m so lucky to be doing what I’m doing and even if it’s not on the scale of those people, I’m so honored to also be recognized by them. Malcolm’s popped out at a couple of my shows and I’ve talked to a lot of the Katseye girls about their experiences and they’ve shared a lot of wisdom with me.
RUSSELL: But it’s good that it’s not a sense of competition.
RIO AMOR: Never. It’s real life inspiration at my fingertips which is great.
RUSSELL: Pivoting a little bit to tour, what are your tour essentials?

RIO AMOR: It’s lots of sweatpants for the bus. It’s hard to put your life in two suitcases, but I always try to bring stuff that feels like home, like little stuffed animals and a lot of pictures of my friends and family so I can remember I’m not going to be here forever. Hand sanitizer is very important to me because I shake so many hands. I have a very bad immune system. I’m very sentimental, so I’ll bring my memory box.
RUSSELL: Oh, that’s sweet. Your tour is really intense, high energy. How are you mentally, physically, and spiritually preparing before you go out on stage?

RIO AMOR: I mean, I have to stay really grounded and remember why I’m doing this because I love it. It’s a lot of mental preparation and getting myself in the right mindset, like turning off my phone and being around the people that I love and—
RUSSELL: Not doing interviews. [Laughs]
RIO AMOR: No, but I’ve now gotten to the point where I’m able to bring a friend, which is great.
RUSSELL: If I was a fan in the crowd and I wanted to get your attention, what is something that I should do?

RIO AMOR: I mean, dude, I get distracted so easily up there. I have to transition and I’m looking at somebody in the front that’s dancing. People that have energy put a huge smile on my face, so that always draws my attention. Sometimes I’ll have so much energy that I hop in the crowd with them because I’m like, “This is so lit.” I also read all the signs.
RUSSELL: What’s your favorite sign that you’ve seen?
RIO AMOR: It was in Orlando, Florida and it said, “Rio, will you be my summerboy?” It was a song that I mentioned I liked a couple times.
RUSSELL: The Lady Gaga song?

RIO AMOR: Yeah, it’s literally one of my favorite songs. It became a little thing and people were giving me “Summerboy” bracelets. I always see fans that make shirts, which is really cute. I’m just happy that people are here, so to see that they went the extra mile always grabs my attention and I always try to interact with them as much as possible.
RUSSELL: Talk to me about the fan participation. I saw on your Instagram story you posted a little Google form.

RIO AMOR: So with these shows, it’s like a talk show set and I hijack the talk show and bring a little gang with me to get the crowd hyped because it’s really fun when people from the stage are participating. I try to get as many kids from the city to come on stage and get people hype. I put them in some fun outfits and we all just have a good time on stage. I call them the leaders of the mosh pit and they do a great job.
RUSSELL: Do you see yourself joining the mosh pit tonight?

RIO AMOR: Yeah, I’ve done all of it. I’ve crowd-surfed. That was a little scary, but I’ve joined the mosh pit almost every show when I was with the boys. These couple shows, I’ve been trying to not get lost in the mosh pit because I see a lot of videos of myself online and I’m always in the mosh pit and I’m like, “Am I even DJing?” [Laughs]
RUSSELL: I know that you’re a Twilight fan. How are we feeling about the James Bond announcement?
RIO AMOR: Oh my god, stop. I was freaking out. We were about to board the plane. I was like, “Oh my god, no way.” I love Rob.
RUSSELL: You’re going to be in that pre-sale.
RIO AMOR: I’ve already told everybody we got to get those seats. He’s an incredible actor.
RUSSELL: In the Rio Amor biopic, he’s taking every single role.
RIO AMOR: The first Gen Z James Bond. [Laughs]
RUSSELL: At 19, you’ve accomplished so much, but you still have so much ahead of you.
RUSSELL: What’s a goal that you have and you want to put on the record, so that way in years from now people can come back to this interview and be like, “Oh fuck, she did it”?
RIO AMOR: I would like to one day play in an arena. I played a lot of festivals, but playing my own show there would change my life. I also want to meet Drake.
RUSSELL: My college job was at this hotel, and when celebrities come to stay, you get their aliases. When we get off the record—
RIO AMOR: Oh my god, tell me!
RUSSELL: Signing off so I can tell Rio Amor Drake’s alias.

items.title: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast
items.description: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast
items.author: Lola Petticrew
paragraphs: Anthony Boyle and Lola Petticrew Are the Matt and Ben of West Belfast

Anthony Boyle is on a generational run. Since his Tony-nominated turn as Scorpius Malfoy on Broadway, the West Belfast-born actor has become prestige TV’s go-to young lead, playing a WWII airman in Masters of the Air, John Wilkes Booth in Manhunt, IRA volunteer Brendan Hughes in Say Nothing, and Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness. Now, he transforms completely as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists, the Netflix limited series about the rise and fall of the crypto empire FTX and the volatile relationship at its center. Here, he talks about the role with his friend of 20 years, the actor Lola Petticrew, who has been his collaborator on screen, and who helps him run lines off it.
SATURDAY 1PM NOVEMBER 7, 2026 BELFAST
LOLA PETTICREW: We always knew this day would come and I’d be interviewing you.
ANTHONY BOYLE: Yeah, only I thought it would be me in a witness stand and you as a judge. So it’s good that it’s for an interview.
PETTICREW: [Laughs] We’ve been friends for 20 years on the dot. Does that make you sick to your stomach?
BOYLE: Jesus Christ. Is that true?
PETTICREW: Yeah. I’m 31 this year.
BOYLE: We’re old. 20 years is a long time. There’s been births, deaths, relationships, terrible hair. We’ve been through so much.
PETTICREW: When you say terrible haircuts, are you referencing when I got a crew cut when I was 14?
BOYLE: I’m thinking of that crew cut that was more of a bowl cut.
PETTICREW: [Laughs] Yeah. So I just want you to talk about our friendship a bit and say nice things about me, maybe for two minutes just to get into it.
BOYLE: Well, I think you’re my favorite actor to work with, my favorite actor to watch.
BOYLE: You got your nails done?
PETTICREW: Yeah, do you want to see them?
BOYLE: What’s that, a little Christmas sparkle we got going on there?
PETTICREW: Yeah. I also got my toes done.
BOYLE: Get the fucking toes out. Nice big black toe. Happy days. Do you want to say nice things about me for a couple of minutes?
PETTICREW: That’s what I’m about to do if you’d let me do my job. You’ve asked me to do this as if I don’t have enough on my plate.
PETTICREW: So you claim to be responsible for my career and we joke about it a lot, but that’s probably quite true if we were being honest.
BOYLE: Thank god this is going to be in print.

PETTICREW: I never would’ve got into drama school if it wasn’t for you because I actually just didn’t apply. And watching you actually go for it was the thing that made me actually go for it. So it’s been really lovely to have someone who’s like family to navigate everything with. There are not a lot of people that get to do that except for Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. So my question is, are we the Matt Damon and Ben Affleck of West Belfast? And if so, who’s Matt and who’s Ben?
BOYLE: I actually think we’re the Ant and Dec of West Belfast, maybe even Jedward. But if we’re going for Matt and Ben, I think…
PETTICREW: I know what I think.
PETTICREW: You’re Matt and I’m Ben.
BOYLE: Why do you think that?
PETTICREW: Because I too love—

PETTICREW: I too love J.Lo. I’m messy, because let’s be serious, Ben is a messy bitch, and I love looking sad and smoking and drinking the Dunkin Donuts coffee. And you’re Matt. You’re the movie star, bro.
BOYLE: Look, I’ll take Matt Damon. I think the Dunkin Donuts and cigarettes and looking sad is definitely your forte, and I’ll take Matt and run with it and be very proud to do so.
PETTICREW: Okay, so I want to talk about The Altruists. My first question is, did you know what altruists meant when you were auditioning or did you have to look?

BOYLE: No. I had to Google it and then I had to Google how to pronounce it. My mom said to me, “What the fuck does altruist mean? You should have just called it Crypto King.” Look, this interview is now a petition to change the name of The Altruists to Crypto King, and they’ll give my mom a bit of the cut. Did you know what altruists meant?
PETTICREW: Yes. So your mom is going to get a cut if we change the name to Crypto King. Do you think that I should get at least 5 percent for helping you with your audition?

BOYLE: Yes, I actually do. Although, do you think I should get 5 percent of all your income for getting you into drama school, getting you an agent, giving you inspiration, showing you what love truly is, showing you what friendship truly means?
PETTICREW: I’m not going to fight that.
BOYLE: Then yes, everyone’s getting paid.
PETTICREW: Everyone’s getting paid.
BOYLE: I can’t believe you’ve actually written questions down. I thought we were just going to talk shit.
PETTICREW: I think I thought if we talked shit, we would go way off, and I thought somebody had to steer the ship.
BOYLE: I will be your shipmate, you will be my captain.

PETTICREW: Great. So when we were shooting I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, you were auditioning for this role and I was helping with your lines, and I therefore was privy to the voice and the accent very early on. Was that something that immediately made you feel like when you dropped into the voice, you had a better hold on this guy?

BOYLE: Yeah, when you’re playing such a big character like this, you see all the YouTube clips and you see all these videos about him and immediately the first thing you start doing is a sort of impression, and then you get a little bit closer to it, and the voice really helps with someone like this because he’s so nervous. It’s two octaves higher than me. It sounds like I’m on fucking helium and he stutters a lot. I feel like he’s got a hundred computer tabs open at once and then when he clicks off one, five come up. So that’s reflected in the way he speaks. He’s going forward, going back, going back, going forward. He also has a Californian no and a Silibant S, those kids that have spent too long on a computer and they speak like this. It’s easy to drop into that and that then informs your physicality and your psyche too.
PETTICREW: It is also probably the only time you have played someone who isn’t conventionally hot. Do you want to speak on that as a conventionally hot guy?
BOYLE: I don’t think I’m conventionally hot.
PETTICREW: I think TikTok begs to differ.
BOYLE: I don’t think Arthur Guinness was conventionally hot.
PETTICREW: Okay. Maybe take out the word conventionally, it’s the first time you’re playing a character without being hot.
BOYLE: Look, beauty is in the eye of the beholder. To be honest, Lola, when you see the rest of the show, there’s something to him.

PETTICREW: Okay. This is not the first time that you’ve played a real person. Did this differ from playing somebody like Brendan Hughes [in Say Nothing] and maybe anxiety or nervousness that you had for portraying a real person?

BOYLE: I’ve played more real people than fictional people. I felt more nervous playing Brendan Hughes because he’s such a huge figure where we live in West Belfast. And because of the subject matter of Say Nothing, which we did together, that made me feel nervous because I wanted to get it right. Whereas this with Sam Bankman-Fried, I didn’t feel that much pressure. I don’t know why, I just thought it was really fun. The script was just really fun, the showrunner was really fun, the director was really fun, Julia [Garner] was really fun. I was like, “Oh, this is just a laugh.”

PETTICREW: Yeah, I remember when you were auditioning for it you were just so excited about the writing. It’s really nice because sometimes when you have an immediate excitement, that doesn’t always last the whole way through, but it seems like it has for you in this.
BOYLE: Yeah. And thank you for bringing up that you helped me with the audition again.
PETTICREW: I just want to make sure people realize that it’s really a team effort when it comes to you and I.
BOYLE: And me helping you with the Furious audition and with your Say Nothing audition.
BOYLE: Let’s talk about Furious, winning all the best reviews in the world and everyone’s saying that you’re the best actor ever. How does that feel?
PETTICREW: Save it for when you interview me for Interview.
PETTICREW: What was it like working with Julia Garner?

BOYLE: Julia is just phenomenal, an incredible artist, an amazing human being. She’s been creating these iconic characters for 10 years and everything’s just so different. She completely transforms and she’s so inventive, so free, but can be so intense. She’s like an athlete or something.
PETTICREW: And you shot it in Vancouver?
PETTICREW: How was Vancouver?
BOYLE: Vancouver is great craic. It’s class, a lot of Irish bars, and loads of Irish people. I didn’t really get much time off to explore because I was filming flat out, but I love Vancouver.

PETTICREW: I remember we found out that you were going to be filming in Vancouver and I was going to be filming in New York, and we thought we were going to be so close to each other that we could just hop across and see each other all the time, and it turns out they’re on two opposite ends.
BOYLE: Geography outside of Belfast and Derry, I’m not really great on, but hey, we got a couple FaceTimes in. It’s all good. What was it like working with Emmy Rossum?
PETTICREW: I’m going to need you to save it for when you interview me for Interview. Stop wasting the magic.
BOYLE: Precious time. Okay, go ahead.
PETTICREW: So I’m going to see you tonight.
BOYLE: Where are you? Give me your exact home address. Let’s dox you in the interview.
PETTICREW: I’m seeing you tonight because I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is closing the Belfast Film Festival.
BOYLE: So exciting. What a long title.
PETTICREW: It’s the longest title in the world, and I’d like people to know that Anthony and I petitioned to change it. Maybe we should call your mom.
BOYLE: It’s a long title and no one’s got it right. People keep saying, “I’m going to see your film, The Building’s on Fire and It’s Raining.”
PETTICREW: Doing I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning was the third time that we’ve worked together. Talk to me a bit about I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, and what drew you to that project?

BOYLE: Well, Clio [Barnard] and Enda [Walsh] wrote me a letter saying that they would love me to do it. Enda was one of my favorite playwrights, and has written some of my favorite films like Hunger. So getting that letter, it’s just a real pinch me moment. Clio was one of the best filmmakers working in England, I think. As soon as I started reading it, I just loved it. I loved the characters, I loved the world, and I was like, “I feel like I could do this role justice and be of service to their vision.”

PETTICREW: It very much felt like the type of film that we always wanted to make, and you and I were always the hugest fans of Enda. But then whenever I got the call, obviously, to ask me to read for it, I couldn’t quite believe that it was going to be Enda, Clio, and then yourself. And even though Say Nothing is set in Belfast and I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is set in Birmingham, it still felt really close to our community.

BOYLE: It’s funny, doing a role like I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, I didn’t have to do any research. Me and you just hung out in the community and got it immediately because it didn’t feel like a world away. Whereas when I’m doing House of Guinness or something, it feels like an anthropological study of who these people are who grew up in private schools. And then adding the element of you playing my wife in it was like I don’t really have to act in a way. Again, we’ve been friends for 20 years, so that means we’ve had ups and downs like in any friendship, and we’ve seen each other go through so much in our lives. I want to be doing a film with you when I’m 50, and I hope we will. That would be a great creative life.
PETTICREW: Yeah, I think there’s an inherent safety there. We have so much to fall back on that nothing that we do in a scene is ever going to be a lie.

PETTICREW: You have that ability that not a lot of actors have, which is that you can play roles that are very close to yourself and also really far from yourself. People are usually only good at one of those, and you have managed to make a career of being able to bounce between both. That’s class. And second of all, is there one of them that feels more exciting for you or more comfortable for you?
BOYLE: It’s so embarrassing to get a compliment from you for some reason. I don’t know why. I’m hiding behind my jumper like, “oh god.” What was the question? Which sort of work do I prefer?
PETTICREW: Not even that you prefer. Is there one that feels more comfortable? More exciting?

BOYLE: Honestly, it always feels like I want to do the opposite of what I’ve just done. I remember I’d done Say Nothing, which felt like an extension of me and everyone I’ve met who can tell a story in a bar in Belfast. And then doing House of Guinness immediately after, which is more of a character piece. It’s a completely different voice and body and psychology. So I guess I want to just do the opposite of what I’ve just done, and right now I’m doing a piece that was written for me and it’s me essentially, and I can’t wait to do a big character piece again. I really like when I get sent something and I’m like, “How the fuck am I going to do this? This is not me at all. How do I get into this?” That’s what really excites me.

PETTICREW: Okay. I would like to end the interview by having you describe to the people of Interview what Goodfellas is, because that’s where I’m going to meet you tonight before we go to the Belfast Film Festival.

BOYLE: Goodfellas is an amazing pizza place in West Belfast where you can bring your own beer. So Lola and I’ll be sat there with our big bottle of Glen’s Vodka on the table. Our mate CJ will bring some Buckfast [Tonic Wine] and we’re going to have some lovely pizza and we’re going to get on a party bus and go to the Belfast Film Festival.
PETTICREW: Can I ask what your Goodfellas order is?

BOYLE: Last night I went for pizza with my family and there was a thing on the menu called a piccante pizza and it was really spicy chicken salami. I’m going to see if I can get something similar tonight. I’ve had pizza three days in a row.
PETTICREW: Well, if you’re looking for a spicy pizza in Goodfellas, it’s going to be a Hot Sicilian.
BOYLE: Okay, then I’ll have a Hot Sicilian this evening.
PETTICREW: Well, I’m going to get a Hot Sicilian. I’m going to get half a pizza, get half Hot Sicilian, and then probably some of the garlic potatoes.
BOYLE: Well, I’ll have to join you on that. And if anyone in America is reading this and finds themself in Ireland, go to Goodfellas.
PETTICREW: Lovely people, lovely craic, great pizza.
BOYLE: I’m actually really excited, Lola, and I think it’s going to be great to screen it. How many people do you have coming? I have 700 people.
PETTICREW: I think your daddy has invited basically all of West Belfast.
BOYLE: Yeah, my dad’s invited everyone he’s ever met, so that’ll be a lot of fun.
PETTICREW: Well, thank you very much for talking to me. I’m going to go and get a shower, shave my legs, and get myself ready to see you in about two hours.
PETTICREW: I love you. Bye.
Groomer: Alice Moore using Moisturise & Revive Daily Moisturiser by Kyushi at The Wall Group.

items.title: Disabled Fans Say the Live-Music Industry Can Do Better: 'We Are Not a Pain in the Ass'
items.description: U ntil recently, I didn’t have to think about disability accommodations at concerts. I could stand and dance for hours, navigate steep stairs, and lose myself in the euphoria of singing alongside friends and strangers. But cancer, a spinal issue, and three sur
items.author: Maribeth Romslo
paragraphs: U ntil recently, I didn’t have to think about disability accommodations at concerts. I could stand and dance for hours, navigate steep stairs, and lose myself in the euphoria of singing alongside friends and strangers. But cancer, a spinal issue, and three surgeries in three years changed my body and my sense of balance. Busy environments now overwhelm my equilibrium, and I often need the stability of a cane to move through the world.

Last October, I attended my first concert as a newly disabled person. My friends and I wore glitter, wigs, and seashell crowns. The four of us had flown to Southern California from around the country to be together for one night of unapologetic joy. That’s what live music can give us as fans — the ability to gather, feel, hear, and sing together. To experience the power of collective vibrations, especially for anyone who has ever felt different, unseen, or too much.

Still, I was unsure what to expect from the outdoor venue, which normally serves as a golf course. It was a general admission event, and the website was vague about accessible seating and capacity. Goldenvoice, the AEG Presents subsidiary managing the tour, only allows one companion per disabled attendee in the accessible (ADA) area. When I emailed ahead asking if my three friends could sit with me, I received a boilerplate response saying I could “switch out” companions by visiting the accessibility tent. Because of my disability, I could only sit with one friend at a time.

I wanted to bring my cane, but without clarity, I opted for a walker, which could double as a seat. At the venue, the accessible rideshare drop-off was nearly a mile from the ADA viewing platform. The route was mostly grass, gravel, and sand. By the time I arrived at the platform more than an hour later, my walker wheels were packed with dirt and the accessible area was full. “First come, first served,” a staffer told me with a shrug. After talking with two more staffers, they squeezed me into the back of an overflow area next to the ADA platform.
When the concert ended, I asked if there was an ADA pickup closer than the original drop-off. “I don’t know,” a staffer said. I pushed my walker back over the same uneven terrain in the dark.

In the weeks after the concert, I filed complaints with the City of Pasadena and California’s Civil Rights Department. Filing a complaint is one of the few formal avenues available to disabled people who believe they have experienced disability discrimination. As I learned more about how ADA complaints are typically resolved through civil enforcement and mediation, I knew a lawsuit wasn’t what I was seeking. I wanted a conversation about how live music could do better.

Over the last year, I’ve spoken with more than 50 people across the disabled community and the entertainment industry about accessibility — its history, its present, and its future. I also attended more shows, where my experiences ranged from frustrating to perfectly fine to genuinely great. But despite bright spots and improvements in the disability landscape, the fact remains that too many disabled people still feel cast aside or left out entirely when it comes to live entertainment.

Kelsey Peterson is a writer, dancer, and podcaster in Wisconsin who uses a wheelchair since sustaining a spinal cord injury in 2012 that left her paralyzed her from her chest down. She told me about seeing her favorite band, Widespread Panic, at Milwaukee’s Riverside Theater last October: “Thirteen years ago, I’d be in the balcony raging with a beautiful view and better sound. Now I’m stuck under the balcony because there’s literally nowhere else for me.”

Peterson continued, “You’re like the afterthought misfits.” The emotional toll, she said, can outweigh the physical one. “You’re not just going to a show to experience joy. You’re going to a show to overcome all the microaggressions. And then try to get to the joy.”

ONE IN FOUR AMERICANS — nearly 70 million adults — live with a disability, according to the most recent CDC data available, from 2024. Those numbers are only growing as America’s population continues to age. Studies indicate a rising trend in people living with disabilities. Researchers describe the Covid-19 pandemic as a “mass disabling event” that has brought millions of newly disabled people into public life and forced spaces to confront long-avoided accessibility failings.

Most able-bodied people tend to think of disability pretty narrowly and visibly: people who use wheelchairs or people born with conditions like cerebral palsy. But disability is widely varied and nuanced. It is the cancer survivor returning to work with less stamina, the veteran reading lips after combat-induced hearing loss, the cyclist learning to trust their body again after an accident. And they all come to live music for the same reasons anyone does: to celebrate artists they love, let go, and feel less alone.

Amy Wood, an accessible events manager for Salesforce who is deaf, says she is often met with surprise when she mentions loving live music. “I can feel the beat, and if I’m really close to the speaker, I can hear some of the music,” she says. “You always are having to dispel these stereotypes or these myths or assumptions about people with disabilities. People with disabilities want to party, too!”

John Kenefick is an Albuquerque artist, military veteran, wheelchair user, and massive EDM fan. He used to feel self-conscious and lonely in his wheelchair, until he transformed it with decorative large-scale papier-mâché sculptures at shows as a way of claiming space and inviting people into conversation. He is now a fierce advocate for fellow disabled veterans who want to enjoy concerts. “They just need to know that they’re wanted and there’s room for them,” he says.

The Americans With Disabilities Act, signed into law in 1990, has spurred much progress in carving out that space. Title III of the ADA requires public-facing businesses like concert venues and music festivals to provide disabled patrons with equal access to “goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages and accommodations.”

To fulfill these terms, venues and festivals should remove architectural and communication barriers for disabled customers, providing ramps, level entry options, and clear and navigable routes to move through spaces. They must also provide reasonable modifications — including accessible signage, websites, and ticketing systems for people who are blind, deaf, or have low vision — so that people with disabilities can participate fully and equally in their services.

In practical terms, this means disabled patrons should be able to buy a ticket as easily as anyone else, get into the venue without extra hurdles, move through the space unimpeded, and have a safe place to experience the show. But in reality, access is often inconsistent or treated as a burden. Disabled concertgoers are still navigating systems that fall short of the law’s intent, even when concert venues and music festivals may be technically ADA compliant.

The ADA regulations for temporary events like outdoor concerts and music festivals were last updated in 2010 and set only the minimum technical requirements for access. As disability has grown in both numbers and visibility, these baseline requirements have become inadequate, advocates say. Compliance can amount to little more than proof that boxes were checked, even when the experience itself can feel exclusionary.

“Whenever I hear that a venue is ‘ADA compliant,’ my antennae go up,” says Jim LeBrecht, a Bay Area filmmaker, Deadhead, and wheelchair user, who co-directed the Oscar-nominated 2020 documentary Crip Camp, about a summer camp for disabled youth, with Nicole Newnham. “When the message is ‘we did what we were required to do,’ what you’re really saying is you don’t care about the intent of the law, which is to make sure people with disabilities can show up for an evening of entertainment like non-disabled people do.”

Disability inclusion, LeBrecht argues, is an opportunity for promoters and cannot stop at technical compliance. “We [disabled people] are not a pain in the ass,” LeBrecht tells me. “We live in a world that wasn’t built for us. If you choose to be in this business, it’s your responsibility to make sure everybody has a good experience. And I mean everybody.”

THE ADA IS A CIVIL RIGHTS law largely regulated and enforced by the Department of Justice. Civil rights laws are largely complaint-driven by design, to avoid overreach and excessive surveillance by the government. However, this setup places the burden on disabled people to recognize discrimination, document it, and push back. Meaningful change usually doesn’t happen until a disabled person has been harmed. And that change can sometimes have unanticipated effects.

In 2019, when Amy Fink was 20 years old, she bought tickets to a reggae-punk fusion show at Red Rocks Amphitheatre, the open-air venue in Colorado. But Fink, who uses a wheelchair, noticed something odd when she tried to buy a ticket. The price of a general admission ticket was $49.99, but when she checked the box to indicate she required accessible seating, the price increased $40. “Why should I have to pay more just because I need a wheelchair-accessible seat?” Fink wondered.
“You’re not just going to a show to experience joy. You have to overcome all the microaggressions. And then try to get to the joy.”
Podcaster and disability advocate Kelsey Peterson

At the time, Fink was undergoing cancer treatments and was fed up with how people treated her when she was using her wheelchair. “People stop you at the grocery store and ask why you’re in a wheelchair. They treat you like you are a nuisance and a leech,” Fink says. “I remember thinking, ‘I’m not going to put up with this. I’m not going to just let this happen to me and other people.’”
So, Fink filed a complaint with the Department of Justice.

Three years later, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado reached a settlement with Red Rocks Amphitheatre and its owner-operator, the City and County of Denver. Between 2018 and 2020, the DOJ determined, Red Rocks overcharged 1,817 accessible tickets across 178 events. Concert promoters Live Nation, AEG, and PBS12 each paid a civil penalty, amounting to a total of $47,950.90 refunded to disabled fans who were overcharged for wheelchair-accessible seats.

“It may not feel like a lot of money to Live Nation or AEG or the city of Denver, but it’s not always about that,” Peter McNeilly, U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado, says. “Money is simply a quantifiable way to say there was not fairness and there wasn’t equal access.”

McNeilly says the Red Rocks case had three goals: to ensure disabled people could access a historic venue, to make whole those who were harmed, and to change how things were done going forward. While settlements like this do not set legal precedent for other venues, he notes, they can create momentum. “If other venues see what Red Rocks did to work this out,” McNeilly tells me, “they may choose to do something similar.”

The DOJ process also prompted broader accessibility improvements at Red Rocks, including expanded accessible parking, rebuilt ramps and plazas, and upgraded accessible bathrooms. Because the amphitheater is built into a mountainside, wheelchair-accessible seating is limited to the very front and very back row. Before the settlement, that setup forced disabled fans into either the highest or lowest ticket prices, excluding them from equal access to purchasing mid-priced tickets available to other fans. Red Rocks now requires all accessible seats to be sold at the lowest ticket price.

But even that victory came at a cost. Red Rocks venue director Tad Bowman says that while the ticketing changes improved the overall experience for disabled fans, they also created an unintended consequence: non-disabled fans buying up wheelchair-accessible tickets just to get a front-row bargain.

“There’s not much we can do about that,” Bowman says. Venues are legally prohibited from requiring proof of a disability, a safeguard meant to protect disabled patrons’ privacy and dignity. Venues have to take a buyer’s word for it when they attest they need an accessible seat. “We can’t go up to someone and say, ‘We don’t think you have a disability, prove it,’ because then we’re also violating the ADA.”

Of the roughly 9,500 seats at Red Rocks, just 121 seats are wheelchair-accessible at each show. When non-disabled people game the system and buy up the limited quantity of accessible seats, disabled fans are excluded from being part of the music. Because of barriers like these, many disabled fans simply stop going to shows, deciding it is not worth the physical toll, the anxiety, or the indignity. It’s the exact opposite result of what cases like the Red Rocks suit are intended to address.

As Mike Foehse, a Minneapolis entrepreneur and musician with low vision and hearing loss, puts it, “How many people are sitting on the sidelines saying, ‘I wish I could go to that show, but I’m just not gonna deal with it’? I can’t do what I used to do, it’s really frustrating. You become less and less relevant. And that’s hard to swallow. Am I obsolete?”

DISABLED MUSICIANS ALSO FEEL the impact of navigating inaccessible venues. In 2018, Portugal. The Man played the Burton Cummings Theatre in Winnipeg. Eric Howk, the band’s guitarist who uses a wheelchair, couldn’t visit the venue’s green room because it was only accessible by a spiral staircase. “I just remember chain smoking alone in the alleyway in February in Manitoba until showtime,” Howk tells me.

But when Howk and the band returned to the venue in 2023, the green room had been updated to be wheelchair accessible. “That wasn’t me shaking my fist or getting on a soapbox,” Howk says. “They saw what the experience was for a disabled musician, determined that it was unacceptable, and fixed it.”

While the Burton Cummings Theatre recognized and addressed the issue, Howk says that outcome is the exception, far from the rule. What frustrates him most is the reflexive apology that typically accompanies the accessibility gap instead, often getting in the way of real problem-solving. “Getting past the apology is 100 percent of the game,” he said. “To start off a concert experience with an apology is a bummer. The apology is a given. Shame becomes a stopping point instead of a starting place. Figure out solutions.”

One challenge is that the music industry still has remarkably little data to guide those solutions. Disabled audiences, artists, and music professionals remain vastly understudied, particularly in the United States.

Recording Artists and Music Professionals with Disabilities (RAMPD), founded by musicians Lachi and Gaelynn Lea, hopes to help change that. Their goal is “to amplify disability culture through the music industry,” says Lachi, a blind recording artist whose music blends EDM, pop, and soul sounds. Or, put another way, “I entertain people into giving a crap about disability.”

Alongside its advocacy work, the organization is conducting one of the first large-scale studies of disabled fans and music professionals in the United States. The results, expected sometime next year, could establish an important baseline for measuring disability access and participation across the American music industry.

Until research efforts like these might encourage broader industry change, progress often depends on individual venues deciding to make improvements on their own. For the Burton Cummings Theatre, that has meant continuing to update the historic 1907 building using the ADA as a benchmark — despite operating in Canada. “We’re inviting people into our building,” Ruben Ramalheiro, director of live entertainment for True North Sports + Entertainment, which operates the theater, says, “so we want people to feel like they would in their own home.”

FESTIVALS AND OUTDOOR SHOWS, of course, present distinct challenges when it comes to accessibility. Some promoters outsource that work to specialized contractors like Accessibility Live.
