Founded by Austin Whitney in 2016, the company is the primary accessibility services provider for both Live Nation and AEG, overseeing accessibility at 120 to 130 concerts and festivals each year. Accessibility Live hires hundreds of temporary seasonal employees to staff teams at large festivals like Coachella, EDC, and more recently Bonnaroo.

Whitney has a very personal view of accessibility across the industry. In 2007, a car accident severed his spinal cord, paralyzing him from the waist down. “I was scared, depressed, and anxious,” he tells me. “I had all sorts of body image issues. I felt alone.” He found solace in experiencing live music when he attended Coachella in 2008 as a new wheelchair user, with his friends helping him overcome the accessibility barriers he encountered at the festival.
“People treat you like you are a nuisance. I thought, ‘I’m not going to put up with this. I’m not going to just let this happen to me and other people.’”
Amy Fink, who filed a civil rights complaint after an experience with Red Rocks

Whitney began working at Coachella in 2011 and started running their accessibility program five years later. He is drawn to temporary infrastructure events, because “it’s a blank slate every year.” Unlike permanent venues, festivals are built and dismantled in a matter of days, requiring accessibility teams to adapt to varied terrain, temporary infrastructure, and changing weather. Those parameters can offer the opportunity for creativity and on-the-fly problem-solving. Yet they don’t always make for lasting change.

“Built infrastructure has memory,” Whitney tells me. “We [festivals] don’t have that, so it relies a lot on people. Most frontline festival staff, they’re temporary. Their training has to be short, repeatable, and specific. That’s where a lot of the breakdowns unfortunately happen.”

Whitney acknowledges that communication is one area where the industry can improve, particularly in giving disabled fans clearer information about what to expect for accessibility accommodations before they arrive.

“People now take in so much different information from different places,” Whitney says, citing social media and online fan communities. “A website with accessible information probably isn’t going to convey enough in order to help prepare fans with disabilities to set expectations for them to have a great time.”

In reporting this story, I struggled to find meaningful public data about disabled fans and live music. I searched high and low for information about how many disabled fans utilize accessibility services at concerts of various sizes and types of venues and how often accommodations reach or exceed capacity. Whitney tells me there are “a lot of data points for any given show.” But, he adds, “It’s data that I can’t really delve into. It’s not my data to share.” Without that information, it is difficult to know how frequently disabled fans encounter barriers, if the same problems recur across events, or how feedback and demand translate into improvements.

The live-music ecosystem is largely controlled by a small number of powerful promoters, namely Live Nation and AEG. When I asked the industry giants how accessibility decisions are made, evaluated, and improved upon, I was met with more caution than candor.

After six weeks of back and forth, Live Nation declined to answer my specific questions about accessibility decision-making, vendors, budgeting, feedback evaluation, and accountability. Instead, the company provided a brief values-based statement from its head of venues and highlighted its partnership with KultureCity, a nonprofit focused on sensory accessibility through venue certification and tools like quiet spaces and sensory bags for neurodiverse patrons.

It is notable that Live Nation created a director of accessibility role in 2023. However, after my repeated requests, the company declined an on-the-record conversation with the person who leads accessibility work at the largest live-entertainment company in the world.

AEG did respond to one of my specific questions about disabled fan feedback and follow-through. Erik Barker, director of risk mitigation for AEG Presents and Goldenvoice, told me via email, “For concerns that are raised through our official channels, fans should expect to receive a response. We strive for a 100 percent response rate. Our email inbox is monitored 24/7, 365 days a year.” Barker added, “The majority of the feedback we get is complimentary.”
Yet, this is not what happened in my experience. After my own accessibility concerns in California last fall, I emailed my feedback to the official AEG accessibility email. I never received a reply.
When I asked major festivals for comment for this story, Bonnaroo and Lollapalooza declined. Coachella did not respond.

Accessibility failures thrive in the dark, where no one has to explain how decisions are made, why capacity isn’t anticipated accurately, or what accessibility actually looks like when thousands of disabled people often have to navigate barriers. The gap between fear and possibility is where progress gets stuck.

Crip Camp co-director Jim LeBrecht puts it more bluntly: “If you’re not willing to be quoted for this article, it speaks to a fear of being called out. Fear that you’re opening yourself up for criticism. If that’s your fear, then maybe you aren’t doing it right. Or you want to let sleeping dogs lie. That you know that there are problems that you’re not fixing. Well, fuck ’em. You can quote me on that.”

IF THE INDUSTRY DOESN’T want to do the right thing for its own sake, concert promoters could consider how much money they’re leaving on the table by ignoring the needs of disabled consumers. Disabled people represent an emerging economic force that businesses systematically under-serve. A 2024 study shows that people with disabilities in North America and Europe control roughly $2.6 trillion in annual disposable income.
“Inclusivity is a term that’s used a lot. [But] if you can’t get in the gate, you can’t go to the festival. If you can’t use the bathroom, you can’t go to the festival.”
ADA coordinator Holly Maniatty

Speaking with many disabled music fans about how they like to spend their money, I learned that those who are treated well tend to be deeply loyal. When access works, when communication is clear, when staff know what they are doing, disabled fans come back. They bring friends. They buy merch. They build community around artists and venues that make them feel welcome.

Carly Webster recently graduated from college in Ohio with a degree in arts management. She also has cerebral palsy, uses a walker, and works VIP and merch booths at concerts and festivals. So Webster understands the accessibility gap from multiple angles, both as a fan and as someone trying to build a career in live music.

“When I first entered the music industry, I wanted to go on tour,” she told me. “But they could just as easily hire somebody who doesn’t have accessibility needs. That’s a hard pill to swallow. But I also want to be visible, out there with my disability. I want younger disabled people to see that they can go to shows and work in the industry.”

Webster speaks bluntly about the business case. “Disabled folks are a valuable investment. If 25 percent of the U.S. population is disabled, imagine the revenue if those people knew your shows were accessible and that you actually cared.”

Last December, business leaders gathered in Tokyo for Sync25, a global summit focused on disability accountability in business. Marcie Roth, CEO and executive director of the World Institute on Disability, said at the gathering that disability inclusion offers “one of the greatest economic opportunities of our time. Companies that fail to include us [disabled people] are not only perpetuating inequity, they are leaving enormous innovation, talent, and market value on the table.”

“We worked really hard to get these rights,” Roth adds. As a mobility scooter user who loves Bruce Springsteen’s music, she channels the Boss’ lyrics when it comes to disability justice: “‘No retreat, no surrender.’ Disabled people just want to boldly go where everybody else has gone before.”

HOLLY MANIATTY IS A CERTIFIED ADA coordinator who started in the industry as an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter for artists like Wu-Tang Clan, Eminem, and Dave Matthews Band. Her accessibility coordination consulting includes large-scale events like NASCAR and 13 years on the accessibility services team at Bonnaroo. Maniatty notes that many of the most meaningful accessibility failures do not boil down to budgets or bottom-line business decisions: “It’s time spent and communication.”

Maniatty’s accessibility approach is rooted in what she calls “experiential equity.” She explains further, “Inclusivity in general is a term that’s used a lot with disability. I think of it more as experiential equity. Because if you can’t get in the gate, you can’t go to the festival. If you can’t use the bathroom, you can’t go to the festival.”

Maniatty finds hope in a growing group of independent festivals that are approaching accessibility as a core value. “These smaller festivals, they’re really raising the bar for the industry giants,” she says.

Colorado’s Meadow Creek Music Festival, launched in 2025 with 10,000 guests in its inaugural year, is one example. “We’re 280 acres in the middle of nowhere Colorado. Everything we do has to be intentional,” founder Jake Frommer says. That included bringing Maniatty into the process early and treating accessibility as foundational. “When Holly said, ‘These are the ways to really make sure everyone feels included,’ we were like, amazing, let’s make this happen.”

Frommer, a longtime producer who’s worked at Electric Forest, Coachella, and Stagecoach festivals, wanted accessibility to be more than a value statement at Meadow Creek. “It’s really easy to write a core value down,” he says. “But how are you actually living that? How are you bringing it to life?”
Maniatty sees that mindset as the real differentiator. “It is about creating a pathway for people to have moments where they feel truly free.”

David Sussman has been navigating live music using a wheelchair longer than most venues have been thinking about accessibility. “There’s lots of opportunities that weren’t there 48 years ago when I became disabled. The world is opening up for us, and has been for many decades. Now we just have to move to the next level, be more inclusive. It just makes for a better world.”

Sussman remembers the 1999 Glastonbury Festival as both frightening and unforgettable. He and his friends were caught in a crush of people trying to reach R.E.M. on a narrow bridge. Sussman grabbed onto his friend and said “Listen, man, this is life or death for me. If I go down in this crowd, I’ll be trampled.”
After his spinal transverse myelitis diagnosis at 15 years old, his father told him, “This sucks. But now go live your life. Don’t look back.”

I REMEMBER MY FIRST CONCERT vividly, piling friends into my tiny Geo Metro on a frigid Iowa night in 1995 to see the Indigo Girls. I’ve been chasing that feeling ever since: watching U2 wail on their guitars in the pouring rain, seeing the Rolling Stones at Soldier Field with brand-new college friends, hearing Mumford & Sons sing “Nothing Compares 2 U” in Minnesota the night Prince died, feeling 17 again at the Eras Tour with my daughter.

Over the last year attending shows as a disabled person, I’ve noticed what makes a difference in accessibility services: infrastructure and personnel training. Permanent venues, as Whitney pointed out, often have an advantage over temporary events as they are built with specific access requirements. Brick-and-mortar facilities also tend to have more regular staff who are trained to understand accommodating disabled guests within their specific location.

I recently saw a show at the Armory in Minneapolis. Before attending, I emailed to figure out my accessibility options for a standing general admission ticket. The box office promptly emailed me back with clear answers, so I knew what to expect. When I arrived, an elevator attendant helped me get to the general admission floor and asked which songs I was most excited to hear. They told me what to do if I needed more assistance before I headed into the crowd with my walker.
None of this was extraordinary. But that’s what made it extraordinary. I didn’t have to spend the night problem-solving my disability. I could just enjoy the show.

Living with disability hasn’t fundamentally changed who I am or what I love. I still want to experience live music the way I always have: immersed, part of the energy, sharing moments of connection and joy with friends and strangers for a few hours. What has changed is my awareness of how often access is treated as optional or an afterthought. Once you experience that gap, you can’t unsee it.

But there is another path forward. One where experiential equity is built in from the beginning, where disabled fans are assumed to be an integral part of the audience, and where live music becomes more expansive.
I’d buy a ticket to that world. Wouldn’t you?

items.title: Patrick Stewart: 10 Essential Roles
items.description: Had Sir Patrick Stewart only played Jean-Luc Picard, commanding officer of the USS Enterprise, or Charles Xavier, leader of the X-Men, the British actor would have secured himself a permanent place in both movie and TV history, as well as nerd fandom. He playe
items.author: David Fear; Andy Greene; CT Jones
paragraphs: Had Sir Patrick Stewart only played Jean-Luc Picard, commanding officer of the USS Enterprise, or Charles Xavier, leader of the X-Men, the British actor would have secured himself a permanent place in both movie and TV history, as well as nerd fandom. He played both, however — as well as a host of roles on stage and screen in a professional career that spanned six decades before his death today at age 86. Rarely has an actor turned a simple phrase like “Make it so” into a baritone-blessed mantra of authority and gravitas.

From those landmark sci-fi and superhero works to his more comedic turns, one half of a classic theater piece’s duo, and voicing a seriously snarky pig’s head — yes, you read that correctly — here are our favorite Patrick Stewart roles.

- ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation’ (1987) Patrick Stewart wasn’t a big Star Trek devotee — or even a real science fiction aficionado — when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987. “Gosh, no!” he told the Los Angeles Times in 1990. “I have no enthusiasm for it whatsoever.” But after some initial hesitation, fans found incredible enthusiasm for Stewart as they watched the classically-trained Shakespeare actor battle the Romulans, find common cause with the Klingons, and even engage in a flirty will they/won’t they with chief medical officer Beverly Crusher (Gates McFadden). And in the two-part “Best of Both Worlds” episode, Picard was transformed by the Borg into the evil Locutus. “Resistance is futile,” he said, in one of the most famous moments in Star Trek history. “Your life, as it has been, is over.” A role like this could have easily typecast Stewart for life, which was the fate for many of the original Star Trek actors. But Stewart was such a titanic talent that it only elevated him to new career heights, and he’d even return to it for the late-career franchise highlight Picard. —Andy Greene

- ‘Robin Hood: Men in Tights’ (1993) Patrick Stewart played many kings throughout his seven decades on the stage and screen — and there’s something delightful about the Sherwood Forest adventure parody ending with Stewart’s swaggering, armor-clad appearance. Thieves, men in tights, and his own brother John begin kneeling in respect. “Throw him in the Tower of London!” he shouts with a smirk, as the peasants drag John away. “Make him part of the tour!” It’s the film’s equivalent of signaling that the adults are back in the room, placing Stewart where people will always remember him — on stage with a crown. —CT Jones

- ‘X-Men’ (2000) Stewart once found himself in a director’s office, pitching himself for a role he desperately wanted, when he stopped cold with a rhetorical question: “Why would I want Captain Picard in my movie?” This was the reason, Sir Patrick later admitted, that he initially said no when he was asked to play Charles Xavier, head of the School for Gifted Mutants. “I already had one glorious albatross around my neck,” he declared. “I don’t need two.” After having lunch with Bryan Singer, however, he eventually agreed to play Professor X — and helped change superhero movies forever. Next to his iconic Star Trek role, Charles Xavier was arguably his best-known part, conveying a sense of authority and offering a moral alternative to Magneto (played by Ian McKellen), his longtime Homo superior frenemy. Stewart would end up playing the wheelchair-bound father figure of Marvel’s mutant team in no fewer than nine times, including one last appearance as Xavier in the upcoming MCU battle-royal epic Avengers: Doomsday. —David Fear

- ‘Match’ (2014) “I love my life,” Stewart’s ballet instructor says. “I regret my life. The lines eventually blur.” His character Tobi is a legendary choreographer who now teaches at Julliard; when asked to sit for an interview with a woman (Carla Gugino) working on her thesis paper and her husband (Matthew Lilliard), he’s happy to wax poetic about his artistic legacy. Then Tobi begins to suspect there’s a secondary agenda behind this encounter, one which will force him to confront a past he’d rather leave in the rearview mirror. Stephen Belber’s underrated screen adaptation of his own play gives Sir Patrick a stage on which to rage, and the actor makes the most of it. You can’t imagine anyone giving the work’s ending the sort of emotional wallop that Stewart delivers — a moment in which someone who’s been dancing as fast as they can from remorseful memories is finally forced to face the music. —D.F.

- ‘Blunt Talk’ (2015) If there was a special Emmy Award for Best Battle With an Airport Toilet in a TV Comedy, Stewart would have easily nabbed it courtesy of this standout sequence from Jonathan Ames’ cracked sitcom. Even without this choice bit of restroom-related slapstick, this chance for Sir Patrick to indulge his inner cringe-comic crank would be memorable for any number of other moments in which his British broadcaster Walter Blunt blunders his way through the brave new world of anything-goes cable news. The show could be crass at times — Family Guy‘s Seth MacFarlane was the executive producer — but this two-season dispatch from the premium-cable fringe has a cult following, and Stewart’s exquisite take on a TV antihero is a big reason why. —D.F.

- ‘Green Room’ (2015) The good news is that, after one of their shows is abruptly cancelled, the up-and-coming punk band the Ain’t Rights manages to secure a last-minute substitute gig and this keep their tour going. The bad news is it’s at a Neo-Nazi club in the rural outskirts of Oregon — and because one of the group’s members have witnessed a murder, they’re trapped inside the joint, with every racist skinhead baying for blood outside the green room’s door. Jeremy Saulnier’s white-knuckle thriller handed Stewart one hell of a villainous role in Darcy Banker, an elderly white supremacist who fancies himself an intellectual yet certainly isn’t above killing these inconvenient interlopers. When the actor read the script, he noted that it “scared the shit out of me” and immediately poured himself a large Scotch to calm his nerves. Then he quickly proceeded to say yes, knowing that it if unnerved him that much on the page, it had a chance to make quite an impact on screen. “Darcy is a bad guy — a really bad guy,” Stewart later said. “And I have to be honest and say it was that aspect that seduced me.” —D.F.

- ‘No Man’s Land’ (2016) There’s an entire other list that could — and should — cover Sir Patrick’s prolific stage work, which ran the gamut from Shakespeare’s Scottish play to Waiting for Godot to his legendary one-man version of A Christmas Carol. For many of us who weren’t able to catch him on Broadway or London’s West End, however, this filmed version of Harold Pinter’s play about a night of drinking that takes a menacing turn — which once again paired Stewart with his longtime friend and fellow thespian Ian McKellen — was one of the few chances to see him flex his theatrical muscles. And Hirst, a man of means who brings home a dissolute poet who he may or may not have met before, is indeed one hell of a role for Stewart, especially as his memory becomes spotty under the fog of booze and possible madness. McKellen’s character may get to describe the imagined lost world of the play’s title, “which never moves, which never changes, which never grows older… but which remains forever, icy and silent.” Sir Patrick is the one who gets the last laugh and the last line, however: “I’ll drink to that!” —D.F.

- ‘Logan’ (2017) Stewart had played Marvel’s Professor X a number of times (see: the X-Men blurb above). But his turn as an alt-universe Charles Xavier, now an old man confused and in pain, bombarded with fractured memories of the past, is so unique that it deserves its own entry. In fact, it feels odd to even call writer-director James Mangold’s take on the “Old Man Logan” comics storyline an X-Men film, because the movie operates less like a formulaic blockbuster and more like a grounded retrospective on the end of an era. And it wouldn’t work without Stewart, a physical representation of a lost lifetime bound to his wheels and a small, abandoned home. Stewart will always be one of the defining faces of cinema’s superhero genre. It’s only fitting he helped change the bounds of what that could look like. —C.T.J.

- ‘The Kid Who Would Be King’ (2019) Sure, Stewart’s onscreen sparring partner Ian McKellen had brought Tolkien’s sagely Gandalf to life. But Sir Patrick proved to be no slouch in the sorcery department by taking on the O.G. of the wizardry world: Merlin. Stewart played the adult version of the resident spellcaster in King Arthur’s court (Angus Imrie is the younger version — long story) in this YA gem about a kid who stumbles across a sword in a construction site. It just so happens to be Excalibur, which brings forth both the wizard and a host of potentially world-ending problems. Every time Merlin switches to his older form, we get the chance to watch Stewart ham it up in a wild hairdo and a ratty Led Zeppelin concert T-shirt. All this, plus he gets a poignant farewell scene. Magic, indeed. —D.F.

- ‘Bait’ (2026) Watching one of England’s greatest national treasures voice a decapitated swine’s head might seem like a hard sell, but there’s nothing more quintessentially Patrick Stewart than his work in this showbiz satire. After all, the late actor had a dedicated track record of supporting actors who were making big, creative leaps — and he loved a good laugh. Created by and starring Riz Ahmed, Bait follows struggling actor Shah Latif, whose life goes through a downward spiral when he’s rumored to be the next James Bond. When a pig’s head is sent to Latif’s family as a clear anti-Muslim threat, Shah’s mental state wavers even further as he starts to hear it speak to him in Stewart’s slow, distinct timbre. To say that Stewart’s readings add an extra cheeky layer to the show’s existing critiques of long-held British establishments would be an understatement. “It was another moment of grace and incredible luck and generosity of the universe… that he said yes,” Ahmed said. “I cherish that man.” —C.T.J.

items.title: The Great Flock Hunt
items.description: C ampus security is on to us. For the past 30 minutes, I’ve been doing laps around a satellite campus of a small Virginia university in the back of a conspicuously rigged-out Toyota Tacoma, a fat disc-shaped antenna magnet-clamped onto its roof and connected t
items.author: Jack Crosbie
paragraphs: C ampus security is on to us. For the past 30 minutes, I’ve been doing laps around a satellite campus of a small Virginia university in the back of a conspicuously rigged-out Toyota Tacoma, a fat disc-shaped antenna magnet-clamped onto its roof and connected to a thick tube of cables that run into a black box by my side. In the front seat are two professional security researchers – call them hackers, if you want – who go by their online pseudonyms Koko and Hedge. Koko and Hedge’s work is all above board, but they still ask me to keep their legal names off the internet. In return, they agree to take me hunting for the cybersecurity world’s greatest enemy: the AI-powered mass-surveillance cameras that have popped up all over America.

We spot our prey, but still need to get the shot — and we’ve already been passed by one city police squad car and another campus cop. Hedge is riding shotgun and navigating, neck bent over two iPhones, the glow lighting his face from below. Koko is watching for cops and keeping an eye on the numbers flashing on a small, homemade device fastened to his windshield. “OK, around this corner,” Hedge says. “We’re going to pass it on the right.” In the back seat, I twist around, trying to line up my phone camera with a night vision scope Koko brought along.

Koko crawls through the intersection. I get the target – a Flock Safety surveillance camera perched above the sidewalk on a long black pole – in frame just as its infrared flash goes off. It’s invisible to the naked eye, but on the night vision scope it’s a blinding pulse of white light. I catch it all on video — but it also catches us: the truck I’m in, the license plate, and almost certainly me, glued to the back window, phone in hand.

Over the past few months, Flock Safety has gone from a little-known, quietly-expanding security camera company into public enemy number one for a vast political coalition. Flock’s critics, which include left-wing anarchists, suburban soccer moms, libertarian computer dorks, and hardline far-right secessionists, have all claimed that the company’s nationwide network of interconnected surveillance cameras violate Americans’ right to privacy in new and frightening ways. That grassroots anger has, in turn, made Flock a defining issue in the 2026 election cycle.

“Little cameras, watching your every move, to collect information about you without you even noticing,” Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said in a new campaign ad on the website X. “That’s all been part of a regime that’s been pushed by, well, this guy: who happens to be the guy I’m running against – Mike Rogers.”

Opposition to Flock has also crossed party lines. In July, Tennessee Republican Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the Protection Against Mass Surveillance Act, a single-page, simple bill that would bar the federal government from “purchasing or accessing” any “mass surveillance” technology, specifically mentioning Flock cameras and devices that use biometric or facial recognition features to profile people.
“We’ve gotta put some guardrails in,” Rep. Burchett tells me over the phone. “You want to follow my ass, get a dadgum warrant.”

Flock, which has been around since 2017, primarily makes cameras known as Automated License Plate Readers, or ALPRs, which it then leases to cities, towns, and homeowners’ organizations, promising their clients an always-on, easily-searchable database of surveillance footage for stopping crime. There are many companies who make ALPRs, many of which offer similar services, but in the past few years, Flock has come to dominate both the market for this technology and the spotlight that it now commands. In some form or another, license-plate capture technology has been around for at least a decade — but privacy experts and security researchers have warned that the Orwellian capabilities and slap-dash vulnerabilities of Flock’s cameras represent a new, drastic security threat for everyday citizens like you and me.

Flock claims its cameras focus only on vehicles — but critics say they’re collecting so much more: giving the government tools to analyze identifying features on vehicles and pedestrians alike, creating profiles that can log everything from a bumper sticker on a car to the color of clothing a jogger wears. That data is held by a private company, which sells it to whoever is willing to pay. And once they have it, anything goes. Across America, rogue cops have used Flock data to stalk ex-wives and girlfriends, held families at gunpoint after faulty readings, and kept one woman in jail for 13 days before admitting that the cameras had led them astray. Mistakes happen in police work, of course, but security researchers also say Flock is also barely bothering to secure their cameras: they’re easy to hack and exploit by anyone with the right gear. All this adds up to a systemic invasion of privacy that is causing sane and rational experts to use words in interviews like “panopticon” and “big brother.” The future is here, and our laws have yet to catch up. Flock did not respond to a detailed list of questions sent by Rolling Stone.

“In the old days, it was just impossible to do these things,” says Andrew Crocker, a senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation who leads the privacy organization’s surveillance cases. “You couldn’t follow someone around 24 hours a day. That was just physically impossible. This technology makes that possible. It changes the relationship of surveillance to people in a really fundamental way.”

Crocker says Flock and other interconnected ALPRs give the government an enormously powerful tool. There are at least 131,000 ALPR cameras in the U.S., over 80 percent of which are owned by Flock. If you have access to Flock’s system, you can plug in a license plate number or even a description of a vehicle and see footage from many of those cameras, effectively telling you almost everywhere their car has been, and sometimes even who was inside it. You can tell what time they arrived somewhere and what time they left. Flock makes all of this information available to its customers at the push of a button, with no warrant or effort required, even if the target isn’t suspected of any crime at all.
“It’s easy for everyone to understand how invasive that could be,” Crocker says. “People get, intuitively, that no one is immune from this sort of surveillance.”

And people, broadly, are pissed: hating Flock is one of the hottest trends on social media. Content creators from across the political spectrum are making guides on the best tools to cut down Flock cameras, blasting them off poles with shotguns, and dissecting every misstep the company makes.

America’s Great Flock Hunt began almost exactly one year ago, when Benn Jordan, a musician and technology YouTuber released a video titled “Breaking the Creepy AI in Police Cameras.” In Jordan’s first video about Flock, he spent much of its runtime figuring out unique ways to fool the cameras’ license plate readers using his own AI programs. But his plain English introduction to what Flock Safety was actually doing is what connected with his audience. Today the video has 3.6 million views.
“It just opened up a rabbit hole that kept going and going,” Jordan tells me. “And it’s still going – now it’s reached critical mass.”

A few months later, he was back with a far more provocative take. Working with a security researcher going by the name GainSec, Jordan showed how Flock’s specific protocols and tech were immensely vulnerable to cyber attacks — some of which would let them tap right into the cameras’ live feeds — in a video called “We Hacked Flock Safety Cameras in 30 Seconds.” Jordan and GainSec found unsecured video feeds they could patch right into and watch, vulnerabilities that let them into back doors in Flock’s database and the camera’s code, and even unsecured databases of Flock’s users, down to the names and addresses of police officers using the system.
Online, the security and hacking world lit up. Here was a company, the consensus went, that was doing almost everything wrong — at the people’s expense.

I started seeing other Flock videos around this time. They came across my feed, at first, through the fringes: 3D-printed gunsmiths, hard-line anti-fascists, weird black-pilled internet denizens, and even some crunchy far-right secessionists in the Pacific Northwest were suddenly all posting about these little black cameras on aluminum poles. Many of them were posting a map on a site called DeFlock.org, which showed the United States as an enormous constellation of lights — thousands upon thousands, with every dot on the map representing an ALPR camera. They were everywhere. To date, DeFlock has mapped more than 131,000 ALPR cameras in the United States, around 80 percent of which are owned and run by Flock Safety. The map, along with a searchable database called HaveIBeenFlocked.com, are the product of a massive public undertaking by a community of hackers who adapted an old A/V-club hobby into a service for the public good. They call themselves “wardrivers,” and for the past year or more, they’ve been fighting to track down every single Flock device active in the United States.

IN MID-AUGUST, I HOPPED IN A rental car and drove from New York to a suburb of DC in Northern Virginia, to meet Koko, a security consultant, entrepreneur, and dedicated wardriver who agreed to take me Flock hunting for a few days. Koko shows me into his house, where his two friendly cats climb all over a dining room table covered in hard-shell Pelican cases — think a boxy briefcase made of industrial plastic — crammed with electrical gear. One of Koko’s friends, another security researcher named Hedge, is along for the ride as well, tinkering with his own gear when we walk in.

Wardriving, they explain, is a relatively simple concept: you pack your car with all the signal-receiving gear you can get and drive around seeing what you catch. Basically every device with a battery or power cable these days is emitting some kind of signal, mostly WiFi or Bluetooth. An extremely simple “wardriving” session, then, would be just traveling along a route and logging the raw number of WiFi and Bluetooth signals you pick up: phones, cameras, computers, cars, et cetera. For some people, that’s the whole hobby — there are online leaderboards of wardrivers competing to put up the most numbers, games that they can play by “capturing” digital territory on real-world maps. Both Koko and Hedge have designed their own specific devices that are tuned to detect Flock cameras as well as other ALPRs and surveillance devices. Doing that is more complex: it requires reading the MAC address — a sort of digital serial number — for a device their gear detects and cross-referencing it with a known list of MAC addresses used by Flock cameras’ manufacturers. (This is in imperfect science. There is one brand of Bluetooth-enabled CPAP machine and certain electric toothbrushes known to have similar MAC addresses to Flock cameras, so sometimes you get false positives if you drive too close to the house of a heavy snorer.)

When you get this deep into the hobby, things get a bit more serious. The gear Koko and Hedge are packing – pocket-sized, 3D-printed boxes with tech inside that they call the Marauder and the Biscuit, respectively — can go beyond passive monitoring. They can spoof WiFi networks, clog up bandwidth, mimic AirTag signals, and all kinds of other mischief. At one point, to demonstrate, Hedge taps in a short command to the Biscuit – which is a 3D-printed mini-computer about the size of a hockey puck that pairs with your smartphone. There’s a brief pause, and then my phone goes haywire, inundated with Bluetooth signal spam — new Airpods connections, contact requests, an avalanche of popups that make my phone basically unusable until Hedge shuts it off.
“We mess with each other all the time,” Hedge laughs. “Usually when someone’s on the toilet, and we know they’ll be on their phone.”

Koko loves the pranks too, but is serious about what this tech can do. On the way back from DEFCON, a hacking conference he attended in early August, several attendees were pulled off a plane by armed air marshals after they set up a malicious WiFi network while on board their flight home.
“This stuff should be seen no differently than owning a firearm,” Koko says. “It all depends on the person wielding it.”
I take his word for it, seeing as he also has a Glock 19 holstered in the front of his waistband.
“So, anyway,” he says. “Want to go do some wardriving?”

Koko quickly dashes my dreams of watching black-clad hacker gangs scrambling sensors and hacking at Flock poles with skill-saws. That’s definitely going on, somewhere, but most wardrivers, like Koko, keep all their activities strictly above board (at one point, for instance, Koko refused to park in a handicapped spot even though the parking lot we were in was entirely deserted at 11 p.m.). We load up Koko’s truck, a four-door 2023 Toyota Tacoma: Koko gets in the drivers’ seat, clipping the Marauder to the windshield. A bigger version of the same tech sits in the back seat, hooked up to a clunky round antenna on the roof. Koko’s truck only has one bumper sticker, an image of a guillotine that says “MAKE CONSEQUENCES GREAT AGAIN.”

Our first stop is the “most controversial,” Koko says: the Lowes parking lot. There are three Flock cameras there and several other non-Flock police cameras. Activists suspect that Flock’s data has been used to plan immigration raids, which frequently target hardware store parking lots where migrant day-laborers often wait for work. We drive around the lot slowly, parking next to one of the cameras to take some photos and video. It’s late in the day, and our gear isn’t picking up the camera’s signature, even though we can see it right there. This is interesting to Koko — he has a theory that some of Flock’s solar-powered cameras shut down their WiFi and Bluetooth signaling after dark to save power, uploading data only through the cell networks, which are much harder to detect.

Stuff like this is all part of the puzzle. It’s what makes it fun for Koko and Hedge, who are in their early 30s. They both make their living primarily through selling the Marauder and Biscuit devices, which are currently selling out as fast as they can make them due to the new influx of privacy-conscious wardrivers. But the mysteries of Flock are also what piss them off: they know better than anyone the kind of data everyday people are giving up to the now-omnipresent cameras in their midst.

“Before, you had more control over the data you put out,” Hedge says. People enjoyed a reasonable amount of privacy in public; they could use cash for purchases and paper tickets for transit. The CCTV footage that did exist was, at best, lazily reviewed by a manager somewhere if and only if there was an incident. Now, he says, the cameras are always on, always taking data. “It’s hard to avoid going to the grocery store.”

Koko and Hedge take me through a couple parking lots and a small condo development that has three new Flock cameras posted right at its entrance. Then we swing back by the house to grab some more gear. As night falls, Koko busts out a military ballistic helmet with a night vision scope attached — crucial for picking up Flock cameras’ infrared flash. We then head to a satellite campus of George Mason University, which the DeFlock map shows us is infested with Flock cameras. Koko wants to test another theory: Flock claims that their cameras are built to collect data from cars, not people, but he is pretty sure they’ll go off even if a person walks past. We do laps around the campus, recording the cameras going off as the truck drives by. Eventually, we find one pointed right at the sidewalk, and hop out. We wait for there to be no cars in sight, and then Koko and Hedge walk past. They make it about five yards past the camera, next to a row of electric scooters, before the IR flash goes off. We repeat the process with one person, then two. The camera snapped us all. Eventually, a campus security cruiser rolls past. We take that as our cue to leave.

IT’S ODD, STANDING IN FRONT of these cameras. I’ve been on TV plenty of times; as a journalist, I’m vaguely used to being treated as a quasi-public figure, albeit an extremely non-famous one. But it’s another thing entirely to stand in front of a lens that you know is recording you on behalf of a private company — not just to make sure you don’t swipe a candy bar at the self-checkout, but to keep a detailed record, if it can, of who you are and how you move about the world. Because we’ve already seen how much power that data conveys. Just last week, Wired reported that Flock had developed a new AI tool for tracking not just vehicles but their specific drivers, matching them with known “associates.” Flock did not dispute any of the capabilities Wired described. In July, 404 Media reported that police departments around the country were running Flock searches for physical descriptions of people, such as “person on skateboard,” or “woman wearing grey shirt, blond hair, black shorts.” Police have used Flock data to search a man’s car on suspicion of possessing marijuana after tracking him traveling between Michigan, where weed is legal, and Wisconsin, where it is not. Local, state, and federal law enforcement are all reportedly tracking social media users who have posted anti-Flock content. Flock’s CEO, Garret Langley, once called DeFlock, the camera-mapping website, a “terroristic organization whose primary motivation is chaos.”
“The fact that they don’t have to get a warrant for [running a search of Flock’s data] is really shocking to me,” Crocker, the EFF lawyer, says. “The law has a hard time keeping up.”

Flock, for its part, claims that its product is solving crimes and saving lives. That’s hard to refute. The technology is clearly powerful — in the right hands, in the right situation, there’s no doubt that an ever-vigilant surveillance net would stop horrific things from happening. Like a gun, it depends on who wields it. The argument against Flock, right now, is that a loophole in the American legal system has allowed a group of tech guys to invent a really, really big gun, which they have then loaned to the government with few restrictions and oversight. That’s not how this country is supposed to work, Koko thinks. He joined the Navy straight out of high school because he wanted to serve his country. He’s proud of that. The Navy taught him cryptography and signals intelligence and crammed years of computer science education into a few focused training units, skills he used on behalf of his country and still wants to use to help the people who live in it.
“I feel like the presence of these cameras kind of undermines the idea that people are entitled to that freedom and their privacy,” Koko says.

The day after the university hunt, we’re talking all this over back in Koko’s office. I notice a post on my phone: Flock Safety, announcing a new slate of privacy and accountability measures. Everyone crowds around Koko’s PC to pore over the statement, trying to puzzle out what the new “default retention period” for camera data means. Koko and Hedge aren’t impressed.
“I mean, this is too little too late,” Koko says.

We pile back in the truck. There’s another subdivision nearby with several cameras Koko and Hedge haven’t been able to pick up. They’re on the DeFlock map, and you can see them with your eyes, but they’re not showing up on the Marauder or Biscuit — perhaps some evidence that Flock is changing some of their tech, or has systems that the two researchers aren’t familiar with.
“I like the idea of understanding something that we’re not fully meant to understand,” Koko says.

On the way back, we drive through a quiet intersection with one camera, facing south, already on the map. As we pull up at the stop sign, I spot something else. “Wait,” I say. “Isn’t that another one?” There’s a second camera, pointing north, affixed to the side of a telephone pole. “Is that on DeFlock?” Hedge asks. We pull out our phones to check. It’s not. Hedge taps away, dropping a pin in the map, putting the new camera in the system, rotating the icon so it shows the exact angle the lens is facing. He zooms out, and the new camera becomes another dot, one of two at that intersection, of a dozen in that town, of hundreds in that part of the state. If you go outside right now and drive around, chances are, you might find one, too. It’s a small comfort, I think, to at least know where these cameras are, to be able to see them for yourself. After all, they’ve already seen you.

items.title: PlaqueBoyMax Wants to Find Your Next Favorite Artist
items.description: It’s been about a year and a half since rapper and streamer PlaqueboyMax first spoke to Rolling Stone. In that time, the music industry has caught up with the popularity of streamers, as a growing set of major names — from Drake to Mariah Carey — have dabbled
items.author: Jeff Ihaza
paragraphs: It’s been about a year and a half since rapper and streamer PlaqueboyMax first spoke to Rolling Stone. In that time, the music industry has caught up with the popularity of streamers, as a growing set of major names — from Drake to Mariah Carey — have dabbled in the format. For Max, who has spent years making music in front of viewers, that means being something of an established figure in an evolving rap landscape.
“It’s been crazy,” he says. “I’m really passionate about music, and I’m just happy that I’m able to merge my worlds and my passions together to make it one big world.”

Max’s recent “Rising Star” competition, something like Star Search or American Idol for the underground rap generation, brought together six rappers with growing fanbases on one livestream where they’d create music and eventually perform for a real audience. The contest has its origins in two of Max’s streaming formats. “In the Booth,” which he started in 2024, lets viewers watch music being made. He was also doing “Song Wars” around then, putting songs up for an audience’s judgment. As he kept doing those streams, he wanted to spend more time with the artists. What else would people want to know about somebody they’d just watched make a song?

“These are concepts where people are making songs and new art is being created live,” he says. “It’s very fascinating. And ‘Rising Star’ is basically a byproduct of these things, but taken even further.”

The weekend format lets the audience spend hours with the contestants, who have personalities and frustrations to contend with as they’re making music. Max would like some of that audience to stick with them afterward.

“My whole premise with ‘Rising Star’ is that I want to find artists of the next generation that are coming up now, as opposed to maybe an already established artist and allow them to showcase what they’re doing and what they’re capable of and who they are as artists through this event.”

He recruited Lil Yachty, with his years of experience making records and maintaining a career, alongside creators Cuffem and Funny Marco. Music advice from the rapper, entertainment from the creators: Max wanted both on the panel, with enough to keep his viewers watching.
“So I would say picking judges came down [to] just me picking people I appreciate, who I mess with, and just bringing them into my world and making it all one amazing product,” he says.
Yachty had plenty to say. Max remembers him taking five minutes to get into an individual artist’s work, which could make for an uncomfortable critique.
“Some of them were getting grilled, but it’s just like he’s giving them real feedback that if they listen, it will help them as an artist, and I love that,” Max says. “That’s what the purpose was.”

Getting grilled in public can’t be much fun. I ask Max if anybody went away upset about it. Some artists were frustrated with the criticism, he says, or with their placement in the fan vote, but he stops short of calling them offended.

“They were frustrated either with their placements or I’d say sometimes the feedback they were getting, but I wouldn’t say that any artist that was competing took it the wrong way,” he says. “They were definitely just working hard and just passionate and hungry.”
But the thing Max remembers most is the show at the Belasco that closed the weekend. He’d spent all that time watching the artists work, and then got to watch them perform.
“It was just so amazing to see everyone work their ass off all weekend and then come together at the show and just put it all out there on stage,” he says. “I love that.”

It would be the buzzing underground rapper Matt Proxy who’d ultimately take the prize. “He really went on that stage and gave it his all, and I respect that so much,” Max tells me. Proxy is known for a dynamic style infused with an experimental-leaning sonic maximalism — 808s rip through speakers like sawblades, punctuated by melodic and emotive vocals, with a lyricism rooted in Proxy’s own life experiences. “He has a star on him for sure,” Max says.

Proxy’s winnings amounted to $25,000 and access to Red Bull’s music studio in Los Angeles, after a weekend spent making music and performing with five other contestants. Max was already a fan. He liked the different influences he could hear in Proxy’s music without being able to pin a genre on it. The set at the Belasco gave him more to go on.
“Matt doesn’t belong in any box, he’s just himself, and I really like that,” Max says. “That’s why I chose him for this because I value creativity greatly.”

Proxy had come to his attention through a video earlier in the year. By the time Max started researching contestants, he knew the music. This is something he already does with his chat: asks them to send him up-and-coming artists he hasn’t heard. People put him on to what they like, and he listens.
“He kind of does things his own way and combines different influences he has to make his own product, and that really fascinates me,” Max says of Proxy.

With this year’s contest finished, Max is pivoting his attention back to his own music. He’s working on his debut album, Elliot, which he says fans can expect soon. As streaming and content creation become a bigger part of the music world, Max says he’s worked all this time to find a balance, splitting his attention between the two. “I love what I do,” he says. “And so it’s just about allocating time to each and staying diligent on that so that I stay up to date and stay moving forward and don’t let anything slip through the cracks.”

items.title: John Turturro Says ‘I Still Consider Myself a Beginner’ as He Gets Marrakech Film Festival Tribute Award: ‘Every Job Is Like a First Love’
items.description: Though his career has spanned over four decades, John Turturro still feels like it’s just the beginning.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Though his career has spanned over four decades, John Turturro still feels like it’s just the beginning.

The 69-year-old actor and filmmaker was honored with a tribute award at Marrakech Film Festival on Sunday night, where he was greeted with roaring applause as he mimed the iconic bowling moves of his “The Big Lebowski” character Jesus Quintana. He then gave a heartfelt speech about his work philosophy, which he said he got from his mom and dad.

“I am a very fortunate person to make a good living as an actor, sometimes as a writer, a director, doing something that I deeply love. To put all of yourself into what you do and give a piece of that away in your work is something that I learned from my parents,” Turturro said. “They taught me that a job well done defines who you are. Building a house, making a dress was done brick by brick, stitch by stitch.”
He called filmmaking the “magic and beauty of life” and “an offering that you hope others will receive with open hearts.”

“A great writer, Cesare Pavese, once said that the only great thing in life is to begin. And I still consider myself a beginner in many ways,” he concluded. “For me, when I do a job, every job is like a first love. And I consider this award an encouragement to continue to try.”

The award was presented to Turturro before a screening of his latest movie, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” with director Noah Segan and producer Rian Johnson also on hand. The crime thriller stars Turturro as an aging pickpocket who steals a valuable USB drive from the heir to a crime family and must race to return it before the life of his disabled wife is threatened. Initially premiering at Sundance Film Festival earlier this year to praise from critics, the film was picked up by Sony Pictures Classics and released wide in U.S. theaters on Oct. 30.

“As you get older, your toolbox of experience becomes fuller,” Turturro said of taking on the role. “You may not be able to jump as high or run as fast, but I absolutely think this is one profession that you can improve your product because you can learn to distill experiences … It was a gift to work on this film.”

Turturro, a longtime champion of independent cinema, is perhaps best known for his collaborations with the Coen Brothers on four movies including “The Big Lebowski” and “Barton Fink,” and with Spike Lee on films including “Do the Right Thing” and “Jungle Fever.” He also starred in the “Transformers” film sereies and as supervillain Carmine Falcone in “The Batman” opposite Robert Pattinson. On the TV side, Turturro won an Emmy Award for his performance in comedy series “Monk” and currently stars in Apple TV’s acclaimed sci-fi thriller show “Severance.”

Turturro’s Marrakech Tribute Award follows that of Jeff Goldblum, who received the honor from his “The Grand Budapest Hotel” co-star Tilda Swinton. Other starry guests at the festival, whose jury is being led by Oscar winner Marion Cotillard, include Rian Johnson, Luca Guadagnino, James Gray, Monica Bellucci and more.
Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

items.title: Box Office: ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Reignites ‘Hunger Games’ Franchise With $120 Million Debut
items.description: “Sunrise on the Reaping” caught fire at the domestic box office, collecting a sensational $120 million in its opening weekend while reinvigorating Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” franchise.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: “Sunrise on the Reaping” caught fire at the domestic box office, collecting a sensational $120 million in its opening weekend while reinvigorating Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” franchise.
Overseas, “Sunrise on the Reaping” generated $105 million from 84 territories for a towering launch of $225 million globally.

The dystopian prequel is one of just five movies this year to launch above $100 million in North America, joining the company of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” ($360 million), “Toy Story 5” ($159 million), “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” ($131 million) and “The Odyssey” ($123 million). All of those films eventually surpassed the $1 billion mark globally.

“‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ posting an impressive $100 million-plus [domestic] debut reinforces just how vital ‘The Hunger Games’ remains as a movie franchise,” says Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” coincided with another big release — albeit not at the movies. Rockstar’s video game “Grand Theft Auto VI” launched after years of anticipation, earning a staggering $3.79 billion on its first day. It’s expected to set a sales record for entertainment across any medium.

“Many have speculated as to whether the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ would hurt ‘The Hunger Games’ at the box office, and I think the marketplace has already spoken,” adds Dergarabedian. “There’s plenty of time to play ‘GTA VI’ and make it to a theater to see ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ this weekend.”

On top of pitched competition at home, initial ticket sales for “Sunrise on the Reaping” are notable because they’re not far off from the original saga. For reference, 2012’s “The Hunger Games” ignited to $152 million, followed by 2013’s “Catching Fire” ($158 million), 2014’s “Mockingjay Part 1” ($121 million) and 2015’s “Mockingjay Part 2” ($102 million). Nearly a decade after those movies, starring Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, concluded their run, the studio revived the young-adult property with 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” an origin story about Panem’s cruel leader, President Coriolanus Snow. That film, set during the 10th Hunger Games, bowed significantly below its predecessors with $44 million. However, the movie stuck around through the holidays and eventually climbed to $363 million globally, registering as a win against a (comparatively leaner) $100 million budget and justifying another prequel for the studio. “Sunrise on the Reaping,” which returns to Panem for the 50th Hunger Games, carries a larger price tag above $150 million, not including the many millions spent on worldwide marketing efforts.

That “Sunrise on the Reaping” managed to recapture the spark of the initial series is impressive as the sixth installment in any property. And the film earned a strong “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls, which bodes well for box office longevity. Analysts attribute the strong debut to several factors, including the franchise’s multi-generational appeal as well as the excitement for the return of fan-favorite characters. This chapter, based on the novel by Suzanne Collins, has a stronger connection to the original saga; the story follows a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada takes on the role originally played by Woody Harrelson) — who eventually mentors Katniss (Lawrence) and Peeta (Hutcherson) in their Hunger Games, a Battle Royale for teens. Francis Lawrence returned to direct, having helmed all but the first chapter in the YA-centric franchise.

“The last ‘Hunger Games’ stumbled when the story went back 64 years without Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This is a strong return.”

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is Lionsgate’s second major theatrical victory in 2026 following “Michael,” which captured a huge $97 million in its debut and became the first biopic ever to cross the $1 billion mark. With this weekend’s haul, the “Hunger Games” series has collectively generated $3.43 billion in global ticket sales, making it the studio’s highest-grossing franchise ever—above “The Twilight Saga” ($3.3 billion worldwide across five films).

“This success is a testament to their remarkable film, the performances of our incredibly talented cast, and ultimately, the love of ‘Hunger Games’ fans worldwide, who embraced a film that told a story they had been asking to see for many years,” said Adam Fogelson, chairman of the Lionsgate Motion Picture Group.

Second place went to “I Play Rocky,” which earned $9.3 million while expanding nationwide to 2,477 theaters. The Amazon MGM movie, which depicts the real-life story of Sylvester Stallone bringing the 1976 classic “Rocky” to the big screen, has generated $10.4 million after two weekends in limited release. Audiences, roughly half of whom were over 45 years old, awarded the feel-good film a rare “A+” grade on CinemaScore. “I Play Rocky,” which hopes to find itself in the Oscar race, cost about $30 million to produce.

Last weekend’s champ “Ebenezer” dropped to third place with $7.7 million from 3,545 venues, a steep 60% decline from its opening. Paramount’s PG-13 take on “A Christmas Carol,” starring Johnny Depp in his first major Hollywood role in eight years, has generated $32.5 million in North America and $78 million globally. It’s not quite a resounding embrace of Depp amid the actor’s return to studio fare. However, it’ll be decently positioned in its theatrical run against a modest $38 million budget. (Theater owners keep half of ticket sales.)

In limited release, the Focus Features drama “Elsinore” earned $240,000 from six locations in New York and Los Angeles, translating to $40,000 per theater. To compare, another awards hopeful, A24’s drama “Club Kid” had a $65,097 per-screen average from six venues, while “I Play Rocky” averaged $49,200 per location in its initial frame. “Elsinore” stars Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor Ian Charleson who secretly battles AIDS while playing “Hamlet” in London. Focus will continue to roll out the film through December.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” provided a nice jolt to the box office ahead of Thanksgiving. This Turkey Day might not cement any theatrical records, but the holiday should be busy for theater owners. “Hunger Games” will continue to draw crowds alongside new offerings like Universal’s comedy “Focker in Law,” with Ariana Grande joining Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, Disney’s animated “Hexed” and Netflix’s Imax release of “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”
“This is a very good weekend,” Gross says. “The weekend before Thanksgiving sets up 10 very strong days. Moviegoing is back on track.”

items.title: How Oobah Butler Scammed His Way to HBO
items.description: I meet Oobah Butler on a wet afternoon in Chinatown outside an empty claw-machine arcade.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: I meet Oobah Butler on a wet afternoon in Chinatown outside an empty claw-machine arcade.
I spot the 34-year-old British hoax artist and gonzo journalist from way down the street, his platinum-blond mop top bobbing between umbrella-wielding tourists.

The reason he picked this interview location — a few blocks from the open-air counterfeit handbag hub of Canal Street — becomes clear when he pulls out his phone. Giddily, he shows me a TikTok page called Clawmaster, an account dedicated to teaching followers how to win prizes out of these notoriously tricky arcade machines.

“Let’s out-scam the scammers,” he says, grinning like the Cheshire Cat. We buy 50 tokens, and, as a bonus, the cashier lets Butler select from a mysterious deck of cards. Butler pulls from the top, revealing a Joker emblazoned with an anime character. She tells him he can redeem it later, so he slips it in his pocket. Butler sets his sights on a Charizard plushie, and we get to work.

Scamming is Butler’s strong suit. Over the last decade, he’s gone viral a dozen or so times, pulling off stunts like listing bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine as an energy drink on the shopping platform and creating the Shed at Dulwich, an entirely fake restaurant that climbed to No. 1 in London on TripAdvisor. During a television press tour for the Shed, Butler auditioned lookalikes to do interviews in his place, fooling journalists around the world.

Now, Butler is preparing to reveal five more fraudulent feats on his new HBO show, “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” which debuts Sunday, Nov. 22. In the series, Butler immerses himself in the worlds of wellness, wine, music and online dating, and scams his way to the top. With a style somewhere between Nathan Fielder and Sacha Baron Cohen, Butler hilariously exposes the bullshit at the heart of our culture.

An example: In the second episode, Butler takes smoke-tainted wine, which is considered so unsellable that vineyards distill it into hand sanitizer, and through clever manipulation and questionable marketing, earns endorsements from two of the world’s top sommeliers and the New York Times wine critic. By the end of the episode, he’s selling it for $500 per bottle.
This penchant for scheming is in Butler’s blood.

“My great-grandfather came to America in the late 19th century and was in the fur trade. It says in our family history that he used to sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine to people,” he says. “So I come from a long line of bullshit artists — or rabbit shit artists.”

By this point, Butler and I have sunk at least 30 tokens into the claw machines with nothing to show for it. Marios, Pokémon and blue aliens in Italian soccer jerseys continue to slip our metal grasp, and we’re starting to doubt the Clawmaster’s expertise. Who is scamming whom?

“He suggested that if you drop the claw right down into the hole, it loosens up,” Butler says. But none of the TikTok tips are working. See, Clawmaster never posts footage of him losing. And, also, he only works on machines where the claw dangles from an elastic cord; the machines here at Anime Claw are much more rigid, dropping down from a taut wire. “For God’s sake, this is infuriating!” Butler yells as another Charizard falls back into the pile. “Clawmaster fucked us.”

Aside from a finale stunt six years in the making, Butler filmed nearly all of “Scams for a Better Tomorrow” in the last few months. He initially pitched the last episode — which is far too ambitious and surprising to spoil here — to A24 as a feature documentary, but the studio passed. Later, its television department reached out to Butler and said, “We want to make this a show.” With the help of Josh Safdie’s Central Pictures and “Nathan for You” production house Abso Lutely, Butler landed a pilot order at HBO, which would turn into a full series.

The first episode sees Butler breaking into the wellness industry with a skin serum made of children’s tears. The influencers love it; Wall Street wants to throw money at it. A real New York dermatologist, after witnessing a group of kids crying into tubes, offers to endorse it — in exchange for a fee, of course.

I ask Butler to define his ethics when it comes to duping people, but his eyes are lasered on a captive Jigglypuff. “Let me do this first, because that’s a harder question,” he says, chuckling. He misses.

“We tried not to punch down,” Butler finally says. The joke is rarely on average people, but rather the highly awarded wine experts or the money-grubbing doctor. “I tried to be fair with people,” he says. Or, in the case of the dermatologist, “I’m being as fair as I need to be.”

Still, Butler says it’s “a bit nerve-racking” that his subjects have yet to see the show. In the edit, he had to cut a few experts from the series, but “I’d have to go off the record to tell you why,” he says, “because it’s a legal thing.”
Despite its puckishness, “Scams for a Better Tomorrow” is not so much a prank show. With each stunt, Butler seeks to reveal something deeper about human psychology.

“Our argument in the wine episode is not that these guys suck because they fell for my trick,” he says. “It’s that the snobbery of that industry is getting in the way of the reality, which is this could be a good product.”

Butler was born Paul Arthur Butler, but his older sister nicknamed him Oobah as a baby. The name stuck, so much so that he legally adopted it in his early 20s. He grew up in Feckenham, a working-class English village of 700 people, and he credits his humble upbringing with instilling in him a confidence that would later come in handy.

“I grew up with this sense that I could talk to anybody — it didn’t matter if it was the lord of the manor or the farmer down at the pub,” he says. “That gave me a sense of acting like I belong in any scenario. It’s a bit of a gift.”

In his 20s, Butler sang and played guitar in a rock band, writing for music publications on the side. His band was so bad at selling records, he says, that it gave him an idea for an article. He would embed himself with the Jehovah’s Witnesses to learn their door-to-door marketing methods, but instead of hawking religion, Butler would go around peddling CDs.
“I wanted to see if it was harder to sell music than God,” he says. In the battle of religion versus music, it turned out, music lost.

He pitched the piece to Vice, which loved the idea, and the magazine brought Butler on as a freelancer. Soon enough he was writing regularly and making videos for Vice’s YouTube page that amassed millions of views. In a few years, Butler had leveraged his internet fame into a hosting gig on the British version of MTV’s “Catfish,” and he made two documentary features for the U.K.’s Channel 4.

In 2024, like his rabbit-shit-peddling ancestor, Butler relocated across the pond. He arrived in the United States with no job and no plans. “I moved here on a whim and a feeling that my work would make sense here,” he says. “I found New York insanely inspiring.”
America proved to be the perfect playground for “Scams for a Better Tomorrow.”
“There’s so much more you can say here that you can’t say back home in the U.K.,” Butler says. “It’s harder in Europe to make claims about things. Here, you get a wider berth to scam — or market.”
Case in point: He advertises that his dirt-cheap smoked wine is “Imported from Florence” but doesn’t exactly disclose that it’s simply been shipped to and from Florence, Massachusetts.

“Inauthenticity is easier than ever now,” he says, mentioning the number of AI-generated commercials he endures while watching “Frasier” reruns. “I find it fascinating how comfortable we’ve become with it.”

Throughout the show, Butler meets with Wall Street investors and tech founders who open their checkbooks and offer to fund his crazy ideas. I ask if he’s ever tempted to turn off the cameras and actually pursue one.
“I find it really hard to be motivated by money,” he says. “It’s chasing the answer to questions, I suppose, that’s motivating to me.”

Fifty-nine minutes into the interview, we suddenly and shockingly win our first prize. Butler lets out a squeak of joy and we instantly embrace, examining the brown plushie — a drumstick with ears. “I think it’s, like, a chicken-bone bear,” Butler says.

The next 15 minutes are wildly prosperous. Clawmaster-style, Butler and I shake the joysticks violently, securing a tuxedoed penguin, a polar bear with a yellow beanie and a miniature Kirby. But as we head toward the exit of the arcade, Butler realizes he never caught the one thing he truly wanted: the Charizard.
He flashes his card at the cashier. “So what do I get with this?”
“Any of the plushies,” she says, and Butler’s face lights up. She escorts us to the Pokémon machine and unlocks the cage.
“This is America,” Butler says, smiling as he clutches his new orange fire breather. “There’s always a Joker card.”

items.title: Katseye Brings Out Camila Cabello for ‘Gabriela’ Dance at Los Angeles Show
items.description: Roughly six songs into their performance on Saturday night, Katseye made a girl group connection with Fifth Harmony member Camila Cabello as Daniela Avanzini brought her out to be the collective’s “Gabriela” for the evening, dancing to the choreography that ac
items.author: Steven J Horowitz
paragraphs: Roughly six songs into their performance on Saturday night, Katseye made a girl group connection with Fifth Harmony member Camila Cabello as Daniela Avanzini brought her out to be the collective’s “Gabriela” for the evening, dancing to the choreography that accompanies the song.

Katseye, who performed as a quartet consisting of Avanzini alongside Lara Raj, Yoonchae and Megan Skindiel, took the stage at around 8:30 p.m. at Los Angeles’ Crypto.com Arena, running through opener “Hootie Frutti” and “Touch” before the girls exited so that Avanzini could bring out Cabello.
“OK, you look stunning,” said Avanzini as Cabello joined her. “Thank you Camila, I have one question for you: Do you know the ‘Gabriela’ dance?”

“I know a little bit, just a little bit,” responded Cabello. “We’re two Latina mamis, I feel like there’s a lot of Latina mamis in here. So even if we get steps wrong, it’s the sazon that counts.” They continued on to do the “Gabriela” dance, hitting the hand-ography before Cabello left the stage and the rest of Katseye joined back up to do a full performance of the single.

Throughout the show, Katseye gave a tour of their discography from the past few years, including hits like “Pinky Up,” “Gnarly” and “Mean Girls.” Katseye, who was recently announced as the recipient of the Group of the Year Award at Variety Hitmakers’ 2026, is currently on its “Wildworld” tour amid a year that saw several members take temporary hiatuses to improve their mental health. Katseye will perform again at Crypto.com Arena on Sunday night before a show in Phoenix and a tour closer at Fort Worth, Texas’ Ariat Arena on December 1.
