items.title: Hailee Steinfeld Confirms ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Return as Kate Bishop
items.description: Hailee Steinfeld will return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Kate Bishop in the forthcoming “Avengers: Doomsday.”
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Hailee Steinfeld will return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Kate Bishop in the forthcoming “Avengers: Doomsday.”

Marvel Studios and Disney Animation announced the news Sunday with an Instagram post featuring Steinfeld. “Hey, so I’m here with my movie ‘Hexed,’ but it looks like they delivered a chair from a different movie,” said the actress before panning to a black director’s chair with her name on it.
“Catch Hailee Steinfeld in Disney’s ‘Hexed’ before she returns in ‘Avengers: Doomsday,'” read the caption.

Steinfeld previously appeared as Bishop in the 2021 Disney+ series “Hawkeye” and in 2023’s “The Marvels.” In “Hawkeye,” the “Sinners” actress shared the screen with Jeremy Renner’s superhero, while she appeared briefly in a post-credits scene alongside Brie Larson, Teyonah Parris, Iman Vellani and more for “The Marvels.”

“It’s really a privilege to be able to play a character that could in any way possibly inspire anyone,” Steinfeld previously told Variety about embodying the beloved comic character. “Kate Bishop is a character that I would have loved to have had growing up — somebody who is completely ambitious, driven and disciplined, and takes it upon herself to do whatever it is she has to do to achieve her goals.”

And while the full list of MCU characters who will appear in “Avengers: Doomsday” may still be a mystery, her former costar Renner has made it clear he didn’t return as Hawkeye. “No, no, no, no. Not in that one,” said Renner when asked if he was returning for “Doomsday” in an Oct. interview. “’Doomsday’ I’m not in, so the Avengers will probably lose, just so you know… they didn’t call me, so it’s their fault. They’re going to lose.”

Prior to Steinfeld’s announcement, Elizabeth Olsen’s Scarlet Witch was most recently revealed to be joining the film via the season finale of “VisionQuest.” A post-credit scene replayed the ending of 2022’s feature film “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” where Wanda Maximoff eradicated the Darkhold from all of the multiverse before (seemingly) being crushed from within a mountain. But this time, the scene continues with Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom appearing, lifting the rubble off Wanda and addressing her, confirming fan speculation that Wanda would return.
“Avengers: Doomsday” hits theaters on Dec. 18.

items.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100M Globally, Becomes First Doc to Hit 1M Letterboxd Watches
items.description: You Can See Everything continues visualizing box office success at a level that puts it in elite company as a documentary.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: You Can See Everything continues visualizing box office success at a level that puts it in elite company as a documentary.

Focusing on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes‘ life in the lead-up to her prison sentence, A24‘s film surpassed $100 million globally over the weekend, a rare feat for any documentary. After opening Oct. 16 in North America, directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s three-hour feature has grossed $93.4 million domestically over its six weekends in release and has more recently been rolling out in international markets. The movie has continued to experience sellout screenings after hitting theaters this weekend in such territories as Australia, the U.K. and Scandinavia, with Sony Pictures handling distribution in some international markets.

Over the weekend, You Can See Everything also became the first documentary film to have been watched by one million Letterboxd members. It becomes the 19th movie released in 2026 to join the “One Million Watched Club,” and with its 4.61 average Letterboxd rating, it is the second-highest-rated feature to hit the milestone, behind only 12 Angry Men with 4.63. You Can See Everything is the highest-rated 2026 film and the second-highest-rated documentary ever, trailing only Stop Making Sense on the social platform.

Among the box office achievements for You Can See Everything include opening with $15.6 million in its debut frame to register the second-biggest domestic launch for a non-music documentary, behind 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11. The Holmes documentary also scored the highest-grossing domestic opening weekend for a release in fewer than 1,000 theaters since 2006’s Borat. You Can See Everything went on become the first documentary to reach No. 1 domestically in its third weekend of release.
The movie remains the second-highest-grossing domestic non-music documentary, with only Fahrenheit 9/11 and its $119.1 million cume to beat.

You Can See Everything stands as a major Oscar contender as awards season heats up. The Hollywood Reporter critic Angie Han called it “smart, funny and full of surprises,” and it holds a 97 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes.

“It was sometimes a tense environment,” cinematographer David Bolen recalled about the shoot during a recent screening at Camerimage. Bolen noted that he would exchange pleasantries with Holmes and partner Billy Evans, but that was generally the extent of their conversations: “I really tried to stay out of the situation as much as possible. Sometimes it would get tense, and you see in the office scene, it gets a little bit tense, and [I would] just try to be quiet and polite and get the cameras out.”

items.title: Mahershala Ali Says “There Are Not Roles for Me” in “Vast Majority of Projects,” Despite Winning Two Oscars
items.description: Mahershala Ali is getting candid about why “there are not roles” for him in “the vast majority of projects,” despite having already won two Oscars.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Mahershala Ali is getting candid about why “there are not roles” for him in “the vast majority of projects,” despite having already won two Oscars.

During a recent interview on Carmelo Anthony and Kazeem “Kaz” Famuyide’s 7PM in Brooklyn podcast, the actor — who previously took home Academy Awards for best supporting actor for 2016’s Moonlight and 2018’s Green Book — opened up about how earning Hollywood’s highest recognition doesn’t guarantee access to great roles.

“There’s a lot of great actors that don’t have Oscars, who are also looking for good material,” he said. “And that’s no disrespect to The Academy or the award at all, but what I’m actually saying is that Oscar or no Oscar, there’s a lot of good actors out there. There’s more good actors than there is good material.”

“It’s not even that all these people are competing for these same spots. It’s just that out of all the material made, there’s only a handful of them that check certain boxes. And then you got to be right for it,” Ali continued. “The vast majority of projects that get greenlit, there are not roles for me in those. You gotta think that way, you know what I mean? So, it doesn’t matter if I got 17 Oscars. If someone is not writing something for you or greenlighting something with you in mind, you’re like everybody else waiting and looking and searching.”
Given the current political climate, Ali later added that rollbacks of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) funding and initiatives also “on some level impact what gets greenlit.”

“I don’t know how much of an impact it has, but I just know that if certain companies are allowed to not feel a pressure to be reflective of the world we live in, they’ll just keep centering who they see in their offices, and it ain’t a bunch of us in those offices,” he said.
The Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star explained that the only other option for actors is to produce and create their own projects; however, “that’s a five-year journey itself.”
Famuyide later asked Ali about the fan notion that Black actors are “validated” only after winning an Oscar. “It’s kind of just talk. It doesn’t translate to anything real,” the actor replied.

“You don’t want to find yourself in a situation where, oh, that’s ‘the diversity project.’ You just want to do great material as a Black person. You’re not thinking of yourself as this exotic other, per se. You just are living your life,” Ali added. “You wake up. You put your pants on like everybody else. You just want to be like, ‘Yo, this is my offering. This is my story. This is my work.’ Opposed to, ‘Man, who are the best Black actors?'”

items.title: Matt Damon on the Oscars, Tarantino, and the Roles That Got Away
items.description: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollyw
items.author: Frazier Tharpe; Richard Burbridge
paragraphs: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollywood, and specifically on a year that will go down as one of that career’s most challenging and rewarding passages.

Damon set 2026 off with The Rip, a throwback pulp thriller that reteamed him with his lifetime BFF Ben Affleck. He then went on to dominate the summer to a degree most actors crossing the other side of 55 wouldn’t dream of, with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey—a noisy, thrilling, engrossing feat of big-budget moviemaking that wouldn’t have worked without an Odysseus compelling enough to command audiences to take the 20-year journey with him. The role demanded everything in Damon’s toolbox, and then some, but the result was a cultural and commercial run that only Spider-Man himself could top.

This is rare air, and Damon knows it. Lightning struck once for him, with Good Will Hunting in 1997—he never thought he’d see that happen again, much less 29 years later. If exhaustion is the price of beating those odds, then so be it. Still readjusting to life on dry land, Damon sat down to unpack the most unlikely filmmaking experience of his career—and begin working out where he might want to go next.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Matt Damon: That is amazing coming from him. Yes, I did hear about it.

Yeah, I think if you talk to any actor my age, any of the usual suspects, they’d probably say the same thing. I think the more you do it, if you’re working with really good people, you’re always improving, you’re getting better. And then you’re living more life and you have your family dynamics, all of your primary relationships kind of fill up your reservoir. I’ve talked to other actors my age about it, Ben included—I think there’s a tendency to push when you’re younger, a little bit, to try to work yourself up, and the older you get, the more available a lot of this stuff is. These very, very, very big emotions are kind of just sitting [near the surface]. And so you can really relax into the work, and it can be very full without being forced.
I think so, yeah. I mean, I’ve never been a part of a movie like The Odyssey that was…. Well, I guess Oppenheimer, to an extent, was somewhat of a phenomenon as well.

My workload was a lot heavier on this one, and everybody’s was, and that was kind of the joy of it. We knew we were the first ones to ever try to do a full film in IMAX [70 mm], and that comes with a whole host of challenges for every single department. We were all, I think, very patient with each other because we knew what was being asked of the other people. So in terms of the acting department—the IMAX load is two and a half minutes or three minutes. And so these big, heavy emotional scenes—you couldn’t play them all the way through. You’d have to cut them up. And the crew was just awesome, very patient with us. It felt like we were explorers, in a way. We got to be the first ones to do it, and that really bonded us.

I never would have expected it. And also, to play a role that’s so physical and, at my age, to even have a role that’s available on a scale like this. I’d always wanted to make a David Lean movie. To have it come at this point in my life, I felt incredibly lucky, not only to be able to do it, but also to be able to contextualize it. I don’t think I would’ve appreciated it as much 20 years ago.

No, I just don’t think I would’ve been able to understand and to hold as much gratitude as I am and as I did throughout the process. It’s all about how you look at things. And in retrospect, yeah, we were probably cold and wet. There was a lot of physical discomfort that was temporary. But because I felt so grateful to be there, I was just so excited. I was just so joyful the whole time that I didn’t really notice any of that.
[Laughs] There are no sure things, man. I think that’s where you get into trouble, being like, Well, this is a surefire hit. I’ve heard that before.

I felt it when I saw it. There is that thing that can happen where you make a movie, and you feel like it’s really good, and it just doesn’t connect, and there’s just nothing you can do about that. But as the audience reactions started to come in and the critical reactions were great as well, it was like, Okay….

Chris [Nolan], the most nervous he is in the entire process, from the very beginning to the very end, is the eve of the film coming out. He’s genuinely nervous. He talks openly about it, because that is the moment that you put it out into the world and you have to live with the reaction. Ultimately, the audience decides. Once it opened and the responses were what they were, I think I felt like, We’re going to be okay. It was a big bet in the sense that it was a big budget. I’m not used to playing in that arena. The numbers that movies have to get to just to break even at that level are just so beyond the movies that I’m known for.

A few of them. But The Martian, which I think is the biggest movie that I’ve ever headlined—I think The Odyssey made three times what that made. And that was a real hit for me. But there’s this other league of these kinds of movies that are in the billions that I’ve just never….
[Laughs] It’s just, like, What?

Well, the thing about a role like that is every single day I was paired with an unbelievable scene partner. One day I’d be working with Annie [Hathaway], and then the next day I’d be working with Himesh [Patel]. It’s following this character through all these different stages of his life and people who are close to him. So every day was a different, exciting little challenge, a little puzzle to figure out. I’ve always said that when you’re working with a great actor, they’re so good that they’re good enough for both of you. And it’s almost like this wave comes and you just stand up on your board and ride it. Then you have Samantha Morton, who literally just picks you up and shoulder-carries you.

It’s very hard to come in and do really intense things in a very short time frame. [Morton’s scenes]—that was under a week of shooting. Each day being incredibly intense. And that was what was so incredible about these actors who would come in. They’re under a lot of pressure. Nobody says that, but we all know the deal. These are critical scenes, and everybody just came in and killed it. It just got more and more exciting as we were going.

I agree. She’s incredible. She’s always been incredible. We had a near-miss working together in 2003—and I got to know her then—in a movie with Heath Ledger. I just think the world of her as an actress, and I was excited when we did the scene. I was like, This one’s going to really work. And I hope—it doesn’t always happen right away, but hopefully it’s lodged her back in the minds of people who are making those decisions, because she’s just extraordinary.

That’s the emotional spine of the movie. A lot of that monologue that I have at the end is in voiceover, but I wrote it all out and I had it on my phone and I would just carry it with me off set. I would just revisit it and run through it a few times, and I was doing that for months and months. Firstly, I thought it was just so beautifully written, but also because I knew that scene had to land. If that lands, then the movie works.

And that also means setting them up as a young couple before he leaves. There’s a lot of engineering that goes into getting to a scene like that and then you have to execute it. I spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about that one.

Well, at that point, the audience has been on the journey with you, and it’s been a hell of a journey, so you don’t have to tell them that. We were tired. That scene I shot with Samantha, oddly, we had come from Iceland, but we were shooting nights, and we came to Scotland, and I had it happen two or three times on this movie where I just didn’t sleep. I was tired and I went to bed, and I’m sure everyone’s had that feeling where you’ve got to get up the next day and you have something that you have to do and you can’t fall asleep and you’re kicking the blanket around and you’re staring at the ceiling. By the time I got to work to do the scene with Sam, I hadn’t slept in 24 hours, and by the end of the day it was 36 or whatever. I remember thinking the great thing about this character is he probably didn’t sleep last night. Don’t worry about it. So the weariness was very real for a lot of the movie.
It’s all in there because it’s what I’m actually feeling. As I was saying before, it’s very easy to relax into what’s real and available and to have access to it.

This was the biggest one that we’ve ever done, and we’ve always had a two-week rule. I think the first stretch [on The Odyssey], I was away for three and a half weeks. The first half of the movie was the hardest because the kids were still in school. And then once the summer hit, they could come to set and we could be together. But that first stretch—luckily they’re huge Chris Nolan fans and they knew that it was this incredible role, so they were really supportive, and it was a sacrifice for them, and they were awesome about it.

He’s turned down a lot of work. And in fact, he really wanted to take on the CEO role at [Damon and Affleck’s production company] Artists Equity because it would keep him home. So when he directs—for instance, Animals, that was all shot in LA. He said to me when we started the company—he’s got joint custody, which means he gets to be with the kids half the time. And he said, “If I go to Estonia and do a movie, it’s not like I get that time back.” So that for him means he’s got to stay in LA.
It’s all downhill from here.

I felt that way when I did Air with Ben. It was such a joyful experience, and we had so much fun, and we really loved the movie we made. We had this discussion about how I don’t want to do [a project] unless it’s joyful and unless it’s really right for my life. So much of being a young actor is you’re afraid it’s going to go away. You’re very much still in touch with that feeling of being unemployed. And so when Ben and I got famous, we both really worked. Buried ourselves in work. Partly because people are suddenly offering you things and you can’t imagine turning anything down, right? It just seems counter to everything you’ve been trying so hard to do for your entire life.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Absolutely.

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And Will was, as he is now, the biggest star. And so it’s like, it’s not Will’s fault. [Laughs] And then I did All the Pretty Horses with Billy Bob [Thornton], and that was a whole fraught experience. There were different ideas between the studio and between Billy Bob about what the movie should be, and so it ended up getting cut in a way that wasn’t to Billy’s liking and it didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

Well, the other thing was that The Bourne Identity was delayed something like a year. And so the word was, That’s going to be a stinker. But in that time, I went right from [filming] Bourne to Ocean’s Eleven. Then there was this whole period of time where nobody was calling, except for Steven Soderbergh, who called and offered me the movie The Informant! And I was so confused. I asked him, “Are you asking me to write it?” Because I couldn’t imagine he was asking me to be in it, because nobody else was calling. He goes, “What? No, Scott Burns is writing it. I want you to be the lead.” And I’ve never forgotten that. He just paid no attention to what everyone else was saying. But anyway, leaving that aside, nobody else was calling. And then The Bourne Identity came out, and it was a big hit.

It’s not personal. It’s business. And people can’t really go out of their way to help you. It’s really a pretty cold calculus that determines whether or not you’re on the list or off the list. And you never know who’s on the list. And the list can be different for different studios, who they’ll greenlight a movie with.

No, no. There’s very, very frank conversations between agents and studio people going like, “I can’t greenlight the movie with X, but I can with Y.” And that list is always changing, and I know that sometimes I’m on it and sometimes I’m not. I just have to remember it’s not personal, but you can feel it if you’re on the list or not.

Yeah. And [the] quality of projects [you’re offered]. I’m sure I’ve worked my way off that list a number of times. I’ve had some movies that didn’t work, and then you got to pay attention. I remember 2012 to 2014-ish, maybe, Patrick [Whitesell], my agent for 35 years, said I was taking a lot of supporting roles—because again, I’m not strategizing at all. I’m just like, Oh, True Grit. I want to work with the Coen brothers. Great.

Yup, George [Clooney directing], great. So there was this string of movies like that. Patrick called me and he said, “You’ll become a supporting actor. We got to think about this next one.” And then what happened to come along was The Martian. But that’s about as much strategizing as we’ve ever done.

Interstellar was in there too. I’m so happy that I’m in that movie. I love the role, even though it’s a tiny part. When Chris offered me [the role], we hadn’t worked together, and [when] he offered me the part in Interstellar, he said, “Do you know that saying ‘There are no small parts, there are only small actors’ ? This is a small part.” But I think he undersold it, because it’s a really kind of pivotal role, and I had a ball doing it.

Yeah, I think I was on a Bourne movie or about to go do Green Zone with Paul Greengrass. That and Milk. I was supposed to play the Dan White part. And I was really excited about it. I’d spoken to Sean [Penn], and I’d started the research. I’d been watching the documentaries about him. Then Sean’s schedule changed and the movie had to push three months, which meant that it was going to conflict with the movie I was going to do with Paul. So I had to bow out, and I just loved that script so much. And I love Gus [Van Sant], obviously. And so that was a bummer. But having said that, they got Josh Brolin, and Josh is absolutely brilliant in the movie. That helped a lot, I think, with this feeling that I have, that I do believe that the right actor gets the part.

I never like to say that, because I don’t want to live with the regret, but I can tell you that I passed on Ted, and I’ve never had this experience where I laughed so hard reading a script. I literally took it to dinner and was reading parts of it out to my friends at dinner. And then I just got too clever by half. I don’t know what I was thinking. I was like, Well, maybe the teddy bear’s actually the best part.…

So I overthought it and I talked myself out of it. And because it shot in Boston, it would’ve been a chance for me to be home—my father’s passed away now, and I look back and I go, Man, that would’ve been six months back [home].
But, again, the right actor got the part. Mark [Wahlberg’s] great, and the movie’s great, and I wouldn’t have made it any better.

They’re really hard to do. And I don’t read a lot [of them]. I don’t think people think of me for comedies a lot. But I love them, and I love watching them, and I love doing them if I can get my hands on one. But they’re few and far between. I think because they don’t travel well. They’re harder to get made because you really have to get all your money back in America. Comedy is so cultural. So the margin for error, I think, is smaller, which is what’s so great when you see a great one.

Anthony [Minghella], I think, was the first, with Talented Mr. Ripley. And he talked openly about it. A lot of these directors do. They want to use whatever it is that you have to offer in a new way and in a fun way and in an unexpected way. Some of those roles are the best roles that I’ve ever had a chance to play. Really interesting, complex people, and I love that.

I shot a scene in a movie theater with [Jack Nicholson], and Jack was working with an earwig. It was just the three of us before the crew came in, and we were just rehearsing. Marty [Scorsese] goes, “Let’s run this and see how we think it’s going to go.” And Jack took the earpiece out and we rehearsed the scene a few times and Jack was letter-perfect with his dialogue. And so Marty went to get the crew, and as people were coming in I said, “Hey, man, what’s the deal with the earwig? You obviously know all your lines—you’re writing stuff.” And it was really interesting because, he goes, “The older you get, the harder it is to remember your lines.” And that feeling of going up on a line, that panic, that surge of adrenaline that you get—he goes, “It just makes me so uncomfortable.” It’s a fail-safe. And if he knows [the earpiece is] there, his body stays in that relaxed state. People might think it was laziness. It was the opposite. He was a grinder. He worked really, really hard. It was more about just protecting himself.

No, no, no, no, no. I think everybody was really focused on Marty. And I remember I was shooting second unit for The Bourne Ultimatum during that Oscars, so I didn’t go. I was living in Miami at the time, and I had an infant. [My wife] Lucy and I were laying in bed watching it and so nervous for Marty. And then when he won, I was jumping up and down in the bedroom and I remember being really excited. And then the next category was best picture, and The Departed won. And I realized in that moment I hadn’t even considered that that could happen. And I turned to Lucy and I was like, “Shit, we should be there!” And then the next few weeks, I got all these calls from all the cast and the studio, like, “Hey, where were you, man?” I totally blew it. And then the next time that that happened was on Oppenheimer, and we had this whole scary thing happen where my wife had a brain aneurysm.

She’s totally fine, thank God, but [she] had this brain surgery the week before the Oscars. But it was the first night she felt good enough to get up and had her energy back. And she surprised me and got a dress and we went out to the after-party, because she remembered that the last time it happened, I didn’t do it. And she was like, “This time we’re going out.” And it was pretty fucking heroic of her to do that and really meaningful.

It’s not something you can control. You got to just do the work, and that’s got to be the reward. Because it’s like, then if you don’t win, do you feel bad about something that was really positive? Don’t turn this into something bad. It’s a tricky one. I always think about old movies when I look at them and it says, “So-and-so won an Oscar, so-and-so didn’t.” You’re judging it in a totally different way. It’s not attached to that anymore. I think the real way they should do them, really, is 20 or 25 years later. You’ll have a really good idea of which movies really endured and really still matter to you. There can be hype in the moment, or it can be a zeitgeist thing, but it doesn’t hold up. The goal for me is to make as many of those movies that are around 20 years later. That’s a cool thing. People come up [to me] about Good Will Hunting and I realize they weren’t born when the movie came out. It’s just very cool for Ben and me to have a new generation of people actually see it.

I don’t know what that means. I live in Brooklyn. [Laughs] If the trail is in that area, yeah. I don’t know what that entails. I will say, the technical side of this movie—I think of someone like Willie Burton, our sound guy, who’s in his 80s and he is a legend in the business.

And I did not loop a line in this movie, which is incredible. And I did not loop a line in Oppenheimer, which is incredible. Willie and Doug [Shamburger], his boom operator, are so good. Every scene on the ship, Willie is down below in the hold mixing in storms. The fact that he salvages all of that dialogue is nothing short of amazing. The technical achievement of our heads of department and their teams were really special. And I just hope that people realize that, realize what it took to do what they did, because from a technical standpoint, I hope they all get their flowers.

I didn’t think I was going to work. And then the Daniels called me and they had this project that was so out there, and it was such a Daniels movie and it’s so different from anything I’ve ever been able to do that I couldn’t pass it up. They’re really good people, and this movie’s like a cosmic love bomb for the world. So it felt like the right place to put my energy, but we’re almost done shooting it, and yeah, I’m going to take a long time off.

I haven’t thought about it. There are a lot of great performances. Paul Newman had some great ones at the end. We have the studio now with Artists Equity, and I feel like we’re just going to do stuff we really want to do, because it’s a very time-consuming job, and if you’re not 100 percent in, it’s just not worth doing. You have to really let it take over your life. I think that was one of the joys of The Odyssey—it dominated our lives.

There was a funny thing that happened on The Odyssey. We were in Scotland. I was with my kids. They’d just come over and gotten out of school, and we were eating dinner in this tiny hotel in this tiny town. And so there was one little dining room, which had 10 little tables in it, and the crew had watched dailies and so they were shuffling in, and I was already eating with my kids—I had jeans and a flannel shirt and a baseball hat on. And Chris came in and he walked by the table and I said, “Hey, Chris.” And he turned and he goes, “Oh, hey, Matt. I didn’t recognize you with the beard.” Chris doesn’t say stupid things—it was definitely the stupidest thing he’s ever said, because we’d been next to each other for six months.

He had just walked out of dailies watching close-ups of me, I’m sure with this giant beard. And I looked at him and he immediately realized what he’d said and he just looked at his shoes and then he looked up, like, Can we just agree that this never happened? And he shuffled off, and my kids go, “Dad, does Chris Nolan not know who you are?” I was like, “No, guys, he’s just exhausted.” He was that tired. He hadn’t seen me out of wardrobe in a while, you know what I mean? We were so tired by the end of that movie.
Well, he should write us a movie. We would be very happy if he did that.

Who knows? I have no right to expect it, let’s put it that way. I don’t want to sound like a broken record, but I have such gratitude for the fact that this came along my path at this point. I have no right to expect anything like that to happen again. But in the meantime, I just want to make good stuff and definitely keep working with Ben, because we’re at that point in our life where we’re like, “Fuck it, why not?” This was our dream as kids, as boys. We got to honor those boys and keep working together if we can. ✦
Photography by Richard Burbridge
Hair by Johnnie Sapong using Leonor Greyl
Tailoring by Susanna Badalyan
Sets by Heath Mattioli for Frank Reps
Production by Kendal Steensen and Felix Cadieu for NEIGHBORS
A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Matt Damon Never Thought 56 Would Be So Epic.”

items.title: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman Is the Scariest Thing You’ll See All Year
items.description: In 2009, Andrew Garfield found a thread. He was preparing to play Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a little-hyped film called The Social Network, and he had located the thing in Zuckerberg’s story that he could pull on—the through line that turns personal exper
items.author: Katherine Stoeffel; Richard Burbridge
paragraphs: In 2009, Andrew Garfield found a thread. He was preparing to play Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a little-hyped film called The Social Network, and he had located the thing in Zuckerberg’s story that he could pull on—the through line that turns personal experience into empathic performance and on into universal storytelling. Then he lost the part to Jesse Eisenberg. Director David Fincher had seen what, today, is obvious: Humanity flows fast and deep through Andrew Garfield. Fincher cast him instead as Eduardo Saverin, the betrayed cofounder and emotional counterweight to Zuckerberg’s opacity, who cries, sneers, throws a feint, and smashes a laptop (that’s one scene).

The movie made him a celebrity, and he brought an unusual depth of emotion to this job too. While serving as Spider-Man, he begged the public, via a handwritten sign held up for paparazzi, to care about a more important cause than what’s up with famous people. While promoting 2021’s Tick, Tick…Boom! on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, he talked about the death of his mother; the clip still gets shared by grieving people.

Now, 15 years after The Social Network, Garfield has picked back up the tech-CEO thread to play Sam Altman in Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s film that covers the founding of OpenAI up to the coup that led to Altman’s firing—and his re-entrenchment. (OpenAI has an agreement with Condé Nast, the owner of GQ, which allows OpenAI to display its content in search results for a limited term.) The movie seems destined to occupy the same orienting role as The Social Network, helping us understand the technology and the men who are shaping our futures, almost in real time. But whereas that film was a legal drama about status (Harvard guy vs. hotter, richer-born Harvard guys), Artificial plays as a horror movie where the monster, AI, is real. (And it just learned how to do theoretical physics.)

Garfield brings Altman to life as a mad guidance counselor: rubbing the shoulders of engineers, taking security meetings cross-legged, and sucking green juice in the faces of his adversaries. Here, finally, is an ascendant tech overlord that makes unsettling use of Garfield’s famous sensitivity. When Garfield-as-Altman cries, you’re not sure whether they’re the tears of a true superintelligence believer or a duplicitous power-seeker. Or which one would be scarier.

When we meet in early October, Garfield is transformed by a beard and shoulder-length hair. He grew it all out to play the magician Roy Horn, of Siegfried and Roy, in next year’s show Wild Things, though they ended up putting a wig on him anyway. He was filming that limited series in Berlin immediately after wrapping The Uprising, a Paul Greengrass movie about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, which shot before Artificial was even technically wrapped. “I did these three things back to back last year, and I did have a bit of burnout, to be honest. I was kind of sleepless in Berlin for a while, and not in a romantic way,” he says. “It was rough, dude. I should have just gone to Berghain and just rode it out.” Now, though, Garfield is visibly buzzing, both from watching Artificial with an audience at the New York Film Festival the night before—and from the chatter coming out of Silicon Valley.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Andrew Garfield: I’ve listened to his podcast.

The walk was a key for me, and the clothes and the physicality. He’s a very slight, slim guy, Sam, and seems to be very image-conscious. Which is interesting to me, which is something that I felt compelled by. There’s a great video of Sam, in what looks like a diner, when he’s talking about Loopt [the company he cofounded before running Y Combinator and cofounding OpenAI], when he’s in his early 20s, and he was much freer with his physicality back then.

Sam did an interview with Vanity Fair [for the magazine’s New Establishment issue]. I think it came out yesterday, the day of our premiere, where he was very sweet about the walk as well. It’s a very generous thing for the boys to acknowledge that the walk was close, a good approximation of Sam and his vibe. I think that’s a very classy thing, to acknowledge the thing that seems to be working. But who knows what’s happening in their hearts and minds right now or within the family? I can project myself into that experience and imagine what it must feel like for an actor to be so presumptuous to play a character called Sam Altman in a major film. I can imagine that must be really strange, and I feel for…. I don’t know. In terms of taking it on, what outweighed that sense of responsibility for me was this sense of it is the defining inevitable invention of our times. It felt like a great responsibility to interrogate not just the machine, if you can even call it that, the kind of the consciousness or the technology itself, but to interrogate the people who are building it and who are putting their hearts and souls and life’s work into it, and where they may or may not be leading us.

That was deeply researched. This is what I gleaned. There’s a lot of people that know Sam. There’s a lot of people that are happy to talk about Sam. Some very, very protective; others, slightly more inside information. And I’m not going to name who these people are. But it was a kind of adding to the cauldron and through my lens of the interpretation of who this person is, combined with what was on the page and the specific cinematic story we’re telling and how we’re telling it, and Luca’s tastes and sensibilities. And, yeah, a lot of people said he would never sit conventionally. He was always sitting like a little boy.

Intimacy, but also ownership of a space—a kind of subtle, very soft dominance of a space. But also, as you say, a kind of, “Hey, we’re all just hanging out doing the coolest job ever. So why can’t we just sit like we’re in a dorm room?” It’s very psychologically interesting to me and smart. And who knows if it’s all calculated? Who knows if it’s not? I don’t know. What was interesting, in tracking his physicality in all the videos I saw is, at the beginning, he’s very free in how he twitches and moves. He’s just freer in his ability to be his true self maybe. And then as he starts to become more and more powerful, and ultimately becoming the face of the new world, this behemoth company that’s going to define where we are going—even if he doesn’t know where we are going, and none of them do—he becomes a slightly more homogenized version of a tech CEO. That was a really, really interesting kind of journey. And you can see, now, in [Altman’s recent interview with Vanity Fair], he’s very image-conscious, and I am too. I think we all are.

I mean, yes. One has to. This is the job. And this is why I wanted to do it: Because with The Social Network, I was getting ready to play Mark Zuckerberg, and then David Fincher calls me in and says, “We found someone that is just going to do it better. It’s Jesse, but we think you could also play this part. And you’re a very emotional actor, Andrew, so why would we waste all of that on someone who doesn’t seem to feel many emotions?” So Eduardo became my kind of guy, and I was very happy with that. But it left a little dangling thread, and I was like, “I need to understand.” Because I started to explore what it takes to win, to win on that level.

I think I’m a competitive person. I’m an athlete. I was raised by a swimming-coach father and, at that time, a proud capitalist. My dad has evolved his view of the world over the course of the last decades, which I find very moving and touching, as I have evolved my view of winning and losing and the beauty of losing and how humility is the only thing that actually grows us. It’s fucking awful. I hate losing.

No. It’s so much easier. Because you’re on this fucking false pedestal and it’s so much easier for the shit to get kicked out. It’s like, Oh, wait a minute. I forgot that I got above my station for a minute, and it’s a wonderful, horrible gift to be forced to crawl back down into the mud of what it is to be a human being. And actually I think it does relate to the story that we’re talking about, the film that we’re talking about.

When I was in my 20s, 30s, it was a time of slaying dragons and trying to plant flags and say, “This is who I am.” And then I think maybe as you enter middle age, a bunch of unresolved wounds from childhood that you kind of patched over with success just go, “Hey, we’re still here, dude.” And then it’s time to realize that there’s still a lot of work to do on maturation. I’m sorry, but to keep bringing it back to the film, I think what we’re dealing with is we’re in a very immature culture. We’re being still defined by this kind of adolescent impulse to win at all costs and that losing is weak and vulnerability is weak and that humility is actually not allowed.

What was that T-shirt in the fashion show that was happening recently? “Bring Back Shame” [in designer Conner Ives’s spring-summer show this past September]. I mean, people will respond to that as they do, but how I respond to it, positively, is, Bring back accountability. Bring back accountability for our inhumanity to each other. Humility is a surefire way to get us back to our collective humanity, I feel. But it’s hard. It’s hard. I love winning. It’s so much easier when things are going great, but I think it’s probably better for your soul when things aren’t going so great.

I’ve had a weird few years just in my own life, in a way that I don’t think it’s appropriate for me to go into, just because it’s my private life that I really care about protecting and holding on [to] for myself. But I think it is related to what I feel in the world in terms of the transition we’re in. It feels like we’re in a falling-apart culture, that there is no center anymore. It’s hard to find our own center within that lack-of-center in the world. A lot of people my age who I speak to are feeling a similar sense of a kind of falling apart, which feels right, because as a thing falls apart, the seeds of the future put back together start to get planted. Something else being born. I don’t mean to be glib, I don’t mean to be evasive, because I do like talking. I remember being a young person and wanting people I saw on magazine covers to say something real. So I feel a responsibility to that young person that is out there as well.

I think I was a real pain in the ass to my family because I was like, “What’s that? What’s happening there? That’s fucked-up.” And they’re like, “Shut the fuck up, Andy. Shut the fuck up.” I was that kid pointing out the stuff that wasn’t being said and was being felt, because I could just feel it all. It’s mysterious to me, but it was a hassle for me as well. I was like, “I don’t want to be so sensitive. I don’t want to hug my bully after he beats the shit out of me.” I could just feel his pain. It would be a lot easier to not have to see and feel all of these things that I may just be making up, but I’m pretty sure I’m not. It was a radar that I’ve had since I was a kid, I guess. I think my family would say the same thing, and I think they would also agree that it was a bit of a pain in the ass.

I need a place to go and express all of the most difficult shit about me to other people in private where they’re expressing their most difficult shit about them. I would venture to say, and this is a bit of a bold statement, that we all need that. I happen to have that in my life because I fucking sought it out and I searched it out and I crawled through the woods and into the dirt to find it. I have a really great group of people.

It really happened when I was doing Spider-Man, and I was like, Oh shit, I’m in danger of losing myself. It’s like what they say about famous, really, really famous people. They walk into any room and they’re like, “Everyone’s so nice.” And it’s like, no. I don’t know this person, but you could say, “No, you’re just Tom Cruise, and everyone wants to hang out with Tom Cruise.” I mean, I do know Tom, and I haven’t seen him in a long time. I only bring him up because he’s one of the most famous people in the world and I happen to know him a little bit and really have enjoyed and have a lot of admiration for him. But for me, it was a big danger that I would start to think that was a reflection of who I am. Do you know what I mean? And so I think in order to hold on to my ability to be messy, my ability to lose, my ability to be “weak,” my ability to be all of the things that our culture says a man should not be or even a person should not be, I sought out places and people and spaces and groups that would allow for me just to stay in touch with all of the messiest parts of myself, all the stuff that I’m not going to talk about here because it’s not safe to talk about them here.

Pleasantly. It was completely unintentional. Literally before I was going on to do the show, Stephen’s assistant came into the dressing room with me and my dad and my brother and said, “Hey, he might bring up this. Is that okay?” And I’m like, “Give me a second.” And I checked in with myself. I was like, “Yeah, sure.” Because I love Stephen, I trust him, and I know that he’s very good with those kinds of topics. He’s a really great container in that way. So it was very spontaneous. And then I think I said a prayer before I went on. I was just like, “Hey, Mom, whatever you got, just let me be the channel. Whatever you want me to say, whatever you don’t want me to say, just use me. I’m here to be used for the good, whatever that means.” And then the rest is just kind of a spontaneous moment that was lucky enough to get captured. I got texts about it yesterday, people who lose people, they get sent that clip. There’s a taboo around the subject in our culture—“No, come on, get on with it. Move forward, move forward, move forward”—and also people are just so scared of dying. We’re all so fucking scared of dying because we’ve somehow been led to believe that “Well, not me. I shouldn’t have to fucking die. I know we’re all going to fucking….” It’s this ascension obsession.

Well, it’s immature, and it’s deluded, and it’s a little adorable. It’s like, Oh, that’s so cute. You think you can outsmart the great mystery? Oh my God, it’s adorable. And it’s kind of sweet, but it’s infantile. And it’s cowardly. It’s the scariest adventure, and we’re all going to go on it. Every single one of us, every single one of us, and it doesn’t make sense. I think that’s the place that I find really exciting, is the not knowing. That’s when people get interesting. And I say that with some irony, I suppose, because we are being led by a bunch of younger guys right now who don’t know where this technology is taking us.

There was an overwhelming amount of reporting done about Sam having a specific relationship with the truth. And it was obviously a really vital ingredient in our story. And so I had to get into that for myself. Because he’s very charming by all accounts. There’s the quote in the movie that if Sam Altman was dropped into an island of cannibals, he would be their king in five years. All of these things were so juicy for me to imagine and to merge with and to interpret. I had to look at myself with my relationship to the truth, to universal truth, to personal truth, to objective truth, to subjective, someone else’s truth about me.

But my relationship to the truth, I try to be rigorous with myself. I try to do a fearless searching moral inventory of myself in every single moment of difficulty or tension. I try my hardest. I’m a human being. I’ve definitely not been a perfect human being. I sound like Sam right now. I think in that Vanity Fair interview, he was like, “I’m not a saint.” I’m the same. I mean, maybe this is a question better asked to people who are closest to me in my life, to be honest. I would say that I wouldn’t be a reliable narrator in terms of that. I think there’s a survival instinct in lying. There’s a self-preservation in the lies we tell each other and the lies we tell ourselves, but I wonder how that plays out in terms of the technology that it’s being baked into.

Yes, I do. I think at that time, before The Social Network came out, people were scoffing at the idea of a Facebook movie. No one was really onto the tech industry and the people that were governing it in the same way, because they didn’t consciously pose as much of a threat to our existence. Now we’re all a bit more hip to it. By the public becoming more hip to it, but also powerful people becoming more hip to it, realizing that that’s where the power lies, means that a company like OpenAI will have much more authority and power. For regular people like you and I, it’s higher stakes because we all feel like we have our eyes slightly more open now to the real-world personal consequences of these technologies. So we’re healthily more invested in shining light where that power lies and where we’re giving our autonomy, but also simultaneously there’s a much larger vested interest in protecting those people and their technology.

I feel afraid now. But it’s outweighed by a faith in humanity, but also a faith in the mystery of life. It’s the artist’s responsibility to reflect the times we’re in, and I think it’s getting harder and harder to do that without fear of consequences from those in power who you are rocking the boat for. I was excited the morning of the premiere yesterday. I woke up because I saw Sam’s interview on Vanity Fair and I was like, Oh shit, I’m playing that guy and people are going to see it tonight. And he’s just been named the most powerful man in the world by this publication. And it was kind of like, this is genuinely a cool thing to be a part of and feels courageous being led by Luca, because he says he’s not afraid, which I really admire and respect. I am afraid, but I’m still willing to put it on the line, but we’ll see.

That being said, there’s another part of me that’s like, “I don’t think this is going to touch them in a way.” You know what I mean? There’s a part that’s like, “I wonder if they’re too big to fail, they’re too big.” They’re able to go, “Well, they got the walk right, but everything else is kind of bullshit.” And then they move on because it’s small potatoes to them. I’m not sure. I’m not in their sphere, but I’m really, really, really curious to see how it all plays out.

But then there’s always people that come out and defend them. It’s so strange. Whether they’re bots or otherwise, I’m not sure, but there’s just an army of people that are like, “Leave those rich guys alone.” I’m like, “What?”

No, I didn’t have a body double. No, I saw that interview and I replayed it a few times to try and discern what he was actually saying, because I was very confused by that. I never had any interaction with him. I’ve never seen him in real life. We were shooting outside of his house. It was an eerie day, for sure. We were told that he wasn’t home and his security people were there. I think I saw one security guard. But, no, I never saw Sam, so he maybe mistook someone else for me. I have no idea, but I’ve never waved at Sam. I’ve never seen him. I was curious about that. [A representative for OpenAI told GQ that Altman was home during the filming and reiterated that he waved at Garfield.]

Yikes. That’s scary. It’s not scary in terms of the link. It’s fine by me. It’s more maybe I’m getting into some survival stuff for myself. I don’t want to make really powerful enemies. I don’t want to do that, but I’m not saying that that’s certainly what’s going to happen, but I don’t know if he’s going to feel warm towards me, and that’s okay. But there’s still a part of me that wants everyone to be okay all the time and therefore I’m okay. You know what I mean? It’s a slightly backtracking impulse, but it’s an interesting position to be in.

I’m not concerned about that. And I don’t think Jesse should be either. I think he’s such an incredible artist and an actor and director [and] writer. I feel safe in that I will make other things and this will be a part of my work and that’s that. And there’ll be other things that take away from that. I know the beginning of my obituary will be “Erstwhile Spider-Man.” You know what I mean?

I haven’t really considered it. My desire is to make work that I feel is speaking from my soul every time. That’s kind of where I’m trying to get to in terms of the feeling of relationship with failure and success. You know what something feels like for you, and you know what it means to you, and then the rest is kind of none of my business. So I’ll make a movie and I love it, and then it just doesn’t work for people or it just doesn’t hit in the same way that something that felt very difficult.
And I’m really glad I had the experience, because it was the ultimate version of fame and visibility. To taste that, and to know what that is, felt really healthy in all of its unhealthiness.

I think I’m the same as everyone else who’s even remotely cognizant of where we are and where we’re heading. I look at my friends who do have kids and the beauty of it obviously, but also the struggle of it and the inescapable agony of young people’s longing to belong to the screen rather than longing to belong to the real world. It gives me pause for sure, like any person, I suppose. That being said, there is that kind of biological imperative, and there is that just kind of instinct, and there’s an image that you live with for so long—I have, anyway—of the concept of being a dad and going on that adventure. It’s mysterious to me.
I know that all tech-CEO people, they’re very, very anti-technology in the house across the board. That just is objectively dark, because they know what it does.

It’s the most obvious cliché stuff. I went to an Ezra Collective gig at the Roundhouse in London. It’s a British kind of conglomerate of amazing musicians in the realm of Afrobeat, jazz-inspired. That was a night where you go, Oh, life and humans and arts and bodies and sweat and creativity. I was in Devon recently with my nephews, and we were surfing and swimming and playing American football on the beach. And eating fish and chips. We had a friends-and-family screening in London for this other film I did with Paul Greengrass called The Uprising, which I’m really proud of and I really love, and I love Paul…. And it’s moments like that when a bunch of friends and family come up, and I don’t care how they feel about the film, but the fact that they want to support and be there and that I can be vulnerable with them after the screening and they can be vulnerable with me. And my friends who I hadn’t seen in a long time, we can catch up and be like, “How you doing?” “I’m struggling a little bit.” “Me, too.” Just as simple as that. ✦

items.title: How Will Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Dress?
items.description: When Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: When Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

“Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”

Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a new look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

“I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” says Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”

The actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser says. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”

Another important factor that contributes to a new Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” says Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”

Tone also plays an important role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

If Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he says, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. As such, he’d opt for longer jackets, both single- and double-breasted, that are fuller through the body, and straight-leg pleated trousers. “It’s not that very, very slim fit that we'd seen for so many years, but it still needs to be refined,” he says. “I don’t think it would be appropriate to put him in wide-leg or baggy trousers. I just don't think it’s right for Bond.”

Given the intense scrutiny on every relaunch of the Bond franchise, and the tendency of fans to get worked up online over perceived mishandling of a beloved character, Pattinson, Villeneuve, and the film’s yet-to-be-announced costume designers have little room for error. Go too conservative and they’ll be accused of playing it safe; make Bond into a fashion guy, and they’ll incur the wrath of the traditionalists.
“He needs to look current, but also timeless,” Spaiser says. “It’s a hard balance to find.”

items.title: Parker Posey Finally Meets Her Match in Artist Kembra Pfahler
items.description: On an unseasonably warm Sunday in October, Parker Posey, who currently stars in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, accepted an invitation to enter Kembra Pfahler’s inner sanctum: a near-empty railroad apartment in Manhattan’s East Village, where the walls, cei
items.author: Alex Hawgood
paragraphs: On an unseasonably warm Sunday in October, Parker Posey, who currently stars in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, accepted an invitation to enter Kembra Pfahler’s inner sanctum: a near-empty railroad apartment in Manhattan’s East Village, where the walls, ceiling, floors, piano, shelves, salt shakers—you name it—are painted in the same tile-red hue.

Pfahler is one of underground New York’s most original figures, a star best known for raw live performances in which she paints her nude body and wears three-tiered fright wigs extending two-and-a-half feet above her blackened snarl. Posey was there “not as a subject to be styled, but as a collaborator to be transformed,” as Pfahler put it, through “bows, wigs, body paint, ritual, humor, and a distinct sense of the theatrical feminine”—or what she calls “the visual language” of her punk–and–performance art project, the Voluptuous Horror of Karen Black. True to Pfahler’s fearless form, the shoot unfolded as a series of provocations: “Is Parker becoming one of Kembra’s collaborators? Is she being initiated? Is she wearing a wig, a balaclava, or body paint? Is she dressed as Kembra, or is she dressed as Parker dressed as Kembra?”

Both Posey, 58, and Pfahler, 65, emerged as emblematic fixtures on New York’s 1990s downtown scene, known for resisting conventions. Posey amassed a following with her breakout film, Party Girl, which fixed her image in the public imagination as an indie It girl and thrift-store clotheshorse who painted the town red; Pfahler gained notoriety as a flesh-baring provocateur who literally painted her body red. Twenty years ago, Posey was walking down a cobblestoned street in SoHo when a shock of color appeared before her. It was Pfahler, naked and painted, surrounded by rapt crowds outside of Jeffrey Deitch’s gallery on Wooster Street. “I only happened upon her by accident,” Posey said. “I’ll never forget seeing her.” Pfahler, for her part, was recently asked by a brand to do a photo shoot modeled after Posey’s librarian transformation in Party Girl.

Despite decades of orbiting cinema and theater scenes—Posey started out in Off Broadway productions and experimental acting workshops, while Pfahler was a regular at museums and underground performance spaces—they had never actually met until this shoot. Predictably, the self-described “indie tramp” and the oft-called “shock-art godmother” turned out to be natural creative partners. “She’s one of my favorite actors,” Pfahler said of Posey. “Her face is so iconic. Basically, any movie she’s ever done is in my top 10.” (She especially loves Best in Show, Josie and the Pussycats, and Superman Returns.) “I felt an immediate kinship,” Posey said. “It was symbiotic. I felt like a sister to her—or like one of her students.” From the beginning, Pfahler wanted the collaboration to be staged in her apartment, where she has lived since the 1980s. Despite its resemblance to an emergency light, the space is monastic. “I don’t have any dishes, any towels, or anything domestic on any level,” she says. (“Empty-shelf syndrome” is how she described her approach to interior design.) The sparseness allows the apartment to be “a launching pad into my new ideas.”

The first of Posey’s outfits was a Gucci gown adorned with a tangle of necklaces sitting like a ruff at her throat. Gathering the diaphanous fabric in one hand, Posey climbed into a freestanding tub in the kitchen, where a black wig the size of a juvenile bear sat on a red table. Posey stood with one leg jutting out of a side slit, as a playlist of 1960s spaghetti western soundtracks twanged from iPhone speakers. The two women then changed into matching cat-eye glasses and black suiting. Pfahler was in her own ensemble, which leaned a smidge sinister; Posey, wearing The Row, was more streamlined. To complete the look, Pfahler wrapped a red headscarf around Posey’s face. “It’s almost more…not tied back…more tight, like a bandage,” Pfahler said, gently knotting the fabric with the exacting precision of an origami sculptor. “I really don’t think there are that many people who have that visage.”

They climbed a small ladder in the next room and sat on the edge of Pfahler’s lofted single bed. On her phone, Pfahler pulled up an image of Carroll Borland, the 1930s actor who more or less invented the idea of the undead ingénue with her waist-length dark hair and minimalist shroud. Posey countered with a different heroine from the madwomen canon: ZaSu Pitts in Greed, Erich von Stroheim’s 1924 silent psychological drama, which originally ran for nine grim hours before being trimmed down to two. “It’s a really creepy movie, and ZaSu Pitts was obviously tormented,” Posey said. “Women are always getting their limits pushed.” Pfahler nodded her wrapped head. “The world is more misogynistic than ever,” she noted.

A longtime model whose tear sheets include a 1996 Calvin Klein Jeans ad and editorials for Italian Vogue and Penthouse, Pfahler grew up at the beach in Los Angeles, around the South Bay. Her father was one of the stars of Bruce Brown’s 1958 surf film Slippery When Wet. Her aunt Karen Rea was a Hollywood casting director whose credits include Ghostbusters and Death Becomes Her. “I was born around the film industry, which meant being born into this atmosphere that was really sexist and racist and kind of appalling,” Pfahler said. She spent her childhood frequenting film sets, and at the age of 9 she was cast in a Kodak commercial. “I really love movies, despite not really getting along too well with the Los Angeles world.”

Pfahler is also, in her own way, a screen siren—or at least a leading face of the Cinema of Transgression, the 1980s and ’90s Lower East Side film movement that rejected polish and professionalism for low-budget Dionysian celebrations of feminism, glamour, and bodily freedom. (Sewing Circle, a 1992 short by Richard Kern, shows Pfahler, clad in a Young Republicans T-shirt, garter belt, and black stockings, “undergoing an unusual form of elective surgery,” as one New York Times critic put it.) Pfahler’s first self-titled monograph, published by Rizzoli in March, documents her more than four decades of body paint, butt prints, and blackened teeth. The editing process was not easy for an artist who abstains from “yesterbating,” a term Pfahler coined for revisiting old works. “I don’t like to think about the past too much,” she said. Still, working on the retrospective gave her “a kind of renewed appreciation for all the hard work that happened over the past four decades.”

Posey, whose favorite color is also red, left Laurel, Mississippi, at 18 to study drama at SUNY Purchase. There, one of her professors mentioned that she reminded him of the ’70s-era character actor Karen Black, whose career bridged pulp and prestige across an oeuvre spanning Dennis Hopper’s 1969 counterculture landmark Easy Rider, Robert Altman’s seminal 1975 satire Nashville, and Rob Zombie’s cult 2003 horror–black comedy House of 1000 Corpses. It was around the time that Posey was a student that Pfahler, recovering from a mugging, caught Trilogy of Terror, the 1975 American made-for-television horror anthology film famous for Black’s portrayal of a woman terrorized in her apartment by a Zuni fetish doll. Pfahler was transfixed, and soon after adopted Black’s name for her stage act, deconstructing B-movie tropes. Karen Black, it turned out, was a North Star for both women, long before either had heard of the other. “It’s interesting how intuition reveals something true,” Posey said.

In her movie roles, Posey has unselfconsciously walked the line between daffiness and depth—whether she’s playing a neurotic stage mother to a Weimaraner in Best in Show or a flamboyantly fascist record executive in Josie and the Pussycats, the Y2K flop turned midnight repertory staple. In The White Lotus, her louche, lorazepam-laced turn as a pouty, privileged wife and mother earned her awards recognition and endless memes. Lately, she has gone broader still. Her role as host of The Mob, Hulu’s new reality competition in which contestants cosplay as Italian Mobsters, feels like an extension of her improvised caricature work in Christopher Guest’s mockumentaries. In a parade of patterned caftans and candy-colored turbans, she slices garlic with a razor blade, tells contestants to “take the whole cannoli,” and delivers lines like “You gotta step it up if you wanna get paid.”

To play the ruddy, sun-worn wife of a CIA agent in Wild Horse Nine, Posey tinted her skin, freckled her face, and gingered her hair. Wearing a leopard-print housecoat onesie and red 1970s bell-bottoms reproduced from her own closet, she nearly steals the movie, despite her brief screen time and a cast that includes Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich, and Steve Buscemi.

“You needed an actress who could come into the film 25 minutes in, grab it and Sam Rockwell by the throat—metaphorically speaking—be funny as hell, then turn on a dime and make the scene far sadder, and their relationship instantly real and deep,” McDonagh said. “You needed someone with unbelievable comedy and acting chops to do that in such a short space of time.” He compared Posey and Rockwell’s telephone tête-à-têtes in the film to “a tennis match with two greats, when both players need to be at the top of their game, like John McEnroe versus Jimmy Connors in the early ’80s.”

Back at the W shoot, the final round of transformations required space beyond the red walls. At a photo studio a few blocks away, Pfahler donned her body paint with the ease of a nurse changing into scrubs. “I’m not really the kind of person who is embraced, and I don’t think the way I present myself will ever be,” she said, applying her own eye makeup using a Sharpie and Wite-Out. “But I’ve always loved transformation.” Posey’s hands, painted red to match Pfahler, were punctuated with black talon-like nails. She would have gone full body paint, she explained, but she was due at a Q&A to promote Wild Horse Nine as soon as she left the set. “I’m an actor,” she asserted matter-of-factly. “I like to look like other people, like characters. I would like to be in Planet of the Apes and go through all that makeup and prosthetics, or at least change my nose for a part if I felt I needed to.”

Then came the manes. Hairstylist Jimmy Paul teased the two wigs, affixing white roses to Posey’s and cutout paper bows to Pfahler’s. When the massive pieces were lowered onto each of their heads, the effect was palpable. Posey was, by any reasonable description, a Pfahler acolyte. Side by side, the two women nearly merged into a single storm cloud. And yet, despite the voluptuousness, Posey was still very much herself. “Parker-ish,” said Pfahler, staring at her collaborator, tears of joy trickling down her red-painted cheeks. For her part, Posey said she has long admired how Pfahler, as well as performance artists such as Christeene, Dynasty Handbag, and Jack Ferver, continue “making their impressions in person. They are bold enough to need that relationship to the act of the art they’re creating. It is a strange and beautiful gift.”

Posey’s friends have, for years, urged her to stage her own one-woman show. “I don’t feel strong enough yet to break out in a solo performance,” she said. “If I ever did, it would feel more like performance art than stand-up, but it takes a lot of guts.” Posey has spent more than three decades working in the film industry, which, whether independent or mainstream, remains male-dominated. “This photo shoot captured a moment where that wasn’t the case,” Posey said. “What registered most, at first and throughout the day, is how much women are excluded from the boys club of art and business.” The collaboration with Pfahler had been something rare: The actor and the artist were one and the same. “She was my muse,” Posey said of Pfahler, “and I was hers.”
Hair by Jimmy Paul at Susan Price NYC; makeup by Yumi Lee at Streeters; manicure by Jin Soon Choi for JinSoon Nails at Home Agency. Set design by Spencer Vrooman.
