items.title: The Actor Chasing Hookups While He’s in Town for a Role
items.description: This week, a guy visiting from Los Angeles enjoys his time off: 30, single, New York
items.author: Alyssa Shelasky
paragraphs: This week, a guy visiting from Los Angeles enjoys his time off: 30, single, New York

8:30 a.m. Wake up in the Hyatt House in the Hudson Valley. I’ve been here the past two nights shooting a small part on a Netflix show with massive stars. I’m an actor normally based in L.A., but I desperately needed a break from the town. I came to New York to chase work and experience the fall out here. So far, so good.
8:45 a.m. Meditate. I’ve been diligent about getting back into my Transcendental Meditation practice. Twice a day, no exceptions.
10 a.m. Check out of the hotel and walk across the highway to a charming diner for an omelet and coffee. They have a whole double-sided menu of just Bloody Marys. I’m tempted, but abstain.

2 p.m. Back at my Harlem sublet. Drop my stuff and head to Alamo Drafthouse Brooklyn to catch Club Kid with my friend Sam. We met in L.A. in our early 20s. They have a frenetic, wild-child magic that you can’t help but get swept up in. They occasionally drive me insane, but I love them deeply. They have a foot fetish, and we’ve dabbled in play together twice. The first time, they sucked and bit on my toes; the second time, we did it to each other, which was much hotter and heavier. Cool to explore, but we’re mostly friends.

5:15 p.m. The movie was amazing. I cried a lot. I’ve thought about being a single gay dad, but I had two single parents, and that always makes me come to my senses. Still, Jordan Firstman made a great case.

8 p.m. Sam and I go to Harlem and chat about life. After a few hours, they’ve been staring at my calf socks for a while, so I allow them to crack my toes and sniff the soles for five minutes. They leave and I go to bed.

9:01 a.m. Late for workout class. I was too Zen after meditation and the gym has locked the doors. Walk up 20 blocks to Barry’s. I’m ClassPassing, so I know I’m going to get charged $30 for the no-show, but I make an inappropriate amount of money from my side gig as an audio erotica voice actor. I started two years ago. My content has blown up, and I’m on retainer for a ridiculous monthly rate. Plus, I’m anonymous, and it opens up time to travel and fund my creative endeavors. It’s the best.

1 p.m. After the gym, I go to the Angelika to catch Paper Tiger. I love going to the movies alone. I love doing a lot of things alone. I ended my last relationship because my ex got really good at making me feel small. Since we broke up, I’ve been hyperindependent. I’m examining it, but I enjoy my own company.
4:30 p.m. The movie was kinda sleepy. I had two beers with lunch before, so that didn’t help. Head back up for a party nap before meeting Sam and some friends for dancing in East Williamsburg.

8:30 p.m. Solo dinner at Peasant in Nolita. A negroni, duck-liver bruschetta with pickled mushrooms, octopus ragù, two glasses of wine, and affogato. During dinner, I tipsily make plans with a Hinge match for two days from now.
10:15 p.m. The club’s cute, but kinda dead. I dance with Sam, their partner, and a few new friends. Make tentative plans to go to Basement with one of them. After, I take a car home.
9 a.m. Gross, rainy morning. I miss L.A. I wanna go back to being a lizard.

10:26 a.m. Text Quentin, another Hinge match, confirming we’re on for drinks tonight. I hate the apps, but I’m lonely and want a relationship, so I have nothing to lose. Head to Barry’s to sweat out the nerves.

6:07 p.m. Waiting at a cocktail bar in Clinton Hill for Quentin, whose train was delayed. Check email. A self-tape request from my agents comes through. Fuck yes! They’re killing it for me lately. It’s for a movie that shoots in Staten Island in February. That sounds horrid, but work is work.

7 p.m. Quentin is a dud. Sweet, affable, no X factor. Kinda basic. He makes us play this drinking game where we make assumptions about each other; the only thing I can come up with is that he looks like he’s been to the Abbey at least five times. I’m obviously correct. It feels like he planned this to avoid awkward conversation. As we walk to the train, he asks to kiss me — but looks over his shoulder first. A pet peeve. Did you forget the blue wave?! It’s our right — nay, our duty — to be gay in public! Chill! I let him kiss me. It’s mid. It all feels by the book. I won’t see him again.
9:15 p.m. Get off the train in Tribeca for oysters and mediocre jambalaya at a Cajun place.

10:30 p.m. Walk up to the Bowery and pop into Bar Monto. This place is poppin’. I’m tipsy and feeling grateful to be young, single, bicoastal — and not a nepo baby — with real money, earned myself, entirely from creative work. It doesn’t look like I thought it would (yet), but it’s an incredible place to be in. Dream your dream, bitch!
11:45 p.m. Horny. There’s a gay dive bar with a darkroom nearby.
12:04 a.m. Check my coat and bag and head to the basement. On top of the date drinks, I had two beers at Bar Monto. Order one more. I’m darkroom drunk, baby.

12:07 a.m. Immediately het rejected left and right. Still, I’ve been craving analog communal experiences. If you can’t learn to enjoy rejection, you’re dead in the water. Nothing is personal, and you never know. Pretty soon, I’m locking lips and jacking off with a shredded, bald sex monolith who’s at least six-foot-six. He bows his head onto my shoulder and lets me kiss his ears and pet his bald head. It’s giving Alien Horse. I’m so turned on. He starts fucking me. I’m hairy and have a deep voice, so a lot of people think I’m daddy, but what they don’t know is that actually? I’m baby. Fool around with a few more guys.

3 a.m. After a half-assed makeout with a string bean of a boy who couldn’t care less about anything or anyone, I turn to leave … and lock eyes with an adorable, lean guy with a mustache and piercings. Let’s call him B. He comes over, and instead of making an explicit pass, I’m compelled to pull him in for a protective hug. Fine — I can absolutely be daddy when I want to. I can tell he’s really into it. We kiss, then trade blowjobs until security comes around with flashlights.

4:45 a.m. B. is home with me. I climb on top and ride him; he returns the favor. It’s drunk sex, so it’s not remarkable, but I feel the night ended on the best possible note. He fingers and kisses me until I come, then curls up next to me and we fall asleep.

10 a.m. Owwwwww. I’m a rotting cadaver. Still rockin’ that morning wood, though. B. wakes up, nuzzles my neck, and peels off my underwear. We give each other sloppy morning kisses. My uncontested favorite. He gives me unreal head. Before he leaves, we exchange numbers.

11 a.m. Text from Hinge date: “Morning! Totally forgot i had brunch plans so if you’re fine with pushing it a little past 2:30 and me being slightly drunk yes were good if not raincheck for tmrw maybe? ;)” Demon twink. I tell him all good and that I’m busy tomorrow. Cancel everything for the day.
11:25 a.m. Take my PrEP and Doxy-PEP. Easy, essential, daily, miraculous!
4 p.m. Catch up on Survivor, read Ari Emanuel’s memoir, order fluff-and-fold laundry, eat pizza.
8 p.m. Film the self-tape. Feel fine about it.

9 a.m. Arrive at my friend Kirsten’s on Third and Bowery. Kirsten’s in her mid-60s. We sat next to each other watching Andrew Scott perform Sea Wall my first week in the city. We struck up a conversation, and I learned she and my mom share a first name and that she’s a fellow meditator. She’s a renowned textile artist who gets commissioned by the top museums in the world. One of the coolest women I’ve ever met. Kirsten leads me, two others, and a Zoom group through a meditation, then we have chai and pastries.

Noon Walk to Kips Bay to meet a friend for Godzilla Minus Zero. We catch up before the movie. He’s just a really solid gay guy. We met at theater camp when we were 17, and he’s become a playwright and poet. We’re developing a play together. He loves to rib me about L.A., but it doesn’t bother me because I know he sees me as an artist. Coming from other people, it’s excruciating. I detest L.A. vs. N.Y. discourse.

3:30 p.m. My friend had never seen a kaiju movie before and was shook by how emotionally resonant it was, and the actual life-threatening stakes for the characters. We then riff a bunch of faggy one-liners about the movie and crack the fuck up. He can queen out like nobody else.
8 p.m. Go over erotica scripts. They’re holiday-themed. Loosely plan to record them tomorrow.
9:30 a.m. My throat is sore, so I need to hold off on recording smut. Sorry, ladies!

1:45 p.m. Call my dad. We went through a turbulent few years after I came out. He’s made progress, and I still love him and am committed to our relationship, but it’s hard. He asks if I’m getting auditions, which I’ve told him not to ask before. The answer is yes, but it’s every actor’s nightmare and always makes me cagey. I try not to react because I know it’s innocent, but fail. Meditate immediately after hanging up.
2:45 p.m. Unprompted, Dad texts an apology. Reiterates that he loves me and wants to be sure things are going well. I don’t give him enough credit.
3 p.m. Take a walk and listen to Remi Wolf’s Mud. Head 40 blocks down to a bar on Amsterdam, order oysters and fries, and read.

5:30 p.m. It’s dark out, and I’m near the entrance to a cruising spot, so decide to go in. I tried a few weeks ago, but wasn’t sure where to go. This time, I go deep into the brush. As my eyes adjust, I see the silhouette of a guy walking past, and it’s hard to describe, but I feel like part of something bigger than myself. This has been a cruising spot for decades, long before AIDS. I think about how many men have walked these trails, through all the different eras of our existence and repression, looking for a release valve for our shame and loneliness and an outlet for our intimacy. I walk around, cruise one guy, and suck his dick for two minutes. Another guy steals him away, but it’s honestly okay. That’s not what the experience was about for me.

8:30 p.m. Dinner at a wine bar on the Upper West Side. The server plies me with Montepulciano and I have burrata, spaghetti, and Broccolini. A Hinge match I’ve been bantering with asks if we can do the NYT “36 Questions” on our first date. I get the ick. Unmatch.
11 p.m. Hurl myself into bed. An L.A. fuck buddy sends me pics, and I send a video of my cumshot.
8:30 a.m. Throat still sore. I need to take rest more seriously.
9 a.m. B. texts asking to get together, but I tell him I’m under the weather. Also, I had fun, but I don’t know if I need to see him again. Will I be alone forever? Would that be the worst thing?

11 a.m. Dive back into the Ari Emanuel memoir. I know people have divided opinions about him, but I love industry memoirs, and his tone is delicious, biting, and strangely optimistic. His stories remind me that the industry has faced extinction many times but has always found a way to adapt.
3 p.m. Tell my therapist all about cruising, the darkroom, the day on set, and my dad. She reflects on how much good has come from my deliberate attempt to loosen my ideas about control. I concur.
6 p.m. Feeling well enough that I knock out my audios. It takes two hours. I clean up and export the files, and drop them in a folder for the editors. That is all I have to do for the entire month.

9:52 p.m. A text from my best friend: Our debut short received its first festival rejection. A year ago, I would’ve been disheartened. As I get ready for bed, I celebrate. I’m trying! The pieces will fall into place. Dream your dream, bitch!
- The Man Sleeping With a Gooner
- The Woman Having Sex on the Floor at a Bar
- The ‘Sex Diaries’ That Brought Roommates Into the Mix

items.title: What Anok Yai, Amanda Seyfried, and Halle Bailey Wore This Month
items.description: This week, we’ll include the greatest ‘fits of November (a challenging task, as there were plenty of great looks). To make things easier, I’m not including any events here that we’ve covered elsewhere, but here are some honorable mentions: Drew Barrymore went
items.author: Jaharia Knowles
paragraphs: This week, we’ll include the greatest ‘fits of November (a challenging task, as there were plenty of great looks). To make things easier, I’m not including any events here that we’ve covered elsewhere, but here are some honorable mentions: Drew Barrymore went full noughties for her look at the MoMA Film Benefit; Tessa Thompson and Zendaya were, by far, the best-dressed at the Governors Awards; and Marion Cotillard proved even a tennis dress can be glamorous (if it’s Chanel!) at the Dia Art Foundation’s fall gala (I also witnessed Pamela Anderson chatting it up with fashion writer Lynn Yaeger at her Friendsgiving dinner with Pandora last week).

In other news, GQ made Men of the Year a three-day affair for the first time this year — and, in my opinion, the women outshone the men on the red carpet. Amelia Dimoldenberg hosted a dinner with Depop to celebrate the season finale of Chicken Shop Date (I’m still in the denial stage of grief for this), Anok Yai made a case for statement coat linings at the Gucci Core launch party, and Amanda Seyfried exuded old Hollywood glamour at Tiffany and Co.’s holiday event. Here are the best celebrity looks.
Most Glamourous: Amanda Seyfried
I know Seyfried’s from Pennsylvania, but she became an honorary New Yorker when she walked through the streets in a black gown and coat.
Best Pop of Color: Anok Yai
The supermodel wore a black fur coat lined with floral print to the Gucci Core launch party. Business on top, party inside? I think it’ll catch on.
Best Thrift Find: Amelia Dimoldenberg
Our favorite awkward girl wore a Blumarine dress she bought from Depop to host a dinner celebrating Chicken Shop Date’s season finale.
Women of the Year: Halle Bailey and Louisa Jacobson
Bailey and Jacobson went edgy for GQ’s Men of the Year party, donning smoky eyes and black leather (Bailey’s dress is Sergio Hudson, while Jacobson’s jacket and skirt are McQueen).
Reunion of the Effies: Elizabeth Banks and Elle Fanning
The method dressing continued at the Hunger Games after-party. Banks took a more subtle approach than Fanning, but I see and acknowledge those power shoulders.
All-American: Laura Harrier and Ryan Destiny
Harrier and Destiny wore red, white, and blue to Ralph Lauren’s celebration of the Polo Blaze Bag.
Opposites Attract: Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts
Paulson and Watts’s outfits and glam at Net-a-Porter’s Friendsgiving party were so different that it seems coordinated, especially since they have matching blonde pixies.
Best Jewels: Pamela Anderson
Fittingly, Anderson accessorized with a stack of jeweled bracelets to her Friendsgiving dinner with Pandora.
Best Pattern-Mixing: Salehe Bembury
The Versace shoe designer and cover star went maximalist-casual for the launch of new Zine Background Check by Backdrop as its inaugural cover star.
The photographer paired her black suit with a lacy top for Loro Piana’s Cashmere of the Year Awards.
Coolest Jackets: Gabriella Khalil and Madison Utendahl
I’m enjoying the belted jackets Khalil and Utendahl wore for the Esha Soni Scarlet Orb bag launch party.
The model gave Carrie Bradshaw at Brianna Capozzi and Jacob Holler’s photo book launch party.

items.title: I Am a Serial Returner. My Latest? My Wedding-Rehearsal Look.
items.description: This week, we have been exploring the many ways shopping anxiety manifests in our lives. How are some people trying to curb their spending stress? By returning — a lot. According to a report from the National Retail Federation, consumers returned approximately
items.author: Isabel Pask
paragraphs: This week, we have been exploring the many ways shopping anxiety manifests in our lives. How are some people trying to curb their spending stress? By returning — a lot. According to a report from the National Retail Federation, consumers returned approximately $850 billion in merchandise in 2025. And, apparently, not all of those buyers went into their purchase thinking they’d keep the final product. Buying and wearing clothes with the intent to return them — sometimes called wardrobing — is not exactly criminal, but it is still deceptive, and it is surprisingly common. So common, in fact, that in recent years brands have been cracking down on serial returners. “Sites like ASOS and Ssense,” this magazine previously reported, “are handing out lifetime shopping bans to longtime shoppers they determine have returned too much too often.” Here, one serial returner explains …

My relationship with returning started when I turned 26. I attended four weddings, two bachelorette parties, a Broadway premiere, and a vow renewal. All of these events required some kind of formalwear.

I scoured the internet for dresses — ones that were beautiful, flattering, unique but not flashy, and most of all, affordable. Dresses that met all of these qualifications were hard to come by. (Since when does even something simple cost $500?) When I wasn’t working as a nanny, hostess, or auditioning, I spent hours rifling through thrift stores. I scrolled through various rental platforms, but the dresses I liked were often out of stock in my size, and even a $90 subscription fee felt extravagant at the time.

For her black-tie wedding, my friend Danielle asked that her bridesmaids wear Champagne. Not taupe. Not tan. Not anywhere near white, of course. Champagne. After months of searching, I ventured out of my price range to an influencer-beloved, private-equity-owned, not-quite-designer but certainly not-cheap retail chain. And there it was. The perfect Champagne dress. I twisted my body to get a look at the tag in the dressing room, where I’d been able to adjust the lighting myself to cast a soft, warm glow. It was $498. Almost exactly what I made in a week’s work at my babysitting job. One-third of my rent. I took off the dress and hung it back on the hanger. As I pulled my jeans back on, I noticed a piece of paper on the floor and picked it up. It was the tag. After briefly panicking at the idea of being forced to actually pay for the dress, I realized something: The tag was attached with a small safety pin. I simply had to pin it back on the dress.

I wore that Champagne dress to Danielle’s wedding. I carefully unpinned the tag and put it in my jewelry box for safekeeping. I bought a powerful 48-hour antiperspirant and opted for white wine instead of red. Afterward, I pinned the tag back on and returned to Soho, where, heart racing, I handed the dress over to the store employee, sure that I would be caught red-handed and banned from the store forever. She didn’t bat an eye. She just dragged the bundle of silk across the counter to herself, blindly groping for the tag and scanning it. $498 went back on my credit card. It was remarkably easy.

In the five or so years since, I’ve gotten bolder. I know which stores have good return policies. I alternate email addresses when I’m frequenting a particular store so that my account isn’t flagged. I don’t wear perfume. I use dress tape to hide a tag when it can’t be easily removed.

My returning has extended beyond events and into my work. I’ve sent back thousands of dollars of props and set dressing, and I’ve costumed actors in clothing I could never afford to buy outright. With each film I’ve made, my collaborators and I create intricate spreadsheets to track return dates and packaging information. My apartment is overtaken by carefully labeled bags and boxes, organized into piles based on where they need to be returned. For my last film, our crew outfitted an entire nursery, from higher-priced items like a crib, rocking chair, and changing table, to 20-dollar purchases including a mobile, stuffed animals, and baby books. After the shoot, we disassembled the furniture and scheduled UPS pickups. We loaded up my laundry cart multiple times with boxes of home décor and niche props, going in shifts to the billionaire-owned grocery chain’s return counter. It’s an imperfect method, but in fighting the uphill battle of making independent films, utilizing it means there’s a far greater chance I can support the costume or set designer in achieving their vision — or at least pay them a rate closer to what they deserve.

I’m not necessarily proud of this pattern. My mother and sister don’t approve, so when I wore and returned a brand-new dress for my own wedding’s rehearsal dinner a few weeks ago, I didn’t tell them. I also didn’t tell them about the full cornhole set that was going back Monday, or the dozens of paper lanterns, string lights, candles, and cups (unused — I’m not a monster!) I boxed up and sent it back. As I’ve often explained to them, I wish I had the disposable income and closet space to buy a gorgeous dress for every occasion, or better, that the very brands I’m “exploiting” weren’t working to create a culture that makes me feel like I need a new dress for every event. It’s wasteful, it’s undignified, and I know that. I feel sick to my stomach when I think about the reality that hundreds of items I’ve sent back have likely been sent to a landfill.

I do my best to justify and examine my own actions. I have rules. No local businesses. No handmade items. No stores where someone actually cares enough to do a thorough inspection or where I’d be screwing with someone’s art or livelihood. I tell myself that stealing from big corporations is actually a sort of righteous rebellion. If I’m lucky enough to have disposable income in a city where the cost of living is astronomically high, I want to spend it on tickets for my friends’ plays, or a trip to Marrakech with my sister. I want to save up to buy a jacket that was hand-painted by someone I went to college with instead of a mass-produced rayon midi dress.

I recently rewatched Never Been Kissed, where 25-year-old investigative reporter Drew Barrymore goes undercover in a high school to research modern teen culture. Desperately searching for a story, Drew calls her boss from her hiding spot behind a mall clothing rack, a trio of popular girls sorting through candy-colored cardigans on the other side. “Gus, listen, it is a great story! They keep the tags on, then they return the clothes after they’ve worn them!” Gus — a beleaguered John C. Reilly — hangs up, uninterested. It’s not the splashy exposé he was after. It’s not new. It’s not dangerous. And I believe that in the larger context of the horrors of late-stage capitalism, my penchant for returns is not actually that big of a deal.

However, I also believe in collective and individual responsibility — to our planet and to local businesses. I know I’m actively choosing to do this — to play this morally dubious, maybe illegal, shockingly easy game. I’m not entirely sure how I feel about it, if it’s right or wrong or somewhere in between. But at least for the present moment, I’ve convinced myself it’s necessary — to make my art, to advance my career, to feel current and stylish and beautiful, and to not feel ashamed when I can’t afford a Champagne-colored dress for my friend’s wedding.
- ‘If He Knew How Much Stuff I Was Buying, He’d See Me Differently’
- ‘My Career in Fashion Hid My Compulsive Shopping Disorder’

items.title: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
items.description: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
items.author: Iva Dixit
paragraphs: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
The Summer I Turned Pretty star — who’s about to light up the holiday season with Clashing Through the Snow — copes with fame by remembering acting is just a job. He still can’t believe it’s his.

“Oh! Somebody watched this?” Years after it happened, Christopher Briney can still summon his incredulity from the first time a stranger asked to take a photo with him, his face screwed up in bewilderment as he starts telling me the story. It was June 2022, a time period that now feels near-Paleolithic, and that little show called The Summer I Turned Pretty had only been live for a day or two, tops. He and his girlfriend were on vacation in Boston, taking a walk through the city, when Briney had the oddest sensation that people were following him. He tried to shake himself loose of that feeling: “Why would they be?” Apart from his new project, he’d only been in one indie movie since graduating from his acting program. “What was extra weird about that for me was: I don’t live here. Like, I’m in Boston?”

But his hunch was, of course, correct. The next thing he knew, some friendly fans of the show had approached him for a picture (he obliged), which proved to be only the tip of the selfie-request iceberg about to come his way.

The Summer I Turned Pretty, the Amazon Prime Video adaptation of Jenny Han’s trilogy of YA novels, was a supernova that only got bigger and brighter over time, and as Conrad Fisher — the primary love interest of Lola Tung’s Isabel “Belly” Conklin, competing for her affections alongside his brother, Jeremiah (Gavin Casalegno) — Briney was at its white-hot center. Last year’s third and final season was the streamer’s most-watched season of television ever for women 18 to 34. The show dominated the cultural conversation to the point that even people who’ve never seen an episode probably have a credible opinion on “Team Conrad versus Team Jeremiah,” and it inspired an online fandom so passionate that the official Summer social media account issued a PSA reminding viewers that this is just a TV program and to please not bully and harass the cast and crew over it.

Briney imbued the elder Fisher brother with a kind of dignified suffering: the golden child of the family bucking under his burdens, including the devastating secret of his mother’s cancer diagnosis. Briney, with those searching blue-green eyes, could translate the storm brewing in Conrad’s head without uttering a single word. There are entire Reddit threads dedicated to screenshots of Briney staring off sullenly, which seem to crystalize something about Gen Z’s taste in heartthrobs. The way to this generation’s heart is through yearning. They want to watch their leading men suffer in thwarted longing. And nobody is yearning onscreen better than Briney.

Briney, 28, wears the mantle with good humor — the only approach when you’re subjected to breathless Leo comparisons — but not without a raised eyebrow at the ridiculousness of it all. His reaction to the idea of having fans hasn’t changed. “I never really expect anyone to like or watch or enjoy anything that I am in or do. I just don’t have that sort of expectation. Not even in, like, a self-deprecating way,” he tells me. But normie civilian activities are harder to pull off than they used to be. “There are definitely times when I’m like, ‘Ah, I wish I didn’t have to walk outside and worry about my privacy today.’” The only reason we’re even able to have our conversation in full public view uninterrupted is because we’re meeting after a photoshoot at 4 p.m. on a Thursday, and the Lower East Side restaurant where we’re talking is completely empty. Remembering that first fan encounter, “I look back and think: He had no idea what was coming.”

Because Briney does world-weary so well, you almost forget he can be a total goofball. Next week, Briney will star in Clashing Through the Snow, a Prime Video holiday rom-com in which he and Landman’s Michelle Randolph play rival employees at a downsizing publishing company who must race to secure the handwritten manuscript of a memoir from a pop star (Julia Fox) to avoid getting laid off. Full of the genre tropes that are somehow only more delightful the farther away you spot them coming — gasp! Enemies-to-lovers in forced proximity! — it arrives for the express purpose of being watched on a 56-inch television by families that are too full and overstimulated to talk to each other but nonetheless want more tryptophan-lulled togetherness. And for Briney, playing a jerky-eating, protein-obsessed wellness bro named Ryan was too much fun to pass up.

“When I met with the director and talked to some producers, they were ready to emphasize, and at least work to find, the comedy of it,” he says. “I don’t know if I would have done it if it were the other way around, where they were like, ‘Yeah, it’s kind of funny at times, but that’s not about you — your story is the romance.’” He recalls filming a scene with NBA stars Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby (cameoing as themselves), in which the athletes bluntly riffed about how annoying Briney’s character is, and how it sent him to actor-nerd heaven. “It made me really happy because I was like, ‘Yesss, you’re down to play!’” he says. “It’s all about making a fool of yourself.”
“I don’t really want someone to send me a tweet about me — unless it’s funny.”

For some actors in Briney’s cohort, you get the sense that they’d scrub the lighter fare of their early career off their IMDb in an instant if they could. That’s not the case with Briney. Those streaming projects fill the void of the midbudget romantic comedies that Hollywood studios used to make, which were essential training grounds in the leading-man ecosystem. You don’t get Matthew McConaughey in Dallas Buyers Club without Matthew McConaughey in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days.

Briney’s only real concern coming out of a show like The Summer I Turned Pretty was being pigeonholed. And he indeed gets plenty of offers to play more overburdened young men transformed by love. “If you do something that does well, everybody wants you to do that again, and you get a lot of offers to do that again somewhere else,” he says. Clashing Through the Snow and its stupid-fun physical comedy is a way around typecasting. But he also seems to be having a wink at his floppy-haired sensitive-boy status, playing Aaron “your hair looks sexy pushed back” Samuels in the 2024 musical Mean Girls movie or a Harry Stylesian rock star on the final season of Hacks. With a French goatee and see-through shirt buttons undone to expose the bad chest tattoo covering one nipple, his character tried to woo Jean Smart’s Deborah Vance — only to have his heart bruised when she calls the paparazzi on their date for publicity, unable to look past his teen-idol star wattage to notice, you know, his actual feelings.

Not that he would put that fine a point on it. “I was like, ‘I’d do anything for Hacks.’ I mean, are you kidding me? Like, this show?” he says. Who wouldn’t want to soak up the brilliance of Jean Smart? “She was wonderful. We got to spend some time between scenes, just chatting — truly a lovely human. I’m grateful that she was willing to spend the time. She didn’t have to, you know? I mean, she owed me nothing.”
“There are definitely times when I’m like, ‘Ah, I wish I didn’t have to walk outside and worry about my privacy today.’”

If anything, Briney wonders sometimes if the success of The Summer I Turned Pretty lifted him to these kinds of opportunities a little too quickly. “I think it’s something that frustrates me with the industry as a whole, but it also benefits me greatly: If people see you in something that does well, they look at you longer, and they’re more willing to hear you out,” he says. “It’s a really rough industry, and the truth is, people making these decisions put so much merit in marketability, if you will. I would argue that the emphasis should be talent, but that’s not really how the world works, unfortunately.”

In September, Briney went to the Toronto International Film Festival to premiere The Julia Set, a coming-of-age drama about a promising mathlete starring Chase Infiniti and Briney as her tutor. “That’s one of the ones where I’m like, ‘I don’t know if I ever could have been in that if it weren’t for the things that came before,’” he says. (Sony Pictures Classics acquired the film, with a U.S. release reportedly planned for 2027.) “I think I could have delivered a performance in it, as any actor with an ego would say to you. But even for a movie that is closer to indie than it is anything else, it’s just hard to get in any room. I’d like to think in some other universe that could have been the first thing I ever did, but I just don’t know if that’s true.” He pauses to think some more. “I don’t know.”

You start to understand Briney’s bafflement at this level of notoriety when you hear him recount the time the universe seemed to slam the door in his face. Briney grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his former-actor parents had decamped after giving up the vocation to raise their two children. They were supportive of any and all of his interests: For a brief moment in his teens, Briney was basically living out the plot of High School Musical, as the junior varsity baseball player who was also auditioning for the school play. But after a summer theater intensive at Wesleyan University, he knew in his bones he was going to do this professionally. “I started applying to only the best theater programs in the country,” he recalls, “which was a stupid idea.”

Why? “Because I didn’t get in anywhere,” he grins. Twelve out of the 13 schools he’d applied to rejected him, including New York University, which he thought was a slam dunk because of the sheer number of acting programs it offered. “I was like, ‘Oh, I’m definitely going to be in one of them,’” he says. “Then I got rejected from NYU, and I remember crying in my car after school.”

He supposes now it was useful practice. “It was maybe a good thing because there’s a lot of rejection in this career, and a lot of people a lot better than me are dealing with more rejection than I have, but still, at any stage, it was a lot of nos,” Briney says. He ended up getting off the waitlist at Pace University, which he calls “one of the best things that’s ever happened for many, many reasons.” It’s where he met his girlfriend, actor Isabel Machado, and some of his closest friends and also got really into the work of director Paul Schrader. (At no point in our conversation is he more animated than discussing Schrader’s classic tome, Transcendental Style in Film: “I could talk about that for a while!”) The school’s emphasis on making a living in a fickle business also resonated with Briney.
“They waited for my heart rate to drop, because they were afraid I got COVID. I was like, ‘No, guys, I just got good news!’”

“The way they always pitched it to us was like, ‘We have nothing but respect for theater programs. We have nothing but respect for the ‘best’ schools’ — you know, like Juilliard and Carnegie and all these things. Like, they’re great programs. But ‘this is acting for acting that pays’ was sort of what our teacher said,” Briney recalls. Film and TV and theater, yes, but also voiceover work and commercials. “They were like, ‘This is what we found, and what we think will help you book jobs in the field.’ And it was never ignorant to training. It was never ignorant to the work that is needed as an actor, but it was practical in a way — as practical as pursuing an art can be.”

Briney graduated in 2020, not exactly a great time for anyone, actor or not, to enter the job market. At one point, two of his roommates caught COVID, so he and another friend partook in a New York City Department of Health program that put people up in hotel rooms if they’d been exposed to someone who had the virus. They thought they were getting something resembling a staycation. Far from it. “It was absolutely awful. They don’t let you out of your room. They bring you food like prison meals twice a day,” he recalls. “No hate to New York public workers. They’re doing God’s work, truly. But I was expecting Cancun resort. We brought a bunch of booze — they took it all. My friend brought his knitting needles — they took them. They took every sharp object.”

But this was where, in between the daily mandatory vital checks, Briney found out that he’d booked his first real job, as Salvador Dalí’s assistant in Dalíland, directed by American Psycho filmmaker Mary Harron. “I couldn’t get my heart rate under 100, so I had to sit on the floor for 30 minutes while they waited for my heart rate to drop, because they were afraid I got COVID,” Briney says. “I was like, ‘No, guys, I just got good news!’”

It got better: He’d be spending a few months filming in England and starring opposite Oscar winner Ben Kingsley. “I was like, ‘You’re flying me to Liverpool? Like, you’re paying for the plane for me to go there? And you’re paying for my housing while I’m there? And I’m working with an Academy Award winner? And all of these really acclaimed people?’ It just blew my mind.”

Occasionally, his gratitude gave way to self-doubt. Once, while standing next to Kingsley in between takes, Briney blurted out that he was nervous about a scene. “I was sort of apologetic for my presence, which I always am,” he says. But instead of coldly staring him down, Kingsley — about to perform a scene in which he delivers a speech in Catalan — replied that so was he. Even towering thespians like Kingsley could experience something as human as jitters in this job. “It was nice to know I wasn’t alone in that, because I felt like I was the green one — I’m the kid here who doesn’t know what he’s doing,” he says. “It was a moment of ‘Oh! None of us know what we’re doing. We’re all figuring it out.’ It settled me a little bit.”

While he was filming Dalíland, Briney booked The Summer I Turned Pretty, which he approached with the same psyched-to-be-employed energy as his last job. “At the time, I was just like, ‘Oh, what an interesting role! What an opportunity to do a TV show!’” He says he wasn’t fully aware of the fandom around Jenny Han projects like Netflix’s To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before (or their crush-minting powers). That Amazon had greenlit the show with a straight-to-series order and renewed it for a second season before the first one even dropped also went over his head. “That should have been a little note to me: Hey, people might actually watch this,” he says. “But I had no idea. I had no clue of the scope.”

Briney says the cast has mostly let each other process the mind-f*ck of its popularity on their own. “I don’t really want someone to send me a tweet about me — unless it’s funny,” he says. “We don’t have that many conversations. Honestly, now that I think about it, Sean [Kaufman, who plays Belly’s brother] — who’s a very close friend of mine — we’re just boys, you know? We just play video games and talk about them and get mad at baseball.”
“I never expect anyone to like or watch or enjoy anything that I am in or do. I just don’t have that expectation. Not even in a self-deprecating way.”

The story isn’t over yet: After the final season dropped, Prime Video announced an upcoming feature-length The Summer I Turned Pretty film, which filmed this year and will serve as the series’ true conclusion. (Briney is a vault on the topic: “I’d get in trouble,” he says. “I’m not really allowed to talk about it. The truth is, I don’t know a lot about it. Like, I don’t know when they want to put it out.”) But as his career has gotten bigger, Briney seems intent on keeping the rest of his life as close to himself as he can, holding onto it exactly as it was. “I’ve intentionally put more of an emphasis on my own privacy and knowing that there are things in my life that I like to keep to myself, and for myself,” he says. “I think I’ve just spent more time with the people in my life that mean a lot to me.”

Briney paints a picture of filming Season 1 in North Carolina, “before we took it for granted.” The housing complex where members of the cast were staying had swimming pools and billiards tables where they’d spend their down hours. “Sean and I played a lot of Wiffle ball, just in the park, and all these things that would require sort of extra carefulness [if we did them now],” he says. “It was like going to college again in a way. When you get there, you’re like, ‘What do you mean I can do whatever I want?’”
I start to ask if he ever thinks about that innocent, pre-fame version of himself, and he answers without hesitation: “Every day.”
