items.title: Inside Amanvari, Aman’s extraordinary new Baja California hideaway
items.description: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally sm
items.author: Lindsay Cohn
paragraphs: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally small, with privacy, serenity and connection to nature of equal importance. The landscape drives the design, acting as both the inspiration and the backdrop for a place so at home in its surroundings it feels as though the land and sea might have given permission to build it.

Set within the exclusive Costa Palmas community on Baja California’s East Cape, Amanvari is positioned to escape it all. Aside from Four Seasons Resort Los Cabos at Costa Palmas, a 10-minute drive away, there’s not much around. And that’s exactly the point. The property is wrapped in nature, removed from tourist-trodden Cabo San Lucas, but accessible enough to venture to a buzzy restaurant or bar should the mood strike – though, speaking from personal experience, you’re not going to want to leave the premises, aside from, perhaps, a day trip snorkelling the ancient coral reefs of Cabo Pulmo National Marine Park or an off-road expedition into the Sierra de la Laguna.

The Baja California landscape – soft sand extending into the deep blue Sea of Cortez, swaying palms, towering cardón cacti, arid desert, an estuary and distant mountains – inspired Elastic Architects’ design. The award-winning firm, with initial contributions from Heah & Co., used local elements, embraced minimalism and spotlighted artistic expression – from contemporary Mexican art to ancestral crafts – to create an indoor-outdoor sanctuary with a deep sense of place.

At the heart of the resort is Casa Grande, an open-plan, atrium-like structure perfectly balanced by a restrained neutral palette with views of the ever-changing sky throughout the day and night. It’s also home to one of Amanvari’s most impressive commissions: an intricate, textured dome, inspired by the spiral chambers of an extinct marine microfossil, which took artists Abi and Luisa Calvete of Extra Neutro more than 1,000 hours to create.

To the left, the curved lounge bar is enveloped in earthy materials, still water and rounded edges, fostering a sense of softness and serenity that’s matched by sweeping Baja vistas. Descend the spiral staircase down to the lower level for the panoramic main pool crafted from Caledonia Black granite as well as three dining venues that follow the same nature-led principles.
Amanvari has 18 stilted casitas, which almost appear to float above the trees.

Contemporary rooms are anchored by white concrete, natural limestone and tropical hardwoods, complemented by bespoke furnishings, textiles in sandy hues and original works by Mexican artisans such as exclusive mixed-media pieces by Arozarena de la Fuente and sculptural ceramics by Tomás Díaz of Disciplina Studio.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
The alfresco living spaces are an extension of the interiors – generous terraces with seating areas for morning coffee, and below, heated pools and outdoor showers.

While all the accommodations are striking, the most soul-stirring views are found in those facing the estuary or situated directly on the sand. I stayed in Casita #4, a short stroll down the path from Casa Grande.

Entering through the large wooden door into the courtyard and through the floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors, the sightlines of the inlet extend, unobstructed to the generous, second-floor terrace, an extension of the white-and-wood interiors.

Below, the heated pool and outdoor shower served as a private holiday haven, an even quieter respite, devoid of other guests (not that I saw many during my stay), where the only sounds were the fish frolicking in the water and the birds chirping.

Back inside, clever choices such as thoughtfully positioned beds and a television that rises and hides at the touch of a button reinforce the idea that the best thing to watch is the outdoors. The bathrooms feature dual limestone vanities on either side, Vermont Beige marble floors and walls, a spacious shower and a soaking tub for the ultimate unwinding experience.
Staying for drinks and dinner?

The curved, open-air lounge bar, which faces the waves on one side and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains on the other, is the place for pre-dinner drinks (I recommend the Bartolo, a clarified concoction of raicilla, mango and habanero) with a soundtrack of soulful live saxophone and the gentle crash of the waves.

Sesui is a sleek Japanese concept, centred around a 10-seat wood counter, illuminated by loofah lanterns the shape of sea urchins. It’s here that Chef Masao Matsubara prepares his ever-changing omakase, spotlighting the culinary conversation between Japan and Baja California. When I dined, highlights included a stunning mix of raw oyster with uni and caviar, dashi broth with shrimp, tempura and nigiri.

Arva, the Italian restaurant, offers seating in the elegant dining room, complete with a full-wall temperature-controlled wine display, and on the fire-warmed terrace below the stars. The menu highlights seasonal produce in dishes such as heirloom tomato and burrata salad, yellowtail crisp with caviar and orange, linguine with clams and fresh catch of the day.
For something more casual, Luma, pairs coastal-influenced Mexican cuisine with an laid-back beachfront setting.

The entire resort. From the moment the car turns down the gravel drive, a sense of calm washes over. Of course, it’s not just the peaceful atmosphere that allows guests to switch off but the thoughtful amenities and services geared towards unwinding.

If you really want to relax, first head to the 600-square-meter Aman Spa, a sanctuary of wellness that leans into ancestral healing traditions from Mexico and across Asia (Aman originated in Phuket, Thailand). Facilities include a stunning white temazcal (sweat lodge) and hydrotherapy houses. Treatments range from purifying facials and body wraps to the signature Desert Damiana, a healing journey that combines reflexology, stretching and an aromatic oil massage that took the post-flight tension straight out of me.

There’s also a 24-hour fitness centre kitted out with the latest Technogym equipment, a movement studio and a yoga pavilion. Though, I would recommend joining the sunrise sessions by the gorgeous pool for a chance to flow with the soundtrack

The service goes above and beyond. Snacks, cold water and Starlink Wi-Fi in the car from the airport. An umbrella to block the midday sun when I emerged from the car. Fresh herb bouquets upon first touring the spa. Pre-breakfast coffee service available on your private terrace. Returning from paddle boarding to find a glass of ice-cold water alongside a tray of sun care essentials beside my beach lounger. Knowledge of my food allergies at every F&B outlet on the property without me having to say it. A personalised WhatsApp group for any additional requests.

Amanvari’s nature-led architecture and exceptional service make it a compelling destination for a restorative escape. If you’re looking for a true escape, a place that welcomes stillness but doesn’t demand solitude, a reset complete with spa treatments, delicious food and an unhurried pace, it’s worth every peso.
Amanvari, Eureka s/n esquina con Sta Maria la Ribera, La Ribera, 23570 Baja California Sur, Mexico

Lindsay Cohn is a freelance travel journalist with a decade of experience writing, editing and jet-setting, and bylines in Vogue, Travel + Leisure, W Mag, Bloomberg, Galerie, and more. In between trips to sunny islands, cobbled villages and bustling cities, you can find her in Los Angeles with her husband and two sons.

items.title: Inside the design of Panem, the dystopian world of The Hunger Games
items.description: The world of Panem is returning to the big screen with Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Directed by Francis Lawrence and based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel, the film takes us back 22 years before Katniss Everdeen’s story. So how do you reimagine the vis
items.author: Annabel Downes
paragraphs: The world of Panem is returning to the big screen with Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Directed by Francis Lawrence and based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel, the film takes us back 22 years before Katniss Everdeen’s story. So how do you reimagine the visual world of one of cinema’s biggest franchises though a 1970s lens? From the brutalist architecture of the Capitol to the deadly beauty of the arena, production designer Uli Hanisch, whose previous credits include The Queen’s Gambit (2020) and Babylon Berlin (2017), reveals how Panem’s latest incarnation came to life.
Wallpaper*: First of all, could you explain the role of a production designer?

Uli: A production designer does for film what a stage designer does for theatre. Essentially, the role is about world-building. We’re responsible for visualising the world in which the story takes place. Whether that means scouting locations or designing sets, it’s about giving that world a visual expression.
Wallpaper*: And what was it about this world that excited you?

I think it’s important to have the film we did before, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), in mind. That was set 70 years before the original films, and 20 before this one. For me, it was the initial step into exploring this kind of fictional period in a fictional world, which is based on our world but slightly different. Usually, you either have a purely invented world or a period world, but here you have a mix of both, which makes it very unique. What I found interesting when working on that film was that, even though these films are meant to be futuristic, they’re actually quite contemporary. They have futuristic elements, like the hovercraft, but much of the world is recognisable.
Wallpaper*: How did that influence your approach to the architecture and design of Panem?

We thought, why not compare Panem’s history with our own? Going back 70 years takes us to the middle of the 20th century, with the Capitol 15 years after a war. So we started looking at Berlin and what it was like 15 years after the Second World War, with its mix of architecture from the Prussian Empire, Nazi Germany, and the Soviet Union. And all that mixed together was a really strong foothold for imagining Panem’s society and its architecture.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Wallpaper*: How did you take those influences forward for this film, set 20 years later?

We simply moved forward 20 years and arrived in the 1970s. So the question became: what makes the architecture and style of that period interesting? How can we use it to tell the story in the right way? And what could we add to Berlin? We also realised that, because of Berlin’s political history, there’s a lot of architecture from that period in the city.
Wallpaper*: And when you discussed this with Francis [Lawrence, the director], what was it about the ‘70s aesthetic that you wanted to draw inspiration from?

Well, I think the first questions we had to ask ourselves were: what do we like about the ‘70s? Why choose this period, and what does it mean? It should never be purely for visual reasons. There has to be a storytelling reason behind it. When we think of the ‘70s in the Western world, we tend to have these hippie-esque, progressive images in our mind. But society at the time was also very adult, conservative, self conscious and wealthy, almost arrogantly so. It was before the economy started to decline and before environmental issues were taken seriously. Cars were enormous, everything was big, strong, and heavy, and there was this sense of being untouchable. That’s what we wanted to translate into Panem: a society at the peak of its power and arrogance, believing itself to be untouchable.
Wallpaper*: So how did you translate those ideas into the film’s design?

We wanted to build on that idea with the arena which is described as overwhelmingly beautiful, but also deadly, poisoned, really evil and mean at the same time. We then carried that contrast into the design of the Capitol. It looks really beautiful, but it’s not meant to be friendly. There’s something misleading about it, which is what propaganda is about in a way: we show you something, but we mean something else. It’s seductive and embracing, but that embrace can be deadly if you’re the wrong person or behave in the wrong way.
Wallpaper*: When you’re building a world like this, where do you start? Do you begin with sketches?

We start with conversations, establishing the overall concept and making decisions about the direction we want to take. I think that’s the most interesting part. Once we have the intention and the concept, we start researching. What’s interesting is that we’re drawing from the ‘70s but it’s not a period movie, so we have the freedom to decide what we take from that era and what we do differently. Something might be authentically ‘70s but not quite work for the world we’re creating. Through research, you gradually develop a sense of what feels right for the film. Then I work with two or three concept artists, because I’m a lousy illustrator myself. We sit down together and discuss what we want to create. In this case, we started with a wide shot of the arena, showing the valley and its landscape. I try to explain what I want to see and I imagine it all coming together.
Wallpaper*: And I understand that almost everything was shot on location, including the arena, which you filmed in Spain?

The entire arena was shot in Asturias, a very remote region of Spain. It took us a long time to find those locations, and we were really happy when we did. But it turned out to be an incredibly complicated decision because the area is so remote, almost inaccessible, with no hotels and infrastructure nearby. For a production of this size, that made things quite difficult at times.
Wallpaper*: How did you maintain visual continuity with the original films, particularly in places like District 12?

For District 12, we found a new location in western Germany, in this huge industrial area where I grew up. I actually shot my very first film there, at an abandoned steel mill that's since been turned into a public park. We'd been looking for locations around Berlin, but nothing was big or complex enough, so eventually I suggested showing Francis this place from my hometown. The beautiful thing is that we didn't really change anything. We added the stage in front of the Hall of Justice, but everything around it was already there. It was wonderful to come back home after all these years.
Wallpaper*: Was there a particular detail or set that you especially loved creating?

I loved all the ‘70s stuff we did for the Capitol, especially the apartment where the tributes stay. We turned it into this bizarre, over-the-top ‘70s space, with lots of colour and white fabrics. You have the tributes sitting on this circular sofa, talking about really serious things, surrounded by these screaming colours. There’s something quite funny about that contrast. It’s a bit silly but it’s meant to be.
Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is out now

items.title: Here's what to catch during Design Miami this year
items.description: As soon as America’s collective tryptophan hangover lifts post-Thanksgiving, the globe’s cultural cognoscenti make a beeline for Florida to attend North America’s largest confluence of art and design: Miami Art Week. The extravaganza, which takes place the fir
items.author: Anna Fixsen
paragraphs: As soon as America’s collective tryptophan hangover lifts post-Thanksgiving, the globe’s cultural cognoscenti make a beeline for Florida to attend North America’s largest confluence of art and design: Miami Art Week. The extravaganza, which takes place the first week of December, is centred primarily around two large international fairs in Miami Beach, Design Miami, an expo of global collectible design, and Art Basel Miami Beach, a major modern and contemporary art fair. Joining them are about 20 other international fairs, in addition to hundreds of events, exhibitions and installations taking place across the city. With so much to see – and so many hotspots at which to be seen – it’s easy to feel overwhelmed. Here are 10 things we’re looking forward to seeing this year, from the fair tents to the beach and beyond.

WHAT: Since it was founded in 2005, Design Miami has become the definitive destination to view collectible design en masse. Now in its 22nd edition, the fair’s influence has gone global, with satellites in Seoul, Paris and – beginning early next year – Dubai. That reach will be felt in the Miami Beach tent, with more than two dozen global galleries present. Highlights include an installation of modern tapestries by Boccara gallery; Lina Bo Bardi-designed furnishings presented by Espasso; and a fun presentation of designer-made mailboxes, courtesy AUTOBODY autobody.
WHERE: Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach, FL 33139

WHAT: Art Basel’s annual showing in Miami Beach is like the Super Bowl of the art world: big, expensive and a prime place to spy a celebrity or three. This year, more than 270 exhibitors from some 40 countries will congregate in the Miami Beach Convention Center, offering a dizzying array of modern and contemporary art up for grabs. If you go, be sure to catch Wallpaper* guest editor Carrie Mae Weems's latest photograph Seaside (1) at Gladstone’s booth; a surrealist garden complete with pearls and skeletons, courtesy Nina Johnson; and Zero 10, a platform devoted to digital art, featuring works by Studio DRIFT, Refik Anadol and Jon Rafman.
WHERE: Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Drive Miami Beach, FL 33139
3. Playboy's ‘Banned’ exhibition

WHAT: Have you heard? Playboy just snapped up the Freehand Miami, with plans to convert the hotel into a private members club. Before that happens, the media and hospitality company is launching a three-day Art Week ‘residency’ called, ‘Banned’, that will explore the idea of censorship through a host of artworks by Andy Warhol, Salvador Dalí and more. Because everyone just reads Playboy for the art, right?
WHERE: 1688 Jefferson Ave, Miami Beach, FL 33139
4. The Miami Design District Annual Design Commission

WHAT: The locus of Design Miami is, of course, the tent. But the fair’s annual Design District commission is a reminder that there’s so much to see beyond Miami Beach. This year, the site-specific installation will be by Objects of Common Interest, a New York- and Athens-based design firm founded by Eleni Petaloti and Leonidas Trampoukis. The duo have created a series of colourful, geometric sculptures with intriguing interactive elements. The totems, installed at various places throughout the tony shopping quarter, will rotate, reflect, emit sounds and even spout vapour. It’s little wonder Objects of Common Interest are calling the activation ‘Out of This World.’ WHEN: 1- 6 December 2026
WHERE: Miami Design District
5. Design Hotels x Play-Doh

WHAT: Miami Beach is basically one gigantic playground during Art Week, so why not channel your inner child? That’s precisely what Design Hotels and Play-Doh have in store at The Shelbourne by Proper. The brands have tapped glass artist Helle Mardahl to create a colourful, site-specific work inspired by the childhood classic modeling clay. Meanwhile, grown-ups can stop by the hotel to work with Play-Doh’s adult line, Blooms, to create Play-Doh flowers and bouquets.
WHERE: The Shelbourne by Proper, 1801 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139
6. 'These Arms of Mine' at the Historic Hampton House

WHAT: Many Art Week events happen in and around hotels, but The Hampton House Motel offers something extraordinary: history. The hotel, which first opened in 1954, had a spot in the Green Book, an essential guide for Black travelers since the mid 1930s, and became a refuge and hub for Black artists, musicians and Civil Rights leaders, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Ella Fitzgerald, Muhammad Ali, Malcolm X and Jackie Robinson. ‘These Arms of Mine,’ named in honour of hotel guest Otis Redding, is an exhibition that examines the body and artistic expressions of it. The show, curated by Zoe Luko and Meg Onli, will feature an extraordinary collection of works by El Anatsui, Felix Gonzalez Torres, Kerry James Marshall, David Hammons, Mickalene Thomas and many more.
WHEN: 1 December 2026 - 28 February 2027
WHERE: 4240 NW 27th Ave, Miami, FL 33142
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
7. Natalia Triantafylli at Villa Paula

WHAT: Villa Paula, the Miami home of gallery The Future Perfect, is another extraordinary venue to add to your list this Art Week. The century-old building, the former home of the Cuban Consul, offers intriguing juxtapositions in its ornate interiors and shaded gardens. Greek-born, London-based artist Natalia Triantafylli is taking over the villa for the first time with her bright ceramic works, which combine hand-sculpting and 3D printing. For this show, ‘Under the Libra Sun,’ Triantafylli will reveal her largest-scale works yet, including chandeliers, tables, and mirrors.
WHEN: Opening November 30, 2026
WHERE: 5811 N Miami Ave, Miami, FL 33127
8. Creative Time's Sandcastle competition

WHAT: Over the years, New York-based arts nonprofit Creative Time would host an artist’s sandcastle competition in Rockaway Beach, a contest in which creatives including Tom Sachs, Duke Riley, Snarkitecture battled it out in the sand. The organisation is dusting off the concept for Art Week on the Miami Edition’s beach. Participating artists for this version include local artist Emmet Moore, filmmaker Jillian Mayer, collage artist Theresa Chromati and sculptor Gabriel Rico. Wallpaper* US400 architect Rafael de Cárdenas, meanwhile, will be the judge. Amid a sea of ‘white cube’ exhibition space, it's the perfect opportunity for artists to get their hands dirty.
WHEN: 1 December, 2026, 2:30 to 4:30 PM
WHERE: The Miami Beach Edition, 2901 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140
9. Germane Barnes' 'Pull Up a Chair' at Untitled Art

WHAT: Can’t wait to see Germane Barnes curate the US Pavilion at the Venice Biennale next year? Catch him in Miami, where his practice, Studio Barnes, is revealing a brand new commission at Untitled Art. 'Pull Up a Chair' explores themes like Southern hospitality and public space by creating a communal seating arrangement in which fairgoers can sit down, rest their legs and, hopefully, discover something new about their neighbour.
WHERE: Untitled Art, Ocean Drive and 12th Street, Miami Beach, FL 33139
10. Reefline's beach ballet

WHAT: Reefline is a seven-mile underwater conservation-focused sculpture park off Miami Beach, masterplanned by OMA’s Shohei Shigematsu. For Art Week, Reefline is adding a new sculpture to its aqueous museum. It’s also going back to the land with a bound-to-be-gorgeous dance performance by Indian artist Subodh Kerkar in partnership with the Miami City Ballet. More than 50 dancers will float across the beach in a mesmerising array, movement that will explore the city’s relationship with its coastline.
WHEN: 1 December 2026, 4pm
WHERE: Beach at Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa, 4041 Collins Ave, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Anna Fixsen is a Brooklyn-based editor and journalist with 13 years of experience reporting on architecture, design, and the way we live. Before joining the Wallpaper* team as the US Editor, she was the Deputy Digital Editor of ELLE DECOR, where she oversaw all aspects of the magazine’s digital footprint.

items.title: AI WEIWEI - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger
paragraphs: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger

The Turbine Hall at London’s Tate Modern is one of the world’s most coveted exhibition spaces, and the next artist to fill it is Ai Weiwei. Although a veteran of major art events such as Documenta 12 and the 48th Venice Biennale, in his home country of China Ai Weiwei is as much known for his activism as he is for his aesthetics. Based in Beijing, where he is under constant surveillance, the artist brazenly flouts the law to bring his view on modern day China to the rest of the world. He is an avid user of fashionable social networking sites, and on an average day he tweets approximately 107 times.
From Fantastic Man n° 12 — 2010
“Okay, let’s start,” says the artist Ai Weiwei, greeting me with a wide smile.

It’s 9am on a sunny Beijing morning – so much for creative types sleeping late – and Ai Weiwei has already been up and at it for several hours. Given his reputation, I assume he’s been irritating the Chinese government and tickling his legions of followers by way of his famously acerbic Twitter feeds. (Consider: “The system doesn’t follow the law. The people don’t believe in the law. So who’s out of luck?”)

I have made what’s been called the ‘ritual pilgrimage’ to the compound Ai designed and built for himself in the city’s northeast outskirts. It’s a journey previously taken by the likes of Gerhard Schröder, Diane von Furstenberg and countless others who fancy themselves sophisticated and international. From the centre of town, you go past unremarkable high rises and light industry zones, beneath highway overpasses and railroad tracks and, finally, along a quiet, gingko-lined road. A blue metal door marks the entrance to Ai’s fabled home and studio, which he shares with his wife, the artist Lu Qing, and which these days also happens to be under surveillance by Chinese authorities.

Inside, the word FUCK is mounted on a garden wall in big neon letters. Otherwise, the scene is quite tranquil. Ai is sitting next to a pleasant, grassy lawn framed by cypress trees, antique stone fragments and thickets of bamboo. He’s accompanied by a member of his 30-or-so-person studio – a young woman, Germanic, I’d say, possibly Scandinavian – and several of his unconfirmed number of cats and dogs. (“We don’t really know how many we have,” he admits.) Ai has close-cropped hair, an unruly beard and an ample belly that together define what you might call the Ai Weiwei look. Wearing a periwinkle T-shirt and shorts, he politely leads me across a patio and into his loft-like, grey-brick home.
“That’s Du Du,” he starts off, catching me glancing at another free-roaming canine as we sit down at a huge wooden table.
“Yeah. And there’s Danny,” he adds, pointing to a female cocker spaniel. “We also have two of her children here.”
Ignoring his pet-naming decisions, I ask how his day is going.

“Normally, I give two interviews in the morning, but today I only have yours,” he says, continuing the small talk. Ai is known to be accessible. “Don’t hesitate to ask me anything you’d like,” he offers.

Ever since 2006, when the architect Jacques Herzog first insisted that I try to meet him – they had collaborated on the design of Beijing’s Bird’s Nest stadium, a project Ai later disavowed as a “fake smile” serving Communist propaganda – the Chinese artist, architect and dangerously outspoken activist has been a distant yet recurring motif in my life.

There he was, popping up at the architecture biennale in Venice and at exhibition openings in Beijing – always with an entourage and rarely without an assistant videotaping his every move. Once, I briefly interviewed him over a bowl of beef noodles. Another time, I visited his studio on a day I was told he wouldn’t be there, only to find him typing away at his computer.

Ai has a knack for being somewhere even when he isn’t. He infiltrates things. As part of a massive, high-concept exercise, he took over Documenta 12 in Kassel, Germany, in 2007 with no less than 1,001 ordinary Chinese whom he’d flown in for the occasion. Earlier this year, he helped organise a protest march on a highly symbolic thoroughfare in central Beijing. The demonstration was totally unauthorised and quickly halted by police, but at least one Communist Party newspaper covered it – and guess whose name was on the photo credit?

Ai, 53, is a conceptual artist who’s become known for his activism and an activist whose provocations verge on art. He named his studio Fake Design, but it’s really his life that his art imitates, and the other way around. This October, Ai will become the latest artist to transform London’s Tate Modern as part of the museum’s blockbuster series of Turbine Hall installations. For many, he’s the godfather of contemporary Chinese art, the man – no, the concept – around which an intriguing image of China begins to emerge.

So who, or what, exactly is Ai Weiwei? A figure of controversy in his home country, for a start. “In China, the newspapers and magazines used to report on me a lot – but mostly fashion publications,” he tells me. (I kid you not: as I write this, a friend has stopped by my home, randomly wearing a Comme Des Garçons T-shirt emblazoned with a watermelon and the words THANKS TO AI WEIWEI.)

“People on the internet have seen me on CCTV” – the Chinese state television network – “and said, ‘Weiwei, what the fuck? You’re on CCTV,’” he says. “Maybe they’re using old programmes, but it’s a big joke because I’ve been censored by them. Officially, they cannot mention my name.” Programmes must sometimes slip through the cracks.
What about the Tate installation? What are you doing for that?
“I really can’t talk about it; they even asked me not to talk to you in particular about this.”
So now you’re being censored by the Tate?
“Partially,” he says with an ironic chuckle.

The proper way to address Ai Weiwei is, in fact, Ai. The Chinese place their surnames first; his is pronounced like ‘eye’. But mostly, Weiwei (‘way-way’), as many call him, is an enigmatic yet omnipresent abstraction, an iconoclastic artist and philosopher whose contours are hard to grasp. He works in a range of media, from sculpture, installations and photography to architecture, film and, for lack of a better word, “actions”, while at various times moonlighting as an antiques trader, gallerist and curator. Until recently, he was also the proprietor of Qu Nar (“Go Where?”), a restaurant specialising in the cuisine of Zhejiang province, at which he frequently held court before it was demolished to make way for a new development last year.

As for his art, Ai is unapologetically irreverent and sardonic. He can be seen flipping his finger at the White House and Eiffel Tower in his well-known Study of Perspective photographs, and he has painted the Coca-Cola logo on ancient pots. All the while, his work often relies on earlier wreckage, the kind of creative destruction that defines China’s contemporary crossroads. There’s Dropping a Han Dynasty Urn (1995), a photographic triptych in which he smashes a 2,000-year-old vase. And Map of China (2003), a hulking, geographically correct sculpture made of wood salvaged from demolished Qing dynasty temples. Ai hits a nerve shared by Chinese and non-Chinese alike. As the artist later puts it: “What does ‘China’ mean?”

Nowadays, however, the more pressing question may be just how far he can push the Chinese authorities. Ai has become a gigantic thorn for the powers that be, a vocal critic of the government – for its corruption, human rights shortcomings and other injustices – in a country where life has been known to get difficult for vocal government critics. He doesn’t go about it quietly and misses few opportunities to act or speak out. During our first interview, he tells me how one week earlier, he’d driven into the mountains to rescue an activist who he says was abandoned there after being beaten by secret police. “He announced it on Twitter, said he didn’t know where he was,” Ai says of the man, an advocate for migrant workers. “We had to go out and find him.”
Then, during our second meeting, he’s interrupted by a phone call. “That was the people from the earthquake area,” he says. “They’re still calling me.”

‘The earthquake’ refers to Ai’s biggest cause to date – more specifically, the thousands of children who died in the 7.9-magnitude tremor that roiled China’s Sichuan province in May 2008. Most of the area’s young perished when their schools collapsed, as a result of shoddy construction that was widely attributed to the negligence and corruption of local officials. Fearing the ensuing outcry, the government silenced protests and failed to produce the names, or even a tally, of the victims.

In response, Ai sent an army of volunteers to the region to help fill the gap. The list they produced grew to more than 5,200 names. Even two years later, Ai daily sends out the names of the victims via Twitter on their birthdays. (Twitter is technically blocked in China, though that’s easy to get around.) For a recent exhibition, he covered the façade of Munich’s Haus der Kunst with 9,000 coloured backpacks forming a quote in Chinese characters taken from one of the children’s mothers. He’s flung open his doors to the press while producing documentaries about the tragedy; they are part of a series tackling a range of issues. “We’ve sent probably 50 or 60 thousand documentaries out on DVD for free,” Ai says, “though millions have seen them on the internet.”

Last year, Chinese censors shut down the popular blog Ai had started writing in 2005. “We had maybe over 50 million readers,” he laments. Meanwhile, he says his email accounts have been hacked, his bank accounts investigated, and his home staked out by mysterious men in parked cars; the latter have since been replaced by closed-circuit cameras.

“The machines are much friendlier,” he says, nodding toward a pair of surveillance cameras, mounted on telephone poles that are aimed at his front gate. “Before that, the guys waiting outside weren’t so nice.” (Even as a mark, Ai is a true gentleman, having once asked his surveillants if they might like some water. When they reacted poorly, he called the police on them.)

If it sounds like Ai is flirting with martyrdom, he’s got the scars to prove it: two of them, on the right side of his head. In August 2009, Ai was in the Sichuanese capital of Chengdu to attend the trial of a fellow earthquake activist when police broke into his room at the Anyi Hotel. It was the middle of the night, and according to Ai, he was roughed up and suffered a blunt blow to the head. A month later, surgeons in Germany had to drill holes in his skull to relieve the pressure from a serious brain haemorrhage.

“It was very dangerous; the doctor said he sees this level of severity, so much blood in the brain, maybe only once every three years,” says the artist, who was in Munich preparing his Haus der Kunst exhibition when the injury was discovered. “If we waited just one day longer, I may have lost my life.” He pauses. “So life is very fragile.”

In fact, Ai learned that lesson early on. His father, Ai Qing, was one of China’s most revered poets. And to understand what happened to him requires placing him in the context of 20th-century Chinese history – which, to put it simply, was a mess. Having first been imprisoned by the Nationalist Party for his leftist sympathies, the elder Ai was later denounced as a “rightist” by the communists. Which, to continue the ideological wheel spinning, was basically an unfounded accusation stemming from the madness of a reactionary purge.

What followed was more than a decade of exile, first to Manchuria and then the remoter Xinjiang region. Ai Qing was relegated to cleaning public toilets, while the family, which also included Ai’s mother and younger brother, had to scavenge for food. During the Cultural Revolution, things got worse: Ai Qing was pelted with stones and, to add to the cruel humiliation, had ink poured over his face. “He couldn’t wash it off, since we didn’t even have soap,” says Ai, who laboured making bricks and working the fields, starting at age ten. “I would have to go out and shit, you know, because there’s no bathroom. And then you look at the sky and you see it’s just yourself there in the desert.”

“My strongest influence on me is my earlier life,” he goes on. “The conditions we were in, how my father was treated, my family facing such insults and punishment. You know, I never believed in the system, and it seems I always had the most sympathy for the weak.”

Much of his art might tap into the suspicions among some of his compatriots that Ai is somehow anti-China. I ask him if he is. “You know, if somebody is critical, the Chinese government always blames it on some kind of anti-China, foreign force,” he says. “So I jump on the internet and say, yeah, I’m anti-China.”
But is he really anti-China? Like, anti-all-of-it?

He thinks for a moment. “I am anti-China. I’m more anti-China than anti-Communist. What’s the big deal?” he says, without losing his cool. “What does ‘China’ mean? Is it the history, the values, the people? What’s the problem with being an individual who’s anti-China, or any other place? This is your own individual position.” Clearly, Ai is not wholly anti-history, anti-values or anti-people, with regard to China or otherwise. He’s obviously quite the opposite. If he is anti-China, it depends on how you define China. But in my mind, Ai is simply anti-being-told-what-to-think-and-do.

After all, he’s exhibited a rebellious streak from the get-go, both in China and the West. Cut to New York, 1981. Ai, now in his mid-20s, has moved into a tiny hovel in the East Village. Back in China, Chairman Mao has died and the Cultural Revolution is over; Ai’s father has been rehabilitated and the family is back in Beijing. Alone in New York, after stops in Philadelphia and Berkeley, Ai soaks up Manhattan’s bohemian vibe. He enrols in Parsons School of Design, drops out, makes art and befriends Allen Ginsberg. He supports himself with odd jobs; in fact, he seems made for New York.

There, he took an interest in gay rights and the Aids epidemic and demonstrated against the first Gulf War. In 1988, in an effort to clean up seedy Tompkins Square Park, the New York City police instituted a curfew. The protests that followed were met by police brutality, and Ai was there to catch it on film. “We took some photos and sent them to the American Civil Liberties Union, got some police dismissed,” he recalls. To his list of occupational titles, one might add photojournalist: while in New York, Ai sold pictures to The New York Times, the New York Daily News and Newsweek.

It’s a little unnerving when Ai points his camera at you, totally without warning. In my experience, it usually happens when you’re talking, in mid-sentence. First, he casually lifts his camera or phone. Then he slyly squints – act natural, you tell yourself, and keep talking – before bringing the lens up close in a way no one besides your dermatologist should do. It’s as if he’s reminding you that he’s watching you as carefully as you are him. Or perhaps it’s his way of bringing you into his orbit; without realising it, you’ve become part of the Ai Weiwei show, a co-conspirator.

Pictures rarely lie. Or at least that’s my explanation for Ai’s obsession with documentation. He makes a point of leaving a paper trail, filing police reports when they’ll likely get him nowhere and invoking China’s equivalent of the Freedom of Information Act knowing full well that a response won’t be coming anytime soon. His first blog posts were like a Warholian scrapbook, filled with images of the minutiae of his life alongside nearly everyone he’d come in contact with. Unlike many others with strong beliefs, Ai has a remarkable capacity for self-reflection. At one point, he tells me the Chinese saying he wants on his tombstone: ‘He was the perfect example of the defects of his time.’

In short, Ai embraces transparency; it’s like he’s on a perpetual fact-finding mission while wanting to prove he has nothing to hide. Yet he also plays with truth. Besides calling his studio Fake Design, he’s made mutant furniture from real antiques, and faux objects (watermelons, sunflower seeds) using only the most authentic craftsmanship (and the former imperial porcelain kilns in Jingdezhen).

At the last Documenta, Ai built a monumental outdoor sculpture from antique wooden windows; a storm unexpectedly sent it crashing down. Two years later, while visiting one of his workshops, I saw the piece being reconstructed – this time in its collapsed state, as if it was always supposed to be that way. “I’m constantly dealing with people’s perception of what is real, what is fake, how we make our value judgment,” he says.
Ai wakes up around 6.30 or 7 in the morning. He spends about four hours working at the computer and receiving the unending stream of museum groups, journalists and others who come by.

Afterwards, he’ll have lunch – he has a penchant for noodles – and work with his studio on its various projects. In the afternoon, he’ll spend time with his only child, a toddler son he fathered with a filmmaker from one of his documentaries. “Then maybe I’ll handle other issues, call friends and have dinner, discuss some matters, you know, have a little bit of a social life,” he says. “Afterwards I’ll come back, jump back to the computer for another four hours or more. So that’s a day.” It sounds oddly prosaic.

In fact, Ai has a funny habit of repeating a phrase that goes something like this: “I had nothing else do to.” He deploys it to explain nearly every turn of his life – such as everything he got up to during his years in New York. (“Basically, I had nothing to do,” he shrugs.) And when he returned to China in 1993, after his father took ill, and started dealing antiques while continuing with his art. (“There was nothing else to do.”) And when, four years after his father died, he built his current home so that he could move out of his mother’s. (“She was annoyed, because I had nothing to do.”)

When he says he had nothing to do, it’s as if Ai is excusing himself for doing whatever he’s done, and has done it despite himself. He says it with humility, and perhaps there are fatalistic tendencies at work: “Life is unpredictable and has unexpected effects,” he emails me at one point. It helps explain his vulnerability to distractions – say, an activist who’s been stranded by the police in the mountains and needs to be saved. But maybe it’s also his way of defusing the criticism that he can seem like a celebrity artist, that he’s a bit overeager to give his audiences what they expect and want.

Therein may lie the biggest irony. If one takes him at his word, Ai has never wanted to be known as a Chinese artist per se. “In the ’80s, when Allen Ginsberg read me his poetry, and I showed him my portfolio, he said, ‘Weiwei, I can’t think of a gallery that wants to show Chinese artists’ work,’” Ai recalls. “At that time, it bothered me. I said, ‘Allen, I don’t think of you as an American poet. You’re just a poet.’”

What’s more, Ai is a champion of what he considers to be universal values. “The only thing I would not accept is regional thinking, because with today’s globalisation and the internet, the world is completely different,” he emails me.

But at the same time, Ai’s resonance depends in large measure on the extent to which he mirrors one’s feelings about China. While few question his integrity, his critics sometimes find him too quick to judge an evolving system that, given the long arc of history, has made dizzyingly rapid strides. On the other hand, his supporters see him as a voice for the underdog, a much-needed reality check for a nation at risk of complacency, of being blinded by its current success.

For some, there’s also the otherness factor. That is to say, he feeds into fears about a rising power they don’t fully understand. When Ai brought those 1,001 Chinese people to Documenta, he tapped into the West’s anxieties about being overrun by the Eastern giant. However, “My intention was focused on the 1,001 people and how this would affect their lives,” he says. “Any work, especially one related to worlds as different as China and the West, can carry completely different, even contradictory, meanings. And in general, people can only approach the surface; this is very normal.”

For him, he says, the piece was more about the process of making it, which included everything from an open call on the internet to securing passports for participants from Chinese minority groups who didn’t have last names. Referencing Kassel’s status as home of the Brothers Grimm, he called the experiment Fairytale.

That said, how Ai’s own story will turn out is impossible to predict. “I can’t answer why the government still hasn’t put me in jail, but I’m ready to face it,” he says, laughing nervously. “I would encourage them to not put me in jail. But I have to be prepared.”
Theories abound as to why Ai has so far avoided imprisonment. One explanation goes that, while he criticises the government, he doesn’t cross the line of questioning its legitimacy.
“That’s wrong,” he shoots back. “From the very beginning I questioned the legitimacy of the Communist Party, though I don’t have to say it all the time.”
Some people say he’s protected by his family background.
“That’s underestimating the system. Look what happened to my father, so what’s that background for?”
Maybe it’s that he’s too established.
“Throughout Chinese history, even those in the highest positions could be punished.”

At one point, I wonder if it’s because he’s avoided hyper-touchy subjects like Tibet. But then he tells me about the meeting, albeit back in 1989, that he had with the Dalai Lama. (“He liked my beard.”) So the most obvious answer, I think, would also help explain why he’s talking to me: in effect, he’s shielded by the international media.
“Could be. But I don’t know, maybe that’s also an illusion. No one’s that influential.”

He’s probably right. Overestimating yourself is risky, since finding your limits often means it’s already too late. But Ai seems fearless, or at least brave enough to face fear. And then he says something that sounds truly hard to believe, at least coming from him: “You know, people forget you from one minute to the next.”

Ai Weiwei first exhibited in 1979, as part of a group show in Beijing called The Stars. Although the show barely happened, due to the authorities shutting it down prematurely, it was a momentous occasion: the first time that experimental artists had dared to exhibit in 30 years of communist rule. The Stars group managed to exhibit a second time in 1980. Many see The Stars as having laid the groundwork for what became the contemporary Chinese art scene. Thirty years later, Ai has yet to be the subject of a retrospective at any major international art institution; his Tate Modern commission is possibly his biggest project in the West yet. As with previous Turbine Hall exhibitors like Carsten Höller, Olafur Eliasson and Louise Bourgeois, nothing about the installation will be revealed until the opening day, on 12 October 2010.

items.title: NOWNESS - Nowness Shorts: Der Mann und sein Haus
items.description: Constructing a celebration of stillness and the cinematic form, Indian-born filmmaker Kriti Dale explores the act of being present by stripping life to its essentials for the short film Der Mann und sein Haus – translated as The Man and His House.
paragraphs: Constructing a celebration of stillness and the cinematic form, Indian-born filmmaker Kriti Dale explores the act of being present by stripping life to its essentials for the short film Der Mann und sein Haus – translated as The Man and His House.

Through the life of 70-year-old Chi-Gong teacher Lambert in Uckermark, North Eastern Germany, the film presents a visual essay on self-sufficiency as both philosophy and daily practice, and the contentment found in mundane tasks. Against the endless skies and rusting birch trees of rural Brandenburg, Lambert chops wood, tends fire, cooks, and cleans the house built with his own hands, finding purpose in unadorned surroundings, and an appreciation of simplicity, quiet, and discipline.

Der Mann und sein Haus is a portrait of a life stripped to its essentials, observed without intervention. Lambert is a close family friend. That familiarity is what made the film possible, allowing the camera to stay at a distance without ever feeling like an intrusion.

Working entirely in available light, with the camera held at a fixed distance, Dale shot on Kodak 500T 16mm film – overexposed and pull-processed to enhance the textures of solitude, from the rich blackness of night, to the soft highlights of open fire and daylight. Building the film around ambient sound – the hum of work and countryside, the call of the region’s native cranes, the crackle of the fire – Dale creates distance from the modern urban world beyond the frame, immersing viewers in a life of chosen stillness with just one lingering question: can a man truly be an island?

items.title: Want a Kinky Watch? Go to Richard Mille
items.description: Want a Kinky Watch? Go to Richard Mille
items.author: Scarlett Baker
paragraphs: Want a Kinky Watch? Go to Richard Mille
Photographed by Charlie Kwai

In the world of horology, legacy is everything. Audemars Piguet just celebrated its 150th anniversary; Vacheron Constantin its 270th. A watch company that is, say, just reaching its 25th year could be seen as barely out of adolescence.

Yet, in that time frame, Swiss watchmaker Richard Mille has managed to inspire something many heritage houses spend generations chasing: allure. “Richard Mille never tried to be fascinating,” says the founder’s son and the brand’s commercial director, Alexandre Mille. “And that’s probably why it is.”

The brand’s Instagram posts are flooded with enthusiasm: “omg stop. I need,” and “I’m not well, [clock emoji, sparkle emoji].” Richard Mille’s watches might cost north of $300,000, unique models aside, but its supporters will follow the cause, even if they don’t have the millions to secure the Mille.

That’s because a lot of Richard Mille is about voyeurism. The brand has managed, almost accidentally, to capitalize on the recurring thrill of wanting the thing you can’t have — and the counterintuitive joy of surrendering to the fact that you probably never will. As Alexandre puts it: “Attachment doesn’t live in the transaction. The communities of enthusiasts who follow Richard Mille closely without ever wearing one on their wrist are not an anomaly. They are, at their core, proof that something sincere is being communicated.”

That something has a lot to do with the sensibility of Richard Mille, which has always run against the grain. After a career working at prestigious firms, notably heading up the watch and jewelry department for Parisian jeweler Mauboussin, Richard Mille’s namesake and co-founder departed to release his own first commercial watch in 2001. It was engineered around one simple idea: Design your dream watch, and worry about production costs later.

The result was a $135,000 timepiece whose mechanics were treated as an artistic feat in their own right. Rather than masking the watch’s movement behind a dial, the cogs, screws, and gears formed the dial itself. The exposed engineering became a part of the watch’s visual identity — a hint of rebelliousness that runs through RM designs today. “For some people it might feel like too much, but that’s exactly the point,” stylist Sofia Popkova says in an email. A Richard Mille watch “doesn’t ask permission to be in the room.”

Richard Mille is willing to experiment with things like whimsy and color, “which you rarely see in watchmaking,” says jeweler Nadine Ghosn. Who else has engineered a watch with three rotating text boxes on the dial, cycling through 216 possible phrases at the push of a button? Among them: “I need to devour your body” or “Let me caress your nipples.” Three guesses why it was christened the RM 69.

The brand has dreamed up everything from diamond-set spiders, snakes, and panda bears to animated flowers that bloom on the dial, hands that rotate counterclockwise to distort your perception of time (after all, it’s a social construct), and the world’s thinnest mechanical watch at the time of its release, at just 1.75mm thick — 0.20mm slimmer than a nickel.

The real headline act, which debuted in 2019 at a Swiss watch fair, is an ensemble of watches inspired by literal candy: 3D marshmallow twists, liquorice swirls, and marbled lollipops, all living within the case. The headlines alone tell the story: “polarizing,” “unexpected,” “most talked about watch of the fair.” In an exclusive run of 10 variations, each piece limited to 30, the average piece retailed at $160,000. The sugar rush continues today; the Bonbon collection remains one of the brand’s most sought-after, with examples seldom appearing at auction and collectors showing little appetite for letting them go.

Beneath the spectacle is some seriously state-of-the-art watchmaking. The brand often uses lightweight, cutting-edge composites that look like a colorful sandwich but weigh less than a slice of bread. These include carbon TPT, quartz TPT, and sapphire — a material so hard and unforgiving that producing a single case takes hundreds of hours.

“Imagine if the greatest engineer and designer and the biggest risk-taker and rule breaker came together” to create a watch, says Olympic fencer and brand ambassador Miles Chamley-Watson. “Try one on, and you will see.”
“We make very serious products without taking ourselves too seriously,” Alexandre adds. “Our products sit at a high price point, but the brand itself remains deeply approachable.”

There are still, of course, the prices to consider. Rebecca Ross, the senior specialist of watches at Christie’s auction house, recalls that in 2022, a Richard Mille with a sapphire crystal case sold for $4 million, then the highest price ever recorded for the brand at auction. One of the best-known owners has to be Drake: “I just, uh, put a Richard on the card,” he raps on “Going Bad” — one of many RM name drops across his catalogue. With him are such figures as Pharrell Williams, LeBron James, Margot Robbie, Kylian Mbappé: people who’ve left some kind of footprint on the culture (and who have the cash flow to show for it).

Then there are the (relative) normies. “It’s like a shameful, secret kink,” says collector Phil Toledano, who recently scooped up his first Richard Mille for “a low hundred” after finally finding a perfectly sized tonneau — the curved-rectangle case shape that the company is known for.

“It’s about status. But it’s fun status,” says Marci Hirshleifer-Penn, a seasoned collector of high horology timepieces. “It’s not like an inherited Rolex. It feels very deliberate and loud. People who wear Richard Mille want you to know they’ve made it.”

Of course, some of Richard Mille’s most enthusiastic admirers may never own one. “Loyalty doesn’t always come from what we can own,” says watch enthusiast Giulia Anselmi, who has spent years surrounded by exceptional watches yet has rarely come across a Richard Mille in person. “The space in between is what gets people hooked.”

Perhaps that’s the real anniversary flex: the in-between space. Richard Mille fans long for something that’s different, but that difference is also what keeps it from them. Chatter is desire, and while desire doesn’t come with a receipt, it certainly keeps you looking.

items.title: Artist Uniform: Menswear Can’t Quit Tommy Vercetti
items.description: In Artist Uniform, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas traces how personal style shapes an artist's identity.
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: In Artist Uniform, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas traces how personal style shapes an artist's identity.

Nobody was cooler to me as a 10-year-old gamer than Tommy Vercetti. The blocky badass at the heart of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City may have spent the game doing very problematic things — murder, extortion, drug dealing — but hey, at least the man had aura.

This was partly because Vice City itself, set in a neon-drenched version of 1980s Miami, was the most stylish GTA ever made, with the best soundtrack in the franchise. (Two accolades I’d argue still hold up 24 years later.) But set aside the worldbuilding, and the Vercetti drip stands on its own.

Vercetti was a relic of mid-’80s fashion, clad in white sneakers and tailored suits, tropical-print shirts and tracksuits, preppy sweaters and normcore graphic tees — the kinds of fits that’ve filtered into runway collections over and over since Vice City’s release in 2002. And as fashion keeps coming back to the ‘80s, it feels like the ghost of Vercetti is haunting every reference.

His iconic teal Hawaiian shirt would slot seamlessly into the range of printed resort shirts from the Prada Spring/Summer 2014 Menswear collection, while the pinstriped two-piece suit and pastel shirt combination feels spiritually linked to everything Haider Ackermann is doing at Tom Ford right now. That tracksuit? Pure adidas, obviously. The cheeky “I completed Vice City and all I got was this lousy t-shirt” piece you get for finishing the game? It’s giving “it’s my birthday and all I got was this overpriced hoodie from Vetements” from the brand’s FW19 season.

Vice City didn’t invent any of these silhouettes, of course. Vercetti’s character design pulled from a constellation of pop culture references, including gangster classics like Goodfellas, plus the super-slick Miami Vice TV series (whose characters regularly wore suits by the likes of Gianni Versace and Hugo Boss). Often, the in-game outfit was almost an exact replica of something seen before, down to the color combination. That Hawaiian shirt? Almost the exact same style Tony Montana wears upon his arrival in Scarface.

Seeing very Vercetti-coded fits pop up across decades simply speaks to the strength of the character’s closet. Paul Smith put Hawaiian shirts under suiting for SS27, Burberry’s SS26 argyle sweater vest looked ready for a day at Vice City’s Leaf Links golf course, and Todd Snyder’s SS26 “La Buena Vida” collection centered on the feeling of stepping off a plane in Miami in the ‘80s — a very Vice City idea, even if Snyder’s fantasy involves a seaplane and his man arriving fitted in linens, not tropical prints and faded jeans. Are these Vercetti references? Likely not. But they do smack of a lingering ‘80s relevance inextricably linked to Vice City’s main man.

With the impending cultural earthquake of Grand Theft Auto VI bringing the franchise back to Vice City for the first time in decades, a new pair of protagonists will reportedly have thousands of outfit options at their disposal. And though Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval may become style icons in their own right, hard to imagine they’ll ever hold the singular sway of Tommy Vercetti.

items.title: Evisu’s Y2K Denim Didn’t Change. It Grew Up. (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Of the many mighty Japanese denim brands, Evisu was the most. The most everything. The most visible, the most popular, the most aggro, the most powerful. No other label in its sphere came close in terms of cultural crossover: just trace its appearances in rap,
items.author: Jake Silbert
paragraphs: Of the many mighty Japanese denim brands, Evisu was the most. The most everything. The most visible, the most popular, the most aggro, the most powerful. No other label in its sphere came close in terms of cultural crossover: just trace its appearances in rap, where Evisu has been shouted out by every generation of rapper since Raekwon, from JAY-Z and Drake to Lils of the Wayne and Tecca variety.

But since its heyday in the aughts, when Evisu was the quintessential cool-guy jeans — and preferably paired with BAPES — the 35-year-old denim label has ebbed and flowed with the times. Its recent return to cultural form was powered more by Y2K fondness than Evisu innovations. But nowadays, the Evisu "seagull" — the signature curves painted on the rear of Evisu jeans — is flying in a fresh direction.

Evisu has stealthily started dropping surprisingly suave collabs with denim-savvy labels as diverse as BEAMS and New York designer Kozaburo. The campaign imagery shared to its Instagram feed is downright tasteful if not aspirational. Its latest collection is a little new, a little old, with Evisu's take on today's omnipresent washed-out cotton jerseys sitting alongside the dark indigo denim it's dished since 1991.
It does feel very of the moment, given the current yen for raw denim, but Evisu didn't get famous for just denim.

Evisu is Evisu because it had attitude. Swagger, if you will. It epitomized a brashness unique in the Japanese denim business, balancing high-end jeans with aggro POV. This new-school Evisu is a little bit of both, but it's a lot more grown-up.

While talking to Scott Watts, a Supreme and Stüssy vet who oversaw the Fall/Winter 2026 shoot's image direction, I was surprised to hear the word "restraint." Yesterday's Evisu earned its fame on the back of jeans with a million painted pockets and enormous screamin' neon gulls, not modesty.

But with age comes wisdom and Evisu is well aware that volume does not necessarily correlate to value. Anyone can scream. Few can claim to have been at the top of the denim game since before kids just now discovering Evisu were even born.
This conversation below, with answers provided by both Watts and the Evisu brand team, has been edited and condensed.
Let's start with timing. Why is Evisu rebranding — and why now?

The overall focus in fashion has shifted back to principles we have always championed. And the topics that are leading the conversation in the industry right now — late-’90s Japanese denim, archive pieces, real craft — are the world Evisu helped build. We’re picking up a thread that began in Osaka in 1991.
What exactly is the "new" Evisu? Is it streetwear? Nostalgia? Denim nerd?

We wouldn’t pocket ourselves in any of those categories; there might have been some street tropes in the past but we started as a denim house. Evisu's Japanese denim helped set the framework for how the rest of the world, particularly Western culture, interacted with Japanese brands.
So, what's actually new about Evisu's product?

What’s new is restraint. The kamome mark now punctuates the garment instead of covering it. And the range goes well beyond jeans. What remains is a commitment to quality products with character that are designed to last.
Is the line going to keep expanding?
We'll add innovations we think the market and consumers deserve.
Speaking of the kamome, what else would you consider an Evisu signature? What makes it distinct?

The hand. The kamome matters because someone painted it — the gesture itself is the signature. We intend to make the hand-painting visible again in our stores and in the way we tell our story. Even as the line expanded into polos, leather, knitwear, and shirting, the focus was on delivering the same quality and cohesive message as you see in our jeans.
I want to drill into that distinction, the factor or factors that make Evisu unique even among other Japanese denim labels.

Well, a lot of Japanese labels take a muted, sterile approach to their product and brand culture. Evisu, both in the past and today, has always been bold and rich in our expression. That's true for our products and our storytelling.
How is Evisu planning to leverage "being bold" to stand out in a far more crowded denim market?
We'll keep developing great products based on our fundamentals.

items.title: Disney is Developing a 'Home Alone' Reboot With Macaulay Culkin, Seth Rogen, and Evan Goldberg
items.description: Disney is currently in early development on a new sequel to the beloved holiday classic 'Home Alone'
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Disney is currently in early development on a new sequel to the beloved holiday classic 'Home Alone'
Original star Macaulay Culkin is collaborating with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg to shape the script
Rogen and Goldberg will also produce the highly anticipated project through their Point Grey banner

Disney is officially in early development on a new Home Alone reboot. Shaping the script alongside original franchise star Macaulay Culkin, comedy heavyweights Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are spearheading the project and will produce the upcoming film through their Point Grey banner.

While official plot details and casting decisions remain strictly under wraps, the announcement arrives following recent reports that Culkin was eyeing a return to the historic franchise. The nostalgic rumors were further reignited after the actor recently reprised his iconic role as a grown-up Kevin McCallister in a Christmas-themed McDonald’s advertisement. Before fully diving into the McCallister universe, Rogen and Goldberg will first finish preparations for an original horror-comedy film they plan to direct for Universal.

The original Home Alone premiered in 1990, starring a nine-year-old Culkin as a resourceful child fending off the infamous Wet Bandits, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern. Directed by Chris Columbus and penned by John Hughes, the blockbuster spawned a massive franchise. While Culkin returned for the 1992 New York-based sequel, subsequent installments featured different leads and varying formats, culminating in the sixth film, Home Sweet Home Alone, which debuted as a Disney+ release.
Release dates and further production details for the upcoming Home Alone project remain strictly under wraps as the film continues early development.
